q.q: Refer to the graph. At AD1 and AS2, the economy is at:

Y1 and P1

q.q: If the economy is below natural output, unemployment is usually:
options: Below the natural rate
Above the natural rate
Zero
Unrelated to output

Point A
Point B
Point D

q.q: Refer to the graph with LRAS. Which output level is natural output?

Y2
P1
Y1

q.q: Refer to the graph with LRAS. Output level Y2 is:
options: Above natural output
Below natural output
Equal to natural output
A price level

q.q: Refer to the graph with LRAS. Output level Y3 is:
options: Above natural output
Equal to natural output
Below natural output
A price level
q.commonError: Ignoring LRAS when judging output gaps.

q.q: A recessionary gap means output is:
options: Above natural output
Below natural output
Equal to the price level
Always at Y2
q.commonError: Reversing recessionary and expansionary gaps.
q.feedback: A recessionary gap occurs when output is below natural output.

q.q: Refer to the graph. If the economy moves from AD1-AS2 to AD2-AS2, what happens?
options: Output rises and the price level rises
Output falls and the price level falls
Output rises and the price level falls
Output falls and the price level rises

Point C
Point B
Point D

Output is above potential

The price level is below zero
q.commonError: Ignoring LRAS when judging gaps.

options: Below the natural rate
Above the natural rate
Equal to zero
Impossible to infer from output

options: An expansionary gap at Y2
A recessionary gap at Y3
Long-run equilibrium at Y1
A leftward SRAS shock
q.commonError: Treating any AD increase as long-run equilibrium.
q.feedback: The move ends at Y2, which is above natural output, creating an expansionary gap.

q.q: Refer to the graph with LRAS. If the economy starts at AD1-AS2 and AD shifts to AD2, what gap appears?
options: Expansionary gap
Recessionary gap
No output gap
Supply gap
q.commonError: Ignoring LRAS after an AD shift.
q.feedback: The economy moves to Y2, which is above natural output, so it creates an expansionary gap.

q.q: A hurricane permanently destroys part of an economy's productive capital, and real GDP falls below its old potential level. Why would it be wrong to assume ordinary recessionary-gap self-correction must restore the old level of output?
options: The loss of productive capital can shift LRAS left, so the economy's new potential output may be lower.
Any fall in real GDP forces aggregate demand to shift permanently left.
Nominal wages cannot adjust after a supply-side disturbance.
SRAS always shifts right enough to restore the pre-shock LRAS position.
q.commonError: Assumes every fall in real GDP is a temporary gap around an unchanged potential-output level.
q.feedback: Before forecasting self-correction back to the old output level, check whether productive capacity changed and LRAS shifted.

q.q: Comparing the original long-run equilibrium C with the new long-run equilibrium B, what is true?
options: GDP returns to 100; prices rise from 125 to 175.
GDP rises to 125; prices remain fixed at 125 throughout.
GDP falls to 75; prices remain fixed at 150 throughout.
GDP stays at 100; prices fall from 125 back to 100.
q.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
q.feedback: LRAS stays at 100, so long-run real GDP returns to 100. The long-run price level is higher at B than at C.

options: AD rises; the economy moves upward along fixed AS0.
AS rises; the economy moves downward along fixed AD0.
AD falls; the economy moves downward along fixed AS0.
Both AD and AS shift; output returns to its starting level.

SRAS shifts left while AD0 and LRAS both stay fixed.
LRAS shifts left while SRAS and AD0 both stay fixed.
SRAS and LRAS shift right while AD0 stays fixed.
q.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
q.feedback: The graph holds AD constant and shows the supply side improving. That raises potential output and lowers the price level.

q.q: In the long-run AD–AS model, natural output is determined mainly by:
options: The current price level alone.
Labor, capital, natural resources, technology, and institutions.
The latest movement in aggregate demand alone.
The nominal money supply with no real-side conditions.
q.commonError: Treating natural output as a price-level or demand choice.
q.feedback: Natural output reflects the economy’s productive capacity and real institutions.

q.q: Refer to the graph. If the economy is operating at Y3 rather than the LRAS level Y1, which condition is consistent with the gap shown?
options: An inflationary gap with unemployment below its natural rate.
Long-run equilibrium with no pressure on wages or expected prices.
A permanent increase in potential output from Y1 to Y3.
A recessionary gap with unemployment above its natural rate.
q.commonError: Confuses the highest output shown with potential output or reverses recessionary and inflationary gaps.
q.feedback: Compare current real output with the LRAS/potential-output level: below potential is recessionary; above potential is inflationary.

q.q: Real GDP is below its old potential level after a permanent decline in labor-force participation. Which diagnostic prevents a mistaken forecast that ordinary self-correction must restore the old output level?
options: Check whether LRAS itself shifted left; if potential output fell, the old level is no longer the long-run anchor.
Assume every output decline is caused by aggregate demand.
Hold LRAS fixed because productive capacity cannot change.
Assume falling wages always restore the pre-shock quantity of labor and output.
q.commonError: Assumes every fall in real GDP is a temporary gap around an unchanged potential-output level.
q.feedback: Before forecasting self-correction back to the old output level, check whether productive capacity changed and LRAS shifted.

q.q: An economy has a recessionary gap after aggregate demand falls. While wages are adjusting downward, a permanent productivity improvement raises productive capacity. Which conclusion best separates the two long-run forces?
options: The productivity gain shifts aggregate demand right while wage adjustment shifts LRAS left, so both forces alter potential output in opposite directions.
The original demand shock permanently fixes real output below potential, so neither wage adjustment nor improved productivity can change the long-run outcome.
SRAS adjustment helps close the demand-created gap, while higher productivity can shift LRAS right and change the potential-output target.
Both changes should be treated as the same SRAS movement, because productive capacity does not affect the location of LRAS in this model.
q.commonError: Assumes every fall in real GDP is a temporary gap around an unchanged potential-output level.
q.feedback: Before forecasting self-correction back to the old output level, check whether productive capacity changed and LRAS shifted.

q.q: When real output is below natural output, unemployment is usually:
options: Above its natural rate
Below its natural rate
Always zero
Unrelated to output
q.feedback: A recessionary gap means firms need fewer workers, so unemployment tends to exceed the natural rate.

q.q: In an AD-AS graph, short-run equilibrium occurs where:
options: Aggregate demand intersects short-run aggregate supply
AD intersects LRAS only
The price level is zero
Unemployment is zero
q.feedback: The intersection of AD and SRAS determines the short-run equilibrium price level and real output.

q.q: If output is below natural output, the economy has:
options: A recessionary gap
An expansionary gap
No output gap
A money multiplier
q.feedback: Output below natural output is a recessionary gap.

q.q: If output is above natural output, the economy has:
options: An expansionary gap
A recessionary gap
No output gap
A reserve gap
q.feedback: Output above natural output is an expansionary gap.

q.q: On an AD-AS graph, natural output is the output level where:
options: Real GDP equals potential output
Inflation is zero
AD is vertical
Unemployment is zero
q.feedback: Natural output is potential output, the economy's sustainable long-run production level.

q.q: Output is $19 trillion while natural output is $20 trillion. The economy has:
options: A recessionary gap
An expansionary gap
No output gap
A Phillips gap
q.feedback: Actual output below natural output is a recessionary gap.

options: Real GDP
The price level
Unemployment
Money supply
q.commonError: Confusing output with the price level.
q.feedback: The vertical axis in the AD-AS model measures the price level.

options: The price level
Inflation expectations
Real GDP
Nominal interest rates
q.commonError: Confusing the AD-AS axes.
q.feedback: The horizontal axis in the AD-AS model measures real GDP or output.

q.q: Which change shifts aggregate demand to the right?
options: A decrease in government spending
An increase in consumer confidence
A negative supply shock
A rise in production costs
q.commonError: Confusing AD shifters with SRAS shifters.

q.q: Which change shifts aggregate demand to the left?
options: A tax increase
A stock market boom
Higher government purchases
Improved consumer confidence
q.commonError: Thinking every policy shifts AD right.
q.feedback: A tax increase reduces spending and shifts aggregate demand left.

q.q: Refer to the graph. Moving from AD1 to AD2 represents:
options: A decrease in aggregate demand
An increase in aggregate demand
A decrease in SRAS
A shift of LRAS
q.commonError: Reversing left and right shifts of AD.
q.feedback: AD2 lies to the right of AD1, so the graph shows an increase in aggregate demand.

q.q: A decrease in household wealth, holding other factors constant, shifts aggregate demand:
options: Not at all because wealth is not part of spending.
Up along the same AD curve.
Left.
Right.
q.commonError: Confusing a spending shifter with a movement along AD.
q.feedback: Lower wealth tends to reduce consumption, shifting aggregate demand left.

An increase in aggregate supply
An increase in aggregate demand
A decrease in aggregate supply

Wealth effect
Exchange-rate effect
Multiplier effect

options: Wealth effect
Interest-rate effect
Exchange-rate effect
Sticky-wage theory

options: Shift left
Shift right
Become vertical
Shift only SRAS
q.commonError: Forgetting net exports are part of AD.
q.feedback: Higher exports raise net exports and shift aggregate demand right.

options: Shift right
Shift left
Shift SRAS right
Shift LRAS right
q.commonError: Treating investment changes as supply changes.
q.feedback: Lower investment reduces total spending and shifts AD left.

q.q: If a price-level increase raises money demand, the interest rate rises, and investment falls. This explains:
options: Why AD slopes downward
Why LRAS slopes upward
Why SRPC shifts down
Why M2 excludes savings
q.commonError: Mixing the AD slope with policy shifts.
q.feedback: This is the interest-rate effect behind the downward-sloping AD curve.

q.q: A lower domestic price level makes domestic goods relatively cheaper to foreign buyers. This supports the downward slope of AD through the:
options: Sticky-wage effect.
Productivity effect.
Exchange-rate effect.
Wealth effect.
q.commonError: Confusing the three reasons aggregate demand slopes downward.
q.feedback: A lower domestic price level can lower interest rates and the currency value, raising net exports.

q.q: Assume SRAS is unchanged. Based on the AD shift shown, what happens to equilibrium real GDP and the price level?
options: Real GDP decreases while the price level increases
Real GDP increases while the price level decreases
Both real GDP and the price level decrease
Both real GDP and the price level increase
q.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
q.feedback: A rightward shift of AD raises spending pressure, so equilibrium output and the price level both rise in the short run.

q.q: Holding SRAS fixed, what short-run equilibrium pattern follows from the demand change in the second AD diagram?
options: Real GDP increases while the price level decreases
Both real GDP and the price level decrease
Real GDP decreases while the price level increases
Both real GDP and the price level increase
q.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift

q.q: Consumer confidence rises while firms become more pessimistic about future sales. What can be concluded about aggregate demand?
options: The net direction is ambiguous without knowing the sizes of the consumption and investment changes.
Aggregate demand must shift left
The economy moves down along the same AD curve
Aggregate demand must shift right
q.commonError: Letting one shifter determine the combined result.
q.feedback: Confidence raises consumption, while pessimism lowers investment; magnitudes determine the net shift.

q.q: The price level falls, but taxes rise at the same time. Which statement is most precise?
options: Both changes cause movement along AD.
The price-level change shifts AD right and the tax increase shifts AD left.
The price-level change causes movement along AD, while the tax increase shifts AD left.
Both changes shift AD left.
q.commonError: Confusing a change in the price level with a nonprice AD shifter.
q.feedback: The price level is on the graph’s vertical axis; taxes are an external shifter.

q.q: Foreign income falls sharply while domestic firms increase investment. The effect on domestic aggregate demand is:
options: A certain rightward shift
A certain leftward shift
Ambiguous because net exports fall while investment rises.
A movement upward along AD
q.commonError: Ignoring offsetting components of aggregate demand.
q.feedback: Lower foreign income reduces exports, while higher investment raises AD.

q.q: A higher price level increases money demand, which raises interest rates and reduces investment. This sequence explains:
options: A rightward shift of LRAS
A rightward shift of AD
A leftward shift of SRAS
A movement upward and leftward along the existing AD curve.
q.commonError: Treating the interest-rate effect as a shift of AD.
q.feedback: The interest-rate effect is one reason quantity of real GDP demanded falls as the price level rises.

q.q: A depreciation of the domestic currency occurs for reasons unrelated to the domestic price level. Holding other factors constant, aggregate demand shifts:
options: Left because net exports fall.
Left because domestic goods become more expensive to foreigners.
Right because exports rise and imports fall.
Nowhere because exchange rates matter only along AD.
q.commonError: Reversing the net-export effect of currency depreciation.
q.feedback: A weaker domestic currency tends to raise net exports and aggregate demand.

q.q: A rise in the price level reduces the real value of household money balances. The immediate AD implication is:
options: Higher net exports and a rightward AD shift.
Higher consumption and a rightward AD shift.
Lower consumption and a movement upward along AD.
Lower investment and a leftward SRAS shift.
q.commonError: Confusing the wealth effect with an AD shifter.
q.feedback: The wealth effect reduces quantity of output demanded as the price level rises.

options: All four components rise automatically.
Only government purchases change.
Consumption falls, investment rises, and net exports fall.
Consumption and net exports rise, while investment falls.
q.commonError: Failing to trace each shifter to the correct AD component.
q.feedback: Confidence affects consumption, expected profits affect investment, and foreign income affects exports.

q.q: The price level rises at the same time that the government cuts taxes. Which graph description is correct?
options: Only movement along AD occurs
There is movement downward along AD plus a leftward shift
Only a rightward shift occurs
There is movement upward along AD plus a rightward shift of the AD curve.
q.commonError: Treating simultaneous movement and shift as mutually exclusive.
q.feedback: The price-level change causes movement along AD; the tax cut shifts the curve.

q.q: Domestic interest rates fall because the central bank expands money supply, while foreign income also falls. What can be said about AD?
options: Investment tends to rise and net exports tend to fall, so the net shift is ambiguous.
Only a movement along AD occurs
AD must shift left
AD must shift right
q.commonError: Ignoring offsetting investment and net-export effects.
q.feedback: The two shifters push different AD components in opposite directions.

q.q: A student says, “Any fall in real GDP means AD shifted left.” What is the best correction?
options: The statement is always correct
Real GDP can fall from movement along AD or from shifts in AD or AS; the graph cause must be identified.
Real GDP changes only when AD shifts
A fall in real GDP always means SRAS shifted right
q.commonError: Inferring a curve shift from an outcome without identifying the cause.
q.feedback: Observed output changes do not by themselves reveal which curve moved.

q.q: A student says AD1 must represent aggregate supply because real GDP is larger. What is the best correction?
options: Any curve farther right must be an aggregate-supply curve.
The graph is LRAS because real GDP is on the horizontal axis.
Both curves are AD; AD1 is the rightward demand shift.
A price-level axis means the curves cannot represent demand.
q.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
q.feedback: The label and downward slope identify the curves as AD. A larger quantity demanded at each price level is an increase in aggregate demand.
q.imageAlt: Aggregate-demand graph with solid AD0 and dashed AD1 to its right on numbered price-level and real-GDP axes.
q.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is real GDP, numbered from 0 to 300; the vertical axis is price level, numbered from 0 to 140. Solid blue AD0 slopes downward from approximately (0,100) to (200,0). Dashed blue AD1 lies above and right of AD0, running from approximately (0,125) to (260,0). At price level 50, AD0 is near GDP 100 and AD1 near GDP 155. These are approximate readings of hand-drawn lines; the diagram has no aggregate-supply curve.

q.q: If policymakers wanted to offset the AD shift shown, which short-run pattern are they responding to?
options: Lower output with downward pressure on the price level
Higher output with upward pressure on the price level
Higher output with downward pressure on the price level
Lower output with upward pressure on the price level
q.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
q.feedback: A decrease in AD lowers both real GDP and the price level in the short run.
q.imageAlt: Aggregate-demand graph with solid AD0 and dashed AD1 to its left on numbered price-level and real-GDP axes.
q.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is real GDP, numbered from 0 to 300; the vertical axis is price level, numbered from 0 to 140. Solid blue AD0 slopes downward from approximately (0,120) to (240,0). Dashed blue AD1 lies below and left of AD0, running from approximately (0,95) to (190,0). At price level 45, AD0 is near GDP 150 and AD1 near GDP 100. These are approximate readings of hand-drawn lines; no aggregate-supply curve is shown.

q.q: The government cuts taxes while the central bank raises interest rates. What is the strongest conclusion about aggregate demand?
options: The net shift is uncertain because the policies oppose each other.
Aggregate demand must rise because tax cuts always dominate.
Aggregate demand must fall because interest rates always dominate.
Both policies reduce consumption and investment.
q.commonError: Declaring a definite aggregate-demand result without comparing opposing policy effects.
q.feedback: The tax cut supports consumption, while higher interest rates restrain investment and durable spending; relative magnitudes determine the net shift.

q.q: The domestic price level rises, consumer confidence strengthens, and foreign income declines. Which analysis is complete?
options: Movement down AD; consumption shifts it right; net exports shift it left
Movement up AD; consumption shifts it right; net exports shift it left
A price rise shifts AD right; both spending changes move along AD
Movement up AD; consumption shifts it left; net exports shift it right
q.commonError: Collapsing simultaneous movement and multiple shifts into one effect.
q.feedback: The price level changes quantity demanded; confidence and foreign income shift the curve in opposite directions.

q.q: A lower price level raises the real value of money balances, lowers interest rates, and makes domestic goods cheaper relative to foreign goods. What happens along AD?
options: Consumption, investment, and net exports all tend to rise.
All three channels shift AD rather than cause movement along it.
Consumption falls while investment and net exports rise.
Only government purchases rise.
q.commonError: Misclassifying the three slope mechanisms.
q.feedback: The wealth, interest-rate, and exchange-rate effects all raise quantity of real GDP demanded at a lower price level.

q.q: Businesses become optimistic, households become pessimistic, and the currency depreciates. Which AD components are initially affected?
options: Only consumption changes.
Investment rises, consumption falls, and net exports rise.
Government purchases and LRAS change.
Investment falls, consumption rises, and net exports fall.
q.commonError: Assigning shifters to the wrong spending components.
q.feedback: Expectations affect I and C, while depreciation affects NX.

q.q: A tax increase and higher government purchases occur together. Which statement is justified without numerical information?
options: The two policies push aggregate demand in opposite directions.
AD must shift left
The policies cause only movement along AD
AD must shift right
q.commonError: Assuming a combined policy has a predetermined net effect.
q.feedback: Higher G raises AD; higher taxes tend to reduce consumption and AD.

q.q: The price level is unchanged, but desired consumption, investment, and net exports all decline. The economy experiences:
options: Movement upward along AD.
A rightward shift of short-run aggregate supply.
Movement downward along AD.
A leftward shift of aggregate demand.
q.commonError: Using movement-along language when the price level is held fixed.
q.feedback: At a given price level, lower planned spending shifts AD left.

q.q: A country’s currency appreciates and foreign economies enter recession while domestic consumer confidence rises. The net AD effect is:
options: Left: consumption and net exports both fall
Right: consumption and net exports both rise
Ambiguous: consumption rises while net exports fall
Unchanged: higher consumption exactly offsets lower net exports
q.commonError: Assuming offsetting forces are equal without evidence.
q.feedback: Confidence raises C, while appreciation and lower foreign income reduce NX.

q.q: Refer to the first AD graph. Purchases rise, private investment partly falls, and the combined spending changes leave the economy on AD1 instead of AD0. The equilibrium price level also rises. Which conclusion separates what the diagram establishes from what still requires evidence?
options: The price increase alone shifted AD0 to AD1; SRAS is unnecessary for identifying equilibrium GDP.
The investment decline proves net AD fell; the rightward curve is only movement along AD0.
The horizontal AD0-to-AD1 distance equals the equilibrium GDP increase even when SRAS slopes upward.
Net desired spending rose at a common price; the equilibrium GDP increase needs the SRAS relationship and cannot be read as the whole horizontal AD shift.
q.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
q.feedback: The rightward shift records a positive net demand change despite an offsetting investment effect. A price change moves along a demand curve. The final intersection and split between price and output responses require supply information absent from this AD-only diagram.
q.imageAlt: Aggregate-demand graph with solid AD0 and dashed AD1 to its right on numbered price-level and real-GDP axes.
q.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is real GDP, numbered from 0 to 300; the vertical axis is price level, numbered from 0 to 140. Solid blue AD0 slopes downward from approximately (0,100) to (200,0). Dashed blue AD1 lies above and right of AD0, running from approximately (0,125) to (260,0). At price level 50, AD0 is near GDP 100 and AD1 near GDP 155. These are approximate readings of hand-drawn lines; the diagram has no aggregate-supply curve.

q.q: Refer to the second AD graph. An economy moves from AD0 to AD1. Falling confidence reduces consumption, while an enacted purchases increase pushes spending in the opposite direction. A lower price level subsequently raises quantity demanded along AD1. Which conclusion is supported, and what remains unidentified?
options: The fiscal expansion outweighs the confidence decline; the lower price level causes the leftward AD shift.
The confidence-related demand reduction outweighs the fiscal expansion at a common price; the diagram does not separately measure the two gross effects.
The lower price level reverses the confidence shock, so the final demand curve must be AD0.
Each gross spending effect equals the net distance between AD0 and AD1, because the shifts have opposite signs.
q.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
q.feedback: AD1 lies left of AD0, so the net demand change is negative at a common price. This identifies which opposing effect dominates, not their individual sizes. A lower price increases quantity demanded along the new curve and does not itself restore the old demand schedule.
q.imageAlt: Aggregate-demand graph with solid AD0 and dashed AD1 to its left on numbered price-level and real-GDP axes.
q.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is real GDP, numbered from 0 to 300; the vertical axis is price level, numbered from 0 to 140. Solid blue AD0 slopes downward from approximately (0,120) to (240,0). Dashed blue AD1 lies below and left of AD0, running from approximately (0,95) to (190,0). At price level 45, AD0 is near GDP 150 and AD1 near GDP 100. These are approximate readings of hand-drawn lines; no aggregate-supply curve is shown.

q.q: Households become more confident about future income and increase planned consumption at every price level. What happens?
options: Short-run aggregate supply shifts right.
Aggregate demand shifts left.
There is movement up along aggregate demand.
Aggregate demand shifts right.
q.commonError: Confusing movement along AD with a rightward shift.
q.feedback: Higher planned consumption at each price level shifts aggregate demand right.

q.q: The horizontal axis of an AD-AS graph measures:
options: The nominal interest rate.
Real output.
The price level.
The money supply.
q.commonError: Reversing the graph axes.
q.feedback: Real GDP or real output appears on the horizontal axis.

q.q: A higher price level, by itself, causes:
options: A leftward shift of AD.
A rightward shift of AD.
A rightward shift of LRAS.
Movement upward along the AD curve.
q.commonError: Treating the price level as an AD shifter.
q.feedback: The price level is on the vertical axis, so its change causes movement along AD.

q.q: Firms expect stronger future sales. Aggregate demand shifts:
options: Left through lower investment.
Nowhere because expectations affect only SRAS.
Right through higher investment.
Right through lower net exports.
q.commonError: Linking business expectations to the wrong component.
q.feedback: More optimistic firms tend to increase investment spending.

q.q: A higher price level reduces real money balances and consumption. This is the:
options: Sticky-wage effect.
Wealth effect.
Multiplier effect.
Exchange-rate effect.
q.commonError: Confusing the slope mechanisms.
q.feedback: The wealth effect works through the purchasing power of money holdings.

q.q: Foreign income falls. Domestic aggregate demand tends to:
options: Move down along AD.
Shift right because imports fall.
Shift left because exports fall.
Stay fixed because foreign income is not domestic.
q.commonError: Ignoring export demand from foreign buyers.
q.feedback: Lower foreign income reduces demand for domestic exports.

q.q: The price level falls while firms cut investment. What occurs?
options: Only movement upward along AD
Only a rightward AD shift
Movement downward along AD plus a leftward AD shift.
A rightward SRAS shift only
q.commonError: Failing to separate price-level movement from a spending shift.
q.feedback: The lower price level changes quantity demanded; lower investment shifts AD left.

q.q: Consumer confidence rises and the currency appreciates. The net AD direction is:
options: No change because the effects are equal
Ambiguous because consumption rises while net exports fall.
Certainly rightward
Certainly leftward
q.commonError: Assuming offsetting shifters cancel exactly.
q.feedback: The two components move in opposite directions, and magnitudes matter.

q.q: Why does a higher price level reduce investment along AD?
options: Higher prices reduce expected input costs.
Higher prices automatically lower taxes.
Higher money demand tends to raise interest rates.
Higher prices directly raise productive capacity.
q.commonError: Confusing AD slope with supply-side changes.
q.feedback: The interest-rate effect links a higher price level to less investment.

q.q: The price level rises, taxes fall, and foreign income falls. Which description is correct?
options: Movement up AD; tax cuts shift AD left; lower foreign income shifts AD right
A price-level increase shifts AD right; tax cuts and foreign income cause movements along AD
Movement up AD; tax cuts shift AD right; lower foreign income shifts AD left
Movement down AD; tax cuts shift AD right; lower foreign income shifts AD right
q.commonError: Combining three distinct forces into one curve change.
q.feedback: The price level causes movement; taxes and foreign income shift AD in opposite directions.

q.q: Consumer confidence falls, investment expectations improve, and the currency depreciates. Which components move?
options: Only government purchases rise.
All components fall.
Consumption falls, investment rises, and net exports rise.
Consumption rises, investment falls, and net exports fall.
q.commonError: Mapping shifters to the wrong components.
q.feedback: Confidence affects C, business expectations affect I, and depreciation affects NX.

q.q: A lower price level raises real balances, lowers interest rates, and weakens the currency. Which AD result follows?
options: SRAS shifts right because interest rates fell
Consumption, investment, and net exports tend to rise along the curve.
Only consumption rises
AD shifts right because the price level fell
q.commonError: Treating movement along AD as a curve shift.
q.feedback: All three classic channels raise quantity demanded at the lower price level.

q.q: The AD curve slopes downward partly because a higher price level reduces:
options: Consumption, investment, and net exports
LRAS, SRAS, and natural output
Taxes, transfers, and debt
Unemployment, inflation, and velocity
q.feedback: A higher price level reduces spending through wealth, interest-rate, and exchange-rate effects.

q.q: Higher consumer confidence shifts AD:
options: Right
Left
Nowhere
Into SRAS
q.feedback: Higher confidence raises consumption and shifts AD right.

q.q: A tax increase usually shifts AD:
options: Left
Right
Up as SRAS
Down as LRAS
q.feedback: A tax increase lowers spending and shifts AD left.

q.q: The vertical axis on a standard AD-AS graph measures:
options: The price level
Real GDP
The unemployment rate
The nominal interest rate
q.feedback: AD-AS graphs place the price level on the vertical axis and real output on the horizontal axis.

q.q: A rightward shift of aggregate demand means:
options: Planned spending is higher at each price level
The price level has moved along AD
Short-run aggregate supply shifted left
Potential output fell
q.feedback: A shift in AD changes total planned spending at every price level.

q.q: A higher price level raises money demand, increases interest rates, and reduces investment. Which AD effect does this illustrate?
options: Interest-rate effect
Wealth effect
Exchange-rate effect
Sticky-wage effect
q.feedback: This is the interest-rate effect behind the downward slope of AD.

q.q: Business investment falls and shifts aggregate demand left. Which analysis determines the economy’s new short-run real output and price level?
options: Find the new intersection of aggregate demand and short-run aggregate supply.
Shift LRAS left by the same amount as investment falls.
Hold output fixed and change only the price level.
Calculate the money multiplier without using the AD–AS equilibrium.
q.feedback: After identifying the AD shift, use its intersection with SRAS to determine the new short-run output and price level.
q.commonError: Stops after identifying an aggregate-demand shift and does not carry it into equilibrium analysis.

q.q: In a fractional reserve banking system, banks
options: hold only part of deposits as reserves and lend out the rest
must keep 100 percent of deposits as cash
cannot affect the money supply
create money by printing currency
q.commonError: thinking banks create money by printing currency
q.feedback: Fractional reserve banking means banks keep some deposits as reserves and lend the rest.

q.q: The money multiplier becomes larger when the reserve ratio
options: falls
rises
equals the inflation rate
equals the nominal interest rate
q.commonError: thinking a higher reserve requirement creates more lending
q.feedback: A lower reserve ratio lets banks lend more of each deposit, which increases the money multiplier.

q.q: For a commercial bank, customer deposits are recorded as:
options: Revenue because deposits increase cash.
Liabilities because the bank owes the funds to depositors.
Bank capital because deposits belong to shareholders.
Assets because the bank physically holds the money.
q.commonError: Treating deposits as bank-owned assets.
q.feedback: Deposits are liabilities: the bank has an obligation to repay depositors.

q.q: A 10 percent reserve rule applies to a $50,000 deposit base. How much must the bank keep rather than lend?
q.commonError: Multiplying by the lending share instead of the reserve ratio.
q.feedback: Ten percent of $50,000 is $5,000.

q.q: When a bank makes a loan from excess reserves, the loan is recorded as:
options: Bank capital only.
An asset of the bank.
A reduction in deposits with no matching asset.
A liability of the bank.
q.commonError: Classifying loans as liabilities.
q.feedback: Borrowers owe repayment to the bank, so loans are bank assets.

q.q: A bank has $300,000 in deposits, a 12 percent reserve requirement, and $50,000 in actual reserves. Excess reserves are:
q.commonError: Forgetting to subtract required reserves from actual reserves.
q.feedback: Required reserves are $36,000, leaving $14,000 in excess reserves.

q.q: A new $2,000 deposit enters a bank with a 20 percent reserve requirement. The bank’s maximum first-round loan is:
q.commonError: Using required reserves as lending or applying the multiplier to the first round.
q.feedback: The bank keeps $400 and may lend $1,600.

q.q: A bank reports $14 million in assets and $12.9 million in liabilities. What is its capital cushion?
options: $26.9 million.
$1.1 million.
$14 million.
$12.9 million.
q.commonError: Adding assets and liabilities or using liabilities alone.
q.feedback: Bank capital equals assets minus liabilities: $1.1 million.

q.q: Why does leverage make banks riskier?
options: A small percentage loss on assets can wipe out a large share of capital.
It guarantees assets never fall in value.
It prevents banks from making loans.
It makes reserves unnecessary.
q.commonError: thinking leverage only increases returns and not risk
q.feedback: Leverage magnifies gains and losses. A small asset loss can hit capital hard.

q.q: A bank originates a loan by crediting its borrower’s checking account. The borrower then pays a supplier at a different bank, and the payment settles in reserves. Which comparison correctly separates origination from settlement?
options: Origination adds a loan and a deposit; settlement reduces the originating bank’s reserves and its borrower’s deposit.
Origination reduces reserves; settlement creates the loan and increases bank capital.
Origination adds reserves and a deposit; settlement leaves both banks’ reserves unchanged.
Origination reduces deposits; settlement cancels the originating bank’s loan asset.
q.commonError: thinking loans reduce assets instead of changing asset composition
q.feedback: Crediting the account initially adds a loan asset and a deposit liability. The later outgoing payment reduces reserves and the deposit liability; the loan remains an asset.

q.q: A bank has $800,000 in deposits, a 10 percent reserve requirement, and $95,000 in reserves. If deposits increase by $100,000 and reserves rise by $20,000, the bank’s new excess reserves are:
q.commonError: Updating deposits or reserves but not both.
q.feedback: New deposits are $900,000, required reserves are $90,000, and actual reserves are $115,000.

q.q: A bank has $25 million in assets and $1.5 million in capital. An 8 percent asset loss occurs. What is the new capital position?
options: $0.5 million.
-$0.5 million.
-$2.0 million.
$1.5 million.
q.commonError: Applying the loss to capital instead of assets.
q.feedback: An 8 percent asset loss is $2 million, reducing $1.5 million of capital to -$0.5 million.

q.q: A banking system has a 10 percent reserve requirement, but banks hold an additional 5 percent of deposits as excess reserves and the public holds no currency. A simple effective deposit multiplier is closest to:
q.commonError: Ignoring voluntary excess reserves.
q.feedback: If 15 percent of deposits is retained, the simple effective multiplier is about 1/0.15 = 6.67.

q.q: Assume the bank cannot obtain extra reserves, sell assets, or retain any new loan proceeds as deposits; every new loan payment would leave the bank. A bank has $900,000 in deposits, a 15 percent reserve requirement, and $135,000 in actual reserves. What can the bank do immediately?
options: It cannot lend more because actual reserves equal required reserves.
It can lend $135,000 because all reserves are excess reserves.
It can lend $765,000 because deposits minus reserves are lendable.
It must borrow $15,000 from the Fed.
q.commonError: treating required reserves as lendable reserves
q.feedback: Required reserves are 0.15 x $900,000 = $135,000. Actual reserves equal required reserves, so there are no excess reserves to lend.

q.q: A bank has $1,200,000 in deposits, $210,000 in reserves, and a 12.5 percent reserve requirement. If it lends all excess reserves, how much can it lend?
q.commonError: lending all reserves instead of only excess reserves
q.feedback: Required reserves are 0.125 x $1,200,000 = $150,000. Excess reserves are $210,000 - $150,000 = $60,000.

q.q: A bank has assets of $50 million and liabilities of $47 million. Asset values fall by 8 percent. What happens to bank capital?
options: Capital falls from $3 million to negative $1 million.
Capital falls from $3 million to $2.76 million.
Capital rises from $3 million to $7 million.
Capital is unchanged because liabilities absorb losses first.
q.commonError: applying the percentage loss to capital instead of assets
q.feedback: Initial capital is $3 million. An 8 percent asset loss on $50 million is $4 million, so capital becomes negative $1 million.

q.q: A bank has $100 million in assets and $92 million in liabilities. If asset values fall by 6 percent, what percentage of initial capital is lost?
options: 75 percent
6 percent
8 percent
60 percent
q.commonError: thinking a 6 percent asset loss means a 6 percent capital loss
q.feedback: Initial capital is $8 million. A 6 percent asset loss is $6 million, which is 75 percent of capital.

q.q: A bank has $1 million in deposits and $90,000 in reserves. The reserve requirement is 10 percent. What is the bank's reserve problem?
options: It is short $10,000 in required reserves.
It has $90,000 in excess reserves.
It can lend $10,000 immediately.
It has exactly enough reserves.
q.commonError: thinking reserves below required levels are still lendable
q.feedback: Required reserves are $100,000. The bank has $90,000, so it is short $10,000.

q.q: If required reserves are $75,000 and the reserve ratio is 15 percent, what are deposits?
q.commonError: multiplying required reserves by the reserve ratio instead of dividing
q.feedback: Required reserves = r x deposits, so deposits = $75,000 / 0.15 = $500,000.

q.q: If excess reserves are $25,000, actual reserves are $85,000, and the reserve ratio is 12 percent, what are deposits?
q.commonError: forgetting to find required reserves before solving deposits
q.feedback: Required reserves are actual minus excess: $85,000 - $25,000 = $60,000. Deposits = $60,000 / 0.12 = $500,000.

q.q: A commercial bank wants to increase lending but is below its required reserves. Which action most directly fixes the reserve shortfall?
options: Borrow reserves or attract new deposits before expanding loans.
Make new loans immediately from required reserves.
Reduce assets by increasing liabilities.
Ignore reserve requirements because lending creates reserves.
q.commonError: thinking banks can lend when already short of required reserves
q.feedback: A bank below required reserves needs reserves before it can safely expand lending.

q.q: A bank has $50 million in assets, $46 million in liabilities, and then suffers a 9 percent asset loss. What is the new capital position?
options: Capital falls from $4 million to negative $500,000.
Capital falls from $4 million to $3.64 million.
Capital rises from $4 million to $8.5 million.
Capital is unchanged because liabilities absorb asset losses first.
q.commonError: applying the loss percentage to capital instead of assets
q.feedback: Initial capital is $4 million. A 9 percent asset loss on $50 million is $4.5 million, so capital becomes negative $500,000.

q.q: A bank has actual reserves of $96,000, excess reserves of $24,000, and a reserve requirement of 12 percent. What are deposits?
q.commonError: dividing actual reserves by the reserve ratio instead of required reserves
q.feedback: Required reserves are actual minus excess: $96,000 - $24,000 = $72,000. Deposits are $72,000 / 0.12 = $600,000.

q.q: A bank’s assets fall by 4 percent while its liabilities remain unchanged. Before the loss, capital was 5 percent of assets. What percentage of the initial capital is lost?
options: 80 percent
4 percent
20 percent
100 percent
q.commonError: thinking a 4 percent asset loss means only 4 percent of capital is lost
q.feedback: Taking initial assets as 100, initial capital is 5. The asset loss is 4, so 4/5 = 80 percent of the initial capital is lost.

q.q: If a bank receives a $1,000 deposit and the reserve requirement is 20 percent, required reserves are:
q.commonError: Subtracting instead of multiplying by the reserve requirement.
q.feedback: Required reserves equal deposits times the reserve requirement, so $1,000 x 0.20 = $200.

q.q: A bank receives $5,000 in new deposits, holds 15 percent required reserves, and lends the rest. What is the maximum first-round loan?
q.commonError: Lending required reserves or using the multiplier too early.
q.feedback: Required reserves are $750, so the bank can lend $4,250 in the first round.

q.q: A bank receives $2,000 in new deposits and faces a 10 percent reserve requirement. If it lends all excess reserves, its first new loan can be:
q.commonError: Lending required reserves.
q.feedback: Required reserves are $200, so excess reserves are $1,800.

q.q: A bank has $50,000 in deposits and must hold 8 percent in reserves. Required reserves equal:
q.commonError: Dividing deposits by the reserve requirement.
q.feedback: Required reserves are $50,000 x 0.08 = $4,000.

q.q: A bank has $500,000 in deposits and a 10 percent reserve requirement. Required reserves equal
q.commonError: using 10 instead of 0.10
q.feedback: Required reserves equal deposits times the reserve ratio: $500,000 x 0.10 = $50,000.

q.q: A bank has $500,000 in deposits, $80,000 in reserves, and a 10 percent reserve requirement. Excess reserves equal
q.commonError: treating all reserves as excess reserves
q.feedback: Required reserves are $50,000, so excess reserves are $80,000 - $50,000 = $30,000.

q.q: A bank receives a new $2,000 deposit and the reserve requirement is 25 percent. How much can the bank initially lend?
q.commonError: lending the entire deposit despite reserve requirements
q.feedback: Required reserves are 0.25 x $2,000 = $500, so the bank can initially lend $1,500.

q.q: If a bank has $1,000 in deposits and the reserve requirement is 10 percent, required reserves are
q.commonError: multiplying by 10 instead of 0.10
q.feedback: Required reserves equal the reserve ratio times deposits: 0.10 x $1,000 = $100.

q.q: If a bank receives a new $1,000 deposit and must hold $100 in required reserves, the bank can initially lend
q.commonError: thinking the full deposit can be lent when reserves are required
q.feedback: The bank can lend excess reserves. $1,000 minus $100 leaves $900 available to lend.

q.q: A bank has $800,000 in deposits, a required reserve ratio of 12.5 percent, and actual reserves of $140,000. How much can it lend before hitting its required reserve level?
q.commonError: treating all actual reserves as lendable reserves
q.feedback: Required reserves are 0.125 x $800,000 = $100,000. Excess reserves are $140,000 - $100,000 = $40,000.

q.q: Use the textbook reserve-constrained model, with no other changes. A bank has $300,000 in deposits and a 10 percent reserve requirement. It currently holds $45,000 in reserves. If it lends all excess reserves, what will its reserves and loans change by? Assume the borrower immediately pays someone at another bank and the entire payment settles in reserves.
options: Reserves fall by $15,000 and loans rise by $15,000.
Reserves fall by $30,000 and loans rise by $30,000.
Reserves fall by $45,000 and loans rise by $45,000.
Reserves rise by $15,000 and loans fall by $15,000.
q.commonError: lending required reserves as if they were excess reserves
q.feedback: Required reserves are $30,000, so excess reserves are $15,000. Lending those lowers reserves by $15,000 and raises loans by $15,000.

q.q: A bank has assets of $10 million and liabilities of $9.4 million. What is bank capital?
options: $9.4 million
$10 million
$19.4 million
q.commonError: adding assets and liabilities instead of subtracting
q.feedback: Bank capital equals assets minus liabilities: $10 million - $9.4 million = $600,000.

q.q: A bank has $2 million in assets and $100,000 in capital. If asset values fall by 5 percent, what happens to capital?
options: It falls to zero.
It falls by $5,000.
It rises to $200,000.
It stays at $100,000.
q.commonError: applying the percentage loss to capital instead of assets
q.feedback: Five percent of $2 million is $100,000. That wipes out the bank's $100,000 in capital.

q.q: A bank has $800,000 in deposits, $110,000 in reserves, and a 10 percent reserve requirement. How much can it lend?
q.commonError: treating all reserves as lendable reserves
q.feedback: Required reserves are $80,000. Excess reserves are $110,000 - $80,000 = $30,000.

q.q: A bank makes a loan from excess reserves. On the bank’s balance sheet, the new loan is:

Capital.
An asset.
A liability.

q.q: A bank has $1.5 million in deposits, a 12 percent reserve requirement, and $240,000 in reserves. Its maximum immediate new lending is:

q.commonError: Confusing required reserves with excess reserves.
q.feedback: Required reserves are $180,000, so excess reserves are $60,000.

q.q: A bank has $30 million in assets and $28.5 million in liabilities. Assets fall 6 percent. New capital is:
options: $1.5 million.
-$1.8 million.
-$0.3 million.
$0.3 million.
q.commonError: Applying the asset loss to the wrong base.

$6 million
$7.2 million
Negative $7.2 million

q.feedback: Initial capital is $6 million. A 9 percent loss on $80 million is $7.2 million, leaving capital at negative $1.2 million.

q.commonError: dividing actual reserves by the reserve ratio instead of required reserves

q.feedback: The bank can lend deposits minus required reserves: $1,000 - $100 = $900.

q.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
q.q: A bank suffers a loss because some of its loan assets lose value. Which balance-sheet item absorbs the loss first?
options: Bank capital
Required reserves
Customer deposits automatically increase
New loans created after the loss
q.feedback: Bank capital absorbs losses first because it is the difference between the bank’s assets and liabilities; a decline in asset value reduces that cushion.

Deposits plus loans
Required reserves minus deposits
Currency plus M2

q.feedback: Required reserves are $1,000, so the bank can lend $3,000.

q.q: A legal maximum price is called:

A price floor
Tax incidence
Consumer surplus

q.q: A price ceiling is binding when it is set:
options: Below equilibrium price
Above equilibrium price
At any seller's preferred price
Only on producers
q.commonError: gets_binding_ceiling_direction_backwards
q.feedback: A ceiling must be below equilibrium to prevent price from rising to equilibrium.

q.q: A binding price ceiling creates:
options: A shortage
A surplus
More supply than demand
A tax wedge
q.commonError: confuses_ceiling_shortage_with_floor_surplus
q.feedback: A binding price ceiling keeps price too low, so quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied.

q.q: A city sets rent at $800 when equilibrium rent is $1,200. This rent ceiling is:
options: Binding
Not binding
A price floor
A tax
q.commonError: misses_ceiling_below_equilibrium

q.q: A price ceiling below equilibrium and a price floor above equilibrium are both:
options: Binding price controls
Examples of market equilibrium
Taxes on sellers
Demand shifters
q.commonError: cannot_distinguish_binding_from_nonbinding_controls

q.q: Which policy would most likely create a shortage?
options: A binding price ceiling
A binding price floor
A tax wedge
An outward PPF shift
q.commonError: confuses_shortage_with_surplus
q.feedback: A binding price ceiling creates a shortage because price is held below equilibrium.

q.q: A legal maximum rent of $1,000 is shown on the apartment-market graph. How should this policy be classified?
options: Binding ceiling: $1,000 is below equilibrium.
Nonbinding ceiling: $1,000 is below equilibrium.
Binding floor: $1,000 is below equilibrium.
Nonbinding floor: $1,000 is above equilibrium.
q.commonError: misreads_graph_or_policy_effect
q.feedback: A price ceiling is binding when it is set below the market equilibrium price. The graph places the ceiling at $1,000, below the $2,000 equilibrium rent.

q.q: The posted price is held below equilibrium, but buyers wait in long lines. What policy most likely caused this?
options: A binding price ceiling
A binding price floor
A tax on sellers
An outward PPF shift
q.commonError: misses_waiting_as_shortage_rationing
q.feedback: A binding price ceiling creates a shortage, so nonprice rationing like waiting can appear.

q.q: A rent ceiling is set above the equilibrium rent. What is the likely result?
options: The ceiling is not binding and has no effect
The ceiling creates a shortage
The ceiling creates a surplus
The ceiling shifts supply right
q.commonError: thinks_all_price_ceilings_bind
q.feedback: A price ceiling above equilibrium does not prevent the market price from reaching equilibrium.

q.q: A binding price ceiling tends to reduce the quality of rental housing because:
options: Landlords have less incentive to maintain units when price cannot rise
Tenants always demand less housing at lower prices
Quantity supplied rises above quantity demanded
The ceiling is above equilibrium
q.commonError: misses_nonprice_effects_of_ceiling
q.feedback: A binding ceiling can create shortages and reduce incentives to maintain quality.

q.q: A binding price ceiling and a tax both reduce market efficiency, but they do so differently. Which statement is correct?
options: A ceiling holds price below equilibrium, while a tax creates a wedge between buyer and seller prices
A ceiling always creates a surplus, while a tax always raises quantity
A tax eliminates scarcity, while a ceiling eliminates opportunity cost
Both policies are the same as a demand increase
q.commonError: confuses_price_control_with_tax_wedge
q.feedback: A price ceiling directly limits price, while a tax creates a gap between what buyers pay and sellers receive.

q.q: A government policy keeps apartment rents below equilibrium. Which outcome is most likely over time?
options: Shortages and nonprice rationing
Surpluses and unsold apartments
A rightward supply shift caused by lower rent
An increase in quantity supplied
q.commonError: misses_nonprice_rationing_under_ceiling
q.feedback: A binding rent ceiling creates shortages, so apartments may be rationed through waiting, search costs, or other nonprice methods.

q.q: Refer to the graph. If the government sets a price ceiling at $20, is the price ceiling binding?
options: Yes, because it is below the equilibrium price
No, because it is below the equilibrium price
Yes, because it is above the equilibrium price
No, because all price ceilings are nonbinding
q.commonError: gets_binding_ceiling_direction_backwards
q.feedback: A price ceiling is binding when it is below equilibrium. Here, $20 is below the $30 equilibrium price.

q.q: Refer to the graph. At a price ceiling of $20, what is quantity demanded?
options: 250 units
150 units
200 units
300 units
q.commonError: reads_supply_curve_instead_of_demand_curve
q.feedback: At $20, the demand curve shows quantity demanded of 250 units.

q.q: Refer to the graph. At a price ceiling of $20, what is quantity supplied?
options: 150 units
250 units
200 units
100 units
q.commonError: reads_demand_curve_instead_of_supply_curve

q.q: Refer to the graph. If the government sets a price ceiling at $40, what is the most likely result?
options: The price ceiling is not binding
A shortage of 100 units occurs
A surplus of 100 units occurs
The equilibrium quantity falls to 150
q.commonError: thinks_all_price_ceilings_bind
q.feedback: A price ceiling above equilibrium is not binding. Since $40 is above the $30 equilibrium price, it does not affect the market.

q.q: At the $1,000 rent ceiling, what shortage is shown?
options: 50 apartments
200 apartments
150 apartments
300 apartments
q.commonError: misreads_graph_or_policy_effect

options: 150 apartments
200 apartments
50 apartments
250 apartments
q.commonError: misreads_graph_or_policy_effect
q.feedback: At $1,000, quantity supplied is only 50 apartments. Even though 250 are demanded, actual transactions cannot exceed the 50 units offered.

q.q: Refer to the graph. Why is the $1,000 rent ceiling binding?
options: The ceiling is 500 dollars above equilibrium
The ceiling is 500 dollars below equilibrium
The ceiling exactly equals the equilibrium price
Supply exceeds demand at the ceiling price

The ceiling must be above equilibrium price

Because all price ceilings create shortages
Because sellers are forced to charge the maximum
Because quantity supplied must equal zero

q.q: A rent ceiling lowers the money rent but causes long search times, side payments, and poorer maintenance. What is the best interpretation?
options: Lower legal rent can be offset by nonmoney costs.
The ceiling eliminated scarcity
The ceiling created a surplus of apartments
The price ceiling shifted demand left

q.feedback: A binding ceiling can lower the legal price but create search costs, rationing, and quality decline.

q.q: Refer to the price-control graph. Officials lower a price ceiling from $50 to $40 and predict that the market price will fall by $10. With demand and supply unchanged, which assessment is correct?
options: Price falls from $50 to $40 because the ceiling sets the transaction price.
Price stays $30 because both legal maxima permit the equilibrium price.
Price rises from $30 to $40 because sellers charge the highest legal price.
Price falls from $30 to $20 because the legal maximum fell by $10.
q.commonError: thinks_all_price_ceilings_bind
q.feedback: The intersection is $30 and 200 units. Both ceilings are above $30, so both are nonbinding. Lowering a nonbinding ceiling while it remains above equilibrium changes the legal limit, not the competitive market outcome.

q.q: Refer to the price-control graph. A policy holds the price at $20. What is the full market result?
options: A binding price ceiling with a shortage of 100 units
A nonbinding price ceiling with no effect
A binding price floor with a surplus of 100 units
A nonbinding price floor with no effect

q.feedback: $20 is below the $30 equilibrium, so it is a binding ceiling. At $20, Qd is 250 and Qs is 150, so the shortage is 100.

q.q: Refer to the price-control graph. At $10, what are quantity demanded and quantity supplied?
options: Quantity demanded is 300 and quantity supplied is 100
Quantity demanded is 100 and quantity supplied is 300
Quantity demanded is 150 and quantity supplied is 250
Quantity demanded is 250 and quantity supplied is 150
q.commonError: reverses_demand_and_supply_at_low_price
q.feedback: At a low price of $10, buyers demand 300 units while sellers supply 100 units.

q.q: Refer to the graph. Relative to the competitive equilibrium, how do quantity demanded and quantity supplied change at the $1,000 ceiling?
options: Quantity demanded -100; quantity supplied +100.
Quantity demanded +200; quantity supplied unchanged.
Quantity demanded unchanged; quantity supplied -200.
Quantity demanded +100; quantity supplied -100.
q.commonError: misreads_graph_or_policy_effect
q.feedback: At equilibrium both quantities are 150. At $1,000, quantity demanded is 250 and quantity supplied is 50. Demand therefore rises by 100 while supply falls by 100, opening a 200-unit shortage.

q.q: Refer to the price-control graph. A price ceiling of $50 is imposed. Which answer is best?
options: The ceiling is nonbinding because it is above the $30 equilibrium price
The ceiling is binding because it is above the $30 equilibrium price

The ceiling creates a shortage because quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied

q.q: Refer to the price-control graph. A $20 price ceiling is imposed. Beyond the lower posted price, what additional market effect should occur?
options: Nonmoney rationing rises because quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied
Nonmoney rationing falls because quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded
Producer competition rises because sellers have excess unsold units
The market clears because the legal price is below equilibrium

q.q: A city caps rent below equilibrium. The advertised rent falls, but apartment searches become longer, maintenance falls, and landlords screen tenants harder. What is the best economic diagnosis?
options: The ceiling lowers the posted price but creates shortage and nonmoney rationing
The ceiling lowers the posted price and therefore eliminates scarcity
The ceiling raises quantity supplied and creates seller competition
The ceiling is nonbinding because landlords still choose tenant quality
q.commonError: focuses_only_on_lower_legal_price
q.feedback: The posted money price is only part of the cost. Binding ceilings create shortage and hidden rationing costs.

q.q: A legal maximum price is set above equilibrium. A student predicts a shortage. What is wrong?
options: A ceiling above equilibrium is nonbinding and does not create a shortage
Any price ceiling always creates a shortage
A ceiling above equilibrium creates a surplus
A ceiling above equilibrium is actually a price floor
q.commonError: thinks_all_ceilings_bind
q.feedback: A price ceiling binds only when it is below equilibrium.

q.q: A binding price ceiling on gasoline leads stations to sell out early. Some stations favor regular customers. What is the best interpretation?
options: The shortage creates nonprice rationing
The market clears because the legal price is low
The ceiling creates a surplus
The ceiling increases supply
q.commonError: thinks_low_legal_price_solves_scarcity
q.feedback: When price cannot ration the good, other methods like waiting, favoritism, and side payments can take over.

q.q: A rent ceiling causes landlords to convert apartments into short-term rentals outside the regulated market. What does this show?
options: The ceiling reduced regulated rental supply by changing landlord incentives.
A ceiling always increases quantity supplied
A ceiling eliminates opportunity cost for landlords
A ceiling is nonbinding if landlords find loopholes
q.commonError: assumes_legal_price_change_does_not_affect_supplier_behavior
q.feedback: A binding ceiling lowers returns in the regulated market and can push suppliers to adjust around the policy.

q.q: Refer to the graph. At the binding $1,000 rent ceiling, what is the maximum number of apartments that can actually be rented?
options: 200 thousand apartments
300 thousand apartments
400 thousand apartments
100 thousand apartments

q.q: A city caps rent below equilibrium to help renters. In the short run, some renters pay less, but many cannot find apartments and landlords reduce maintenance. Which answer best explains the full economic result?
options: The legal price falls, but shortage, rationing, and quality decline create hidden costs
The policy eliminates scarcity because rent is lower
The policy creates a surplus because quantity supplied rises
The market reaches equilibrium because demand and supply adjust immediately
q.commonError: focuses_only_on_lower_legal_price
q.feedback: A binding rent ceiling lowers the legal price but creates a shortage, rationing, search costs, and weaker maintenance incentives.

q.q: A city creates a low legal parking fee below equilibrium. Drivers spend extra time circling for spaces, miss class, and compete for limited spots. What is the best economic interpretation?
options: The ceiling lowers the money price but raises nonmoney costs through shortage and rationing
The ceiling creates a surplus of parking spaces
The ceiling is nonbinding because drivers still pay with time
The ceiling shifts demand left
q.commonError: ignores_time_cost_as_part_of_full_price
q.feedback: A binding price ceiling can lower the posted price while raising search and waiting costs.

q.q: A binding rent ceiling lowers the rent paid by tenants who retain apartments by $300. At that rent, 28,000 more households want apartments than landlords offer. Which conclusion is warranted?
options: Continuing tenants save on rent, but the shortage does not identify how many former tenants lost housing
All 28,000 unmatched households must previously have rented apartments
Every household is better off because the legal rent is lower
The rent saving proves aggregate consumer surplus increased
q.commonError: assumes_target_group_all_benefits
q.feedback: The shortage compares current quantities demanded and supplied; it is not a count of displaced former tenants. Continuing tenants save on rent, but the net effects on all households also depend on lost access, allocation and any search costs.

q.q: A city subsidizes apartment construction while also imposing a binding rent ceiling. Which combined result is most likely?
options: More supply can ease—but not necessarily end—rationing under a binding ceiling.
The subsidy makes the ceiling irrelevant in all cases
The ceiling shifts demand left and eliminates scarcity
The policy must create a surplus because supply increases
q.commonError: assumes_one_policy_fully_cancels_the_other
q.feedback: A supply subsidy can ease shortage pressure, but a binding ceiling can still hold price below equilibrium and cause rationing.

q.q: Refer to the apartment graph. Under the displayed ceiling, what is the maximum number of rentals and the excess demand, assuming landlords offer the quantity on S0?
options: At most 50 rentals and excess demand of 200 apartments
At most 250 rentals and excess demand of 200 apartments
At most 150 rentals and excess demand of 100 apartments
At most 50 rentals and excess supply of 200 apartments
q.commonError: misreads_graph_or_policy_effect
q.feedback: The ceiling is below the $2,000 equilibrium rent. At $1,000, supply is 50 and demand is 250. Supply limits possible rentals to 50, while excess demand is 250 − 50 = 200. Actual matching could be lower; the graph alone establishes a maximum.

q.q: Refer to the graph. Compare a $20 ceiling with a $40 ceiling, assuming efficient matching and no other restrictions. Which policy comparison is correct?
options: $20 permits 150 trades and creates a 100-unit shortage; $40 allows the 200-unit equilibrium
$20 permits 250 trades and creates a 100-unit shortage; $40 allows the 200-unit equilibrium
$20 permits 150 trades; $40 forces 250 trades and a 100-unit surplus
Both ceilings leave the market at 200 trades because both are legal maximum prices
q.commonError: cannot_connect_binding_status_to_shortage_size
q.feedback: Equilibrium is $30 and 200 units. The $20 maximum binds: Qs = 150 and Qd = 250, so the shortage is 100 and at most 150 units trade. The $40 maximum allows the equilibrium price below it; it does not force the market to charge $40.

q.q: A binding ceiling reduces the number of apartments rented. Under which allocation would it create an additional loss beyond the gains from the missing rentals?
options: Some available apartments go to lower-value applicants while higher-value applicants go without
The remaining apartments all go to the highest-value applicants
The lower rent transfers money from landlords to continuing tenants
Landlords supply exactly the number of apartments willing buyers rent
q.commonError: judges_policy_only_by_lower_price_for_some_buyers
q.feedback: A quantity reduction loses gains from missing beneficial trades. A further allocation loss arises if a lower-value recipient displaces a higher-value applicant. A ceiling does not by itself prove that this misallocation occurs.

q.q: At a binding rent ceiling, 4,000 households demand apartments and landlords offer 2,700. A construction program adds 500 apartments at that rent, while new arrivals raise quantity demanded by 200. Assuming all offered apartments are rented, what changes?
options: Rentals rise by 500 and the shortage falls by 300
Rentals rise by 500 and the shortage falls by 500
Rentals rise by 200 and the shortage falls by 700
Rentals rise by 700 and the shortage stays unchanged
q.commonError: reverses_qd_and_qs
q.feedback: Initially the shortage is 4,000 − 2,700 = 1,300. Afterward demand is 4,200 and supply is 3,200, so rentals rise by 500 and the shortage is 1,000, down 300. Additional demand partly offsets the construction program.

q.q: Refer to the apartment graph. One tenant keeps the same apartment after the displayed ceiling is imposed but now spends time searching and queuing valued at $1,100 per month. With apartment quality unchanged, which evaluation is correct?
options: The tenant gains $1,000 net, and the market has excess demand of 200 apartments
The tenant loses $100 net, and the market has excess demand of 200 apartments
The tenant loses $100 net, and all 200 unmatched applicants must be former tenants
The tenant gains $100 net, and the market has excess supply of 200 apartments
q.commonError: misreads_graph_or_policy_effect
q.feedback: The graph shows rent falling from $2,000 to $1,000, a $1,000 saving. Subtract the stated $1,100 time cost: the continuing tenant loses $100 net. At the ceiling, Qd = 250 and Qs = 50, giving excess demand of 200. The time cost is specified for this tenant, not asserted for every ceiling.

q.q: Refer to the graph. A student says a $2,000 rent ceiling binds and creates a 200-thousand-apartment shortage. Which diagnosis corrects both errors and identifies the policy that could sustain the gap at $2,000?

Nonbinding ceiling: $1,500 and 200 thousand; at $2,000, Qd > Qs by 200 thousand, consistent with a binding ceiling.
Nonbinding ceiling: $1,500 and 200 thousand; at $2,000, Qs > Qd by 200 thousand, consistent with a binding floor.
Binding ceiling: $2,000 and 300 thousand; Qs > Qd by 200 thousand, consistent with a binding ceiling.

q.commonError: misreads_graph_relationship
q.feedback: Equilibrium is $1,500 and 200 thousand. A maximum of $2,000 permits that equilibrium and does not force price up. At $2,000, Qs=300 thousand and Qd=100 thousand: the hypothetical gap is a 200-thousand surplus. A floor at $2,000, not the stated ceiling, could hold price above equilibrium.

q.q: Refer to the price-control graph. If a price ceiling is set at $10, what shortage results?
options: 200 units
100 units
300 units
400 units
q.commonError: adds_qd_and_qs_instead_of_subtracting
q.feedback: At $10, quantity demanded is 300 and quantity supplied is 100. The shortage is 300 - 100 = 200 units.

q.q: A rent ceiling is set below equilibrium. Quantity demanded is 900 apartments and quantity supplied is 600. What occurs?
options: A shortage of 300 apartments
A surplus of 300 apartments
A shortage of 1,500 apartments
No effect because ceilings are minimum prices
q.commonError: adds_qd_and_qs_instead_of_subtracting
q.feedback: The shortage is quantity demanded minus quantity supplied: 900 - 600 = 300.

q.q: Refer to the graph. If the government sets a price ceiling at $20, what shortage results?
options: 100 units
50 units
150 units
400 units
q.commonError: adds_qd_and_qs_instead_of_subtracting
q.feedback: At $20, quantity demanded is 250 and quantity supplied is 150. The shortage is 250 - 150 = 100 units.

q.q: A city sets a price ceiling below equilibrium to make apartments affordable. The legal rent falls, but renters wait longer, landlords reduce maintenance, and some units are rented off-book. What is the strongest economic conclusion?
options: The posted price falls, but shortage shifts part of the cost into waiting, quality loss, and rationing
The posted price falls, so the policy removes the main cost renters face in the market
The posted price falls, but the shortage means sellers now compete harder for renters
The posted price falls, so the market clears through a lower equilibrium rent
q.commonError: focuses_only_on_lower_legal_price
q.feedback: A binding ceiling can lower the posted price while creating shortage, search costs, lower quality, rationing, and misallocation.

q.q: Refer to the price-control graph and treat the plotted curves as straight lines. An enforced ceiling rises from $20 to $25. All units sellers offer are purchased, and there are no side payments or other changes. What happens to the shortage and quantity actually traded?
options: Shortage falls by 25 units; quantity traded rises by 50 units.
Shortage rises by 50 units; quantity traded falls by 25 units.
Shortage falls by 50 units; quantity traded falls by 25 units.
Shortage falls by 50 units; quantity traded rises by 25 units.
q.commonError: subtracts_quantity_demanded_from_quantity_supplied
q.feedback: At $20, Qd=250 and Qs=150: shortage is 100 and trades are 150. Halfway to the $30 equilibrium, at $25, Qd=225 and Qs=175: shortage is 50 and trades are 175. The smaller gap reflects both lower quantity demanded and higher quantity supplied; trades are limited by the latter.

q.q: Initially Qd=140-2P and Qs=2P, with a price ceiling of $40. Later demand becomes Qd=200-2P while supply stays fixed. What happens to the ceiling’s effect?
options: Initially nonbinding at equilibrium $35; later binding at $40, with Qd=120, Qs=80 and a shortage of 40.
Initially binding at $40 with a shortage of 20; later nonbinding because demand growth raises equilibrium above the ceiling.
Initially nonbinding at $35; later nonbinding at $50 because a ceiling never changes when only demand shifts.
Initially nonbinding at $35; later binding at $40, with a surplus of 40 because sellers supply more than buyers demand.
q.commonError: thinks_all_price_ceilings_bind
q.feedback: Initially 140-2P=2P gives P=35. Later 200-2P=2P gives P=50, above the ceiling. At P=40, demand is 120 and supply 80, so the previously nonbinding maximum becomes binding and creates a 40-unit shortage.

q.q: A binding price ceiling reduces the legal price from $100 to $70. At $70, buyers want 500 units and sellers offer 300 units. Which outcome is most likely?
options: A shortage of 200 units and rationing by waiting, favoritism, or side payments
A surplus of 200 units and falling inventories
No shortage because the legal price is lower
A demand decrease because buyers dislike lower prices
q.commonError: ignores_nonprice_rationing
q.feedback: At the ceiling, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied by 200 units. Because price cannot rise, the good must be rationed some other way.

q.q: A policy lowers the legal price, creates a shortage, reduces product quality, and causes buyers to spend time searching. Which policy best matches this pattern?
options: A binding price ceiling
A binding price floor
A nonbinding price floor
A seller tax with perfectly elastic demand
q.commonError: misidentifies_shortage_policy
q.feedback: Lower legal price plus shortage and search costs points to a binding price ceiling.

q.q: A binding rent ceiling creates a 200-unit shortage. The city allocates apartments to whoever waits in line longest. Which conclusion best completes the analysis?
options: The money price is lower, but time costs rise and apartments may not go to those who value them most
The lower money price eliminates the economic cost of housing
Waiting lines prove that quantity supplied now exceeds quantity demanded
The allocation is efficient because every renter faces the same legal price
q.commonError: ignores_nonmoney_price_and_misallocation
q.feedback: A binding ceiling lowers the posted price but can replace money costs with waiting, search, quality loss, and inefficient rationing.

q.q: At a binding rent ceiling, Qd=8,000 and Qs=5,600. Of the supplied units, 400 are assigned by waiting list; they are not additional apartments. Later, 300 landlords withdraw units while Qd at the ceiling is unchanged. An official subtracts the 400 waiting-list allocations from the later shortage. What is the correct diagnosis?
options: Shortage rises from 2,000 to 2,300; waiting-list allocation reduces excess demand independently of the supplied apartments.
Shortage rises from 2,400 to 2,700; waiting lists allocate existing supply and do not add units or reduce the underlying gap.
Shortage falls from 2,400 to 2,100; withdrawals remove potential renters as well as the landlords’ supplied units.
Shortage stays 2,400; nonprice allocation prevents a change in the shortage when legal rent is unchanged.
q.feedback: Initial excess demand is 8000-5600=2400. Supply then falls to 5300, giving 8000-5300=2700. The 400 apartments are already counted in supply, so subtracting them again double counts an allocation as new capacity.

q.q: A rental market has Qd=10,000-2P and Qs=1,000+P. A $2,000 ceiling is introduced. Over time, 500 units are converted out of the regulated market at every rent, while demand is unchanged. Which sequence follows, and what can be inferred about tenants?
options: Equilibrium was $3,000; surplus is initially 3,000 and later 3,500 units, so all tenants necessarily gain from easier apartment access.
Equilibrium was $3,000; shortage is initially 3,000 and later 3,500 units, while search and quality costs can offset some tenants’ posted-rent savings.
Equilibrium was $2,000; the ceiling is nonbinding initially, and conversion creates a 500-unit shortage only because demand shifts right.
Equilibrium was $3,000; shortage falls from 3,000 to 2,500 units, and lower legal rent guarantees every prospective tenant is better off.
q.commonError: assumes_legal_price_change_does_not_affect_supplier_behavior
q.feedback: Set 10000-2P=1000+P to get P=3000 and Q=4000. At P=2000, Qd=6000 and Qs=3000, a shortage of 3000. Conversion lowers supply to 2500 and raises shortage to 3500. Lower posted rent does not ensure access or exclude search and quality costs.

q.q: A maximum legal price is binding only when it is set:
options: Below equilibrium price
Above equilibrium price
Exactly at zero
Above quantity supplied
q.commonError: gets_binding_ceiling_direction_backwards
q.feedback: A price ceiling binds only when it is below equilibrium price.

q.q: A binding price ceiling usually creates:

A surplus
A tax wedge
An outward PPF shift

60 units
90 units
150 units

options: A shortage of 45 units

No shortage

q.q: A rent ceiling is set at $900 when equilibrium rent is $1,300. What happens?
options: The ceiling is binding and creates a shortage
The ceiling is nonbinding and has no effect
The ceiling creates a surplus
The ceiling shifts supply right
q.commonError: gets_binding_ceiling_direction_backwards
q.feedback: A ceiling below equilibrium is binding and creates a shortage.

q.q: A legal maximum price is above equilibrium. Why is it nonbinding?
options: The market price remains below the legal maximum
All ceilings create shortages
Sellers must charge the maximum
Demand must fall to zero
q.commonError: thinks_all_price_ceilings_bind

q.q: A legal maximum below equilibrium and a legal minimum above equilibrium have what in common?
options: Both are binding price controls
Both create market equilibrium
Both create tax wedges
Both increase quantity traded
q.commonError: cannot_distinguish_binding_from_nonbinding_controls
q.feedback: A ceiling below equilibrium and a floor above equilibrium both bind because they prevent the market from reaching equilibrium.

q.q: Which policy-price pairing is nonbinding?
options: A price ceiling above equilibrium
A price ceiling below equilibrium
A price floor above equilibrium
A rent ceiling below market rent
q.commonError: thinks_all_controls_bind
q.feedback: A price ceiling above equilibrium is nonbinding because the market price can settle below it.

q.q: A rental schedule lists monthly rent, apartments wanted and apartments offered: $800: 120, 60; $1,000: 100, 80; $1,200: 90, 90. An enforced rent ceiling is $1,000. What shortage follows?
options: 20 apartments
80 apartments
180 apartments
0 apartments
q.commonError: adds_qd_and_qs_instead_of_subtracting
q.feedback: Use the $1,000 row, not the equilibrium row at $1,200. At the ceiling, buyers want 100 apartments and owners offer 80, so the shortage is 100 - 80 = 20. Adding the quantities does not measure unmet demand.

q.q: At a binding cap on storage-unit rents, 150 customers each want one unit and owners offer 110 units. All offered units are rented. A manager reports, "The shortage is 110 units because that is how many were rented." Which correction is accurate?
options: 40 units are unfilled demand; 110 units are rented.
110 units are unfilled demand; 40 units are rented.
40 units are excess supply; 110 units are rented.
260 units are unfilled demand; 110 units are rented.
q.commonError: reverses_shortage_formula
q.feedback: The 110 rentals are actual transactions, not the shortage. Unfilled demand is 150 - 110 = 40 units. Because customers want more than owners offer, the gap is a shortage rather than a surplus.

q.q: A legal minimum price is called:
options: A price floor
A price ceiling
A shortage
A demand shift
q.commonError: confuses_floor_with_ceiling
q.feedback: A price floor is a legal minimum price.

q.q: A price floor is binding when it is set:

Only on buyers

q.q: A binding price floor creates:

A binding price ceiling
A decrease in supply

q.q: Refer to the price-control graph. At $50, what are quantity demanded and quantity supplied?
