Quantity of labor supplied increases by 150 thousand; quantity demanded is unchanged.
Quantity of labor supplied is unchanged; quantity demanded decreases by 150 thousand.

q.q: Refer to the graph. A $40 floor is enforced. Private buyers purchase their quantity demanded, and government buys 50 additional units at the floor. If sellers produce the quantity on supply, what remains unsold and what does government spend?

460 units
700 units
1,160 units
q.commonError: adds_qs_and_qd_instead_of_subtracting
q.feedback: Surplus is Qs - Qd: 700 - 460 = 240 units.

q.q: A minimum wage is set at $16 when equilibrium wage is $12. At $16, labor supplied is 95,000 and labor demanded is 72,000. What is the labor surplus?
options: 23,000 workers
72,000 workers
95,000 workers
167,000 workers
q.commonError: adds_labor_supplied_and_labor_demanded
q.feedback: The labor surplus is labor supplied minus labor demanded: 95,000 - 72,000 = 23,000.

q.q: Refer to the price-control graph. If a price floor is set at $50, what surplus results?
options: 200 units
100 units
300 units
400 units
q.commonError: adds_qs_and_qd_instead_of_subtracting
q.feedback: At $50, quantity supplied is 300 and quantity demanded is 100. The surplus is 300 - 100 = 200 units.

q.q: A minimum wage is set above equilibrium. Labor supplied is 120,000 and labor demanded is 80,000. What is the labor surplus?
options: 40,000 workers
80,000 workers
120,000 workers
200,000 workers
q.commonError: adds_qs_and_qd_instead_of_subtracting
q.feedback: The surplus is quantity supplied minus quantity demanded: 120,000 - 80,000 = 40,000.

q.q: Refer to the graph. If the government sets a price floor at $40, what surplus results?
options: 100 units
50 units
150 units
400 units
q.commonError: adds_qs_and_qd_instead_of_subtracting
q.feedback: At $40, quantity supplied is 250 and quantity demanded is 150. The surplus is 250 - 150 = 100 units.

q.q: A minimum wage is set at $16 when the equilibrium wage is $12. At $16, firms demand 70,000 workers and 110,000 workers want jobs. What is the best diagnosis?
options: The floor is binding and creates a labor surplus of 40,000 workers
The floor is binding and creates a labor shortage of 40,000 workers
The floor is nonbinding because workers prefer higher wages
The floor increases labor demand by 40,000 workers
q.commonError: confuses_labor_surplus_with_shortage
q.feedback: A price floor above equilibrium is binding. Labor surplus equals quantity supplied minus quantity demanded, so 110,000 - 70,000 = 40,000 workers.

q.q: A minimum wage raises pay for workers who keep their jobs, but firms hire fewer workers and more workers seek jobs. Which statement gives the best economic interpretation?
options: The policy helps some employed workers, but it also creates a labor surplus among workers seeking jobs
The policy helps workers as a group because the higher wage applies to anyone willing to work
The policy helps firms attract more workers, so labor demand rises with the legal wage
The policy leaves employment unchanged because only the legal wage has changed
q.commonError: counts_only_workers_who_keep_jobs
q.feedback: A binding minimum wage creates winners and losers. Some employed workers earn more, but firms hire fewer workers and a labor surplus appears.

q.q: A labor market initially has Qd=440-10W and Qs=10W. A minimum wage of $18 is imposed. Later labor demand falls to Qd=280-10W, with supply unchanged. Which account is correct?
options: The floor is initially nonbinding at $22; later it binds at $18, with 100 employed and a labor surplus of 80.
The floor initially binds at $18; later it becomes nonbinding at $14, with 180 employed and no surplus.
The floor is initially nonbinding at $22; later it binds at $18, with 180 employed and a labor shortage of 80.
The floor stays nonbinding because its statutory value is unchanged, so employment remains at the original 220.
q.commonError: thinks_all_price_floors_bind
q.feedback: Initial equilibrium solves 440-10W=10W, giving W=22. Later equilibrium would be W=14. At the $18 floor, labor demand is 100 and supply 180; employment is demand-limited and excess supply is 80.

q.q: A binding price floor raises the legal price from $30 to $45. At $45, sellers offer 900 units and buyers want 600 units. Which outcome is most likely?
options: A surplus of 300 units and extra effort by sellers to unload the good
A shortage of 300 units and long lines for buyers
No surplus because sellers prefer the higher price
A demand increase because the higher price signals quality
q.commonError: ignores_quantity_demanded_response
q.feedback: At the floor, quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded by 300 units. Sellers compete to find buyers, often through nonprice margins.

q.q: A policy raises the legal price, creates unsold output, and benefits some sellers while making buyers purchase less. Which policy best matches this pattern?
options: A binding price floor
A binding price ceiling
A nonbinding price ceiling
A buyer tax that leaves quantity unchanged
q.commonError: misidentifies_surplus_policy
q.feedback: Higher legal price plus unsold output points to a binding price floor.

q.q: The government sets a crop price floor above equilibrium and promises to buy any unsold output. Which result is most likely?
options: Farmers produce more than consumers buy, so the government purchases and stores the surplus
Consumers buy more because the legal price is higher
The policy creates a shortage because quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied
The floor is nonbinding because the government participates in the market
q.commonError: confuses_government_purchase_with_market_clearing
q.feedback: A binding price floor creates excess supply. A purchase guarantee shifts the unsold surplus to the government rather than making it disappear.

q.q: A wage floor of $16 is initially below an $18 equilibrium wage. Demand then falls; without the floor the new wage would be $14. At $16, firms now demand 90 workers and 130 want jobs. With all demanded jobs filled, what is the correct diagnosis?
options: The floor remains nonbinding, with 130 employed and no surplus
The floor changes from nonbinding to binding, with 130 employed and a 40-worker shortage
The floor changes from nonbinding to binding, with 90 employed and a 40-worker surplus
The floor was binding in both periods, with employment fixed at 90
q.commonError: confuses_labor_surplus_with_shortage
q.feedback: Initially the legal minimum of $16 permits the $18 equilibrium. After demand falls, it prevents adjustment to $14. Labor demand limits employment to 90, while 130 − 90 = 40 willing workers are unmatched. Binding status depends on the current equilibrium.

q.q: At a binding price floor, sellers offer 1,900 units and buyers demand 1,250. The government purchases 300 units. How much unsold surplus remains?
q.commonError: confuses_government_purchase_with_market_clearing
q.feedback: Initial surplus is 650 units. Government purchases of 300 leave 350 unsold.

q.q: A binding agricultural price floor is removed. Holding other conditions constant, which adjustment is expected?
options: Price rises, quantity demanded falls, and quantity supplied rises
Price falls, quantity demanded rises, and quantity supplied falls
Price and quantity supplied both rise
A shortage necessarily replaces the surplus
q.commonError: ignores_quantity_demanded_response
q.feedback: Removing the floor allows price to fall toward equilibrium, raising demand and reducing supply.

q.q: A minimum legal price is binding only when it is set:
options: Above equilibrium price
Below equilibrium price
Exactly at zero
Below quantity demanded
q.commonError: gets_binding_floor_direction_backwards
q.feedback: A price floor binds only when it is above equilibrium price.

q.q: A binding price floor usually creates:
options: A surplus
A shortage
A tax wedge
A demand increase
q.commonError: confuses_floor_surplus_with_ceiling_shortage
q.feedback: A binding floor keeps price too high, so quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded.

q.q: At a binding price floor, Qs = 110 and Qd = 80. What is the surplus?
options: 30 units
80 units
110 units
190 units
q.commonError: adds_qs_and_qd_instead_of_subtracting
q.feedback: Surplus equals Qs - Qd: 110 - 80 = 30.

q.q: At a binding floor, sellers offer 140 units and buyers want 95 units. What happens?
options: A surplus of 45 units
A shortage of 45 units
A surplus of 235 units
No surplus
q.commonError: reverses_surplus_formula
q.feedback: The surplus is quantity supplied minus quantity demanded: 140 - 95 = 45.

q.q: A minimum wage is set at $15 when equilibrium wage is $11. What happens?
options: The floor is binding and creates a labor surplus
The floor is nonbinding and has no effect
The floor creates a labor shortage
The floor shifts labor demand right
q.commonError: gets_binding_floor_direction_backwards
q.feedback: A floor above equilibrium is binding and creates a surplus.

q.q: A legal minimum price is below equilibrium. Why is it nonbinding?
options: The market price remains above the legal minimum
All floors create surpluses
Buyers must pay the lowest possible price
Supply must fall to zero
q.commonError: thinks_all_price_floors_bind
q.feedback: A floor below equilibrium does not stop the market from reaching equilibrium.

q.q: A grain schedule lists price per sack, sacks buyers want and sacks growers offer: $4: 100, 40; $6: 70, 70; $8: 50, 90. An enforced price floor is $8. What surplus follows?
options: 40 sacks
50 sacks
140 sacks
0 sacks
q.commonError: adds_qs_and_qd_instead_of_subtracting
q.feedback: Use the $8 floor row, not the $6 equilibrium row. Growers offer 90 sacks and buyers want 50, so surplus is 90 - 50 = 40. Adding supply and demand does not measure unsold output.

q.q: At a binding minimum price for milk, farms offer 700 cartons and households want 455. There are no government purchases, and households buy all 455. A clerk calls the 455 sold cartons "the surplus." Which correction is accurate?
options: 245 cartons are unsold; 455 cartons are purchased.
455 cartons are unsold; 245 cartons are purchased.
245 cartons are unmet demand; 455 cartons are purchased.
1,155 cartons are unsold; 455 cartons are purchased.
q.commonError: reverses_surplus_formula
q.feedback: Purchases are 455 cartons. The surplus is the amount offered but not purchased: 700 - 455 = 245 cartons. Supply exceeds demand, so the gap is unsold output, not unmet demand.

q.q: When federal outlays exceed federal revenues during a fiscal year, what is the result?
options: A budget deficit
A budget surplus
A balanced budget
A reduction in gross debt
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Budget Accounting.
q.feedback: A deficit occurs because annual outlays are greater than annual revenues.

q.q: Which fiscal position exists when annual federal revenues exceed annual outlays?
options: A budget deficit
A budget surplus
A balanced budget
A debt rollover
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Budget Accounting.
q.feedback: Revenues greater than outlays produce a positive budget balance, called a surplus.

q.q: Why is federal borrowing not classified as federal revenue in budget accounting?
options: It counts as revenue when interest rates fall
It becomes a transfer payment received by households
It finances a shortfall rather than counting as revenue
It is included in government purchases when debt is issued
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Budget Accounting.
q.feedback: Debt issuance supplies financing, but it does not turn the borrowed funds into budget revenue.

q.q: In the identity public saving = T − G, what must T represent in this accounting framework?
options: Net tax revenue after relevant transfers
Total federal outlays including transfers and net interest
Gross tax collections before subtracting any transfer payments
The accumulated federal debt stock at a specific date
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Public Saving.
q.feedback: The shorthand is valid here only when T is defined net of transfers and G is government purchases.

q.q: Under public saving = T − G, with T defined as net tax revenue and G as government purchases, what does negative public saving mean?
options: Private saving must also be below zero
T is less than G
Nominal GDP must be declining during the year
The government can have no outstanding federal debt
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Public Saving.
q.feedback: Public saving is negative when net tax revenue T is below government purchases G.

q.q: A Social Security benefit payment is best classified as what from the federal budget perspective?
options: Federal revenue from payroll taxes
Government purchases included in GDP when paid
Intragovernmental holdings of federal debt
A transfer payment within federal outlays
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Revenues and Outlays.
q.feedback: The payment is an outlay that transfers income; it is not a purchase of current output when issued.

q.q: The federal government buys newly produced rescue equipment. How is the transaction classified?
options: An outlay and a government purchase
A transfer payment without a current purchase
Federal revenue
Debt held by the public
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Revenues and Outlays.
q.feedback: Paying for newly produced equipment is both an outlay and government purchases in GDP.

q.q: Federal revenues are $4.8 trillion and outlays are $6.2 trillion. Using revenues minus outlays, what is the budget balance?
options: +$1.4 trillion
−$11.0 trillion
+$11.0 trillion
−$1.4 trillion
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Budget Accounting.
q.feedback: Revenues minus outlays equals $4.8 trillion minus $6.2 trillion, or −$1.4 trillion, a deficit.

q.q: A federal budget balance is reported as +$120 billion. What does the positive sign mean?
options: Revenues exceed outlays by $120 billion
Outlays exceed revenues by $120 billion
Federal debt equals $120 billion
Borrowing increased by exactly $120 billion
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Budget Accounting.
q.feedback: Under the stated revenues-minus-outlays convention, a positive balance is a surplus.

q.q: Federal revenues total $5.1 trillion and outlays total $5.9 trillion. What is the deficit expressed as a positive magnitude?
options: −$0.8 trillion
$0.8 trillion
$5.1 trillion
$11.0 trillion
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Budget Accounting.
q.feedback: Outlays exceed revenues by $0.8 trillion, so the deficit magnitude is reported as positive $0.8 trillion.

q.q: Net tax revenue T is $3.2 trillion and government purchases G are $3.8 trillion. What is public saving?
options: +$0.6 trillion
$3.2 trillion
−$0.6 trillion
$7.0 trillion
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Public Saving.
q.feedback: Using the stated identity, public saving is T minus G, or $3.2 trillion minus $3.8 trillion.

q.q: Suppose T is explicitly defined as net tax revenue and equals $2.9 trillion, while government purchases G equal $2.5 trillion. What is public saving?
options: −$0.4 trillion
$2.5 trillion
$5.4 trillion
+$0.4 trillion
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Public Saving.
q.feedback: With the variables defined, T − G equals +$0.4 trillion, indicating positive public saving.

q.q: Which statement accurately distinguishes mandatory and discretionary spending?
options: Mandatory spending cannot change
Mandatory follows standing law; discretionary depends on appropriations
Discretionary spending has no economically important uses
Every federal transfer payment belongs to discretionary spending
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Revenues and Outlays.
q.feedback: The labels describe budget processes, not whether spending matters or can ever be changed by law.

q.q: Interest paid on outstanding federal debt belongs in which budget category?
options: Federal revenue from outstanding Treasury securities
A transfer payment counted as government purchases in GDP
Net interest outlays, not government purchases
Intragovernmental holdings in federal trust-fund accounts
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Revenues and Outlays.
q.feedback: Interest outlays service prior borrowing; they are not purchases of newly produced goods and services.

q.q: One table reports a budget balance of −$900 billion; another describes a deficit of $900 billion. Are the reports consistent?
options: No; both reports must show the shortfall with a negative sign
No; balance and deficit figures cannot have the same magnitude
Yes; one is signed and the other gives the deficit magnitude
Yes; both figures describe a $900 billion budget surplus
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Budget Accounting.
q.feedback: A negative revenues-minus-outlays balance and a positive deficit magnitude can describe the same shortfall.

q.q: Revenues rise from $4.9 trillion to $5.2 trillion while outlays rise from $6.0 trillion to $6.1 trillion. How does the budget balance change?
options: It worsens by $0.2 trillion
It improves by $0.3 trillion and becomes a budget surplus
It remains unchanged as both rise
It improves by $0.2 trillion but remains negative
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Budget Accounting.
q.feedback: The balance moves from −$1.1 trillion to −$0.9 trillion, an improvement of $0.2 trillion.

q.q: A table gives total federal revenues of $5 trillion and total outlays, including transfers and interest, of $6 trillion. What should revenues minus outlays be called?
options: A $1 trillion federal budget deficit
Public saving of −$1 trillion under T − G
Private saving of $1 trillion
Government purchases of $6 trillion
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Public Saving.
q.feedback: Total revenues minus total outlays is the budget balance. In the T − G public-saving shorthand, T must be net tax revenue and G must be government purchases.

q.q: Holding the relevant definitions and other items fixed, what is the basic public-saving implication of a larger budget deficit?
options: Public saving is necessarily higher
Public saving is lower
Private saving becomes zero by identity
Government purchases are no longer part of GDP
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Public Saving.
q.feedback: A wider fiscal shortfall reduces the government's contribution to national saving under the introductory accounting link.

q.q: A benefit payment and a purchase of new federal vehicles are both outlays. What distinguishes their GDP treatment?
options: Both enter G
Neither enters GDP
Only the benefit payment enters G directly when Treasury pays it
Only the vehicle purchase enters G when paid
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Revenues and Outlays.
q.feedback: A transfer redistributes income, whereas the vehicle purchase pays for current production.

q.q: Taxes raise $4.7 trillion and borrowing supplies $1.1 trillion. Which amount is federal revenue?
options: $4.7 trillion
$1.1 trillion
$5.8 trillion
Neither amount
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Revenues and Outlays.
q.feedback: Taxes are receipts; borrowing finances the gap and is not recorded as revenue.

q.q: A published table rounds revenues to $5.6 trillion, outlays to $7.4 trillion, and the deficit to $1.9 trillion. Why need the rounded entries not subtract exactly?
options: The displayed figures were rounded independently
The deficit excludes displayed revenues
Borrowing is added to both displayed revenues and displayed outlays
The deficit uses calendar-year data
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Budget Accounting.
q.feedback: Independent rounding can make displayed components differ slightly from an identity calculated with unrounded values.

q.q: A budget worksheet reports $920 billion of cash inflows, including $180 billion from issuing new debt, and $870 billion of total outlays. All remaining inflows are revenues; there are no other financing adjustments. What are the budget balance and the amount of new borrowing left to increase cash balances?
options: A $50 billion surplus and no borrowing needed for the outlays
A $130 billion deficit and a $50 billion cash increase
A $130 billion deficit and a $180 billion cash increase
A $310 billion deficit and a $130 billion cash decrease
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Budget Accounting.
q.feedback: Revenues exclude borrowing: 920 − 180 = $740 billion. Revenues minus outlays equal 740 − 870 = −$130 billion. Of the $180 billion borrowed, $130 billion finances the deficit and $50 billion increases cash balances.

q.q: A simplified fiscal account reports gross tax receipts of $900 billion, transfers of $180 billion, government purchases of $660 billion and interest payments of $70 billion. These are all revenues and outlays. For this exercise define T as gross taxes minus transfers, excluding interest. Which pair gives textbook public saving T − G and the full budget balance?
options: Public saving is $240 billion; the full budget has a $60 billion surplus
Public saving is −$10 billion; the full budget also has a $10 billion deficit
Public saving is $60 billion; the full budget has a $10 billion deficit
Public saving is $60 billion; the full budget has a $60 billion surplus
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Public Saving.
q.feedback: Under the stated convention, T = 900 − 180 = $720 billion and T − G = $60 billion. Total outlays are 180 + 660 + 70 = $910 billion, giving a $10 billion deficit. The $70 billion difference is interest, which this exercise excludes from net taxes. Transfers are already deducted in T and must not be deducted a second time.

q.q: A speaker calls all discretionary outlays “optional” and all mandatory outlays “uncontrollable.” What is wrong with the claim?
options: Discretionary outlays are made without any congressional appropriations
The labels describe funding rules, not permanence or importance
Mandatory programs never transfer
Net interest outlays are classified as federal budget revenues
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Revenues and Outlays.
q.feedback: Process labels do not settle importance, desirability, or whether future law can alter spending.

q.q: A government starts the year with $3,600 billion of debt. Revenues are $760 billion and outlays are $940 billion. It issues $500 billion of debt, including debt used to repay $270 billion of maturing principal; remaining financing may change cash balances. With no other debt or financing adjustments, which reconciliation is correct?
options: A $180 billion deficit, ending debt of $4,100 billion, and a $320 billion increase in cash
A $320 billion surplus, ending debt of $3,830 billion, and a $50 billion increase in cash
A $180 billion deficit, ending debt of $3,830 billion, and a $50 billion increase in cash
A $450 billion deficit, ending debt of $3,780 billion, and unchanged cash
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Budget Accounting.
q.feedback: The deficit is 940 − 760 = $180 billion; debt issuance is financing, not revenue. Net issuance is 500 − 270 = $230 billion, so ending debt is $3,830 billion. Net financing exceeds the deficit by $50 billion, increasing cash. Principal repayment is not counted again as a budget outlay.

q.q: Annual federal revenues equal $5.0 trillion and outlays equal $5.3 trillion. Which fiscal position is shown?
options: A $0.3 trillion surplus
A balanced budget
A $5.3 trillion debt stock
A $0.3 trillion deficit
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Budget Accounting.
q.feedback: Outlays exceed revenues by $0.3 trillion, so the annual budget is in deficit.

q.q: According to CBO's February 2026 baseline, FY2026 revenues are projected at about $5.6 trillion and outlays at about $7.4 trillion. What fiscal position is projected?
options: A deficit because projected outlays exceed projected revenues
A surplus because projected revenues are positive
A balanced budget because both values are projections
A debt stock of $1.8 trillion
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Budget Accounting.
q.feedback: CBO projects outlays above revenues, which is a deficit; the published rounded deficit is about $1.9 trillion.

q.q: With T defined as net tax revenue and G as government purchases, T equals $800 billion and G equals $900 billion. What is public saving?
options: +$100 billion
$800 billion
$1.7 trillion
−$100 billion
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Public Saving.
q.feedback: T − G equals −$100 billion, so public saving is negative.

q.q: Which statement uses the public-saving convention correctly?
options: T − G, with T net of transfers and G purchases
Total revenues minus all federal outlays is always T − G public saving
T means gross collections and G includes transfers
Public saving is the federal debt stock
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Public Saving.
q.feedback: The notation is valid only when T is net tax revenue, net of transfers, and G is government purchases.

q.q: The government collects payroll taxes, sends pension benefits, and buys medical equipment. Which classification is correct?
options: Taxes, benefits, and equipment purchases are all federal revenue
Benefits and equipment both enter government purchases in GDP when paid
Taxes are revenue; both payments are outlays; only equipment is G
Payroll taxes are borrowing
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Revenues and Outlays.
q.feedback: Budget and GDP classifications overlap but are not identical: transfers are outlays without entering G when paid.

q.q: A simplified government has only three outlay categories: purchases of current domestic goods and services, transfers, and interest. Purchases rise from $400 billion to $430 billion, transfers from $300 billion to $350 billion, and interest from $50 billion to $70 billion. Revenues rise by $60 billion. Which comparison is correct?
options: The deficit widens by $40 billion, while the direct increase in GDP government purchases is $100 billion
The deficit narrows by $30 billion, while the direct increase in GDP government purchases is $40 billion
The deficit widens by $100 billion, while the direct increase in GDP government purchases is $30 billion
The deficit widens by $40 billion, while the direct increase in GDP government purchases is $30 billion
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Revenues and Outlays.
q.feedback: Outlays rise by 30 + 50 + 20 = $100 billion. With revenues up $60 billion, the deficit widens $40 billion. Only the $30 billion increase in current purchases directly increases G; transfers and interest are budget outlays without being current government purchases. No induced output response is being calculated.

q.q: Federal revenues are $5 trillion and outlays are $6 trillion. Is the budget in surplus or deficit?
options: Surplus
Deficit
Balanced
Debt-free
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Budget Accounting.
q.feedback: Outlays exceed revenues by $1 trillion, so the federal budget is in deficit.

q.q: T is net tax revenue of $700 billion and G is purchases of $600 billion. What is public saving?
options: −$100 billion
+$100 billion
$600 billion
$1.3 trillion
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Public Saving.
q.feedback: Subtract government purchases from net tax revenue: $700 billion minus $600 billion equals +$100 billion.

q.q: Which transaction is a government purchase rather than a transfer?
options: The federal purchase of new computers
A pension benefit payment
An unemployment benefit payment
An interest payment on debt
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Revenues and Outlays.
q.feedback: Buying current goods is a government purchase; benefits and interest are outlays but not G purchases.

q.q: A federal budget records revenues below outlays. What financing issue follows from that accounting result?
options: The shortfall becomes additional tax revenue in the same year
Government purchases become zero
The shortfall must be financed, commonly through borrowing
Existing federal debt disappears
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Budget Accounting.
q.feedback: A deficit is an annual financing gap; borrowing is a common way to cover it.

q.q: Why does negative public saving matter beyond the federal budget?
options: It directly fixes the economy's nominal exchange rate
It makes positive private saving impossible by definition
It reduces one component of national saving
It determines the national money supply without monetary policy
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Public Saving.
q.feedback: Negative public saving lowers national saving, all else equal, and therefore reduces the funds available to finance investment in the loanable-funds model.

q.q: A federal benefit payment is an outlay but not government purchases in GDP when paid. When can it affect measured GDP?
options: When Treasury classifies the benefit as mandatory spending
When recipients buy newly produced goods or services
Immediately, because every federal outlay enters G in GDP
Only after the outstanding federal debt stock begins to fall
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Federal Revenues and Outlays.
q.feedback: The transfer itself is not production; later consumption of current final output can enter GDP.

q.q: Net capital outflow equals domestic purchases of foreign assets minus:
options: Exports of domestic goods
Domestic investment spending
Foreign purchases of domestic assets
Domestic purchases of domestic assets
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: The second side of NCO records foreign acquisition of domestic assets.

q.q: A U.S. resident buys a bond issued by the German government. This transaction:
options: Counts as U.S. domestic investment
Increases U.S. NCO
Decreases U.S. NCO
Increases U.S. imports
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: A domestic purchase of a foreign asset is a capital outflow and enters positively in NCO.

q.q: A Japanese pension fund buys shares in a U.S. company. For the United States, this transaction:
options: Decreases NCO
Increases NCO
Increases exports by the share price
Reduces domestic investment
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: A foreign purchase of a domestic asset is subtracted when calculating domestic NCO.

q.q: Negative NCO is also called:
options: Net capital outflow
A trade surplus
Balanced asset trade
Net capital inflow
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: When foreign purchases of domestic assets are larger, funds flow into the country on net.

q.q: In the standard model, a higher domestic real interest rate tends to make domestic assets:
options: Identical to foreign assets
Unrelated to capital flows
More attractive relative to foreign assets
Less attractive relative to foreign assets
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: A higher return draws funds toward domestic assets, other things equal.

q.q: Political instability that causes residents to seek foreign assets is called:
options: Balanced trade
Capital flight
Crowding in
Purchasing-power parity
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: Capital flight is a sharp increase in desired purchases of foreign assets prompted by risk or instability.

q.q: Residents buy $180 billion of foreign assets, and foreigners buy $125 billion of domestic assets. What is NCO?
options: $125 billion
$305 billion
$55 billion
−$55 billion
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: NCO = $180 billion − $125 billion = $55 billion.

q.q: Residents buy $90 billion of foreign assets while foreigners buy $140 billion of domestic assets. Which description fits?
options: NCO is zero because both sides trade assets
NCO is −$50 billion, a net capital inflow
NCO is $50 billion, a net capital outflow
NCO is $230 billion, a net capital inflow
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: The difference is $90 billion − $140 billion = −$50 billion.

q.q: Domestic real interest rates rise relative to foreign rates. What happens to NCO in the standard model?
options: NCO falls
NCO rises
NCO becomes equal to domestic investment
NCO is fixed by the trade balance alone
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: Domestic assets become relatively attractive, reducing domestic purchases abroad and encouraging foreign purchases at home.

q.q: Foreign interest rates rise while the domestic real interest rate is unchanged. What is the likely effect on domestic NCO?
options: It falls
It becomes zero
It must equal national saving
It rises
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: Higher foreign returns make foreign assets more attractive to domestic investors, increasing NCO.

q.q: A domestic firm builds a factory abroad. How is the acquisition classified for the home country?
options: An import of consumer goods
Domestic residential investment
A domestic purchase of a foreign asset
A foreign purchase of a domestic asset
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: Ownership of productive capital abroad is a foreign asset held by a domestic resident.

q.q: Foreign confidence in domestic institutions improves. Holding returns fixed, what capital-flow response is most plausible?
options: NCO remains fixed because risk cannot affect asset demand
Foreign purchases of domestic assets rise, reducing NCO
Domestic purchases of foreign assets rise, increasing NCO
Foreign purchases of domestic goods fall, raising NCO
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: Lower perceived risk raises foreign demand for domestic assets, increasing the term subtracted from NCO.

q.q: Domestic purchases of foreign assets rise by $70 billion, while foreign purchases of domestic assets rise by $95 billion. How does NCO change?
options: It rises by $25 billion
It rises by $165 billion
It falls by $165 billion
It falls by $25 billion
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: The change in NCO is +$70 billion − $95 billion = −$25 billion.

q.q: The domestic real interest rate rises, but political risk also rises sharply. What can be concluded about NCO?
options: NCO rises because risk determines flows independently of returns
NCO is unchanged because NX = NCO forces the channels to cancel
The direction is ambiguous because the two forces push NCO oppositely
NCO falls because interest returns determine flows independently of risk
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: Higher domestic returns tend to lower NCO, while greater domestic risk tends to raise it; relative magnitudes are needed.

q.q: A student says a capital inflow means domestic residents purchased more foreign assets. What is the correction?
options: The statement is correct whenever interest rates rise
A net inflow means foreign purchases of domestic assets exceeded domestic purchases abroad
A net inflow means both asset-purchase flows were zero
A net inflow is the same as positive NCO
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: Negative NCO is generated when the foreign acquisition of domestic assets is the larger flow.

q.q: National saving is $520 billion, domestic investment is $610 billion, and domestic residents buy $160 billion of foreign assets. How much do foreigners buy in domestic assets?
options: $250 billion
$70 billion
$160 billion
$770 billion
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: NCO = S − I = −$90 billion. Since −90 = 160 − foreign purchases, foreign purchases are $250 billion.

q.q: Foreign investors reduce new purchases of domestic bonds while domestic investors do not change their foreign-asset purchases. What happens to NCO?
options: It falls
It is unchanged
It becomes equal to the bond price
It rises
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: A smaller foreign purchase flow reduces the term subtracted from domestic purchases abroad, raising NCO.

q.q: Why does a higher domestic real interest rate lower NCO rather than raise it in the standard model?
options: It makes foreign assets relatively more attractive to domestic savers
It raises outward investment by increasing the return on foreign bonds
It favors domestic assets over foreign assets for both domestic and foreign investors
It attracts foreign funds that enter positively in the definition of NCO
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: The relative-return change keeps more domestic funds at home and attracts more foreign funds.

q.q: Domestic rates rise 2 percentage points, foreign rates rise 3 points, and domestic political risk falls. What can be inferred about NCO?
options: It falls two percentage points because domestic risk and rates move together
It is unchanged because domestic and foreign rates both increased
Its direction is ambiguous: the relative-rate change raises NCO while lower domestic risk reduces it
It rises one percentage point because flow quantities equal rate differentials
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: Foreign returns rise one point relative to domestic returns, tending to raise NCO, while safer domestic assets tend to lower it; magnitudes decide the net effect.

q.q: Gross capital outflows rise while NCO falls. Which change can explain both facts?
options: The trade balance becomes unrelated to NCO
Gross capital inflows rise by more than gross outflows
Gross inflows fall by the same amount
Domestic purchases of foreign assets become zero
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: NCO is a net measure; it can fall despite larger outflows if foreign purchases of domestic assets rise even more.

q.q: Residents initially buy $220 billion abroad and foreigners buy $260 billion domestically. Resident purchases later rise 25 percent. What range of growth in foreign purchases would leave a net inflow that is smaller than the initial net inflow?
options: Approximately 0% < growth < 5.77%
Approximately 21.15% < growth < 25%
Approximately 25% < growth < 40%
Approximately 5.77% < growth < 21.15%
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: Resident purchases become 275. For −40 < NCO < 0, require −40 < 275 − 260(1+g) < 0. Thus 275 < 260(1+g) < 315, giving 5.77% < g < 21.15%. Endpoints correspond to balance or the original inflow, so they are excluded.

q.q: Domestic real returns rise while perceived domestic political risk also rises. An analyst observes that NCO increased and concludes that higher interest rates caused capital flight. Holding other determinants fixed, which inference separates the observed change from the interest-rate effect?
options: The positive NCO response proves that higher domestic rates increase desired foreign purchases
The identity NX = NCO requires risk and interest-rate effects to have equal size
The risk-driven outward shift dominated the rate-induced reduction in NCO; the observation does not reverse the rate mechanism
The rate increase must have preceded the risk shock because NCO rose
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: The return effect lowers NCO, while the domestic risk shock raises it. Positive net change under these two channels shows that risk dominated, not that the partial interest-rate slope reversed. Timing is not identified.

q.q: NCO moves from −$80 billion to $30 billion while domestic foreign-asset purchases rise $40 billion. How must foreign purchases of domestic assets change?
options: They must rise by $150 billion
They must fall by $70 billion
They must rise by $70 billion
They must fall by $110 billion
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: NCO rises $110 billion. With domestic foreign purchases up $40 billion, foreign domestic-asset purchases must fall $70 billion to make the net rise $110 billion.

q.q: In a period, residents acquire $300 billion of foreign securities. Foreign acquisitions of domestic factories are known only to lie between $180 and $240 billion; foreign acquisitions of domestic bonds lie between $50 and $90 billion. There are no other asset flows. What can be inferred about NCO?
options: It lies between −$30 and +$70 billion; its sign needs the combined inflow
It must be positive because securities purchases exceed either inflow separately
It must be negative because there are two types of inward purchases
It equals $30 billion because the component ranges cancel
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: Total inflow is between 230 and 330, so NCO = 300 − inflow lies between −30 and +70. The sign depends on whether combined inflow exceeds 300; counting the types of transactions is insufficient.

q.q: Political instability raises desired foreign-asset purchases, and the domestic real interest rate rises in response. How should the second effect be interpreted?
options: The higher rate reinforces NCO by making foreign assets more attractive
The rate converts the capital outflow into domestic investment
The rate leaves NCO unchanged because capital flight is permanent
The higher rate partly restrains the initial increase in NCO
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: Capital flight shifts desired NCO outward, while the higher domestic return produces movement toward domestic assets along the new relationship.

q.q: Gross outward and inward asset purchases are reported as $3,045 billion and $3,000 billion. Each figure could independently be revised up or down by $30 billion. Does the reported positive NCO establish a robust direction of net capital flow?
options: Yes; any revisions preserve the reported +$45 billion
Yes; the maximum revision to NCO is only $30 billion
No; admissible NCO ranges from −$15 to +$105 billion
No; the revisions imply exactly zero NCO
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: Reported NCO is 45. Independent errors can reduce it by 30 + 30 = 60 or raise it by 60, so its interval is [−15,105]. Large nearly offsetting gross flows make the sign sensitive to revisions.

q.q: A foreign company buys a domestic office building. For the domestic economy, this is:
options: A capital inflow that lowers NCO
A capital outflow that raises NCO
An export that raises NCO
Domestic saving that leaves NCO fixed
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: Foreign acquisition of a domestic real asset is a foreign purchase of a domestic asset.

q.q: If domestic purchases abroad equal foreign purchases at home, NCO is:
options: Positive
Negative
Equal to investment
Zero
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: Equal gross asset-purchase flows produce a zero net difference.

q.q: Which change tends to reduce NCO?
options: A rise in foreign asset returns
Residents seeking more foreign diversification
A rise in the domestic real interest rate
A rise in perceived domestic political risk
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: Higher domestic returns make home assets more attractive relative to foreign assets.

q.q: Outward asset purchases are $340 billion and inward purchases are $410 billion. What is NCO?
options: $70 billion
$340 billion
$750 billion
−$70 billion
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: Subtracting $410 billion from $340 billion gives −$70 billion.

q.q: Foreign demand for domestic bonds rises with domestic purchases abroad unchanged. Which result follows?
options: NCO remains unchanged
Gross outflows increase
NCO decreases
NCO increases
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: The foreign-purchase term is subtracted, so a larger inflow reduces NCO.

q.q: Why can a net capital inflow help finance domestic investment above national saving?
options: Domestic investment is subtracted from GDP
Foreign purchases of domestic assets provide external financing
Imports are counted as domestic saving
NCO becomes positive when investment exceeds saving
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: When I exceeds S, NCO = S − I is negative; the counterpart is net financing from abroad.

q.q: A country's NCO is −$120 billion and residents purchase $200 billion of foreign assets. What are foreign purchases of domestic assets?
options: $120 billion
$200 billion
$320 billion
$80 billion
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: −120 = 200 − foreign purchases, so foreign purchases equal $320 billion.

q.q: Domestic rates rise while foreign risk also rises. What is the likely combined effect on domestic NCO?
options: The effects necessarily cancel
Both changes tend to reduce it
Both changes tend to increase it
The rate raises it while foreign risk lowers it
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: Higher domestic returns favor home assets, and riskier foreign assets further discourage purchases abroad.

q.q: Residents reduce net acquisition of foreign assets by selling assets and repatriating funds. Foreign net acquisition of domestic assets is unchanged. What happens to residents’ net outward asset flow and NCO?
options: Both fall
Both rise
The outward asset flow falls while NCO rises
NCO is unchanged because foreign investors did not act
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: Resident net acquisition of foreign assets enters positively in NCO; a reduction lowers NCO when foreign net acquisition of domestic assets is fixed. This statement concerns period asset flows, not revaluations of existing holdings.

q.q: Initially gross outward purchases are $500 billion and inward purchases $560 billion. Later inward purchases are $650 billion, investment has risen $75 billion and saving has risen $105 billion. What later outward purchases reconcile the accounts, and does the country still receive a net inflow?
options: $680 billion; no, a $30 billion net outflow
$620 billion; yes, a $30 billion net inflow
$650 billion; no, the asset account balances
$590 billion; yes, a $60 billion net inflow
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: Initial NCO is −60. Its change equals ΔS − ΔI = 105 − 75 = 30, so final NCO is −30. Outward purchases must satisfy outward − 650 = −30, hence 620. Negative NCO remains a net inflow.

q.q: At the original interest rate, a risk shock raises residents’ intended foreign purchases by $140 billion and lowers foreign intended domestic purchases by $60 billion. The new equilibrium shows NCO up $125 billion. What interest-rate feedback is required, and which portfolio pattern could produce it?
options: Feedback lowers NCO $75 billion; resident purchases fall $45 billion and foreign purchases rise $30 billion relative to the shifted schedule
Feedback raises NCO $75 billion; resident purchases rise $45 billion and foreign purchases fall $30 billion
Feedback lowers NCO $15 billion; both gross purchase flows fall $75 billion
Feedback lowers NCO $200 billion; all desired purchases return to their original levels
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: The initial NCO shift is 140 − (−60) = 200. The realized increase of 125 requires feedback of −75. A −45 resident-flow response minus a +30 foreign-flow response gives −75, consistent with more attractive domestic returns.

q.q: Domestic investment rises $90 billion while national saving rises $20 billion. If residents' foreign purchases fall $30 billion, what change in foreign purchases of domestic assets is consistent?
options: They fall by $40 billion
They rise by $100 billion
They fall by $100 billion
They rise by $40 billion
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: NCO must fall $70 billion. Its first gross-flow component falls $30 billion, so foreign purchases must rise $40 billion to produce the remaining $40 billion decline.

q.q: A student labels positive NCO a capital inflow. Which correction is accurate?
options: Positive NCO means foreign purchases dominate
Positive NCO is a net capital outflow
Positive NCO is a net capital inflow
The sign of NCO has no interpretation
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: Positive NCO means domestic purchases of foreign assets exceed foreign purchases of domestic assets.

q.q: The domestic real interest rate rises and NCO falls. How does this change reach the foreign-exchange market?
options: A lower NCO raises demand for domestic currency
A higher rate makes foreign-exchange supply horizontal
NCO affects only goods markets
A lower NCO reduces the supply of domestic currency
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: With fewer net foreign-asset purchases, residents exchange less domestic currency for foreign currency, so FX supply shifts left.

q.q: What is the central bank of the United States?
options: The Treasury Department
Congress
The Federal Reserve
The FDIC
q.commonError: Confusing the Fed with fiscal agencies.
q.feedback: The Federal Reserve is the central bank of the United States.

q.q: Which group directs open-market operations?
options: Federal Open Market Committee
Congressional Budget Office
Bureau of Labor Statistics
Internal Revenue Service
q.commonError: Confusing monetary policy agencies with data or tax agencies.
q.feedback: The FOMC directs open-market operations as part of monetary policy.

q.q: One major role of the Federal Reserve is to act as
options: a lender of last resort for banks
the agency that collects personal income taxes
the branch of government that writes spending bills
the organization that produces real GDP data
q.commonError: confusing the Federal Reserve with fiscal agencies
q.feedback: The Fed can serve as a lender of last resort by lending to banks when they need liquidity.

q.q: The discount rate is the interest rate
options: the Fed charges banks for loans
banks charge each other on overnight loans
households earn on checking accounts
Congress pays on tax refunds
q.commonError: confusing the discount rate with the federal funds rate
q.feedback: The discount rate is the interest rate the Fed charges banks when it lends to them.

q.q: The federal funds rate is best described as the interest rate
options: banks charge each other for short-term overnight loans
the Fed charges households for mortgages
Congress sets on government spending
firms pay workers as a wage
q.commonError: thinking the federal funds rate is directly charged to consumers by the Fed
q.feedback: The federal funds rate is the rate banks charge each other for overnight loans.

q.q: The Federal Reserve is best described as
options: the central bank of the United States
the agency that writes the federal budget
a private commercial bank that lends only to households
the part of Congress that sets tax rates
q.commonError: confusing the Fed with fiscal policymakers
q.feedback: The Federal Reserve is the central bank of the United States and conducts monetary policy.

q.q: The Federal Open Market Committee is most directly responsible for
options: conducting open-market operations
setting federal income tax rates
writing government spending bills
calculating the unemployment rate
q.commonError: confusing monetary policy with fiscal policy
q.feedback: The FOMC conducts monetary policy largely through buying and selling government bonds.

q.q: Which statement best describes the FOMC's role?
options: It guides monetary policy and open-market operations.
It sets federal income tax brackets.
It calculates the CPI.
It decides how much Congress spends.
q.commonError: confusing the FOMC with fiscal policymakers
q.feedback: The FOMC is central to monetary policy, especially open-market operations.

q.q: The Fed is called a lender of last resort because it can
options: lend to banks facing liquidity problems
lend directly to every household for groceries
write spending bills for Congress
set all market prices
q.commonError: thinking lender of last resort means normal consumer lending
q.feedback: The Fed can lend to banks when they face liquidity stress, which is why it is called a lender of last resort.

q.q: Why does central bank independence matter?
options: It can help monetary policy avoid short-run political pressure.
It lets the Fed collect income taxes.
It prevents banks from holding reserves.
It means the Fed is owned by Congress.
q.commonError: thinking independence means no public role or accountability
q.feedback: Central bank independence can help keep monetary policy from being driven by short-run political incentives.

q.q: Which distinction between the Federal Reserve and the U.S. Treasury is correct?
options: The Treasury sets the federal funds rate, while the Fed writes tax laws.
The Fed passes the federal budget, while the Treasury regulates inflation expectations.
The Fed conducts monetary policy, while the Treasury manages federal finances and debt operations.
Both institutions perform exactly the same functions.
q.commonError: Treating the central bank and fiscal authority as the same institution.
q.feedback: The Fed is the monetary authority; the Treasury is part of the executive branch and manages federal finances.

q.q: A commercial bank approves a loan and credits the borrower’s checking account. In a separate transaction, the Federal Reserve credits a bank’s reserve account during an asset purchase. Which distinction is correct?
options: The commercial bank creates a deposit liability; the Fed creates central-bank reserves
The Fed creates the borrower’s commercial-bank deposit, while the bank creates central-bank reserves
Both transactions create only physical currency held by the public
Neither transaction changes any bank liability or reserve balance
q.commonError: Treats commercial-bank deposits and central-bank reserves as the same liability issued by the same institution.
q.feedback: Commercial banks create deposit liabilities when they lend; the central bank creates reserve balances/base money used by banks.

q.q: A headline says, “The Treasury raised the federal funds rate to conduct monetary policy.” What is the best correction?
options: The statement is correct because the Treasury and Federal Reserve are the same institution
The federal funds rate is set by commercial banks with no connection to Federal Reserve policy
The Treasury sets monetary policy while the Federal Reserve determines tax rates and federal spending
Monetary policy and the federal funds rate are associated with the Federal Reserve, while the Treasury manages federal finances and debt operations
q.commonError: Treats the Federal Reserve and Treasury as interchangeable agencies.
q.feedback: The Federal Reserve conducts monetary policy and supports the banking/payments system; the Treasury manages federal finances and debt operations.

q.q: During a panic, a solvent bank cannot obtain short-term funding even though its assets exceed its liabilities. What central-bank response best fits the lender-of-last-resort role?
options: Guarantee every bank loss without conditions.
Finance a permanent tax cut.
Raise reserve requirements solely to remove liquidity.
Provide temporary liquidity against sound collateral.
q.commonError: Confusing liquidity support with an unconditional bailout of insolvent institutions.
q.feedback: Lender-of-last-resort support addresses temporary liquidity problems while safeguards limit losses and moral hazard.

q.q: Which institutional arrangement best combines central-bank independence with democratic accountability?
options: Public officials set the mandate; the central bank chooses instruments and reports transparently.
The central bank chooses national goals and never explains its decisions to the public.
Elected officials directly set policy interest rates before every national election.
The Treasury secretly directs monetary operations without a published mandate.
q.commonError: Treating independence as freedom from any public mandate or oversight.
q.feedback: Instrument independence can coexist with a legislated mandate, transparency, and public accountability.

q.q: When the central bank buys a large quantity of longer-term securities, what happens directly on its balance sheet?
options: Tax revenue rises while currency liabilities disappear from the balance sheet.
Its securities assets and reserve liabilities usually both rise.
Government purchases of goods rise automatically with the securities purchase.
Commercial-bank capital is converted directly into federal tax receipts.
q.commonError: Treating asset purchases as ordinary fiscal spending.
q.feedback: A central-bank asset purchase expands its asset holdings and typically creates reserve liabilities.

q.q: The short-term policy rate is near its effective lower bound. Which action is still a monetary-policy option?
options: Change federal income-tax rates through the banking system.
Authorize a new congressional spending program immediately.
Use forward guidance or buy longer-term securities.
Set private-sector wages and prices by administrative order.
q.commonError: Assuming monetary policy has no remaining tools when a short-term rate is very low.
q.feedback: Central banks may use communication and balance-sheet tools when conventional rate cuts are constrained.

q.q: During a panic, a bank has valuable assets but cannot obtain enough short-term funding to meet payments. Later analysis shows another bank’s assets are worth less than its liabilities. Why should a central bank treat the two cases differently?
options: Liquidity can address the first bank’s funding problem, but it cannot erase the second bank’s insolvency
Both banks should receive unlimited central-bank loans because any funding problem proves that losses and insolvency are irrelevant
The insolvent bank needs only a lower reserve requirement, while the solvent bank must be closed immediately
The central bank should finance both banks permanently because recognizing losses is a fiscal-policy function
q.commonError: Treats emergency central-bank liquidity as a way to erase losses at an insolvent institution.
q.feedback: Lender-of-last-resort support addresses temporary liquidity problems; insolvency requires losses to be recognized and capital restored through other mechanisms.

q.q: A central-bank asset purchase sharply increases reserve balances, yet commercial-bank lending changes little. Which statement best separates the institutions’ roles?
options: The central bank failed to create any reserve balances because commercial banks did not expand loans after the asset purchase
Commercial banks create central-bank reserves whenever they choose not to lend
Reserve balances are identical to bank capital, so unchanged lending proves capital was unchanged
The central bank creates reserves; commercial-bank deposit creation still depends on lending and borrowing
q.commonError: Assumes that creating reserves automatically forces commercial banks to make loans and expand deposits.
q.feedback: The central bank can supply reserves, but broad deposit creation also depends on banks, borrowers, and redepositing behavior.

q.q: A government persistently pressures its central bank to create money to finance large deficits. What institutional risk is most relevant?
options: The natural rate of unemployment automatically becomes zero.
The money supply becomes unrelated to the central bank.
Budget deficits cease to have opportunity costs.
Fiscal dominance can weaken price stability and central-bank credibility.
q.commonError: Ignoring how fiscal pressure can compromise monetary-policy objectives.
q.feedback: Under fiscal dominance, debt-financing pressure can subordinate monetary policy and raise inflation risk.

q.q: Emergency lending stops a bank run, but banks now expect rescue whenever they take large risks. What tradeoff does the central bank face?
options: Financial stability today versus greater moral hazard tomorrow.
Lower inflation today versus a permanently lower natural rate.
Higher taxes today versus lower government spending tomorrow.
More exports today versus fewer imports tomorrow.
q.commonError: Evaluating emergency lending without considering future risk-taking incentives.
q.feedback: Liquidity support can stabilize the system, but poorly designed guarantees can encourage excessive risk.

q.q: A country has no central bank independence. Before elections, policymakers pressure the central bank to buy bonds and expand money aggressively. Which long-run risk is most consistent with the course logic?
options: Political pressure may create excessive money growth and inflation.
Political pressure guarantees higher real output forever.
Bond purchases permanently lower the price level.
Money becomes commodity money.
q.commonError: thinking central bank independence is irrelevant to inflation outcomes
q.feedback: Central bank independence can help reduce politically motivated money growth that risks inflation.

q.q: Why does central-bank independence not mean the central bank should be free to choose any social objective it wants?
options: Independence requires all monetary-policy decisions to remain secret.
Independence covers instrument choice within a publicly established mandate.
The central bank must directly control federal taxes and spending.
Independence means elected institutions have no legitimate policy role.
q.commonError: Equating instrument independence with unlimited policy authority.
q.feedback: A legitimate framework separates public goal setting from day-to-day instrument choices and requires accountability.

q.q: Inflation is well above target and output is near potential, but elected officials demand easier money before an election. What is the strongest case for central-bank independence?
options: It guarantees that monetary tightening has no short-run output cost.
It allows the central bank to eliminate every federal budget deficit.
It resists election-driven easing and protects price-stability credibility.
It permanently fixes unemployment below the natural rate.
q.commonError: Assuming independence removes policy tradeoffs rather than improving commitment.
q.feedback: Independence can support credible commitment to price stability even when near-term political incentives favor expansion.

q.q: A crisis program has two parts: the central bank lends temporarily against sound collateral to solvent banks, while the fiscal authority injects taxpayer capital into an insolvent institution. What principle best distinguishes the two actions?
options: Central-bank liquidity support addresses funding; fiscal recapitalization addresses losses and solvency
Both actions are ordinary open-market operations because each changes a financial balance sheet
The central bank is conducting fiscal policy in both cases because all emergency lending uses tax revenue
The fiscal authority is acting as lender of last resort while the central bank is collecting taxes
q.commonError: Treats emergency central-bank liquidity as a way to erase losses at an insolvent institution.
q.feedback: Lender-of-last-resort support addresses temporary liquidity problems; insolvency requires losses to be recognized and capital restored through other mechanisms.

q.q: The central bank expands its balance sheet and reserve balances surge. Banks, however, tighten underwriting and firms postpone borrowing because sales prospects are weak. Which conclusion is strongest?
options: The central bank did not actually create reserves because bank lending failed to rise
Weak borrowing proves that commercial banks, not the central bank, issue reserve balances
The simple multiplier guarantees the same deposit expansion regardless of banks or borrowers
Creating reserves does not mechanically force commercial-bank lending or deposit expansion
q.commonError: Assumes that creating reserves automatically forces commercial banks to make loans and expand deposits.
q.feedback: The central bank can supply reserves, but broad deposit creation also depends on banks, borrowers, and redepositing behavior.

q.q: A student argues that the Federal Reserve must be part of the Treasury because its actions can affect government-security markets. Which response is most accurate?
options: The Treasury conducts monetary policy whenever the Fed buys a government security
Government securities cannot appear on a central-bank balance sheet unless Congress sets the policy rate directly
The Fed is a distinct central bank even though its operations can involve government securities
The Fed is legally just a Treasury checking account because both institutions handle government securities
q.commonError: Treats the Federal Reserve and Treasury as interchangeable agencies.
q.feedback: The Federal Reserve conducts monetary policy and supports the banking/payments system; the Treasury manages federal finances and debt operations.

q.q: Which description correctly identifies the Federal Reserve?
options: the central bank of the United States
the agency that writes federal spending bills
the agency that collects income taxes
a private household lender
q.commonError: confusing the Fed with fiscal agencies
q.feedback: The Fed is the U.S. central bank. It handles monetary policy, not tax law.

q.q: The FOMC is most directly connected to
options: open-market operations and monetary policy
writing the federal budget
calculating the CPI
setting income tax brackets
q.commonError: confusing FOMC actions with fiscal policy
q.feedback: The FOMC conducts monetary policy largely through open-market operations.

q.q: A central bank faces political pressure to expand money before an election. Why does central bank independence matter here?
options: It limits political pressure for excessive money growth.
It lets the Fed set income tax rates.
It prevents all inflation forever.
It makes banks stop lending.
q.commonError: thinking Fed independence has nothing to do with inflation risk
q.feedback: Independence can help keep monetary policy from being pushed around for short-run political gain.

q.q: A solvent bank cannot obtain overnight funding during a panic, while an insolvent bank has losses larger than its capital. Which central-bank principle is most important?
options: Neither bank can receive liquidity because central banks deal only with government budgets
Liquidity lending can help the solvent bank, but it cannot by itself restore the insolvent bank’s capital
Both problems are identical and can be solved by unlimited reserve creation
Only the insolvent bank qualifies for lender-of-last-resort support because it has larger losses
q.commonError: Treats emergency central-bank liquidity as a way to erase losses at an insolvent institution.
q.feedback: Lender-of-last-resort support addresses temporary liquidity problems; insolvency requires losses to be recognized and capital restored through other mechanisms.

q.q: The government establishes the central bank’s mandate, but elected officials cannot order a pre-election interest-rate change. The bank must explain its decisions publicly. What does this arrangement combine?
options: Instrument independence with democratic accountability
Complete independence from any public mandate
Fiscal dominance with no central-bank discretion
Commercial-bank control of the monetary-policy mandate
q.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
q.feedback: Elected institutions establish the public mandate, while the central bank retains day-to-day instrument choice and reports its decisions, combining operational independence with accountability.

q.q: The central bank adds reserves through an asset purchase, but banks and borrowers do not expand credit. What can still be said with confidence?
options: The asset purchase could not have occurred because every reserve increase must create the maximum amount of loans
Commercial banks must have created the reserve balances before the central bank could buy the asset
The lack of new lending means the action was fiscal rather than monetary
The central bank changed reserve conditions even though broader deposit creation did not respond mechanically
q.commonError: Assumes that creating reserves automatically forces commercial banks to make loans and expand deposits.
q.feedback: The central bank can supply reserves, but broad deposit creation also depends on banks, borrowers, and redepositing behavior.

q.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes the Federal Reserve from a commercial bank?
options: The Fed can create reserve balances; a commercial bank creates deposits when it makes loans
The commercial bank creates Federal Reserve reserve liabilities for the payment system, while the Fed creates private bank capital for each lender
Both institutions issue only physical currency and neither creates account balances
The Fed accepts household checking deposits in the same way as a retail bank
q.commonError: Treats commercial-bank deposits and central-bank reserves as the same liability issued by the same institution.
q.feedback: Commercial banks create deposit liabilities when they lend; the central bank creates reserve balances/base money used by banks.

q.q: Which statement best distinguishes the Federal Reserve from the U.S. Treasury?
options: The Treasury conducts monetary policy and determines bank reserve conditions; the Fed sets federal tax rates for Congress
The two names refer to the same institution
The Fed manages congressional spending while the Treasury supplies bank reserves
The Fed conducts monetary policy; the Treasury manages federal finances and debt operations
q.commonError: Treats the Federal Reserve and Treasury as interchangeable agencies.
q.feedback: The Federal Reserve conducts monetary policy and supports the banking/payments system; the Treasury manages federal finances and debt operations.

q.q: A central-bank committee decides to change monetary conditions. Which institutional description is most accurate?
options: The committee determines federal tax rates and appropriations for the entire national budget
The committee measures M1 but has no connection to monetary policy
The policy-making body chooses monetary actions within the central bank’s mandate
The committee directly approves household mortgages at commercial banks
q.commonError: Treats the Federal Reserve and Treasury as interchangeable agencies.
q.feedback: The Federal Reserve conducts monetary policy and supports the banking/payments system; the Treasury manages federal finances and debt operations.

q.q: A central bank under political pressure buys bonds aggressively before an election. Banks lend most of the new reserves, and output is already near potential. Which long-run risk is most consistent with the chapter logic?
options: Excessive money growth creates inflation pressure without lasting real-output gains.
Real output permanently rises because more money creates more resources.
The price level falls because bond purchases reduce reserves.
Money demand becomes zero.
q.commonError: thinking money growth permanently raises real output
q.feedback: If output is near potential, aggressive money growth mainly risks inflation rather than permanent real gains.

q.q: A commercial bank makes a loan by crediting a deposit, while the Federal Reserve supplies reserve balances to banks. Which statement best separates the two forms of money creation?
options: Commercial banks create deposits; the central bank creates reserves and base money
Commercial banks issue reserve balances; the central bank issues all checking deposits
Both institutions can create only physical currency
Neither institution can create a financial liability
q.commonError: Treats commercial-bank deposits and central-bank reserves as the same liability issued by the same institution.
q.feedback: Commercial banks create deposit liabilities when they lend; the central bank creates reserve balances/base money used by banks.

q.q: A bank is solvent but temporarily unable to meet payments because short-term funding markets freeze. Which central-bank response best fits the lender-of-last-resort principle?
options: Use tax revenue to replace every risky bank asset permanently
Refuse all liquidity because a funding shortage proves assets are worthless
Order the Treasury to guarantee every future bank loss
Provide temporary liquidity against sound collateral to an otherwise solvent bank
q.commonError: Treats emergency central-bank liquidity as a way to erase losses at an insolvent institution.
q.feedback: Lender-of-last-resort support addresses temporary liquidity problems; insolvency requires losses to be recognized and capital restored through other mechanisms.

q.q: What is the central bank of the United States?
options: The Federal Reserve
The Treasury
Congress
The IRS
q.feedback: The Federal Reserve is the central bank of the United States.

q.q: Which group directs open-market operations?
options: FOMC
IRS
BLS
CBO
q.feedback: The Federal Open Market Committee directs open-market operations.

q.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
q.q: A solvent bank has sound assets but cannot obtain short-term funding during a panic. Which central-bank role is designed for this situation?
options: Lender of last resort
Collector of federal income taxes
Issuer of corporate stock
Manager of the congressional budget
q.feedback: A lender of last resort provides temporary liquidity to a solvent bank facing a funding panic.

q.commonError: Confusing monetary policy with fiscal policy.
q.q: The Fed mainly conducts:
options: Monetary policy
Fiscal policy
Trade policy
Tax collection
q.feedback: The Fed handles monetary policy, not taxes and government spending.

q.commonError: Confusing the FOMC with Congress.
q.q: The FOMC is most closely tied to:
options: Open-market operations
Income tax rates
Federal spending bills
GDP measurement
q.feedback: The FOMC helps direct monetary policy through open-market operations.

q.commonError: Thinking FOMC decisions are fiscal policy.
q.q: When the FOMC buys or sells bonds, it is using:
options: Monetary policy
Fiscal policy
Trade policy
Labor policy
q.feedback: Buying and selling bonds is monetary policy.

q.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
q.q: Elected officials establish a central bank’s mandate, while the bank chooses how to use its policy instruments and reports its decisions publicly. What principle does this arrangement illustrate?
options: Instrument independence combined with public accountability
Complete independence from any publicly established mandate
Fiscal dominance because elected officials choose tax rates
Abolition of central-bank discretion over policy instruments
q.feedback: The arrangement gives the bank instrument independence within a public mandate and requires it to explain its decisions, preserving democratic accountability.

q.commonError: Missing the link between political pressure and inflation risk.
q.q: Political pressure to print money can create risk of:
options: Inflation
Deflation always
Zero money demand
No nominal prices
q.feedback: Politically driven money growth can create inflation pressure.

q.q: A financial panic hits and the banking system needs a lender-of-last-resort institution. Which institution fits?
options: Federal Reserve
Bureau of Labor Statistics
Congressional Budget Office
Internal Revenue Service
q.feedback: The Fed acts as the central bank and lender of last resort.

q.q: The FOMC decides that monetary conditions should be easier and authorizes purchases of securities. What connection is being made?
options: The FOMC is choosing a monetary-policy tool that adds reserves
The Treasury is using fiscal policy to change government purchases
A commercial bank is deciding how much capital to issue to shareholders
Households are changing M1 by moving funds from checking to savings
q.feedback: When the FOMC authorizes securities purchases, it is using an expansionary monetary-policy tool that adds reserve balances to banks.
q.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
Confusing the Fed with Congress or the Treasury.
q.q: If a policy changes bank reserves and interest rates, it is most likely:
options: Monetary policy by the Fed
Fiscal policy by Congress
Trade policy
GDP accounting
q.feedback: Changes in reserves and interest rates are monetary policy territory.

q.q: A competitive market has:
options: Many buyers and sellers, none with much price control
One seller who controls the price
Only government buyers
No price signals
q.commonError: confuses_competitive_market_with_one_dominant_seller
q.feedback: A competitive market has many buyers and sellers, each with little control over price.

q.q: A price taker is a buyer or seller who:
options: Accepts the market price as given
Sets the market price alone
