q.q: A government restricts foreign direct investment to protect domestic firms. What is a possible long-run cost?
options: Less capital, technology, and productivity growth
Guaranteed faster catch-up growth
No effect on capital accumulation
Automatic increase in human capital
q.feedback: Foreign investment can bring capital and technology, so restricting it may slow productivity growth.

q.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
q.q: Why can research and development policies raise living standards even if they do not immediately raise output?
options: They expand technology and future productivity
They directly count as discouraged workers
They lower GDP by definition
They only change the CPI basket
q.feedback: R&D can improve production methods and technologies that raise future output per worker.

q.q: GROWTH-01 shows that capital deepening can move an economy from A toward B, but the curve becomes flatter. Which policy implication is strongest?
options: Capital raises output, while sustained growth also needs broader productivity gains
Capital accumulation becomes completely useless as soon as the economy reaches point B on the graph
The graph implies that low-capital economies should stop investment before they approach point B
Long-run growth can rely on repeated physical-capital accumulation forever without complementary productivity improvements
q.commonError: Treats a one-time demand boost as a substitute for policies that raise productive capacity.
q.feedback: Capital deepening raises output but faces diminishing returns; sustained growth also requires skills, technology, and sound institutions.

q.q: A government uses a temporary spending surge that raises current output but does not change capital, worker skills, technology, or institutions. What is the main long-run limitation?
options: It permanently doubles output per worker even though productive capacity is unchanged
It guarantees a permanently lower natural unemployment rate without changing labor-market institutions
It eliminates diminishing returns to capital even though the capital stock is unchanged
It does not directly strengthen long-run productivity fundamentals
q.commonError: Treats a one-time demand boost as a substitute for policies that raise productive capacity.
q.feedback: A temporary spending surge can raise current demand/output, but without stronger fundamentals it does not directly raise long-run productivity.

q.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
q.q: A government wants growth but repeatedly changes tax rules, seizes assets, and restricts courts. Which policy failure matters most?
options: Unstable property rights discourage investment
Too much human capital
Too much technological knowledge
Too much labor-force accuracy
q.feedback: Unstable property rights reduce incentives to invest and innovate.

q.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
q.q: Why might openness to foreign investment raise productivity?
options: Capital, technology, management, and market links
It guarantees no domestic firms fail
It lowers productivity by definition
It only changes the CPI basket
q.feedback: Foreign investment can increase capital and transmit technology or business practices.

q.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
q.q: A country funds education but blocks firms from adopting new technologies and discourages investment. What is the likely issue?
options: Skills need complementary capital and technology
Education alone guarantees growth
Technology restrictions raise productivity
Investment is unrelated to output per worker
q.feedback: Productivity growth usually requires complementary gains in skills, capital, and technology.

q.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
q.q: A country wants continuing productivity growth after a one-time equipment grant has raised capital per worker. Which package best addresses the limitation imposed by diminishing returns?
options: Maintain useful investment while improving skills, research and adoption of better methods
Repeat equal equipment grants and assume each creates a larger marginal output gain
Increase working hours and treat all additional output as higher hourly productivity
Replace training with equipment because physical and human capital cannot complement each other
q.feedback: Additional capital can still raise output, but its marginal contribution may diminish with other inputs fixed. Skills and technological progress complement capital and support productivity growth beyond a single level increase.

q.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
q.q: A country raises saving incentives, yet surveyed firms postpone equipment purchases because contracts are often unenforceable. A proposed response doubles the saving subsidy without changing courts. Which recommendation is best supported?
options: Address enforcement risk alongside finance; more saving alone may not make productive investment attractive
Double the subsidy because every extra saved dollar necessarily becomes domestic machinery
Reduce worker training because courts and skills are substitute measures of the same input
Infer that physical capital has zero marginal product because investment is currently weak
q.feedback: The evidence identifies insecure returns as a barrier between available funds and investment. Predictable enforcement can complement financing. The survey does not establish an optimal subsidy or prove capital has no productive value.

q.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
q.q: A government blocks foreign investment to protect domestic firms. What long-run growth cost is most plausible?
options: Less capital inflow, less technology transfer, and weaker productivity growth
Higher productivity from isolation by definition
Immediate doubling of human capital
Elimination of diminishing returns
q.feedback: Foreign investment can bring capital, technology, and management know-how.

q.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
q.q: A region has trained engineers and funds for new equipment, but a rule prevents firms from using improved production methods. A review proposes more of the same training while keeping that rule. Which response best addresses the stated constraint?
options: Permit useful method adoption while maintaining skills and investment; training alone may not release the constraint
Purchase equipment alone because methods cannot affect output with machines fixed
Keep the rule because a stock of trained workers guarantees continuing productivity growth
Stop all training because technological knowledge makes human capital unproductive
q.feedback: The constrained margin is adopting better methods. Technology, skills and equipment can complement one another; repeating one input policy while blocking another can limit the gain. This is a conditional recommendation from the stated evidence.

q.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
q.q: A policy package improves contract enforcement, funds technical training, and supports research trials. After two years, capital and skill measures rise but output growth remains modest. Which assessment best separates a coherent strategy from a guaranteed result?
options: The package targets productivity determinants; implementation, diffusion and time still matter for realized growth
The package failed in principle because research must raise output immediately
The capital increase proves the research trials caused all future growth
The modest output change proves institutions cannot affect investment incentives
q.feedback: The instruments address institutions, human capital and technological knowledge. These are plausible growth channels, but observed short-run output alone neither guarantees eventual success nor disproves the channels. Implementation and technology diffusion must be evaluated.

q.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
q.q: Why can population growth reduce GDP per person even while raising total GDP?
options: Total GDP may rise while output per person falls
Population growth always raises productivity
GDP per person ignores population
Capital per worker automatically rises with population
q.feedback: Population growth can dilute capital per worker unless investment keeps pace.

q.q: A country saves heavily and imports machinery, yet productivity barely rises because schools are weak, power is unreliable, and contracts are insecure. Which conclusion is strongest?
options: Capital alone may not deliver catch-up when complementary conditions are weak
High saving guarantees convergence even when schools, infrastructure, and institutions remain persistently weak
The country should restrict technological adoption so scarce capital continues to have a high marginal product
The catch-up effect requires poorer economies to have lower productivity growth than richer economies
q.commonError: Treats a one-time demand boost as a substitute for policies that raise productive capacity.
q.feedback: Investment needs complementary human capital, infrastructure, technology, and secure institutions; capital alone may not deliver catch-up.

q.q: A government subsidizes investment for five years, raising capital per worker, but it makes no lasting change to research, education, or institutions. Which long-run caution is most appropriate?
options: The temporary subsidy guarantees a permanently higher growth rate even after capital deepening slows
Research and education matter only for short-run aggregate demand
Institutions become irrelevant once the capital stock has increased
The capital increase can raise the output level, but sustained productivity growth needs broader continuing sources
q.commonError: Treats a one-time demand boost as a substitute for policies that raise productive capacity.
q.feedback: More capital can raise the output level, but continuing productivity growth requires ongoing gains in skills, technology, and institutions.

q.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
q.q: One policy that can support long-run productivity growth is:
options: Encouraging saving and investment
Discouraging education
Weakening property rights
Blocking research and development
q.feedback: Saving and investment can build capital and raise productivity.

q.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
q.q: Why can higher saving support future growth?
options: It can finance investment in capital goods
It immediately raises consumption only
It eliminates diminishing returns
It makes inflation impossible
q.feedback: Saving can provide funds for investment, which builds productive capital.

q.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
q.q: A country saves more, and firms use those funds to buy machines and build factories. Which growth channel is operating?
options: Capital accumulation
CPI substitution
Frictional unemployment
Transfer payments
q.feedback: Saving can finance investment, and investment builds physical capital.

q.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
q.q: Property rights matter for growth because they:
options: Protect returns from investment
Make inflation impossible
Replace human capital
Eliminate all imports
q.feedback: Secure property rights encourage people and firms to invest.

q.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
q.q: A country has skilled workers and natural resources, but businesses fear the government may seize assets. What is likely to happen to investment?
options: Investment is likely to be weaker
Investment must rise
Productivity automatically doubles
GDP per person cannot change
q.feedback: Weak property rights and political instability discourage investment.

q.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
q.q: Which policy environment is most growth-friendly?
options: Secure property rights and predictable rules
Frequent asset seizure and unclear laws
Banning investment
Reducing education and infrastructure
q.feedback: Growth is more likely when institutions support investment and long-run planning.

q.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
q.q: Education supports growth mainly by increasing:
options: Human capital
Natural resource deposits
The unemployment rate
Used goods sales
q.feedback: Education increases human capital, which can raise productivity.

q.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
q.q: Why can openness to trade support productivity growth?
options: Specialization plus better inputs, ideas, and markets
It guarantees every firm survives
It eliminates scarcity
It makes domestic production irrelevant
q.feedback: Trade can improve productivity through specialization, competition, and access to inputs and ideas.

q.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
q.q: A government funds universities, public health, infrastructure, and research. What is it mainly trying to improve?
options: Long-run productivity growth
Used-good sales
Short-run CPI measurement only
The resale value of old goods
q.feedback: Education, health, infrastructure, and research can all support long-run productivity growth.

q.q: Which policy most directly strengthens incentives for private long-term investment?
options: Secure property rights with predictable contract enforcement
Frequent asset seizure that makes long-term investment returns highly uncertain
Unpredictable contract enforcement that raises risk for firms making long-term investments
Bans on productive capital formation that prevent firms from expanding productive capacity
q.commonError: Treats a one-time demand boost as a substitute for policies that raise productive capacity.
q.feedback: Secure property rights and predictable contract enforcement protect investment returns, strengthening incentives for private long-term investment.

q.q: Which policy most directly builds human capital?
options: Reducing access to schooling and limiting opportunities for workers to acquire new skills
Making private research illegal and restricting firms from adopting outside technologies
Replacing productive investment with longer workweeks while worker skills remain unchanged
Improving education, job training, and basic health
q.commonError: Treats a one-time demand boost as a substitute for policies that raise productive capacity.
q.feedback: Education, job training, and basic health build workers’ human capital and can raise productivity.

q.q: Which policy most directly supports technological knowledge?
options: Increasing transfer payments without changing productive capacity
Restricting all business investment
Research, innovation, and diffusion of better production methods
Discouraging adoption of new methods
q.commonError: Treats a one-time demand boost as a substitute for policies that raise productive capacity.
q.feedback: Research and innovation create technological knowledge, while diffusion spreads more productive methods to firms.

q.q: A policy raises current consumer spending but leaves physical capital, human capital, technology, and institutions unchanged. Why is it not a complete long-run growth strategy?
options: Productivity falls whenever consumption rises
It does not directly raise productivity fundamentals
Consumer spending can never affect measured GDP
Long-run growth is determined only by population
q.commonError: Treats a one-time demand boost as a substitute for policies that raise productive capacity.
q.feedback: Higher current spending can raise demand, but leaving capital, skills, technology, and institutions unchanged does not raise the core productivity fundamentals.

q.q: A poor economy has little capital but weak schools, unreliable infrastructure, and insecure property rights. Which policy package best supports conditional catch-up?
options: Improve institutions and human capital while enabling productive investment and technology adoption
Rely only on its low starting income to guarantee convergence
Block new technology so existing capital remains scarce
Raise population growth without expanding capital or skills
q.commonError: Treats a one-time demand boost as a substitute for policies that raise productive capacity.
q.feedback: Conditional catch-up requires institutions and skills that let investment and technology adoption work productively, not just more capital.

q.q: In GROWTH-01, moving from A toward B through capital accumulation raises output per worker, but the curve flattens. Which policy best complements continued capital deepening?
options: A policy that prevents workers from learning new methods
A ban on technology adoption
A policy that makes investment returns less secure
Policies that improve skills, innovation, and productive institutions
q.commonError: Treats a one-time demand boost as a substitute for policies that raise productive capacity.
q.feedback: Once capital deepening faces diminishing returns, better skills, innovation, and productive institutions provide complementary sources of productivity growth.

q.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
q.q: Boss Audit: A government wants sustained growth. Which combination is strongest?
options: Property rights, investment, education, trade, infrastructure, and R&D
Price controls, weak courts, and blocked technology
Transfers only, with no investment or training
Higher population growth with no capital deepening
q.feedback: Sustained productivity growth requires institutions, capital, human capital, technology, and openness.

q.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
q.q: Boss Audit: A country saves more, but political instability causes investors to hold funds abroad instead of building domestic capital. What went wrong?
options: Saving did not translate into domestic investment
Saving always guarantees domestic capital accumulation
Political instability raises productivity
Capital flight increases GDP by definition
q.feedback: Saving supports growth only when institutions allow savings to become productive investment.

q.q: GROWTH-01 shows a low-capital economy at A with catch-up potential. Its government wants that potential to become sustained growth rather than remain a possibility. Which strategy is strongest?
options: Support productive investment while strengthening human capital, technology adoption, infrastructure, and institutions
Assume low initial capital alone guarantees convergence
Rely only on repeated additions of physical capital with no complementary improvements
Discourage investment so the marginal product of capital stays high
q.commonError: Treats a one-time demand boost as a substitute for policies that raise productive capacity.
q.feedback: Turning catch-up potential into sustained growth requires productive investment plus human capital, technology adoption, infrastructure, and secure institutions.

q.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
q.q: Which policy supports long-run productivity growth?
options: Encouraging saving and investment
Weakening property rights
Blocking education
Banning technology
q.feedback: Saving and investment can build capital and support productivity.

q.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
q.q: Secure property rights support growth because they:
options: Encourage investment
Eliminate scarcity
Make CPI unnecessary
Reduce all population growth
q.feedback: People invest more when they can keep the returns.

q.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
q.q: A government improves courts, property rights, schools, and infrastructure. What is it trying to support?
options: Long-run productivity growth
Used-good sales
CPI measurement only
Discouraged workers
q.feedback: Those policies support investment, skills, and productivity.

q.q: An economist estimates a policy’s effects, then recommends adoption. What two roles appear?
options: Scientist for the estimate and adviser for the recommendation
Adviser for both because policy is mentioned
Scientist for both because evidence is used
Legislator for the estimate and judge for the advice
q.commonError: Giving economists authority to choose society’s values.
q.feedback: Economists can estimate consequences; recommendations also require value judgments.

q.q: When an economist estimates how a tax will affect employment, the economist is primarily:
options: Making a moral judgment about fairness.
Providing positive analysis about likely consequences.
Guaranteeing the policy will pass.
Setting the tax rate by law.
q.commonError: Confusing analysis with political authority.
q.feedback: Economists can estimate consequences without deciding the policy.

q.q: When policymakers ask an economist to compare costs and benefits, the economist should:
options: Hide uncertainty to sound decisive.
Replace evidence with personal preference.
State assumptions and identify relevant tradeoffs.
Ignore who bears the costs.
q.commonError: Treating policy advice as assumption-free.
q.feedback: Good advice makes assumptions, tradeoffs, and uncertainty visible.

q.q: Which activity is most clearly part of an economist’s policy role?
options: Voting on behalf of the legislature.
Enforcing the final regulation.
Declaring one value judgment scientifically correct.
Evaluating evidence about likely behavioral responses.
q.commonError: Giving economists powers they do not possess.
q.feedback: Economists analyze incentives, evidence, and tradeoffs; elected officials make policy choices.

q.q: An economist estimates how a bus fee changes ridership. What role is primary?
options: Scientist analyzing a testable consequence
Adviser making a value judgment about whether the fee is fair
Policymaker deciding whether the fee should be adopted
Administrator responsible for enforcing the fee.
q.commonError: Giving economists authority to choose society’s values.
q.feedback: Economists can estimate consequences; recommendations also require value judgments.

q.q: An adviser compares costs borne by commuters and taxpayers. What should the adviser make explicit?
options: The combined cost alone, without showing how it is divided between the two groups.
The costs each group bears and the tradeoffs between the policy alternatives.
The adviser’s preferred outcome alone, without showing the costs of other choices.
The taxpayers’ costs alone, without including the costs borne by commuters.
q.commonError: Treating efficiency as the only criterion of social desirability.
q.feedback: An informative comparison identifies which costs fall on commuters and which fall on taxpayers, and how those costs change across policy alternatives. A single total can conceal the distribution of costs and the tradeoffs facing the decision maker.

q.q: Why can economics inform but not dictate a school policy?
options: Economics cannot measure the effects of school policies
School policies have no economic tradeoffs
The final choice also depends on social values
Evidence cannot help identify the likely consequences of alternative policies.
q.commonError: Giving economists authority to choose society’s values.
q.feedback: Economists can estimate consequences; recommendations also require value judgments.

q.q: A forecast gives a range rather than one number. Why?
options: The range identifies which policy society should prefer
A range means the evidence is too weak to be useful
Every value inside the range is equally likely.
Policy effects are uncertain, not guaranteed
q.commonError: Presenting an estimate as a guarantee.
q.feedback: Responsible advice reports assumptions, uncertainty, and plausible unintended consequences.

q.q: Two economists use different estimates of demand elasticity and reach different tax projections. What best explains the disagreement?
options: They may share the same framework but use different empirical assumptions.
One of them must reject opportunity cost.
Economic analysis cannot use evidence.
Normative values are the only possible source of disagreement.
q.commonError: Assuming disagreement proves the discipline has no method.
q.feedback: Different estimates and assumptions can produce different forecasts.

q.q: An economist reports that a policy raises total surplus but imposes concentrated losses on one group. What should the report do next?
options: Conclude that everyone benefits.
Separate the efficiency finding from the distributional consequence.
Ignore the losing group because total surplus rose.
Call the distributional judgment a positive fact.
q.commonError: Collapsing efficiency and equity into one claim.
q.feedback: Policy analysis should distinguish aggregate efficiency from distribution.

q.q: A forecast is highly sensitive to one uncertain parameter. The best policy advice is to:
options: Use only the most favorable value.
Present one estimate as certain.
Report the sensitivity and show results under plausible values.
Remove the parameter from the model.
q.commonError: Hiding model sensitivity.
q.feedback: Decision makers need to know when conclusions depend heavily on uncertain inputs.

q.q: A mayor asks whether rent control is “good.” What is the economist’s most useful first response?
options: Answer solely from personal ideology.
Promise there will be no unintended consequences.
Treat the word good as a measurable price.
Clarify the objectives and analyze likely effects and tradeoffs.
q.commonError: Treating vague policy goals as self-defining.
q.feedback: Policy evaluation requires explicit objectives and evidence about consequences.

q.q: Two economists use different demand estimates. What can explain different forecasts?
options: Different scientific judgments about evidence
One economist must have made an arithmetic mistake
Different forecasts can only come from different value judgments
Empirical disagreements cannot be informed by additional evidence.
q.commonError: Assuming all economist disagreement is partisan or all is empirical.
q.feedback: Disagreement can reflect evidence, models, uncertainty, or different values.

q.q: Two advisers share one forecast but rank equity differently. What differs?
options: Their estimates of the policy’s effects
Their normative values
Their definitions of the economic variables
One adviser must have interpreted the data incorrectly.
q.commonError: Assuming all economist disagreement is partisan or all is empirical.
q.feedback: Disagreement can reflect evidence, models, uncertainty, or different values.

q.q: A policy raises total surplus but harms one region. What should analysis report?
options: Only the increase in total surplus
Only the regional loss, because any loser makes the policy inefficient
Efficiency and distribution separately
A single efficiency conclusion without reporting who gains and loses.
q.commonError: Treating efficiency as the only criterion of social desirability.
q.feedback: Economic analysis clarifies tradeoffs but does not uniquely rank every social goal.

q.q: A rule changes incentives in an unexpected way. What should advisers examine?
options: Only the response the rule was intended to create
Treat unexpected behavior as irrelevant to the policy analysis
Assume the original behavioral prediction remains correct.
Likely behavioral responses and unintended effects
q.commonError: Presenting an estimate as a guarantee.
q.feedback: Responsible advice reports assumptions, uncertainty, and plausible unintended consequences.

q.q: A model omits enforcement costs. What should the policy estimate do?
options: Include feasible implementation and administration costs
Ignore enforcement costs if the policy objective is worthwhile
Count only the direct statutory cost of the program
Assume administration uses no scarce resources.
q.commonError: Confusing statutory design with actual implementation.
q.feedback: Enforcement and administration use scarce staff time, equipment and other resources. A feasible policy estimate must include those implementation costs when comparing benefits with costs. Omitting them can overstate net benefits even if the policy’s stated goal is desirable.

q.q: A policy model predicts large benefits, but the data come from a different population and period. What is the central concern?
options: Whether the evidence generalizes to the current setting.
Whether the policy has a money price.
Whether economists may use models.
Whether positive analysis is always normative.
q.commonError: Assuming evidence transfers automatically across settings.
q.feedback: Policy advice must consider whether evidence is applicable to the target population and context.

q.q: An economist is employed by an agency that benefits from a favorable estimate. What practice best protects credibility?
options: Publish the preferred specification with full calculations, omitting the agency relationship to keep the report technical.
Disclose the agency interest, assumptions, alternatives and uncertainty so others can assess the estimate.
Have an agency colleague check the arithmetic, then report one point estimate to avoid confusing readers.
Report an interval from the chosen model, leaving model selection and alternative specifications to the agency.
q.commonError: Ignoring incentives facing analysts.
q.feedback: Disclosure must address both the institutional interest and methodological discretion. Arithmetic review or an uncertainty interval alone does not reveal how model selection could favor the agency.

q.q: A policy has a positive expected net benefit but a small chance of catastrophic loss. Which addition is necessary?
options: A claim that averages eliminate risk.
Removal of all low-probability outcomes.
Risk analysis beyond the expected-value calculation.
A conclusion based only on sunk costs.
q.commonError: Treating expected value as a complete policy criterion.
q.feedback: Low-probability, high-cost outcomes may matter even when expected net benefits are positive.

q.q: A pilot worked elsewhere but institutions differ locally. What is the key warning?
options: A successful pilot automatically generalizes to other settings
Institutional differences matter only for normative judgments
A large effect elsewhere guarantees a large local effect.
Evidence may not transfer to the new setting
q.commonError: Presenting an estimate as a guarantee.
q.feedback: Responsible advice reports assumptions, uncertainty, and plausible unintended consequences.

q.q: An efficient proposal conflicts with a legal-rights goal. What follows?
options: The efficient proposal must be adopted
Efficiency evidence does not uniquely decide social desirability
The legal-rights goal is irrelevant to policy evaluation
The conflict proves the proposal is economically inefficient.
q.commonError: Treating efficiency as the only criterion of social desirability.
q.feedback: Economic analysis clarifies tradeoffs but does not uniquely rank every social goal.

q.q: A recommendation changes under plausible assumptions. What should the economist do?
options: Report only the baseline estimate
Use the assumption that produces the most favorable result
Report sensitivity rather than one certain answer
Delay all advice until uncertainty is eliminated.
q.commonError: Presenting an estimate as a guarantee.
q.feedback: Responsible advice reports assumptions, uncertainty, and plausible unintended consequences.

q.q: Two advisers accept the same estimate: consolidating offices saves staff time but lengthens rural travel. One favors consolidation and the other opposes it. Which information best explains their different recommendations?
options: Which adviser used more decimal places in the shared estimate
Whether the two advisers agree that travel is measurable
Whether consolidation is being proposed by a public institution
How each weighs staff savings against rural access
q.commonError: Assuming all economist disagreement is partisan or all is empirical.
q.feedback: Agreement about effects leaves room for different weights on efficiency and access. Those priorities can explain the recommendations without inventing a forecast disagreement.

q.q: An economist recommends a policy because it maximizes total surplus, while citizens prioritize equal treatment. The disagreement is primarily about:
options: The arithmetic definition of surplus.
The normative criterion used to rank outcomes.
Whether incentives exist.
The distinction between micro and macro topics.
q.commonError: Calling a value disagreement an empirical error.
q.feedback: Economic analysis can measure consequences, but ranking competing values requires a normative criterion.

q.q: Two studies estimate opposite effects because one uses a credible natural experiment and the other compares self-selected groups. The strongest appraisal emphasizes:
options: Differences in causal identification.
Which result has the larger number.
Which author supports the preferred policy.
Whether both studies use percentages.
q.commonError: Treating all empirical designs as equally informative.
q.feedback: Policy advice should weigh evidence by its ability to identify causal effects.

q.q: Volunteers in a training pilot earn more later. A second study assigns training by lottery and finds little effect. Before recommending expansion, what should the adviser resolve?
options: Whether volunteer enthusiasm proves the training caused their earnings
Whether the lottery result makes all participant preferences irrelevant
Whether selection explains the first result and whether the lottery setting fits expansion
Whether the larger positive estimate is easier to communicate
q.commonError: Treating all empirical designs as equally informative.
q.feedback: Volunteers can differ before training. The lottery helps separate selection from treatment, while its population and implementation still need to fit the expansion setting.

q.q: A report favors plan A because paid-work savings exceed its cash cost. A requires relatives to provide unpaid care; plan B purchases the same care. What comparison would correct the scope of the advice?
options: Value caregiving time under both plans alongside cash and paid-work effects
Add unpaid care only to B because B records an invoice
Treat unpaid care as free because relatives are not paid
Remove paid-work savings so both plans contain only budget costs
q.commonError: Ignoring nonmarket opportunity costs.
q.feedback: Unpaid time has alternative uses. Comparable benefit-cost scope includes caregiving burdens for A and avoids ignoring a resource merely because B buys it explicitly.

q.q: A model favors a recycling program if most households sort correctly. A pilot reports high collection but does not measure contamination; sorting is harder in the rollout area. What should precede the recommendation?
options: Declare the program undesirable solely because compliance is uncertain
Measure correct sorting and test whether the ranking survives realistic rollout compliance
Treat collected tonnage as proof of the required compliance
Use the pilot average unchanged because the same program name is used
q.commonError: Confusing statutory design with actual implementation.
q.feedback: Collection is not the assumed correct sorting. Advice needs the relevant compliance measure and sensitivity to the more difficult rollout setting.

q.q: A consolidation plan has aggregate gains but losses for remote users. A report says compensation makes everyone better off, although no compensation is funded. Which conclusion is warranted?
options: An unfunded transfer can be counted as income already received
Any remote loss proves aggregate gains are mathematically impossible
Potential compensation does not establish actual gains for remote users; report the implemented distribution
Positive total gains mean the remote users must gain indirectly
q.commonError: Using averages to hide variation.
q.feedback: Aggregate gains can create scope for compensation. Without an implemented transfer, the remote users' losses remain part of the actual policy outcome.

q.q: Two access plans have the same total measured benefit. One imposes concentrated losses on residents with few alternatives; the other spreads smaller losses. What additional step supports a defensible recommendation?
options: Choose either plan because equal totals establish identical welfare for every resident
Increase numerical precision until one value criterion becomes unnecessary
Count only beneficiaries because costs are already reflected in the total
State how concentrated hardship is weighed, and show each plan's distribution
q.commonError: Treating efficiency as the only criterion of social desirability.
q.feedback: Equal totals conceal different distributions. A recommendation needs an explicit evaluation of concentrated hardship and evidence about who gains and loses.

q.q: A permit reform saves time for compliant firms but increases inspections. It has positive net benefit at high compliance and negative net benefit at low compliance. Local compliance is unmeasured. What advice is best supported?
options: Present the conditional ranking and seek local compliance evidence before a firm recommendation
Recommend adoption because the favorable scenario is feasible
Reject because one plausible scenario has losses
Average the two outcomes without assessing how likely each is
q.commonError: Presenting an estimate as a guarantee.
q.feedback: The sign depends on an unresolved local behavior. Reporting that dependence and obtaining relevant evidence is more defensible than selecting or mechanically averaging scenarios.

q.q: A school schedule saves paid staff hours but shifts supervision to families. The measured gain disappears when family time is valued at its next-best use. Which revision follows?
options: Treat the original cash saving as false because the wider net gain disappeared
Report the wider resource comparison and explain why a budget saving need not be a social gain
Keep the original conclusion because only paid hours use scarce resources
Count the family time twice, once as cost and once as a separate loss of the same activity
q.commonError: Treating efficiency as the only criterion of social desirability.
q.feedback: The budget saving can be real while the wider net benefit vanishes. Count the forgone family activity once and distinguish fiscal effects from resource effects.

q.q: An adviser reports a narrow forecast interval based on one assumed take-up rate. Credible alternative take-up rates reverse the recommendation. What uncertainty is missing?
options: A value judgment proving which take-up rate is true
Evidence that no economic forecast can ever inform a choice
Uncertainty about the behavioral assumption, beyond precision conditional on that assumption
Only rounding uncertainty in the reported forecast
q.commonError: Presenting an estimate as a guarantee.
q.feedback: A precise estimate conditional on one rate does not capture uncertainty about the rate itself. Report the alternative assumptions and the recommendation reversal.

q.q: Two policy models fit the pilot. One attributes improved attendance to transport; the other to reminders sent at the same time. The rollout can fund only one. What evidence most directly helps the adviser choose?
options: A larger pilot that always combines both services
The political popularity of the combined pilot as proof of causality
The pilot's total attendance without a breakdown of interventions
Comparable groups receiving transport alone and reminders alone
q.commonError: Assuming all economist disagreement is partisan or all is empirical.
q.feedback: Separating the interventions tests the competing mechanisms relevant to the actual funding choice. More bundled observations cannot identify which component drove the gain.

q.q: An economist identifies the schedule with the highest total measured benefit. Citizens prefer another because it guarantees a minimum service level to every district. Which advice respects both roles?
options: Explain the cost of the service guarantee and make the ranking criterion explicit
Treat the citizens' preference as a statistical error in the benefit estimate
Describe the maximizing schedule as morally required by the calculation
Alter the benefit numbers until both schedules receive the same ranking
q.commonError: Giving economists authority to choose society’s values.
q.feedback: Economic analysis can estimate the tradeoff created by the guarantee. Deciding how strongly to value equal minimum access goes beyond identifying the aggregate maximum.

q.q: A small pilot pays shops to repair items and records strong gains. Nationwide adoption induces shops to relabel routine maintenance as repairs. What should a follow-up evaluation change?
options: Infer zero genuine gains solely because some reporting changed
Measure additional genuine repairs and account for the changed reporting incentive
Use reimbursement counts unchanged because the pilot already validated the measure
Treat all repairs after adoption as caused by the payment
q.commonError: Presenting an estimate as a guarantee.
q.feedback: Scaling changes incentives and can change what the metric measures. Estimate genuine additional repairs against a credible comparison rather than equating paid claims with benefits.

q.q: What can an economist contribute without choosing society’s values?
options: Evidence about likely consequences
Choose society’s moral priorities
Decide which policy lawmakers must adopt
Guarantee that the chosen policy will succeed.
q.commonError: Giving economists authority to choose society’s values.
q.feedback: Economists can estimate consequences; recommendations also require value judgments.

q.q: A projection includes a confidence range. What does it acknowledge?
options: The true effect is guaranteed to lie inside the range
Uncertainty in the predicted effect
The range identifies the policy society should prefer
Every value in the range is equally likely.
q.commonError: Presenting an estimate as a guarantee.
q.feedback: Responsible advice reports assumptions, uncertainty, and plausible unintended consequences.

q.q: A policy creates winners and losers. What should analysis show?
options: Only the total effect on surplus
Only which groups lose
The distribution as well as the total effect
Ignore distribution whenever the aggregate effect is positive.
q.commonError: Treating efficiency as the only criterion of social desirability.
q.feedback: Economic analysis clarifies tradeoffs but does not uniquely rank every social goal.

q.q: Policy A creates $40 million of gains for high-income households and $10 million of losses for low-income households. Policy B creates $22 million of gains for low-income households and costs high-income households $5 million. With no other effects, which advice distinguishes efficiency from distribution?
options: A has the larger unweighted net gain, while B favors low-income households; the ranking depends on the stated social criterion.
B has the larger unweighted net gain, while A favors low-income households; efficiency alone therefore selects B.
A has the larger unweighted net gain, so it necessarily satisfies a goal of improving low-income households’ welfare.
B favors low-income households, so A cannot have a positive unweighted net gain even if its benefits exceed losses.
q.commonError: Treating efficiency as the only criterion of social desirability.
q.feedback: Unweighted net gains are 40-10=30 for A and 22-5=17 for B. Efficiency totals and incidence differ. Choosing between them requires stating how distribution enters the social ranking.

q.q: A subsidy model estimated that firms would add 100 jobs when credit was available at 5%. Credit is now rationed and borrowing costs 12%; the model still predicts 100 jobs because it treats financing as fixed. What is the best next analysis?
options: Keep the 100-job forecast because the subsidy is unchanged; treat financing as an unrelated macroeconomic detail.
Reestimate firms’ financing responses and compare predictions under feasible credit conditions before transferring the old forecast.
Replace 100 jobs with the latest observed hiring total; that difference directly measures the subsidy’s causal effect.
Reject all subsidy models because one institutional change means simplified forecasts cannot provide policy evidence.
q.commonError: Presenting an estimate as a guarantee.
q.feedback: Credit conditions affect the mechanism through which firms finance expansion. The old forecast is conditional on assumptions that changed; observed hiring alone does not identify a counterfactual subsidy effect.

q.q: Two advisers agree that a flood barrier yields $60 million in avoided damage, costs $35 million and relocates 200 households. One favors it; the other rejects involuntary relocation. Which further step would clarify rather than merely repeat their disagreement?
options: Collect a more precise construction-cost estimate until both advisers must adopt the same view of relocation.
Add the number of relocated households directly to the dollar cost and select the policy with the smallest sum.
State the relocation criterion, examine feasible less-displacing alternatives and show how each changes net benefits and affected households.
Treat the shared positive net benefit as evidence that objections to relocation are errors in economic forecasting.
q.commonError: Giving economists authority to choose society’s values.
q.feedback: The advisers share the main predictions but differ over a social criterion. Examining feasible alternatives and explicit tradeoffs informs the choice; greater forecast precision cannot itself settle the value judgment.

q.q: Economists disagree because one trusts a different study. What differs?
options: Their scientific judgment about evidence
Their normative values must differ
One economist must be irrational
Evidence becomes irrelevant once economists disagree.
q.commonError: Assuming all economist disagreement is partisan or all is empirical.
q.feedback: Disagreement can reflect evidence, models, uncertainty, or different values.

q.q: They agree on effects but rank fairness differently. What differs?
options: Their scientific forecasts
Their normative evaluation
One economist must have misread the data
Economic analysis cannot distinguish factual claims from value judgments.
q.commonError: Assuming all economist disagreement is partisan or all is empirical.
q.feedback: Disagreement can reflect evidence, models, uncertainty, or different values.

q.q: Why examine enforcement before recommending a rule?
options: Enforcement affects legality but not economic outcomes
Assume full compliance when evaluating a proposed rule
Implementation changes costs and behavior
Implementation costs are irrelevant before adoption.
q.commonError: Presenting an estimate as a guarantee.
q.feedback: Responsible advice reports assumptions, uncertainty, and plausible unintended consequences.

q.q: A proposed tax is projected to create $80 million in national efficiency gains but $50 million in losses concentrated in one region. Those regional losses are already included in the national estimate. A domestic transfer could offset them at $8 million of administrative cost, but the regional loss estimate is uncertain. Which advice is sound?
options: Net expected national gain after administration is $72 million; test regional-loss scenarios and compensation feasibility before making a distributional recommendation.
Net expected national gain after compensation is $22 million; subtract the regional losses again because concentration makes them additional costs.
Net expected national gain after compensation is $122 million; add the transfer because recipients experience it as a benefit.
Net expected national gain is $80 million under every scenario; positive national gains guarantee each region can implement compensation itself.
q.commonError: Treating efficiency as the only criterion of social desirability.
q.feedback: The $50 million loss is already in the national ledger and a domestic transfer is redistribution. Administration reduces expected gain to 72. Uncertain regional effects still matter for funding, implementation and social priorities.

q.q: Model A predicts a transit subsidy raises ridership mainly by attracting former drivers. Model B predicts the same total increase mainly by shifting riders from unsubsidized buses. Both fit current totals. The policy goal is fewer car trips. What evidence best discriminates between the models for this decision?
options: Collect more precise total ridership counts after the subsidy; equal predictions imply either model establishes equal car-trip reductions.
Track prior travel modes and changes against a credible untreated comparison; total ridership fit alone cannot identify car-trip displacement.
Choose A because its mechanism matches the goal; a policy-relevant mechanism needs no separate test once totals fit.
Average the predicted ridership increases; averaging identical totals also identifies how many riders switched from cars.
q.commonError: Assuming all economist disagreement is partisan or all is empirical.
q.feedback: Identical ridership predictions can hide different substitution channels. Prior-mode and counterfactual evidence tests whether observed new riders actually displaced car travel.

q.q: A school policy has estimated net benefits of $12 million and reduces access for rural pupils. An alternative yields $8 million and preserves access. The adopted charter requires preserving rural access unless no feasible alternative exists. What conclusion follows from the estimates and criterion together?
options: The first policy must satisfy the charter because its larger net benefit proves no economically feasible alternative exists.
The alternative’s access benefit proves its unweighted net benefit exceeds $12 million even though the estimate is $8 million.
The first policy leads on unweighted net benefits, but the feasible alternative satisfies the stated access constraint; surplus alone does not justify overriding it.
Neither estimate is positive analysis because the access constraint makes factual policy comparisons inherently normative.
q.commonError: Treating efficiency as the only criterion of social desirability.
q.feedback: The estimates are factual claims about consequences; the charter supplies a normative constraint. A feasible access-preserving alternative exists, so maximizing the listed net benefit is not the only decision rule.

q.q: A safety rule would prevent $10 million of harm with full compliance and require $4 million of compliance resources. Current enforcement induces only half the affected firms to comply; assume benefits and compliance costs scale proportionally. An extra $1 million enforcement program would raise compliance to 80%. Which assessment is correct?
options: Net benefit rises from $3 million to $4.8 million; enforcement spending is a transfer and should not reduce the gain.
Net benefit falls from $6 million to $3.8 million; compare actual enforcement with the original full-compliance forecast.
Net benefit stays $6 million; the legal rule fixes compliance benefits regardless of enforcement behavior.
Net benefit rises from $3 million to $3.8 million; the extra enforcement gains $0.8 million despite falling short of full compliance.
q.commonError: Presenting an estimate as a guarantee.
q.feedback: Current net benefit is 0.5(10-4)=3. With stronger enforcement it is 0.8(10-4)-1=3.8. The incremental gain is 0.8, and the correct baseline is current feasible compliance rather than the full-compliance forecast.

q.q: Positive policy analysis asks:
options: What consequences are likely to occur.
Which outcome is morally best.
Which party should win.
Which value judgment is scientifically true.
q.commonError: Confusing prediction with value judgment.
q.feedback: Positive analysis describes or predicts consequences.

q.q: When a policy conclusion depends on an assumption, the economist should:
options: Hide it from decision makers.
State the assumption and test how much it matters.
Treat it as a proven fact.
Replace it with a slogan.
q.commonError: Treating assumptions as invisible facts.
q.feedback: Transparent assumptions and sensitivity checks strengthen policy advice.

q.q: Can economists scientifically determine society’s values?
options: Yes; economic expertise identifies the morally best outcome
Yes; estimating consequences also determines which values society should hold
No; they can clarify consequences and tradeoffs
Yes; economists receive decision-making authority from their technical expertise.
q.commonError: Giving economists authority to choose society’s values.
q.feedback: Economists can estimate consequences; recommendations also require value judgments.

q.q: Does efficiency prove a policy is socially best?
options: Yes; efficiency incorporates every social objective
Yes; distribution does not matter when total surplus rises
Yes; economists can rank competing social values scientifically.
No; other values and distribution may matter
q.commonError: Treating efficiency as the only criterion of social desirability.
q.feedback: Economic analysis clarifies tradeoffs but does not uniquely rank every social goal.

q.q: Is a policy forecast a guarantee?
options: No; it depends on evidence and assumptions
Yes, if the forecast comes from a strong model
Yes, if the confidence interval is narrow
Yes, if the economist has no conflict of interest.
q.commonError: Presenting an estimate as a guarantee.
q.feedback: Responsible advice reports assumptions, uncertainty, and plausible unintended consequences.

q.q: Must economist disagreement be political?
options: Yes; all disagreement among economists is ideological
No; evidence, models, or values can differ
Yes; economists using the same field must otherwise agree
Yes; empirical evidence cannot produce different interpretations.
q.commonError: Assuming all economist disagreement is partisan or all is empirical.
q.feedback: Disagreement can reflect evidence, models, uncertainty, or different values.

q.q: The economist's role in policy analysis is primarily to:
options: Clarify likely tradeoffs and consequences
Choose everyone's values
Guarantee a policy works
Eliminate scarcity
q.feedback: Economics can analyze consequences and tradeoffs, while value judgments remain separate choices.

q.q: A faculty committee asks whether a new attendance rule will improve learning. An economist would first:
options: Identify the behavioral mechanism and evidence needed to test it.
Declare the rule fair or unfair without analysis.
Assume attendance and learning are identical.
Ignore incentives created by the rule.
q.commonError: Failing to transfer policy-analysis logic outside government.
q.feedback: Economic policy reasoning applies to any rule that changes incentives and outcomes.

q.q: A policy forecast is testable, but the economist also recommends adoption. How should the forecast and recommendation be distinguished?
options: Both are positive claims because the recommendation follows evidence
Positive analysis informs a separate normative choice
Both are normative because the topic is public policy
The forecast itself determines whether the policy should be adopted.
q.commonError: Giving economists authority to choose society’s values.
q.feedback: Economists can estimate consequences; recommendations also require value judgments.

q.q: A model works only under one assumption. What should advice report?
options: Report only the baseline result
Drop the assumption from the analysis
How the conclusion changes when the assumption changes
Delay all advice until the assumption can be proven true.
q.commonError: Presenting an estimate as a guarantee.
q.feedback: Responsible advice reports assumptions, uncertainty, and plausible unintended consequences.

q.q: A subsidy changes behavior beyond its intended target. Which economic idea helps explain these additional responses?
options: Only the directly targeted behavior should be included in the analysis
Responses outside the target are irrelevant to the policy’s effects
Unintended responses occur only when enforcement fails.
Incentives can create unintended consequences
q.commonError: misses_unintended_consequence_of_incentives
q.feedback: A subsidy changes the payoff from an action. People may adjust related choices as well as the behavior the policy targets, creating effects the designer did not intend. Those responses belong in the policy’s benefit-and-cost analysis even when the subsidy is enforced as designed.

q.q: The multiplier effect means that government spending can shift AD by:
options: Less than the initial spending only
More than the initial spending
Exactly zero
Only changing LRAS
q.commonError: Ignoring induced consumption.
q.feedback: The multiplier effect occurs when initial spending creates additional rounds of income and consumption.

q.q: Crowding out occurs when fiscal expansion raises interest rates and reduces:
options: Private investment
The price level
Money demand
The natural rate instantly
q.commonError: Missing the interest-rate channel.
q.feedback: Crowding out reduces private investment when fiscal expansion raises interest rates.

q.q: The multiplier effect occurs because an initial increase in spending
options: raises income and causes additional consumption spending
always raises interest rates enough to cancel itself completely
reduces every household's income
makes money demand vertical
q.commonError: thinking the multiplier is only the first round of spending
q.feedback: The multiplier effect happens because one person's spending becomes another person's income, causing additional consumption.

q.q: The marginal propensity to consume is the fraction of extra income that households
options: consume
save
pay only in taxes
hold only as bonds
q.commonError: confusing MPC with the fraction saved
q.feedback: MPC is the fraction of extra income that households consume rather than save.

q.q: The simple spending multiplier is calculated as
options: 1 - MPC
MPC / 100
MPC x tax rate
q.commonError: using MPC itself as the multiplier
q.feedback: The simple spending multiplier is 1 divided by 1 minus MPC.

q.q: Crowding out occurs when expansionary fiscal policy raises interest rates and reduces
options: investment spending
government spending automatically
money supply by definition
the price level immediately
q.commonError: thinking crowding out makes government spending disappear
q.feedback: Crowding out occurs when higher interest rates reduce private investment spending.

q.q: If fiscal expansion raises interest rates and reduces investment, the final AD shift is likely:
options: Larger because crowding out amplifies it
Smaller because crowding out offsets it
Zero because fiscal policy cannot affect AD
Negative because taxes always rise
q.commonError: Thinking the multiplier is never offset.
q.feedback: Crowding out weakens the final effect of fiscal expansion on AD.

q.q: The multiplier effect exists because one person's spending becomes
options: another person's income
a lower reserve requirement
a decrease in government spending
a fall in money demand every time
q.commonError: thinking the multiplier is only the initial spending increase
q.feedback: The multiplier works because spending becomes income, and some of that income gets spent again.

q.q: The movement from the first AD shift to the larger final AD shift represents
options: the multiplier effect
monetary neutrality
the Fisher effect
a reserve requirement
q.commonError: confusing the multiplier effect with monetary policy
q.feedback: The multiplier effect is the extra AD shift caused by income leading to additional consumption spending.

q.q: The initial shift in aggregate demand from higher government spending is followed by a larger shift because
options: higher income leads to additional consumption spending
higher taxes reduce disposable income
money supply automatically falls
interest rates always fall to zero
q.commonError: thinking only the first round of government spending matters
q.feedback: The first increase in spending raises income, which causes more consumption and a further AD shift.

q.q: Crowding out weakens fiscal expansion because higher government spending can raise interest rates and reduce
options: private investment
tax collections automatically to zero
the price level immediately
the money multiplier to infinity
q.commonError: thinking crowding out strengthens fiscal stimulus
q.feedback: Crowding out offsets fiscal expansion by reducing private investment when interest rates rise.

q.q: Which situation would make the multiplier effect larger?
options: A higher MPC
A lower MPC
More crowding out
A higher reserve requirement
q.commonError: thinking a lower MPC creates a larger multiplier
q.feedback: A higher MPC means more extra income is spent, which makes the multiplier larger.

q.q: Which situation would make fiscal stimulus less powerful?
options: Strong crowding out
A high MPC with no interest-rate effect
A large initial increase in government spending
A high willingness to consume extra income
q.commonError: ignoring offsetting effects from interest rates
q.feedback: Crowding out weakens fiscal stimulus by reducing private investment.

q.q: Refer to the AD multiplier graph. For this application, assign Y1 = $500 billion, Y2 = $560 billion, and Y3 = $620 billion at the marked price P. Starting on AD1, purchases increase by $40 billion and MPC = 0.5. Use the simple spending multiplier. Crowding out creates a total $20 billion AD offset, already including induced spending effects. Which drawn AD curve represents the net result at P?
options: AD2, because the net rightward shift is $60 billion.
AD3, because the net rightward shift is $120 billion.
AD1, because the $20 billion offset cancels all induced spending and direct purchases.
No drawn curve, because $80 billion is the net shift after crowding out.
q.commonError: Confusing the initial shift with the multiplied shift.
q.feedback: The multiplier is 2. Gross AD increases by $80 billion; subtract the already-total $20 billion offset to obtain $60 billion. At P, desired output is therefore 500 + 60 = $560 billion, on AD2. The diagram does not contain an SRAS curve, so this locates demand at P rather than a final macro equilibrium.

q.q: Refer to the AD multiplier graph. If crowding out occurs after AD reaches AD3, the final AD position may move back toward:
options: AD2
AD4
SRAS
LRPC
q.commonError: Thinking crowding out amplifies AD.
q.feedback: Crowding out offsets part of fiscal expansion, pulling the final effect back from AD3 toward AD2.

q.q: If the initial government spending increase shifts AD by $20 billion, why might the final shift be larger?
options: The spending raises income, which triggers additional consumption spending.
The spending lowers income, which reduces consumption.
The spending automatically reduces money supply.
The spending makes MPC equal zero.
q.commonError: thinking only the first spending round matters
q.feedback: The multiplier effect comes from income causing additional consumption, which pushes AD farther.

q.q: If MPC is higher, the distance between the initial AD shift and the final AD shift should
options: increase
decrease
become zero
turn into money demand
q.commonError: thinking a higher MPC weakens the multiplier
q.feedback: A higher MPC means more extra income is spent, so the final AD shift is larger.

q.q: If expansionary fiscal policy raises interest rates, which effect offsets part of the multiplier?
options: Crowding out
The Fisher effect
Monetary neutrality
Commodity backing
q.commonError: confusing crowding out with the multiplier effect itself
q.feedback: Crowding out occurs when higher interest rates reduce private investment, offsetting fiscal stimulus.

q.q: Which fiscal policy has the strongest predicted multiplier effect before crowding out?
options: MPC = 0.9 and government spending rises by $50 billion
MPC = 0.5 and government spending rises by $50 billion
MPC = 0.25 and government spending rises by $50 billion
MPC = 0.1 and government spending rises by $50 billion
q.commonError: thinking lower MPC creates a stronger multiplier
q.feedback: Higher MPC means a larger multiplier. MPC = 0.9 gives the strongest multiplier here.

q.q: Fiscal expansion raises AD through the multiplier, but interest rates rise and investment falls. Which description best fits the final result?
options: Initial AD shift partly offset by crowding out
SRAS shift fully offset by lower taxes
LRPC shift partly offset by higher inflation
Money demand shift fully offset by M1
q.commonError: Treating the multiplier as the final effect every time.
q.feedback: Fiscal expansion can be amplified by the multiplier but weakened by crowding out.

q.q: Refer to the multiplier graph. Direct purchases shift AD1 to AD2; induced spending makes the gross prediction AD3. Crowding out creates a positive total AD offset. Which additional restriction is needed to conclude that the final AD curve lies strictly between AD2 and AD3?
options: The total offset must be smaller than the horizontal AD2-to-AD3 distance at the reference price.
The total offset must be smaller than the full AD1-to-AD3 distance, with no further restriction.
The total offset must equal the full AD1-to-AD3 distance.
The total offset must exceed the AD2-to-AD3 distance but remain below the AD1-to-AD3 distance.
q.commonError: Ignoring crowding out after multiplier expansion.
q.feedback: To finish to the right of AD2, subtract less than the extra induced-spending distance from AD2 to AD3. A positive offset puts the result left of AD3. Merely retaining some net stimulus relative to AD1 does not guarantee finishing beyond AD2.

q.q: If government spending rises, MPC is high, and interest rates do not rise, which effect dominates?
options: Multiplier effect
Crowding out
Monetary neutrality
Adverse supply shock
q.commonError: Assuming crowding out always dominates fiscal policy.
q.feedback: A high MPC strengthens the multiplier, and little interest-rate increase means crowding out is weak.

q.q: If government spending rises, MPC is low, and interest rates rise sharply, which concern dominates?
options: Weak multiplier with strong crowding out
Strong multiplier with no crowding out
Money neutrality with no AD change
Expected inflation with SRPC falling
q.commonError: Ignoring both MPC size and interest-rate effects.
q.feedback: A low MPC weakens the multiplier, while higher rates crowd out private investment.

q.q: If government spending initially shifts AD right by $40 billion and MPC is 0.75, what is the total shift before crowding out?
options: $160 billion
$70 billion
$40 billion
$30 billion
q.commonError: using MPC as the multiplier instead of 1 divided by 1 minus MPC
q.feedback: With MPC = 0.75, the multiplier is 4. A $40 billion initial shift becomes $160 billion before crowding out.

q.q: If the initial AD shift is $30 billion and the final shift is $150 billion, what MPC is implied by the simple multiplier?
q.commonError: using final shift divided by initial shift as MPC instead of multiplier
q.feedback: The multiplier is 150/30 = 5. If 1/(1-MPC)=5, then MPC = 0.8.

q.q: If the initial shift is $50 billion and MPC falls from 0.8 to 0.5, what happens to the final AD shift before crowding out?
options: It falls from $250 billion to $100 billion.
It rises from $100 billion to $250 billion.
It stays at $50 billion.
It falls from $250 billion to $50 billion.
q.commonError: thinking a lower MPC creates a larger multiplier
q.feedback: MPC 0.8 gives multiplier 5, so $250 billion. MPC 0.5 gives multiplier 2, so $100 billion.

q.q: A fiscal package produces a gross $200 billion rightward AD shift in a simplified expenditure model. Crowding out produces a total $60 billion leftward AD offset, including all induced spending effects of the displaced investment. What net AD increase should policy analysis use?
options: $140 billion
$260 billion
$200 billion
$60 billion
q.commonError: adding crowding out instead of subtracting it
q.feedback: The two magnitudes are both total AD changes: 200 − 60 = $140 billion. Do not multiply the stated total offset again. This is an AD shift, not a guaranteed equal increase in equilibrium GDP.

q.q: If policymakers expect the multiplier shift to close a recessionary gap exactly, but crowding out is stronger than expected, what is the likely result?
options: AD does not shift far enough right to fully close the gap.
AD shifts too far right because crowding out magnifies fiscal policy.
AD shifts left because government spending is not part of AD.
The multiplier becomes infinite.
q.commonError: thinking crowding out strengthens the fiscal multiplier
q.feedback: Stronger crowding out reduces the net AD shift, so stimulus may fall short.

q.q: Government purchases increase by $60 billion. MPC = 0.75; use the simple spending multiplier, with no other leakages. Crowding out produces a total $50 billion AD offset, including its induced spending effects. What is the net rightward AD shift?
options: $190 billion
$240 billion
$110 billion
$10 billion
q.commonError: forgetting to apply the multiplier before subtracting crowding out
q.feedback: Multiplier is 4, so the gross shift is $240 billion. Subtract $50 billion crowding out for a net $190 billion. The offset is already a total AD change and is subtracted after multiplication; the sequence is an analytical decomposition, not a claim about separate calendar stages.

q.q: A government spending increase raises income, consumption, and AD, but also raises interest rates and lowers investment. Which answer correctly names both effects?
options: Multiplier effect and crowding-out effect
Fisher effect and monetary neutrality
Liquidity trap and fiat money
Reserve requirement and inflation tax
q.commonError: treating all fiscal policy effects as multiplier effects only
q.feedback: The multiplier amplifies the AD increase; crowding out offsets part of it by reducing investment.

q.q: A student says fiscal expansion raises AD and therefore can never crowd out investment. What is the best correction?
options: Fiscal expansion can raise AD while higher rates reduce private investment.
Fiscal expansion lowers rates because government borrowing reduces money demand.
Fiscal expansion shifts SRAS right because firms face lower costs.
Fiscal expansion eliminates the multiplier because taxes disappear.
q.commonError: Thinking multiplier effects rule out crowding out.
q.feedback: Fiscal expansion can increase AD, but rising interest rates can reduce investment and offset part of the effect.

q.q: Refer to the aggregate-demand multiplier graph. AD moves from AD1 to AD2, then from AD2 to AD3, followed by a partial move back. Which interpretation fits?
options: Initial fiscal shift, multiplier expansion, then crowding out offset.
Initial monetary contraction, SRAS expansion, then LRPC adjustment.
Initial supply shock, expected price decline, then AD collapse.
Initial inflation tax, M1 expansion, then velocity collapse.
q.commonError: Confusing multiplier and crowding-out stages.
q.feedback: Fiscal policy can shift AD right, the multiplier can push it farther, and crowding out can pull the final effect back.

q.q: Government spending rises by $70 billion and MPC = 0.8. What is the correct order of AD shifts before crowding out?
options: AD first shifts right by $70 billion, then shifts farther right to a total of $350 billion.
AD first shifts right by $350 billion, then shifts back to $70 billion.
AD shifts left by $70 billion, then left by $350 billion.
AD does not shift because the multiplier only affects money demand.
q.commonError: confusing the initial AD shift with the final multiplier shift
q.feedback: The first AD shift is the direct $70 billion increase in G. With MPC = 0.8, the multiplier is 5, so the final AD shift is $350 billion.

q.q: Government spending rises by $60 billion and the final AD shift is $300 billion. What order of AD shifts and implied MPC fit these data?
options: AD shifts right first by $60 billion, then to a final $300 billion shift; MPC = 0.8.
AD shifts right first by $300 billion, then back to $60 billion; MPC = 0.8.
AD shifts left first by $60 billion, then left by $300 billion; MPC = 0.2.
AD shifts right first by $60 billion, then to a final $300 billion shift; MPC = 0.6.
q.commonError: treating final shift divided by initial shift as MPC instead of the multiplier
q.feedback: The multiplier is $300/$60 = 5. If 1/(1 - MPC) = 5, then MPC = 0.8.

q.q: Government spending rises by $40 billion. If MPC rises from 0.5 to 0.8, how does the order of AD shifts change?
options: The initial AD shift stays $40 billion, but the final shift rises from $80 billion to $200 billion.
The initial AD shift rises from $80 billion to $200 billion, but the final shift stays $40 billion.
Both the initial and final AD shifts stay $40 billion.
The initial AD shift becomes $200 billion and the final shift becomes $80 billion.
q.commonError: thinking same initial government spending creates same final AD shift regardless of MPC
q.feedback: The initial shift is still $40 billion. With MPC = 0.5, multiplier is 2 and final shift is $80 billion. With MPC = 0.8, multiplier is 5 and final shift is $200 billion.

q.q: Government purchases increase by $100 billion. MPC = 0.6; use the simple spending multiplier, with no other leakages. Crowding out produces a total $75 billion AD offset, including its induced spending effects. Which sequence separates the direct purchases, gross multiplier prediction, and net AD shift?
options: AD first shifts right $100 billion, then the multiplier pushes the gross shift to $250 billion, then crowding out leaves a net $175 billion shift.
AD first shifts right $250 billion, then crowding out increases it to $325 billion.
AD first shifts left $100 billion, then the multiplier pushes it left $250 billion, then crowding out leaves $175 billion.
AD shifts right $100 billion only because crowding out cancels the multiplier.
q.commonError: adding crowding out instead of subtracting it from the gross multiplier shift
q.feedback: MPC = 0.6 gives multiplier 2.5. The $100 billion initial shift becomes $250 billion, then crowding out reduces the net shift to $175 billion. The offset is already a total AD change and is subtracted after multiplication; the sequence is an analytical decomposition, not a claim about separate calendar stages.

q.q: Two governments each increase purchases by $60 billion. Economy A has MPC 0.80 and $100 billion of crowding out; Economy B has MPC 0.60 and $20 billion of crowding out. Using the simple multiplier and the stated offsets, which comparison is correct?
options: Economy A has a $200 billion net AD increase, which is $70 billion larger than Economy B.
Economy A has a $300 billion net increase and Economy B has a $150 billion net increase because crowding out does not affect AD.
Economy B has a $200 billion net increase, which is $70 billion larger than Economy A.
Both economies have the same $180 billion net AD increase because the initial spending changes are equal.
q.commonError: Compares gross multiplier effects without subtracting the private spending displaced by higher interest rates.
q.feedback: For the simplified model used here, compare each policy’s gross multiplier effect and then subtract its stated crowding-out offset.

q.q: Government purchases rise by $80 billion and MPC is 0.75. The observed net increase in aggregate demand is $230 billion after crowding out. Under the simple model used in this bank, how much of the gross multiplier effect was crowded out?
options: $230 billion.
$320 billion.
$10 billion.
$90 billion.

q.feedback: First compute the gross multiplier effect, then infer the crowding-out offset from the difference between gross and observed net AD.

q.q: If the MPC is 0.75, the simple government purchases multiplier is:
q.commonError: Using MPC as the multiplier.

q.q: If government spending rises by $80 billion, MPC is 0.75, and crowding out offsets $100 billion, final AD rises by:

q.q: If MPC rises from 0.5 to 0.8, the government purchases multiplier changes from:
options: 2 to 5
5 to 2
q.commonError: Using MPC itself as the multiplier.
q.feedback: The multiplier is 1/(1-MPC), so it rises from 2 to 5.

q.q: If the government raises spending by $50 billion and the multiplier is 3, the first-pass AD increase before crowding out is:
options: $50 billion
$100 billion
$150 billion
$200 billion
q.commonError: Using the spending change instead of multiplying it.
q.feedback: The initial multiplier effect is $50 billion x 3 = $150 billion.

q.commonError: using the saved portion instead of MPC
