options: $250 billion
$40 billion
$62.5 billion
$50 billion
q.commonError: multiplying by MPC instead of the multiplier
q.feedback: With MPC = 0.8, the multiplier is 5. Total increase is 5 x $50 billion = $250 billion.

q.q: If government spending rises by $80 billion and MPC = 0.75, what is the simple multiplier and total AD increase before crowding out?
options: Multiplier = 4; AD increase = $320 billion
Multiplier = 3; AD increase = $240 billion
Multiplier = 0.75; AD increase = $60 billion
Multiplier = 1.33; AD increase = $106.4 billion
q.commonError: multiplying by MPC instead of the multiplier
q.feedback: Multiplier = 1 / (1 - 0.75) = 4. Total AD increase = 4 x $80 billion = $320 billion.

q.q: If MPC = 0.9 and government spending increases by $25 billion, what is the simple multiplier effect on AD before crowding out?
options: $250 billion
$22.5 billion
$27.8 billion
$225 billion
q.commonError: using 0.9 as the multiplier instead of 10
q.feedback: With MPC = 0.9, the multiplier is 10. AD increases by 10 x $25 billion = $250 billion.

q.q: A fiscal package produces a gross $300 billion rightward AD shift in a simplified expenditure model. Crowding out produces a total $80 billion leftward AD offset, including all induced spending effects of the displaced investment. What net AD increase should policy analysis use?
options: $220 billion
$380 billion
$80 billion
$300 billion
q.commonError: adding crowding out instead of subtracting it
q.feedback: The two magnitudes are both total AD changes: 300 − 80 = $220 billion. Do not multiply the stated total offset again. This is an AD shift, not a guaranteed equal increase in equilibrium GDP.

q.q: If MPC = 0.8, then a $100 increase in income raises consumption by
q.commonError: using the saved portion instead of the consumed portion
q.feedback: Consumption rises by MPC times the income increase: 0.8 x $100 = $80.

q.q: If MPC = 0.75, the simple spending multiplier equals
q.commonError: dividing MPC by 1 instead of using 1 divided by 1 minus MPC
q.feedback: The multiplier is 1 / (1 - 0.75) = 1 / 0.25 = 4.

q.q: Why can an initial increase in spending generate a larger total increase in aggregate demand?
options: raises income and causes additional consumption spending
always fully crowds out investment
lowers income and reduces consumption
makes money demand disappear
q.commonError: thinking the multiplier is only the first spending round
q.feedback: The multiplier happens because spending becomes income, and part of that income is spent again.

q.q: If government spending rises by $80 billion and MPC = 0.75, what is the gross AD shift before crowding out?
options: $320 billion
$80 billion
$60 billion
$106.7 billion
q.commonError: using MPC instead of the multiplier
q.feedback: MPC 0.75 gives multiplier 4. Gross AD shift is $80 billion x 4 = $320 billion.

q.q: Government purchases increase by $80 billion. MPC = 0.75; use the simple spending multiplier, with no other leakages. Crowding out produces a total $70 billion AD offset, including its induced spending effects. What is the net rightward AD shift?
options: +$250 billion
+$320 billion
+$70 billion
+$150 billion
q.commonError: forgetting to subtract crowding out after applying the multiplier
q.feedback: Gross AD shift is $320 billion. Subtract $70 billion of crowding out, leaving $250 billion. The offset is already a total AD change and is subtracted after multiplication; the sequence is an analytical decomposition, not a claim about separate calendar stages.

q.q: Households spend 75 cents of each additional dollar of disposable income. What does that imply?
options: The marginal propensity to save is 0.75, so the multiplier equals one.
The government-purchases multiplier must be 0.75.
The MPC is 0.75, so repeated spending creates a multiplier greater than one.
Crowding out must eliminate every later spending round.
q.commonError: Confusing the marginal propensity to consume with the multiplier itself.
q.feedback: An MPC of 0.75 means each spending round passes along 75 percent of added income, generating further rounds of expenditure.

q.q: What is the central mechanism of crowding out?
options: Fiscal expansion lowers interest rates and increases private investment.
Higher government spending directly reduces the money supply.
A larger multiplier forces households to stop consuming.
Fiscal expansion raises interest rates and reduces some private investment spending.
q.commonError: Reversing the interest-rate and investment effects of fiscal expansion.
q.feedback: Government borrowing and stronger money demand can raise interest rates, discouraging private investment.

q.q: Holding other factors constant, which change makes the simple spending multiplier larger?
options: A lower marginal propensity to save.
A higher marginal propensity to save.
A larger amount of crowding out.
A smaller initial change in government purchases.
q.commonError: Treating more saving as a force that strengthens repeated spending rounds.
q.feedback: A lower marginal propensity to save means a larger MPC, so more income is respent in each round.

q.q: Government purchases rise by $20 billion and the MPC is 0.50. Ignoring crowding out, what is the predicted total increase in aggregate demand?
options: $10 billion.
$40 billion.
$20 billion.
$80 billion.
q.commonError: Using the MPC itself as the multiplier or ignoring the repeated-spending process.
q.feedback: The multiplier is 1/(1 - 0.50) = 2, so a $20 billion increase produces a $40 billion gross shift.

q.q: A fiscal package produces a gross $120 billion rightward AD shift in a simplified expenditure model. Crowding out produces a total $25 billion leftward AD offset, including all induced spending effects of the displaced investment. What net AD increase should policy analysis use?
options: Aggregate demand rises by $145 billion.
Aggregate demand rises by $25 billion.
Aggregate demand rises by $95 billion.
Aggregate demand falls by $95 billion.
q.commonError: Adding the crowded-out investment to the gross effect rather than subtracting it.
q.feedback: The two magnitudes are both total AD changes: 120 − 25 = $95 billion. Do not multiply the stated total offset again. This is an AD shift, not a guaranteed equal increase in equilibrium GDP.

q.q: Why can an equal-dollar tax cut create a smaller initial aggregate-demand shift than an equal increase in government purchases?
options: Tax cuts always raise interest rates before households receive them.
Government purchases do not pass through the multiplier process.
Tax cuts reduce disposable income before they affect consumption.
Tax cuts are partly saved; government purchases enter aggregate demand directly.
q.commonError: Assuming every dollar of a tax cut is spent immediately.
q.feedback: Only the consumed portion of a tax cut enters the first spending round, whereas government purchases are direct expenditure.

q.q: Government purchases increase by $90 billion. MPC = 0.8; use the simple spending multiplier, with no other leakages. Crowding out produces a total $180 billion AD offset, including its induced spending effects. Which sequence separates the direct purchases, gross multiplier prediction, and net AD shift?
options: AD first shifts right $90 billion, then the multiplier pushes the gross shift to $450 billion, then crowding out leaves a net $270 billion shift.
AD first shifts right $450 billion, then crowding out increases the shift to $630 billion.
AD first shifts left $90 billion, then the multiplier pushes it left $450 billion, then crowding out leaves $270 billion.
AD shifts right only $90 billion because crowding out eliminates the multiplier.
q.commonError: not following initial shift, multiplier shift, then crowding-out offset
q.feedback: MPC 0.8 gives multiplier 5. The $90 billion initial shift becomes $450 billion, then crowding out reduces the net shift to $270 billion. The offset is already a total AD change and is subtracted after multiplication; the sequence is an analytical decomposition, not a claim about separate calendar stages.

q.q: The initial government-spending shift is $100 billion and the final AD shift is $400 billion. What MPC is implied, and what is the correct shift order?
options: AD first shifts right $100 billion, then to $400 billion; MPC = 0.75.
AD first shifts right $400 billion, then back to $100 billion; MPC = 0.75.
AD first shifts left $100 billion, then left $400 billion; MPC = 0.25.
AD first shifts right $100 billion, then to $400 billion; MPC = 0.8.
q.commonError: treating final shift divided by initial shift as MPC instead of multiplier
q.feedback: The multiplier is 400/100 = 4. If 1/(1 - MPC) = 4, MPC = 0.75.

q.q: Money demand shifts right while money supply is fixed. Expansionary fiscal policy also raises interest rates through crowding out. What happens to investment if both effects occur?
options: Investment falls from both interest-rate channels.
Investment rises from both interest-rate channels.
Investment rises from the money-demand channel but falls from crowding out.
Investment is unaffected because r is not connected to investment.
q.commonError: tracking only one interest-rate channel
q.feedback: Higher money demand raises r. Crowding out also raises r. Higher r reduces investment.

q.q: If MPC = 0.5, the government purchases multiplier is:
q.feedback: The multiplier is 1/(1-MPC), so 1/(1-0.5)=2.

q.q: Crowding out happens when fiscal expansion raises rates and reduces:
options: Private investment
Currency
LRAS
Expected output
q.feedback: Crowding out weakens fiscal expansion by reducing private investment.

q.q: Why might a tax cut have a smaller immediate effect than an equal increase in government purchases?
options: Households may save part of the tax cut
Tax cuts never affect AD
Government purchases are not part of GDP
Taxes shift SRAS directly
q.feedback: Some of a tax cut is saved, so its initial spending effect can be smaller than direct government purchases.

q.q: The multiplier effect means an initial spending increase can raise AD by:
options: More than the initial spending
Exactly zero
Only less than the initial spending
Only changing SRAS
q.feedback: The multiplier occurs when spending creates additional rounds of income and consumption.

q.q: The multiplier effect means an initial increase in government spending can:
options: Create a larger total increase in aggregate demand and output
Affect only the first recipient of spending
Reduce GDP by the same amount
Shift LRAS immediately
q.feedback: Initial spending becomes income for others, whose further spending magnifies the total effect.

q.commonError: Using MPC as the multiplier.
q.q: The simple spending multiplier equals:
options: MPC
1 - MPC
MPC / 100
q.feedback: The multiplier is 1 divided by 1 minus MPC.

q.commonError: Using MPC directly as the multiplier.
q.q: If MPC = 0.75, the multiplier is:

q.commonError: Adding crowding out instead of subtracting it.
q.q: Crowding out reduces the effect of fiscal expansion by reducing:
options: Private investment
Government spending automatically
Money demand
Taxes
q.feedback: Crowding out happens when higher interest rates reduce private investment.

q.commonError: Adding the crowding-out amount to the multiplier effect.
q.q: If gross AD rises $200 billion and crowding out is $50 billion, net AD rises:
options: $150 billion
$250 billion
$200 billion
$50 billion
q.feedback: Crowding out subtracts from the gross effect: $200 - $50 = $150 billion.

q.q: If MPC = 0.8, the government purchases multiplier is:
q.feedback: The multiplier is 1/(1-0.8)=5.

q.q: Fiscal expansion raises interest rates. Which part of spending is most likely crowded out?
options: Private investment
Government purchases
Currency in M1
Natural output
q.feedback: Higher interest rates reduce private investment.

q.q: Government spending rises by $20 billion and the multiplier is 3. Before crowding out, AD rises by:
options: $60 billion
$20 billion
$23 billion
$6.7 billion
q.feedback: The multiplier effect is $20 billion x 3 = $60 billion.

q.commonError: Stops at the first-round fiscal impulse and treats it as the full aggregate-demand effect.
q.q: Government purchases rise $50 billion and MPC is 0.75. Which statement correctly connects the fiscal action to the multiplier concept?
options: The $50 billion first-round AD impulse is magnified to $200 billion before any crowding-out offset.
The $50 billion first-round impulse remains $50 billion because later spending rounds do not affect AD.
The multiplier reduces the initial AD impulse to $37.5 billion.
The fiscal action shifts LRAS rather than aggregate demand.
q.feedback: After the first-round spending change, the multiplier process traces additional income-consumption rounds; crowding out can then reduce the net effect.

q.commonError: Carries the gross fiscal impulse into stabilization analysis even after an offset has been specified.
q.q: A stabilization analyst receives two model estimates: a $300 billion gross rightward AD shift from fiscal expansion and a total $80 billion AD reduction from displaced investment, including its induced spending effects. Which AD impulse should the analyst carry into the stabilization forecast?
options: $220 billion net increase.
$380 billion net increase.
$300 billion because stabilization uses only the gross multiplier effect.
$80 billion because crowding out replaces the fiscal impulse.
q.feedback: The two magnitudes are both total AD changes: 300 − 80 = $220 billion. Do not multiply the stated total offset again. This is an AD shift, not a guaranteed equal increase in equilibrium GDP.

q.q: Higher government spending usually shifts aggregate demand:
options: Right
Left
Nowhere
Into LRAS
q.commonError: Reversing expansionary fiscal policy.
q.feedback: Higher government spending raises aggregate demand.

options: Left
Right
Down the SRPC only
Into money demand
q.commonError: Confusing tax cuts and tax increases.
q.feedback: A tax cut raises disposable income and consumption, shifting AD right.

q.q: Expansionary fiscal policy includes
options: higher government spending or lower taxes
lower government spending or higher taxes
a decrease in the money supply
a higher reserve requirement only
q.commonError: confusing fiscal policy with monetary policy

q.q: Contractionary fiscal policy includes
options: lower government spending or higher taxes

a decrease in interest on reserves only
the Fed buying bonds
q.commonError: confusing fiscal tightening with monetary tightening
q.feedback: Contractionary fiscal policy means lower government spending or higher taxes, which reduces aggregate demand.

q.q: A decrease in taxes usually shifts aggregate demand
options: right
left
nowhere because taxes are not related to spending

q.commonError: thinking tax cuts reduce consumption
q.feedback: Lower taxes raise disposable income, which can raise consumption and shift AD right.

q.q: Refer to the AD graph with constant price level P. Moving from AD1 to AD2 changes output from:

q.feedback: At the same price level, output rises from Y1 to Y2 when AD shifts from AD1 to AD2.

Selling government bonds by the Fed
Raising reserve requirements
Increasing the discount rate

q.feedback: Expansionary fiscal policy uses higher government spending or lower taxes to raise aggregate demand.

options: Increasing taxes
Buying government bonds by the Fed
Lowering reserve requirements
Cutting the discount rate
q.commonError: confusing fiscal and monetary policy tools
q.feedback: Higher taxes are contractionary fiscal policy because they reduce disposable income and aggregate demand.

q.q: A tax cut shifts aggregate demand right mainly because it
options: raises disposable income and consumption
raises reserve requirements
lowers the money multiplier directly
forces banks to hold more reserves
q.commonError: thinking tax cuts work through bank reserves
q.feedback: A tax cut raises disposable income, which can increase consumption and shift AD right.

q.q: A cut in government purchases shifts aggregate demand left because
options: government spending is a component of aggregate demand
money demand automatically rises
banks stop creating money
MPC becomes zero
q.commonError: forgetting that G is directly part of AD
q.feedback: Government purchases are part of AD, so reducing G shifts AD left.

q.q: If Congress increases infrastructure spending during a recession, the direct effect is to
options: shift aggregate demand right
shift aggregate demand left
reduce the money supply
raise reserve requirements
q.commonError: treating fiscal stimulus like contractionary policy
q.feedback: Higher infrastructure spending raises G and shifts AD right.

q.q: If the government raises taxes during an expansion, the likely AD effect is
options: AD shifts left
AD shifts right
AD becomes vertical
money supply increases automatically
q.commonError: thinking tax increases raise consumption
q.feedback: Higher taxes reduce disposable income and consumption, shifting AD left.

q.q: Congress increases government purchases by $80 billion while households cut consumption by $50 billion for unrelated reasons. Before multiplier effects, the net direct change in aggregate demand is:
options: A $30 billion decrease.
No change.
A $30 billion increase.
A $130 billion increase.
q.commonError: Adding changes without respecting their directions.
q.feedback: Government purchases add $80 billion while consumption subtracts $50 billion.

q.q: A $120 billion tax rebate is issued and households spend 65 percent of the added disposable income initially. What is the first-round consumption increase?
options: $42 billion.
$184.6 billion.
$78 billion.
$120 billion.
q.commonError: Using the MPS or the full tax cut as first-round consumption.
q.feedback: First-round consumption is 0.65 × $120 billion = $78 billion.

q.q: A government raises taxes and increases purchases by the same dollar amount. Which statement is most precise about the immediate AD effects?
options: The two actions must cancel exactly before behavior is considered.
Both actions shift AD right by the same amount.
Taxes enter AD directly as a negative component.
Purchases enter AD directly, while higher taxes reduce consumption indirectly.
q.commonError: Treating taxes as a direct component of aggregate demand.
q.feedback: Government purchases are part of AD; taxes work through disposable income and consumption.

q.q: A temporary tax cut is mostly saved because households expect it to be reversed next year. Compared with a tax cut that is mostly spent, the AD shift is:
options: Smaller.
Necessarily leftward.
Identical.
Larger.
q.commonError: Ignoring household spending behavior.
q.feedback: A smaller consumption response weakens the tax cut’s effect on aggregate demand.

q.q: The government cuts purchases during a recession but also cuts taxes. Which conclusion is valid without knowing the magnitudes and household response?
options: Aggregate demand must rise.
The two policies always cancel exactly.
The net direction of aggregate demand is ambiguous.
Aggregate demand must fall.
q.commonError: Assuming one policy label determines the combined outcome.
q.feedback: A spending cut shifts AD left, while a tax cut tends to shift it right; magnitudes matter.

q.q: A tax increase of $60 billion reduces consumption by $42 billion in the first round. The implied MPC is:
q.commonError: Dividing in the wrong direction or using the MPS.
q.feedback: MPC = $42 billion / $60 billion = 0.70.

q.q: A tax cut occurs while households expect future taxes to rise and save much of the extra income. What happens to the tax multiplier?
options: It is weaker than simple models predict
It becomes infinite automatically
It shifts SRAS instead of AD
It eliminates crowding out
q.commonError: Assuming every tax cut creates the same consumption response.
q.feedback: If households save much of the tax cut, the increase in consumption and AD is weaker.

q.q: An economy faces a positive AD shock of $240 billion. If policymakers use a tax increase that reduces disposable income by $100 billion and MPC is 0.8, what is the first-round consumption reduction?
options: $80 billion
$100 billion
$20 billion
$500 billion
q.commonError: using the saved portion instead of MPC
q.feedback: The first-round consumption reduction is MPC times the disposable income change: 0.8 x $100 billion = $80 billion.

q.q: A fiscal package raises government purchases by $120 billion and taxes by $100 billion. If MPC = 0.8, the package’s first-round effect on AD is:
options: A $20 billion increase.
A $200 billion increase.
A $40 billion increase.
A $40 billion decrease.
q.commonError: Ignoring that the tax increase reduces consumption by MPC times the tax change.
q.feedback: Purchases add $120 billion; the tax increase reduces consumption by $80 billion.

q.q: A tax cut is announced, but credit-constrained households spend 90 percent while high-income households spend 30 percent. Which feature matters most for the AD effect?
options: The long-run natural rate of output
Whether government purchases are counted in GDP
Only the statutory size of the tax cut
How the tax cut is distributed across groups with different marginal propensities to consume.
q.commonError: Assuming every dollar of tax reduction produces the same consumption response.
q.feedback: The aggregate consumption response depends on who receives the tax cut and how much they spend.

q.q: A government increases purchases by $50 billion and raises taxes by $50 billion. MPC is 0.75. Before subsequent multiplier rounds, the net first-round AD change is:
options: No change.
A $12.5 billion increase.
A $37.5 billion decrease.
A $100 billion increase.
q.commonError: Assuming equal spending and tax changes have equal direct AD effects.
q.feedback: Purchases add $50 billion; the tax increase cuts consumption by $37.5 billion.

q.q: A tax cut raises disposable income by $160 billion. Households spend 60 percent of the increase initially. If later rounds follow a simple spending multiplier of 2.5, the total AD increase before other offsets is:
options: $400 billion.
$64 billion.
$240 billion.
$96 billion.
q.commonError: Applying the multiplier to the full tax cut instead of the first-round consumption change.
q.feedback: First-round consumption rises $96 billion; multiplying by 2.5 gives $240 billion.

q.q: The government increases infrastructure purchases, but imports rise sharply because much of the equipment is purchased abroad. Relative to a package using domestic inputs, the increase in domestic aggregate demand is likely:
options: Leftward because any import increase reduces government purchases.
Identical because all government spending counts equally.
Smaller because part of the spending leaks into imports.
Larger because imports are part of domestic production.
q.commonError: Ignoring import leakage from domestic demand.
q.feedback: Spending on imports does not directly purchase domestically produced output.

q.q: Two equal-cost fiscal packages provide either a targeted transfer or a broad tax rebate. Recipients of the transfer have the higher MPC, but most transfer payments arrive after a planned stabilization deadline, while the rebates arrive before it. A minister concludes that the transfer must create more AD by the deadline. Which additional comparison is needed?
options: Compare each package’s amount actually received and spent by the deadline, including induced spending completed by then.
Compare only the recipients’ MPCs; the timing of payment cannot affect AD by the deadline.
Count every transfer dollar as purchases immediately, then compare that total with rebate consumption.
Compare the eventual multipliers only; completion of spending rounds before the deadline is irrelevant.
q.commonError: Ignoring differences in marginal propensity to consume.
q.feedback: A higher MPC raises consumption from each dollar received, other things equal, but it does not guarantee a larger effect by a date when fewer dollars have been paid. Timely receipts, consumption and induced rounds jointly determine the relevant short-run AD effect.

q.q: A government wants to reduce aggregate demand while expanding targeted transfers. Under a simple closed-economy expenditure model, MPC = 0.6 for all households, taxes stay fixed, and no crowding-out or price feedback occurs. Transfers rise by $30 billion. What minimum purchases cut produces a $45 billion leftward AD shift rather than merely cancelling the transfer stimulus?
options: $18 billion: cancelling the first-round transfer consumption also provides the full target contraction.
$45 billion: the target AD shift is itself the required purchases cut.
$75 billion: add the full transfer amount to the desired AD reduction.
$36 billion: offset $18 billion of induced first-round consumption and add $18 billion of net autonomous contraction.
q.commonError: Mixing expansionary and contractionary tools.
q.feedback: Transfers first add 0.6 × 30 = $18 billion of consumption. The spending multiplier is 2.5, so a $45 billion AD reduction requires $18 billion of net autonomous contraction. Purchases must fall by 18 + 18 = $36 billion. The transfer is not itself a government purchase.

q.q: A recessionary economy receives a temporary tax rebate. Households use half to repay debt, save one quarter, and spend one quarter. The immediate consumption channel equals:
options: 50 percent of the rebate.
100 percent of the rebate.
75 percent of the rebate.
25 percent of the rebate.
q.commonError: Treating saving or debt repayment as immediate consumption.
q.feedback: Only the portion spent on current consumption directly raises the consumption component of AD.

q.q: A $120 billion refundable tax credit can be allocated between two household groups, with MPCs of 0.90 and 0.40. The government wants a first-round consumption increase of $84 billion, before any induced spending. How should the credit be allocated, and why would the same $120 billion of government purchases have a different first-round AD effect?
options: $72 billion to the higher-MPC group and $48 billion to the other; purchases enter AD directly, whereas some credit is saved.
$48 billion to the higher-MPC group and $72 billion to the other; purchases and credits enter AD directly in full.
$60 billion to each group; averaging MPCs guarantees the target regardless of allocation.
$84 billion to the higher-MPC group and $36 billion to the other; each dollar of credit is a dollar of purchases.
q.commonError: Applies one MPC to the entire tax change even when recipient groups have different spending responses.
q.feedback: Let x go to the higher-MPC group. Then 0.90x + 0.40(120 − x) = 84, giving x = $72 billion and $48 billion to the other group. Their consumption responses are $64.8 billion and $19.2 billion. Government purchases would directly add $120 billion to AD; a credit affects disposable income and only the spent portion enters first-round consumption.

q.q: Congress replaces $100 billion of government purchases with a $100 billion tax cut. Households have MPC 0.80. Holding other AD determinants fixed and looking only at the first round, what happens to aggregate demand?
options: AD is unchanged because the two fiscal changes are equal.
AD rises by $20 billion.
AD rises by $80 billion.
AD falls by $20 billion.
q.commonError: Treats equal-dollar spending and tax changes as having identical direct effects on aggregate demand.
q.feedback: Government purchases enter AD directly, while tax changes affect AD through the share of disposable income households spend.

q.q: A tax cut raises disposable income by $100 billion. If MPC = 0.8, what is the first-round increase in consumption?
options: $80 billion
$20 billion
$100 billion
$125 billion
q.commonError: using the saved portion instead of the consumed portion
q.feedback: The first-round consumption increase is MPC times disposable income: 0.8 x $100 billion = $80 billion.

q.q: Which policy combination is expansionary fiscal policy?
options: higher government spending or lower taxes
lower government spending or higher taxes
selling bonds by the Fed
raising interest on reserves
q.commonError: confusing fiscal policy with monetary policy
q.feedback: Fiscal policy uses government spending and taxes. Expansionary fiscal policy raises G or lowers T.

q.q: A tax cut raises disposable income by $120 billion. If MPC = 0.8, what is the first-round increase in consumption?
options: $96 billion
$120 billion
$24 billion
$150 billion
q.commonError: using the saved portion instead of MPC
q.feedback: First-round consumption rises by MPC times the tax cut: 0.8 x $120 billion = $96 billion.

q.q: A tax cut raises disposable income by $120 billion. MPC = 0.8. If the first-round consumption increase enters the multiplier process, what is the total AD increase before crowding out?
options: $480 billion
$600 billion
$120 billion
$96 billion
q.commonError: multiplying the full tax cut by the multiplier before applying MPC
q.feedback: The first-round consumption increase is $96 billion. With MPC 0.8, the multiplier is 5, so AD rises $480 billion.

q.q: Expansionary fiscal policy most directly includes:
options: Higher government purchases or lower taxes.
Lower government purchases or higher taxes.
Higher reserve requirements only.
Lower consumer confidence.
q.commonError: Confusing fiscal policy with monetary policy or private behavior.
q.feedback: Expansionary fiscal policy raises government demand or supports private spending.

q.q: Which fiscal action shifts aggregate demand left through lower disposable income?
options: A tax cut.
A tax increase.
Higher government purchases.
Higher transfer payments.
q.commonError: Reversing the effect of taxes on disposable income and consumption.
q.feedback: A tax increase reduces disposable income and tends to reduce consumption.

q.q: Government purchases are:
options: The same as household saving.
A direct component of aggregate demand.
A direct component of short-run aggregate supply.
Excluded from GDP.
q.commonError: Misplacing government purchases in the macro model.
q.feedback: Government purchases are included directly in C + I + G + NX.

q.q: A $100 billion tax cut with MPC 0.8 raises first-round consumption by:
options: $500 billion.
$80 billion.
$20 billion.
$100 billion.
q.commonError: Using the MPS or multiplier too early.
q.feedback: MPC times the tax cut gives the first-round consumption increase.

q.q: A cut in government purchases shifts AD left because it directly reduces:
options: Labor-force participation
The money multiplier
The government-purchases component of spending.
The economy’s productive capacity
q.commonError: Confusing an AD shift with an AS or banking change.
q.feedback: Government purchases enter aggregate demand directly.

q.q: A tax cut has a weak AD effect when households:
options: Spend most of it immediately.
Save most of the increase in disposable income.
Face a high marginal propensity to consume.
Increase consumption by more than the tax cut.
q.commonError: Ignoring the consumption response.
q.feedback: More saving means less immediate consumption and a smaller rightward AD shift.

q.q: Refer to the multiplier graph. A $60 billion tax cut raises disposable income, and MPC = 0.75. What is the correct order of AD effects before crowding out?
options: Consumption first rises $45 billion, then the multiplier expands the AD shift to $180 billion.
AD first rises $60 billion, then the multiplier expands it to $240 billion.
Consumption first rises $15 billion, then AD rises $60 billion.
AD falls $45 billion, then the multiplier reduces it by $180 billion.
q.commonError: multiplying the full tax cut by the spending multiplier without first applying MPC
q.feedback: First-round consumption rises 0.75 x $60 billion = $45 billion. Multiplier is 4, so AD rises $180 billion.

q.q: Government purchases rise $90 billion and taxes rise $60 billion. MPC is 0.75. What is the net first-round change in AD?
options: A $135 billion increase.
A $45 billion increase.
A $30 billion increase.
A $45 billion decrease.
q.commonError: Failing to distinguish the direct spending effect from the tax-induced consumption effect.
q.feedback: Purchases add $90 billion; taxes reduce consumption by $45 billion.

q.q: A $200 billion tax cut reaches two equal groups. One group spends 80 percent and the other spends 40 percent. What is the combined first-round consumption increase?
options: $160 billion.
$120 billion.
$240 billion.
$80 billion.
q.commonError: Applying one group’s MPC to the entire tax cut.
q.feedback: Each group receives $100 billion; spending rises $80 billion plus $40 billion.

q.q: Congress increases government purchases while taxes and other aggregate-demand determinants are unchanged. Which change should a student predict in the AD-AS model?
options: Aggregate demand shifts right.
Aggregate demand shifts left.
Short-run aggregate supply shifts right.
Long-run aggregate supply shifts left.
q.feedback: Government purchases and tax-induced consumption changes work primarily through aggregate demand in this Principles model.
q.commonError: Confuses a fiscal-policy change with an aggregate-supply shift.

q.q: A $40 billion tax cut raises disposable income and MPC is 0.75. Before later multiplier rounds, how much does consumption increase?
options: $30 billion.
$40 billion.
$10 billion.
$53.3 billion.
q.feedback: The first-round consumption effect equals the change in disposable income times MPC.
q.commonError: Treats the full tax cut as immediate consumption.
Classifies fiscal policy from the state of the economy rather than from what government purchases and taxes actually do.
q.q: Congress lowers government purchases and raises taxes in the same bill to reduce excessive aggregate demand. How should the package be classified?
options: Contractionary fiscal policy.
Expansionary fiscal policy.
Expansionary monetary policy.
An automatic stabilizer.
q.feedback: Classify the package from its fiscal actions: higher purchases/lower taxes are expansionary; lower purchases/higher taxes are contractionary.

q.commonError: Thinking fiscal expansion shifts AD left.
q.q: Higher government spending usually shifts AD:
options: Right
Left
Nowhere
Into money demand
q.feedback: Government spending is part of AD, so higher G shifts AD right.

q.commonError: Forgetting taxes work through disposable income and consumption.
q.q: A tax cut usually increases:
options: Disposable income
Reserve requirements
Money demand only
Imports only
q.feedback: A tax cut raises disposable income.

q.commonError: Jumps from a tax change directly to total output without identifying the first spending channel.
q.q: Why can a tax cut shift aggregate demand to the right in the short run?
options: It raises disposable income, which can raise consumption spending.
It directly increases the money supply.
It directly lowers firms’ production costs and shifts SRAS right.
It automatically increases potential output.
q.feedback: A tax change first changes disposable income, then consumption according to MPC, which shifts aggregate demand.

q.q: The government cuts spending during a recession. What happens to AD?
options: AD shifts left
AD shifts right
SRAS shifts right
LRPC shifts left
q.feedback: Lower government spending reduces aggregate demand.

q.q: A tax cut raises disposable income and consumption. What happens to AD?
options: AD shifts right
AD shifts left
SRAS shifts left
LRAS shifts left
q.feedback: Higher consumption shifts aggregate demand right.

q.commonError: Stops at the first-round fiscal impulse and treats it as the full aggregate-demand effect.
q.q: A tax cut produces an $80 billion first-round increase in consumption. Which next idea is needed to move from that first-round fiscal impulse to the larger total aggregate-demand effect?
options: The multiplier process traces additional income-and-spending rounds.
Long-run aggregate supply shifts by the same $80 billion.
The inflation tax converts the consumption increase into government revenue.
The natural rate of unemployment determines the tax cut directly.
q.feedback: After the first-round spending change, the multiplier process traces additional income-consumption rounds; crowding out can then reduce the net effect.

q.q: If expected inflation rises and the real interest rate is unchanged, the nominal interest rate should:
options: Fall
Rise
Become zero
Equal real GDP
q.commonError: Reversing the Fisher effect.
q.feedback: Nominal interest rates include expected inflation, so they rise when expected inflation rises.

q.q: The Fisher effect says that when expected inflation rises, the nominal interest rate tends to
options: rise
fall
stay fixed forever
become equal to real GDP growth
q.commonError: thinking inflation lowers nominal interest rates
q.feedback: The Fisher effect says higher expected inflation tends to raise nominal interest rates.

q.q: The Fisher equation is most commonly written as
options: nominal interest rate = real interest rate + expected inflation
real interest rate = nominal interest rate + expected inflation
expected inflation = real GDP + money supply
nominal interest rate = velocity divided by output
q.commonError: adding inflation to the wrong side of the equation
q.feedback: The Fisher equation links nominal rates, real rates, and expected inflation: nominal rate equals real rate plus expected inflation.

q.q: If expected inflation rises from 2 percent to 5 percent and the real interest rate is unchanged, the nominal interest rate should
options: rise by about 3 percentage points
fall by about 3 percentage points
stay exactly the same
fall to zero
q.commonError: thinking nominal rates ignore expected inflation
q.feedback: If the real rate is unchanged, a 3-point rise in expected inflation raises the nominal rate by about 3 points.

q.q: Under the Fisher effect, a country with persistently higher inflation will tend to have
options: higher nominal interest rates
lower nominal interest rates
no nominal interest rates
unchanged price levels forever
q.commonError: thinking high inflation means low nominal rates
q.feedback: Higher expected inflation tends to be built into higher nominal interest rates.

q.q: Lenders begin expecting inflation to be 4 percentage points higher, while the long-run real interest rate is unchanged. What does the Fisher effect predict?
options: Nominal interest rates tend to rise by about 4 percentage points.
Nominal interest rates tend to fall by about 4 percentage points.
Real interest rates must rise by exactly 4 percentage points.
Actual inflation must immediately equal the new nominal interest rate.
q.commonError: Uses actual inflation instead of expected inflation when applying the Fisher effect.
q.feedback: The Fisher effect links expected inflation to the nominal interest rate, holding the underlying real interest rate constant in the long-run comparison.

q.q: A bank sets a fixed nominal loan rate today for next year. Which inflation concept is most relevant to the Fisher effect when that rate is chosen?
options: Only inflation that has already occurred.
The current unemployment rate by itself.
Only the realized inflation rate known after repayment.
Expected inflation over the loan period.
q.commonError: Uses realized inflation to explain a nominal rate chosen before the loan was made.
q.feedback: The nominal rate written into a contract reflects expected inflation at the time the contract is set; realized inflation determines the ex post real return.

q.q: If expected inflation rises while the real interest rate is unchanged, lenders will require
options: a higher nominal interest rate
a lower nominal interest rate
no repayment
a lower price level
q.commonError: thinking lenders ignore expected inflation
q.feedback: Lenders care about purchasing power, so higher expected inflation is built into higher nominal interest rates.

q.q: Two otherwise similar economies have the same long-run real interest rate, but expected inflation is 2 percent in one and 7 percent in the other. What should differ under the Fisher effect?
options: The second economy should tend to have a nominal interest rate about 5 percentage points higher.
The first economy should have a nominal interest rate about 5 percentage points higher instead because lower expected inflation raises nominal rates.
Both nominal rates must be identical because real rates match.
The second economy must have a real rate 5 points higher.
q.commonError: Uses actual inflation instead of expected inflation when applying the Fisher effect.
q.feedback: The Fisher effect links expected inflation to the nominal interest rate, holding the underlying real interest rate constant in the long-run comparison.

q.q: Expected inflation falls from 6 percent to 2 percent while the long-run real interest rate remains 3 percent. What nominal-rate change is predicted?
options: The nominal rate rises from about 5 percent to about 9 percent.
The real rate falls from 3 percent to negative 1 percent automatically.
The nominal rate stays at 9 percent because only actual inflation matters.
The nominal rate falls from about 9 percent to about 5 percent.
q.commonError: Uses actual inflation instead of expected inflation when applying the Fisher effect.
q.feedback: The Fisher effect links expected inflation to the nominal interest rate, holding the underlying real interest rate constant in the long-run comparison.

q.q: A one-year loan is priced when inflation is expected to be 3 percent. Actual inflation later turns out to be 8 percent. Which statement separates the Fisher effect from the realized return?
options: The Fisher effect uses actual inflation only and ignores expectations.
Unexpected inflation raises both parties’ realized real returns by the same amount.
The nominal rate reflected expected inflation when set; the unexpectedly high actual inflation changes the ex post real return.
The nominal rate must be rewritten after actual inflation is observed so the original expected rate no longer matters.
q.commonError: Uses realized inflation to explain a nominal rate chosen before the loan was made.
q.feedback: The nominal rate written into a contract reflects expected inflation at the time the contract is set; realized inflation determines the ex post real return.

q.q: Expected inflation rises 6 percentage points while the equilibrium real interest rate falls 2 percentage points. What happens to the nominal interest rate approximately?
options: It rises about 4 percentage points because both expected inflation and the real rate matter.
It rises exactly 6 percentage points because the Fisher effect requires the real rate to remain fixed in every comparison.
It falls about 8 percentage points because expected inflation lowers nominal rates.
It is unchanged because the two components must always offset completely.
q.commonError: Assumes nominal rates must move one-for-one with expected inflation even when the real rate also changes.
q.feedback: The one-for-one Fisher prediction requires holding the real interest rate fixed; if the real rate changes too, combine both changes.

q.q: Country A has expected inflation of 8 percent and a real interest rate of 1 percent. Country B has expected inflation of 3 percent and a real interest rate of 5 percent. Which statement is correct?
options: Country A must have a nominal rate exactly 5 points above Country B.
Country B must have the lower nominal interest rate because lower expected inflation always dominates any real-rate difference.
The Fisher effect says real interest rates are always identical across countries.
A one-for-one comparison of nominal rates cannot use expected inflation alone because the real rates differ too.
q.commonError: Assumes nominal rates must move one-for-one with expected inflation even when the real rate also changes.
q.feedback: The one-for-one Fisher prediction requires holding the real interest rate fixed; if the real rate changes too, combine both changes.

q.q: Expected inflation falls sharply after a credible long-run policy change, but productive opportunities and saving behavior leave the real rate roughly unchanged. What does the Fisher effect predict?
options: Real interest rates must fall by exactly the same amount as expected inflation.
Nominal rates should stay fixed because only realized inflation affects contracts.
Nominal interest rates should fall as the inflation premium falls.
Nominal interest rates should rise because lower expected inflation raises the inflation premium.
q.commonError: Uses actual inflation instead of expected inflation when applying the Fisher effect.
q.feedback: The Fisher effect links expected inflation to the nominal interest rate, holding the underlying real interest rate constant in the long-run comparison.

q.q: A lender receives a 10 percent nominal rate that was set when expected inflation was 4 percent. Actual inflation is later 9 percent. Which statement is most accurate?
options: Expected inflation is irrelevant once a fixed nominal rate has been written.
The ex ante pricing reflected roughly a 6 percent real return, but the realized real return is much lower.
The Fisher effect predicted a 1 percent real return when the loan was made.
The nominal rate automatically rises to 15 percent after inflation is observed because fixed-rate contracts always adjust retroactively after the fact.
q.commonError: Uses realized inflation to explain a nominal rate chosen before the loan was made.
q.feedback: The nominal rate written into a contract reflects expected inflation at the time the contract is set; realized inflation determines the ex post real return.

q.q: Nominal interest rates rise from 7 to 11 percent at the same time expected inflation rises from 3 to 8 percent. Can we conclude the real rate was unchanged?
options: No. The nominal rate rose 4 points while expected inflation rose 5, so the implied real rate actually fell about 1 point.
Yes. Any rise in nominal rates alongside expected inflation proves the real rate is unchanged.
Yes. The Fisher effect requires nominal rates to rise exactly half as much as expected inflation regardless of changes in real rates.
No. The implied real rate rose about 9 percentage points.
q.commonError: Assumes nominal rates must move one-for-one with expected inflation even when the real rate also changes.
q.feedback: The one-for-one Fisher prediction requires holding the real interest rate fixed; if the real rate changes too, combine both changes.

q.q: A lender expected 4 percent inflation and charged 9 percent nominal interest. Actual inflation was 8 percent. What happened to the realized real return?
options: It was lower than expected
It was higher than expected
It was unchanged
It became nominal GDP
q.commonError: Ignoring unexpected inflation after a loan is written.
q.feedback: Higher-than-expected inflation lowers the realized real return to lenders.

q.q: Use the Fisher approximation. A borrower signs a loan at 9 percent nominal interest when expected inflation is 4 percent. Actual inflation is 7 percent. What happened to the realized real interest rate compared with what the lender expected?
options: It fell from 5 percent expected to 2 percent realized.
It rose from 5 percent expected to 7 percent realized.
It stayed at 5 percent because nominal interest was fixed.
It fell from 9 percent expected to 4 percent realized.
q.commonError: using expected inflation for the realized real rate
q.feedback: Expected real rate was 9 - 4 = 5 percent. Realized real rate was 9 - 7 = 2 percent.

q.q: Use the Fisher approximation. Expected inflation rises from 2 percent to 9 percent. If the real interest rate is stable at 3 percent, what should happen to the nominal interest rate under the Fisher effect?
options: It rises from 5 percent to 12 percent.
It falls from 5 percent to 3 percent.
It rises from 2 percent to 9 percent.
It stays at 3 percent.
q.commonError: forgetting the real interest rate is part of nominal interest
q.feedback: Nominal rate equals real rate plus expected inflation. It rises from 3 + 2 = 5 to 3 + 9 = 12 percent.

q.q: A lender’s one-year fixed nominal contract pays 12 percent. Expected inflation when written was 5 percent, but actual inflation is 9 percent. Use exact gross returns. What are the expected and realized real returns, and what nominal rate on a new loan would preserve the original expected real return if expected inflation is now 9 percent?
options: About 6.67 percent, 2.75 percent, and 16.27 percent.
7 percent, 3 percent, and 16 percent exactly.
About 2.75 percent, 6.67 percent, and 12 percent.
About 6.67 percent, 2.75 percent, and 12 percent.
q.commonError: using expected inflation for both expected and realized real rates
q.feedback: Expected real return is 1.12/1.05 − 1 = 6.67 percent; realized is 1.12/1.09 − 1 = 2.75 percent. Preserving the original gross real return on a new loan requires (1.12/1.05) × 1.09 − 1 = 16.27 percent nominal.

q.q: Use the Fisher approximation. Expected inflation rises from 4 percent to 11 percent. The real interest rate falls from 3 percent to 2 percent. What happens to the nominal interest rate?
options: It rises from 7 percent to 13 percent.
It rises from 4 percent to 11 percent.
It falls from 7 percent to 2 percent.
It stays at 7 percent.
q.commonError: assuming the real rate is constant when it is explicitly changed
q.feedback: Initial nominal rate is 3 + 4 = 7 percent. New nominal rate is 2 + 11 = 13 percent.

q.q: A one-time monetary expansion lowers the value of money today. Credible guidance says the money-growth rate will then return to its previous path. The long-run real interest rate is unchanged. An analyst concludes that nominal interest rates must remain permanently higher. Which evaluation is strongest?
options: A one-time price-level rise does not establish permanently higher expected inflation, so the lasting nominal-rate claim is unsupported.
The higher price level guarantees permanently higher inflation, so the nominal-rate claim follows.
The lower value of money proves the real interest rate falls permanently, so nominal rates must fall.
Monetary neutrality makes expected inflation irrelevant to nominal rates, so the Fisher relationship does not apply.
q.commonError: confusing short-run liquidity effects with long-run Fisher effect
q.feedback: The Fisher effect relates nominal rates to expected inflation over the loan horizon. A level adjustment alone does not establish a continuing inflation-rate increase. The real-rate assumption therefore does not complete the analyst’s argument.

q.q: Money growth rises from 8 percent to 20 percent. Velocity growth is zero and output growth is 4 percent. If expected inflation adjusts fully, what happens to nominal rates when the real rate stays at 3 percent?
options: Nominal rates rise from about 7 percent to about 19 percent.
Nominal rates fall from 7 percent to 3 percent.
Nominal rates rise from 8 percent to 20 percent exactly.
Nominal rates stay at 3 percent.
q.commonError: not converting money growth into inflation before applying Fisher
q.feedback: Inflation rises from 8 - 4 = 4 percent to 20 - 4 = 16 percent. With real rate 3 percent, nominal rates rise from 7 to 19 percent.

q.q: A country establishes a credible low-inflation regime. Expected inflation falls from 9 percent to 3 percent, while saving and investment conditions leave the long-run real interest rate near 2 percent. Which outcome best fits the Fisher effect?
options: The nominal interest rate tends to fall from about 11 percent to about 5 percent.
The nominal interest rate tends to rise from about 5 percent to about 11 percent.
The real interest rate must fall from 2 percent to negative 4 percent.
The nominal interest rate should stay near 11 percent because credibility affects only actual inflation.
q.commonError: Uses actual inflation instead of expected inflation when applying the Fisher effect.
q.feedback: The Fisher effect links expected inflation to the nominal interest rate, holding the underlying real interest rate constant in the long-run comparison.

q.q: Two long-run episodes have identical expected inflation, but the equilibrium real interest rate is higher in the second because investment demand is stronger. What should happen to the nominal rate?
options: It must be unchanged because identical expected inflation always forces identical nominal interest rates even when real saving and investment conditions differ.
It must be lower because stronger investment demand reduces nominal rates.
It must equal expected inflation because real rates disappear in the long run.
It should also be higher, showing that Fisher comparisons must account for the real-rate component as well as expected inflation.
q.commonError: Assumes nominal rates must move one-for-one with expected inflation even when the real rate also changes.
q.feedback: The one-for-one Fisher prediction requires holding the real interest rate fixed; if the real rate changes too, combine both changes.

q.q: Use the Fisher approximation. If the real interest rate is 3 percent and expected inflation rises from 4 percent to 9 percent, the Fisher effect predicts the nominal rate rises by:
options: 3 points
4 points
5 points
9 points
q.commonError: Using the final inflation rate instead of the change.
q.feedback: Expected inflation rises by 5 percentage points, so the nominal rate rises by 5 points.

q.q: Use the Fisher approximation. Expected inflation rises from 3 percent to 6 percent while the real interest rate stays at 2 percent. The nominal rate becomes:
options: 3 percent
5 percent
6 percent
8 percent
q.commonError: Forgetting to add expected inflation to the real rate.
q.feedback: Nominal interest rate equals real interest rate plus expected inflation, so 2 + 6 = 8 percent.

q.q: If the nominal interest rate is 9 percent and expected inflation is 4 percent, the real interest rate is approximately
options: 5 percent
13 percent
4 percent
36 percent
q.commonError: adding inflation when solving for the real rate
q.feedback: Real interest rate is approximately nominal rate minus expected inflation: 9 - 4 = 5 percent.

q.q: If the real interest rate is 2 percent and expected inflation is 6 percent, the nominal interest rate is approximately
options: 8 percent
4 percent
3 percent
12 percent
q.commonError: subtracting inflation from the real rate when solving for nominal rate
q.feedback: Nominal interest rate is approximately real interest rate plus expected inflation: 2 + 6 = 8 percent.

q.q: Use the Fisher approximation. The nominal interest rate is 11 percent and expected inflation is 7 percent. If actual inflation turns out to be 10 percent, what is the realized real interest rate?
options: 1 percent
4 percent
3 percent
21 percent
q.commonError: using expected inflation instead of actual inflation for realized real rate
q.feedback: The realized real rate uses actual inflation: 11 - 10 = 1 percent.

q.q: Use the Fisher approximation. If expected inflation rises from 3 percent to 8 percent and the real interest rate remains 2 percent, what happens to the nominal interest rate?
options: It rises from 5 percent to 10 percent.
It falls from 5 percent to 2 percent.
It rises from 3 percent to 8 percent.
It stays at 2 percent.
q.commonError: forgetting to include the real interest rate in both periods
q.feedback: Nominal rate = real rate + expected inflation. It rises from 2 + 3 = 5 to 2 + 8 = 10.

q.q: If the real interest rate is 3 percent and expected inflation is 2 percent, the nominal interest rate is approximately
options: 5 percent
1 percent
2 percent
6 percent
q.commonError: subtracting inflation from the real rate when solving for nominal rate
q.feedback: The nominal interest rate is approximately the real interest rate plus expected inflation: 3 + 2 = 5 percent.

q.q: If the nominal interest rate is 7 percent and expected inflation is 3 percent, the real interest rate is approximately
options: 4 percent
10 percent
3 percent
21 percent
q.commonError: adding expected inflation when solving for the real interest rate
q.feedback: Real interest rate is approximately nominal interest rate minus expected inflation: 7 - 3 = 4 percent.

q.q: The Fisher effect links expected inflation to
options: nominal interest rates
real GDP only
reserve requirements
M1 only
q.commonError: thinking expected inflation is unrelated to nominal rates
q.feedback: The Fisher effect says higher expected inflation tends to raise nominal interest rates.

q.q: If the real interest rate is 2 percent and expected inflation is 7 percent, the nominal interest rate is about
options: 9 percent
5 percent
7 percent
14 percent
q.commonError: subtracting expected inflation when solving for nominal rate
q.feedback: Nominal interest is real interest plus expected inflation: 2 + 7 = 9 percent.

q.q: Use the Fisher approximation. Expected inflation rises from 3 percent to 8 percent while the real interest rate falls from 4 percent to 2 percent. What happens to the nominal interest rate?
options: It rises from 7 percent to 10 percent.
It falls from 7 percent to 2 percent.
It rises from 3 percent to 8 percent.
It stays at 7 percent.
q.commonError: tracking only expected inflation and ignoring the real rate change
q.feedback: Initial nominal rate is 4 + 3 = 7 percent. New nominal rate is 2 + 8 = 10 percent.

q.q: If expected inflation rises while the long-run real interest rate is unchanged, the Fisher effect predicts that the nominal interest rate will:
options: Rise.
Fall.
Remain fixed by definition.
Become equal to real GDP growth.
q.commonError: Uses actual inflation instead of expected inflation when applying the Fisher effect.
q.feedback: The Fisher effect links expected inflation to the nominal interest rate, holding the underlying real interest rate constant in the long-run comparison.

q.q: Which inflation rate matters when lenders set a nominal rate today for a future loan period?
options: Only last year’s inflation.
Only inflation observed after repayment.
The unemployment rate instead of inflation.
Expected inflation.
q.commonError: Uses realized inflation to explain a nominal rate chosen before the loan was made.
q.feedback: The nominal rate written into a contract reflects expected inflation at the time the contract is set; realized inflation determines the ex post real return.

q.q: The real interest rate is 3 percent and expected inflation is 5 percent. The Fisher approximation gives a nominal rate near:
options: 3 percent.
15 percent.
8 percent.
2 percent.
q.commonError: Uses actual inflation instead of expected inflation when applying the Fisher effect.
q.feedback: The Fisher effect links expected inflation to the nominal interest rate, holding the underlying real interest rate constant in the long-run comparison.

q.q: Expected inflation rises from 4 to 10 percent while the equilibrium real rate falls from 3 to 1 percent. What happens to the nominal rate approximately?
options: It remains at about 7 percent because expected inflation and real rates always offset.
It rises from about 7 to about 11 percent.
It rises from about 7 to about 13 percent because the real-rate change is irrelevant.
It falls from about 7 to about 5 percent.
q.commonError: Assumes nominal rates must move one-for-one with expected inflation even when the real rate also changes.
q.feedback: The one-for-one Fisher prediction requires holding the real interest rate fixed; if the real rate changes too, combine both changes.

q.q: A fixed-rate loan was written when expected inflation was 2 percent, but actual inflation turns out to be 8 percent. Which statement is correct?
options: Expected inflation helped determine the original nominal rate; the surprise changes the realized real return.
The Fisher effect requires the bank to retroactively reset the nominal rate to actual inflation.
Unexpected inflation leaves the realized real return unchanged on a fixed-rate contract.
The nominal rate was based only on actual inflation, which was already known.
q.commonError: Uses realized inflation to explain a nominal rate chosen before the loan was made.
q.feedback: The nominal rate written into a contract reflects expected inflation at the time the contract is set; realized inflation determines the ex post real return.

q.q: Nominal interest rates rise 3 percentage points while expected inflation rises 5 points. What does the Fisher decomposition imply about the real-rate component?
options: It rose by about 8 percentage points.
It rose by exactly 5 percentage points.
It must have remained unchanged because nominal rates increased.
It fell by about 2 percentage points.
q.commonError: Assumes nominal rates must move one-for-one with expected inflation even when the real rate also changes.
q.feedback: The one-for-one Fisher prediction requires holding the real interest rate fixed; if the real rate changes too, combine both changes.

q.q: Use the Fisher approximation. If MS shifts right and the value of money falls, expected inflation rises from 3 percent to 9 percent. If the real interest rate stays at 2 percent, what happens to the nominal interest rate?
options: It rises from 5 percent to 11 percent.
It falls from 5 percent to 2 percent.
It rises from 3 percent to 9 percent.
It stays at 5 percent.
q.commonError: forgetting to add the real interest rate to expected inflation
q.feedback: Nominal rate equals real rate plus expected inflation. It rises from 2 + 3 = 5 to 2 + 9 = 11 percent.

q.q: Use the Fisher approximation. Expected inflation rises from 2 percent to 10 percent while the real rate falls from 4 percent to 1 percent. What happens to the nominal interest rate, and why is this not a contradiction?
options: It rises from 6 percent to 11 percent because expected inflation rose more than the real rate fell.
It falls from 6 percent to 1 percent because the real rate fell.
It stays at 6 percent because changes cancel exactly.
It rises from 2 percent to 10 percent because real rates do not matter.
q.commonError: tracking only the real rate or only expected inflation
q.feedback: Initial nominal rate is 4 + 2 = 6 percent. New nominal rate is 1 + 10 = 11 percent. Expected inflation rose more than the real rate fell.

q.q: A country’s nominal loan rate falls from 16 to 9 percent while expected inflation falls from 12 to 4 percent. Using the Fisher approximation, what happens to the expected real rate, and by how much would the new nominal rate have had to fall further to preserve its original expected real rate?
options: The expected real rate rises from 4 to 5 percent; a further 1-point nominal cut was needed.
The expected real rate falls from 4 to 3 percent; a further 1-point nominal cut was needed.
The expected real rate stays at 4 percent; no further nominal change was needed.
The expected real rate rises from 4 to 5 percent; a further 5-point nominal cut was needed.
q.commonError: assuming lower nominal rates always mean lower real rates

q.q: A borrower says the Fisher effect is found by subtracting this year’s actual inflation from a loan rate set last year. What is the key mistake?
