q.feedback: The tariff is collected on imported units, not on every unit consumed.

labels: Analyze tariff effects on price, quantities, revenue, and total surplus.

q.q: A learner says all consumer surplus lost under a tariff is deadweight loss. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Producer gains are not part of total surplus
Government revenue is always deadweight loss
Some loss is transferred to producers and government; only the unrecovered portion is deadweight loss
All consumer loss disappears from national welfare
q.commonError: counts_transfers_as_social_losses
q.feedback: Tariff welfare analysis separates transfers from production and consumption distortions.

labels: Analyze tariff effects on price, quantities, revenue, and total surplus.

q.q: A learner says quota rent is automatically government revenue. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Quota rent is always collected as a tariff
Quota rent equals domestic producer surplus
Quota rent exists only when the quota is nonbinding
Quota rent goes to whoever holds the valuable import rights unless the government auctions them
q.commonError: assigns_quota_rents_to_government_automatically
q.feedback: Unlike tariff revenue, quota rent depends on who receives or buys the import licenses.

labels: Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.

q.q: A learner says equal-price tariffs and quotas must have identical national effects. What key issue is missing?
options: Whether imports exist
Whether domestic firms produce anything
Who receives the quota rents
Whether consumers face a price
q.commonError: assumes_tariff_and_quota_are_always_identical
q.feedback: If foreign license holders capture quota rents, national surplus differs from an equivalent tariff with domestic government revenue.

labels: Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.

q.q: What surplus concept separates tariff revenue from deadweight loss?
options: All consumer losses are deadweight loss
All producer gains are deadweight loss
Transfers change recipients; deadweight loss removes mutually beneficial trades
Revenue is never part of welfare
q.commonError: counts_transfers_as_social_losses
q.feedback: Tariff revenue is a transfer to the government, while deadweight loss represents gains from trade that disappear because the tariff distorts production and consumption.

labels: Analyze tariff effects on price, quantities, revenue, and total surplus.

q.q: How does comparative advantage support gains from international trade?
options: It requires absolute advantage in every good
It eliminates scarcity
It guarantees equal gains
Specialization follows lower opportunity cost and exchange expands consumption possibilities
q.commonError: confuses_trade_with_one_sided_loss
q.feedback: Comparative advantage identifies the goods each side can produce at lower opportunity cost. Specialization on that basis can create gains that exchange allows both sides to share.

labels: Explain world price, imports, exports, and the small-country trade model.

q.q: Can a country gain from trade if it is less productive in every good?
options: Yes, if opportunity costs differ and it specializes by comparative advantage
No, absolute disadvantage prevents all gains
Only if it bans imports
Only if wages are identical
q.commonError: confuses_trade_with_one_sided_loss
q.feedback: Yes. Even a country with an absolute disadvantage in every good can gain from trade when opportunity costs differ and it specializes according to comparative advantage.

labels: Explain world price, imports, exports, and the small-country trade model.

q.q: Two small countries open their wheat markets to free trade. Before trade, wheat sells for $40 per sack in Alder and $24 in Birch. The world price is $30 per sack, with no transport costs or trade barriers. Which trade pattern follows?
options: Alder exports; Birch imports.
Alder imports; Birch exports.
Both countries import wheat.
Both countries export wheat.
q.commonError: reverses_world_price_comparison_for_imports_and_exports
q.feedback: Compare the $30 world price with each country's no-trade price. In Alder, $30 is below $40, so domestic demand exceeds domestic supply and imports fill the gap. In Birch, $30 is above $24, so domestic supply exceeds domestic demand and the excess is exported. Both face the same world price; their different no-trade prices explain their different trade directions.

labels: Explain world price, imports, exports, and the small-country trade model.

q.q: How can supply elasticity affect domestic production response to a tariff?
options: Elasticity eliminates tariff revenue
Elasticity fixes import quantity under every policy
Elasticity makes marginal cost irrelevant
More responsive supply creates a larger production increase and distortion
q.commonError: misses_high_cost_domestic_expansion
q.feedback: When domestic supply is more responsive to price, the tariff-induced price increase produces a larger increase in domestic output and therefore a larger production distortion, other things equal.

labels: Analyze tariff effects on price, quantities, revenue, and total surplus.

q.q: How is a tariff connected to a tax wedge?
options: It creates a gap between the domestic buyer price and the world resource price
It creates a gap between domestic quantity supplied and domestic quantity demanded, measured as tax per unit.
It creates a gap between the government’s total tariff receipts and the per-unit price paid for imports.
It creates a gap between the lower domestic buyer price and the unchanged world price after the tariff.
q.commonError: predicts_tariff_lowers_domestic_price
q.feedback: In the small-country importing model, a tariff raises the domestic price above the world price while imports continue. That price difference is the per-unit tax wedge. The import quantity and total tariff revenue are different measures, and the tariff does not lower the domestic buyer price.

labels: Analyze tariff effects on price, quantities, revenue, and total surplus.

q.q: How is tariff deadweight loss connected to lost gains from exchange?
options: It equals tariff revenue
The tariff prevents beneficial imports and induces higher-cost production
It equals all consumer expenditure
It is a payment to foreign firms
q.commonError: counts_transfers_as_social_losses
q.feedback: The tariff prevents some imports whose value to domestic buyers exceeds their world resource cost and also induces higher-cost domestic production. Those foregone gains create deadweight loss.

labels: Analyze tariff effects on price, quantities, revenue, and total surplus.

q.q: How can trade move consumption beyond a country’s production possibilities frontier?
options: Trade moves domestic production outside physical constraints
A tariff expands resources automatically
Specialization and exchange separate what is consumed from what is domestically produced
Imports eliminate opportunity cost
q.commonError: confuses_trade_with_one_sided_loss
q.feedback: Trade does not move domestic production beyond the PPF. Specialization and exchange can instead allow the country to consume a combination of goods that it could not produce by itself.

labels: Explain world price, imports, exports, and the small-country trade model.

q.q: What does the PPF contribute to trade analysis?
options: It directly calculates tariff revenue
It fixes the world price
It identifies quota rents
It shows opportunity costs and the production tradeoffs behind comparative advantage
q.commonError: confuses_trade_with_one_sided_loss
q.feedback: The PPF shows the production tradeoffs that determine opportunity costs. Those opportunity costs help identify comparative advantage and the basis for specialization.

labels: Explain world price, imports, exports, and the small-country trade model.

q.q: What efficiency question should be separated from the equity question in trade?
options: Whether total surplus rises versus how gains and losses are distributed
Whether imports equal exports versus whether prices exist
Whether firms earn revenue versus whether consumers buy
Whether quotas are legal versus whether supply slopes upward
q.commonError: equates_efficiency_with_fairness
q.feedback: Efficiency asks whether trade raises total surplus. Equity asks how the resulting gains and losses are distributed across people, firms, industries, or regions.

labels: Evaluate trade-policy arguments using efficiency, distribution, and evidence.

q.q: Why might adjustment assistance be discussed even when trade raises total surplus?
options: Trade eliminates all consumer gains
Some workers and communities can bear concentrated transition costs
Efficiency requires equal outcomes
Imports always reduce total employment
q.commonError: equates_efficiency_with_fairness
q.feedback: Trade can raise total surplus while imposing concentrated transition costs on particular workers and communities. Adjustment assistance addresses those distributional costs without denying the aggregate gains.

labels: Evaluate trade-policy arguments using efficiency, distribution, and evidence.

q.q: How does a tariff connect to the tax-wedge idea from domestic markets?
options: It guarantees the legal and economic burden are identical
It creates a wedge between the world price and the domestic buyer/seller price
It eliminates the role of price
It shifts world demand only
q.feedback: A tariff acts like a tax on imports and raises the domestic price above the world price in the small-country model.

labels: Analyze tariff effects on price, quantities, revenue, and total surplus.

q.q: How does tariff deadweight loss connect to surplus analysis?
options: It is the total surplus destroyed by production and consumption distortions
It is the full transfer from consumers to producers
It equals tariff revenue
It is producer surplus after the tariff
q.commonError: counts_transfers_as_social_losses
q.feedback: The surplus framework identifies the trades and resource uses that no longer maximize gains.

labels: Analyze tariff effects on price, quantities, revenue, and total surplus.

q.q: How does a binding quota connect to ordinary supply-and-demand pressure?
options: Import restrictions make domestic supply irrelevant
Restricting imports reduces available supply to the domestic market and raises the domestic price
A quota shifts domestic demand left automatically
A quota fixes the world price and domestic price at zero
q.commonError: assumes_quota_leaves_price_at_world_price
q.feedback: The quantity restriction tightens the domestic market and raises price until the permitted import gap is satisfied.

labels: Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.

q.q: How does quota rent connect to economic rent more generally?
options: A scarce legal right can acquire value because it permits profitable access
Quota rent is a payment for labor only
Economic rent requires a perfectly competitive labor market
Quota rent equals consumer surplus by definition
q.feedback: Import licenses become valuable because the restriction creates a price gap.

labels: Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.

q.q: Why can auctioning quota licenses make a quota look more like a tariff in national-welfare accounting?
options: Auctioning eliminates the domestic price increase
Auctioning makes imports unlimited
Auctioning turns the quota into an export subsidy
The government captures the quota rent much like tariff revenue
q.commonError: miscompares_tariff_and_quota
q.feedback: Who receives the rent is a major difference between quotas and tariffs.

labels: Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.

q.q: A demand increase occurs under a fixed quota. What does the quota teach about quantity controls versus price-based barriers?
options: Both price and imports must stay unchanged
The quota automatically becomes a tariff
The import quantity stays capped while domestic price can rise further
Domestic price stays fixed while imports expand freely
q.commonError: assumes_tariff_and_quota_are_always_identical
q.feedback: A hard quantity limit adjusts differently from a fixed per-unit tariff when market conditions change.

labels: Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.

q.q: A voluntary export restraint gives foreign firms free shipment rights. How does national-welfare accounting connect this arrangement to an equivalent tariff?
options: Count the rents as domestic tax receipts because domestic consumers pay them
Include the same distortions, but subtract rents sent abroad instead of counting domestic tariff revenue
Count only producer gains because no import tax is collected
Treat rents and distortion triangles as the same loss in world welfare
q.commonError: assigns_quota_rents_to_government_automatically
q.feedback: With the same prices and quantities, the distortions match. Foreign rents are a transfer abroad that lowers importing-country welfare relative to domestic tariff receipts; they are not themselves destroyed world surplus.

labels: Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.

q.q: How does a quota-versus-tariff comparison connect to policy design?
options: Two policies can create similar price and quantity effects but differ in who receives the transfer
Two policies with matching price and quantity effects must give their revenue or rents to the same recipients.
Two policies with matching import quantities must raise equal government revenue, even when quota licenses are given away.
Two policies can raise the same domestic price, but only the quota distorts domestic production and consumption.
q.commonError: assumes_tariff_and_quota_are_always_identical
q.feedback: An equivalent tariff and binding quota can produce similar prices and quantities, yet tariff revenue goes to government while quota rents go to the holders of import rights unless those rights are auctioned. Both can distort production and consumption. Policy design must therefore track who receives revenue or rents as well as efficiency effects.

labels: Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.

q.q: How does evaluating protection connect positive and normative economics?
options: Positive economics decides which distribution is fair
Normative economics calculates tariff revenue mechanically
The two approaches are identical in trade policy
Positive analysis estimates costs and benefits; normative judgment weighs goals and distribution
q.commonError: confuses_policy_analysis_with_policy_preference
q.feedback: Trade-policy evaluation separates what a policy does from judgments about whether its goals justify those effects.

labels: Evaluate trade-policy arguments using efficiency, distribution, and evidence.

q.q: Net exports equal which difference?
options: National saving minus consumption
Domestic investment minus national saving
Exports minus imports
Imports minus exports
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: Net exports measure domestic sales abroad less domestic purchases of foreign goods and services.

q.q: When exports exceed imports, how is the trade balance described?
options: A net capital inflow by definition
A trade surplus
A trade deficit
Balanced trade
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: Exports greater than imports make net exports positive, which is a trade surplus.

q.q: Which transaction is a U.S. export?
options: A Canadian household buys software produced by a U.S. firm
A U.S. household buys a television produced in Korea
A U.S. fund buys bonds issued by Canada
A German firm buys shares issued by a U.S. firm
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: An export is a domestically produced good or service purchased by a foreign buyer.

q.q: In the standard open-economy accounts, which identity links trade in goods and services to trade in assets?
options: NX = C + I
NCO = G − T
S = C + NX
NX = NCO
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: Net exports equal net capital outflow as an accounting identity.

q.q: Positive net capital outflow means that domestic residents' purchases of foreign assets are:
options: Equal to domestic investment
Excluded from the international accounts
Greater than foreign purchases of domestic assets
Less than foreign purchases of domestic assets
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: NCO subtracts foreign purchases of domestic assets from domestic purchases of foreign assets.

q.q: Why are imports subtracted in the expenditure approach to GDP?
options: Because imports are transfers rather than purchases
To remove foreign production already included in C, I, or G
Because buying imports reduces domestic production by the same amount
To treat imports as domestic intermediate goods
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: Imported spending can first appear in C, I, or G, so subtracting imports prevents foreign production from being counted as domestic output.

q.q: Exports are $720 billion and imports are $810 billion. What is net exports?
options: −$1.53 trillion
$1.53 trillion
−$90 billion
$90 billion
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: NX = $720 billion − $810 billion = −$90 billion, a trade deficit.

q.q: An economy has national saving of $640 billion and domestic investment of $500 billion. What is NCO?
options: $1.14 trillion
$140 billion
−$140 billion
$500 billion
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: From S = I + NCO, NCO = $640 billion − $500 billion = $140 billion.

q.q: A country records NCO of −$60 billion. What must its net exports equal?
options: −$60 billion
$60 billion
An amount that cannot be inferred
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: NX and NCO are equal in the accounts, so negative NCO implies an equal trade deficit.

q.q: Domestic residents buy $240 billion of foreign assets while foreigners buy $310 billion of domestic assets. What is NCO?
options: $70 billion
$240 billion
$550 billion
−$70 billion
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: NCO = $240 billion − $310 billion = −$70 billion, indicating net capital inflow.

q.q: A household buys a $2,000 imported computer with no other economic change. What does GDP accounting do?
options: Investment rises by $2,000 and GDP rises by $2,000
Net exports rise by $2,000 while consumption is unchanged
Consumption rises by $2,000 and imports rise by $2,000, leaving GDP unchanged
GDP falls by $2,000 because imports are subtracted
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: The purchase enters consumption, while the import subtraction removes the foreign-produced computer from domestic GDP.

q.q: If national saving is less than domestic investment, which combination is consistent with the identities?
options: Zero NCO and a trade deficit
Negative NCO and a trade deficit
Positive NCO and a trade surplus
Positive NCO and balanced trade
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: S − I equals NCO, so S below I makes NCO negative; NX = NCO makes net exports negative as well.

q.q: Output is $2.4 trillion, consumption is $1.5 trillion, investment is $0.4 trillion, and government purchases are $0.6 trillion. What are NX and NCO?
options: Both are $0.1 trillion
NX is −$0.1 trillion and NCO is $0.1 trillion
NX is $0.5 trillion and NCO is −$0.1 trillion
Both are −$0.1 trillion
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: NX = Y − C − I − G = 2.4 − 1.5 − 0.4 − 0.6 = −0.1 trillion; NX = NCO.

q.q: Private saving is $420 billion, public saving is −$80 billion, and domestic investment is $390 billion. What follows?
options: National saving is $340 billion, so NCO and NX are $50 billion
National saving is −$50 billion, so NCO and NX are −$390 billion
National saving is $340 billion, so NCO and NX are −$50 billion
National saving is $500 billion, so NCO and NX are $110 billion
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: National saving is $420 billion − $80 billion = $340 billion. Subtracting $390 billion of investment gives NCO = NX = −$50 billion.

q.q: A student says a trade deficit proves imports destroyed an equal amount of domestic output. Which correction is best?
options: The deficit proves national saving exceeds domestic investment
The deficit records imports above exports; it does not identify the separate response of domestic production
The claim is correct because imports are subtracted from GDP
A trade deficit means domestic consumption must be falling
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: Imports are subtracted to exclude foreign production from GDP. The trade balance alone does not show how domestic output changed.

q.q: Exports rise by $40 billion and imports rise by $65 billion while other GDP components are unchanged. How do NX and GDP change?
options: Both fall by $25 billion
Both rise by $105 billion
NX falls by $25 billion while GDP rises by $25 billion
NX rises by $25 billion while GDP is unchanged
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: Net exports change by $40 billion − $65 billion = −$25 billion, so the expenditure identity lowers measured GDP by $25 billion when other components are fixed.

q.q: A country has a $90 billion trade surplus and domestic investment of $260 billion. What national saving is consistent with the accounts?
options: $170 billion
$260 billion
$440 billion
$350 billion
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: NX = NCO = $90 billion, and S = I + NCO = $260 billion + $90 billion = $350 billion.

q.q: Across two consistently measured periods, foreign purchases of domestic bonds rise while domestic purchases of foreign assets are unchanged. Which accounting change follows, without identifying how quickly trade adjusts?
options: NCO is unchanged, while NX falls
NCO falls, while NX must rise
NCO falls, and NX must be lower in the accounts
NCO rises, and NX must be higher
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: The larger foreign-purchase flow lowers NCO. NX must match NCO in consistent period accounts; this identity alone does not establish an immediate trade response to a particular bond purchase.

q.q: Exports and imports both rise, foreign purchases of domestic assets increase, and domestic purchases of foreign assets also increase. Which conclusion is justified without magnitudes?
options: NCO must fall because foreign asset purchases increased
NX and NCO can take different values because both sides changed
The signs of NX and NCO are indeterminate, but the two balances must remain equal
NX must rise because exports increased
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: Each balance depends on a difference whose sign requires magnitudes; the accounting identity still requires NX = NCO.

q.q: National saving rises by $70 billion, domestic investment rises by $30 billion, exports rise by $55 billion, and imports rise by $15 billion. Are the changes mutually consistent?
options: Yes; both balances rise by $70 billion
Yes; both NCO and NX rise by $40 billion
No; NCO rises by $100 billion while NX rises by $40 billion
No; NCO falls by $40 billion while NX rises by $70 billion
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: ΔNCO = ΔS − ΔI = $40 billion, and ΔNX = ΔX − ΔM = $40 billion, so the identities reconcile.

q.q: In one period, consumption rises $96 billion, of which $72 billion is imported. Measured investment rises $35 billion, including $11 billion of imported equipment. Exports rise $18 billion; G and other imports are unchanged. A report claims GDP rose $149 billion. Which correction also reconciles the change in national saving?
options: GDP rises $149 billion and national saving rises $53 billion
GDP rises $66 billion and national saving rises $30 billion
GDP rises $83 billion and national saving falls $13 billion
GDP rises $66 billion and national saving falls $30 billion
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.

q.q: Two countries initially have S = $700 billion and I = $750 billion. In Alder, saving rises $65 billion while investment rises an unknown amount. In Brin, saving rises $40 billion and investment rises $25 billion. What condition makes Alder end with a smaller trade deficit than Brin but still a deficit?
options: Alder investment rises by less than $15 billion
Alder investment rises by more than $50 billion but less than $65 billion
Alder investment rises by more than $15 billion but less than $50 billion
Alder investment rises by exactly $65 billion
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: Brin ends with NX = −50 + 40 − 25 = −35. Alder ends at NX = −50 + 65 − ΔI = 15 − ΔI. Requiring −35 < 15 − ΔI < 0 gives 15 < ΔI < 50, in billions.

q.q: Initially NX and NCO are zero. Residents increase foreign-asset purchases by $126 billion. Exports then rise $54 billion and imports rise $18 billion. What change in foreign purchases of domestic assets reconciles both accounts, and what does it establish about the causal sequence?
options: They rise $162 billion; capital inflow necessarily causes the export increase
They rise $90 billion; the identities do not establish which flow caused the trade change
They fall $90 billion; the identities establish that trade moved first
They rise $36 billion; the asset and trade balances need not match
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: ΔNX = 54 − 18 = 36, so ΔNCO = 36 = 126 − Δinflow. Therefore inflow rises 90. Period accounting reconciles the totals but does not identify the behavioral timing.

q.q: Imports increased, national saving fell, and domestic investment also fell. A commentator says these observations prove that the trade deficit widened. Which additional comparison would resolve the claim while allowing an independent trade-account check?
options: Compare the saving decline with the investment decline, and compare the import rise with the export change
Compare the saving decline with the import rise; exports are unnecessary
Compare the investment decline with the import rise; saving is unnecessary
Compare the levels of saving and exports; their changes are unnecessary
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: ΔNX = ΔS − ΔI, so falling saving and investment alone do not sign the change. Independently, ΔNX = ΔX − ΔM; exports must be compared with imports. Either complete accounting comparison should produce the same answer.

q.q: A deficit lowers public saving $74 billion. Private saving rises by an unknown amount, domestic investment falls $22 billion, and NX falls $31 billion. Which private-saving response and interpretation reconcile the accounts?
options: Private saving rises $43 billion; NX must fall by the full deficit increase
Private saving falls $21 billion; investment crowding out enlarges the NX decline
Private saving rises $105 billion; the deficit necessarily produces a trade surplus
Private saving rises $21 billion; the NX decline is smaller than the deficit increase
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: Let p be the private-saving rise. ΔNX = (p − 74) − (−22) = p − 52 = −31, so p = 21. Offsetting private saving and lower investment both cushion the external-balance effect.

q.q: For the same period, a data release reports S = $480 billion, I = $525 billion, X = $210 billion, M = $240 billion, foreign-asset purchases by residents of $70 billion, and domestic-asset purchases by foreigners of $115 billion. If exactly one trade figure is wrong and all other figures are correct, which correction is admissible, and is its location identified?
options: Raise X to $225 billion or lower M to $225 billion; the identity does not select between them
Raise M to $255 billion; the identity proves that imports alone are wrong
Raise M to $255 billion or lower X to $195 billion; the identity does not select between them
Lower X to $195 billion; the identity proves that exports alone are wrong
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: S − I = −45 and asset NCO = 70 − 115 = −45, but reported NX is −30. Trade must fall another 15: either M rises from 240 to 255 or X falls from 210 to 195. The stated data do not identify which trade entry is erroneous.

q.q: Exports are $500 billion and imports are $620 billion. Which trade balance is correct?
options: A $120 billion deficit
A $120 billion surplus
A $1.12 trillion deficit
Balanced trade
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: Exports minus imports equals −$120 billion, so imports exceed exports by $120 billion.

q.q: Which equation correctly allocates national saving in an open economy?
options: S = C + G
I = S + NX
NCO = imports − exports
S = I + NCO
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: National saving finances domestic investment plus net purchases of foreign assets.

q.q: A negative value of NCO describes which situation?
options: A trade surplus
No international asset trade
A net capital inflow
A net capital outflow
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: Negative NCO means foreign purchases of domestic assets exceed domestic purchases of foreign assets.

q.q: National saving is $300 billion and investment is $360 billion. Which external balance follows?
options: NCO and NX are $60 billion
NCO is −$60 billion and NX is $60 billion
Both balances are $660 billion
NCO and NX are −$60 billion
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: S − I = −$60 billion, and the identity makes both NCO and NX equal to that amount.

q.q: A domestic airline buys a newly produced aircraft from France. How does the purchase enter domestic GDP accounting?
options: It enters consumption but not imports
It directly reduces domestic output
It raises investment and imports by the same amount
It lowers investment and raises exports
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: The aircraft is business investment, but its foreign production is removed through the import term.

q.q: If the trade account is balanced, what must be true of NCO in the same consistent accounts?
options: NCO equals domestic investment
NCO equals zero
NCO is positive
NCO is negative
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: Balanced trade means NX = 0, and NX = NCO requires NCO = 0.

q.q: Private saving rises by $40 billion, public saving falls by $15 billion, and investment rises by $10 billion. What is the change in NX?
options: An increase of $35 billion
An increase of $65 billion
An increase of $15 billion
A decrease of $15 billion
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: National saving rises by $25 billion. Subtracting the $10 billion investment increase leaves NCO and NX up $15 billion.

q.q: Imports rise by $70 billion and exports rise by $20 billion, while consumption rises by $70 billion entirely because of the new imports. Other domestic spending is unchanged. What happens to GDP?
options: GDP is unchanged
GDP rises by $20 billion
GDP falls by $50 billion
GDP rises by $70 billion
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: The import-driven $70 billion rise in consumption is offset by imports; the $20 billion export increase adds domestic production.

q.q: A country has positive NCO but a reported trade deficit. Within the same consistently measured period, which statement is correct?
options: At least one reported balance is inconsistent with the accounting identity
The combination is expected whenever saving is high
Positive NCO mechanically creates a trade deficit
The signs can differ whenever exchange rates float
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: The identity NX = NCO requires the two balances to share the same value and sign.

q.q: Output is $5.0 trillion, consumption $3.1 trillion, government purchases $0.9 trillion, and investment $1.2 trillion. Domestic purchases of foreign assets are $260 billion. How much must foreigners purchase in domestic assets?
options: $660 billion
$460 billion
$60 billion
$260 billion
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.
q.feedback: NX = 5.0 − 3.1 − 0.9 − 1.2 = −$0.2 trillion, so NCO is −$200 billion. With NCO = $260 billion − foreign purchases, foreign purchases equal $460 billion.

q.q: A $100 billion rise in exports accompanies a $130 billion rise in imports. National saving rises by $50 billion. What change in domestic investment preserves all identities?
options: An increase of $80 billion
An increase of $20 billion
A decrease of $20 billion
An increase of $180 billion
q.commonError: Confuses the direction or accounting relationship tested in this question.

Lower prices increase money demand, raise interest rates, and lower investment.

Lower prices eliminate the need for investment.
q.commonError: thinking lower prices raise money demand

q.q: If money demand shifts right while money supply stays fixed, what must happen to restore money-market equilibrium?

The interest rate falls.
Money supply shifts left automatically.
Aggregate demand becomes vertical.

q.q: A rise in real income shifts money demand right. If the Fed holds money supply fixed, what happens next?

Interest rates fall.
Money supply rises automatically.
Investment rises because borrowing is cheaper.

q.feedback: Higher income increases money demand. With fixed money supply, the interest rate rises.

q.q: A fall in the price level shifts money demand left. If money supply is fixed, what happens to the interest rate?

It stays fixed because money demand cannot shift.
It becomes the inflation rate.
q.commonError: thinking a lower price level increases money demand

The quantity of money demanded rises.

q.q: If income rises and the Fed prevents interest rates from rising, what policy shift is needed?
options: Increase money supply as money demand rises
Decrease money supply as money demand rises
Increase money demand as money supply falls
Decrease money demand as interest rates rise
q.commonError: Forgetting the Fed must offset higher money demand.
q.feedback: Higher income raises money demand; to hold rates down, the Fed must increase money supply.

q.q: If the Fed cuts money supply while money demand rises, what happens to the interest rate pressure?
options: It rises from both forces
It falls from both forces
It rises from supply but falls from demand
It falls from supply but rises from demand
q.commonError: Missing that both shifts raise rates.
q.feedback: Lower money supply and higher money demand both push the interest rate upward.

q.q: Starting in money-market equilibrium, the price level rises. Which full chain explains the interest-rate effect on aggregate demand?
options: Higher P raises money demand, raises r, lowers investment, and lowers quantity of goods and services demanded.

Higher P raises money supply, lowers r, raises investment, and shifts AD right.
Higher P lowers money supply, raises r, and shifts money demand left.
q.commonError: reversing the price-level effect on money demand
q.feedback: Higher prices require more money for transactions. That raises money demand, raises interest rates, lowers investment, and reduces quantity demanded.

options: Money demand falls, r falls, investment rises, and output demanded rises.
Money demand rises, r rises, investment falls, and output demanded falls.
Money supply falls, r rises, and AD shifts left.
Money demand falls, r rises, and investment falls.
q.commonError: thinking lower prices increase money demand
q.feedback: A lower price level reduces money demand, lowers interest rates, raises investment, and increases quantity demanded.

q.q: Money demand shifts from MD1 to MD2 while money supply remains fixed. What is the likely effect on r and investment?
options: r rises and investment falls.
r falls and investment rises.
r rises and investment rises.
r falls and investment falls.
q.commonError: thinking higher money demand lowers the interest rate
q.feedback: With fixed money supply, a rightward shift in money demand raises the interest rate, which lowers investment.

q.q: Money demand shifts left while money supply remains fixed. What chain follows?
options: r falls, investment rises, and AD tends to increase.
r rises, investment falls, and AD tends to decrease.
r falls, investment falls, and AD tends to decrease.
r rises, investment rises, and AD tends to increase.
q.commonError: missing the investment response after the money-market movement
q.feedback: Lower money demand reduces the equilibrium interest rate, which supports investment and AD.

q.q: If a rise in the price level shifts money demand right and the Fed does not change money supply, why does this help explain the downward slope of AD?
options: Higher P raises r and lowers investment, reducing quantity demanded.
Higher P lowers r and raises investment, increasing quantity demanded.
Higher P shifts AD right by increasing investment.
Higher P makes money supply rise automatically.
q.commonError: missing that this is movement along AD, not an AD shift
q.feedback: Higher P raises money demand and interest rates, lowering investment and quantity demanded along the AD curve.

q.q: If an increase in Y raises money demand and the Fed wants to prevent r from rising, what should the Fed do?
options: Increase money supply to match the higher money demand.
Decrease money supply to reduce money demand.
Raise taxes because money supply cannot shift.
Reduce government spending to make MD vertical.
q.commonError: thinking the Fed should reduce money supply when money demand rises
q.feedback: If money demand rises, increasing money supply can prevent the equilibrium interest rate from rising.

q.q: If P rises, money demand shifts right. If the Fed also increases money supply enough to hold r constant, what happens to the interest-rate effect on AD?
options: It is offset because r does not rise to reduce investment.
It becomes stronger because r rises more.
It reverses because investment must fall more.
It disappears because AD is no longer related to spending.
q.commonError: ignoring that Fed policy can offset money-demand pressure on r
q.feedback: If the Fed accommodates the higher money demand, r does not rise, so the investment channel behind the interest-rate effect is muted.

q.q: A student says a fall in the interest rate from 8 percent to 6 percent would shift MD0 to the right. What is the best correction?

Interest-rate changes shift MD0 because the rate is on the axis.
Interest-rate changes shift MS0 while MD0 stays fixed.
Interest-rate changes shift both MD0 and MS0 together.
q.commonError: misreads_money_market_or_transmission
q.feedback: The interest rate is the price variable on the money-demand curve. Changing it moves the economy along MD0.

Interest rates fall because fixed money supply means more lending.
q.commonError: Reversing income effects on money demand.
q.feedback: Higher income raises money demand; with fixed money supply, interest rates rise.

q.q: Money demand rises while the Fed increases money supply. Which conclusion is safest?
options: The interest-rate effect is ambiguous without knowing relative shift sizes.
Interest rates must rise because money demand always dominates.
Interest rates must fall because money supply always dominates.
Interest rates must stay fixed because both curves shifted.
q.commonError: Assuming one shift always dominates.
q.feedback: When money demand and money supply both increase, the interest-rate effect depends on which shift is larger.

q.q: Money demand rises because income rises, while the Fed cuts the money supply. Which memo is strongest?
options: Both forces push interest rates upward and pressure AD downward.
Both forces push interest rates downward and pressure AD upward.
Money demand raises rates, but lower money supply lowers rates.
Money demand lowers rates, but lower money supply raises rates.
q.commonError: Missing that both shifts raise interest rates.
q.feedback: Higher money demand and lower money supply both raise interest rates, weakening investment and AD.

q.q: Money demand falls while the Fed expands money supply. Which memo is strongest?
options: Both forces push interest rates downward and support AD.
Both forces push interest rates upward and weaken AD.
Money demand lowers rates, but higher money supply raises rates.
Money demand raises rates, but higher money supply lowers rates.
q.commonError: Missing that both shifts lower interest rates.
q.feedback: Lower money demand and higher money supply both push interest rates down, supporting investment and AD.

q.q: Money demand shifts right while money supply is fixed. If the Fed wants to prevent the resulting interest-rate increase, what should it do?
options: Increase money supply enough to offset the rightward money-demand shift.
Decrease money supply to reinforce the money-demand shift.
Raise taxes because taxes directly shift money demand left.
Do nothing because r must fall when money demand rises.
q.commonError: thinking the Fed should reduce money supply when money demand rises
q.feedback: A rightward money-demand shift raises r if MS is fixed. Increasing MS can offset that pressure.

q.q: Real income rises and the central bank increases the money supply enough to leave the equilibrium interest rate unchanged. What must be true?
options: Money demand stayed fixed even though higher income increased transaction volume.
The money supply shifted left by enough to offset the rise in money demand.
The price level fell to zero and eliminated the need to hold transaction balances.
The money-supply increase offset the rise in money demand.
q.commonError: Assuming an unchanged interest rate means neither curve shifted.
q.feedback: Higher income raises money demand. A sufficiently large increase in money supply can offset that pressure and leave the equilibrium interest rate unchanged.

q.q: If the nominal interest rate were temporarily above point A while MS0 stayed fixed, what adjustment pressure would the graph imply?
options: Excess money demand pushes the rate farther above A.
Excess money supply pushes the rate down toward A.
Money supply shifts right until the rate rises above A.
Money demand shifts left until the rate remains above A.
q.commonError: misreads_money_market_or_transmission
q.feedback: Above equilibrium, the quantity of money demanded is less than the fixed money supply. Portfolio adjustment pushes the interest rate back down toward equilibrium.
