q.q: After the money-supply change from MS0 to MS1 shown in the graph, which spending-and-AD response should follow?
options: Higher rates raise interest-sensitive spending and shift AD right.
Higher rates cut interest-sensitive spending and shift AD left.
Lower rates cut interest-sensitive spending and shift AD left.
Lower rates raise interest-sensitive spending and shift AD right.
q.commonError: misreads_money_market_or_transmission
q.feedback: The standard contractionary chain runs from less money to higher interest rates to less interest-sensitive spending and lower aggregate demand.
q.imageAlt: Money-market diagram with MD0 and vertical MS0 and MS1.
q.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is quantity of money and the vertical axis is nominal interest rate. The straight downward MD0 line runs from (0,12) to (150,0). Solid MS0 is vertical at quantity 100; its MD0 intersection is at rate 4. Dashed MS1 is vertical at quantity 75; its MD0 intersection is at rate 6. Horizontal dashed guides mark rates 4 and 6.

q.q: Refer to the graph. The economy starts at B with MD0 and MS0. Money demand changes to MD1. The central bank increases money supply to MS1, but wants to restore B’s original nominal interest rate. If the straight MD1 line continues as drawn, approximately how much additional money beyond MS1 is needed?
options: 25 units; a total money quantity of 125.
No additional money; C already restores the original rate.
75 units; a total money quantity of 175.
12.5 units; a total money quantity of 112.5.
q.commonError: misreads_money_market_or_transmission
q.feedback: B’s rate is 3. MD1 passes through A at (75,6) and C at (100,4), a fall of 2 rate points per 25 money units. A further 1-point fall requires 12.5 additional units, beyond MS1 at 100.
q.imageAlt: Money-market diagram with two vertical MS lines, two downward MD lines and labeled points A, B, C and D.
q.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is quantity of money; the vertical axis is nominal interest rate. Solid MS0 is vertical at 75 and dashed MS1 at 100. Solid MD0 is the lower straight downward line, through B (75,3) and D (100,1). Dashed MD1 is the upper parallel line, through A (75,6) and C (100,4). MD1 crosses the vertical axis at 12 and the horizontal axis at 150. MD0 crosses the vertical axis at 9. All four points are marked with black dots.

q.q: Which complete chain is consistent with the two-panel graph?
options: MD ↑; rate ↓; interest-sensitive spending ↑; AD →; GDP and prices ↑.
MD ↑; rate ↑; interest-sensitive spending ↓; AD ←; GDP and prices ↓.
MS ↑; rate ↑; interest-sensitive spending ↓; AD ←; GDP and prices ↑.
MD ↓; rate ↑; interest-sensitive spending ↑; AD →; GDP and prices ↑.
q.commonError: misreads_money_market_or_transmission
q.feedback: The panels show the full liquidity-preference transmission from a money-demand increase to a higher rate and lower aggregate demand.
q.imageAlt: Two panels with MS0, MD0 and MD1 on the left and AD0, AD1 and SRAS on the right.
q.graphDescription: Left panel axes: quantity of money horizontally and nominal interest rate (%) vertically. MS0 is vertical at 75. Solid downward MD0 passes through A (75,2); upper dashed MD1 passes through B (75,4). Right panel axes: real GDP horizontally and price level vertically. Solid AD0 and lower dashed AD1 slope downward; red SRAS slopes upward. AD0 and SRAS meet at A (150,55); AD1 and SRAS meet at B (105,45). Dashed guides identify the point coordinates.

q.q: Refer to the money-market graph. Starting at point e (MS1 with MD1), both money demand and money supply shift right to MD2 and MS2. The new equilibrium is point d. What does the change from r2 to r3 imply?
options: The rightward money-demand shift exerts more upward pressure on the interest rate than the rightward money-supply shift offsets.
The money-supply shift must have dominated because any increase in money supply mechanically raises interest rates more than a simultaneous money-demand shift can affect them.
Both rightward shifts necessarily leave the interest rate unchanged.
The new equilibrium shows that money demand fell relative to money supply.
q.commonError: Assumes the direction of one curve shift determines the interest rate even when both money demand and money supply move.
q.feedback: When money demand and money supply both shift, compare the new equilibrium with the old one; the interest-rate direction depends on their relative effects.
q.imageAlt: Money-market graph with two vertical money-supply curves and two downward-sloping money-demand curves.
q.graphDescription: The vertical axis is interest rate r and the horizontal axis is quantity of money Qm. MS1 is vertical at Qm1 and MS2 is vertical to its right at Qm2. MD1 slopes downward through e at Qm1, r2 and g at Qm2, r1. MD2 is shifted right/up and slopes downward through a at Qm1, r4 and d at Qm2, r3. Additional labeled points are b at Qm2, r4; c at Qm1, r3; and f at Qm1, r1.

q.q: Refer to the money-market graph. With MD2 and MS2, the equilibrium is point d at r3. If the interest rate is temporarily at point b on MS2 at r4, what adjustment should occur?
options: There is excess money demand, so households sell interest-bearing assets; bond prices fall and the interest rate rises farther above r4 before the market can clear.
Point b is already the equilibrium because it lies on MS2.
Money demand must shift right again before the interest rate can change.
There is excess money supply; people try to buy interest-bearing assets, putting downward pressure on the interest rate toward r3.
q.commonError: Treats a labeled point on a money-supply line as an equilibrium even when it is not on the active money-demand curve.
q.feedback: At an interest rate above equilibrium, money supplied exceeds money demanded and asset-market adjustment pushes the rate down; below equilibrium, excess money demand pushes it up.
q.imageAlt: Money-market graph with two vertical money-supply curves and two downward-sloping money-demand curves.
q.graphDescription: The vertical axis is interest rate r and the horizontal axis is quantity of money Qm. MS1 is vertical at Qm1 and MS2 is vertical to its right at Qm2. MD1 slopes downward through e at Qm1, r2 and g at Qm2, r1. MD2 is shifted right/up and slopes downward through a at Qm1, r4 and d at Qm2, r3. Additional labeled points are b at Qm2, r4; c at Qm1, r3; and f at Qm1, r1.

q.q: Refer to the money-market graph. With MD1 and MS1, equilibrium is point e at r2. If the interest rate is temporarily at r1, what pressure moves the market back toward equilibrium?
options: The market remains at r1 because a vertical money-supply curve prevents interest-rate adjustment.
The central bank must reduce the fixed money supply before households can obtain enough money balances and the interest rate can move back toward equilibrium.
Quantity of money demanded exceeds the fixed money supply, so attempts to raise money by selling interest-bearing assets put upward pressure on the interest rate.
Quantity of money supplied exceeds money demanded, so asset purchases push the interest rate lower.
q.commonError: Treats a labeled point on a money-supply line as an equilibrium even when it is not on the active money-demand curve.
q.feedback: At an interest rate above equilibrium, money supplied exceeds money demanded and asset-market adjustment pushes the rate down; below equilibrium, excess money demand pushes it up.
q.imageAlt: Money-market graph with two vertical money-supply curves and two downward-sloping money-demand curves.
q.graphDescription: The vertical axis is interest rate r and the horizontal axis is quantity of money Qm. MS1 is vertical at Qm1 and MS2 is vertical to its right at Qm2. MD1 slopes downward through e at Qm1, r2 and g at Qm2, r1. MD2 is shifted right/up and slopes downward through a at Qm1, r4 and d at Qm2, r3. Additional labeled points are b at Qm2, r4; c at Qm1, r3; and f at Qm1, r1.

q.q: Real income rises while the overall price level falls. With money supply fixed, what can be concluded about the equilibrium interest rate from liquidity-preference theory alone?
options: It cannot change because income and the price level never shift money demand.
The direction is ambiguous because higher income raises money demand while a lower price level reduces money demand.
It must rise because every increase in real income dominates every change in the price level.
It must fall because the price-level effect always dominates the income effect.
q.commonError: Assumes the direction of one curve shift determines the interest rate even when both money demand and money supply move.
q.feedback: When money demand and money supply both shift, compare the new equilibrium with the old one; the interest-rate direction depends on their relative effects.

q.q: The central bank increases the money supply and the equilibrium interest rate falls while income and the price level are unchanged. A student says, “Money demand shifted left.” What is the best correction?
options: The fall in the interest rate is a movement along the existing money-demand curve unless a money-demand shifter also changed.
The student is correct because any fall in interest rates shifts the entire money-demand curve left at every quantity, even when income and the price level are unchanged.
Money demand shifts right whenever money supply increases.
Money demand becomes horizontal after an expansionary money-supply change.
q.commonError: Calls an interest-rate-induced movement along a money-demand curve a shift of the curve.
q.feedback: A change in the interest rate causes movement along a given money-demand curve. Income or the price level can shift the money-demand curve.

q.q: Refer to the money-market graph. The economy begins at e with MD1 and MS1. Money demand shifts to MD2, and the central bank also expands money supply to MS2. Is the increase in money supply large enough to keep the interest rate at r2?
options: Yes. Any rightward money-supply shift exactly offsets any rightward money-demand shift.
Yes. Point d lies on MS2, so the interest rate must still equal r2.
No. The central bank would need to reduce money supply to keep the interest rate from rising.
No. The new equilibrium d is at r3, so the central bank would need a larger rightward money-supply shift to hold the rate at r2.
q.commonError: Uses a contractionary money-supply response to offset a rightward money-demand shift.
q.feedback: If money demand shifts right and the central bank wants to prevent the interest rate from rising, it must increase money supply enough to accommodate the higher demand.
q.imageAlt: Money-market graph with two vertical money-supply curves and two downward-sloping money-demand curves.
q.graphDescription: The vertical axis is interest rate r and the horizontal axis is quantity of money Qm. MS1 is vertical at Qm1 and MS2 is vertical to its right at Qm2. MD1 slopes downward through e at Qm1, r2 and g at Qm2, r1. MD2 is shifted right/up and slopes downward through a at Qm1, r4 and d at Qm2, r3. Additional labeled points are b at Qm2, r4; c at Qm1, r3; and f at Qm1, r1.

q.q: Real income rises, shifting money demand right, yet the observed equilibrium interest rate falls. Which inference is most consistent with the liquidity-preference model?
options: Money demand could not have risen because income never affects transaction demand.
The central bank must have held money supply fixed because a fixed supply guarantees a lower rate.
Money supply must have increased enough to more than offset the upward interest-rate pressure from higher money demand.
Money supply must have fallen because lower supply always lowers interest rates.
q.commonError: Ignores the opposing pressure from a money-demand increase when interpreting a falling interest rate.
q.feedback: If money demand rises but the equilibrium interest rate falls, money supply must have risen by enough to more than offset the upward interest-rate pressure from money demand.

q.q: In liquidity preference theory, the interest rate balances which two quantities?
options: money supply and money demand
taxes and government spending
exports and imports
labor supply and labor demand
q.commonError: confusing money market equilibrium with AD-AS equilibrium
q.feedback: The interest rate balances money supply and money demand.

q.q: If the price level rises, what happens in the money market?
options: Money demand rises and interest rates rise.
Money demand falls and interest rates fall.
Money supply rises and interest rates fall.
Money supply falls and interest rates fall.
q.commonError: thinking higher prices reduce money demand
q.feedback: Higher prices mean people need more money for transactions, so money demand rises and interest rates rise.

q.q: A higher price level raises money demand, interest rates rise, and investment falls by $40 billion. If MPC = 0.75, what is the total AD decrease from this channel?
options: $160 billion
$40 billion
$53.3 billion
$30 billion
q.commonError: using MPC instead of the multiplier
q.feedback: MPC 0.75 gives multiplier 4. A $40 billion investment fall reduces AD by $160 billion.

q.q: In the liquidity-preference model, the opportunity cost of holding money is the:
options: Interest income forgone by not holding interest-bearing assets.
The current price level paid for goods and services during the year.
The required reserve ratio applied to deposits held by commercial banks.
The previous year’s inflation rate reported by the statistical agency.
q.commonError: Confusing the opportunity cost of money with a price index or reserve rule.
q.feedback: Holding money sacrifices the interest that could have been earned on bonds or other interest-bearing assets.

q.q: If the money supply increases while money demand is unchanged, the equilibrium interest rate tends to:
options: Rise.
Fall.
Remain fixed by definition.
Become equal to the inflation rate.
q.commonError: Reversing the interest-rate effect of a rightward money-supply shift.
q.feedback: More money supplied at each interest rate creates excess money balances until the interest rate falls.

q.q: Which event shifts money demand to the right?
options: An open-market purchase that increases money supply.
A decrease in the amount of currency printed.
An increase in real income and transactions.
A lower required reserve ratio by itself.
q.commonError: Selecting a money-supply event as a money-demand shifter.
q.feedback: Higher income generates more transactions and raises the quantity of money people want to hold at each interest rate.

q.q: The price level rises while the nominal money supply is fixed. What happens in the money market?
options: Money demand falls and the equilibrium interest rate decreases.
Money supply rises and the equilibrium interest rate decreases.
Both curves remain fixed because only prices changed.
Money demand rises and the equilibrium interest rate increases.
q.commonError: Ignoring the transaction-money demand created by a higher price level.
q.feedback: A higher price level increases nominal transaction needs, shifting money demand right and raising the interest rate with fixed supply.

q.q: The central bank increases the money supply. Through the interest-rate effect, what happens next?
options: The interest rate falls, encouraging investment and aggregate demand.
The interest rate rises, reducing investment and aggregate demand.
The price level falls before the interest rate changes.
Money demand shifts left because reserves increased.
q.commonError: Reversing the monetary-policy transmission chain.
q.feedback: A larger money supply lowers the equilibrium interest rate, which tends to increase interest-sensitive spending.

q.q: Real income falls while the money supply is fixed. What is the likely equilibrium change?
options: Money demand rises and the interest rate increases.
Money demand falls and the interest rate decreases.
Money supply falls and the interest rate increases.
Money demand is unchanged because income is real.
q.commonError: Reversing the money-demand response to lower transaction volume.
q.feedback: Lower real income reduces transactions, shifts money demand left, and lowers the equilibrium interest rate.

q.q: Money demand shifts right while money supply is fixed. If the investment response to the interest-rate change is $50 billion and MPC = 0.75, what is the correct AD effect?
options: Money demand shifts right, r rises, investment falls, and AD decreases by $200 billion.
Money demand shifts right, r falls, investment rises, and AD increases by $200 billion.
Money supply shifts right, r falls, investment rises, and AD increases by $50 billion.
Money demand shifts left, r rises, investment falls, and AD decreases by $50 billion.
q.commonError: using the multiplier but reading the money-market movement backward
q.feedback: With fixed MS, higher MD raises r and lowers investment. MPC = 0.75 gives multiplier 4, so AD falls by $200 billion.

q.q: Money demand shifts left while money supply is fixed. If the investment response is $45 billion and MPC = 0.5, what is the correct AD effect?
options: MD shifts left, r falls, investment rises, and AD increases by $90 billion.
MD shifts left, r rises, investment falls, and AD decreases by $90 billion.
MD shifts right, r rises, investment falls, and AD decreases by $45 billion.
MD shifts right, r falls, investment rises, and AD increases by $45 billion.
q.commonError: claiming a price-level movement when the graph is a money-market shift
q.feedback: A leftward MD shift lowers r and raises investment. MPC 0.5 gives multiplier 2, so AD rises $90 billion.

q.q: The price level rises and shifts money demand right. The central bank wants to keep the interest rate unchanged. What action fits the model?
options: Decrease the money supply by selling securities.
Hold money supply fixed and require less investment.
Increase the money supply enough to match the higher money demand.
Shift aggregate supply left to reduce money demand.
q.commonError: Using contractionary policy to offset a rightward money-demand shift.
q.feedback: To prevent the interest rate from rising when money demand shifts right, the central bank must shift money supply right as well.

q.q: Refer to the money-market graph. With MD2 and MS2, point b is above the equilibrium interest rate at d. Which adjustment best explains movement toward equilibrium?
options: An excess supply of money leads people to buy interest-bearing assets, pushing the interest rate down toward r3.
An excess demand for money leads people to sell interest-bearing assets, lowering bond prices and pushing the interest rate farther above r4 until the central bank expands money supply.
Because MS2 is vertical, point b is an equilibrium regardless of money demand.
The central bank must shift MS2 left before any interest-rate adjustment can occur.
q.commonError: Treats a labeled point on a money-supply line as an equilibrium even when it is not on the active money-demand curve.
q.feedback: At an interest rate above equilibrium, money supplied exceeds money demanded and asset-market adjustment pushes the rate down; below equilibrium, excess money demand pushes it up.
q.imageAlt: Money-market graph with two vertical money-supply curves and two downward-sloping money-demand curves.
q.graphDescription: The vertical axis is interest rate r and the horizontal axis is quantity of money Qm. MS1 is vertical at Qm1 and MS2 is vertical to its right at Qm2. MD1 slopes downward through e at Qm1, r2 and g at Qm2, r1. MD2 is shifted right/up and slopes downward through a at Qm1, r4 and d at Qm2, r3. Additional labeled points are b at Qm2, r4; c at Qm1, r3; and f at Qm1, r1.

q.q: Refer to the money-market graph. The economy moves from e to d because both money demand and money supply shift right. Which conclusion is supported by the final interest rate?
options: The supply shift dominates, because every increase in money supply raises the interest rate.
The two shifts exactly offset, because both curves move right.
Money demand must have shifted left, because the equilibrium quantity of money rises.
The demand shift dominates the supply shift’s interest-rate effect, because the equilibrium rate rises from r2 to r3.
q.commonError: Assumes the direction of one curve shift determines the interest rate even when both money demand and money supply move.
q.feedback: When money demand and money supply both shift, compare the new equilibrium with the old one; the interest-rate direction depends on their relative effects.
q.imageAlt: Money-market graph with two vertical money-supply curves and two downward-sloping money-demand curves.
q.graphDescription: The vertical axis is interest rate r and the horizontal axis is quantity of money Qm. MS1 is vertical at Qm1 and MS2 is vertical to its right at Qm2. MD1 slopes downward through e at Qm1, r2 and g at Qm2, r1. MD2 is shifted right/up and slopes downward through a at Qm1, r4 and d at Qm2, r3. Additional labeled points are b at Qm2, r4; c at Qm1, r3; and f at Qm1, r1.

q.q: In liquidity preference theory, the interest rate balances:
options: Money supply and money demand
Taxes and transfers
Exports and imports
Inflation and unemployment
q.feedback: The interest rate adjusts to balance money supply and money demand.

q.q: If money demand rises and money supply is fixed, the interest rate tends to:
options: Rise
Fall
Become zero
Become GDP
q.feedback: Higher money demand pushes interest rates up when money supply is fixed.

q.q: In the money market, the equilibrium interest rate occurs where:
options: Money demand equals money supply
AD equals SRAS
Saving equals investment only
Government spending equals taxes
q.feedback: The money-market interest rate adjusts until the quantity of money demanded equals the quantity supplied.

q.commonError: Calls an interest-rate-induced movement along a money-demand curve a shift of the curve.
q.q: The central bank increases the money supply while income and the price level stay unchanged. The equilibrium interest rate falls. What happens to money demand in the standard diagram?
options: There is a movement down along the existing money-demand curve; the curve itself need not shift.
The money-demand curve shifts left because the lower interest rate changes households’ desired money holdings at every possible interest rate, not just at the new equilibrium.
The money-demand curve shifts right because the central bank supplied more money.
Money demand becomes vertical because the money supply changed.
q.feedback: A change in the interest rate causes movement along a given money-demand curve. Income or the price level can shift the money-demand curve.

q.commonError: Treats a labeled point on a money-supply line as an equilibrium even when it is not on the active money-demand curve.
q.q: At the current interest rate, households want to hold more money than the fixed money supply provides. Which adjustment moves the market toward equilibrium?
options: People try to obtain money by selling interest-bearing assets, putting upward pressure on the interest rate.
People buy interest-bearing assets, pushing the interest rate downward.
The money-demand curve automatically shifts left until it equals money supply.
The central bank must change money supply because the interest rate cannot adjust.
q.feedback: At an interest rate above equilibrium, money supplied exceeds money demanded and asset-market adjustment pushes the rate down; below equilibrium, excess money demand pushes it up.

q.commonError: Reversing the effect of price level on money demand.
q.q: When the price level rises, money demand usually:
options: Rises
Falls
Becomes zero
Turns into money supply
q.feedback: Higher prices mean people need more money for transactions.

q.commonError: Missing the investment step in the interest-rate effect.
q.q: Higher interest rates tend to make investment:
options: Fall
Rise
Become government spending
Equal money demand
q.feedback: Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive, so investment falls.

q.q: In the money market, if the interest rate is too low, quantity of money demanded is usually:
options: Greater than money supplied
Less than money supplied
Equal to zero
Equal to LRAS
q.feedback: At too low an interest rate, people demand more money than is supplied, pushing rates up.

q.q: Income rises, so people want to hold more money. If money supply is fixed, interest rates:
options: Rise
Fall
Become zero
Become inflation
q.feedback: Higher money demand with fixed money supply raises interest rates.

q.commonError: Confusing money-market and AD-AS equilibrium.
q.q: Money demand shifts right while money supply is fixed. What happens to the interest rate?
options: It rises
It falls
It becomes zero
It turns into the price level
q.feedback: With fixed money supply, higher money demand pushes the interest rate up.

q.commonError: Stops after finding the new money-market interest rate and does not carry the result into spending and aggregate demand.
q.q: A higher price level shifts money demand right while money supply is fixed, so the equilibrium interest rate rises. To carry that money-market result into the policy-transmission model, what happens next?
options: Interest-sensitive investment falls, putting downward pressure on aggregate demand.
Investment rises because higher rates make borrowing cheaper, shifting aggregate demand right.
Aggregate demand shifts left directly because the price level changed, with no spending channel involved.
The higher interest rate shifts money demand farther right but has no effect on spending.
q.feedback: After solving the money market, use the interest-rate change to infer the direction of investment and other rate-sensitive spending, then the aggregate-demand shift.

q.q: Money demand shifts right while money supply is fixed, raising the equilibrium interest rate. What is the next step if the student is bridging from the money market to monetary-policy transmission?
options: Higher borrowing costs reduce interest-sensitive investment and put downward pressure on aggregate demand.
Higher borrowing costs raise investment because firms earn more interest.
The higher interest rate directly increases government purchases.
Aggregate demand is unaffected because interest rates matter only inside the money-market graph.
q.commonError: Stops after finding the new money-market interest rate and does not carry the result into spending and aggregate demand.
q.feedback: After solving the money market, use the interest-rate change to infer the direction of investment and other rate-sensitive spending, then the aggregate-demand shift.

q.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
q.q: Economic growth is usually measured by increases in:
options: Real GDP per person
Nominal prices only
The unemployment rate
Imports only
q.feedback: Real GDP per person is commonly used to compare living standards and growth.

q.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
q.q: Why do small differences in growth rates matter over long periods?
options: They compound into large differences in income
They immediately eliminate unemployment
They make inflation impossible
They force imports to equal exports
q.feedback: Growth compounds, so small annual differences can become large over decades.

q.commonError: Forgetting that doubling time is approximately 70 divided by the growth rate.
q.q: The Rule of 70 estimates:
options: How long it takes a variable to double
The unemployment rate
The CPI basket cost
The size of net exports
q.feedback: The Rule of 70 estimates doubling time by dividing 70 by the growth rate.

q.q: Which measure is generally more useful than total real GDP for comparing average material living standards across countries of different sizes?
options: Nominal GDP.
The population growth rate alone.
The current price level.
Real GDP per person.
q.commonError: Using total output without adjusting for population size.
q.feedback: Real GDP per person relates inflation-adjusted output to the number of people sharing that output.

q.q: Over long periods, the most important source of rising average living standards is usually growth in:
options: Productivity, meaning more output produced from each unit of labor input.
The current price level, meaning higher prices for the same output.
The money supply, even when physical production remains unchanged.
One month’s unemployment rate, regardless of long-run output per worker.
q.commonError: Treating nominal variables as the main source of sustained real living-standard growth.
q.feedback: Higher productivity lets an economy produce more goods and services from its available labor and resources.

q.q: If real GDP grows 2 percent and population grows 3 percent, real GDP per person will approximately:
options: Rise 1 percent.
Fall 1 percent.
Rise 5 percent.
Remain unchanged.
q.commonError: Adding population growth to output growth.
q.feedback: Approximate per-person growth is 2% − 3% = −1%.

q.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
q.q: Country A grows at 1% per year and Country B grows at 4% per year. What is the most likely long-run result?
options: The income gap can become much larger over time
Both countries must end with the same income
Country A must always become richer
Growth rates do not affect living standards
q.feedback: Small growth-rate differences compound into large long-run income differences.

q.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
q.q: Why can a country that is poor today become much richer over several decades?
options: Sustained productivity growth can raise real GDP per person
Poor countries cannot grow
Only inflation can increase income
Unemployment must disappear first
q.feedback: Long-run growth in productivity can dramatically raise living standards.

q.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
q.q: Which comparison best captures differences in living standards across countries?
options: Real GDP per person
Nominal interest rates only
The number of banks
The unemployment rate alone
q.feedback: Real GDP per person is commonly used to compare living standards.

q.q: A country’s real GDP grows 4 percent and population grows 1 percent. Approximate growth in real GDP per person is:
options: 1 percent.
4 percent.
3 percent.
5 percent.
q.commonError: Using total GDP growth without adjusting for population.
q.feedback: Approximate real GDP per person growth is 4% − 1% = 3%.

q.q: A country raises output mainly by requiring much longer workweeks, while output per hour is unchanged. What is the most careful interpretation?
options: Productivity must rise because total output increased after workers supplied more hours.
Living standards must fall because any increase in work hours necessarily reduces output.
Real GDP per person cannot change when total hours worked change but output per hour does not.
Real GDP may rise, but productivity is unchanged and lost leisure can limit the welfare gain.
q.commonError: Equating more total labor input with higher productivity and complete welfare improvement.
q.feedback: More hours can raise output without raising output per hour, and GDP does not fully value lost leisure.

q.q: Why can a country with lower initial income eventually catch a richer country?
options: A persistently higher growth rate can compound enough to close the initial income gap.
Lower initial income automatically guarantees convergence even without faster growth.
Nominal GDP always grows faster in poorer countries because their prices are lower.
Population growth alone raises real output per person without any productivity change.
q.commonError: Assuming starting income permanently fixes a country’s relative position.
q.feedback: Sustained differences in growth rates compound over time and can outweigh an initial income gap.

q.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
q.q: A country with lower current income grows rapidly for several decades and catches up to richer countries. Which concept best explains this possibility?
options: Sustained growth and the catch-up effect
CPI substitution bias
Cyclical unemployment
Transfer payment accounting
q.feedback: Growth compounds over time, and poorer countries may grow faster when capital is scarce.

q.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
q.q: Which country likely has the higher living standard, holding other quality-of-life factors aside?
options: Country A with real GDP of $1T and population of 10M
Country B with real GDP of $2T and population of 80M
Country C with nominal GDP of $3T but unknown prices
Country D with higher inflation
q.feedback: Country A has real GDP per person of $100,000; Country B has $25,000.

q.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
q.q: Why can rankings of countries by income change dramatically over time?
options: Different growth rates compound over many years
Nominal GDP is always constant
Population never changes
The Rule of 70 prevents poor countries from growing
q.feedback: Long-run differences in growth rates can greatly change relative income levels.

q.q: Real GDP rises from $1.20 trillion to $1.32 trillion while population rises from 40 million to 42 million. Approximately how does real GDP per person change?
options: It rises from $30,000 to $33,000, a gain of exactly 10 percent.
It rises from $30,000 to about $31,429, a gain of roughly 4.8 percent.
It falls from $30,000 to about $28,571 as population increases.
It stays at $30,000 because both real GDP and population rose.
q.commonError: Comparing total GDP growth without recomputing output per person.

q.q: A country’s real GDP per person rises 3 percent, but most of the gain goes to a small share of households. What can be concluded?
options: Every household’s real income must have risen by exactly 3 percent.
Real GDP per person must have fallen because the distribution changed.
Average output per person rose, but the typical household may have gained less.
The price level must have increased by the same 3 percent.
q.commonError: Treating an average as a description of every household’s experience.
q.feedback: Real GDP per person is an average and does not reveal how income or output gains are distributed.

q.q: A country’s real GDP grows 3 percent while its population grows 4 percent. Approximately what happens to real GDP per person?
options: It rises about 7 percent.
It rises about 1 percent.
It remains unchanged.
It falls about 1 percent.
q.commonError: Adding population growth to output growth instead of subtracting it.
q.feedback: Approximate per-person growth equals real GDP growth minus population growth: 3% − 4% = −1%.

q.commonError: Forgetting that doubling time is approximately 70 divided by the growth rate.
q.q: Country A has real GDP per person of $20,000 and grows at 2%. Country B has real GDP per person of $10,000 and grows at 6%. Using the Rule of 70, what is the strongest long-run implication?
options: B can catch up because it doubles much faster than A
A must always remain richer because it starts ahead
B cannot grow because it is poorer
Both double every 35 years
q.feedback: A doubles in about 35 years; B doubles in about 11.7 years, so B can catch up if growth persists.

q.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
q.q: A country grows real GDP by 6% while population grows by 2%. Approximately what happens to real GDP per person?
options: It rises by about 4%
It rises by 8%
It falls by 4%
It is unchanged
q.feedback: Real GDP per person grows roughly by real GDP growth minus population growth, or about 4%.

q.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
q.q: A country with rapid population growth sees total real GDP rise but real GDP per person stay flat. What is the best interpretation?
options: Output is rising, but not faster than population
Living standards must be rising quickly
Productivity must have doubled
Inflation explains all growth
q.feedback: Living standards are better captured by output per person, not total output alone.

q.commonError: Forgetting that doubling time is approximately 70 divided by the growth rate.
q.q: Using the Rule of 70, Country X growing at 3.5% doubles in about how many years, and Country Y growing at 1.75% doubles in about how many years?
options: 20 years and 40 years
10 years and 20 years
35 years and 70 years
40 years and 20 years

q.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
q.q: Two economies have equally scarce capital and similar access to technology. One has reliable electricity and trained operators; the other has frequent outages and little training. Which evidence best limits a claim that both must catch up equally fast?
options: The complementary inputs differ, so equal capital scarcity does not imply equal realized gains
Scarce capital has a low marginal product in both, regardless of complementary inputs
Technology access proves training and infrastructure no longer matter
A country’s current income ranking fixes its future growth ranking
q.feedback: Capital scarcity can create high-return opportunities, but skilled workers and usable infrastructure help realize them. Catch-up is conditional; equal starting capital alone does not establish equal productivity growth.

q.commonError: Forgetting that doubling time is approximately 70 divided by the growth rate.
q.q: At the start, real GDP per person is $32,000 in Alder and $8,000 in Birch. Their persistent growth rates are 1.75% and 7%. Using the Rule of 70, which comparison follows after 40 years?
options: Alder is near $64,000 and Birch near $128,000; matching Alder’s initial level earlier was not yet catching its moving level
Both are near $64,000 because Birch began at one-quarter of Alder’s level
Alder is near $64,000 and Birch near $32,000; count only one doubling for Birch
Birch stays poorer because a lower starting level cannot be overcome
q.feedback: Approximate doubling times are 40 years for Alder and 10 for Birch. Over 40 years Alder doubles once to 64,000, while Birch doubles four times to 128,000. Reaching a rival’s initial level is distinct from catching a rival that also grows.

q.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
q.q: Over a decade, real GDP rises 12%, population rises 5%, and total labor hours rise 20%. Which pair best evaluates average material output and hourly productivity, to one decimal place?
options: Real GDP per person rises 6.7%; output per hour falls 6.7%
Both rise 12% because total real GDP rose
Real GDP per person rises 7%; output per hour falls exactly 8%
Real GDP per person falls 6.7%; output per hour rises 6.7%
q.feedback: Per-person output changes by 1.12/1.05 - 1 ≈ 6.7%; hourly output changes by 1.12/1.20 - 1 ≈ -6.7%. More total hours can raise average output even while productivity per hour falls.

q.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
q.q: Cedar reports nominal GDP of $960 billion, a deflator of 120, and 32 million residents. Delta reports $1,320 billion, a deflator of 150, and 44 million residents. Which current real-GDP-per-person comparison is supported using comparable base prices?
options: Cedar $25,000; Delta $20,000, so higher nominal total does not imply higher average real output
Cedar $30,000; Delta $30,000, so average real output is equal
Cedar $25,000; Delta $30,000, because only Cedar needs deflation
Cedar $20,000; Delta $25,000, because the larger deflator raises real output
q.feedback: Real GDP is 960/1.20 = 800 billion for Cedar and 1,320/1.50 = 880 billion for Delta. Divide by populations: 25,000 and 20,000 per person. The larger nominal aggregate does not settle the living-standard comparison.

q.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
q.q: A poor country grows quickly after gaining stable property rights, schools, and foreign investment. Which explanation is strongest?
options: Catch-up potential plus growth-supporting institutions
Growth must be caused only by inflation
Poor countries grow automatically regardless of policy
Property rights reduce investment
q.feedback: Catch-up growth is more likely when institutions support investment, human capital, and technology adoption.

q.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
q.q: Real output per hour rises 10%, annual hours per employed person fall 5%, and the employed share of the population falls from 60% to 58%. Which conclusion about real GDP per person follows, assuming these cover all production?
options: It rises about 1.0%; the other two factors offset much of the productivity gain
It rises 10%; hourly productivity alone determines the exact change
It falls 7%; add the percentage and percentage-point declines
It rises 5%; the employed share does not enter output per person
q.feedback: Output per person equals output/hour × hours/worker × workers/person. Its factor is 1.10 × 0.95 × (58/60) ≈ 1.01017. Average output rises about 1.0%, much less than the hourly-productivity increase.

q.q: Real GDP per person rises, but average leisure falls sharply and pollution worsens. What is the most careful conclusion?
options: Market output per person rose, but overall well-being may have changed differently.
Living standards rose by exactly the same rate because GDP per person captures all welfare changes.
GDP per person becomes unusable whenever leisure or environmental quality changes.
Pollution and lost leisure are already fully subtracted from measured real GDP.
q.commonError: Treating real GDP per person as a complete measure of welfare.
q.feedback: Real GDP per person is useful for material output, but it does not fully capture leisure, environmental quality, distribution, or nonmarket activity.

q.commonError: Forgetting that doubling time is approximately 70 divided by the growth rate.
q.q: If a country grows at 2% per year, the Rule of 70 says income doubles in about:
options: 35 years
70 years
14 years
2 years
q.feedback: 70 divided by 2 equals about 35 years.

q.commonError: Forgetting that doubling time is approximately 70 divided by the growth rate.
q.q: If a country grows at 7% per year, income doubles in about:
options: 10 years
20 years
70 years
7 years
q.feedback: 70 divided by 7 equals about 10 years.

q.commonError: Forgetting that doubling time is approximately 70 divided by the growth rate.
q.q: Country A grows at 2% and Country B grows at 5%. Using the Rule of 70, how much sooner does Country B double its income?
options: About 21 years sooner
About 3 years sooner
About 35 years sooner
About 70 years sooner
q.feedback: Country A doubles in about 35 years; Country B doubles in about 14 years, so B doubles about 21 years sooner.

q.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
q.q: If real GDP per person rises from $20,000 to $26,000, what is the percentage increase?

q.commonError: Forgetting that doubling time is approximately 70 divided by the growth rate.
q.q: Using the Rule of 70, a country growing at 5% per year doubles its income in about:
options: 7 years
14 years
35 years
70 years
q.feedback: 70 divided by 5 equals about 14 years.

q.commonError: Forgetting that doubling time is approximately 70 divided by the growth rate.
q.q: Using the Rule of 70, a country growing at 1% per year doubles its income in about:
options: 1 year
10 years
35 years
70 years
q.feedback: 70 divided by 1 equals about 70 years.

q.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
q.q: An economist asks: why do small differences in annual growth rates matter so much over long periods?
options: Because growth compounds over time
Because inflation always disappears
Because unemployment becomes impossible
Because GDP stops using prices
q.feedback: Small growth differences compound and can create large income gaps over decades.

q.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
q.q: Country A grows at 2% while Country B grows at 5%. What should you expect over several decades?
options: Country B's income will rise much faster if the growth rates persist
Both countries will end with the same income
Country A must grow faster because it starts slower
Growth rates do not affect living standards
q.feedback: Higher sustained growth leads to much larger long-run income gains.

q.commonError: Forgetting that doubling time is approximately 70 divided by the growth rate.
q.q: Using the Rule of 70, how long does it take income to double at a 5% annual growth rate?
options: 14 years
35 years
70 years
5 years
q.feedback: The Rule of 70 gives 70 / 5 = 14 years.

q.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
q.q: An economist points to two countries. Which measure is usually better for comparing average living standards?
options: Real GDP per person
Total nominal GDP
The unemployment rate alone
The number of firms
q.feedback: Real GDP per person is usually better for comparing average material living standards.

q.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
q.q: Country A has higher total GDP than Country B, but also has a much larger population. What should you check before comparing living standards?
options: GDP per person
Only total exports
Only the CPI basket
Only nominal interest rates
q.feedback: Total GDP can be misleading when countries have different population sizes.

q.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
q.q: Country A has real GDP of $2 trillion and a population of 50 million. What is real GDP per person?
q.feedback: Real GDP per person = $2 trillion / 50 million = $40,000.

q.q: A country reports $750 billion in inflation-adjusted output and 25 million residents. Which real-GDP-per-person figure is correct?
q.commonError: Dividing by the wrong population scale.
q.feedback: $750 billion ÷ 25 million residents = $30,000 per person.

q.q: Using the Rule of 70, income growing at 3.5 percent per year doubles in about:
options: 10 years.
35 years.
20 years.
70 years.
q.commonError: Multiplying 70 by the growth rate instead of dividing.

q.q: If population grows faster than real GDP, real GDP per person will generally:
options: Rise.
Remain unchanged.
Equal nominal GDP.
Fall.
q.commonError: Ignoring population growth when evaluating average output.
q.feedback: Per-person output falls when the population denominator grows faster than total real output.

q.q: Country A grows 2 percent annually and Country B grows 4 percent. Using the Rule of 70, their approximate doubling times are:
options: 35 years for A and 17.5 years for B.
14 years for A and 28 years for B.
17.5 years for A and 35 years for B.
70 years for both countries.
q.commonError: Reversing the relationship between growth rates and doubling times.
q.feedback: Doubling time is 70 divided by the growth rate: 70/2 = 35 and 70/4 = 17.5.

q.q: Country A has real GDP of $2 trillion and 100 million people. Country B has real GDP of $1.5 trillion and 50 million people. Which has higher real GDP per person?
options: Country A: $40,000 versus Country B’s $15,000.
Country B: $30,000 versus Country A’s $20,000.
Country A because its total real GDP is larger.
They are equal because both figures are measured in real terms.
q.commonError: Ranking living standards by total GDP rather than GDP per person.
q.feedback: A has $20,000 per person; B has $30,000 per person, so B has the higher average output per person.

q.q: Real GDP grows 5 percent and population grows 2 percent. Approximate real GDP per person growth is:
options: 2 percent.
7 percent.
3 percent.
10 percent.
q.commonError: Adding population growth to output growth.
q.feedback: Approximate per-person growth is 5% − 2% = 3%.

q.q: Country A doubles nominal wages while prices also double. Country B raises output per worker by 25% with stable prices. Which country has the clearer improvement in living standards?
options: Country A, because nominal wages doubled
Country B, because productivity and real output per worker increased
Both improved equally because wages and output are both economic variables
Neither can improve living standards without a price ceiling
q.commonError: confuses_nominal_income_growth_with_real_living_standard_growth
q.feedback: Higher nominal wages do not help if prices rise equally. Higher productivity supports higher real living standards.

q.q: Which factor best explains how a country can support higher wages and living standards over time?
options: Higher productivity allows workers to produce more output per hour
Higher nominal prices automatically create more real wealth
A price ceiling always increases available goods
Unemployment insurance directly raises productivity
q.commonError: confuses_higher_prices_with_higher_real_output
q.feedback: Long-run living standards depend heavily on productivity, meaning output produced per worker or per hour.

q.commonError: Forgetting that doubling time is approximately 70 divided by the growth rate.
q.q: Boss Audit: Country A starts at $60,000 per person and grows at 2%. Country B starts at $30,000 and grows at 7%. Using Rule of 70, what is the best implication?
options: B reaches $60,000 in about 10 years; A doubles in about 35
B cannot catch up because it starts lower
A doubles faster than B
Both double in 20 years
q.feedback: B doubles in about 10 years; A doubles in about 35 years.

q.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
q.q: Boss Audit: Real GDP rises 4%, population rises 1.5%, and output per worker rises 2%. What is approximate real GDP per person growth?
options: About 2.5%
About 5.5%
About 2%
About 4%
q.feedback: Real GDP per person growth is roughly real GDP growth minus population growth: 4 - 1.5 = 2.5%.

q.q: Country A starts at $48,000 real GDP per person and grows 2 percent annually. Country B starts at $24,000 and grows 4 percent. Using the Rule of 70, what is the strongest implication after about 35 years?
options: A remains twice as rich because starting income determines the permanent ranking.
B reaches only $48,000 because a 4 percent rate doubles once in 35 years.
A reaches $192,000 while B remains at $24,000.
Both are near $96,000 per person because A doubles once and B doubles twice.
q.commonError: Ignoring compounding and different doubling times when comparing convergence.
q.feedback: At 2 percent A doubles in about 35 years. At 4 percent B doubles in about 17.5 years, so it doubles twice in roughly 35 years.

q.q: Country A has nominal wages rise 12% while prices rise 12%. Country B has nominal wages rise 5%, prices rise 1%, and output per worker rises. Which country shows the stronger evidence of improved real living standards?
options: Country A, because nominal wages rose faster
Both are equal because both have wage growth
Country B, because real wages and productivity rose
Country A, because inflation confirms higher productivity
q.commonError: chooses_larger_nominal_wage_growth
q.feedback: Country B has real wage growth and rising productivity. Country A's nominal wage gain is wiped out by inflation.

q.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
q.q: Real GDP per person is calculated as:
options: Real GDP divided by population
Population divided by CPI
Exports minus imports
Labor force divided by unemployment
q.feedback: Real GDP per person is real GDP divided by population.

q.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
q.q: If real GDP is $1 trillion and population is 50 million, real GDP per person is:
q.feedback: $1 trillion / 50 million = $20,000.

q.commonError: Forgetting that doubling time is approximately 70 divided by the growth rate.
q.q: Which doubling-time question can be answered with the Rule of 70?
options: How long it takes income to double
The unemployment rate
The CPI basket cost
Net exports
q.feedback: The Rule of 70 estimates doubling time.

q.commonError: Forgetting that doubling time is approximately 70 divided by the growth rate.
q.q: At 2% growth, income doubles in about:
options: 35 years
2 years
70 years
14 years

q.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
q.q: Real GDP is $3 trillion and population is 100 million. What is real GDP per person?
q.feedback: $3 trillion / 100 million = $30,000.

q.commonError: Forgetting that doubling time is approximately 70 divided by the growth rate.
q.q: A country grows at 4% per year. About how long does income take to double?
options: 17.5 years

options: More projects pass the profitability test at higher rates

Investment demand shifts right automatically
Public saving becomes negative

A movement up along saving supply

q.q: New technology raises expected returns on capital at every real interest rate. What changes?
options: There is only movement along investment demand
Saving supply shifts left
The quantity axis shifts
Investment demand shifts right

q.q: Businesses become pessimistic about future sales. What is the correct diagrammatic treatment?

Investment demand shifts left
Saving supply moves upward along itself

An investment-demand shift
Movement along the saving curve
A change in public saving

q.q: A larger budget deficit lowers public saving while private-saving behavior and investment determinants remain unchanged. Which complete loanable-funds sequence follows?
options: National saving falls, investment demand shifts left, and both the rate and quantity fall
National saving rises, supply shifts right, and investment falls along demand
National saving is unchanged because public saving is not part of loanable-funds supply
Supply shifts left, raising the rate and reducing investment
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Loanable-Funds Equilibrium.
q.feedback: Public saving is part of national saving, which supplies loanable funds. A deficit lowers that supply, raises the equilibrium real interest rate, and crowds out investment along unchanged demand.

q.q: The real interest rate is above equilibrium with loanable-funds curves unchanged. Which adjustment moves the market back toward equilibrium?
options: Excess investment demand pushes the rate up, increasing the imbalance
Excess saving pushes the rate down toward equilibrium
Saving supply shifts left until all planned investment disappears
Investment demand shifts right because the high rate makes more projects profitable
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Loanable-Funds Equilibrium.
q.feedback: Above equilibrium, the quantity of funds supplied exceeds the quantity demanded. Downward pressure on the rate causes movements along both curves until planned saving and investment are equal.

q.q: Households become more willing to save at every real interest rate. The resulting equilibrium rate falls, and firms undertake more projects. Which description separates the initial cause from the response?
options: Investment demand shifts right first; saving rises through movement along unchanged supply
Both saving supply and investment demand shift right merely because their quantities rise
Saving supply shifts right; investment rises through movement down along unchanged demand
The lower rate shifts saving supply left and shifts investment demand right
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Movement Along Versus Shift.
q.feedback: Greater willingness to save shifts supply right. The lower equilibrium rate then makes more projects profitable, increasing investment as movement along the original investment-demand curve.

q.q: A retirement incentive increases saving at every real rate, while improved technology raises expected returns on investment. Which conclusion follows without knowing shift sizes?
options: Only saving supply shifts right, so the real rate must fall
Both curves shift right and equilibrium quantity rises; the real-rate direction is ambiguous
Both curves shift right and the real rate must remain unchanged
Saving supply shifts left while investment demand shifts right, so quantity is ambiguous
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Movement Along Versus Shift.
q.feedback: The saving incentive shifts supply right, while improved technology shifts investment demand right. Both changes raise equilibrium quantity, but their pressures on the real interest rate oppose one another.

q.q: Refer to the graph above. Treat the displayed curves as straight lines. At a temporary real interest rate of 10 percent, how large is the planned imbalance, and what adjustment returns this market toward A?

An 80-unit excess supply; a falling rate reduces saving supplied and increases investment demanded
An 80-unit excess demand; a rising rate reduces investment demanded and increases saving supplied
A 40-unit excess demand; a rising rate shifts saving supply right
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Loanable-Funds Equilibrium.
q.feedback: At 10 percent, S0 supplies 180 units and D0 demands 100, leaving excess supply of 80. A lower rate moves down along S0 and D0 toward their intersection at 140 units and 8 percent; neither curve must shift.

Movement along supply, followed by a rightward supply shift
The higher rate shifts supply right, while the incentive causes movement along the curve
Both changes cause movement along the original saving curve because neither affects demand
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Loanable-Funds Equilibrium.

q.q: A saving incentive shifts loanable-funds supply right. The lower equilibrium real rate makes more investment projects profitable, and firms also become more optimistic about future sales. Which description is complete?
options: Both investment increases are movements along demand because firms ultimately borrow more
Both investment increases shift demand because the equilibrium rate changes
The saving incentive shifts investment demand right, while optimism moves firms along that curve
Movement along demand, followed by a separate rightward demand shift
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Movement Along Versus Shift.
q.feedback: The saving shock lowers the rate and causes movement along the existing investment-demand curve. Optimism changes desired investment at every rate, so it separately shifts demand right.

q.q: Refer to the graph above. Treat the lines as straight. Starting at A, a technology change shifts D0 horizontally right while S0 stays fixed. The new equilibrium real rate is 10 percent, although the new demand curve is not drawn. What can be inferred about the shift and the quantity response?
options: Demand shifted right by 40 units; equilibrium investment rose by 40 through a rightward shift of S0
Demand shifted right by 80 units; equilibrium investment rose by 80 because saving must match the shift
Demand shifted right by 40 units; equilibrium investment rose by 80 through movement along D0
Demand shifted right by 80 units; equilibrium investment rose by 40 through movement along S0
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Loanable-Funds Equilibrium.
q.feedback: On S0, a 10 percent rate corresponds to 180 units. Old D0 demands 100 units at that rate, so the new demand schedule must be 80 units to the right. Equilibrium investment rises from 140 to 180, or 40 units. The unchanged saving schedule accommodates that quantity through a rate-induced movement; an accounting identity does not force a saving-supply shift.

q.q: At a real interest rate below equilibrium, desired investment exceeds desired saving. A student claims this disproves S = I in a closed economy. Which response correctly separates the accounting statement from the market adjustment?
options: Realized saving exceeds realized investment until the rate rises; inventory changes are excluded from investment
Realized investment equals desired investment at every rate; the saving identity applies only after the rate adjusts
Realized saving includes the financing gap as foreign saving; the rate rises until that gap disappears
Realized investment, including unplanned inventories, equals realized saving; excess demand for funds puts upward pressure on the rate
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Loanable-Funds Equilibrium.
q.feedback: S = I is an ex-post closed-economy accounting identity, including inventory investment. Planned quantities can disagree at a posted rate; that behavioral imbalance creates upward pressure on the real rate. Market clearing explains compatible plans, not the validity of the identity.

q.q: Initially, desired investment is I = 300 − 10r, with I in billions of dollars and r measured in percentage points. Technology changes only the intercept. The real rate rises from 4 to 7 percent, and equilibrium investment rises by $20 billion. What happened to investment demand, and what would investment have been at the original rate after the technology change?
options: Demand shifted right by $20 billion; investment at 4 percent would be $280 billion
Demand shifted right by $50 billion; investment at 4 percent would be $310 billion
Demand shifted right by $30 billion; investment at 4 percent would be $290 billion
Demand shifted right by $50 billion; investment at 4 percent would be $280 billion
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Movement Along Versus Shift.
q.feedback: Initial investment is 300 − 10(4) = $260 billion, so the new equilibrium quantity is $280 billion. The 3-point rate increase reduces quantity demanded by $30 billion along the new schedule. Technology therefore raises demand by $50 billion at every rate, making investment $310 billion at 4 percent.

q.feedback: Borrowers demand funds to finance desired investment, while national saving provides the funds supplied.

A $40 billion increase at every rate; public saving is excluded when constructing the saving-supply curve

q.feedback: At 6 percent, S0 and D0 each have quantity 40, while S1 and D1 each have quantity 80. Each schedule shifts right by $40 billion. Since national saving combines private and public saving, the private shift must satisfy private change − 10 = 40, giving +$50 billion. The two shifts leave the depicted equilibrium rate at 6 percent.
q.imageAlt: Loanable-funds graph with S0, S1, D0, D1 and labeled intersections A and B.
