The quantity axis has no currency scale. All curves are straight. The solid red line labeled S0 slopes upward through (0, 4) and (40, 6). The dashed red line labeled S1 slopes upward through (0, 2) and (80, 6). The solid blue line labeled D0 slopes downward through (0, 8) and (160, 0). The dashed blue line labeled D1 slopes downward through (0, 10) and (200, 0). Point A marks the S0–D0 intersection at (40, 6). Point B marks the S1–D1 intersection at (80, 6). A numbered grid provides the coordinate scale.
q.loanableFundsScenario: Saving and investment demand both increase

q.q: If national saving increases, which curve shifts?
options: Investment demand shifts right
Investment demand shifts left
Saving supply shifts left
The supply of loanable funds shifts right
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Changes in Saving.
q.feedback: National saving is the supply of loanable funds, so an increase shifts that curve right.

q.q: How does greater national saving connect to investment?
options: More supply raises financing cost and lowers investment
Saving shifts investment demand left by definition
More supply lowers financing cost and raises equilibrium investment
Saving removes all funds from financial markets
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Changes in Saving.
q.feedback: The supply shift lowers the real interest rate, encouraging more investment projects to be financed.

q.q: Which curve is vertical in the long run?
options: AD
SRAS
LRAS
Money demand
q.commonError: Confusing SRAS and LRAS.
q.feedback: LRAS is vertical because long-run output depends on resources, capital, technology, and institutions.

q.q: A rise in economy-wide productivity shifts long-run aggregate supply:
options: Not at all because productivity affects only demand.
Left.
Right.
Up along the same curve.
q.commonError: Confusing productive capacity with aggregate demand.
q.feedback: Higher productivity raises the economy’s sustainable level of output.

q.q: A hurricane destroys factories and transport infrastructure. Which long-run effect is most likely?
options: LRAS shifts left because productive capacity falls.
SRAS shifts right because inputs are scarcer.
LRAS shifts right because rebuilding spending rises.
Only AD shifts right.
q.commonError: Focusing on reconstruction spending while ignoring lost capacity.
q.feedback: Destroyed capital reduces the economy’s potential output.

q.q: A productivity improvement lowers production costs and raises potential output over time. Which curves are most likely affected?
options: SRAS right and LRAS right
AD left and SRAS left
SRPC up and AD left
MD right and MS left
q.commonError: Treating productivity only as demand.
q.feedback: Higher productivity can shift SRAS right and increase long-run aggregate supply.

q.q: A permanent labor-force increase raises productive capacity and tends to expand short-run supply. A simultaneous temporary energy-price spike tends to reduce short-run supply. No relative magnitudes are given. What can be concluded about LRAS and the net SRAS shift?
options: LRAS shifts right; the net SRAS direction is not determined.
LRAS shifts right; SRAS necessarily shifts left.
LRAS shifts left; SRAS necessarily shifts right.
LRAS stays fixed; SRAS necessarily shifts right.
q.commonError: Combining long-run capacity and short-run cost changes incorrectly.
q.feedback: The labor-force increase raises potential output, shifting LRAS right. The two events exert opposing pressures on SRAS, so their relative effects are needed to determine its net direction. A temporary energy-price spike does not by itself remove productive capacity.

q.q: A country receives a permanent productivity improvement and a temporary spike in imported input prices. Which graph change best fits?
options: Both curves shift left permanently
LRAS shifts left and SRAS right
Only aggregate demand shifts
LRAS shifts right, while SRAS may shift left initially.
q.commonError: Failing to separate permanent capacity from temporary production costs.
q.feedback: Productivity raises potential output; costly imported inputs can reduce short-run supply.

q.q: A permanent tax credit raises capital investment, while a temporary wage subsidy lowers current labor costs. Which supply changes are most likely?
options: LRAS shifts right over time and SRAS shifts right immediately.
SRAS shifts left because subsidies raise wages
LRAS shifts left and SRAS right
Only AD shifts right
q.commonError: Failing to distinguish capacity growth from current cost reduction.
q.feedback: More capital raises potential output, while the subsidy lowers short-run production cost.

q.q: For this capacity calculation only, potential output equals usable capital multiplied by output per unit of usable capital; other inputs are sufficient and unchanged. Usable capital falls by 5 percent while output per unit rises by 8 percent. A planner claims that any productivity gain above 5 percent would restore the original LRAS position. Which assessment is correct?
options: Potential output rises by 2.6 percent, but exactly restoring it would require a productivity gain of about 5.26 percent.
Potential output rises by 3 percent, and a 5 percent productivity gain would exactly restore it.
Potential output falls by 2.6 percent, and an 8 percent productivity gain cannot offset the capital loss.
Potential output is unchanged because the two percentage changes cancel exactly.
q.commonError: Comparing raw percentages that apply to different economic quantities.
q.feedback: Capacity becomes 0.95 × 1.08 = 1.026 times its original value, a 2.6 percent increase and a rightward LRAS shift. The break-even productivity factor is 1/0.95, or a gain of approximately 5.26 percent. Percentages with different bases cannot simply be subtracted.

q.q: A permanent improvement in education raises worker productivity, but a new regulation raises current compliance costs. Which statement is most complete?
options: LRAS shifts right; opposing SRAS effects make its net shift uncertain
LRAS shifts left; both changes move SRAS to the left
LRAS is unchanged; both changes move SRAS to the right
LRAS shifts right; compliance costs necessarily outweigh productivity gains
q.commonError: Treating permanent productivity and current cost changes as identical.
q.feedback: Education raises capacity; compliance costs can reduce short-run supply.

q.q: LRAS is vertical because long-run output depends primarily on:
options: Labor, capital, resources, and technology.
The current price level.
The nominal money supply alone.
Consumer confidence.
q.commonError: Treating the price level as the source of long-run output.
q.feedback: Potential output is determined by productive capacity.

q.q: A permanent rise in productivity most directly shifts:
options: AD right only.
LRAS right.
SRAS left only.
LRAS left.
q.commonError: Misclassifying a capacity improvement.
q.feedback: Higher productivity raises potential output.

q.q: A larger permanent labor force adds productive capacity and supports short-run supply, but a temporary oil-price spike pushes short-run supply in the opposite direction. Before their relative sizes are known, which conclusion should an AD-AS analysis carry forward?
options: LRAS shifts right; SRAS necessarily shifts left.
LRAS shifts left; SRAS necessarily shifts right.
LRAS shifts right; the net SRAS direction is not determined.
LRAS stays fixed; SRAS necessarily shifts right.
q.commonError: Combining capacity and cost changes incorrectly.
q.feedback: The labor-force increase raises potential output, shifting LRAS right. The two events exert opposing pressures on SRAS, so their relative effects are needed to determine its net direction. A temporary energy-price spike does not by itself remove productive capacity.

q.q: Capital is destroyed while a new technology raises productivity. Which LRAS conclusion is valid?
options: LRAS cannot shift because the forces differ
LRAS must shift left
LRAS must shift right
The net direction is ambiguous without the relative output effects.
q.commonError: Comparing opposing capacity changes without magnitudes.
q.feedback: Lost capital and better technology push potential output in opposite directions.

q.q: LRAS is vertical because long-run output depends mainly on:
options: Resources, capital, technology, and institutions
The current price level only
Short-run money demand only
Temporary inflation surprises only
q.feedback: LRAS reflects productive capacity, not the current price level.

q.q: Better technology and more productive capital most directly shift which long-run curve?
options: LRAS right
AD left
SRPC up
Money demand left
q.feedback: Better productive capacity shifts LRAS right.

q.q: In the long run, an economy returns to natural output because:
options: Nominal wages and expectations adjust
AD becomes vertical
Money demand disappears
Taxes must equal zero
q.commonError: Thinking short-run gaps last forever.
q.feedback: Over time, wages, prices, and expectations adjust, moving output back toward natural output.

q.q: Real GDP is below potential and labor-market slack is putting downward pressure on nominal wage growth. If aggregate demand does not change again, which adjustment helps the economy self-correct?
options: SRAS shifts right as wage and production-cost pressures ease.
AD shifts right automatically because unemployment is high.
LRAS shifts left until it reaches the depressed output level.
SRAS shifts left because firms are producing below potential.
q.commonError: Assumes aggregate demand must shift back on its own for the economy to return to potential output.
q.feedback: With aggregate demand unchanged, wage, cost, and price-expectation adjustment can shift SRAS so real output returns toward potential.

q.q: A boom in foreign economies raises net exports and pushes output above potential. In the long run, expected prices likely:
options: Rise and shift SRAS left
Fall and shift SRAS right
Stay fixed forever
Shift AD farther right
q.commonError: Thinking output stays above potential forever.
q.feedback: When output is above potential, pressures raise expected prices and shift SRAS left over time.

q.q: A negative demand shock pushes output below potential. If policymakers do nothing, long-run adjustment likely involves:
options: Falling expected prices and SRAS shifting right
Rising expected prices and SRAS shifting left
LRAS shifting left permanently
AD becoming horizontal
q.commonError: Missing self-correction through expectations.
q.feedback: Below-potential output puts downward pressure on wages and expected prices, shifting SRAS right.

q.q: An increase in demand that remains in place pushes production above potential. Policymakers do nothing, and wage contracts are gradually renegotiated as workers and firms revise price expectations upward. Which change is most consistent with self-correction?
options: Higher wages and input costs shift SRAS left while aggregate demand stays at its post-boom position.
Aggregate demand shifts left automatically as soon as wages rise.
LRAS shifts right because the economy briefly produced above potential.
SRAS shifts right because firms respond to the higher price level by cutting costs.
q.commonError: Assumes aggregate demand must shift back on its own for the economy to return to potential output.
q.feedback: With aggregate demand unchanged, wage, cost, and price-expectation adjustment can shift SRAS so real output returns toward potential.

q.q: Refer to the graph with LRAS. Starting at AD2-AS2, long-run self-correction most likely shifts:
options: SRAS left toward AS1
SRAS right toward AS2
AD left toward AD1
LRAS right toward Y2
q.commonError: Missing expected price adjustment after an expansionary gap.
q.feedback: At Y2 output is above potential, so rising wages and expected prices shift SRAS left.

q.q: Refer to the graph with LRAS. Starting at AD1-AS1, long-run self-correction most likely shifts:
options: SRAS right toward AS2
SRAS left toward AS1
AD right toward AD2
LRAS left toward Y3
q.commonError: Missing expected price adjustment after a recessionary gap.
q.feedback: At Y3 output is below potential, so wages and expected prices tend to fall, shifting SRAS right.

q.q: A negative AD shock lowers output and prices. What long-run adjustment restores output if no policy responds?
options: Wages and expected prices fall
Wages and expected prices rise
Money demand rises permanently
LRPC shifts right
q.commonError: Thinking recessionary gaps cannot self-correct.
q.feedback: Lower wages and expected prices shift SRAS right and help output return to natural.

q.q: A positive AD shock pushes output above potential. What long-run adjustment restores output if no policy responds?
options: Wages and expected prices rise
Wages and expected prices fall
SRAS shifts right immediately
LRAS shifts to AD2
q.commonError: Thinking booms above potential persist forever.
q.feedback: Higher wages and expected prices shift SRAS left and return output to potential.

q.q: Which statement best describes the macro outcome shown by the move from A to B?
options: Recession with accelerating inflation pressure.
Demand-pull inflation with no long-run growth.
Long-run growth with lower price pressure.
No change in either output or the price level.
q.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
q.feedback: Higher LRAS and SRAS support more output alongside a lower price level.
q.imageAlt: AD-AS graph with AD0, SRAS0, SRAS1, vertical LRAS0 and LRAS1, and intersections A and B.
q.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is real GDP and the vertical axis is price level. Blue AD0 slopes downward. Red SRAS0 slopes upward; dashed SRAS1 lies below and right of SRAS0. LRAS0 is vertical at GDP 100 and dashed LRAS1 is vertical to its right at GDP 115. A, the AD0-SRAS0-LRAS0 intersection, is at (100,125). B, the AD0-SRAS1-LRAS1 intersection, is at (115,110). Dashed guides connect A and B to the axes.

q.q: Refer to the graph with LRAS. Starting at AD2-AS2, which long-run adjustment is most consistent with self-correction?
options: SRAS shifts left until output returns to Y1
SRAS shifts right until output reaches Y3
AD shifts right until output reaches Y2
LRAS shifts right until it reaches Y2
q.commonError: Moving LRAS instead of SRAS during short-run self-correction.
q.feedback: At Y2, output is above natural output, so rising wages and expected prices shift SRAS left toward long-run equilibrium.

q.q: Refer to the graph with LRAS. Starting at AD1-AS1, which long-run adjustment is most consistent with self-correction?
options: SRAS shifts right until output returns to Y1
SRAS shifts left until output returns to Y3
AD shifts left until output returns to Y3
LRAS shifts left until it reaches Y3
q.commonError: Moving AD or LRAS instead of SRAS during self-correction.
q.feedback: At Y3, output is below natural output, so falling wages and expected prices shift SRAS right toward long-run equilibrium.

q.q: Output initially exceeds potential after a lasting AD expansion. Compare two separate responses, each sufficient to restore potential output: a demand policy with SRAS held fixed, or wage/expectation adjustment with AD held fixed. How do their price-level effects compare with the initial short-run equilibrium?
options: Contractionary policy lowers the price level; wage adjustment raises it.
Both responses lower the price level because both reduce output.
Contractionary policy raises the price level; wage adjustment lowers it.
Neither response changes the price level because both restore potential output.
q.commonError: Pairing the wrong policy with the wrong output gap.
q.feedback: AD contraction moves down along fixed SRAS, lowering output and price. Rising wages shift SRAS left, lowering output but raising price along fixed AD. The two paths share an output target, not a price outcome.

q.q: Output initially lies below potential after a lasting AD decline. Compare two separate responses, each sufficient to restore potential output: a demand policy with SRAS held fixed, or wage/expectation adjustment with AD held fixed. How do their price-level effects compare with the initial short-run equilibrium?
options: Expansionary policy raises the price level; wage adjustment lowers it.
Both responses raise the price level because both raise output.
Expansionary policy lowers the price level; wage adjustment raises it.
Neither response changes the price level because both restore potential output.
q.commonError: Pairing recessionary gaps with contractionary policy.
q.feedback: AD expansion moves up along fixed SRAS, raising output and price. Falling wages shift SRAS right, raising output but lowering price along fixed AD. The two paths share an output target, not a price outcome.

q.q: An economy begins at natural output. AD rises unexpectedly, then expected prices rise. Which sequence is most likely?
options: Output rises first, then SRAS shifts left
Output falls first, then SRAS shifts right
Prices fall first, then AD shifts left
LRAS shifts right, then output falls
q.commonError: Skipping the short-run expansion before long-run adjustment.
q.feedback: An unexpected AD increase raises output in the short run, but higher expected prices later shift SRAS left.

q.q: An economy begins at natural output. AD falls unexpectedly, then expected prices fall. Which sequence is most likely?
options: Output falls first, then SRAS shifts right
Output rises first, then SRAS shifts left
Prices rise first, then LRAS shifts left
AD rises first, then unemployment rises
q.commonError: Skipping the short-run recession before self-correction.
q.feedback: An unexpected AD decrease lowers output first, then lower expected prices shift SRAS right over time.

q.q: Refer to the graph with LRAS. Starting at AD1-AS2, a lasting demand expansion moves AD to AD2. Wage adjustment then moves SRAS all the way to AS1. Only after this adjustment does a delayed fiscal contraction return AD to AD1. With wages slow to change again, why does this delayed action fail to restore the original equilibrium immediately?
options: It leaves the economy at Y3/P2, below potential; restoring the original Y1/P1 with AD1 requires SRAS to move back to AS2.
It leaves the economy at Y1/P1 immediately, because restoring AD always restores the original equilibrium.
It leaves the economy at Y2/P2, because wage adjustment shifted LRAS to Y2.
It leaves the economy at Y1/P3, because a contraction cannot change output once wages have adjusted.
q.commonError: Confusing short-run output with long-run potential output.
q.feedback: The sequence is AD1-AS2 at Y1/P1, AD2-AS2 at Y2/P2, AD2-AS1 at Y1/P3, then AD1-AS1 at Y3/P2. After wages adjusted to the demand expansion, simply restoring old demand creates a new recessionary gap. Subsequent lower wage and expected-price pressures can return SRAS toward AS2.

q.q: Refer to the graph with LRAS. The economy starts at AD1-AS1, below potential. Two separate counterfactuals restore Y1: leave AD fixed and allow SRAS to reach AS2, or hold AS1 fixed and expand AD to AD2. If policymakers implement the full demand expansion after SRAS has already reached AS2, what happens and why?
options: Output reaches Y2/P2, above potential, because each full remedy was sized for the original gap rather than the already-adjusted economy.
Output remains Y1/P1 because self-correction prevents fiscal policy from changing demand.
Output remains Y1/P3 because a policy calibrated to the original gap automatically shrinks as wages adjust.
Output falls to Y3/P2 because combining two output-restoring changes reverses both shifts.
q.commonError: Moving LRAS instead of SRAS during self-correction.
q.feedback: Self-correction alone gives AD1-AS2 at Y1/P1; the policy alone gives AD2-AS1 at Y1/P3. Combining both full changes gives AD2-AS2 at Y2/P2. A policy appropriate before cost adjustment can be excessive after the gap has closed.

q.q: A one-time aggregate-demand decline that remains in place lowers output below potential. With no policy response and flexible wages and expected prices over time, what is the long-run outcome?
options: SRAS shifts right and output returns to potential at a lower price level.
Output remains permanently below potential with the original price level.
LRAS shifts left until productive capacity matches the recession output.
Aggregate demand automatically shifts right because unemployment increased.
q.commonError: Treating a temporary demand shock as a permanent change in productive capacity.
q.feedback: Falling wages and expected prices shift SRAS right, restoring natural output while leaving the price level lower.

q.q: Refer to the graph. A demand increase has moved the economy to the intersection of AD2 and AS2 at Y2 and P2. If no policy reverses AD2 and long-run adjustment is completed, which comparison between the short-run and long-run effects is supported by the graph?
options: The temporary output gain disappears as output returns to Y1, while the price level rises further toward P3.
Output remains at Y2 because long-run adjustment changes only the price level, which falls all the way back toward P1.
Output falls to Y3 as SRAS shifts left past AS1, while the price level stays fixed at the short-run level P2.
Both real output and the price level return to their original Y1 and P1 values once wage contracts and expectations adjust.
q.commonError: Assumes aggregate demand must shift back on its own for the economy to return to potential output.
q.feedback: With aggregate demand unchanged, wage, cost, and price-expectation adjustment can shift SRAS so real output returns toward potential.

q.q: Two economies have identical recessionary gaps. In Economy A, most wages can be reset monthly; in Economy B, most wages are fixed by three-year contracts. With no policy response, which prediction best follows from the long-run adjustment model?
options: Economy B should self-correct faster because longer wage contracts make SRAS respond more quickly to the recessionary gap.
Both economies must return to potential at exactly the same speed because a vertical LRAS fixes the timing as well as the destination.
Neither economy can self-correct without an aggregate-demand policy change because wage and cost adjustment cannot move SRAS.
Economy A should tend to self-correct faster because wages and production costs can adjust sooner.
q.commonError: Assumes self-correction is instantaneous even when wages and expectations are sticky.
q.feedback: Long-run adjustment can take time because wage contracts, input costs, and price expectations may change gradually.

q.q: After a negative aggregate-demand shock, real output begins recovering toward potential even though policymakers make no fiscal or monetary change. Nominal wage growth has slowed and firms report easing unit labor costs. What is the strongest interpretation?
options: The evidence requires LRAS to have shifted left until it met current output, converting the recessionary gap into long-run equilibrium.
The recovery shows wage adjustment is irrelevant because only changes in aggregate demand can move real output back toward potential.
The evidence is consistent with self-correction through a rightward SRAS shift, not necessarily an active stabilization policy.
The recovery proves aggregate demand was shifted right by discretionary policy even though no fiscal or monetary action is observed.
q.commonError: Attributes any recovery toward potential to active policy even when wages and expectations are adjusting with no policy change.
q.feedback: Self-correction is the endogenous SRAS response to an output gap; stabilization policy is a separate deliberate intervention.

q.q: An economy has a recessionary gap and policymakers do nothing. Which self-correcting sequence is most consistent with the model?
options: Higher wages shift SRAS left and deepen the recessionary gap.
LRAS shifts left until potential output equals the depressed output level.
Lower wage and price expectations shift SRAS right toward potential.
Aggregate demand rises automatically because the current price level is fixed.
q.commonError: Reversing the wage and SRAS adjustment in a recessionary gap.
q.feedback: Below-potential output puts downward pressure on wages and expected prices, allowing SRAS to shift right.

q.q: Demand growth pushes output above potential. If no stabilization policy is used, which long-run adjustment is most likely?
options: Falling wages shift SRAS right and push output farther above potential.
LRAS shifts right solely because the current price level has increased.
Output stays permanently above potential without creating inflation pressure.
Rising costs shift SRAS left, returning output to potential at a higher price level.
q.commonError: Using recessionary-gap adjustment for an inflationary gap.
q.feedback: An overheated labor market raises costs and expected prices, shifting SRAS left and closing the inflationary gap.

q.q: Output is below potential and unemployment is unusually high. If policymakers do nothing, which pressure is part of the opening self-correction mechanism?
options: Weak labor demand restrains wage and cost growth, creating pressure for SRAS to shift right.
High unemployment automatically shifts aggregate demand right.
Weak labor demand shifts LRAS left by definition.
High unemployment causes SRAS to shift left through higher wage growth.
q.commonError: Assumes aggregate demand must shift back on its own for the economy to return to potential output.
q.feedback: With aggregate demand unchanged, wage, cost, and price-expectation adjustment can shift SRAS so real output returns toward potential.

q.q: Refer to the graph. The economy begins at AD1-AS2 at Y1 and then a demand boom shifts AD to AD2, moving output to Y2. With no policy response, which pair of changes completes long-run adjustment?
options: AD shifts back to AD1 automatically; output returns to Y1 at P1.
LRAS shifts right to Y2; output remains above its original potential.
SRAS shifts right beyond AS2; output rises further while the price level falls.
SRAS shifts left toward AS1; output returns to Y1 while the price level rises toward P3.
q.commonError: Assumes aggregate demand must shift back on its own for the economy to return to potential output.
q.feedback: With aggregate demand unchanged, wage, cost, and price-expectation adjustment can shift SRAS so real output returns toward potential.

q.q: An economy is above potential because of a temporary surge in household spending. Which observation would be the strongest evidence that long-run self-correction has begun?
options: Aggregate demand is automatically shifting left with no change in spending.
Nominal wage growth is falling, pushing SRAS farther to the right.
Nominal wage and unit-cost growth are rising, putting leftward pressure on SRAS.
Potential output is falling simply because current output is high.
q.commonError: Assumes aggregate demand must shift back on its own for the economy to return to potential output.
q.feedback: With aggregate demand unchanged, wage, cost, and price-expectation adjustment can shift SRAS so real output returns toward potential.

q.q: Refer to the graph. At AD1 and AS1 the economy is at Y3, below Y1. If AD1 remains fixed, which change must occur for self-correction toward Y1?
options: SRAS shifts farther left from AS1, reducing output below Y3.
Falling wage and price expectations shift SRAS right from AS1 toward AS2.
Aggregate demand shifts from AD1 to AD2 while SRAS remains at AS1.
LRAS shifts left from Y1 to Y3 because output is currently low.
q.commonError: Assumes aggregate demand must shift back on its own for the economy to return to potential output.
q.feedback: With aggregate demand unchanged, wage, cost, and price-expectation adjustment can shift SRAS so real output returns toward potential.

q.q: A negative demand shock leaves the economy below potential, and no policy response occurs. Which statement best identifies the long-run adjustment mechanism before tracing the details?
options: Slack puts downward pressure on wages and expected prices, allowing SRAS to shift right.
Aggregate demand must automatically shift right enough to restore potential output without any change in wages or expectations.
LRAS must move left until it passes through current output, eliminating the gap without any cost adjustment.
High unemployment raises wage growth and shifts SRAS left, moving output even farther below potential.
q.commonError: Assumes aggregate demand must shift back on its own for the economy to return to potential output.
q.feedback: With aggregate demand unchanged, wage, cost, and price-expectation adjustment can shift SRAS so real output returns toward potential.

q.q: Refer to the graph. Starting at AD1-AS1 at Y3, expected prices and nominal cost pressures fall gradually while AD1 stays fixed. Which sequence is consistent with the model?
options: SRAS moves farther left from AS1, pushing output below Y3 while the price level rises above its starting point.
AD shifts to AD2 and output jumps to Y2 even though the prompt holds aggregate demand fixed throughout the adjustment.
LRAS shifts left from Y1 to Y3, redefining the depressed output level as potential without any wage or expectation adjustment.
SRAS moves toward AS2, output rises toward Y1, and the price level falls toward P1.
q.commonError: Assumes aggregate demand must shift back on its own for the economy to return to potential output.
q.feedback: With aggregate demand unchanged, wage, cost, and price-expectation adjustment can shift SRAS so real output returns toward potential.

q.q: If output is below natural output, falling wages and expected prices shift SRAS:
options: Right
Left
Into AD
Into LRPC
q.feedback: A recessionary gap tends to push wages and expected prices down, shifting SRAS right.

q.q: If output is above natural output, rising wages and expected prices shift SRAS:
options: Left
Right
Into AD
Into money supply
q.feedback: An expansionary gap tends to push wages and expected prices up, shifting SRAS left.

q.q: Output is above potential and self-correction through rising wages and costs is expected to be slow. Which stabilization-policy question becomes relevant?
options: Stabilization policy—whether and how to use an active policy response instead of waiting for self-correction.
Money measurement—whether currency should be counted in M1 or M2.
Growth accounting—how much of productivity comes from capital deepening.
CPI measurement—whether the market basket overstates cost-of-living changes.
q.feedback: Long-run adjustment describes self-correction; stabilization policy asks whether policymakers should actively shift aggregate demand rather than wait.
q.commonError: Treats passive long-run adjustment and deliberate stabilization as the same mechanism.

q.q: The long-run Phillips curve is vertical at:
options: The natural rate of unemployment
Zero inflation
The money supply
The highest price level
q.commonError: Confusing SRPC with LRPC.
q.feedback: The LRPC is vertical at the natural rate of unemployment.

q.q: Refer to the graph. Which unemployment rate is the natural rate?
options: U1
U2
U3
I1
q.commonError: Ignoring the vertical LRPC.
q.feedback: The LRPC is drawn at U2, so U2 is the natural rate of unemployment.
q.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves and a vertical long-run Phillips curve at unemployment rate U2, with labeled points a through d.
q.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. A vertical LRPC stands at U2. SRPC1 is the lower/left downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/right downward-sloping curve. Point a is at U1/I2 on SRPC1, point b is at U2/I2 where SRPC2 meets the LRPC, point c is at U2/I1 where SRPC1 meets the LRPC, and point d is at U3/I1 on SRPC2. Dashed guides mark unemployment rates U1-U3 and inflation rates I1-I2.

q.q: Refer to the graph. At U3, SRPC2 has inflation rate:
options: I1
I2
I3
I4
q.commonError: Reading the wrong curve at the same unemployment rate.
q.feedback: At U3, the upper curve SRPC2 is at I4.
q.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves, labeled unemployment rates U1 through U4, inflation rates I1 through I4, and points a through f.
q.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. SRPC1 is the lower downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/rightward downward-sloping curve. On SRPC1, point a is at U1/I4, b at U2/I3, c at U3/I2, and d at U4/I1. On SRPC2, point f is at U3/I4 and point e is at U4/I3. Dashed guides connect the labeled points to unemployment rates U1-U4 and inflation rates I1-I4.

q.q: Refer to the graph. At U4 on SRPC1, inflation is:
options: I1

q.q: Assume a fixed natural rate, no supply shocks, and an unchanged Phillips slope. Each year expected inflation equals the previous year’s actual inflation. Policy keeps unemployment the same fixed distance below natural. What must happen to actual inflation and the inflation surprise?

q.commonError: Assuming one expansion can hold unemployment below the natural rate forever.
q.feedback: With an unchanged slope and unemployment gap, the required actual-minus-expected inflation gap is constant. Because expectations catch up to the previous actual rate, actual inflation must rise again by that same amount. Ever-higher inflation does not require ever-larger forecast errors.

q.q: Two economies have the same natural unemployment rate but very different average inflation rates over many years. Which observation is most consistent with a vertical long-run Phillips curve?

q.q: A matching reform lowers the natural unemployment rate from 6.4 percent to 5.6 percent. At the same time, an unexpected demand expansion lowers actual unemployment to 4.9 percent. LRPC shifts to 5.6 percent, but expectations adjustment permanently fixes unemployment at 4.9 percent.

q.commonError: Confusing a change in the natural rate with a movement caused by inflation.
q.feedback: The structural shift is 6.4 − 5.6 = 0.8 percentage point. Actual unemployment is temporarily 5.6 − 4.9 = 0.7 point below the new natural rate. Once the demand surprise disappears, the long-run anchor is 5.6, not the old 6.4 or temporary 4.9.

Total-benefit reasoning without considering added cost
q.commonError: Missing the one-more-unit focus of marginal analysis.
q.feedback: The question compares the benefit and cost created by one additional hour.

A reason to continue so the payment is not wasted.
