q.commonError: Adding benefit and cost or reporting only one side.
q.feedback: Net marginal benefit is $70 minus $52.

q.q: A store has already paid monthly rent. When deciding whether to stay open one more hour, how should that rent be treated?
options: As a sunk cost that does not change with the hour
As the marginal cost of every extra hour
As the marginal benefit of added sales
As an avoidable cost only if sales are low
q.commonError: Assigning a fixed past payment to the next-hour decision.
q.feedback: Only costs that change with the additional hour are marginal.

q.q: A clinic can treat one more patient. Which question is marginal?
options: What added benefit and added cost will this patient create?
What have all patients cost since the clinic opened?
What is average benefit across all patients?
How large was the clinic’s original construction budget?
q.commonError: Substituting total, average, or historical values for the next increment.
q.feedback: Marginal analysis asks what changes because of one additional patient.

q.q: A business owner already spent $2,000 on a project. Finishing the project costs another $500 and will bring in $800. What should matter for the decision?
options: The extra $500 cost and extra $800 benefit
The full $2,500 spent across the whole project
Only the sunk $2,000
Only whether the project feels successful
q.commonError: includes_sunk_cost_in_marginal_decision
q.feedback: The decision should compare the additional cost of finishing with the additional benefit.

q.q: The marginal benefit of the fourth unit is $18 and its marginal cost is $14. The fourth unit should be:
options: Produced or consumed because marginal benefit exceeds marginal cost.
Rejected because any positive marginal cost makes the unit undesirable
Accepted only if no sunk costs were incurred earlier
Rejected unless average benefit also rises.
q.commonError: Using total or average values instead of the next unit.
q.feedback: The fourth unit adds $4 in net benefit.

q.q: A firm has already spent $50,000 developing a product. Finishing it will cost another $12,000 and is expected to generate $18,000. The firm should:
options: Cancel because total spending would reach $62,000
Finish so the original $50,000 is not wasted
Finish the product because the future benefit exceeds the future cost.
Ignore the $18,000 expected revenue because it is uncertain.
q.commonError: Including sunk development spending in the marginal comparison.
q.feedback: The $50,000 is unrecoverable; the relevant comparison is $18,000 versus $12,000.

q.q: A museum stays open an extra hour. The added admissions revenue is $900 and added staffing and utility cost is $1,100. Marginal analysis says:
options: Stay open because total daily revenue is high
Stay open to recover fixed building costs
Close at the normal time because marginal cost exceeds marginal benefit.
Close only if average cost rises.
q.commonError: Using totals or fixed costs rather than incremental values.
q.feedback: The extra hour reduces net benefit by $200.

q.q: A factory’s average cost is $14, while producing unit 101 raises total cost from $1,400 to $1,418. Which cost is relevant to the unit-101 decision?
options: The $18 marginal cost of unit 101
The $14 average cost of existing output
The $1,418 total cost after production
The $1,400 cost already incurred
q.commonError: Using average or total cost instead of the added cost.
q.feedback: Unit 101 changes total cost by $18; that increment is its marginal cost.

q.q: A student studies an additional hour. The expected grade benefit is valued at 9 points and fatigue cost at 6 points. The net marginal benefit is:
options: 3 points.
15 points.
6 points.
9 points.
q.commonError: Adding benefit and cost or reporting only one side.
q.feedback: Net marginal benefit equals 9 minus 6.

q.q: Total benefit rises from $140 to $158 when a fifth unit is added, while total cost rises from $92 to $107. What is the fifth unit’s net marginal benefit?
q.commonError: Comparing totals or adding the two marginal changes.
q.feedback: MB is $18 and MC is $15, so net marginal benefit is $3.

q.q: A warehouse’s average handling cost is $9 per box, but the next box costs $13 to handle and creates $15 in margin. What should it do?
options: Handle it because $15 exceeds the $13 marginal cost
Reject it because marginal cost exceeds average cost
Handle it only if average cost falls below $9
Reject it because total handling cost rises
q.commonError: Using average cost instead of the next box’s cost.
q.feedback: The box adds $2 in profit even though its marginal cost exceeds average cost.

q.q: A firm can run up to four ads. Their marginal benefits are $90, $70, $45, and $20; each ad costs $50. How many ads should run?
options: Two ads
One ad
Three ads
Four ads
q.commonError: Stopping early or continuing after MB falls below MC.
q.feedback: Only the first two ads have marginal benefit at least $50.

q.q: A project has an unrecoverable $8,000 design cost. Finishing costs $3,000 and yields $4,200; cancellation costs $400. Which comparison is relevant?
options: Finish for a $1,200 future gain versus paying $400 to cancel
Compare the full $11,000 spending with $4,200 revenue
Finish only to recover the $8,000 design cost
Cancel because any remaining cost is harmful
q.commonError: Including sunk design cost or ignoring the cancellation alternative.
q.feedback: The future choices are a $1,200 net gain from finishing or a $400 cancellation cost.

q.q: A sixth quality inspection lowers expected defect losses by $260 and costs $210 in labor. What is the correct next-step decision?
options: Perform it because avoided loss is a marginal benefit above cost
Skip it because inspection creates a positive labor cost
Perform it only if total defect losses become zero
Skip it unless average inspection cost falls
q.commonError: Ignoring avoided cost as benefit or using totals and averages.
q.feedback: The inspection creates $50 in net marginal benefit.

q.q: One more worker adds $620 in output but requires $480 in wages and $90 in added equipment use. What is the worker’s net marginal contribution?
q.commonError: Omitting a cost component or reporting gross output.
q.feedback: $620 minus $480 minus $90 equals $50.

q.q: A software team has spent six months on a feature. Completing it requires 200 more hours and is expected to save users 140 hours. The strongest decision is:
options: Stop unless there are additional future benefits not yet counted.
Continue because six months have already been invested.
Ignore the remaining 200 hours because the project is nearly done.
Continue because users receive some benefit.
q.commonError: Escalating commitment based on past effort.
q.feedback: Past effort is sunk; the remaining cost exceeds the identified future benefit.

q.q: A cyber-security team can run one more audit. It costs 90 staff-hours and is expected to prevent 120 hours of incident response, but the audit also displaces training worth 20 hours. What is the net marginal effect?
options: A gain of 10 staff-hours
A gain of 30 staff-hours
A loss of 70 staff-hours
A gain of 210 staff-hours
q.commonError: Ignoring the displaced alternative or adding costs and benefits.
q.feedback: Net marginal effect is 120 minus 90 direct hours minus 20 displaced training hours.

q.q: A platform can add one feature now for $80,000. It yields $95,000 in direct benefit but delays a security upgrade worth $25,000. What is the feature’s net marginal effect?
q.commonError: Ignoring the displaced incremental alternative.
q.feedback: $95,000 minus $80,000 direct cost minus $25,000 opportunity cost equals -$10,000.

q.q: An airline’s next flight frequency adds $80,000 in revenue, $54,000 in operating cost, and $18,000 in expected delay costs imposed on other flights. What is net marginal benefit?
q.commonError: Ignoring congestion cost or adding benefit and costs.

q.q: A police department considers one more patrol. Crime reduction is valued at $120,000, added payroll is $75,000, and the officers would forgo training worth $38,000. What is net marginal benefit?
q.commonError: Ignoring forgone training or adding values.

q.q: A firm can produce units with marginal benefits of $20, $16, $12, and $8 and marginal costs of $6, $10, $13, and $15. How many units maximize net benefit?
options: Two units.
Four units.
One unit.
Three units.
q.commonError: Continuing after marginal cost exceeds marginal benefit.
q.feedback: The first two units add net benefit; the third and fourth would reduce it.

q.q: A city has spent $4 million on a stadium design. Construction will cost another $30 million and generate benefits valued at $24 million. What should marginal analysis recommend?
options: Build because total benefits are positive.
Do not build because the future cost exceeds the future benefit.
Ignore construction cost because design work is complete.
Build because abandoning the design wastes $4 million.
q.commonError: Using sunk design cost to justify a negative future decision.
q.feedback: The $4 million is sunk; the relevant comparison is $24 million in benefits versus $30 million in future cost.

q.q: A clinic can extend hours. The first extra hour has MB $5,000 and MC $2,000; the second has MB $3,000 and MC $2,500; the third has MB $1,500 and MC $2,200. The optimal extension is:
options: Zero hours.
Three hours.
One hour.
Two hours.
q.commonError: Using total benefit without checking each additional hour.
q.feedback: Extend through the second hour and stop before the third, where MC exceeds MB.

q.q: A company’s average profit per customer is positive, but the next customer is expected to cost $140 to serve and generate $110 in revenue. The company should:
options: Accept the customer to spread fixed costs over more customers
Accept because average profit is positive
Accept because total revenue will increase.
Reject the next customer because marginal cost exceeds marginal benefit.
q.commonError: Using average profitability to justify a negative marginal transaction.
q.feedback: The next customer lowers profit by $30.

q.q: A farmer has already applied fertilizer. One additional unit raises crop value by $45 and costs $38, but also causes $10 in expected runoff damage. Including the external cost, the farmer should:
options: Ignore runoff because it is not paid directly by the farmer.
Apply because total crop value is positive.
Apply because private marginal cost is only $38.
Not apply the additional unit because marginal social cost is $48.
q.commonError: Ignoring a relevant marginal cost borne by others.
q.feedback: The added social cost is $38 plus $10, which exceeds the $45 marginal benefit.

q.q: An airline can sell one more seat for $240. Added catering and handling cost $35, and accepting the passenger displaces cargo margin of $170. What is net marginal benefit?
q.commonError: Ignoring opportunity cost or adding benefit and costs.
q.feedback: Net benefit is $240 minus $35 direct cost minus $170 forgone cargo margin.

q.q: A city considers a third congestion-reduction measure. Driver time savings are $1.4 million, implementation costs $900,000, and added neighborhood noise costs $600,000. What should it do?
options: Reject because marginal social cost is $1.5 million
Adopt because private implementation cost is below benefit
Adopt because total time savings remain positive
Reject only if average program cost rises
q.commonError: Ignoring an external marginal cost.
q.feedback: Implementation plus noise costs exceed the next measure’s benefit.

q.q: Total revenue at 200 units is $18,000 and at 201 units is $18,075. Total cost rises from $14,400 to $14,482. Should unit 201 be produced?
options: No, because marginal revenue $75 is below marginal cost $82
Yes, because total revenue remains above total cost
Yes, because average profit is positive
No, because total cost rises when the unit is produced
q.commonError: Using positive total or average profit instead of the next unit.
q.feedback: Unit 201 reduces profit by $7.

q.q: A hospital can add a night shift. Expected benefit is $31,000; added payroll is $22,000; and using the nurses displaces training worth $11,000. Which decision is best?
options: Do not add it because relevant marginal cost is $33,000
Add it because payroll alone is below benefit
Add it because total hospital benefit is large
Do not add it because any displaced activity is sunk
q.commonError: Ignoring the next-best alternative use of staff time.
q.feedback: Payroll plus forgone training exceeds the shift’s expected benefit.

q.q: A research grant has spent $2 million. Another experiment costs $180,000 and has a 40% chance of producing evidence worth $600,000. Ignoring other outcomes, should it run?
options: Run because expected marginal benefit is $240,000
Stop because the $600,000 benefit is uncertain
Run only to justify the $2 million already spent
Stop because total spending would rise
q.commonError: Ignoring probability or including sunk grant spending.
q.feedback: Expected added benefit exceeds the $180,000 experiment cost.

q.q: A retailer’s first three added inventory batches have net marginal benefits of $6,000, $2,000, and -$1,500. A fourth would have +$500 only if the third is purchased. What is the best discrete choice?
options: Buy two batches
Buy four batches
Buy three batches
Buy one batch
q.commonError: Crossing a negative increment to reach a smaller later positive one.
q.feedback: Buying batches three and four together would reduce net benefit by $1,000.

q.q: A nonprofit is considering one more meal-delivery route. The route would generate $900 in attributable donations, cost $620 for food and fuel, and use volunteer time that would otherwise provide tutoring worth $310. Should the nonprofit add the route?
options: Do not add it because relevant marginal cost is $930
Add it because direct cost is below donations
Add it because volunteer time is unpaid
Do not add it because total program costs are high
q.commonError: Treating unpaid resources as zero marginal cost.
q.feedback: Direct plus forgone volunteer value exceeds added donations.

q.q: A factory’s next three pollution-control units have marginal benefits of $90, $70, and $45 and marginal costs of $40, $65, and $60. How many units should be installed?
options: One unit.
Three units.
Zero units.
Two units.
q.commonError: Installing every beneficial unit without comparing the final unit’s marginal cost.
q.feedback: The first two units have MB at least as large as MC; the third does not.

q.q: A hospital considers one more diagnostic test. Expected patient benefit is $420, direct test cost is $250, and expected false-positive follow-up cost is $190. The marginal social decision is:
options: Ignore false-positive costs because they occur later.
Do not add the test because total marginal cost is $440.
Add because the direct cost is below the benefit.
Add because some patients benefit.
q.commonError: Ignoring expected downstream marginal cost.
q.feedback: Relevant marginal cost includes direct and expected follow-up costs.

q.q: A pollution rule’s next reduction step yields $4.8 million in health benefits, costs firms $3.6 million, and reduces recreational value by $1.5 million. Based on social marginal analysis, should the additional reduction be required?
options: Do not require it because social marginal cost is $5.1 million
Require it because compliance cost alone is below benefit
Require it because total prior health benefits are large
Do not require it because all environmental policy is costly
q.commonError: Ignoring a relevant external or opportunity cost.
q.feedback: The next step’s combined social costs exceed its benefit.

q.q: A utility considers one more conservation rebate. Expected energy savings are $130, rebate administration costs $90, and customer hassle is valued at $45. What is the social decision?
options: Do not offer it because marginal social cost is $135
Offer it because administrative cost is below savings
Offer it because total energy savings remain positive
Do not offer it because rebates are transfers
q.commonError: Ignoring a nonbudget marginal cost.
q.feedback: The next rebate’s social cost exceeds its benefit by $5.

q.q: An emergency agency can pre-position one more team. Expected response benefit is $500,000, deployment costs $320,000, and the team’s best alternative assignment is worth $210,000. What should it do?
options: Do not deploy because relevant marginal cost is $530,000
Deploy because direct cost is below expected benefit
Deploy because emergency benefits are not monetary
Do not deploy because prior readiness spending is sunk
q.commonError: Ignoring the alternative assignment of the next team.
q.feedback: Direct plus opportunity cost exceeds expected response benefit.

q.q: A farm’s next fertilizer application raises crop value by $1,100, costs $760, and increases expected water cleanup by $390. Which statement is correct?
options: Do not apply because marginal social cost exceeds benefit by $50
Apply because private marginal profit is $340
Apply because total crop revenue is positive
Do not apply because fertilizer cost is sunk
q.commonError: Using only private marginal cost.
q.feedback: Combined marginal cost is $1,150, above the $1,100 benefit.

q.q: A data center’s next cooling upgrade saves $140,000 in expected outages, costs $100,000, and uses technicians who could complete security work worth $50,000. What should it do?
options: Do not upgrade because relevant marginal cost is $150,000
Upgrade because outage savings exceed direct cost
Upgrade because technicians are already salaried
Do not upgrade because total cooling spending is high
q.commonError: Ignoring the next-best use of salaried labor.
q.feedback: Direct and opportunity costs exceed the expected outage savings.

q.q: A school intervention’s next class has gross benefit 44 points, delivery cost 30, and teacher fatigue cost 9. A later class would yield gross benefit 50 but requires this class first. What should the school do now?
options: Deliver the next class because its net marginal benefit is 5
Skip to the later class because its gross benefit is higher
Stop because combined cost is positive
Deliver only if average class benefit rises
q.commonError: Skipping a required increment or using gross and average values.
q.feedback: The current required class has positive net marginal benefit.

q.q: A vaccine trial can enroll one more site. The site has a 60% chance of producing evidence worth $50,000 and costs $24,000 to operate. Ignoring other effects, what does expected marginal analysis recommend?
options: Enroll because expected marginal benefit is $30,000, above cost
Reject because the full $50,000 benefit is uncertain
Enroll only if earlier research spending is recovered
Reject because the $24,000 cost raises total trial spending
q.commonError: Ignoring probability or including sunk research spending.
q.feedback: Expected added benefit is 0.60 × $50,000 = $30,000, which exceeds $24,000.

q.q: A project already cost $8 million. Finishing costs $5 million. Expected future benefits are $4 million, but cancellation requires a $0.5 million cleanup cost. What is the best choice?
options: Cancel, because cancellation costs $0.5 million while finishing has a $1 million negative future net benefit.
Finish because future benefits exceed the $0.5 million cleanup cost
Cancel because total project cost exceeds total benefit
Finish so the $8 million already spent is not wasted.
q.commonError: Ignoring the relevant alternatives after a sunk cost.
q.feedback: Compare future choices: finish yields -$1 million; cancel costs $0.5 million.

q.q: A training firm must decide whether to accept one additional client. A nonrefundable $4,000 license fee is already paid, and existing contracts will earn $50,000 profit either way. The new client will pay $18,000 with probability 0.75 and $10,000 otherwise. Service costs $11,000, support costs $2,000, and using the specialists forgoes another job's $4,000 net profit. All figures concern the firm; there are no other effects. Which marginal decision maximizes expected profit?
options: Reject: relevant expected marginal profit is -$1,000.
Accept: relevant expected marginal profit is +$3,000.
Reject: relevant expected marginal profit is -$5,000.
Accept: relevant expected marginal profit is +$49,000.
q.commonError: Ignoring opportunity cost, counting sunk expense, or comparing total rather than incremental profit.
q.feedback: Expected marginal revenue is 0.75 × $18,000 + 0.25 × $10,000 = $16,000. Relevant marginal cost is $11,000 + $2,000 + $4,000 = $17,000, so accepting lowers expected profit by $1,000. The paid license fee is sunk and the $50,000 from existing contracts is unchanged. Omitting the forgone job, adding the sunk fee, or including existing profit gives the distractor results.

q.q: A flood barrier segment has a 30% chance of preventing $10 million in damage, costs $2.4 million, and creates $900,000 in expected habitat loss. What does social marginal analysis recommend?
options: Do not build because expected benefit is $3 million and social cost is $3.3 million
Build because expected damage avoided exceeds construction cost
Build because the possible gross benefit is $10 million
Do not build because uncertain benefits should count as zero
q.commonError: Ignoring probability or external marginal cost.
q.feedback: Expected benefit is below construction plus habitat cost.

q.q: A project's next three stages have benefits of 14, 8 and 19 points and costs of 9, 12 and 10 points. Stages must occur in order. A manager would stop after stage one because stage two loses points. What is the best decision?
options: Complete all three; their total net benefit is 10 points
Stop after one; any negative increment rules out later stages
Complete only stage three; it has the largest net benefit
Complete two; positive total benefits justify the second stage
q.commonError: Stopping at the first negative increment without evaluating feasible complementary later steps.
q.feedback: Feasible cumulative net benefits are 0, 5, 1 and 10. Stages two and three together add 5 points. The last stage cannot be taken alone.

q.q: A firm spent $12 million on a prototype. Completing it costs $7 million. Selling the finished product yields $6 million, while selling the unfinished prototype now yields $1.5 million. How much better is the best current choice than completing it?
options: $4.5 million better by completing
$10.5 million better by selling now
$2.5 million better by selling now
$1 million better by selling now
q.commonError: Comparing gross future revenue without considering the alternative and remaining cost.
q.feedback: Completion yields $6m - $7m = -$1m from now; selling now yields $1.5m. Selling is better by $2.5m. The $12m already spent is common and sunk.

q.q: A producer earns a positive total profit. The next indivisible batch adds $320 in revenue and $350 in cost, but is required for a second batch adding $410 in revenue and $340 in cost. Which choice maximizes additional profit?
options: Produce both batches for a $40 gain
Produce neither because the first batch loses $30
Produce the second batch alone for a $70 gain
Produce the first alone to spread fixed cost
q.commonError: Using total profit or average cost rather than the marginal comparison.
q.feedback: The feasible additions yield $0, -$30 and +$40. Although the first batch loses money, the required pair gains $40. The second batch is not independently feasible.

q.q: A policy has already spent $2 billion. Continuing for one year costs $600 million and produces expected benefits of $520 million; ending it costs $30 million in transition expenses. What is the best marginal choice?
options: End the policy because $30 million is less costly than an $80 million negative continuation margin.
End because total cost since the program began exceeds total benefit
Continue so the $2 billion already spent is not wasted
Continue because the $520 million in benefits exceeds the $30 million transition cost.
q.commonError: Letting sunk spending or an irrelevant total comparison drive the decision.
q.feedback: The decision should compare future alternatives: continue loses $80 million; ending costs $30 million.

q.q: A treatment slot yields 88 benefit points and uses supplies costing 42 points. The staff time would otherwise support readiness worth 35 points. A method cuts supply cost by 8 but reduces the treatment benefit by 12. Which version is preferable to leaving staff in readiness?
options: The original slot, with an 11-point net gain
The cheaper method, with a 15-point net gain
Neither, because readiness must be added to benefit
Both versions give the same gain because both save supplies
q.commonError: Ignoring the best alternative use of the next slot.
q.feedback: Original net gain is 88 - 42 - 35 = 11. The cheaper method gives 76 - 34 - 35 = 7. Both beat the alternative, but cost saving alone does not make the revised method better.

q.q: A software team’s next sprint has a 50% chance of creating $180,000 in value and costs $70,000. It also delays maintenance worth $25,000. What should it do?
options: Do not run it because expected benefit $90,000 is below relevant cost $95,000
Run it because possible benefit is $180,000
Run it because sprint cost alone is below expected benefit
Do not run it because uncertainty makes expected benefit zero
q.commonError: Ignoring probability or displaced maintenance.
q.feedback: Expected benefit is $90,000; direct plus opportunity cost is $95,000.

q.q: The next two maintenance zones add benefits of 18 and 13 points and operating costs of 10 and 11 points. Opening either requires a one-time setup cost of 9 points. Zones must be opened in order. Which option has the greatest net benefit?
options: Open both zones, gaining 1 point
Open neither, because the first zone alone loses 1 point
Open only the first, gaining 8 points
Open both, gaining 10 points
q.commonError: Continuing after MC exceeds MB or stopping too soon.
q.feedback: Including setup once, one zone gives 18 - 10 - 9 = -1; both give 31 - 21 - 9 = 1. The second zone covers the remaining setup loss and adds a net gain.

q.q: Total benefit at five inspection stations is $900,000 and total cost is $610,000. At six they are $970,000 and $688,000. Station six also displaces a separate activity worth $9,000. How much added benefit would make station six break even?
q.commonError: Using favorable totals instead of unfavorable margins.
q.feedback: Station six adds $70,000 in benefit and $78,000 in direct cost plus $9,000 forgone value. It is short by $17,000; the positive total surplus does not settle the incremental choice.

q.q: Sequential grants have expected net benefits of $2.0m, $0.7m, -$0.4m and $0.6m. Each later grant requires all earlier grants. How many maximize total expected net benefit?
options: Four grants, yielding $2.9m
Two grants, yielding $2.7m
Three grants, yielding $2.3m
One grant, yielding $2.0m
q.commonError: Stopping at the first negative increment without evaluating feasible complementary later steps.
q.feedback: Feasible totals for zero through four grants are 0, 2.0, 2.7, 2.3 and 2.9 million. Grants three and four jointly add $0.2m, so stopping at the first negative increment misses the best feasible package.

q.q: A program's average benefit is 16 points per participant. The next participant adds 9 benefit points and 7 cost points; accommodating that participant also lowers benefits to existing participants by 3 points. What is the correct marginal decision?
options: Reject; the overall incremental net benefit is -1 point
Accept; 9 exceeds the direct cost of 7
Reject solely because 9 is below the average of 16
Accept; a positive average establishes a positive marginal gain
q.commonError: Using an average benchmark instead of MB versus MC.
q.feedback: Count the 3-point loss to existing participants as an added consequence: 9 - 7 - 3 = -1. The existing average is not the relevant comparison.

q.q: A plant's prepaid lease is unchanged. An extra order earns $760 and needs $490 in materials and $140 in overtime. It also occupies capacity that could earn $160 net on another order. What minimum price increase makes accepting it break even?
q.commonError: Allocating fixed or total cost to the next-unit rule.
q.feedback: Relevant cost is $490 + $140 + $160 = $790, against $760 in revenue. Another $30 reaches break-even; the unchanged lease does not enter.

q.q: A campaign has already spent $400,000. A final placement costs $60,000 and yields additional revenue of $100,000 if it succeeds, otherwise zero. With no other effects, which success probability makes the placement break even?
options: A probability above 100% because past spending must be recovered
q.commonError: Ignoring probability or including sunk campaign spending.
q.feedback: Set expected incremental revenue equal to avoidable cost: p times $100,000 = $60,000, so p = 0.60. Past campaign expenditure is sunk.

q.q: At 12 trips a route has total benefits of 840 points and costs of 610. At 13 trips these become 892 and 655. At 14 they become 930 and 699. With no later trips available, which expansion from 12 is best?
options: Add one trip; the two increments net +7 and -6 points
Add two trips because total benefit still exceeds total cost
Add neither because both trips raise total cost
Add two trips because 14 trips has the highest total benefit
q.commonError: Comparing totals or reporting one marginal change.
q.feedback: Trip 13 adds 52 - 45 = 7 points. Trip 14 adds 38 - 44 = -6. Relative to 12 trips, the feasible gains are 0, 7 and 1; add only trip 13.

q.q: A university pilot has spent $6 million. Extending it costs $900,000 and yields $1.1 million in expected benefit, while ending now requires $250,000 in transition cost. What is best?
options: Extend because its future net gain exceeds the cost of ending
End because total spending is already too high
Extend only to avoid wasting the $6 million
End because transition cost is less than extension cost
q.commonError: Comparing gross future costs or sunk totals instead of future alternatives.
q.feedback: Extending gains $200,000, while ending loses $250,000.

q.q: A city adds park lighting in blocks. Marginal benefits are 100, 82, 61, and 40; private costs are 55 each, but marginal light-pollution costs are 10, 18, 25, and 32. How many blocks should be lit?
options: Two blocks
One block
Three blocks
Four blocks
q.commonError: Ignoring changing external costs or continuing one unit too far.
q.feedback: Social MC is 65, 73, 80, and 87; only the first two pass.

q.q: An inspection costs $70,000 and prevents $500,000 in repairs if it finds a defect in time, otherwise saving nothing. It displaces work worth $20,000. What detection probability makes the inspection break even?
q.commonError: Using gross possible savings or ignoring probability.
q.feedback: Expected benefit is p times $500,000. Direct plus opportunity cost is $90,000, so break-even requires p = 90,000 / 500,000 = 18%.

q.q: If the marginal benefit of an action is $30 and the marginal cost is $20, what should a rational person do?
options: Take the action
Avoid the action
Ignore the marginal benefit
Choose only by total cost
q.commonError: gets_mb_mc_rule_backwards
q.feedback: Because marginal benefit is greater than marginal cost, the action is worth taking.

q.q: A firm already spent $5,000 designing a product. It can spend $1,200 more to launch it and earn $1,700 in revenue. What should it do if it is using marginal reasoning?
options: Launch, because the marginal benefit exceeds the marginal cost by $500
Do not launch, because total spending is $6,200
Do not launch, because the $5,000 sunk cost is too large
Launch only if total revenue exceeds all past costs
q.commonError: includes_sunk_cost_in_marginal_decision
q.feedback: The $5,000 is sunk. The launch decision compares the extra $1,200 cost with the extra $1,700 revenue.

q.q: A bookstore considers staying open one more hour. The hour adds $240 in sales margin and $170 in staffing and utility cost. Which comparison matters?
options: The $240 added benefit versus the $170 added cost
Total yearly sales versus total yearly operating and staffing cost
Average hourly sales versus the original opening expense
Past rent payments versus today’s entire revenue
q.commonError: Using total, average, or sunk values instead of next-hour changes.
q.feedback: Marginal analysis isolates what changes during the additional hour.

q.q: A business can earn $900 from one more project, but completing it costs $650. What should it do?
options: Complete it because marginal benefit exceeds marginal cost
Reject the project because any cost is bad
Ignore the extra revenue
Complete the project only if GDP rises
q.commonError: gets_mb_mc_rule_backwards
q.feedback: The marginal benefit is greater than the marginal cost, so the project adds net benefit.

q.q: A nurse can make one more follow-up call. The expected patient benefit is 12 points and the fatigue cost is 8 points. What should the nurse do?
options: Make the call because its marginal benefit exceeds its marginal cost
Skip the call because fatigue creates any positive cost
Make the call only if average benefit per call rises
Skip the call unless total benefit exceeds all past costs
q.commonError: Reversing the MB-MC rule or using averages and totals.
q.feedback: The next call adds 4 points of net benefit.

q.q: A grocer can stock one more crate. Expected sales margin is $45, spoilage risk costs $12, and shelf labor costs $18. What should the grocer do?
options: Stock it because the $45 benefit exceeds the $30 added cost
Reject it because spoilage risk makes total benefit uncertain
Stock it only if the store’s average profit increases
Reject it because adding the crate increases total store costs.
q.commonError: Ignoring a cost component or adding benefit and cost.
q.feedback: Marginal cost is $30, leaving $15 in net marginal benefit.

q.q: A vendor already spent 100 tokens setting up a stall. Staying open one more hour costs 12 tokens and brings in 20 tokens. What should matter now?
options: The extra 12-token cost and extra 20-token benefit
The full 112 tokens spent
Only the original 100-token setup cost
Only whether the stall looks impressive
q.commonError: includes_sunk_cost_in_marginal_decision
q.feedback: The setup cost is sunk. The current decision compares the extra cost and extra benefit of staying open.

q.q: The next unit has marginal benefit $24 and marginal cost $19. What should happen?
options: Continue only because past costs are sunk.
Stop because cost is positive.
Stop unless average benefit rises.
Produce or consume the next unit.
q.commonError: Rejecting a unit whenever it has any cost.
q.feedback: The next unit adds $5 in net benefit.

q.q: A fee has already been paid, but its refund terms have not yet been checked. When should it affect the current decision?
options: Only if some part of it can still be recovered or avoided.
Only when total benefits are positive.
Always, because past spending must be recovered.
Never, even if a refund remains available.
q.commonError: Using a blanket rule without checking whether the cost is truly sunk.
q.feedback: Check whether the current choice changes how much of the fee can be recovered. A refund available under one choice but not another is relevant; a payment that cannot be recovered or changed is sunk. Having paid the fee does not by itself establish that it is irrelevant, and a desire to recover past spending is not a marginal benefit.

q.q: A school considers one more tutoring session. Total benefit would rise from 72 to 80 points and total cost from 48 to 54 points. Which values should be compared?
options: Marginal benefit 8 and marginal cost 6
Total benefit 80 and total cost 54
Average benefit 76 and average cost 51
Prior benefit 72 and prior cost 48
q.commonError: Comparing totals or averages instead of their changes.
q.feedback: The additional session adds 8 benefit points and 6 cost points.

q.q: MB values for units 1 through 4 are 30, 22, 14, and 8; MC values are 10, 16, 15, and 12. Which production plan is optimal?
options: Produce only unit 1
Produce all four units
Produce the first three units
Produce the first two units
q.commonError: Continuing after marginal cost first exceeds marginal benefit.
q.feedback: Units 1 and 2 add net benefit; unit 3 would reduce it.

q.q: A project has spent $5 million irreversibly. Finishing now costs $3 million and produces $2 million in future benefits. Abandoning it costs $1.5 million in required restoration, with no future benefits. Delaying changes neither future cost nor benefit. Which choice minimizes the remaining loss?
options: Abandon: $2 million of benefits is below $3 million of cost, regardless of the restoration alternative.
Finish: the $5 million already spent must be counted as an additional benefit from completion.
Finish: the $1 million future loss is smaller than the $1.5 million abandonment loss.
Delay: postponement removes the restoration cost even though the stated future alternatives are unchanged.
q.commonError: Escalating commitment based on sunk cost.
q.feedback: Finishing nets 2-3=-1 million. Abandoning nets -1.5 million. Finishing is preferable by 0.5 million, despite its negative standalone future net value, because the feasible alternative is worse. Sunk spending is irrelevant.

q.q: A firm can accept a rush order for $30,000 or decline it. Internal production requires $16,000 in materials and labor plus $2,000 in extra maintenance, and displaces a job with $9,000 net profit. Outsourcing costs $24,000 plus $1,000 for inspection and leaves that other job intact. A $6,000 design fee is already paid and nonrefundable under every choice. Both production methods are feasible and give the same revenue. Which plan maximizes incremental private profit?
options: Produce internally; incremental profit is $12,000.
Outsource production; incremental profit is $5,000.
Reject the order; the best production option loses $1,000.
Produce internally; incremental profit is $3,000.
q.commonError: Ignoring a displaced private profit opportunity or counting an unavoidable sunk fee.
q.feedback: Internal production adds $30,000 - $16,000 - $2,000 - $9,000 = $3,000 after accounting for the displaced job. Outsourcing adds $30,000 - $24,000 - $1,000 = $5,000 and preserves that job, so outsourcing is best. The $6,000 design fee is sunk and does not enter either comparison.

q.q: A firm’s average profit is positive. The next order adds $180 in revenue and $205 in avoidable cost. What should it do?
options: Reject the order because its marginal contribution is negative
Accept because average profit across all prior orders remains positive
Accept because total revenue will rise
Reject only if fixed cost also rises
q.commonError: Using positive average profit instead of the next order’s margin.
q.feedback: The order reduces profit by $25.

q.q: Total benefit rises from 300 to 336 with one more unit; total cost rises from 210 to 242. What should happen?
options: Add the unit because MB 36 exceeds MC 32
Stop because total cost rises by 32
Add only if average benefit increases
Stop because total cost remains positive
q.commonError: Using totals or treating any added cost as disqualifying.
q.feedback: The next unit adds 4 in net benefit.

q.q: A project has $10 million in sunk spending. Completion costs $3 million, yields $3.4 million, and displaces another project worth $0.6 million. What is the decision?
options: Do not complete because relevant marginal cost is $3.6 million
Complete because future revenue exceeds direct cost
Complete to recover the $10 million
Do not complete because total project cost is high
q.commonError: Ignoring the displaced project or including sunk spending.
q.feedback: Direct plus opportunity cost exceeds future benefit.

q.q: One more factory inspection avoids expected losses of $95,000, costs $62,000, and creates $38,000 in delay costs for customers. What is the social choice?
options: Skip it because marginal social cost is $100,000
Perform it because direct cost is below avoided loss
Perform it because total quality benefit is positive
Skip it because all delay costs are sunk
q.commonError: Ignoring an external marginal cost.
q.feedback: The inspection’s combined added cost exceeds avoided loss.

q.q: A warehouse has packed 900 orders; that work is irreversible. The last 100 avoid $2,100 of penalties if completed tonight. Overtime costs $1,600 and displaces training worth $700. An outside packer can finish them for $1,900 without using warehouse staff. Which decision maximizes incremental value?
options: Use the outside packer: its $200 gain exceeds overtime’s $200 loss and leaving the orders unfinished.
Use overtime: its $500 gain exceeds the outside packer’s $200 gain because training is not a cash payment.
Leave them unfinished: both methods cost more than zero, and previous packing costs must be recovered first.
Use overtime: the 900 completed orders make finishing the final 100 worthwhile regardless of displaced training.
q.commonError: Ignoring avoided costs or relying on total and average values.
q.feedback: Relative to leaving the orders unfinished, overtime yields 2100-1600-700=-200; outsourcing yields 2100-1900=200. The prior 900 orders are sunk. The relevant choice compares complete incremental costs across feasible methods.

q.q: A software firm has spent $2 million irreversibly. Updating costs $90,000 and adds $70,000 in revenue. Canceling avoids the update but triggers a $35,000 support-termination payment. Selling the unfinished code yields $15,000 and requires $10,000 of handover work, with no termination payment. Which option is best from today?
options: Sell: its $5,000 net receipt exceeds updating’s $20,000 loss and cancellation’s $35,000 loss.
Update: its $70,000 revenue exceeds the sale receipt, so the remaining $90,000 cost should be ignored.
Cancel: avoiding the $90,000 update cost is sufficient even though selling has a positive net receipt.
Update: the $2 million already spent makes the smallest additional cash outlay the relevant criterion.
q.commonError: Letting sunk investment override a negative next increment.
q.feedback: Future net values are 70-90=-20 thousand for updating, -35 thousand for canceling and 15-10=5 thousand for selling. The historical $2 million is common to every alternative and cannot justify continuation.

q.q: A transit line can add up to three buses in order. Their direct marginal benefits are $140k, $105k and $78k; each costs $100k. Adding any buses requires $30k of dispatch setup. Only a three-bus plan also enables transfers worth $60k. Which plan has the highest net benefit?
options: Three buses: net benefit is $53k, exceeding $15k for two and $10k for one.
Two buses: stop before the third because its direct $78k benefit is below its $100k cost.
One bus: its $40k direct surplus exceeds the second bus’s $5k direct surplus.
No buses: dispatch setup makes every positive-size plan have negative net benefit.
q.commonError: Stopping early or continuing after MB falls below MC.
q.feedback: One bus nets 140-100-30=10. Two net 140+105-200-30=15. Three net 140+105+78+60-300-30=53. The third enables a complementary benefit, so its relevant incremental benefit is 78+60.

q.q: A city can buy sensors sequentially. Direct MBs are 90, 72, 50 and 31; MCs are 40, 60, 55 and 48. A linked alert system worth 25 becomes feasible only with at least three sensors and costs no more. Which number maximizes total net benefit?
options: Three: totals are 50, 62, 82 and 65 for one through four sensors.
Two: the third direct MB is below MC, so any linked benefit must be excluded.
Four: four sensors have the largest total direct benefit regardless of incremental cost.
One: its individual net benefit is largest, so later positive gains should be ignored.
q.commonError: Continuing after MC exceeds MB or stopping early.
q.feedback: Cumulative direct net gains are 50, 62, 57 and 40. Add 25 for plans with at least three sensors: 82 and 65. Three is optimal because the third unlocks an additional benefit while the fourth does not.

q.q: A project has spent $5 million irreversibly. Finishing costs $900,000 and yields $1 million. Canceling costs $180,000. Selling the project as-is brings $350,000 but requires $120,000 of transfer work and avoids cancellation fees. Which choice is best?
options: Sell: its $230,000 future net value exceeds finishing’s $100,000 and canceling’s -$180,000.
Finish: the $1 million receipt is the largest, and the sunk investment should be recovered before considering a sale.
Cancel: its $180,000 outlay is below finishing cost, so the sale receipt should not affect the comparison.
Finish: the relevant sale alternative is $350,000 minus the entire $5 million already spent.
q.commonError: Comparing gross future costs or sunk totals instead of net alternatives.
q.feedback: Compare future net values: 1,000,000-900,000=100,000; -180,000; 350,000-120,000=230,000. Selling wins. The historical $5 million is unchanged by the decision.

q.q: A hospital can add a mobile unit with expected benefits of $700,000 and direct costs of $520,000. Its team would abandon prevention work worth $210,000. Hiring temporary prevention staff costs $140,000 and preserves all that work; no other constraints change. Which plan maximizes incremental benefit?
options: Add the unit and hire temporary staff: net gain is $40,000, versus a $30,000 loss if prevention is displaced.
Do not add the unit: the $210,000 prevention value must be lost under every plan.
Add the unit without replacement: its $180,000 cash surplus establishes the largest social gain.
Add the unit and hire staff: net gain is $250,000 because preserved prevention is an extra benefit above the baseline.
q.commonError: Ignoring the forgone use of the next resource increment.
q.feedback: Without replacement the incremental gain is 700-520-210=-30 thousand. With replacement it is 700-520-140=40 thousand; the preserved prevention service is already in the baseline, not an extra 210 gain.

q.q: A manufacturer can hire a worker for one job that adds $1,400 in output. Wages are $980 and equipment costs $260 but can be resold for $100 after the job. The worker’s workstation could instead be rented out for $190 during the job. Which net contribution is relevant?
options: $70: subtract wages, net equipment cost and forgone workstation rent.
$260: subtract wages and net equipment cost but ignore the owned workstation.
$160: subtract wages and the full equipment purchase but ignore resale and rent.
-$30: subtract wages, the full equipment purchase and rent, ignoring resale.
q.commonError: Omitting a cost component or reporting gross output.
q.feedback: Net equipment use costs 260-100=160. Relevant contribution is 1400-980-160-190=70. Ownership does not remove forgone rental income, and recoverable resale value reduces the equipment cost.

q.q: A cleanup method yields $500 in health benefits, costs the operator $370 and damages habitat by $150. A gentler method gives the same health benefit, costs $430 and causes $20 of habitat damage. Which method is socially preferable, and what would an operator ignoring habitat costs choose?
options: Society prefers the gentler method ($50 net); the operator prefers the original ($130 private net versus $70).
Society prefers the original ($130 net); the operator prefers the gentler method because its habitat damage is lower.
Both prefer the original because its cash cost is lower and habitat losses are transfers between users.
Both reject cleanup because the original method’s $520 social cost proves every available method has negative net benefit.
q.commonError: Ignoring external marginal cost.
q.feedback: Original social net benefit is 500-370-150=-20; gentler net benefit is 500-430-20=50. Ignoring habitat, private nets are 130 and 70, so private and social rankings differ.

q.q: A preventable failure has a 25% probability and would cost $800,000. Prevention costs $170,000 and eliminates the loss. A perfect test costs $20,000 and permits prevention only when failure would otherwise occur. For a risk-neutral decision maker, which strategy has the lowest expected cost?
options: Test then prevent if needed: $62,500, versus $170,000 for unconditional prevention and $200,000 for no action.
Prevent unconditionally: $170,000, versus $220,000 for testing because testing cannot change the failure probability.
Take no action: $0, because a 25% possible loss is not a current cash outlay.
Test then prevent if needed: $190,000, because prevention must be paid even after a negative test.
q.commonError: Ignoring probability or sunk testing expenditure.
q.feedback: No action costs 0.25×800000=200000 in expectation. Unconditional prevention costs 170000. Testing allows conditional prevention, costing 20000+0.25×170000=62500. Information has value because it changes action in the no-failure state.

q.q: Marginal benefit is:
options: The added benefit from one more unit.
A past benefit that cannot change.
Average benefit per unit.
Total benefit from all units.
q.commonError: Confusing marginal, total, and average values.
q.feedback: Marginal benefit measures the change from one additional unit.

q.q: A cost is sunk when it:
options: Will occur only if one more unit is chosen.
Has already occurred and cannot be recovered.
Changes with the current decision.
Equals the next-best alternative.
q.commonError: Calling future or avoidable costs sunk.
q.feedback: Sunk costs are past and unrecoverable.

q.q: The marginal rule says to continue while:
options: Marginal benefit is at least as large as marginal cost.
Average cost is falling
Total benefit is positive
Past spending is large.
q.commonError: Using totals, averages, or sunk costs.
q.feedback: The next unit should be chosen when its added benefit covers its added cost.

q.q: Total benefit is 50 and average benefit is 10. One more unit raises total benefit to 57. What is marginal benefit?
q.commonError: Reporting total or average benefit instead of the change.
q.feedback: Marginal benefit is 57 minus 50.

q.q: Marginal cost is $12 and marginal benefit is $17. What should happen?
options: Take the next unit because benefit exceeds cost
Stop because the unit has a positive cost
Add $12 and $17 before deciding
Use average cost instead of marginal cost
q.commonError: Reversing the marginal rule or adding MB and MC.
q.feedback: Compare MB with MC; the next unit adds $5 in net benefit.

q.q: Which value is average rather than marginal?
options: Total cost divided by all units produced
The change in cost from one more unit
The benefit added by the next unit
A future cost avoided by stopping now
q.commonError: Treating an average per unit as the next unit’s change.
q.feedback: Average divides a total across units; marginal measures a change.

q.q: A $100 fee is refundable if a project stops today. Is it sunk for today’s decision?
options: No, because stopping can still recover it
Yes, because it was paid in the past
Yes, because every prior payment is sunk
No, because future costs can never matter
q.commonError: Calling a recoverable or avoidable cost sunk.
q.feedback: A cost is sunk only if the current choice cannot recover or avoid it.

q.q: One more sale brings $30 in revenue and requires $22 in added cost. What is net marginal benefit?
q.commonError: Adding benefit and cost or reporting gross revenue.
q.feedback: Net marginal benefit equals $30 minus $22.

q.q: A decision should continue when:
options: Marginal benefit is at least marginal cost
Total cost is zero
Average cost is falling
Demand is perfectly elastic
q.feedback: Marginal reasoning compares the next benefit with the next cost.

q.q: Scarcity limits a community’s emergency crews. How does marginal analysis help decide whether to assign one more crew-hour to inspections?
options: Compare the added inspection benefit with the best use of that crew-hour forgone
Add the value of every program the community cannot fund
Use total inspection benefit without considering the next hour’s cost
Treat all prior emergency spending as the next hour’s marginal cost
q.commonError: Failing to connect scarce-resource tradeoffs to the next increment.
q.feedback: Scarcity makes the crew-hour costly; marginal analysis tests whether its added inspection benefit covers that cost.

q.q: A worker could earn $25 during one more study hour. How does opportunity cost enter the marginal study decision?
options: The forgone $25 is part of the marginal cost of that hour
The $25 is a sunk cost because work has not occurred
All lifetime wages become the marginal cost of studying
Opportunity cost matters only for the first study hour
q.commonError: Ignoring the best alternative use of the next increment.
q.feedback: The next hour’s opportunity cost belongs in its marginal cost.

q.q: A firm expands output while the revenue from one more unit exceeds the cost of that unit. How does this connect marginal analysis to profit maximization?
options: Each positive marginal contribution raises profit until the next unit turns negative
Profit is maximized whenever total revenue is positive
Fixed cost determines whether every additional unit is produced
Average revenue must exceed total cost for the next unit
q.commonError: Using totals or fixed costs instead of incremental profit.
q.feedback: Profit rises while marginal revenue covers marginal cost.

q.q: A factory’s next unit creates pollution damage not paid by the factory. How does that affect marginal analysis?
options: The external damage belongs in social marginal cost
The damage is sunk because outsiders bear it
Only private production cost can be marginal
External damage matters only after all output is produced
q.commonError: Leaving external incremental harm out of social decisions.
q.feedback: Social marginal analysis counts costs imposed on others.

q.q: A public program considers one additional service. How does marginal analysis implement cost-benefit reasoning?
options: Compare the added social benefit with the added social cost
Compare lifetime total program spending with the current year’s available budget
Add average benefit and average cost together
Continue whenever any participant receives a benefit
q.commonError: Replacing the next increment with totals or averages.
q.feedback: Cost-benefit analysis at the margin asks whether the next increment creates net social benefit.

q.q: A consumer buys another unit while its added satisfaction exceeds the price and other next-unit costs. What connection is being made?
options: Consumer choice can use the same MB-versus-MC rule
Consumer choice depends only on total satisfaction accumulated from every prior purchase
The price becomes sunk before the purchase decision
Average satisfaction determines every additional purchase
q.commonError: Failing to transfer marginal comparison to an individual purchase.
q.feedback: The consumer continues while the next unit’s marginal benefit covers its marginal cost.

q.q: Market equilibrium occurs where:
options: Quantity demanded equals quantity supplied
Quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied, creating a shortage
Quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded, creating a surplus
The demand curve reaches the price axis
q.commonError: confuses_equilibrium_with_highest_price
q.feedback: At equilibrium, quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.

q.q: If the market price is above equilibrium, the market has:
options: A surplus
A shortage
A binding price ceiling
No quantity supplied
q.commonError: reverses_surplus_and_shortage
q.feedback: A price above equilibrium creates a surplus because quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded.

q.q: If the market price is below equilibrium, the market has:
options: A shortage
A surplus
Excess supply
No demand
q.commonError: reverses_surplus_and_shortage
q.feedback: A price below equilibrium creates a shortage because quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied.

q.q: A popular endorsement increases demand for a product while production conditions remain unchanged. How does the market's equilibrium price respond?
options: It increases
It decreases
It remains unchanged
It becomes a shortage at every price
q.commonError: gets_demand_shift_price_effect_backwards
q.feedback: The endorsement shifts demand right. With supply unchanged, buyers compete for the product and the equilibrium price rises.

q.q: If supply increases and demand does not change, what happens to equilibrium price?
options: It decreases
It increases
It remains unchanged because demand did not change.
It increases because more units are available for sale.
q.commonError: gets_supply_shift_price_effect_backwards
q.feedback: An increase in supply lowers equilibrium price when demand is unchanged.

q.q: At the equilibrium price, quantity demanded is:
options: Greater than quantity supplied.
Equal to quantity supplied.
Less than quantity supplied.
Unrelated to quantity supplied.
q.commonError: Defining equilibrium as a shortage, surplus, or unrelated quantities.
q.feedback: Market equilibrium occurs at the price where buyers’ quantity demanded equals sellers’ quantity supplied.

q.q: What equilibrium price and quantity are shown in the displayed gas market?
options: $3 per gallon and 150 thousand gallons
$2 per gallon and 200 thousand gallons
$4 per gallon and 100 thousand gallons
$3 per gallon and 300 thousand gallons
q.commonError: misreads_graph_or_confuses_shift_with_movement
q.feedback: D0 and S0 intersect at a price of $3 per gallon and a quantity of 150 thousand gallons.

q.q: Before either curve shifts, what equilibrium is formed by D0 and S0 in the displayed gas market?
options: $4 and 100 thousand units
$4 and 200 thousand units
$3 and 150 thousand units
$5 and 150 thousand units
q.commonError: misreads_graph_or_confuses_shift_with_movement
q.feedback: The original curves D0 and S0 intersect at price $3 and quantity 150 thousand.

q.q: A product goes viral while firms' production conditions remain unchanged. How do the resulting demand shift and movement along supply change equilibrium?
options: Price rises and quantity rises
Price falls and quantity falls
Price rises and quantity falls
Price falls and quantity rises
q.commonError: gets_demand_increase_effect_backwards
q.feedback: The viral interest shifts demand right. With supply fixed, the new intersection lies higher and farther right, so equilibrium price and quantity both rise.

q.q: Supply for a product decreases while demand stays the same. What happens to equilibrium price and quantity?
options: Price rises and quantity falls
Price falls and quantity rises
Price rises and quantity rises
Price falls and quantity falls
q.commonError: gets_supply_decrease_effect_backwards
q.feedback: A decrease in supply raises equilibrium price and lowers equilibrium quantity.

q.q: A market price is too low. Quantity demanded is greater than quantity supplied. What pressure should occur in an unregulated market?
options: Price should rise
Price should fall
Supply should vanish
Demand must be zero
q.commonError: gets_shortage_price_pressure_backwards
q.feedback: A shortage creates upward pressure on price as buyers compete for limited goods.

q.q: A market price is too high. Quantity supplied is greater than quantity demanded. What pressure should occur in an unregulated market?
options: Price should fall
Price should rise
Demand shifts right in response to unsold inventory
Supply shifts left before price can adjust
q.commonError: gets_surplus_price_pressure_backwards
q.feedback: A surplus creates downward pressure on price as sellers compete to sell the extra output.

q.q: A hurricane destroys part of the orange crop. What is the likely result in the orange market?
options: Supply decreases, price rises, and quantity falls
Demand increases, price rises, and quantity rises
Supply increases, price falls, and quantity rises
Quantity demanded rises because supply fell
q.commonError: confuses_supply_shock_with_demand_increase
q.feedback: A crop loss reduces supply, which raises price and lowers equilibrium quantity.

q.q: A new health report says blueberries are especially beneficial. What likely happens in the blueberry market?
options: Demand increases, price rises, and quantity rises
Supply decreases, price rises, and quantity falls
Demand decreases, price falls, and quantity falls
Quantity supplied falls because demand rose
q.commonError: confuses_demand_shift_with_supply_shift
q.feedback: A favorable taste or information change increases demand, raising price and quantity.

q.q: Refer to the supply and demand graph. Which equilibrium is formed by D1 and S2?
options: Price P1 and Quantity Q2
Price P2 and Quantity Q1
Price P3 and Quantity Q2
Price P2 and Quantity Q3
q.commonError: misreads_intersection_of_named_curves
q.feedback: D1 and S2 intersect at the middle vertical guide and the lowest horizontal guide, which is Price P1 and Quantity Q2.

q.q: Refer to the supply and demand graph. Which equilibrium is formed by D1 and S1?
options: Price P2 and Quantity Q1
Price P1 and Quantity Q2
Price P3 and Quantity Q2
Price P2 and Quantity Q3
q.commonError: misreads_intersection_of_named_curves
q.feedback: D1 and S1 intersect at the left vertical guide and the middle horizontal guide, which is Price P2 and Quantity Q1.

q.q: Refer to the supply and demand graph. Which equilibrium is formed by D2 and S2?
options: Price P2 and Quantity Q3
Price P1 and Quantity Q2
Price P3 and Quantity Q2
Price P2 and Quantity Q1
q.commonError: misreads_intersection_of_named_curves
q.feedback: D2 and S2 intersect at the right vertical guide and the middle horizontal guide, which is Price P2 and Quantity Q3.

q.q: Refer to the graph. A production improvement shifts supply from S1 to S2 while demand remains D1. Which explanation connects the curve shift to the new equilibrium?
options: Equilibrium moves from P2, Q1 to P1, Q2, so price falls and quantity rises
Equilibrium moves from P1, Q2 to P2, Q3, so price and quantity rise
Equilibrium moves from P3, Q2 to P2, Q3, so price falls and quantity rises
Equilibrium moves from P2, Q3 to P3, Q2, so price rises and quantity falls
q.commonError: gets_supply_shift_effect_backwards
q.feedback: The production improvement shifts supply right to S2. Along unchanged D1, the intersection moves from P2, Q1 to P1, Q2.

q.q: Refer to the supply and demand graph. If demand shifts from D1 to D2 while supply remains at S2, what happens to equilibrium price and quantity?
options: Price rises and quantity rises
Price falls and quantity falls
Price rises and quantity falls
Price falls and quantity rises
q.commonError: gets_demand_shift_effect_backwards
q.feedback: Moving from D1 with S2 to D2 with S2 raises equilibrium price from P1 to P2 and raises equilibrium quantity from Q2 to Q3.

q.q: Refer to the supply and demand graph. Compared with the equilibrium at D1 and S1, the equilibrium at D2 and S2 shows:
options: The same price but a higher quantity
A lower price and a lower quantity
A higher price and a lower quantity
A lower price and the same quantity
q.commonError: cannot_compare_two_equilibria_correctly
q.feedback: D1 and S1 gives Price P2 and Quantity Q1, while D2 and S2 gives Price P2 and Quantity Q3, so price is the same and quantity is higher.

q.q: Refer to the supply and demand graph. The market begins at D1 and S1. Supply then increases, followed by an increase in demand. What is the final equilibrium?
options: Price P2 and Quantity Q3
Price P1 and Quantity Q2
Price P2 and Quantity Q1
Price P3 and Quantity Q2
q.commonError: fails_to_track_two_step_shift_sequence
q.feedback: Starting at D1 and S1 gives P2, Q1. A supply increase moves equilibrium to P1, Q2. Then a demand increase moves equilibrium to P2, Q3.

q.q: Refer to the price-control graph. What is the market equilibrium price and quantity?
options: $30 and 200 units
$20 and 250 units
$40 and 150 units
$50 and 300 units
q.commonError: misreads_intersection_of_supply_and_demand
q.feedback: Equilibrium occurs where supply and demand intersect, which is $30 and 200 units.

q.q: At a price of $2 per gallon in the displayed gas market, what imbalance exists?
options: A surplus of 100 thousand gallons
A shortage of 100 thousand gallons
A shortage of 200 thousand gallons
No shortage or surplus
q.commonError: misreads_graph_or_confuses_shift_with_movement
q.feedback: At $2, quantity demanded is 200 thousand and quantity supplied is 100 thousand, so the shortage is 100 thousand gallons.

options: $5 and 150 thousand units

q.q: Demand increases while supply decreases, and the observed equilibrium quantity is unchanged. Which inference best reconciles the two shifts with that observation?
options: Equilibrium price rises, and the opposing quantity effects happen to offset

Equilibrium quantity is unchanged because neither curve shifts
Equilibrium price is unchanged because the demand and supply shifts are equal

q.q: Demand decreases while supply increases. What can be predicted with certainty?
options: Equilibrium price falls
Equilibrium quantity rises
Equilibrium price rises
Equilibrium quantity falls
q.commonError: claims_quantity_change_is_certain_in_opposing_shifts

q.q: Demand and supply both increase. What can be predicted with certainty?

Equilibrium price rises

q.q: Demand and supply both decrease. What can be predicted with certainty?

Equilibrium price rises

q.q: A drought reduces wheat supply while a health trend increases demand for wheat bread. Explain which equilibrium effect is certain and which depends on the relative shift sizes.

q.q: Production technology lowers costs while consumer interest in the good falls. Explain which equilibrium effect is certain and which depends on the relative shift sizes.
options: Price falls; quantity is ambiguous because the shifts have opposing quantity effects
Price rises; quantity falls because both shifts reduce market availability
Price falls; quantity rises because supply determines both outcomes
Price is ambiguous; quantity falls because demand determines both outcomes
q.commonError: assumes_quantity_moves_with_supply_only

q.q: Refer to the graph. Starting at D1/S1, demand and supply both increase to D2/S2. Which explanation compares the general prediction with the particular equilibrium drawn?
options: Quantity rises for certain; price is generally ambiguous but remains at P2 in this drawing

Both price and quantity are generally fixed because the curves shift together
Quantity falls for certain; price is generally ambiguous but falls to P1 here

q.q: Refer to the graph. Demand increases from D1 to D2 while supply decreases from S2 to S1. Infer what theory guarantees, then use the plotted equilibria to explain the quantity outcome.
options: Price rises for certain; quantity is generally ambiguous but stays at Q2 in this drawing
Quantity rises for certain; price is generally ambiguous but stays at P2 in this drawing
Price falls for certain; quantity stays at Q2 because both curves shift right
Quantity falls for certain; price stays at P1 because the shifts offset
q.commonError: misses_quantity_can_remain_same_with_opposing_shifts
q.feedback: The demand increase and supply decrease both raise price. Their quantity effects oppose; the graph shows those effects offset at Q2 for this particular pair of shifts.

q.q: Refer to the supply and demand shift graph. Starting from D2/S1, demand decreases to D1 while supply increases to S2. What happens?
options: Price falls and quantity stays the same
Price rises and quantity stays the same
Price stays the same and quantity rises
Price falls and quantity falls

q.q: Refer to the supply and demand shift graph. If demand and supply both increase, what does this graph show is possible?
options: Quantity rises while price stays the same
Quantity rises while price rises because the demand shift has the larger price effect
Quantity rises while price falls because the supply shift has the larger price effect
Price rises while quantity stays the same because the shifts have equal quantity effects
q.commonError: thinks_double_shift_has_one_forced_price_result
q.feedback: The graph shows D1/S1 to D2/S2. Both demand and supply increase, quantity rises, and price remains unchanged.

q.q: Refer to the supply and demand shift graph. If demand increases and supply decreases, what does this graph show is possible?
options: Price rises while quantity stays the same
Price falls while quantity rises
Price stays the same while quantity rises
Price falls while quantity stays the same
q.commonError: thinks_quantity_must_change_when_both_curves_shift
q.feedback: The graph shows D1/S2 to D2/S1. Demand rises and supply falls, causing price to rise while quantity stays at Q2.

q.q: Refer to the graph. Calculate the disequilibrium at $1 per gallon and explain the price pressure that follows from buyers' and sellers' incentives.
options: A 200-thousand surplus; downward price pressure
A 50-thousand shortage; no price pressure

A 200-thousand shortage; upward price pressure

q.q: Refer to the graph. How do equilibrium price and quantity change from A to B?
options: Price rises 4 dollars; quantity stays 200 thousand
Price rises 4 dollars; quantity rises 200 thousand
Price falls 4 dollars; quantity stays 200 thousand

q.q: Refer to the graph. Tastes shift demand from D1 to D2 while supply remains S1. Which explanation uses both intersections to distinguish the demand shift from the market's movement along supply?
options: Demand shifts right, and equilibrium moves along S1 from P2, Q1 to P3, Q2
Supply shifts right, and equilibrium moves along D1 from P2, Q1 to P1, Q2
Demand shifts left, and equilibrium moves along S1 from P3, Q2 to P2, Q1
Supply shifts left, and equilibrium moves along D2 from P2, Q3 to P3, Q2

q.q: A market price is above equilibrium. What pressure does the market create and why?
options: Downward pressure on price because quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded
Upward pressure on price because quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied
No pressure because high prices clear every market

q.q: A market price is below equilibrium. What pressure does the market create and why?

Downward pressure on price because quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded
No pressure because buyers prefer low prices
A supply increase because the legal price is low

q.q: Refer to the supply and demand graph with D1, D2, S1, and S2. Starting at D2 and S1, supply increases to S2 while demand stays at D2. What happens?
options: Equilibrium moves from P3, Q2 to P2, Q3.

Supply decreased while demand increased, creating offsetting quantity effects.

q.q: Refer to the graph. Which statement distinguishes the general prediction for these simultaneous shifts from the particular outcome shown?

Price falls by $2 and quantity rises to 250; the graph shows only a supply increase.

q.q: Refer to the graph. Compare two adjustment paths from D to B: demand changes first in one path; supply changes first in the other. Which claim about the intermediate quantity and final equilibrium is correct?
options: Demand first takes quantity to A; supply first takes it to C; both paths end at B.
Demand first takes quantity to C; supply first takes it to A; both paths end at B.
Demand first takes quantity to C; supply first takes it to A; the paths end at different equilibria.
Either first shift keeps quantity at D; only the second shift moves quantity to B.
q.imageAlt: The gasoline market has price in dollars vertically and quantity in thousands of gallons per day horizontally. D1 is right of D0 and S1 is left of S0. Intersections are A at D0-S1, quantity 150 and price 5; B at D1-S1, quantity 200 and price 6; C at D1-S0, quantity 250 and price 5; and D at D0-S0, quantity 200 and price 4.

q.q: Refer to the graph. The taco market begins at point D. Tacos are a normal good. Consumer income rises while the cost of an important production input increases. Compare the two determinant effects and infer which labeled point becomes the new equilibrium.
options: B — the intersection of D1 and S1
C — the intersection of D1 and S0
A — the intersection of D0 and S1
D — the intersection of D0 and S0

q.feedback: Because tacos are a normal good, higher consumer income shifts demand from D0 to D1. The higher input cost shifts supply from S0 to S1. The new D1-S1 equilibrium is point B.

q.q: Refer to the graph. Compare the market at $2 with the market at $4, then infer how the two opposite price-adjustment forces both move the market toward the $3 equilibrium.
options: Surplus at $2 pushes price down; shortage at $4 pushes price up.
Shortage at $2 pushes price up; surplus at $4 pushes price down.
Shortage at both prices pushes the market price steadily upward.
Surplus at both prices pushes the market price steadily downward.
q.commonError: misreads_graph_or_confuses_shift_with_movement
q.feedback: A shortage creates upward price pressure and a surplus creates downward pressure. Both adjustment forces point toward the $3 equilibrium.

q.q: Refer to the graph. The market moves from D1/S1 to D2/S2. An analyst claims that simultaneous demand and supply increases must leave price unchanged. Then part of the supply increase is reversed: supply lies strictly between S1 and S2 at every shown price, while demand stays D2. Which assessment is correct?
options: The original offset is specific to the graph; afterward price is between P2 and P3 and quantity between Q2 and Q3.
The original offset is a general rule; afterward price stays P2 and quantity stays Q3.
The original offset is specific to the graph; afterward price is between P1 and P2 and quantity exceeds Q3.
The original offset is a general rule; afterward price reaches P3 and quantity falls below Q1.
q.commonError: claims_price_change_is_certain_when_both_curves_shift_right
q.feedback: Both initial increases raise quantity, but their opposing price effects need not cancel in general. They happen to cancel at P2 in this drawing. With D2 fixed, partially reversing S2 toward S1 places the new intersection between (P2,Q3) and (P3,Q2). Price rises above P2, and quantity falls from Q3 but remains above Q2 and the original Q1.

q.q: A disease reduces berry supply while a nutrition trend raises berry demand. The final quantity is above its original level. Which conclusion follows with ordinary downward demand and upward supply?
options: Price is higher; the demand increase more than offsets the supply reduction’s effect on quantity.
Price is lower; greater final quantity proves that supply increased.
Price is unchanged; the higher quantity shows that the two shifts offset completely.
Price is higher; the observed quantity proves that the supply reduction dominated demand.
q.commonError: assumes_supply_effect_dominates_demand_effect
q.feedback: Both shifts raise price. Supply reduction alone lowers equilibrium quantity, so the observed quantity increase requires the demand effect to outweigh that reduction in the final outcome.

q.q: Two initially identical device markets face the same increase in demand. Only Market Y also loses a component supplier. Compared with Market X’s final equilibrium, what must be true in Market Y?
options: Y has a higher price and lower quantity, although its quantity relative to the original equilibrium is uncertain.
Y has a lower price and higher quantity, although its quantity relative to the original equilibrium is uncertain.
Y has a higher price and quantity, because both changes increase demand.
Y has the same price and quantity, because both markets face the same demand change.
q.commonError: forces_quantity_direction_without_curve_size
q.feedback: Starting from X’s final equilibrium, the additional supply reduction in Y raises price and lowers quantity. Compared with the common original equilibrium, Y’s demand increase and supply decrease have opposing quantity effects.

q.q: Lunch-delivery demand falls while improved routing lowers delivery costs. Final price is lower and the number of deliveries is unchanged. Which explanation is consistent?
options: Demand fell and supply rose; their quantity effects offset at the final equilibrium.
Demand and supply both fell; their quantity effects offset at the final equilibrium.
Demand and supply both rose; unchanged deliveries reflect offsetting quantity effects.
Only demand fell; a fixed upward-sloping supply curve kept deliveries unchanged.
q.commonError: assumes_quantity_must_follow_demand_shift_only
q.feedback: Lower demand and higher supply both reduce price but have opposite quantity effects. The observed unchanged quantity reflects an offset in this case; it is not a general prediction of those shifts.

q.q: Bicycles are a normal good. Income and production-input costs rise, yet equilibrium bicycle sales fall. A manager concludes that bicycle demand must have fallen. Evaluate the conclusion.
options: Incorrect: demand rose, but the supply reduction more than offset its effect on quantity; price rose.
Correct: lower equilibrium sales establish a demand decrease even when income rises.
Incorrect: supply rose, but demand fell enough to reduce both price and quantity.
Correct: higher input costs reduce bicycle demand directly while supply stays fixed.
q.commonError: tracks_only_one_curve_shift
q.feedback: Higher income increases demand for a normal good; higher input costs reduce supply. Both raise price. Lower sales can result when the supply effect dominates quantity, so sales alone do not identify a demand shift.

q.q: A production improvement increases supply while tastes shift away from the product. An analyst predicts that price and quantity must both fall. What is the precise correction?
options: Price must fall, but quantity falls only if the demand reduction outweighs the supply increase’s quantity effect.
Quantity must fall, but price falls only if the production improvement outweighs the taste change.
Price must rise, but quantity can rise or fall depending on the relative shifts.
Neither direction can be inferred because simultaneous shifts make both variables indeterminate.
q.commonError: claims_quantity_change_is_certain_in_opposing_shifts
q.feedback: Both changes lower equilibrium price. Lower demand reduces quantity while higher supply increases it, so the analyst needs relative effects to assert a quantity decline.

q.q: A coffee shop sees more customers after a celebrity endorsement. At the same time, wages for baristas rise. If the relative sizes of the two shifts are unknown, which equilibrium outcome can be predicted with certainty?
options: Price rises; quantity is ambiguous
Quantity rises; price is ambiguous
Both price and quantity fall
Price falls; quantity rises
q.commonError: assumes_popularity_always_raises_quantity
q.feedback: Demand increases and supply decreases. Both raise price, but quantity depends on which shift is larger.

q.q: A new production method makes shoes cheaper to produce. At the same time, a fashion shift makes shoes less popular. What is certain?
options: Price falls; quantity is ambiguous
Quantity falls; price is ambiguous
Both price and quantity rise
Price rises; quantity falls
q.commonError: assumes_less_popularity_always_lowers_quantity_and_price_only
q.feedback: Supply increases and demand decreases. Both lower price, but quantity is ambiguous.

q.q: A hurricane disrupts production and reduces supply while households expect prices to rise tomorrow and rush to buy today. What is the strongest prediction for today’s market?
options: Price rises; quantity is ambiguous
Quantity rises; price is ambiguous
Both price and quantity fall
Price falls; quantity rises
q.commonError: ignores_expectations_as_demand_shifter
