q.q: A housing model predicts lower purchases when price rises, holding neighborhood quality fixed. In the data, renovated neighborhoods have both higher prices and more purchases. A critic calls this a refutation. Which evaluation and test are most informative?
options: Higher purchases prove demand slopes upward; controlling for quality would remove economically relevant evidence and invalidate the test.
Quality changes may confound the comparison; compare price changes within similar-quality neighborhoods before rejecting the conditional prediction.
The prediction is immune to data because holding quality fixed is an assumption; no observed comparison can challenge it.
Renovation proves quality causes all purchases; the model’s price mechanism is established even without a conditional comparison.
q.commonError: Rejecting a focused assumption merely because the held-constant factor varies in reality.
q.feedback: The model makes a ceteris-paribus prediction. Varying quality may shift demand while price changes, so the raw correlation does not isolate the price effect. Comparable-quality evidence can test the relevant conditional prediction.

q.q: Two models predict different effects of a tax because one assumes fixed supply and the other allows firms to enter. What should economists do first?
options: Average both tax predictions without examining their assumptions
Choose the model containing the greater number of equations
Match assumptions to the relevant time horizon and evidence
Reject both models simply because their predictions disagree
q.commonError: Choosing between models without matching entry assumptions to the time horizon.
q.feedback: Whether firms can enter depends on the horizon and evidence, so the assumptions determine applicability.

q.q: A model predicts that a price ceiling causes a shortage, but observed quantity sold does not fall. Which finding would most strongly preserve the model rather than refute it?
options: The ceiling was above the market-clearing price
Consumers preferred other products during the policy
The market included many buyers and sellers
Officials described the ceiling as a fair policy
q.commonError: Applying a binding-ceiling prediction when the legal ceiling may be nonbinding.
q.feedback: A ceiling above equilibrium is nonbinding, so the shortage prediction does not apply.

q.q: A labor model predicts a payroll subsidy lowers hiring costs and expands employment at flexible wages. In a new region, bargaining agreements guarantee workers the entire subsidy as higher wages while firms’ net hiring costs stay unchanged. Which transfer of the model is defensible?
options: Keep the original employment forecast; a subsidy of the same statutory size must have the same effect under any bargaining rule.
Reject the original model in its own region; failure to transfer proves flexible wages never mattered for employment.
Rework the wage-setting mechanism; the unchanged net hiring cost removes the model’s stated employment-expansion channel.
Predict an equal employment contraction; workers receiving the subsidy necessarily shifts firms’ labor demand left by the same amount.
q.commonError: Transferring a result without checking context or omitted factors.
q.feedback: The original mechanism depends on a reduction in firms’ net labor cost. If wage bargaining absorbs the subsidy completely, that channel is absent. The model may still describe its original institutions, but needs revision for the new setting.

q.q: Two models fit past recessions equally well. One says reduced credit supply cuts investment; the other says weak expected sales reduce both borrowing and investment. A new policy randomly expands credit access for some otherwise comparable firms. Which observation best distinguishes the proposed mechanisms?
options: Borrowing and investment remain correlated in the historical sample after adding more recession years.
Investment rises among newly credit-eligible firms relative to controls without a prior relative improvement in expected sales.
Both models continue to predict the same national investment total during the experiment.
Firms with the strongest expected sales borrow most before the randomized eligibility change.
q.commonError: Treating shared historical fit as proof of one mechanism.
q.feedback: Randomized credit access creates variation separate from firms’ preexisting sales outlook. A relative investment response supports the credit-supply channel; historical co-movement alone is compatible with both mechanisms.

q.q: A simple model forecasts regional employment with 5% out-of-sample error and recommends policy A across plausible parameter values. A complex model lowers error to 4.8%, but small plausible parameter changes reverse its A-versus-B policy ranking. The decision concerns a costly irreversible policy. Which next step is strongest?
options: Report the modest prediction gain and unstable ranking, test sensitive parameters, and assess whether the policy choice is robust enough for this decision.
Choose the complex model because any lower forecast error establishes a more reliable policy ranking.
Choose A solely because the simple model is stable, treating stability as proof that its mechanism and recommendation are correct.
Average the two point recommendations without examining parameters, because averaging eliminates structural uncertainty.
q.commonError: Assuming additional detail automatically improves a model.
q.feedback: Predictive error and decision robustness are different criteria. A small fit improvement may not justify a sensitive irreversible recommendation; testing influential assumptions and reporting ranking uncertainty is more useful than automatic complexity or simplicity.

q.q: What role does an assumption play in a model?
options: It replaces the evidence used to test predictions
It makes the model a policy recommendation
It states a condition used to focus the analysis
It guarantees that every result is factually certain
q.commonError: Treating a conditional assumption as a universal fact.
q.feedback: An assumption states a condition held fixed or treated as given so the model can trace a particular relationship.

q.q: Must a model be rejected because it simplifies reality?
options: No; but only when the model includes a graph
No; judge whether the simplification fits its purpose
Yes; useful models reproduce every real-world detail
Yes; evidence cannot support a simplified explanation
q.commonError: Using the model without checking its purpose, assumptions, or evidence.
q.feedback: Simplification is a design feature; rejection is warranted only when omitted details undermine the model’s purpose or performance.

q.q: Does adding more detail automatically improve a model?
options: Yes; every extra variable improves every model
Yes; realism is the only useful model criterion
No; because simple models never make errors
No; complexity can reduce clarity or prediction quality
q.commonError: Assuming additional detail automatically improves a model.
q.feedback: More detail helps only when it improves relevant explanation or prediction enough to justify added complexity and fragility.

q.q: A prediction assumes income stays fixed. What if income changes?
options: Income must be ignored to protect the model
The assumption proves income never changes
The prediction may need revision because its condition changed
The prediction becomes true by definition
q.commonError: Treating a conditional assumption as a universal fact.
q.feedback: If income changes, the fixed-income prediction no longer isolates price and must be adjusted for an income-driven demand shift.

q.q: A model fit past data well. Does that prove its proposed mechanism?
options: No; models cannot provide any useful evidence
No; different mechanisms can fit the same observations
Yes; fit proves every assumed causal step
Yes; past fit guarantees future accuracy
q.commonError: Treating shared historical fit as proof of one mechanism.
q.feedback: Past fit shows descriptive performance, but competing-mechanism evidence is needed to establish the model’s causal explanation.

q.q: When should a model be applied to a new setting?
options: When its important assumptions remain reasonable there
Whenever it worked once in any setting
Only when it contains every possible detail
Whenever it supports the preferred conclusion
q.commonError: Transferring a result without checking context or omitted factors.
q.feedback: A model should transfer only when its important assumptions and mechanisms remain plausible in the new setting.

q.q: Economists use models mainly to:
options: Simplify reality and isolate important relationships
Include every detail of the economy
Eliminate the need for assumptions
Guarantee policy success
q.feedback: Models deliberately simplify so the important causal relationships can be studied.
q.commonError: Treating a model as either a complete copy of reality or a guaranteed prediction.

q.q: A demand model predicts fewer purchases after a price increase. How should this positive prediction be evaluated?
options: Compare the conditional prediction with observed evidence
Treat the prediction as a statement of what ought to happen
Accept the mechanism because the prediction sounds plausible
Reject all models whenever one observation differs
q.commonError: Using the model without checking its purpose, assumptions, or evidence.
q.feedback: The demand model makes a testable positive prediction, but its conclusion should be limited to settings where its assumptions describe the relevant buying decision.

q.q: A PPF uses only two goods. Why can this simplification still be useful for analyzing scarcity and opportunity cost?
options: The two-good assumption removes scarcity from production
The PPF proves real economies produce only two goods
The graph replaces the need to compare alternatives
The simplification makes the tradeoff easier to see
q.commonError: Rejecting a PPF because its two-good simplification is not literal.
q.feedback: The two-good abstraction exposes scarcity and opportunity cost without describing every output.

q.q: A supply-and-demand model holds buyer income fixed. What role does the ceteris paribus assumption play in this analysis?
options: Income is assumed never to change in real markets
The model makes income irrelevant to demand
Ceteris paribus guarantees the prediction is exact
Holding income fixed isolates the price relationship
q.commonError: Using the model without checking its purpose, assumptions, or evidence.
q.feedback: Holding buyer income fixed is the ceteris-paribus condition that lets the model isolate movement caused by price.

q.q: A policy model predicts lower emissions after a fee. What should an analyst check before relying on that prediction in the policy setting?
options: Ignore uncertainty because the model is quantitative
Choose assumptions that produce the preferred result
Test whether behavioral assumptions fit the policy setting
Treat the prediction as proof the policy is desirable
q.commonError: Using the model without checking its purpose, assumptions, or evidence.
q.feedback: The emissions prediction is positive analysis; policy evaluation still requires evidence that the fee changes the modeled behavioral margin.

q.q: Why is the Fed's control over the money supply not perfect?
options: M1 and M2 are always equal
Currency is not money
The Fed cannot buy bonds
Banks and depositors also influence lending
q.commonError: Assuming the Fed controls every dollar directly.
q.feedback: The Fed influences the money supply, but banks and depositors affect reserves, lending, and deposits.

q.q: The Fed's control over the money supply is imperfect partly because
options: banks may choose to hold excess reserves
Congress directly controls every bank loan
money demand is always zero
currency cannot be held by the public
q.commonError: thinking the Fed can force banks to lend every excess reserve
q.feedback: The Fed can influence lending conditions, but banks may still choose to hold excess reserves.

q.q: The Fed's control over the money supply is imperfect partly because households can choose to hold more money as
options: currency instead of deposits
real GDP instead of inflation
tax revenue instead of government spending
imports instead of exports
q.commonError: forgetting that currency held by the public affects bank reserves and deposit creation
q.feedback: If people hold more currency instead of deposits, banks have fewer deposits to lend out, limiting money creation.

q.q: If banks become nervous and stop lending excess reserves, the money multiplier will
options: be smaller than the simple multiplier predicts
be larger than the simple multiplier predicts
be exactly equal to the inflation rate
stop depending on reserves
q.commonError: thinking the simple multiplier always predicts the exact real-world result
q.feedback: If banks hold excess reserves instead of lending them, deposit creation is weaker than the simple multiplier suggests.

q.q: Why might a Fed policy action fail to increase the money supply as much as expected?
options: Banks may not lend all available excess reserves.
The Fed cannot buy government bonds.
Fiat money must have intrinsic value.
The price level is always fixed.
q.commonError: assuming central bank policy mechanically creates lending one-for-one
q.feedback: Fed actions influence the money supply, but the final effect depends partly on bank lending decisions.

q.q: Interest on reserves can affect monetary control because it changes banks' incentive to
options: hold reserves instead of lending them
calculate real GDP
set tax rates
issue commodity money
q.commonError: thinking interest on reserves has nothing to do with bank lending
q.feedback: Paying interest on reserves can encourage banks to hold reserves rather than lend them, affecting money creation.

q.q: If banks decide to hold more excess reserves, the money creation process becomes:
options: Stronger because lending rises
Weaker because lending falls
Unchanged because reserves do not matter
Infinite because deposits disappear
q.commonError: Ignoring bank behavior in monetary control.
q.feedback: When banks hold more excess reserves, they lend less, so deposit creation weakens.

q.q: Why is the simple money multiplier only a rough prediction in the real world?
options: Banks may hold excess reserves and people may hold currency.
The Fed cannot affect reserves in any way.
Deposits are not part of the money supply.
Banks always lend exactly zero.
q.commonError: thinking the simple multiplier always predicts the exact result
q.feedback: The simple multiplier assumes banks lend all excess reserves and the public holds no currency; excess reserves and currency holdings make actual money creation smaller.

q.q: If households decide to hold more currency and fewer bank deposits, banks will have
options: fewer deposits available to support loans
more deposits available to support loans
no reserve requirement
a larger required reserve ratio automatically
q.commonError: thinking currency holdings do not affect bank lending
q.feedback: When people hold more currency, fewer funds sit in deposits, which limits bank lending and money creation.

q.q: A bank holds excess reserves during a financial panic. What happens to deposit creation compared with the simple multiplier prediction?
options: Deposit creation is weaker.
Deposit creation is stronger.
Deposit creation is exactly unchanged.
Deposit creation becomes unrelated to reserves.
q.commonError: ignoring bank behavior in money creation
q.feedback: If banks hold excess reserves, they lend less, so deposit creation is weaker than the simple multiplier predicts.

q.q: Which situation makes the Fed's control over the money supply less precise?
options: Banks change how much they want to lend.
The Fed exists as a central bank.
Money has three functions.
Prices are quoted in dollars.
q.commonError: thinking central bank control is mechanically perfect
q.feedback: The Fed influences the money supply, but bank lending decisions affect the final amount of money created.

q.q: The central bank supplies ample reserves and banks are willing to lend, but households and firms become reluctant to borrow. What happens to deposit creation relative to the simple multiplier maximum?
options: Weak loan demand can keep deposit creation below the simple-multiplier maximum
It must equal the maximum because reserve supply alone determines every loan
It must exceed the maximum because unborrowed reserves count twice
It becomes fiscal policy because borrowers are not requesting loans
q.commonError: Assumes banks can expand loans to the textbook maximum even when creditworthy customers do not want to borrow.
q.feedback: Reserve availability is only one condition for lending; weak loan demand can make broad money expand by less than a simple multiplier suggests.

q.q: The Fed buys bonds, but banks hold the new reserves instead of lending them. What happens to the money multiplier process?
options: It weakens despite higher reserves
It strengthens despite no lending
It becomes unrelated to banks
It eliminates currency from M1
q.commonError: Assuming Fed purchases always create full deposit expansion.
q.feedback: Fed purchases raise reserves, but deposit expansion is weaker if banks do not lend those reserves.

q.q: A student says, 'The Fed can perfectly control the money supply because it controls reserves.' What is the best correction?
options: Bank reserves and public currency choices affect final money creation.
The Fed cannot influence reserves at all.
Banks cannot create money in a fractional reserve system.
Currency held by the public always increases deposits.
q.commonError: assuming Fed control over reserves equals perfect control over money supply
q.feedback: The Fed has powerful tools, but final money creation depends partly on banks and the public.

q.q: During a panic, banks hold excess reserves and households withdraw deposits into currency. What happens to the money multiplier?
options: It falls below the simple multiplier prediction.
It rises above the simple multiplier prediction.
It becomes equal to the reserve requirement.
It becomes unrelated to bank behavior.
q.commonError: using the simple multiplier mechanically during financial stress
q.feedback: Both excess reserves and currency withdrawals weaken deposit creation, so the actual multiplier falls.

q.q: If the Fed injects reserves but banks choose not to lend them, why might the money supply grow less than expected?
options: The reserves remain idle instead of supporting new deposits.
The reserve requirement must have become 100 percent by law.
The public must have stopped using money entirely.
The Fed's bond purchase automatically reduced deposits.
q.commonError: assuming injected reserves are always fully multiplied
q.feedback: Reserves only multiply into deposits if banks lend and borrowers redeposit. If banks sit on reserves, the multiplier weakens.

q.q: A higher interest rate paid on reserves can make monetary policy tighter because it
options: raises the reward for banks to hold reserves instead of lending
forces households to hold more commodity money
automatically lowers all taxes
makes money demand zero
q.commonError: thinking interest on reserves cannot affect lending incentives
q.feedback: If reserves pay more, banks may prefer holding reserves over making loans, which can restrain money creation.

q.q: If the public suddenly deposits more currency into banks and banks lend excess reserves, what happens to the banking system's ability to create money?
options: It increases because deposits and reserves available for lending rise.
It decreases because deposits destroy reserves.
It stays unchanged because deposits are never lent.
It disappears because money becomes fiat.
q.commonError: thinking moving currency into banks weakens lending
q.feedback: When currency becomes bank deposits, banks have more deposits and reserves to support lending.

q.q: A central bank wants to expand lending but banks are already holding large excess reserves. Which issue is most relevant?
options: Bank willingness to lend may limit money creation.
Commodity money must replace fiat money.
M1 must exclude checking deposits.
Velocity must be exactly zero.
q.commonError: thinking more reserves automatically guarantees more loans
q.feedback: More reserves do not guarantee more lending if banks are unwilling to lend.

q.q: A Fed bond purchase increases reserves, but households convert much of the new deposits into currency. What is the likely result?
options: The money supply rises by less than the simple multiplier predicts.
The money supply rises by more than the simple multiplier predicts.
The money supply cannot rise at all because bonds were purchased.
Currency holdings make the reserve requirement negative.
q.commonError: ignoring leakages from deposits into currency
q.feedback: Currency drain limits redepositing, so the multiplier effect is weaker.

q.q: Which statement best explains why banks cannot make society rich simply by creating more money through lending?
options: Money creation can increase nominal balances, but it does not automatically create real goods and services.
Every bank loan creates new factories instantly.
Money creation permanently increases real output without limits.
The money supply is unrelated to prices or output.
q.commonError: thinking more money means more real wealth automatically
q.feedback: Banks can help create money, but real wealth depends on real goods, services, labor, capital, and productivity.

q.q: A bank receives new deposits, the Fed pays higher interest on reserves, and banks choose to hold more excess reserves. What is the likely result?
options: Money creation weakens because lending falls
Money creation strengthens because deposits rose
The multiplier becomes unrelated to reserves
M1 falls because deposits are excluded
q.commonError: Assuming deposits automatically create full lending expansion.
q.feedback: Deposits increase lending potential, but higher interest on reserves can make banks hold reserves instead of lending them.

q.q: The Fed buys bonds during a banking panic, but households increase currency holdings and banks increase excess reserves. What should students infer?
options: Fed control is limited by depositor and bank behavior
The money multiplier must rise to its maximum
Open-market purchases cannot affect reserves
Currency holdings are excluded from M1
q.commonError: Ignoring leakage from currency holdings and excess reserves.
q.feedback: Fed purchases add reserves, but currency withdrawals and excess reserve holdings can weaken money creation.

q.q: The Fed buys $30 million in bonds. The reserve ratio is 10 percent, but banks hold half of new reserves as excess reserves. Which answer best describes the actual result compared with the simple multiplier maximum?
options: The actual money increase is less than the $300 million simple multiplier maximum.
The actual money increase equals exactly $300 million.
The actual money increase exceeds $300 million because excess reserves multiply faster.
The money supply must fall because bond purchases are contractionary.
q.commonError: using the simple multiplier even when banks hold excess reserves
q.feedback: The simple maximum would be $30 million x 10 = $300 million, but excess reserve holding weakens the actual expansion.

q.q: A student says, 'If the Fed lowers reserve requirements, the money supply must always rise by the maximum multiplier amount.' What is the best correction?
options: The maximum depends on banks lending excess reserves and borrowers redepositing funds.
Lower reserve requirements always eliminate excess reserves.
The money supply must fall when reserve requirements fall.
Reserve requirements affect only fiscal policy.
q.commonError: treating the simple multiplier as a guaranteed result
q.feedback: The simple multiplier is a maximum under strict assumptions. Banks and the public can weaken the actual money creation process.

q.q: Use a hypothetical banking system initially holding exactly its required reserves. The stated reserve ratio stays fixed, banks lend all excess reserves, every loan payment is fully redeposited, and there is no currency drain or other lending constraint. The initial deposit comes from currency previously held by the public, and total deposit expansion includes that initial deposit. The public moves $50 million from currency into checking deposits. The reserve ratio is 10 percent and banks lend all excess reserves. What is the maximum total deposit expansion supported by this shift?
options: $500 million
$50 million
$45 million
$5 million
q.commonError: thinking currency deposited into banks cannot support money creation
q.feedback: Moving currency into deposits gives banks reserves to support lending. With a multiplier of 10, $50 million can support up to $500 million in deposits. The initial cash deposit itself replaces public currency with deposits; it is not net new money.

q.q: The public withdraws $50 million from checking deposits into currency. The reserve ratio is 10 percent. Why can the final money supply fall by more than $50 million?
options: The withdrawal removes reserves from banks and reduces further deposit creation.
Currency automatically multiplies faster than deposits.
Banks gain excess reserves from the withdrawal.
Reserve requirements become negative.
q.commonError: thinking a currency withdrawal affects only the first $50 million
q.feedback: A currency drain reduces bank reserves and shrinks the base for additional lending, so the total effect can exceed the initial withdrawal.

q.q: Which scenario best illustrates why Fed control is powerful but not perfect?
options: The Fed injects reserves, but banks hold them because loan risk is high.
The Fed buys bonds and every bank must lend every reserve by law.
The Fed sets M1 exactly by counting every dollar daily.
The Fed controls household spending by setting tax brackets.
q.commonError: assuming Fed reserve injections automatically become loans
q.feedback: Fed tools matter, but banks still decide whether they are willing to lend.

q.q: If the Fed buys $100 million in bonds but the public holds all proceeds as currency instead of depositing them, which part of the simple multiplier process breaks?
options: Redepositing into banks, which limits further lending.
The initial Fed injection, which never occurs.
The definition of fiat money.
The unit of account function.
q.commonError: thinking currency held by the public supports the same lending as deposits
q.feedback: The money enters the public's hands, but if it is not deposited, banks cannot use it as reserves for further lending.

q.q: Which answer best explains why lowering the discount rate may not create much lending during a crisis?
options: Banks may still avoid borrowing or lending if they see borrowers as too risky.
Lower borrowing costs always force banks to lend.
The discount rate controls tax rates, not bank borrowing.
Lower discount rates automatically create commodity money.
q.commonError: assuming cheaper Fed credit guarantees private lending
q.feedback: Lowering the discount rate helps only if banks are willing to borrow and lend.

q.q: The Fed buys $80 million in bonds. The simple reserve ratio is 20 percent, but banks hold 25 percent of new reserves as excess reserves instead of lending them. Which answer best describes the result?
options: The money supply rises by less than the $400 million simple multiplier maximum.
The money supply rises by exactly $400 million.
The money supply rises by more than $400 million because excess reserves multiply.
The money supply falls because bond purchases are contractionary.
q.commonError: using the simple multiplier even when excess reserves are explicitly introduced
q.feedback: The simple multiplier maximum is 1/0.20 = 5, so $80 million could become $400 million. But excess reserve holding weakens the actual expansion.

q.q: In a hypothetical fully loaned-up system with a fixed 10 percent reserve ratio and no excess reserves, the public permanently switches $36 million from deposits to currency. The monetary base stays fixed. Banks restore their reserve ratios through loan repayments that destroy deposits; there are no defaults or other changes. What are the final changes in deposits and in currency plus deposits?
options: Deposits fall $360 million; money falls $324 million.
Deposits fall $36 million; money is unchanged.
Deposits fall $360 million; money falls $396 million.
Deposits fall $324 million; money falls $360 million.
q.commonError: thinking currency withdrawal only changes the location of money with no multiplier effect
q.feedback: Currency rises $36 million and reserves fall $36 million. At reserves/deposits = 0.10, deposits must fall $360 million in total. Money changes by +$36 million − $360 million = −$324 million.

q.q: The Fed sells $75 million in bonds. The multiplier is 4, but the public responds by moving additional funds out of banks into currency. What should we expect relative to the simple multiplier result?
options: The contraction may exceed $300 million because currency drain further weakens deposit creation.
The contraction must equal exactly $300 million.
The money supply must increase because bond sales add reserves.
The contraction must be smaller because currency drain raises bank reserves.
q.commonError: treating the simple multiplier as exact even with added currency drain
q.feedback: The simple contraction is $75 million x 4 = $300 million, but currency drain can make the banking contraction larger.

q.q: A bank has a reserve shortfall of $20,000. The Fed lowers the discount rate, but the bank still refuses to borrow because it fears insolvency. What does this show?
options: A lower discount rate may not restore lending if bank risk concerns dominate.
The discount rate only affects fiscal policy.
Lower discount rates always force borrowing.
Reserve shortfalls increase lending capacity.
q.commonError: thinking a lower policy rate automatically fixes bank behavior
q.feedback: The Fed can make borrowing cheaper, but banks may still avoid borrowing or lending when risk dominates.

q.q: Use a hypothetical banking system initially holding exactly its required reserves. The stated reserve ratio stays fixed, banks lend all excess reserves, every loan payment is fully redeposited, and there is no currency drain or other lending constraint. The initial deposit comes from currency previously held by the public, and total deposit expansion includes that initial deposit. If the public deposits $30 million in currency into banks, the reserve ratio is 15 percent, and banks lend all excess reserves, what is the maximum total deposit expansion?
options: $200 million
$30 million
$25.5 million
$4.5 million
q.commonError: calculating only the first-round loan instead of total deposit expansion
q.feedback: The multiplier is 1/0.15 = 6.666..., so $30 million can support about $200 million in total deposits. The initial cash deposit itself replaces public currency with deposits; it is not net new money.

q.q: A student says, 'If banks create money through loans, loans must create real goods too.' What is the best correction?
options: Loans create deposits; real output still needs productive resources.
Loans automatically create real output one-for-one.
Deposits are not money.
Banks create commodity money with every loan.
q.commonError: thinking money creation equals real wealth creation
q.feedback: Bank lending can expand money and spending power, but it does not automatically create more real goods and services.

q.q: A new $100,000 deposit enters the banking system. The required reserve ratio is 10 percent, but the public withdraws 20 percent of every new loan as currency before redepositing the rest. What happens relative to the simple multiplier?
options: The final expansion is smaller than the simple $1,000,000 maximum.
The final expansion equals exactly $1,000,000.
The final expansion is larger because currency leakage increases reserves.
The money supply must contract because deposits increase.
q.commonError: using the simple multiplier despite a stated currency leakage
q.feedback: The simple maximum is $100,000 x 10 = $1,000,000, but currency leakage reduces redeposits and weakens money creation.

q.q: Which statement best combines Chapter 30's banking model with monetary-control limits?
options: Excess reserves and currency holdings weaken deposit multiplication.
Fractional reserve banking guarantees exact Fed control of M1.
The multiplier works only with commodity money.
Currency drain increases bank reserves and expands lending.
q.commonError: thinking the multiplier mechanism is automatic and exact
q.feedback: Fractional-reserve banking can multiply deposits, but excess reserves and currency holdings can make the actual expansion smaller than the simple model predicts.

q.q: A bank has $2 million in assets and $120,000 in capital. If asset values fall by 4 percent, capital falls to:
q.commonError: Applying the loss percentage to capital instead of assets.
q.feedback: A 4 percent asset loss is $80,000, so capital falls from $120,000 to $40,000.

q.q: A bank has assets of $1,000,000 and capital of $80,000. If assets fall by $40,000, bank capital becomes:
q.commonError: Thinking losses reduce liabilities first.
q.feedback: Losses reduce bank capital. $80,000 - $40,000 = $40,000.

q.q: Why is the Fed's control over the money supply imperfect?
options: Excess reserves and public currency holdings.
The Fed cannot influence reserves.
Banks cannot lend money.
Currency is not money.
q.commonError: assuming Fed control is mechanically perfect
q.feedback: The Fed can influence money creation, but banks and the public also matter.

q.q: The Fed injects reserves, but banks choose not to lend because they are worried about risk. What happens relative to the simple multiplier?
options: Money creation is weaker than predicted.
Money creation is stronger than predicted.
The money supply must fall to zero.
The simple multiplier becomes infinite.
q.commonError: thinking reserves automatically become loans
q.feedback: If banks hold reserves instead of lending, deposit creation is weaker than the simple multiplier predicts.

q.q: The Fed buys bonds, banks hold some excess reserves, and households keep some proceeds as currency. What is the best conclusion?
options: The money supply rises by less than the simple multiplier predicts.
The money supply rises by exactly the simple multiplier amount.
The money supply must fall because households hold currency.
The Fed has perfect control over final money creation.
q.commonError: treating the simple multiplier as guaranteed
q.feedback: Excess reserves and currency drain both weaken the multiplier. The Fed is powerful, not magical.

q.q: After a reserve injection, banks hold extra reserves, the public keeps some loan proceeds as currency, and firms reduce borrowing. Relative to the simple multiplier model, what should we expect?
options: No change in broad money because reserve injections affect only bank capital
A substantially smaller expansion because several leakages interrupt repeated lending and redepositing
The exact simple multiplier maximum because the three effects cancel automatically
A larger expansion because every leakage creates additional bank reserves
q.commonError: Treats the central bank as having mechanical one-for-one control over broad money.
q.feedback: The central bank controls its own balance sheet and reserve conditions more directly than broad money, which also depends on banks, borrowers, and the public.

q.q: Which statement best describes what the central bank controls most directly?
options: Its own balance sheet and reserve conditions, not the exact final quantity of broad money
The exact quantity of bank loans made to every borrower
The public’s desired split between currency and deposits
The amount every commercial bank must want to lend regardless of risk
q.commonError: Treats the central bank as having mechanical one-for-one control over broad money.
q.feedback: The central bank controls its own balance sheet and reserve conditions more directly than broad money, which also depends on banks, borrowers, and the public.

q.q: The central bank lowers a policy-related borrowing rate, but banks still see borrowers as risky and firms do not want new loans. Why can the monetary response remain weak?
options: A lower central-bank lending rate automatically raises required reserves
The policy turns into a tax change when private borrowing is weak
Commercial banks are legally required to stop lending whenever the central bank lowers a rate
Cheaper central-bank liquidity does not eliminate bank risk concerns or weak credit demand
q.commonError: Assumes banks can expand loans to the textbook maximum even when creditworthy customers do not want to borrow.
q.feedback: Reserve availability is only one condition for lending; weak loan demand can make broad money expand by less than a simple multiplier suggests.

q.q: The central bank adds reserves, but banks choose to hold much of them as excess reserves. What is the likely result?
options: Broad deposit creation is smaller than the simple multiplier maximum
Deposit creation must equal the maximum because reserves increased
The money supply must fall by the amount of the reserve injection
Required reserves disappear from bank balance sheets
q.commonError: Treats the central bank as having mechanical one-for-one control over broad money.
q.feedback: The central bank controls its own balance sheet and reserve conditions more directly than broad money, which also depends on banks, borrowers, and the public.

q.q: Households convert part of each new bank deposit into currency rather than leaving the funds in banks. What happens to the deposit-multiplication process?
options: It strengthens because currency held by the public becomes excess reserves
It is unchanged because currency and bank reserves are identical
It guarantees a larger simple multiplier regardless of the reserve ratio
It weakens because less money is redeposited into banks for additional lending
q.commonError: Treats the central bank as having mechanical one-for-one control over broad money.
q.feedback: When households keep currency, less of each loan is redeposited; fewer redeposits support fewer subsequent lending rounds, weakening deposit multiplication.

q.q: Banks have ample reserves and are willing to lend, but creditworthy firms postpone borrowing during a severe slump. Which limitation is illustrated?
options: Household currency holdings must have fallen to zero
Bank capital automatically rises whenever firms reject loans
Weak loan demand can keep money creation below the textbook maximum
The central bank has lost the legal authority to create reserves
q.commonError: Assumes banks can expand loans to the textbook maximum even when creditworthy customers do not want to borrow.
q.feedback: Reserve availability is only one condition for lending; weak loan demand can make broad money expand by less than a simple multiplier suggests.

q.q: The Fed buys $120 million in bonds. The reserve ratio is 10 percent, but banks hold 30 percent of new reserves as excess reserves. Which result is most accurate?
options: The money supply rises by less than the $1.2 billion simple multiplier maximum.
The money supply rises by exactly $1.2 billion.
The money supply falls because bond purchases drain reserves.
The money supply rises by more than $1.2 billion because excess reserves multiply faster.
q.commonError: using the simple multiplier as exact when excess reserves are stated
q.feedback: The simple maximum is $120 million x 10 = $1.2 billion, but excess reserve holding weakens the actual expansion.

q.q: A bank has $2 million in deposits, $260,000 in reserves, and a 10 percent reserve requirement. The public then withdraws $100,000 in currency from deposits. If deposits and reserves both fall by $100,000, what is the bank's reserve position after the withdrawal?
options: It is short $30,000 in reserves.
It has $70,000 in excess reserves.
It has exactly required reserves.
It can lend $160,000.
q.commonError: not reducing both deposits and reserves after currency withdrawal
q.feedback: After withdrawal, deposits are $1.9 million and reserves are $160,000. Required reserves are $190,000, so the bank is short $30,000.

q.q: In a hypothetical banking system initially without excess reserves, the public deposits $56,000 of existing currency. The required-reserve ratio stays at 20 percent. Each bank lends all excess reserves; after every loan, 25 percent stays as currency and 75 percent reaches the next bank. No other constraint binds. Including the initial deposit, what is the eventual deposit increase, and what is the net increase in currency plus deposits?
options: Deposits rise $140,000; net money rises $112,000.
Deposits rise $280,000; net money rises $224,000.
Deposits rise $140,000; net money rises $140,000.
Deposits rise $112,000; net money rises $84,000.
q.commonError: ignoring the currency leakage stated in the question
q.feedback: Successive deposits have ratio 0.80 × 0.75 = 0.60, so their sum is $56,000/(1 − 0.60) = $140,000. Total loans are 0.80 × $140,000 = $112,000; $28,000 returns to public currency. Currency changes by −$56,000 + $28,000, so net money rises $112,000.

q.q: A policy memo claims that supplying more reserves guarantees the full textbook deposit expansion, even when creditworthy firms postpone borrowing and banks retain excess reserves. Which correction addresses both breaks in the argument?
options: Banks must be willing to lend and borrowers willing to borrow; unused reserves do not guarantee new deposits.
Only the reserve requirement matters; banks and borrowers cannot alter the predicted expansion.
Borrower caution raises the multiplier because fewer loans consume fewer reserves.
Excess reserves are already customer deposits, so the predicted expansion has occurred.
q.commonError: assuming reserve injections guarantee full lending
q.feedback: The reserve injection is an input to a conditional model. Both bank decisions and credit demand can prevent the lending and redepositing needed to reach its maximum.

q.q: If a bank’s assets fall, what absorbs the loss first?
options: Bank capital
Currency
M1
The CPI
q.feedback: Losses reduce bank capital.

q.q: Why is Fed control of the money supply imperfect?
options: Banks and depositors affect lending and reserves
The Fed cannot buy bonds
Currency is not money
Deposits never change
q.feedback: The Fed influences the money supply, but banks and depositors also affect it.

q.commonError: Treating the simple multiplier as guaranteed.
q.q: The simple multiplier overpredicts money creation when banks:
options: Hold excess reserves
Lend all excess reserves
Face a lower reserve ratio
Receive new deposits
q.feedback: If banks hold excess reserves, less money is created through lending.

q.commonError: Ignoring public currency holdings.
q.q: If people hold more currency instead of deposits, bank money creation usually:
options: Weakens
Strengthens
Becomes unlimited
Is unaffected by reserves
q.feedback: Currency held outside banks cannot support deposit creation the same way bank deposits can.

q.q: A bank has $500,000 in assets and $30,000 in capital. If assets fall by $20,000, capital becomes:
q.feedback: Losses reduce capital, so $30,000 - $20,000 = $10,000.

q.q: The Fed buys bonds, but banks hold excess reserves. What should happen to deposit creation?
options: It is weaker than the simple multiplier predicts
It reaches the full multiplier automatically
It becomes unrelated to lending
It eliminates currency from M1
q.feedback: If banks do not lend excess reserves, the deposit expansion process weakens.

q.commonError: Treating the simple multiplier as guaranteed.
q.q: The Fed injects reserves, but banks hold half of them as excess reserves. What happens?
options: Money creation is less than the simple multiplier predicts
Money creation is exactly the simple maximum
Money creation is larger than the simple maximum
Money supply must fall
q.feedback: Excess reserve holding weakens the multiplier process.

q.q: Which variable is nominal?
options: Real GDP
Nominal wage
Relative price
Quantity of labor
q.commonError: Confusing money-measured variables with real variables.
q.feedback: A nominal wage is measured in dollars.

q.q: Which variable is real?
options: Nominal GDP
Dollar wage
Relative price
Price level
q.commonError: Treating all prices as nominal variables.
q.feedback: A relative price compares one good to another, so it is a real variable.

q.q: Monetary neutrality says that in the long run, a change in the money supply affects:
options: Nominal variables, not real variables
Real output only
The natural rate only
Technology only
q.commonError: Thinking money changes real variables permanently in the long run.
q.feedback: Monetary neutrality means money affects nominal variables in the long run, not real output or employment.

q.q: A nominal variable is measured in
options: monetary units
physical units
hours only
percent changes only
q.commonError: confusing nominal with real
q.feedback: Nominal variables are measured in monetary units, such as dollars.

q.q: A real variable is measured in
options: physical units or purchasing power
only current dollars
only bank deposits
only government bonds
q.commonError: thinking all economic variables are nominal
q.feedback: Real variables are measured in physical units or purchasing power, not just dollars.

q.q: Which of the following is a nominal variable?
options: Nominal wage in dollars per hour
Real wage in goods per hour
Real GDP in units of output
Relative price of apples in terms of oranges
q.commonError: mistaking real purchasing power for a dollar amount
q.feedback: A nominal wage is measured in dollars per hour, so it is a nominal variable.

q.q: Which of the following is a real variable?
options: Real GDP
Nominal GDP
Nominal wage
The price level
q.commonError: thinking GDP is always nominal
q.feedback: Real GDP measures output adjusted for prices, so it is a real variable.

q.q: The classical dichotomy separates variables into
options: nominal and real variables
supply and demand variables
public and private variables
short-run and long-run bonds
q.commonError: thinking the dichotomy separates fiscal and monetary policy
q.feedback: The classical dichotomy separates nominal variables from real variables.

q.q: Monetary neutrality means changes in the money supply do not affect
options: real variables in the long run
nominal prices in the long run
the price level
the inflation rate
q.commonError: thinking money neutrality means money has no effect on prices
q.feedback: Monetary neutrality means money growth affects nominal variables but not real variables in the long run.

q.q: Over the long run, all dollar wages and prices are twice as high while output per worker and hours worked are unchanged. Which interpretation best fits monetary neutrality?
options: Nominal variables changed, but the listed real variables did not.
Real variables doubled because every dollar price doubled.
Output per worker must have doubled because wages doubled.
The price level is a real variable, so nothing nominal changed.
q.commonError: Compares dollar values without adjusting for the price level.
q.feedback: Separate nominal from real variables. A proportional change in nominal wages and prices can leave purchasing power unchanged.

q.q: If all nominal prices and wages double while relative prices stay unchanged, this illustrates:
options: Monetary neutrality
Crowding out
A supply shock
A liquidity trap
q.commonError: Missing the real versus nominal distinction.
q.feedback: Monetary neutrality says nominal variables can change while real variables remain unchanged in the long run.

q.q: If all nominal prices double but relative prices stay the same, this illustrates
options: monetary neutrality
crowding out
the multiplier effect
liquidity preference
q.commonError: thinking changes in nominal prices automatically change relative prices
q.feedback: Monetary neutrality says money affects nominal variables but not real variables in the long run.

q.q: Which statement is consistent with the classical dichotomy?
options: Money growth can affect nominal wages without changing real wages in the long run.
Money growth changes only real variables and never nominal variables.
Nominal and real variables are always identical.
The price level is a real variable.
q.commonError: thinking nominal and real variables move identically
q.feedback: Under the classical dichotomy, money affects nominal variables, while real variables are determined by real factors in the long run.

q.q: A nominal wage rises from $15 to $30 while the price level doubles. What happens to the real wage?
options: It stays the same.
It doubles.
It falls by half.
It becomes zero.
q.commonError: thinking a higher nominal wage always means a higher real wage
q.feedback: If nominal wages and the price level both double, the real wage is unchanged.

q.q: After a sustained monetary expansion, the long-run price level is higher and nominal wages are higher by roughly the same proportion. What happens to the real wage if productivity is unchanged?
options: It can return to about its previous level because both the wage and price level rose together.
It must rise in the same proportion as the nominal wage because a larger dollar wage always guarantees more purchasing power.
It must fall to zero because money growth raises prices.
It becomes equal to the money-supply growth rate.
q.commonError: Compares dollar values without adjusting for the price level.
q.feedback: Separate nominal from real variables. A proportional change in nominal wages and prices can leave purchasing power unchanged.

q.q: If nominal wages double, prices double, and real output is unchanged, the result best illustrates:
options: Monetary neutrality
Crowding out
Sticky prices
Fiscal stimulus
q.commonError: Treating nominal changes as real changes.
q.feedback: If nominal variables double while real variables stay unchanged, that is monetary neutrality.

q.q: A textbook says money is neutral in the long run. Which outcome is most consistent with that idea after the money supply doubles?
options: Nominal prices double while relative prices and real output are unchanged.
Real output doubles while nominal prices are unchanged.
Relative prices double while nominal prices are unchanged.
The price level falls and real wages double.
q.commonError: thinking money neutrality means prices do not change
q.feedback: Money neutrality means money changes nominal variables, not real variables, in the long run.

q.q: If every nominal price and nominal wage doubles, why might employment and output be unchanged in the long run?
options: Real wages and relative prices are unchanged.
Workers receive twice as many physical goods per hour.
Money demand must fall to zero.
The reserve requirement doubles automatically.
q.commonError: thinking nominal doubling changes real incentives by itself
q.feedback: If all nominal values double together, real wages and relative prices do not change, so real decisions need not change.

q.q: Which pair correctly classifies the variables?
options: Nominal GDP is nominal; real GDP is real.
Nominal GDP is real; real GDP is nominal.
The price level is real; real wage is nominal.
Relative price is nominal; dollar wage is real.
q.commonError: labeling anything involving GDP as real
q.feedback: Nominal GDP is measured in dollars. Real GDP is measured in output adjusted for price changes.

q.q: A country doubles its money supply and, in the long run, all dollar prices double. What happens to the value of money?
options: It falls by half.
It doubles.
It stays unchanged.
It becomes equal to real GDP.
q.commonError: thinking money supply doubling doubles the value of money
q.feedback: If the price level doubles, the value of money, 1/P, falls by half.

q.q: A monetary expansion raises output temporarily, but years later output returns to its prior real trend while the price level remains permanently higher. Why is this consistent with monetary neutrality?
options: Neutrality describes the long-run separation of nominal changes from real output, not the absence of short-run real effects.
Neutrality requires the price level to return fully to its original level after every monetary expansion, even in the long run.
Neutrality means real output must remain permanently above trend after money growth.
Neutrality applies only when both output and prices are unchanged at every horizon.
q.commonError: Treats monetary neutrality as a claim that money can never affect real activity.
q.feedback: Monetary neutrality is a long-run proposition: nominal variables can change while real output and other real variables return to levels determined by real factors.

q.q: A central bank doubles the money supply, output is unchanged, and all nominal wages and prices double. Which claim is strongest?
options: Real wages and relative prices are unchanged
Real wages double with nominal wages
Relative prices double with prices
Output must double with money
q.commonError: Confusing nominal doubling with real doubling.
q.feedback: If wages and prices double together, real wages and relative prices remain unchanged.

q.q: A worker’s nominal wage rises 6 percent while the price level rises 9 percent. What happens to the real wage?
options: It falls by about 3 percent
It rises by about 3 percent
It rises by about 15 percent
It stays unchanged
q.commonError: Treating nominal wage growth as real wage growth.
q.feedback: Real wage growth is approximately nominal wage growth minus inflation, so 6 - 9 = -3 percent.

q.q: Refer to the value-of-money graph. The economy moves from a to b. Velocity is allowed to change. In a long-run comparison, a nominal wage rises by the same proportion as the price level inferred from those points, and technology and labor supplies are unchanged. Which comparison fits monetary neutrality?
options: The price level and nominal wage rise by one-third; the real wage need not change.
The price level falls by one-quarter; the real wage must rise.
The price level doubles; unchanged real resources require output to double.
The price level rises by one-third; the real wage must also rise by one-third.
q.commonError: confusing nominal price-level changes with real-output changes
q.feedback: The graph gives value of money 2 at a and 1.5 at b. Their reciprocal price levels are 1/2 and 2/3, a one-third increase. Proportional nominal wage growth leaves the real wage unchanged; nominal changes alone do not raise real productive capacity. With real output fixed, this graph requires velocity to fall to two-thirds of its initial value; it is not the fixed-velocity quantity-theory case.
q.imageAlt: Money graph with downward-sloping MD, vertical MS1 and MS2, and labeled points a, b, and c.
q.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is Q_M and the vertical axis is V_M. MD slopes downward from upper left to lower right. MS1 is a vertical line at Q_M = 2,500 and MS2 is a vertical line at Q_M = 5,000. Point a lies where MS1 meets MD at V_M = 2. Point b lies where MS2 meets MD at V_M = 1.5. Point c lies on MD at Q_M = 7,500 and V_M = 1. Dashed guides mark the labeled V_M and Q_M values.

q.q: A country doubles all nominal wages and prices, while output, employment, and relative prices are unchanged. Which concept explains this outcome?
options: Monetary neutrality
Crowding out
The liquidity trap
Shoeleather costs
q.commonError: thinking nominal doubling must increase real output
q.feedback: If nominal variables change but real variables do not, that is monetary neutrality.

q.q: Nominal wages rise 12 percent while the price level rises 8 percent. Approximately what happens to the real wage?
options: It rises by about 4 percent.
It falls by about 4 percent.
It rises by about 20 percent.
It is unchanged.
q.commonError: looking only at nominal wage growth
q.feedback: Real wage growth is roughly nominal wage growth minus inflation: 12 percent - 8 percent = 4 percent.

q.q: If nominal GDP rises 10 percent while real GDP rises 4 percent, what happened to the price level approximately?
options: It rose about 6 percent.
It rose about 14 percent.
It fell about 6 percent.
It stayed fixed.
q.commonError: adding real growth to nominal growth instead of subtracting
q.feedback: Nominal GDP growth is roughly inflation plus real GDP growth, so price level growth is about 10 - 4 = 6 percent.

q.q: A student says nominal wages rose 8 percent, so workers are better off. Inflation was 11 percent. What correction survives?
options: Real wages fell because prices rose faster than nominal wages.
Real wages rose because nominal wages increased above zero.
Real wages were unchanged because all inflation is neutral immediately.
Real wages doubled because nominal wages are measured in dollars.
q.commonError: Confusing nominal wage growth with real wage growth.
q.feedback: Real wage growth is approximately nominal wage growth minus inflation, so workers lost purchasing power.

q.q: A student says, 'Since money is neutral, monetary policy cannot affect output during recessions.' Which correction is strongest?
options: Neutrality is a long-run claim; short-run sticky prices allow AD effects on output.
Neutrality means money changes output permanently but not prices.
Neutrality applies only to fiscal policy and never to money.
Neutrality means the Phillips curve slopes downward in the long run.
q.commonError: Applying long-run neutrality to every short-run case.
q.feedback: Money is neutral in the long run, but monetary policy can affect output in the short run through aggregate demand.

q.q: Nominal GDP rises 12 percent while real GDP rises 5 percent. What happened to the price level, and which kind of variable changed?
options: The price level rose about 7 percent; that is a nominal change.
The price level rose about 17 percent; that is a real change.
The price level fell about 7 percent; that is a nominal change.
The price level was unchanged; only real output changed.
q.commonError: adding nominal and real growth instead of subtracting
q.feedback: Nominal GDP growth is roughly inflation plus real GDP growth, so price growth is about 12 - 5 = 7 percent. The price level is nominal.

q.q: A worker's nominal wage rises from $24 to $30 while the price level rises from 6 to 10. What happens to the real wage?
options: It falls from 4 units to 3 units.
It rises from 4 units to 5 units.
It stays at 4 units.
It rises from 6 units to 10 units.
q.commonError: looking only at the nominal wage increase
q.feedback: Real wage is W/P. It falls from 24/6 = 4 to 30/10 = 3 units.

q.q: All nominal prices double except wages, which rise only 50 percent. What happens to real wages?
options: Real wages fall because nominal wages rise less than the price level.
Real wages rise because nominal wages rose.
Real wages are unchanged because all prices rose.
Real wages double because prices doubled.
q.commonError: thinking any nominal wage increase raises the real wage
q.feedback: Real wages depend on wages relative to prices. If wages rise 50 percent while prices double, real wages fall.

q.q: A country's price level rises from 100 to 140, nominal wages rise from $20 to $24, and workers complain their purchasing power fell. What happened to real wages?
options: They fell because wages rose 20 percent while prices rose 40 percent.
They rose because nominal wages rose.
They stayed the same because both wages and prices rose.
They doubled because the price level rose.
q.commonError: thinking nominal wage growth automatically raises purchasing power
q.feedback: Nominal wages rose 20 percent, but prices rose 40 percent. Real wages fell.

q.q: A policy causes all nominal prices, nominal wages, and nominal debts to double, but output and employment remain unchanged. Which outcome best fits long-run monetary neutrality?
options: Nominal variables changed while real variables stayed unchanged.
Real variables changed while nominal variables stayed unchanged.
Money had no effect on the price level.
Relative prices doubled.
q.commonError: thinking monetary neutrality means money has no nominal effects
q.feedback: Long-run monetary neutrality means money affects nominal variables but not real output or employment.

q.q: A worker earns $20 per hour, and the price level is 5. The real wage is
options: 4 units of output per hour
$25 per hour
100 units of output per hour
0.25 units of output per hour
q.commonError: multiplying wage by price level instead of dividing
q.feedback: Real wage equals nominal wage divided by price level: 20 / 5 = 4 units of output per hour.

q.q: If the price of pizza rises from $10 to $20 and the price of soda rises from $2 to $4, the relative price of pizza in terms of soda
options: is unchanged
doubles
falls by half
becomes zero
q.commonError: thinking nominal price increases always change relative prices
q.feedback: Pizza was 5 sodas before and 5 sodas after. The relative price is unchanged.

q.q: A worker's nominal wage rises from $20 to $30 while the price level rises from 4 to 5. What happens to the real wage?
options: It rises from 5 to 6 units of output.
It falls from 5 to 4 units of output.
It stays at 5 units of output.
It rises from 4 to 5 units of output.
q.commonError: looking only at the nominal wage increase
q.feedback: Real wage is W/P. It rises from 20/4 = 5 to 30/5 = 6.

q.q: The price of coffee rises from $4 to $8 while the price of tea rises from $2 to $3. What happens to the relative price of coffee in terms of tea?
options: It rises from 2 teas to about 2.67 teas.
It stays at 2 teas.
It falls from 2 teas to 1.5 teas.
It becomes 8 teas.
q.commonError: thinking all nominal price increases leave relative prices unchanged
q.feedback: Coffee was 4/2 = 2 teas. It becomes 8/3, or about 2.67 teas.

q.q: Which unit is used to express a nominal variable?
options: monetary units
physical units
real output units
labor hours only
q.commonError: confusing nominal with real
q.feedback: Nominal variables are measured in money terms, such as dollars.

q.q: A nominal wage rises from $20 to $30 while the price level rises from 4 to 6. What happens to the real wage?
options: It stays at 5 units of output.
It rises from 5 to 6 units.
It falls from 5 to 3.33 units.
It doubles.
q.commonError: looking only at nominal wage growth
q.feedback: Real wage is W/P. It starts at 20/4 = 5 and ends at 30/6 = 5.

q.q: A country's money supply doubles, and in the long run all nominal prices and wages double while output is unchanged. Which concept does this illustrate?
options: Monetary neutrality
Crowding out
Liquidity trap
Menu costs
q.commonError: thinking money neutrality means prices do not change
q.feedback: Monetary neutrality means money affects nominal variables but not real variables in the long run.

q.q: Which outcome is most consistent with long-run monetary neutrality after a one-time increase in the money supply?
options: A higher price level with real output determined by real productive factors.
Permanently higher real output with no change in nominal prices.
Permanently lower prices because more money makes each dollar more valuable.
A permanently higher real wage solely because the number of dollars increased.
q.commonError: Treats monetary neutrality as a claim that money can never affect real activity.
q.feedback: Monetary neutrality is a long-run proposition: nominal variables can change while real output and other real variables return to levels determined by real factors.

q.q: A worker’s nominal wage and the price level both rise 10 percent while productivity is unchanged. What happens to the worker’s real wage approximately?
options: It rises about 20 percent.
It rises exactly 10 percent.
It falls exactly 10 percent.
It is roughly unchanged.
q.commonError: Compares dollar values without adjusting for the price level.
q.feedback: Separate nominal from real variables. A proportional change in nominal wages and prices can leave purchasing power unchanged.

q.q: Which variable is nominal rather than real?
options: Hours of labor used to produce haircuts.
Haircuts produced per worker.
The dollar price of a haircut.
The quantity of haircuts produced.
q.commonError: Compares dollar values without adjusting for the price level.
q.feedback: Separate nominal from real variables. A proportional change in nominal wages and prices can leave purchasing power unchanged.

q.q: Money growth accelerates for several years. In the long-run neutrality framework, which comparison is most defensible?
options: Neutrality requires money growth to leave every nominal price and wage unchanged in the long run.
Nominal prices can be persistently higher even though money growth does not permanently raise productive capacity.
Productive capacity must rise one-for-one with the price level.
A higher price level proves long-run real output rose by the same percentage.
q.commonError: Treats a one-time nominal level change as permanent real growth.
q.feedback: A one-time monetary expansion can raise nominal levels; long-run real growth requires changes in real productive capacity.

q.q: A country redenominates so every old 100-unit price becomes 1 new unit, with contracts and wages converted proportionally. What has changed economically?
options: The nominal unit of account changed, while real quantities and relative prices need not change.
Real output fell by 99 percent because smaller numbers on price tags necessarily mean less production.
Productivity rose because fewer currency units are needed per transaction.
The natural rate of unemployment must fall because nominal wages were converted.
q.commonError: Compares dollar values without adjusting for the price level.
q.feedback: Separate nominal from real variables. A proportional change in nominal wages and prices can leave purchasing power unchanged.

q.q: The central bank unexpectedly expands money, real activity rises for a time, and later output returns to potential while nominal prices remain higher. Which statement best reconciles the episode?
options: Long-run neutrality is disproved whenever any short-run real effect occurs.
Neutrality requires output to remain permanently above potential.
The episode can be neutral only if the price level eventually falls below its starting point.
Short-run real effects can coexist with long-run monetary neutrality.
q.commonError: Treats monetary neutrality as a claim that money can never affect real activity.
q.feedback: Monetary neutrality is a long-run proposition: nominal variables can change while real output and other real variables return to levels determined by real factors.

q.q: Refer to the value-of-money graph. A worker earns $24 at point a and $30 at point b. Treat each point’s price level as the reciprocal of its displayed value of money. What happens to the worker’s real wage, and what nominal wage at b would instead preserve the original purchasing power?
options: Real wage falls from 48 to 45 output units; $32 would preserve it.
Real wage rises from 12 to 20 output units; $18 would preserve it.
Real wage rises from 48 to 60 output units; $24 would preserve it.
Real wage falls from 48 to 45 output units; $36 would preserve it.
q.commonError: not converting value of money into price level before calculating real wage
q.feedback: P is 1/2 at a and 2/3 at b. Real wages are 24/(1/2) = 48 and 30/(2/3) = 45. To retain 48 units at b requires 48 × 2/3 = $32.
q.imageAlt: Money graph with downward-sloping MD, vertical MS1 and MS2, and labeled points a, b, and c.
q.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is Q_M and the vertical axis is V_M. MD slopes downward from upper left to lower right. MS1 is a vertical line at Q_M = 2,500 and MS2 is a vertical line at Q_M = 5,000. Point a lies where MS1 meets MD at V_M = 2. Point b lies where MS2 meets MD at V_M = 1.5. Point c lies on MD at Q_M = 7,500 and V_M = 1. Dashed guides mark the labeled V_M and Q_M values.

q.q: Nominal GDP rises 15 percent, real GDP rises 6 percent, and nominal wages rise 8 percent. What happens to the price level and real wages approximately?
options: P rises about 9 percent; real wages fall about 1 percent.
P rises about 21 percent; real wages rise about 8 percent.
P falls about 9 percent; real wages rise about 17 percent.
P rises about 6 percent; real wages rise about 2 percent.
q.commonError: not comparing nominal wage growth to inflation
q.feedback: Inflation is about 15 - 6 = 9 percent. Nominal wages rise 8 percent, so real wages fall about 1 percent.

q.q: A country doubles the number of currency units used to quote every wage and price, while production technology, labor, and relative prices are unchanged. What is the best first inference?
options: The change is nominal; the economy has not doubled its real productive capacity.
Real productive capacity doubled because every nominal amount doubled.
The natural rate of unemployment doubled because the currency unit changed.
The country necessarily experienced a permanent doubling of output per worker because every quoted nominal price and wage also doubled.
q.commonError: Treats monetary neutrality as a claim that money can never affect real activity.
q.feedback: Monetary neutrality is a long-run proposition: nominal variables can change while real output and other real variables return to levels determined by real factors.

q.q: A student says, “If money is neutral, monetary policy can never affect real output.” What is the best correction?
options: Neutrality is a long-run claim; short-run real effects can occur even if long-run real output returns to a level set by real factors.
Neutrality means money changes only real output and never prices at any horizon, so even temporary short-run changes in prices, spending, or production cannot occur.
Neutrality applies only during recessions, not in long-run comparisons of nominal and real economic variables.
Neutrality means every monetary-policy action has exactly zero effect on prices, output, employment, and interest rates at every horizon.
q.feedback: Monetary neutrality is a long-run proposition: nominal variables can change while real output and other real variables return to levels determined by real factors.
q.commonError: Treats monetary neutrality as a claim that money can never affect real activity.

q.q: A wage measured in dollars is:
options: Nominal
Real
Relative
Imported
q.feedback: A dollar wage is a nominal variable.

q.q: A wage adjusted for the price level is:
options: Real
Nominal
Fiat
Reserve
q.feedback: A wage adjusted for prices is a real wage.

q.commonError: Looking only at the nominal wage.
q.q: Real wage equals:
options: Nominal wage divided by price level
Nominal wage times price level
Price level divided by nominal wage
Money supply divided by wage
q.feedback: Real wage adjusts the dollar wage for the price level.

q.commonError: Thinking a higher nominal wage always means higher purchasing power.
q.q: If nominal wage is $20 and the price level is 4, real wage is:
options: 5 units
80 units
16 units
24 units
q.feedback: Real wage is 20 / 4 = 5 units.

q.commonError: Thinking neutrality means money has no effect on prices.
q.q: Monetary neutrality means money growth affects:
options: Long-run nominal variables
Only real variables
Neither prices nor wages
Only unemployment
q.feedback: Money neutrality means money affects nominal variables but not real variables in the long run.

q.commonError: Thinking money neutrality means prices are fixed.
q.q: If all nominal prices double but real output is unchanged, this fits:
options: Monetary neutrality
Crowding out
Liquidity trap
Menu costs only
q.feedback: Nominal variables changed, but real output did not.

q.q: If all nominal prices and wages double but real output is unchanged, this supports:
options: Monetary neutrality
Crowding out
Sticky wage theory only
A liquidity trap
q.feedback: Monetary neutrality means nominal variables can change without changing real variables in the long run.

q.q: A worker’s nominal wage rises 5 percent while inflation is 8 percent. The real wage:
options: Falls by about 3 percent
Rises by about 3 percent
Rises by about 13 percent
Does not change
q.feedback: Real wage growth is approximately nominal wage growth minus inflation: 5 - 8 = -3 percent.

q.commonError: Looking only at nominal wage growth.
q.q: Nominal wage rises from $20 to $30 and the price level rises from 4 to 6. What happens to real wage?
options: It stays at 5 units
It rises to 6 units
It falls to 3.33 units
It doubles
q.feedback: Real wage is 20/4 = 5 and 30/6 = 5.

q.commonError: Thinking neutrality means no price changes.
q.q: Money supply doubles, all nominal prices double, and real output is unchanged. This illustrates:
options: Monetary neutrality
Crowding out
Liquidity trap
Shoeleather costs
q.feedback: Nominal variables changed, but real output did not.

q.q: The quantity theory predicts that sustained money growth faster than real output growth can raise inflation. In the long-run neutrality framework, what should a student infer about real productive capacity?
options: Faster money growth can raise nominal prices without permanently increasing productive capacity.
Faster money growth must permanently raise productive capacity by the same percentage.
Higher inflation proves output per worker rose by the same amount.
Long-run neutrality requires inflation to be zero whenever money growth exceeds output growth.
q.commonError: Stops after predicting the price-level effect and does not separate nominal from real outcomes.
q.feedback: Use the quantity-theory result for nominal spending and prices, then apply long-run neutrality to ask which real variables need not rise permanently.

q.q: If the Fed buys bonds in open-market operations, what happens first?
options: Bank reserves tend to fall
Bank reserves tend to rise
SRAS shifts left
The natural rate falls
q.commonError: Reversing bond purchases and bond sales.
q.feedback: Fed bond purchases inject reserves into the banking system.

q.q: When the Fed buys government bonds in open-market operations, the money supply tends to
options: increase
decrease
stay fixed by law
turn into commodity money
q.commonError: thinking bond purchases reduce the money supply
q.feedback: When the Fed buys bonds, it injects money into the banking system, so the money supply tends to increase.

q.q: When the Fed sells government bonds in open-market operations, the money supply tends to
options: decrease
increase
become equal to real GDP
stop depending on banks
q.commonError: thinking bond sales add money to the economy
q.feedback: When the Fed sells bonds, buyers pay money to the Fed, so money is pulled out of circulation.

q.q: A lower discount rate tends to make banks
options: more willing to borrow from the Fed
less willing to lend
hold exactly 100 percent reserves
stop creating deposits
q.commonError: thinking a lower borrowing cost discourages borrowing
q.feedback: A lower discount rate makes borrowing from the Fed cheaper, which can encourage bank lending.

q.q: If the Fed wants to expand the money supply using open-market operations, it should
options: buy government bonds
sell government bonds
raise taxes
cut government purchases
q.commonError: thinking bond purchases take money out of circulation
q.feedback: Buying government bonds injects money into the banking system and expands the money supply.

q.q: If the Fed wants to contract the money supply using open-market operations, it should
options: sell government bonds
buy government bonds
increase government spending
lower income taxes
q.commonError: thinking bond sales add money to banks
q.feedback: Selling government bonds pulls money out of the banking system and contracts the money supply.

q.q: If the Fed lowers reserve requirements, banks can usually create
options: more money through lending
less money through lending
no deposits at all
commodity money instead of fiat money
q.commonError: thinking lower reserve requirements reduce bank lending
q.feedback: Lower reserve requirements free up reserves, allowing banks to lend more and expand deposits.

q.q: If the Fed wants to reduce the money supply through open-market operations, it should:
options: Buy bonds from banks
Sell bonds to the public
Lower reserve requirements
Lower the discount rate
q.commonError: Reversing open-market purchases and sales.
q.feedback: Selling bonds pulls reserves out of the banking system and reduces the money supply.

q.q: Which sequence correctly describes an open-market purchase?
options: Fed buys bonds, reserves rise, money supply can expand
Fed sells bonds, reserves rise, lending expands
Fed buys bonds, reserves fall, money supply contracts
Fed sells bonds, reserves fall, money demand vanishes
q.commonError: Breaking the reserves-to-money-supply chain.
q.feedback: A Fed bond purchase adds reserves and can support money supply expansion.

q.q: A higher interest rate paid on reserves most directly encourages banks to:
options: Hold more reserves
Hold fewer reserves
Ignore the Fed
Create commodity money
q.commonError: Thinking interest on reserves always increases lending.
q.feedback: Paying more on reserves makes holding reserves more attractive to banks.

q.q: The Fed wants to increase the money supply. Which open-market operation matches that goal?
options: Buy government bonds from the public.
Sell government bonds to the public.
Raise taxes on households.
Reduce government purchases.
q.commonError: thinking Fed bond purchases remove money from circulation
q.feedback: When the Fed buys bonds, it pays money into the economy, increasing the money supply.

q.q: The Fed wants to reduce the money supply. Which open-market operation matches that goal?
options: Sell government bonds to the public.
Buy government bonds from the public.
Cut the discount rate.
Lower reserve requirements.
q.commonError: thinking Fed bond sales inject money
q.feedback: When the Fed sells bonds, the public pays money to the Fed, reducing the money supply.

q.q: If the Fed lowers the discount rate, which effect is most likely?
options: Banks find it cheaper to borrow from the Fed.
Banks are required to hold more reserves.
The money supply must fall.
Currency becomes commodity money.
q.commonError: thinking a lower discount rate discourages borrowing
q.feedback: A lower discount rate makes borrowing from the Fed cheaper for banks.

q.q: If the Fed raises reserve requirements, the banking system's ability to create money usually
options: decreases
increases
becomes unlimited
does not depend on deposits anymore
q.commonError: thinking higher required reserves create more lending
q.feedback: Higher reserve requirements force banks to hold more reserves and lend less, reducing money creation.

q.q: If the Fed pays a higher interest rate on reserves, banks may respond by
options: holding more reserves and lending less
holding fewer reserves and lending more
creating commodity money
eliminating demand deposits
q.commonError: thinking interest on reserves cannot affect lending
q.feedback: Higher interest on reserves can make banks more willing to hold reserves instead of lending.

q.q: Which sequence best describes a contractionary open-market operation?
options: Sell bonds, reserves fall, lending weakens
Buy bonds, reserves fall, lending weakens
Sell bonds, reserves rise, lending expands
Buy bonds, reserves rise, lending contracts
q.commonError: Reversing bond sales and purchases.
