q.feedback: Selling bonds drains reserves, weakens lending, and reduces money creation.

q.q: The Fed raises the discount rate and also raises interest on reserves. Which combined effect is most likely?
options: Banks borrow less from the Fed and may hold more reserves.
Banks borrow more from the Fed and lend every reserve.
Households automatically hold fewer dollars because taxes fall.
The money multiplier becomes infinite.
q.commonError: treating all Fed tools as expansionary regardless of direction
q.feedback: A higher discount rate discourages bank borrowing, and higher interest on reserves can encourage banks to hold reserves.

q.q: Which Fed action is most clearly contractionary?
options: Selling bonds and raising reserve requirements
Buying bonds and lowering reserve requirements
Buying bonds and lowering the discount rate
Lowering interest on reserves and buying bonds
q.commonError: mixing expansionary and contractionary tools
q.feedback: Selling bonds pulls money out, and raising reserve requirements restricts lending. That is contractionary.

q.q: Which Fed action is most clearly expansionary?
options: Buying bonds and lowering reserve requirements
Selling bonds and raising reserve requirements
Raising the discount rate and raising interest on reserves
Selling bonds and lowering bank lending
q.commonError: thinking bond purchases are contractionary
q.feedback: Buying bonds injects money, and lower reserve requirements support more lending. That is expansionary.

q.q: If the Fed wants looser money but also raises interest on reserves, what tension does this create?
options: It injects reserves but may also encourage banks to hold them instead of lending.
It lowers reserves and forces banks to lend more.
It turns deposits into commodity money.
It makes fiscal policy impossible.
q.commonError: assuming all policy tools point in the same direction
q.feedback: More reserves can support lending, but higher interest on reserves may make banks sit on those reserves.

q.q: The central bank raises the interest rate paid on reserve balances. What response is most likely, other things equal?
options: Banks are more willing to hold reserves and less willing to expand lending.
Banks reduce reserve holdings and expand lending because reserves now pay more.
Households move currency directly into government spending when reserves earn more.
The required reserve ratio automatically falls when reserve interest increases.
q.commonError: Reversing the incentive effect of higher interest paid on reserves.
q.feedback: A higher return on reserve balances makes reserve holding more attractive and tends to restrain lending and money creation.

q.q: The Fed wants the money supply to fall by $180 million. If the money multiplier is 6 and banks fully lend according to the simple model, what open-market operation should the Fed conduct?
options: Sell $30 million in bonds.
Buy $30 million in bonds.
Sell $180 million in bonds.
Buy $1.08 billion in bonds.
q.commonError: multiplying the desired money change by the multiplier instead of dividing
q.feedback: To reduce money by $180 million with a multiplier of 6, the Fed sells $30 million in bonds.

q.q: The Fed buys bonds while also increasing interest on reserves. Which answer best captures the policy conflict?
options: Bond purchases add reserves, but higher interest on reserves may reduce banks' willingness to lend them.
Bond purchases remove reserves, while higher interest on reserves forces banks to lend more.
Both actions clearly reduce reserves and contract lending.
Both actions clearly eliminate money demand.
q.commonError: assuming every Fed action in a scenario pushes the same direction
q.feedback: Buying bonds is expansionary, but higher interest on reserves can make banks hold reserves instead of lending them.

q.q: Which policy package most strongly reduces bank lending capacity?
options: Fed sells bonds, raises reserve requirements, and raises interest on reserves.
Fed buys bonds, lowers reserve requirements, and lowers interest on reserves.
Fed buys bonds and lowers the discount rate.
Fed lowers reserve requirements and buys bonds.
q.commonError: failing to combine multiple contractionary tools
q.feedback: Selling bonds drains reserves, higher reserve requirements restrict lending, and higher interest on reserves encourages banks to hold reserves.

q.q: Which policy package most strongly expands bank lending capacity?
options: Fed buys bonds, lowers reserve requirements, and lowers interest on reserves.
Fed sells bonds, raises reserve requirements, and raises interest on reserves.
Fed sells bonds and raises the discount rate.
Fed raises reserve requirements and pays banks more to hold reserves.
q.commonError: missing that lower interest on reserves can encourage lending
q.feedback: Buying bonds adds reserves, lower reserve requirements free reserves, and lower interest on reserves weakens the incentive to sit on reserves.

q.q: A bank has $400,000 in deposits and $80,000 in reserves. The required reserve ratio rises from 10 percent to 20 percent. What happens to excess reserves?
options: They fall from $40,000 to $0.
They rise from $40,000 to $80,000.
They fall from $80,000 to $40,000.
They stay at $80,000.
q.commonError: forgetting required reserves change when the ratio changes
q.feedback: At 10 percent, required reserves are $40,000 and excess reserves are $40,000. At 20 percent, required reserves are $80,000 and excess reserves are $0.

q.q: A bank has $400,000 in deposits and $80,000 in reserves. The required reserve ratio falls from 20 percent to 10 percent. What new lending capacity is created?
q.commonError: thinking lower reserve requirements reduce excess reserves
q.feedback: Required reserves fall from $80,000 to $40,000, creating $40,000 in excess reserves.

q.q: If the Fed sells bonds and the public pays with checking deposits, what is the direct effect on bank reserves and the money supply process?
options: Bank reserves fall, weakening deposit creation.
Bank reserves rise, strengthening deposit creation.
Bank reserves stay fixed, but taxes rise.
Bank reserves become commodity money.
q.commonError: thinking Fed bond sales add reserves to banks
q.feedback: When the Fed sells bonds, payment leaves bank deposits and reserves fall, reducing money creation.

q.q: If the Fed buys bonds from the public and sellers deposit the proceeds, what is the direct effect on bank reserves and the money supply process?
options: Bank reserves rise, supporting deposit creation.
Bank reserves fall, weakening deposit creation.
Taxes rise, reducing consumption.
Reserve requirements automatically rise to 100 percent.
q.commonError: thinking Fed bond purchases drain reserves
q.feedback: When the Fed buys bonds, money enters bank deposits and reserves rise, supporting lending and deposit creation.

q.q: A bank has $2,400,000 in deposits, $360,000 in reserves, and a reserve requirement of 10 percent. The reserve requirement then rises to 15 percent. What happens to excess reserves?
options: They fall from $120,000 to $0.
They rise from $120,000 to $360,000.
They fall from $360,000 to $240,000.
They rise from $0 to $120,000.
q.commonError: forgetting to recalculate required reserves after the policy change
q.feedback: At 10 percent, required reserves are $240,000, so excess reserves are $120,000. At 15 percent, required reserves are $360,000, leaving zero excess reserves.

q.q: In a hypothetical steady-state banking model, the required-reserve ratio is 10 percent, banks hold excess reserves equal to 5 percent of deposits, and the public holds currency equal to 25 percent of deposits. These ratios remain fixed. Money is currency plus deposits; the monetary base is currency plus total reserves. What base increase is needed for a $250 million money increase, and why is the simple 1/required-ratio estimate too small?
options: $80 million; both currency holdings and excess reserves absorb base money.
$25 million; every base dollar supports ten dollars of money.
$100 million; currency is excluded from the money measure.
$62.5 million; retaining a fixed fraction once describes every lending round.
q.commonError: ignoring the 80 percent lending adjustment
q.feedback: With deposits D, money is 1.25D and the base is (0.25 + 0.10 + 0.05)D = 0.40D. The money/base ratio is 3.125, so the base must rise $250/3.125 = $80 million. The simple multiplier ignores both leakages.

q.q: A hypothetical bank has $600,000 in deposits and $90,000 in reserves. The required-reserve ratio rises from 10 to 15 percent. The bank cannot obtain new reserves, and any additional loan payment would settle at another bank. Which conclusion distinguishes its reserve position from its ability to expand?
options: It meets the new requirement exactly, but has no excess reserves for an outgoing loan.
It has a $30,000 reserve deficit and must obtain reserves just to comply.
It retains $30,000 of excess reserves because deposits have not changed.
It must shrink deposits by $90,000 even if it makes no new loan.
q.commonError: thinking a higher reserve requirement creates more excess reserves
q.feedback: Required reserves rise from $60,000 to $90,000, exactly equal to actual reserves. The bank is compliant but the specified settlement constraint prevents further outgoing lending without adjustment.

q.q: The Fed cuts the discount rate, buys bonds, and lowers interest on reserves. What is the most complete expected effect?
options: Bank borrowing and reserves rise, lending incentives strengthen, and the money supply tends to expand.
Bank reserves fall, lending incentives weaken, and the money supply contracts.
Taxes fall, consumption rises, and fiscal policy expands.
The money supply is unaffected because only fiscal policy matters.
q.commonError: treating Fed tools as unrelated one-off facts
q.feedback: All three actions push toward monetary expansion: cheaper Fed borrowing, more reserves, and less reward for holding reserves idle.

q.q: The Fed raises the discount rate, sells bonds, and raises interest on reserves. What is the most complete expected effect?
options: Borrowing becomes costlier, reserves fall, banks may hold more reserves, and money creation weakens.
Borrowing becomes cheaper, reserves rise, and lending expands.
Government spending rises and taxes fall.
Money demand becomes zero.
q.commonError: missing that higher interest on reserves can be contractionary
q.feedback: That policy package tightens money through costlier borrowing, fewer reserves, and stronger incentives to hold reserves.

q.q: A bank has $10 million in deposits and a 10 percent reserve requirement. It holds $1.4 million in reserves. The Fed raises the reserve requirement to 12 percent and banks lend all remaining excess reserves. How much can the bank lend after the change?
options: $1.2 million
$1.4 million
q.commonError: using the old reserve requirement after the policy change
q.feedback: New required reserves are 0.12 x $10 million = $1.2 million. With $1.4 million in reserves, the bank can lend $200,000.

q.q: If the Fed buys $40 million in bonds and the money multiplier is 4, what is the maximum possible increase in the money supply?
options: $160 million
$40 million
$10 million
$44 million
q.commonError: dividing by the multiplier instead of multiplying
q.feedback: A bond purchase injects reserves. Maximum money expansion is $40 million x 4 = $160 million.

q.q: If the Fed wants to reduce the money supply by exactly $120 million and the money multiplier is 6, how many bonds should it sell?
options: $20 million
$120 million
$720 million
$6 million
q.commonError: multiplying target money change by the multiplier instead of dividing
q.feedback: To reduce money by $120 million with a multiplier of 6, the Fed sells $20 million in bonds.

q.q: If the Fed buys government bonds, the money supply tends to
options: increase
decrease
stay fixed
turn into commodity money
q.commonError: thinking bond purchases remove money from circulation
q.feedback: Buying bonds injects reserves and tends to increase the money supply.

q.q: If the Fed wants to reduce the money supply using open-market operations, what should it do?
options: Sell government bonds.
Buy government bonds.
Lower reserve requirements.
Lower the discount rate.
q.commonError: thinking bond sales add reserves
q.feedback: Selling bonds pulls money out of the banking system and contracts the money supply.

q.q: The Fed sells $20 million in bonds and the money multiplier is 5. Under the simple model, what is the maximum decrease in the money supply?
options: $100 million
$20 million
$4 million
$25 million
q.commonError: dividing by the multiplier instead of multiplying
q.feedback: A $20 million bond sale times multiplier 5 gives a maximum $100 million money-supply decrease.

q.q: To increase banking-system reserves through open-market operations, the central bank should:
options: Sell government securities.
Buy government securities.
Raise taxes.
Increase reserve requirements.
q.commonError: Reversing the reserve effect of an open-market purchase.
q.feedback: When the central bank buys securities, it pays by adding reserves to the banking system.

q.q: What is the usual effect of lowering the discount rate?
options: Banks must hold a larger fraction of deposits as reserves.
The central bank removes reserves by selling bonds.
Borrowing from the central bank becomes less costly for banks.
Households are required to reduce currency holdings.
q.commonError: Confusing the discount rate with reserve requirements or open-market sales.
q.feedback: A lower discount rate reduces the cost of borrowing reserves directly from the central bank.

q.q: Which policy action is contractionary?
options: Buying government securities in the open market.
Lowering the interest paid on reserve balances.
Lowering reserve requirements.
Selling government securities in the open market.
q.commonError: Selecting an expansionary tool as contractionary.
q.feedback: An open-market sale withdraws reserves and tends to reduce money and credit expansion.

q.q: The central bank buys securities but simultaneously raises the interest paid on reserves. Why might lending rise by less than expected?
options: The purchase adds reserves, but the higher reserve return encourages banks to hold them.
Both actions remove reserves and directly reduce the banking system’s lending capacity.
The bond purchase automatically raises reserve requirements and blocks new loans.
The higher reserve return forces banks to lend every newly created reserve dollar.
q.commonError: Assuming every tool in a policy package pushes bank lending in the same direction.
q.feedback: The open-market purchase is expansionary, while a higher return on reserves can weaken the lending response.

q.q: A central bank wants to drain reserves quickly without changing reserve requirements. Which action is most direct?
options: Buy government securities and credit reserve accounts.
Sell government securities and debit reserve accounts.
Lower the discount rate to make reserve borrowing cheaper.
Lower interest paid on reserves to discourage reserve holding.
q.commonError: Choosing an expansionary action when the goal is to remove reserves.
q.feedback: An open-market sale receives payment from the banking system and reduces reserves directly.

q.q: Reserve requirements are lowered, but banks expect severe loan losses and keep the newly available reserves idle. What does this illustrate?
options: Lower reserve requirements always produce the full textbook deposit multiplier.
Banks lose the legal ability to hold excess reserves after requirements decline.
Policy can expand lending capacity without guaranteeing that banks will lend.
The central bank shifts aggregate supply left whenever it changes reserve rules.
q.commonError: Treating potential money creation as automatic actual money creation.
q.feedback: Lower reserve requirements free reserves for lending, but risk perceptions and bank choices can weaken the actual expansion.

q.q: A bank has $3,000,000 in deposits, $510,000 in reserves, and a 12 percent reserve requirement. The Fed raises the reserve requirement to 15 percent. How much lending capacity remains after the change?
q.commonError: using the old reserve requirement after the Fed changes policy
q.feedback: New required reserves are 0.15 x $3,000,000 = $450,000. With $510,000 in reserves, lending capacity is $60,000.

q.q: The Fed wants to reduce the money supply by $480 million. The money multiplier is 6, but currency drain is expected to make the actual multiplier closer to 4. What bond sale is closest to the needed action?
options: Sell $120 million in bonds.
Sell $80 million in bonds.
Buy $120 million in bonds.
Buy $80 million in bonds.
q.commonError: using the simple multiplier instead of the adjusted multiplier
q.feedback: With the actual multiplier closer to 4, the Fed sells $480 million / 4 = $120 million in bonds.

q.q: The Fed buys bonds, lowers the discount rate, but raises interest on reserves sharply. Which answer best explains why the final lending response may be muted?
options: Reserve expansion may be offset if banks prefer earning interest on reserves.
All three actions are contractionary and must reduce reserves.
Higher interest on reserves forces banks to lend every dollar.
The discount rate only affects government spending.
q.commonError: assuming all listed Fed actions push lending the same way
q.feedback: Bond purchases and a lower discount rate are expansionary, but higher interest on reserves can weaken lending.

q.q: The Fed wants a $900 million maximum money expansion. The reserve ratio is 12.5 percent. Under the simple model, how large should the bond purchase be?
options: $112.5 million
$900 million
$7.2 billion
$125 million
q.commonError: multiplying the target expansion by the multiplier
q.feedback: The multiplier is 1/0.125 = 8. Required bond purchase is $900 million / 8 = $112.5 million.

q.q: If the Fed buys bonds, bank reserves usually:
options: Rise
Fall
Become zero
Turn into taxes
q.feedback: Fed bond purchases add reserves to the banking system.

q.q: If the Fed sells bonds, bank reserves usually:
options: Fall
Rise
Double
Become M2
q.feedback: Fed bond sales drain reserves from the banking system.

q.q: Raising the interest rate paid on bank reserves tends to:
options: Encourage banks to hold reserves rather than lend
Force banks to lend all reserves
Raise the money multiplier automatically
Shift SRAS right
q.feedback: A higher return on reserves increases the incentive to hold reserves, which can restrain lending.

q.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
q.q: If the reserve requirement is lowered, other things equal, what happens to the amount of deposits banks must hold as required reserves?
options: It falls, leaving more reserves potentially available for lending
It rises, leaving fewer reserves potentially available for lending
It is unchanged because reserve requirements affect only currency
It becomes equal to total bank capital
q.feedback: A lower reserve requirement reduces the amount of deposits that must be held as required reserves, leaving more reserves potentially available for lending.

q.commonError: Missing that bond purchases add reserves.
q.q: A Fed bond purchase adds money to:
options: The banking system
The tax code
Imports only
Used goods markets only
q.feedback: Bond purchases add reserves to the banking system.

q.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
q.q: If the central bank lowers the rate it charges banks for direct loans, what is the immediate textbook effect?
options: Borrowing from the central bank becomes less costly for banks
Required reserves automatically rise for every bank
The Treasury must reduce government spending
The public is forced to hold less currency
q.feedback: A lower discount rate reduces the cost to banks of borrowing directly from the central bank.

q.commonError: Missing that bond sales drain reserves.
q.q: A Fed bond sale usually causes bank reserves to:
options: Fall
Rise
Double automatically
Become taxes

Interest rates fall, AD rises, and inflation disappears cleanly.
Interest rates rise, SRAS shifts right, and output returns to potential.
Interest rates fall, LRAS shifts left, and unemployment returns to natural.
q.commonError: Missing the danger of tightening into weak demand.
q.feedback: A lower money supply raises interest rates and shifts AD left, which can worsen a recessionary gap.

q.q: A student says expansionary monetary policy raises AD by directly increasing government purchases. What is the best correction?
options: Monetary policy works mainly through money supply, interest rates, and investment.
Monetary policy works by changing G before interest rates can move.
Monetary policy works only by shifting LRAS through technology.
Monetary policy works by raising taxes and lowering consumption.
q.commonError: Confusing monetary and fiscal policy channels.
q.feedback: Monetary policy affects AD primarily through money supply, interest rates, and investment spending.

q.q: A student says, 'If the Fed buys bonds, inflation must rise immediately and real output cannot move.' Which correction is strongest?
options: In the short run, lower rates can raise AD and output before long-run price adjustment dominates.
Bond purchases only change fiscal spending, so inflation and output are unaffected.
Bond purchases lower AD because reserves rise and lending must fall.
In the long run, bond purchases permanently reduce unemployment.
q.commonError: Skipping the short-run transmission channel.
q.feedback: Open-market purchases lower interest rates and can raise AD and output in the short run.

q.q: Refer to the graph. What policy movement is shown across the two panels?
options: Money supply shifts left from MS1 to MS2, r rises from r1 to r2, AD shifts left from AD1 to AD2, and output falls from Y1 to Y2.
Money supply shifts right from MS2 to MS1, r falls from r2 to r1, AD shifts right from AD2 to AD1, and output rises from Y2 to Y1.
Money demand shifts left, r falls, investment rises, and AD shifts right.
The price level falls and the economy moves along AD1 from Y1 to Y2.
q.commonError: reading the leftward money-supply shift as expansionary policy
q.feedback: The graph shows contractionary monetary policy: MS shifts left, r rises, AD shifts left, and output falls.
q.imageAlt: Two panels with vertical MS1 and MS2, downward MD, and downward AD1 and AD2.

q.q: Refer to the graph. If the investment change caused by the MS1 to MS2 movement is $80 billion and MPC = 0.6, what is the correct full AD effect?
options: MS shifts left, r rises, investment falls, and AD decreases by $200 billion.
MS shifts right, r falls, investment rises, and AD increases by $200 billion.
MS shifts left, r falls, investment rises, and AD increases by $200 billion.
MS shifts right, r rises, investment falls, and AD decreases by $80 billion.
q.commonError: using the multiplier correctly but reading the graph direction backward
q.feedback: The graph shows MS shifting left and r rising, so investment falls. MPC = 0.6 gives multiplier 2.5, so AD falls by $200 billion.

q.q: Refer to the graph. The Fed moves the money supply from MS1 to MS2. If the resulting investment change is $60 billion and MPC = 0.75, what is the correct full effect on AD?
options: MS shifts left, r rises, investment falls, and AD decreases by $240 billion.
MS shifts right, r falls, investment rises, and AD increases by $240 billion.
MS shifts left, r falls, investment rises, and AD increases by $240 billion.
MS shifts right, r rises, investment falls, and AD decreases by $60 billion.
q.commonError: letting the arithmetic hide a bad graph read
q.feedback: The graph shows MS shifting left from MS1 to MS2, which raises r and reduces investment. MPC = 0.75 gives multiplier 4, so AD falls by $240 billion.

q.q: Refer to the graph. The Fed moves MS from MS1 to MS2. If the investment response is $40 billion and MPC = 0.5, what is the correct AD result?
options: MS shifts left, r rises, investment falls, and AD decreases by $80 billion.

MS shifts left, r falls, investment rises, and AD increases by $40 billion.
MS shifts right, r rises, investment falls, and AD decreases by $20 billion.

q.q: Refer to the graph. If the MS1 to MS2 movement causes only a $20 billion investment response and MPC = 0.8, what is the correct AD interpretation?

The graph shows expansionary monetary policy, and AD increases by $100 billion.
The graph shows contractionary monetary policy, and AD decreases by only $20 billion.

AD shifts right by $200 billion.
AD shifts left by $40 billion.
AD shifts right by $50 billion.
q.commonError: using MPC as the multiplier or reading the AD shift backward
q.feedback: The graph shows contractionary monetary policy, so AD shifts left. MPC = 0.8 gives multiplier 5, so $40 billion becomes $200 billion.

Output stays at Y1.

q.feedback: At P1, the leftward AD shift moves output from Y1 to Y2.

The graph shows AD shifting right because money supply rises and r falls.
The graph shows a lower price level causing movement along AD1.
The graph shows fiscal expansion through higher government spending.
q.commonError: confusing an AD shift with movement along a fixed AD curve
q.feedback: This is not movement along AD. It is a leftward AD shift caused by tighter monetary policy.

q.q: Refer to the graph. Which graph feature shows that the monetary policy is contractionary rather than expansionary?
options: MS moves left from MS1 to MS2 and AD moves left from AD1 to AD2.
MS moves right from MS2 to MS1 and AD moves right from AD2 to AD1.
Money demand moves left and AD stays fixed.
The price level falls along AD1.
q.commonError: not using the labels MS1, MS2, AD1, and AD2 to identify policy direction
q.feedback: The key evidence is MS1 to MS2 and AD1 to AD2, both leftward shifts.

q.q: Refer to the graph. The policy direction shown needs to move AD left by $300 billion. If MPC = 0.5 and each 1-point increase in r lowers investment by $50 billion, how much must r rise?

6 percentage points
1.5 percentage points
2 percentage points
q.commonError: not dividing the AD target by the multiplier before solving for investment
q.feedback: The graph calls for a rise in r. MPC = 0.5 gives multiplier 2, so investment must fall $150 billion. At $50 billion per point, r must rise 3 points.

q.q: Refer to the graph. If the investment response to the MS1 to MS2 movement is $50 billion and MPC = 0.6, what is the correct order of effects?
options: MS shifts left, r rises, investment falls $50 billion, and AD shifts left by $125 billion.
MS shifts right, r falls, investment rises $50 billion, and AD shifts right by $125 billion.
MS shifts left, r falls, investment rises $50 billion, and AD shifts right by $125 billion.
MS shifts left, r rises, investment falls $50 billion, and AD shifts left by $50 billion only.
q.commonError: stopping at the investment decline instead of applying the multiplier
q.feedback: The graph shows MS shifting left and r rising. MPC = 0.6 gives multiplier 2.5, so a $50 billion investment fall shifts AD left by $125 billion.

q.q: Refer to the two-panel graph. Between A and B, the central bank expands money supply while SRAS stays fixed. A commentator says output and prices rose by the same percentage because they both rose. Which numerical comparison and inference are supported?
options: Output rises 12.5 percent and the price level 25 percent; their responses must be proportional.
Both rise 25 percent; equal directions establish equal percentage changes.
Both rise 6.25 percent; a common point label establishes a common percentage change.
Output rises 25 percent and the price level 12.5 percent; their responses need not be proportional.
q.commonError: misreads_money_market_or_transmission
q.feedback: Read output 100 to 125 and P 50 to 56.25. Their percentage changes are 25/100 = 25 percent and 6.25/50 = 12.5 percent. The diagram supplies distinct responses along fixed SRAS.

The illustrated tightening raises rates and lowers both GDP and the price level.

The illustrated tightening lowers GDP while raising the price level.

q.q: Through the interest-rate channel, expansionary monetary policy shifts aggregate demand in which direction?
options: right
left
nowhere
only along short-run aggregate supply
q.commonError: thinking expansionary money shifts AD left
q.feedback: Expansionary monetary policy lowers interest rates, raises investment, and shifts AD right.

q.q: If the Fed increases money supply, what chain follows?
options: Interest rates fall, investment rises, and AD shifts right.
Interest rates rise, investment falls, and AD shifts left.
Interest rates fall, investment falls, and AD shifts left.
Interest rates rise, investment rises, and AD shifts right.
q.commonError: thinking more money raises interest rates in this model
q.feedback: More money lowers interest rates, raises investment, and shifts AD right.

q.q: The Fed increases money supply and investment rises by $70 billion. If MPC = 0.6, what is the total AD increase?
options: $175 billion
$70 billion
$42 billion
$116.7 billion
q.commonError: stopping at the investment increase without applying the multiplier
q.feedback: MPC 0.6 gives multiplier 2.5. A $70 billion investment increase raises AD by $175 billion.

q.q: The central bank buys government bonds from the public. What is the first link in the usual expansionary transmission chain?
options: Reserves and the money supply rise, pushing interest rates down.
Bank reserves fall and interest rates rise immediately.
Government purchases increase before the money market changes.
Aggregate supply shifts right because banks hold more bonds.
q.commonError: Skipping the money-supply and interest-rate links after an open-market purchase.
q.feedback: A bond purchase adds reserves to the banking system, supports money creation, and tends to lower market interest rates.

q.q: Why can lower interest rates increase aggregate demand in the short run?
options: They automatically reduce all product prices.
They increase investment and other rate-sensitive spending.
They raise required reserve ratios for banks.
They directly increase government purchases.
q.commonError: Treating monetary policy as a direct change in government spending or product prices.
q.feedback: Lower borrowing costs encourage investment and some durable consumption, shifting aggregate demand to the right.

q.q: Money supply shifts right while money demand is unchanged. What happens at the new money-market equilibrium?
options: The equilibrium interest rate rises.
The price level must fall immediately.
The equilibrium interest rate falls.
Real output must remain permanently fixed.
q.commonError: Reversing the interest-rate effect of a rightward money-supply shift.
q.feedback: With money demand fixed, a larger money supply lowers the equilibrium interest rate.

q.q: The central bank adds reserves, but banks choose to hold most of them as excess reserves. How does this affect the transmission mechanism?
options: Money and credit expand more, making aggregate demand rise farther.
The policy becomes contractionary because excess reserves reduce taxes.
Aggregate demand rises by the same amount because reserve use never matters.
Money and credit expand less, weakening the interest-rate and aggregate-demand response.
q.commonError: Assuming reserve injections always create the same money and credit expansion.
q.feedback: When banks hold added reserves rather than lending them, money creation and the downstream spending response are weaker.

q.q: Interest rates fall after an expansionary policy, but firms believe future sales will remain weak. What is the likely result?
options: Investment responds only modestly, so the rightward shift of aggregate demand is limited.
Investment surges because interest rates are the only influence on firms.
Aggregate demand shifts left because lower rates reduce borrowing.
The money supply contracts automatically when firms are pessimistic.
q.commonError: Assuming lower rates guarantee a large investment response regardless of expectations.
q.feedback: Weak expected sales can make firms reluctant to invest even when borrowing costs fall, weakening policy transmission.

q.q: Which sequence correctly traces a contractionary open-market operation through aggregate demand?
options: Bond sales raise reserves, lower interest rates, and shift aggregate demand right.
Bond sales drain reserves, raise interest rates, reduce investment, and shift aggregate demand left.
Bond purchases reduce reserves, raise investment, and shift aggregate demand left.
Higher taxes reduce reserves, lower interest rates, and shift aggregate demand right.
q.commonError: Reversing the reserve, interest-rate, or spending links in contractionary policy.
q.feedback: Selling bonds drains reserves, contracts money and credit, raises rates, reduces interest-sensitive spending, and lowers aggregate demand.

q.q: Refer to the graph showing MS1 to MS2. In a fixed-price spending model, the resulting investment loss is $90 billion, while an independent recovery in business expectations adds $30 billion of autonomous investment. MPC is 0.6; there are no taxes, imports or further interest-rate feedbacks. What is the net shift in aggregate demand, and what independent investment recovery would exactly cancel the monetary effect?
options: AD shifts left $150 billion; a $90 billion recovery would cancel it.
AD shifts left $225 billion; a $30 billion recovery would cancel it.
AD shifts left $60 billion; a $150 billion recovery would cancel it.
AD shifts right $150 billion; a $90 billion recovery would cancel it.
q.commonError: multiplying before finding the net spending impulse or reading the graph backward
q.feedback: The graph supplies contractionary direction. Net autonomous investment is −90 + 30 = −60. With multiplier 1/(1 − 0.6) = 2.5, AD shifts left $150 billion. Exact cancellation requires a $90 billion independent recovery, before multiplication.
q.imageAlt: Two panels with vertical MS1 and MS2, downward MD, and downward AD1 and AD2.
