Every imaginable room use must be added together
Only borrowed rooms can have opportunity costs
q.commonError: Assuming owned resources have no opportunity cost.
q.feedback: The best forgone use of an owned resource is an implicit cost.

q.q: A worker takes two unpaid hours off instead of working for $18 per hour. What wage value is forgone?
q.commonError: Ignoring duration or assuming unpaid time has no opportunity cost.
q.feedback: Two forgone work hours at $18 each equal $36.

q.q: If choosing one option means giving up the next-best alternative, the value given up is:
options: Opportunity cost
A sunk cost
A price ceiling
Consumer surplus
q.feedback: Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best alternative forgone.

q.q: Scarcity means a community cannot fund every valued program. If the community funds a clinic, what determines the clinic’s opportunity cost?
options: Funding the clinic requires giving up the best alternative program
Scarcity makes the clinic’s historical spending a sunk cost
Opportunity cost disappears once officials approve a budget
Every unfunded program must be added together as the cost
q.commonError: Seeing scarcity and opportunity cost as unrelated definitions.
q.feedback: Scarcity forces a choice; the best forgone use created by that choice is its opportunity cost.

q.q: Moving along a production possibilities frontier from more food toward more machinery requires giving up food. What does the food forgone measure?
options: The opportunity cost of the additional machinery
The sunk cost of previously produced food
The money price of machinery in the product market
The total value of all unattainable production points
q.commonError: Failing to connect a production tradeoff with opportunity cost.
q.feedback: The output surrendered when production shifts measures the opportunity cost along a PPF.

q.q: Two producers can make the same goods, but one gives up fewer shirts for each bicycle. How does opportunity cost identify comparative advantage?
options: The producer giving up fewer shirts has comparative advantage in bicycles
The producer making more total goods in both industries must have comparative advantage
The producer with the higher bicycle opportunity cost should specialize
Comparative advantage depends only on money prices of the goods
q.commonError: Assigning comparative advantage to absolute output or higher opportunity cost.
q.feedback: Comparative advantage belongs to the producer with the lower opportunity cost.

q.q: A firm considers producing one additional unit. How does opportunity cost enter a marginal decision?
options: The forgone value of resources used for that unit is compared with its added benefit
Every past expense and every earlier unit’s benefit are added to the next unit’s marginal cost
The total benefit of all earlier units determines the next unit’s cost
Opportunity cost matters only before the first unit is produced
q.commonError: Using sunk or total values instead of additional benefit and cost.
q.feedback: Marginal analysis compares added benefit with the opportunity cost of the next unit.

q.q: An entrepreneur uses a personally owned building and unpaid owner labor. How do these opportunity costs connect to economic profit?
options: Forgone rent and salary are implicit costs subtracted from accounting profit
Owned inputs disappear from both accounting and economic analysis
Historical purchase prices plus every owner cash withdrawal are charged again each period
Economic profit subtracts every rejected business idea
q.commonError: Treating owner-supplied inputs as free when moving from accounting to economic profit.
q.feedback: Implicit opportunity costs explain why economic profit can be below accounting profit.

q.q: A workshop gives up progressively more chairs for each additional table. What connection does this create between opportunity cost and the production tradeoff?
options: The opportunity cost of later tables rises as more chairs are forgone
Opportunity cost stays equal to the money price of a table in every production decision
Past chair production becomes a sunk cost of every table
The tradeoff disappears because both goods use the same workshop
q.commonError: Failing to interpret forgone output as the cost of additional production.
q.feedback: The amount of one good forgone measures the opportunity cost of producing more of the other.

q.q: Refer to the graph. Moving from point a to point b most likely shows:
options: Expected inflation adjusting upward
Money demand disappearing
LRPC shifting left
Unemployment becoming zero
q.commonError: Thinking unemployment stays below natural permanently.
q.feedback: After inflation expectations adjust upward, the SRPC shifts and unemployment returns to the natural rate at point b.
q.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves and a vertical long-run Phillips curve at unemployment rate U2, with labeled points a through d.

SRPC1 is the lower/left downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/right downward-sloping curve. Dashed guides mark unemployment rates U1-U3 and inflation rates I1-I2.

q.q: If expected inflation rises, the short-run Phillips curve shifts:
options: Down and left
Up and right
Into the AD curve
Into the money multiplier
q.commonError: Reversing expected inflation shifts.
q.feedback: Higher expected inflation shifts the SRPC up and right.

q.q: Refer to the graph. SRPC2 compared with SRPC1 represents:
options: A higher expected inflation curve
A lower expected inflation curve
A lower natural rate only
A fall in money supply only
q.commonError: Missing that the higher SRPC reflects worse inflation expectations.
q.feedback: SRPC2 is above SRPC1, meaning higher expected inflation or a worse tradeoff. With other shifters explicitly excluded, the upward shift identifies higher expected inflation.
q.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves, labeled unemployment rates U1 through U4, inflation rates I1 through I4, and points a through f.

SRPC1 is the lower downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/rightward downward-sloping curve. On SRPC1, point a is at U1/I4, b at U2/I3, c at U3/I2, and d at U4/I1. On SRPC2, point f is at U3/I4 and point e is at U4/I3. Dashed guides connect the labeled points to unemployment rates U1-U4 and inflation rates I1-I4.

q.q: An adverse supply shock shifts the short-run Phillips curve:
options: Up and right
Down and left
Nowhere
Into LRAS
q.commonError: Treating supply shocks as movement along the same SRPC.
q.feedback: An adverse supply shock worsens the tradeoff by shifting the SRPC up and right.

q.q: A surge in oil prices can cause inflation and unemployment to:
options: Both rise
Both fall
Move in opposite directions only
Become zero
q.commonError: Thinking inflation and unemployment always move opposite ways.
q.feedback: A negative supply shock can raise inflation and unemployment together.

q.q: Compared with point A, what combination is shown at point B?
options: Higher unemployment and more inflation
Lower unemployment and more inflation
Higher unemployment and less inflation
Lower unemployment and less inflation
q.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
q.feedback: Point A is at 5 percent unemployment and 3 percent inflation, while point B is at 6 percent unemployment and 6 percent inflation.
q.imageAlt: Phillips graph with two downward-sloping SRPCs, vertical LRPC, and points A and B.

Solid blue SRPC0 is a straight downward-sloping line through (0,6), A at (5,3), and (10,0). Dashed purple SRPC1 is parallel above it, running through (0,9.6), B at (6,6), and (10,3.6). Green LRPC is vertical at unemployment 5 and intersects SRPC0 at A and SRPC1 at inflation 6.6. Dashed guides mark A at (5,3) and B at (6,6).

q.q: Workers and firms begin expecting higher inflation next year. Holding unemployment fixed, what happens to the short-run Phillips curve?
options: It shifts upward
It shifts downward
The economy moves down one unchanged curve
The vertical LRPC shifts left
q.commonError: Moves along the SRPC instead of shifting it when expected inflation changes.
q.feedback: Higher expected inflation shifts the SRPC upward; lower expected inflation shifts it downward.

q.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Starting at point a, expected inflation adjusts upward. The long-run movement is to:
options: b
c
d
U3
q.commonError: Keeping unemployment below natural forever.
q.feedback: Expectations adjust upward, SRPC shifts up, and unemployment returns to U2 at point b.
q.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves and a vertical long-run Phillips curve at unemployment rate U2, with labeled points a through d.

SRPC1 is the lower/left downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/right downward-sloping curve. Dashed guides mark unemployment rates U1-U3 and inflation rates I1-I2.

q.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Moving from d to c most likely reflects:
options: Expected inflation falling
Expected inflation rising
Natural unemployment rising
AD shifting right
q.commonError: Missing downward expectations adjustment.
q.feedback: As expected inflation falls, the SRPC shifts downward and unemployment returns to U2 at point c.
q.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves and a vertical long-run Phillips curve at unemployment rate U2, with labeled points a through d.
q.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. A vertical LRPC stands at U2. SRPC1 is the lower/left downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/right downward-sloping curve. Point a is at U1/I2 on SRPC1, point b is at U2/I2 where SRPC2 meets the LRPC, point c is at U2/I1 where SRPC1 meets the LRPC, and point d is at U3/I1 on SRPC2. Dashed guides mark unemployment rates U1-U3 and inflation rates I1-I2.

q.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. Moving from SRPC1 to SRPC2 at the same unemployment rate means:
options: Inflation is higher at the same unemployment rate
Inflation is lower at the same unemployment rate
Unemployment disappears
LRPC shifts right
q.commonError: Missing the upward SRPC shift.
q.feedback: SRPC2 is above SRPC1, so inflation is higher for a given unemployment rate.
q.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves, labeled unemployment rates U1 through U4, inflation rates I1 through I4, and points a through f.
q.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. SRPC1 is the lower downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/rightward downward-sloping curve. On SRPC1, point a is at U1/I4, b at U2/I3, c at U3/I2, and d at U4/I1. On SRPC2, point f is at U3/I4 and point e is at U4/I3. Dashed guides connect the labeled points to unemployment rates U1-U4 and inflation rates I1-I4.

q.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. Assume supply conditions and the natural rate are unchanged; only expected inflation can shift the curve. If the economy moves from c on SRPC1 to the upper point at the same unemployment rate, the likely cause is:
options: Higher expected inflation
Lower expected inflation
A fall in actual inflation only
A lower natural rate
q.commonError: Confusing a curve shift with movement along one curve.
q.feedback: At the same unemployment rate, a higher SRPC reflects higher expected inflation or a worse tradeoff. With other shifters explicitly excluded, the upward shift identifies higher expected inflation.
q.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves, labeled unemployment rates U1 through U4, inflation rates I1 through I4, and points a through f.

SRPC1 is the lower downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/rightward downward-sloping curve. On SRPC1, point a is at U1/I4, b at U2/I3, c at U3/I2, and d at U4/I1. On SRPC2, point f is at U3/I4 and point e is at U4/I3. Dashed guides connect the labeled points to unemployment rates U1-U4 and inflation rates I1-I4.

q.q: An adverse supply shock affects the Phillips curve by:
options: Shifting SRPC up and right
Moving down along the same SRPC
Shifting LRPC to zero unemployment
Eliminating expected inflation
q.commonError: Treating supply shocks as normal AD movements.
q.feedback: An adverse supply shock worsens the inflation-unemployment tradeoff.

q.q: If policymakers expand AD to reduce unemployment below the natural rate, what happens after expectations adjust?
options: Unemployment returns to natural and inflation stays higher
Unemployment stays permanently lower
Inflation falls below expected inflation
LRPC becomes downward sloping
q.commonError: Believing in a permanent policy tradeoff.
q.feedback: Higher expected inflation shifts the SRPC up, returning unemployment to natural at higher inflation.

q.q: Suppose expected inflation rises while the natural rate is unchanged. Which curve change shown is consistent with that assumption?
options: SRPC0 shifts downward away from SRPC1
SRPC0 shifts upward to SRPC1
LRPC shifts left to a lower natural rate
The economy only moves along unchanged SRPC0
q.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
q.feedback: An upward shift of the short-run Phillips curve is the standard way to show higher expected inflation or an adverse supply shock with the natural rate unchanged.

Solid blue SRPC0 is a straight downward-sloping line through (0,6), A at (5,3), and (10,0). Dashed purple SRPC1 is parallel above it, running through (0,9.6), B at (6,6), and (10,3.6). Green LRPC is vertical at unemployment 5 and intersects SRPC0 at A and SRPC1 at inflation 6.6. Dashed guides mark A at (5,3) and B at (6,6).

q.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Starting at c, which sequence matches expansionary policy and expectations adjustment?
options: c to a to b
c to b to a
c to d to b
c to a to d
q.commonError: Skipping the short-run movement along SRPC.
q.feedback: Expansion moves from c to a in the short run; expected inflation rises and moves the economy to b.

SRPC1 is the lower/left downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/right downward-sloping curve. Point a is at U1/I2 on SRPC1, point b is at U2/I2 where SRPC2 meets the LRPC, point c is at U2/I1 where SRPC1 meets the LRPC, and point d is at U3/I1 on SRPC2. Dashed guides mark unemployment rates U1-U3 and inflation rates I1-I2.

q.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Which movement shows expectations falling after contractionary policy?
options: d to c
c to a
a to b
b to a
q.commonError: Reversing expectation shifts.
q.feedback: Moving from d to c reflects lower expected inflation and return to the natural unemployment rate.

options: Higher on SRPC2
Lower on SRPC2
The same on both curves
Zero on both curves
q.commonError: Missing worse tradeoff at the same inflation rate.

q.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. A shift from SRPC1 to SRPC2 is most consistent with:
options: Higher expected inflation or adverse supply shock
Lower expected inflation or favorable supply shock
Higher money supply with expectations fixed
Lower unemployment at every inflation rate
q.commonError: Treating SRPC shifts as ordinary movement along a curve.
q.feedback: The upward SRPC shift reflects higher expected inflation or a worsened supply-side tradeoff.

q.q: If the Fed unexpectedly increases inflation while expected inflation is fixed, unemployment moves:
options: Below the natural rate temporarily
Above the natural rate permanently
To zero permanently
Unchanged in every period
q.commonError: Ignoring the gap between actual and expected inflation.
q.feedback: When actual inflation exceeds expected inflation, unemployment can temporarily fall below the natural rate.

q.q: Which event shifts both SRAS left and SRPC up-right?
options: Oil price surge
Tax cut
Open-market purchase
Consumer confidence boom
q.commonError: Confusing supply shocks with AD shocks.
q.feedback: An oil price surge raises production costs and worsens the inflation-unemployment tradeoff.

q.q: Initially actual inflation equals expected inflation and unemployment is at its natural rate. Supply conditions and the natural rate stay unchanged. If expected inflation rises while actual inflation is held at its original rate, what happens to unemployment?
options: Rise above natural
Fall below natural
Stay zero
Become inflation
q.commonError: Ignoring expected inflation in the Phillips curve equation.
q.feedback: Higher expected inflation shifts SRPC up, so unchanged actual inflation corresponds to higher unemployment. The stated initial equality makes the new inflation surprise negative.

q.q: Initially actual inflation equals expected inflation and unemployment is at its natural rate. Supply conditions and the natural rate stay unchanged. If expected inflation falls while actual inflation is held at its original rate, what happens to unemployment?
options: Fall below natural
Rise above natural
Stay at zero
Equal the price level
q.commonError: Reversing the effect of lower expected inflation.
q.feedback: Lower expected inflation shifts SRPC down, so the same actual inflation can mean lower unemployment. The stated initial equality makes the new inflation surprise positive.

q.q: A student says an oil shock causes only movement along the SRPC. What is the correction?
options: It shifts SRPC because costs and prices change directly
It shifts only AD because spending changes directly
It shifts only LRPC because inflation changes
It moves only along LRAS because output changes
q.commonError: Treating supply shocks as AD movements.
q.feedback: A supply shock shifts the SRPC because it directly changes firms' costs and inflation pressure.

q.q: A student says higher expected inflation lowers unemployment permanently. What is the correction?
options: It shifts SRPC upward and worsens the short-run tradeoff
It shifts LRPC left and improves the long-run tradeoff
It shifts AD right and lowers prices
It raises money demand and lowers rates
q.commonError: Treating expected inflation as beneficial stimulus.
q.feedback: Higher expected inflation shifts the SRPC upward, giving higher inflation at each unemployment rate.

q.q: At a given unemployment rate, how does SRPC1 compare with SRPC0?
options: SRPC1 shows a lower inflation rate
SRPC1 shows the same inflation rate
SRPC1 shows a lower natural rate
SRPC1 shows a higher inflation rate
q.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
q.feedback: Point B lies on a different short-run Phillips curve, SRPC1, so the graph is showing a curve shift rather than a movement along SRPC0.

q.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. A move from c on SRPC1 to the upper point at U3 on SRPC2 means:
options: Same unemployment with higher inflation
Same inflation with lower unemployment
Lower inflation with same unemployment
Higher unemployment with same inflation
q.commonError: Reading the curve shift as movement along SRPC1.
q.feedback: At U3, SRPC2 shows a higher inflation rate than SRPC1.

q.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. At inflation I3, comparing SRPC1 and SRPC2 shows:
options: SRPC2 has higher unemployment
SRPC2 has lower unemployment
Both curves have U3
Both curves have U1
q.commonError: Missing the worse tradeoff after SRPC shifts upward.
q.feedback: At the same inflation rate, the higher SRPC shows higher unemployment.

On SRPC2, point f is at U3/I4 and point e is at U4/I3. Dashed guides connect the labeled points to unemployment rates U1-U4 and inflation rates I1-I4.

q.q: A central bank unexpectedly expands AD. Later, workers build the higher inflation into wage demands. Which sequence is most accurate?
options: Move along SRPC, then SRPC shifts up
SRPC shifts down, then move along LRPC
LRPC shifts left, then AD falls
Move along LRAS, then M1 falls
q.commonError: Confusing immediate inflation surprise with later expectation adjustment.
q.feedback: Unexpected AD expansion first moves along the SRPC; later expected inflation rises and shifts SRPC upward.

q.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. Which labeled move isolates an upward SRPC shift at unemployment U3?
options: The move from point c to point f
The move from point a to point f
The move from point b to point e
The move from point c to point a
q.commonError: Compares points with different unemployment rates, so movement and shift effects are mixed.
q.feedback: Points c and f share unemployment U3; moving from c on SRPC1 to f on SRPC2 isolates higher inflation at the same unemployment rate.

q.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. The economy moves from SRPC1 to SRPC2. Which statement should be rejected?
options: The tradeoff improved because higher inflation now buys lower unemployment at every point.
The tradeoff worsened because inflation is higher at a given unemployment rate.
Expected inflation may have increased and shifted the curve upward.
An adverse supply shock may have raised both inflation pressure and unemployment risk.
q.commonError: Calling an upward SRPC shift an improvement.
q.feedback: An upward SRPC shift worsens the tradeoff because inflation is higher at the same unemployment rate.

On SRPC2, point f is at U3/I4 and point e is at U4/I3. Dashed guides connect the labeled points to unemployment rates U1-U4 and inflation rates I1-I4.

q.q: A policymaker says, 'Inflation is high, so unemployment must be low.' What is the best correction?
options: That only fits demand pressure; supply shocks can raise inflation and unemployment together.
That is always true because the Phillips curve never shifts.
That is false only when M1 is larger than M2.
That is true in the long run because LRPC slopes downward.
q.commonError: Treating the Phillips curve as fixed under every shock.
q.feedback: The short-run tradeoff can worsen when SRPC shifts up, so inflation and unemployment can rise together.

q.q: Refer to the SRPC graph. The economy is on SRPC2 rather than SRPC1. Which conclusion is most careful?
options: The tradeoff worsened, but the cause could be expected inflation or a supply shock.
The tradeoff improved, and policymakers can now lower unemployment without cost.
The LRPC shifted left, so natural unemployment must have fallen.
AD must have shifted right, so SRPC cannot have moved.
q.commonError: Assuming every SRPC shift has only one cause.
q.feedback: An upward SRPC shift can come from higher expected inflation or an adverse supply shock, and both worsen the tradeoff.

On SRPC2, point f is at U3/I4 and point e is at U4/I3. Dashed guides connect the labeled points to unemployment rates U1-U4 and inflation rates I1-I4.

q.q: Refer to the graph with SRPC0, SRPC1, A and B. Use the model inflation = expected inflation − 0.6 × (unemployment − 5) + supply offset, with all rates in percent and differences in percentage points. At B the separately measured supply offset is +1.1 points. What expected inflation is consistent with B, and could the graph alone identify that expectation if the supply offset were unknown?
options: Expected inflation is 6 percent; actual inflation equals expectations at every point on an SRPC.
Expected inflation is 5.5 percent; without the supply-offset measurement, only expected inflation plus the offset is identified.
Expected inflation is 6.6 percent; the supply offset can be ignored even though it is positive.
Expected inflation is 4.3 percent; both the unemployment gap and the supply offset must be subtracted from actual inflation.
q.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
q.feedback: B has unemployment 6 and actual inflation 6. Thus 6 = expected inflation − 0.6 + 1.1, implying expected inflation 5.5. Without the offset measurement the graph identifies only expected inflation + offset = 6.6. The higher curve does not by itself isolate an expectations change.
q.imageAlt: Phillips graph with two downward-sloping SRPCs, vertical LRPC, and points A and B.
q.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is Unemployment rate (%) from 0 to 10; the vertical axis is Inflation rate (%) from 0 to 10. Solid blue SRPC0 is a straight downward-sloping line through (0,6), A at (5,3), and (10,0). Dashed purple SRPC1 is parallel above it, running through (0,9.6), B at (6,6), and (10,3.6). Green LRPC is vertical at unemployment 5 and intersects SRPC0 at A and SRPC1 at inflation 6.6. Dashed guides mark A at (5,3) and B at (6,6).

q.q: Refer to the graph with A and B on SRPC0. Initially expected inflation is the inflation rate at A, and the economy is at B. Next period expected inflation equals this period’s actual inflation. Hold the natural rate and supply conditions fixed; each one-point expectations change shifts the SRPC vertically by one point with slope unchanged. Compare keeping unemployment at B’s rate with instead keeping actual inflation at B’s current rate. Which next-period outcome follows?
options: Keeping unemployment at 3 percent requires unchanged 3.5 percent inflation; holding inflation fixed shifts LRPC to 3 percent.
Keeping unemployment at 3 percent requires 4.5 percent inflation; holding inflation at 3.5 percent instead returns unemployment to 5 percent.
Keeping unemployment at 3 percent requires 2.5 percent inflation; holding inflation at 3.5 percent raises unemployment to 7 percent.
Both targets give the same unchanged point B because adaptive expectations cannot shift an SRPC.
q.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
q.feedback: Expectations rise from 2.5 to 3.5, shifting the curve up one point. At unemployment 3, inflation therefore rises from 3.5 to 4.5. Alternatively, actual inflation equal to the new expectation gives natural unemployment at 5. A fixed unemployment target and a fixed inflation target are different continuations.
q.imageAlt: Phillips graph with A and B on SRPC0 and vertical LRPC through A.
q.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is Unemployment rate (%) and the vertical axis is Inflation rate (%). Blue SRPC0 is a straight downward-sloping line from (0,5) through B at (3,3.5) and A at (5,2.5) to (10,0). Green LRPC is vertical at unemployment 5 and passes through A. B lies above and left of A on the same curve. Dashed horizontal and vertical guides mark both point coordinates.

q.q: Refer to the graph with B to the right of A on SRPC0. Initially actual inflation is B’s rate and expected inflation is A’s rate. Each period expectations equal the previous period’s actual inflation; each one-point expectations change shifts SRPC vertically by one point with slope unchanged. Natural unemployment and supply conditions stay fixed. Policy holds unemployment at B’s rate for one additional period, then requires inflation to be nonnegative in the following period. What inflation occurs in the additional period, and what is the highest unemployment rate compatible with that later inflation constraint?
options: Inflation stays 1.5 percent, then unemployment can remain at 7 percent.
Inflation is 0.5 percent, then unemployment can remain at 7 percent without deflation.
Inflation is 2.5 percent, then unemployment can be at most 5 percent.
Inflation is 0.5 percent, then unemployment can be at most 6 percent.
q.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
q.feedback: The plotted slope is (1.5 − 2.5)/(7 − 5) = −0.5. Expectations first fall from 2.5 to 1.5, so holding unemployment at 7 gives inflation 0.5. Next expectations are 0.5; nonnegative inflation requires 0.5 − 0.5 × (unemployment − 5) ≥ 0, or unemployment no greater than 6. Maintaining 7 would instead produce −0.5 percent inflation.
q.imageAlt: Phillips graph with A and B on SRPC0 and vertical LRPC through A.
q.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is Unemployment rate (%) and the vertical axis is Inflation rate (%). Blue SRPC0 is a straight downward-sloping line from (0,5) through A at (5,2.5) and B at (7,1.5) to (10,0). Green LRPC is vertical at unemployment 5 and passes through A. B lies below and right of A on the same curve. Dashed horizontal and vertical guides mark both point coordinates.

q.q: A temporary supply disruption raises inflation while existing contracts still reflect the original expected inflation. Wage setters update forecasts using the observed inflation, but the disruption ends before the new contracts take effect. Expected inflation nevertheless remains above its original level. With natural unemployment unchanged, what can be concluded about the final SRPC relative to its original position and its position during the disruption?
options: It must return exactly to its original position because the physical disruption ended.
It must lie above the disruption-period curve because any expectations rise exceeds any removed supply offset.
It must lie below the original curve because the original supply shock was temporary.
It remains above its original position, but its position relative to the disruption-period curve depends on the expectations rise versus the removed supply offset.
q.commonError: Assumes a surprise to actual inflation remains a surprise indefinitely.
q.feedback: The original curve has neither the supply offset nor the higher expectation. The final curve retains only the expectation increase, so it is above the original. Comparing it with the disruption-period curve requires the two offset magnitudes. Observed inflation alone does not identify their relative sizes.

q.q: Two central banks announce the same lower inflation target. One has a stronger record of meeting targets. Under otherwise similar conditions, what can differ?
options: Actual inflation must reach zero with no output cost
The less credible bank must cause immediate deflation
Expected inflation may fall faster where the announcement is more credible
The natural rate must immediately fall only in the credible economy
q.commonError: Assumes credibility mechanically eliminates every short-run output cost.
q.feedback: Credibility can speed expectations adjustment, but disinflation costs depend on model assumptions and wage-price adjustment.

q.q: Actual inflation is 5% while wage setters expected 3%, temporarily pushing unemployment below natural. What erodes that effect?
options: The price level returns to its initial value automatically
Forecasts adjust upward, shifting the SRPC until unemployment returns toward natural
The LRPC shifts left because actual inflation is above expected
Forecasts adjust downward, moving unemployment farther below natural
q.commonError: Assumes a surprise to actual inflation remains a surprise indefinitely.
q.feedback: As expected inflation adapts, the temporary unemployment effect fades and the SRPC shifts.

q.commonError: Treating expected inflation as movement along the same SRPC.
q.q: What happens to the short-run Phillips curve when expected inflation rises?
options: It shifts downward
It shifts upward
It becomes horizontal
It becomes the money demand curve
q.feedback: Higher expected inflation shifts the short-run Phillips curve upward.

q.commonError: Keeping unemployment below natural forever after an inflation surprise.
q.q: Refer to the graph. Starting at c, expansionary policy moves the economy to a. After expected inflation rises, where does the economy move?
options: b
c
d
U1
q.feedback: After expected inflation rises, the SRPC shifts up and the economy moves to b at the natural rate of unemployment.
q.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves and a vertical long-run Phillips curve at unemployment rate U2, with labeled points a through d.
q.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. A vertical LRPC stands at U2. SRPC1 is the lower/left downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/right downward-sloping curve. Point a is at U1/I2 on SRPC1, point b is at U2/I2 where SRPC2 meets the LRPC, point c is at U2/I1 where SRPC1 meets the LRPC, and point d is at U3/I1 on SRPC2. Dashed guides mark unemployment rates U1-U3 and inflation rates I1-I2.

q.q: A sharp oil-price increase raises firms’ costs. What happens to the short-run Phillips curve, other things equal?
options: It shifts down and to the left.
The economy only moves along an unchanged curve.
It shifts up and to the right.
It becomes vertical at zero unemployment.
q.commonError: Treating an adverse supply shock as a movement along a fixed SRPC.
q.feedback: An adverse supply shock can raise both inflation and unemployment, shifting the SRPC up-right.

q.q: If expected inflation increases, which SRPC change follows?
options: An upward shift
A downward shift
Only movement down the same curve
A horizontal LRPC shift
q.commonError: Moves along the SRPC instead of shifting it when expected inflation changes.
q.feedback: Higher expected inflation shifts the SRPC upward; lower expected inflation shifts it downward.

q.q: If expected inflation decreases, which SRPC change follows?
options: An upward shift
Only movement up the same curve
A vertical AD shift
A downward shift
q.commonError: Moves along the SRPC instead of shifting it when expected inflation changes.
q.feedback: Higher expected inflation shifts the SRPC upward; lower expected inflation shifts it downward.

q.q: Why can actual inflation above expected inflation temporarily reduce unemployment?
options: Higher inflation permanently raises labor productivity
The LRPC becomes downward sloping
Some wages and prices were set using the lower forecast
The natural rate immediately becomes lower
q.commonError: Assumes a surprise to actual inflation remains a surprise indefinitely.
q.feedback: As expected inflation adapts, the temporary unemployment effect fades and the SRPC shifts.

q.q: Under rational expectations, wage setters use available information, including credible policy announcements; forecasts can still be wrong when new information arrives. A credible lower-inflation target changes their forecasts before much demand contraction occurs, but some contracts remain fixed. Which assessment follows?
options: Rational expectations guarantee exact forecasts and eliminate every unemployment cost even with fixed contracts.
The SRPC can shift downward sooner, reducing the transition cost, while fixed contracts can leave some temporary unemployment increase.
Expected inflation must wait for past inflation to decline because announcements cannot enter a forecast.
A credible nominal target permanently shifts LRPC left even when labor-market structure is unchanged.
q.commonError: Assumes credibility mechanically eliminates every short-run output cost.
q.feedback: Available-information forecasting can incorporate credible policy news before actual inflation falls. It does not imply perfect foresight or instantly flexible contracts. Earlier expectations adjustment can reduce disinflation costs without guaranteeing zero costs.

q.q: Actual inflation remains above expected inflation for several contract cycles. Which sequence best fits adaptive expectations?
options: Expected inflation rises, shifting SRPC upward and undoing the temporary unemployment gain
Expected inflation falls, shifting SRPC downward and preserving the unemployment gain indefinitely
LRPC shifts left, locking in unemployment below natural after contracts renew
SRPC stays fixed because only actual inflation matters for wage setting
q.commonError: Assumes a surprise to actual inflation remains a surprise indefinitely.
q.feedback: As expected inflation adapts, the temporary unemployment effect fades and the SRPC shifts.

q.q: A supply shock raises inflation without a demand boom. Why might a simple expectations-only diagnosis be incomplete?
options: Expected inflation is the only possible SRPC shifter in the introductory model
Every inflation increase is movement along a fixed SRPC regardless of its cause
Supply shocks shift only the vertical LRPC while leaving SRPC unchanged
The shock can shift the SRPC even before expectations adapt
q.commonError: Calls a supply or expectations shock a movement along one unchanged SRPC.
q.feedback: A changed inflation-unemployment relationship shifts the SRPC; it is not movement along the same curve.

q.q: A surprise expansion lifts inflation from 2% to 5% while expected inflation remains 2%. What makes the unemployment effect temporary?
options: Expected inflation falls below 2% and shifts SRPC downward after workers observe prices
The LRPC becomes flatter as actual inflation rises above expected inflation
Expected inflation eventually rises toward actual inflation and shifts the SRPC upward
The natural rate permanently falls three points once actual inflation exceeds its forecast
q.commonError: Assumes a surprise to actual inflation remains a surprise indefinitely.
q.feedback: As expected inflation adapts, the temporary unemployment effect fades and the SRPC shifts.

q.q: A disinflation announcement is only partly credible and wage contracts reset slowly. Which conclusion is appropriately bounded?
options: The announcement necessarily causes the price level to fall for several years
Expectations may fall gradually, so some short-run output cost can remain
Partial credibility must eliminate every unemployment cost as soon as policy is announced
Expected inflation cannot change until actual inflation reaches the announced target
q.commonError: Assumes credibility mechanically eliminates every short-run output cost.
q.feedback: Credibility can speed expectations adjustment, but disinflation costs depend on model assumptions and wage-price adjustment.

q.q: An adverse supply shock raises actual inflation, then wage setters incorporate it into next year’s contracts. What are the two stages?
options: An initial SRPC shift followed by reinforcement through higher expected inflation
Two movements along one fixed SRPC with no change in the inflation-unemployment relation
An LRPC shift followed by lower expected inflation when contracts renew
A demand contraction followed by an SRPC shift downward at each unemployment rate
q.commonError: Assumes a surprise to actual inflation remains a surprise indefinitely.
q.feedback: The supply shock first shifts SRPC upward even with expectations unchanged. Incorporating the higher observed inflation into contracts adds an expectations-driven upward shift. This reinforces inflation pressure rather than describing the disappearance of a demand-created unemployment gain.

q.q: Expected inflation rises from 2% to 4%. At a given unemployment rate, how does the SRPC move?
options: It shifts upward
It shifts downward
The economy moves down the same SRPC
The LRPC shifts right
q.feedback: Higher expected inflation shifts the SRPC upward; lower expected inflation shifts it downward.
q.commonError: Moves along the SRPC instead of shifting it when expected inflation changes.

q.q: Actual inflation repeatedly exceeds the rate workers expected. Which forecast adjustment is likely?
options: Expected inflation falls
Expected inflation becomes permanently zero
Expected inflation cannot respond
Expected inflation rises
q.feedback: As expected inflation adapts, the temporary unemployment effect fades and the SRPC shifts.
q.commonError: Assumes a surprise to actual inflation remains a surprise indefinitely.

q.q: Does a credible announcement guarantee costless disinflation?
options: Yes; unemployment must immediately fall
No; credibility can never affect expectations
No; it can reduce costs without always eliminating them
Yes; credibility removes all nominal rigidities
q.feedback: Credibility can speed expectations adjustment, but disinflation costs depend on model assumptions and wage-price adjustment.
q.commonError: Assumes credibility mechanically eliminates every short-run output cost.

q.q: The economy moves up-left along SRPC after a demand surprise. Wage setters then revise forecasts upward. What connection is required?
options: A movement along SRPC becomes an upward shift as expectations adjust
The LRPC shifts left as aggregate demand rises and nominal wages renew
The same fixed SRPC supports permanently lower unemployment after forecasts update
A downward expectations shift reinforces the initial unemployment gain
q.feedback: As expected inflation adapts, the temporary unemployment effect fades and the SRPC shifts.
q.commonError: Assumes a surprise to actual inflation remains a surprise indefinitely.

q.q: Expected inflation falls during a credible disinflation. Which applied family slice uses that change to assess policy costs?
options: GDP components
Money creation
Economic growth policy
Disinflation and policy
q.feedback: Credibility can speed expectations adjustment, but disinflation costs depend on model assumptions and wage-price adjustment.
q.commonError: Assumes credibility mechanically eliminates every short-run output cost.

q.q: Expectations fully catch up after repeated inflation surprises. Which curve summarizes the long-run unemployment result?
options: The money-demand curve
The production possibilities frontier
The LRPC at the natural rate
The SRPC as a permanent menu
q.feedback: The LRPC is vertical at the natural rate because expected inflation adjusts in the long run.
q.commonError: Infers a permanent unemployment gain from the downward-sloping SRPC.

q.q: A transit study predicts that a lower fare will increase ridership. Why is this positive?
options: Evidence could test the predicted change
The prediction must be socially desirable
The result is guaranteed to be true
Transit policy contains no value judgment
q.commonError: Treating positive as good, true, or politically neutral.
q.feedback: A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.

q.q: A council member says parks should receive more funding because access is fair. Why is this normative?
options: It includes a government budget
It ranks outcomes using a value judgment
It predicts a measurable funding change
It must be supported by all voters
q.commonError: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
q.feedback: A normative claim ranks outcomes or says what ought to be done.

q.q: Which statement is positive?
options: The city should make rent cheaper.
Rent control is unfair.
A binding rent ceiling reduces apartment supply
The best policy is always lower rent.
q.commonError: uses_policy_topic_to_assume_normative
q.feedback: This is positive because it makes a testable claim about what the policy will do.

q.q: A library reports that Sunday hours increased visits. What makes this positive?
options: The increase in visits is a desirable outcome
Library officials support Sunday hours
The report is written confidently, so the claim must be true.
Visit records could test the claimed increase
q.commonError: Treating positive as good, true, or politically neutral.
q.feedback: A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.

q.q: “The library should stay open Sundays because access matters.” Why is this normative?
options: It recommends a choice using a value judgment
Sunday visits can be counted
The statement concerns a public institution
Evidence could show whether Sunday hours increase attendance.
q.commonError: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
q.feedback: A normative claim ranks outcomes or says what ought to be done.

q.q: A forecast that later proves false can still be positive when:
options: The forecast was made by an expert
Evidence could in principle have tested it
The forecast described an outcome people wanted
The forecast was stated with certainty.
q.commonError: Treating positive as good, true, or politically neutral.
q.feedback: A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.

q.q: Which claim is normative in a school debate?
options: Average class size fell by two students last year
Smaller classes increased per-student spending
The district ought to favor smaller classes despite higher costs
Enrollment is projected to rise next year.

q.feedback: A normative claim ranks outcomes or says what ought to be done.

q.q: Which claim is positive in a transit debate?
options: The city should make transit more affordable
Lower fares are fairer to low-income riders
Expanding transit access is more important than balancing the transit budget.
A lower fare increased weekday ridership
q.commonError: Treating positive as good, true, or politically neutral.
q.feedback: A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.

options: Positive
Normative
A price floor
A circular-flow claim
q.commonError: assumes_policy_topic_means_normative
q.feedback: This is positive because it makes a testable claim about cause and effect.

q.q: A commissioner says the city ought to favor safer streets even if travel takes longer. What makes this normative?
options: The ability to measure travel time
The ranking of safety against travel time
The prediction that streets can change
The reference to a city decision
q.commonError: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
q.feedback: A normative claim ranks outcomes or says what ought to be done.

options: The claim that the fee reduced waste
The measured amount of waste reduction
The judgment that the fee is fair
The fact that a fee was imposed.
q.commonError: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
q.feedback: Separate testable predictions from the value judgment used to recommend a choice.

q.q: A weakly supported prediction later fails. What classification remains possible?
options: Normative, because the prediction turned out to be false
Normative, because the evidence supporting it was weak
Neither positive nor normative until the prediction is confirmed.
Positive, because testability does not require truth
q.commonError: Treating positive as good, true, or politically neutral.
q.feedback: A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.

q.q: “Costs rose 8%, so the city should respond.” What is present?
options: A positive measurement plus a normative recommendation
A purely positive statement because it includes a measured percentage
A purely normative statement because it recommends action
Two positive claims because both parts refer to economic conditions.
q.commonError: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
q.feedback: Separate testable predictions from the value judgment used to recommend a choice.

q.q: A program “works,” but no outcome is named. What is missing?
options: A statement that the program is desirable
A measurable claim that evidence could contradict
A recommendation about whether the program should continue
A larger sample of people who support the program.
q.commonError: Assuming objective wording alone makes a claim positive.
q.feedback: Identify what observation could support or contradict the testable component.

q.q: “Equal access matters more than maximum output.” What is this?
options: A positive claim because access and output can both be measured
A positive claim because it compares two economic outcomes
A normative ranking of competing values
Neither positive nor normative because no policy is named.
q.commonError: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
q.feedback: A normative claim ranks outcomes or says what ought to be done.

q.q: A tax study uses the word efficient for a measurable revenue criterion. Is it necessarily normative?
options: Yes; the word efficient always expresses a value judgment
Yes; any claim about taxes is normative
Yes; a policy criterion cannot be evaluated with evidence.
No; the stated criterion can be tested with evidence
q.commonError: Treating positive as good, true, or politically neutral.
q.feedback: A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.

q.q: Which statement is positive rather than normative?
options: A binding rent ceiling reduces the quantity of rental housing supplied
The city should cap rents to protect tenants
Housing is too important to leave to markets
Fair rents matter more than landlord profits
q.commonError: mistakes_policy_topic_for_normative_statement
q.feedback: The claim that a binding rent ceiling reduces the quantity of rental housing supplied is a testable prediction. The other claims prescribe what the city should do or express judgments about fairness and priorities.

q.q: An economist says, 'The city should accept some efficiency loss to make housing more affordable.' What makes this normative?
options: It can be tested with rental data alone
It uses a value judgment about what policy should do
It describes only current prices
It states the law of demand
q.commonError: misses_should_and_value_tradeoff
q.feedback: The statement recommends what policy should do, so it is normative.

q.q: A report predicts that extending library hours will increase weekly visits. Another recommends the extension because access is worth the staffing cost. Which assessment is correct?
options: The visit prediction is testable; the recommendation adds a value judgment
Both claims are normative because a public agency is involved
The recommendation is positive because staffing costs can be measured
The visit prediction is normative until the extension occurs
q.commonError: assumes_controversial_policy_claim_is_normative
q.feedback: Evidence can test the predicted visit change. Calling improved access worth its cost also ranks outcomes; future predictions can be positive before observation.

q.q: A subsidy is predicted to raise enrollment and is therefore recommended. Which split is correct?
options: Both parts are positive because enrollment can be measured
Both parts are normative because a subsidy is a policy
The forecast is positive; the recommendation is normative
The forecast is normative; the recommendation is positive.
q.commonError: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
q.feedback: Separate testable predictions from the value judgment used to recommend a choice.

q.q: “The policy benefits most residents, so it is just.” Where is the normative step?
options: The claim that most residents benefit
The number of residents affected by the policy
The measured size of the benefits.
Calling the distribution just
q.commonError: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
q.feedback: A normative claim ranks outcomes or says what ought to be done.

q.q: What could test the claim that a road fee reduces congestion?
options: Traffic counts around comparable fee changes
A survey asking whether drivers think the fee is fair
A city council vote on the fee
A statement from officials that the fee will work.
q.commonError: Assuming objective wording alone makes a claim positive.
q.feedback: Identify what observation could support or contradict the testable component.

q.q: When can “the project has positive net benefits” be positive?
options: Always, because net benefits are measured in dollars
When inputs and the net-benefit rule are empirically checkable
Never, because the word benefits is inherently normative
Only when everyone agrees the project is desirable.
q.commonError: Treating positive as good, true, or politically neutral.
q.feedback: A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.

q.q: “The only acceptable policy is universal access.” Why is this normative?
options: Universal access can be measured
The statement refers to a policy outcome
It embeds a value standard despite objective wording
The sentence does not include a numerical prediction.
q.commonError: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
q.feedback: A normative claim ranks outcomes or says what ought to be done.

q.q: A rule lowers costs but is called morally wrong. What can evidence settle?
options: Both the cost effect and whether the rule is morally wrong
Only whether the rule is morally wrong
Neither claim, because the rule is a policy.
The cost effect, but not the moral conclusion by itself
q.commonError: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
q.feedback: Separate testable predictions from the value judgment used to recommend a choice.

q.q: An economist says, 'A rent ceiling below equilibrium will reduce housing quality over time.' Another says, 'The city should accept that cost to help low-income renters.' Which pairing is correct?
options: First is positive; second is normative
First is normative; second is positive
Both are positive
Both are normative
q.commonError: treats_all_policy_discussion_as_normative
q.feedback: The first is testable. The second recommends what policy should do, so it is normative.

q.q: A report defines success only as maximum total surplus. What choice is normative?
options: Calculating total surplus from observed prices and quantities
Selecting total surplus as the sole ranking criterion
Measuring how total surplus changes after the policy
Estimating the policy’s effect on output.
q.commonError: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
q.feedback: A normative claim ranks outcomes or says what ought to be done.

q.q: Two analysts agree that an archive plan preserves more records but delays public access. One recommends it; the other rejects it. What additional finding would show a factual disagreement as well as a value disagreement?
options: They agree on the delay but differ on whether it is acceptable
They use the same probabilities but prefer different distributions of access
They assign different probabilities to permanent record loss under the alternative
They give different ethical priority to immediate public access
q.commonError: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
q.feedback: Probabilities of record loss are empirical assessments. The other differences concern how agreed consequences should be valued.

q.q: An evaluator says, "Option A saves more staff time, so it is the best policy." Which reply separates the testable component from the hidden value premise?
options: Measure the time savings, then ask why that objective should outrank other consequences
Treat the entire sentence as positive because staff time is measurable
Treat the time-saving estimate as normative because it supports a recommendation
Conclude more accurate timing data will uniquely determine the preferred policy
q.commonError: confuses_policy_analysis_with_policy_preference
q.feedback: Time savings can be tested. Moving from that estimate to "best" requires a criterion for weighing time against other outcomes.

q.q: A board ranks plans only by the number of people served and selects A. New evidence shows B serves more people but offers less privacy. Which conclusion distinguishes logic from values?
options: Choosing A would necessarily show the new service count is false
Its stated rule now favors B; preferring A would require changing or qualifying that rule
The privacy difference makes the service-count evidence normative
More people served proves B is morally superior under every criterion
q.commonError: confuses_policy_analysis_with_policy_preference
q.feedback: A fixed criterion has implications that evidence can change. Preferring privacy can justify a different criterion, but does not refute the service-count evidence.

q.q: A forecast says a digitization plan will reduce waiting. A recommendation says it should be adopted only if access for people without internet is protected. Waiting falls but offline access worsens. Which inference is sound?
options: Observed waiting reductions prove the plan satisfies the value criterion
The forecast becomes normative because implementation affected access
The forecast is supported, while the recommendation's stated condition is unmet
The failed access condition refutes the waiting-time forecast
q.commonError: classifies_all_policy_claims_as_normative
q.feedback: The observed waiting result bears on the positive claim. Protecting offline access is a separate condition in the recommendation; success on one outcome does not satisfy it.

q.q: A report states that volunteers prefer evening shifts and therefore evening-only service is fair. A representative survey confirms the preference. What remains unresolved?
options: Whether a confirmed preference statement can count as positive
Whether using a survey converts the fairness conclusion into a measured fact
Whether the fairness judgment proves daytime users have no unmet needs
Whether fairness should be judged by volunteer preferences rather than users' access
q.commonError: mistakes_policy_topic_for_normative_statement
q.feedback: A preference claim is empirically testable. The move from measured volunteer preferences to fairness requires a value premise about whose interests count.

q.q: A rule gives priority to people facing the greatest hardship. New data show that a different group meets that description. What change is consistent with keeping the same normative principle?
options: Change the priority group because the evidence changed who satisfies the criterion
Keep the old group because normative principles cannot use evidence
Declare hardship measurement normative solely because it informs policy
Treat the data as proof that greatest-hardship priority is the only fair principle
q.commonError: treats_economic_vocabulary_as_making_claim_positive
q.feedback: A stable value criterion can lead to a different recommendation when facts change. Evidence identifies its beneficiaries without uniquely establishing the criterion itself.

q.q: A researcher predicts that simplifying an application raises completion when eligibility is unchanged. A trial simplifies the form and broadens eligibility; completion rises. Which statement is justified?
options: Only recommendations can be evaluated when two policies change together
The prediction is positive, but the joint change does not isolate the form's effect
The rise proves the form alone caused every added completion
The extra eligibility change makes the original claim normative
q.commonError: classifies_controversial_topic_as_normative_even_when_claim_is_testable
q.feedback: The conditional causal prediction is testable. Because eligibility changed too, the observation does not by itself identify the effect of form simplification.

q.q: A report finds that a shuttle saves travelers time but increases neighborhood noise. It recommends adoption using travelers' gains alone. Which critique is precise?
options: Time savings become normative when expressed in money
Adding more precise effect estimates removes the need to decide whose welfare counts
The effects are testable; excluding neighbors from the recommendation embeds a value choice
Noise estimates are normative because neighbors dislike the outcome
q.commonError: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
q.feedback: Time and noise effects can be measured. Counting only travelers when recommending a policy assigns standing to one group and excludes another, which is a value choice.

q.q: Two forecasts disagree about whether a new scheduling rule will shorten next year's queues. Both specify measurable waiting times and comparable staffing. What would change their status as positive claims?
options: The forecast with the larger benefit is positive; the other is normative
Both become normative until next year's data exist
Agreement by the forecasters is required before evidence can test them
Neither disagreement nor the future date changes their testable status
q.commonError: Treating positive as good, true, or politically neutral.
q.feedback: Positive status depends on empirical testability, not agreement, truth, desirability or whether the outcome has occurred. Later evidence can support one forecast over the other.

q.q: An analyst rejects a delivery plan because predicted delays exceed her stated acceptable limit. Better evidence places delays below that limit, but she still rejects it on privacy grounds. Which interpretation fits?
options: The factual case changed, and the rejection now requires an additional value criterion
The original delay forecast was normative because it supported rejection
The unchanged decision proves the new delay estimate is irrelevant to the original argument
Privacy concerns establish that the revised forecast is false
q.commonError: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
q.feedback: The delay objection no longer follows from the updated evidence and original threshold. A privacy objection can support rejection, but it is a separate normative premise.

q.q: A planner defines "optimal" as maximizing visits, then claims the chosen schedule is objectively best. Another schedule serves fewer visitors but reaches people with greater need. Which statement is most defensible?
options: A numerical criterion cannot contain a value judgment
Visit maximization identifies an optimum under one criterion, not a uniquely justified social ranking
Calling a result optimal makes its criterion empirically true
The need difference disproves the measured visit counts
q.commonError: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
q.feedback: Optimization can be objective conditional on a criterion. Choosing visits rather than need as the social objective remains a normative judgment.

q.q: What is a positive statement?
options: A testable claim about how the world is
A claim about how the world should be
A statement that is always morally good
A policy recommendation
q.commonError: confuses_positive_with_good_or_approval
q.feedback: A positive statement describes or predicts how the world is.

q.q: An instructor presents this claim: 'A price ceiling below equilibrium creates a shortage.' What kind of statement is this?
options: Normative
Positive
A value judgment
A policy recommendation
q.commonError: assumes_policy_topic_means_normative
q.feedback: This is positive because it is a testable cause-and-effect claim.

q.q: An instructor gives two claims. Claim 1: 'Rent control reduces housing supply.' Claim 2: 'The city should use rent control anyway.' Which pairing is correct?
options: Claim 1 is normative; Claim 2 is positive
Both claims are positive
Claim 1 is positive; Claim 2 is normative
Both claims are normative
q.commonError: treats_all_policy_claims_as_normative
q.feedback: The first claim is testable. The second claim recommends what should happen, so it is normative.

q.q: A report predicts gains and calls them worth unequal losses. What is normative?
options: The judgment that gains justify the losses
The prediction that the policy creates gains
The estimated size of the gains
The measured distribution of gains and losses.
q.commonError: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
q.feedback: Separate testable predictions from the value judgment used to recommend a choice.

q.q: What best tests “a fee reduces congestion”?
options: A survey asking whether residents support the fee
Traffic counts before and after comparable changes
A council vote to adopt the fee
A statement from officials that congestion will fall.
q.commonError: Assuming objective wording alone makes a claim positive.
q.feedback: Identify what observation could support or contradict the testable component.

q.q: Why is “Policy A is responsible” not automatically positive?
options: The statement mentions a policy
The word responsible refers to a measurable outcome
Responsible may hide an unstated value standard
Any sentence about policy performance is positive.
q.commonError: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
q.feedback: A normative claim ranks outcomes or says what ought to be done.

q.q: “A bus lane reduced travel time.” What kind of claim is this?
options: Positive and empirically testable
Normative because reduced travel time is desirable
Normative because the statement concerns transportation policy
Neither, because one observed result cannot be tested.
q.commonError: Treating positive as good, true, or politically neutral.
q.feedback: A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.

q.q: “The city ought to accept higher costs for cleaner air.” What kind?
options: Positive because costs and air quality can be measured
Normative because it ranks a tradeoff
Positive because the statement describes a policy tradeoff
Neither, because the statement contains no numerical estimate.
q.commonError: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
q.feedback: A normative claim ranks outcomes or says what ought to be done.

q.q: When does a false forecast remain positive?
options: Only when the forecast describes a desirable outcome
Only when an expert made the forecast
When evidence could have tested the forecast
Never; a false claim cannot be positive.
q.commonError: Treating positive as good, true, or politically neutral.
q.feedback: A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.

q.q: An adviser predicts a wage rule raises employed teenagers’ annual income by $8 million but reduces teenage employment by 3%. She recommends it because the income gain is worth the employment loss. A pilot instead finds a 1% job loss. Which conclusion separates evidence from values?
options: The pilot makes the original employment prediction normative because a positive statement cannot be contradicted by data.
The pilot challenges the size of the positive employment prediction; it does not by itself establish the adviser’s tradeoff criterion.
The smaller loss proves the recommendation objectively correct, regardless of how the affected teenagers value work and income.
The recommendation makes both numerical predictions normative, so neither can be evaluated using pilot evidence.
q.commonError: misses_should_and_value_tradeoff
q.feedback: Predictions about income and employment are testable positive claims even when inaccurate. Calling one outcome worth another introduces a value judgment. New evidence informs the tradeoff but cannot supply the normative weighting by itself.

q.q: A report states: (1) a tax reduces cigarette purchases; (2) the tax burden falls heavily on low-income smokers; (3) therefore the tax is unjust. Which classification is correct?
options: All three are positive, because technical wording removes every value judgment
Only statement 1 is positive
Statements 1 and 2 are positive; statement 3 is normative
Statements 2 and 3 are normative
q.commonError: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
q.feedback: The first two claims can be tested empirically. The conclusion that the policy is unjust is normative.

q.q: School plan A is predicted to raise scores by 6 points and reduce free time by 4 hours weekly. Plan B raises scores by 4 points and reduces free time by 1 hour. A board declares A preferable because each extra score point is worth at least 2 hours of free time. Which assessment is exact?
options: The outcome predictions are normative; the board’s numerical weighting is positive, and A’s extra 2 points cost 3 hours.
All claims are positive because they contain numbers; A dominates B on both scores and free time.
The weighting is normative, so the score and time predictions cannot be tested against observed outcomes.
The outcome predictions are positive; the board’s weighting is normative, and A’s extra 2 points cost 3 hours relative to B.
q.commonError: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
q.feedback: Comparative predictions imply A adds 2 score points while costing 3 more hours, or 1.5 hours per extra point. Whether that is worthwhile depends on the board’s stated value criterion, not merely on the accuracy of the predictions.

q.q: A positive statement is best described as:
options: A testable claim about how the world is
A claim about how the world should be
A statement that is always good
A policy recommendation
q.commonError: confuses_positive_with_good
q.feedback: Positive statements describe or predict how the world is.

q.q: A statement using 'should' is usually:
options: Positive
Normative
A demand shifter
A supply schedule
q.commonError: misses_should_language
q.feedback: Normative statements make value judgments about what should happen.

q.q: Does positive mean good or favorable?
options: Yes; positive means the outcome is desirable
Yes; positive claims support the policy being discussed
No; it means testable in principle
Yes; positive claims are facts that must be true.
q.commonError: Treating positive as good, true, or politically neutral.
q.feedback: A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.

q.q: Does false automatically mean normative?
options: Yes; normative claims are the claims that turn out to be false
Yes; positive claims must be factually correct
Yes; a claim becomes normative once evidence rejects it.
No; a false claim can still be testable
q.commonError: Treating positive as good, true, or politically neutral.
q.feedback: A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.

q.q: Is every policy statement normative?
options: No; policy predictions can be positive
Yes; any statement about government policy is normative
Yes; policy effects cannot be tested with evidence
Yes; mentioning a recommendation makes every related claim normative.
q.commonError: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
q.feedback: Separate testable predictions from the value judgment used to recommend a choice.

q.q: Does technical tone guarantee a positive claim?
options: Yes; technical language makes a statement factual
No; technical wording can conceal a value judgment
Yes; numerical language removes value judgments
Yes; professional wording means the claim can be tested.
q.commonError: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
q.feedback: A normative claim ranks outcomes or says what ought to be done.

q.q: A price-support study predicts more output, then recommends the policy as fair. How should these two claims be evaluated?
options: Test the output prediction separately from the fairness judgment
Ignore the prediction once advice appears
Treat both parts as positive because evidence exists
Treat both parts as normative because policy is involved
q.commonError: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
q.feedback: Separate testable predictions from the value judgment used to recommend a choice.

q.q: An analyst writes: "A congestion charge will reduce downtown car trips by 10%. That reduction is worth the added financial burden on commuters." How are the two claims classified?
options: First normative; second positive.
Both positive.
First positive; second normative.
Both normative.
q.commonError: confuses_testable_prediction_with_value_judgment
q.feedback: The 10% traffic prediction can be tested against evidence, whether or not it proves true. Saying the reduction is worth the burden ranks competing outcomes; that judgment needs a value premise that traffic data alone cannot establish.

q.q: An economist predicts job losses and recommends against a rule. What additional judgment turns the prediction into policy advice?
options: The existence of a measurable employment effect
The fact that the rule is a government policy
The recommendation adds a value judgment about the predicted cost
The use of an economic forecast.
q.commonError: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
q.feedback: Separate testable predictions from the value judgment used to recommend a choice.

q.q: A model predicts a tax effect under stated assumptions. Why is it positive?
options: Because the prediction supports the tax
Because the model is written in technical language
Because the prediction must be true if the assumptions are stated.
Evidence could test the conditional prediction
q.commonError: Assuming objective wording alone makes a claim positive.
q.feedback: Identify what observation could support or contradict the testable component.

q.q: The circular-flow model shows how dollars, goods and services, and resources move between:
options: Households and firms
Banks and foreign governments
Workers and tax agencies
Retailers and central banks
q.commonError: confuses_circular_flow_with_ppf
q.feedback: The circular-flow model shows flows between households and firms.

q.q: In the simple circular-flow model, households usually supply:
options: Finished goods and services
Factors of production
Price ceilings
Tax wedges
q.commonError: reverses_household_and_firm_roles
q.feedback: Households supply factors of production such as labor, land, and capital.

q.q: In the simple circular-flow model, firms usually supply:
options: Labor services to households
Household income to product markets
Goods and services
Tax revenue to resource markets
q.commonError: reverses_firm_and_household_roles
q.feedback: Firms produce and sell goods and services.

q.q: A production possibilities frontier shows:
options: The exact market price of each good
Government’s preferred production mix
The economy’s current unemployment rate
Currently feasible combinations of two goods
q.commonError: confuses_ppf_with_market_supply_curve
q.feedback: A PPF shows possible production combinations with current resources and technology.

q.q: A point inside the PPF usually means:
options: Resources are not being used efficiently
The point is unattainable
The economy has no tradeoffs
The economy is beyond its resources
q.commonError: confuses_inside_ppf_with_unattainable
q.feedback: A point inside the PPF is attainable but inefficient.

q.q: A point outside the PPF is:
options: Efficient but always chosen
Unattainable with current resources and technology
A price floor
A market surplus
q.commonError: confuses_outside_ppf_with_efficient
q.feedback: A point outside the PPF cannot be reached with current resources and technology.

q.q: Moving along a PPF usually means:
options: Producing more of every good without cost
Creating a tax wedge
Producing more of one good and less of another
Changing only the price level
q.commonError: misses_tradeoff_on_ppf
q.feedback: Moving along the PPF shows a tradeoff between two goods.

q.q: An outward shift of the PPF usually represents:
options: A shortage
A binding price ceiling
A decrease in demand
Economic growth
q.commonError: confuses_growth_with_movement_along_ppf
q.feedback: An outward shift means the economy can produce more than before.

q.q: A circular-flow model shows households supplying labor to firms and receiving wages. Which market is being described?
options: The market for factors of production
The market for final goods and services
The market for price ceilings
The market for tax revenue
q.commonError: reverses_product_and_factor_markets
q.feedback: Households provide factors of production such as labor in factor markets and receive income.

q.q: A PPF is bowed outward. Moving from low production of Good X to high production of Good X requires giving up larger and larger amounts of Good Y. What principle does this show?
options: Increasing opportunity cost
Constant opportunity cost
A binding price floor
A tax wedge
q.commonError: misses_bowed_ppf_as_increasing_cost
q.feedback: A bowed-out PPF shows increasing opportunity cost as resources are shifted toward one good.

q.q: An economist uses a PPF to show how producing more military goods requires producing fewer consumer goods. What is the model showing?
options: Tradeoffs and opportunity cost
Tax incidence
A binding price ceiling
A market surplus
q.commonError: misses_ppf_as_tradeoff_model
q.feedback: The PPF shows tradeoffs because producing more of one good requires giving up some of another.

q.q: An economy moves from a point inside its PPF to a point on the PPF. What happened?
options: It reached an unattainable point
It used idle resources more efficiently
It created a tax wedge
It shifted demand left
q.commonError: confuses_movement_to_frontier_with_growth
q.feedback: Moving from inside the PPF to the frontier means resources are being used more efficiently.

q.q: An economy gets better technology for producing both goods. What happens to its PPF?
options: It shifts inward
It becomes a price ceiling
It shifts outward
It creates a shortage
q.commonError: confuses_growth_with_movement_along_ppf
q.feedback: Better technology increases productive capacity, shifting the PPF outward.

q.q: A point is outside the PPF today but becomes attainable after an increase in capital and technology. What changed?
options: The market price was fixed
Demand decreased
The economy moved inside the PPF
The economy's productive capacity increased
q.commonError: does_not_connect_growth_to_attainability
q.feedback: More capital and better technology increase what the economy can produce.

q.q: Refer to the PPF graph. Which points are efficient production points?
options: A, B, C, D, and E
F, because it is attainable inside the frontier
G, because it represents greater output
B, C, and D, because only interior points on the frontier are efficient.
q.commonError: confuses_points_on_ppf_with_inside_or_outside_points
q.feedback: Points on the PPF are efficient because the economy is using its available resources fully.

q.q: Refer to the PPF graph. Which point is attainable but inefficient?
options: G
F
C
E
q.commonError: confuses_inside_ppf_with_unattainable
q.feedback: Point F is inside the PPF, so it is attainable but inefficient.

q.q: Refer to the PPF graph. Which point is currently unattainable?
options: F
A
G
D
q.commonError: confuses_outside_ppf_with_efficient
q.feedback: Point G is outside the PPF, so it is unattainable with current resources and technology.

q.q: Refer to the PPF graph. What does the bowed-out shape of the PPF suggest?
options: Opportunity cost remains constant along the frontier
Opportunity cost falls as more Good X is produced
The economy has idle resources at each frontier point
Opportunity cost rises as more Good X is produced
q.commonError: misses_bowed_shape_as_increasing_opportunity_cost
q.feedback: A bowed-out PPF shows increasing opportunity cost as resources are shifted toward producing more of one good.

q.q: Refer to the PPF graph. If the economy moves from F to C, what has happened?
options: The economy has moved from inefficient production to efficient production
The economy has moved from unattainable production to attainable production
The economy has reduced both goods
The economy has moved outside the PPF
q.commonError: confuses_inside_point_with_outside_point
q.feedback: Point F is inside the PPF and point C is on the PPF, so the economy moved from inefficient to efficient production.

q.q: Refer to the graph. Moving from A to B, what is the opportunity cost per additional pizza?
options: 1 robot
2 robots
0.5 robot
40 robots
q.imageAlt: A bowed PPF0 has pizzas on the horizontal axis and robots on the vertical axis. Point A is at 20 pizzas and 120 robots; point B is at 60 pizzas and 80 robots. The frontier reaches about 125 robots at zero pizzas and 100 pizzas at zero robots.
q.commonError: misreads_graph_relationship
q.feedback: The move gains 40 pizzas and gives up 40 robots, so each pizza costs 1 robot.
q.graphDescription: A bowed PPF0 has pizzas on the horizontal axis and robots on the vertical axis. Point A is at 20 pizzas and 120 robots; point B is at 60 pizzas and 80 robots. The frontier reaches about 125 robots at zero pizzas and 100 pizzas at zero robots.

q.q: A household buys groceries in the product market and sells labor in the factor market. In the circular-flow model, which flow goes from firms to households in factor markets?
options: Income such as wages, rent, and profit
Goods and services
Consumer spending from households to firms.
Price ceilings
q.commonError: reverses_money_and_resource_flows
q.feedback: Households provide factors of production, and firms pay income for those factors.
