Equal to unemployment
q.feedback: A deflator above 100 means current prices are above base-year prices.

q.commonError: Infers output growth directly from nominal GDP growth.
q.q: Nominal GDP rises while quantities are unchanged. Does that prove production increased?
options: No; higher current prices can raise nominal GDP
Yes; nominal GDP measures only changes in physical quantities
Yes; every nominal increase establishes the same real growth
No; nominal GDP deliberately excludes every change in prices
q.feedback: Compare nominal and real GDP to separate price changes from changes in production.

q.commonError: Mixes current and base-year prices while valuing current output.
q.q: Is real GDP calculated by simply subtracting the inflation rate from nominal GDP?
options: Yes; subtract the inflation percentage directly from the nominal dollar level
Yes; but only when the measured inflation rate remains positive
No; value current quantities at current prices in both measures
No; value current quantities at consistent base-year prices
q.feedback: Multiply current quantities by the designated base-year prices and add across final goods.

q.commonError: Mixes current and base-year prices while valuing current output.
q.q: GDP measurement identifies current final output. Which added step makes output comparable across years with changing prices?
options: Value current quantities at consistent base-year prices
Subtract all imports from every year twice
Add transfer payments to nominal GDP
Replace quantities with current interest rates
q.feedback: Multiply current quantities by the designated base-year prices and add across final goods.

q.commonError: Treats GDP as either a complete welfare index or a useless statistic.
q.q: Real GDP per person rises, but leisure and environmental quality worsen. Which family destination evaluates the remaining question?
options: GDP components and the expenditure identity alone
Inventory investment and unsold production accounting
Nominal GDP measured only with current market prices
Limits of GDP and welfare measurement
q.feedback: GDP is a strong measure of market production for its purpose, but it omits some dimensions of welfare.

q.commonError: Forgetting to subtract inflation from the nominal interest rate.
q.q: The nominal interest rate is:
options: The interest rate usually reported before correcting for inflation
The interest rate after subtracting inflation
Always equal to zero
The same as the unemployment rate
q.feedback: The nominal interest rate is the stated or reported interest rate before adjusting for inflation.

q.commonError: Forgetting to subtract inflation from the nominal interest rate.
q.q: The real interest rate is approximately:
options: Nominal interest rate minus inflation rate
Nominal interest rate plus inflation rate
Inflation rate minus unemployment rate
GDP divided by population
q.feedback: The real interest rate adjusts the nominal rate for inflation.

q.commonError: Forgetting to subtract inflation from the nominal interest rate.
q.q: If inflation rises while the nominal interest rate stays the same, the real interest rate:
options: Falls
Rises
Does not change
Becomes the CPI
q.feedback: Higher inflation reduces the real interest rate when the nominal rate is unchanged.

q.q: Inflation is higher than the nominal interest earned on an account. What is true of the approximate real return?
options: It is negative
It is greater than the nominal rate
It must equal zero
It is unrelated to purchasing power
q.commonError: Uses the nominal rate alone to infer the purchasing-power return.
q.feedback: For introductory approximation, real interest is nominal interest minus inflation.

q.q: What does a real interest rate describe that a nominal rate does not?
options: The number of dollars deposited
The current CPI basket composition
The long-run money-supply growth rate
The change in purchasing power
q.commonError: Uses the nominal rate alone to infer the purchasing-power return.
q.feedback: For introductory approximation, real interest is nominal interest minus inflation.

q.q: Unexpected inflation is higher than lenders and borrowers expected on a fixed-rate loan. Who generally benefits?
options: Both gain the same purchasing power
Neither party’s real outcome changes
The borrower
The lender
q.commonError: Misses how unexpected inflation changes the real burden of a fixed nominal loan.
q.feedback: Higher-than-expected inflation lowers the realized real repayment burden and shifts purchasing power from lender to borrower.

q.commonError: Forgetting to subtract inflation from the nominal interest rate.
q.q: A bank pays 6% interest and inflation is 2%. What happened to purchasing power in the account?
options: It rose by about 4%
It fell by about 4%
It rose by 8%
It was unchanged
q.feedback: The real interest rate is about 4%, so purchasing power rises by about 4%.

q.commonError: Forgetting to subtract inflation from the nominal interest rate.
q.q: Which borrower benefits most from unexpectedly high inflation?
options: A borrower with a fixed nominal interest rate
A lender with a fixed nominal interest rate
A saver earning a low fixed rate
A worker paid only in real wages
q.feedback: Unexpected inflation reduces the real burden of fixed nominal debt.

q.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes ex ante and ex post real interest rates?
options: Both measures subtract actual inflation from the nominal rate.
Ex ante adds expected inflation to the nominal interest rate.
Ex post is known with certainty when the loan contract is signed.
Ex ante uses expected inflation; ex post uses actual inflation.
q.commonError: Using actual inflation for both the expected and realized real return.
q.feedback: The expected real return is based on expected inflation, while the realized real return uses actual inflation.

q.q: Actual inflation exceeds expected inflation while a loan’s nominal rate is fixed. What happens to the lender’s realized real return?
options: It is lower than expected
It is higher than expected
It equals the nominal rate
It becomes independent of inflation
q.commonError: Uses actual inflation to describe an expected return or expected inflation to describe the realized return.
q.feedback: Ex ante real interest uses expected inflation; ex post real interest uses actual inflation.

q.q: Actual inflation is lower than expected on a fixed nominal loan. Who bears a higher real repayment burden than anticipated?
options: The lender
The central bank
The price-index compiler
The borrower
q.commonError: Misses how unexpected inflation changes the real burden of a fixed nominal loan.
q.feedback: Because actual inflation is lower than expected, the repayment dollars retain more purchasing power than anticipated, increasing the borrower’s real burden.

q.q: Which inflation rate belongs in an ex post real-interest calculation?
options: The base-year CPI level
Long-run money growth
Actual inflation
Expected inflation only
q.commonError: Uses actual inflation to describe an expected return or expected inflation to describe the realized return.
q.feedback: Ex ante real interest uses expected inflation; ex post real interest uses actual inflation.

q.commonError: Forgetting to subtract inflation from the nominal interest rate.
q.q: A borrower agrees to repay a loan at 6% nominal interest. Inflation unexpectedly rises from 2% to 8%. Who is helped, other things equal?
options: The borrower, because the real repayment burden falls
The lender, because the real return rises
Neither side, because inflation does not affect real payments
Only the government, because GDP falls
q.feedback: Unexpected inflation lowers the real value of fixed nominal repayments, helping borrowers.

q.commonError: Forgetting to subtract inflation from the nominal interest rate.
q.q: If nominal interest is 4% and inflation is 7%, what does the real interest rate imply?
options: Purchasing power falls by about 3%
Purchasing power rises by about 11%
Purchasing power rises by 4%
Inflation is irrelevant
q.feedback: Real interest = 4% - 7% = -3%, so purchasing power falls.

q.commonError: Forgetting to subtract inflation from the nominal interest rate.
q.q: Which statement best explains why inflation matters for interest rates?
options: Nominal rate shows dollar growth; real rate shows buying-power growth
The real rate ignores inflation
The nominal rate is always lower than inflation
Inflation only affects unemployment, not borrowing
q.feedback: The real rate adjusts nominal interest for inflation to show changes in purchasing power.

q.q: A savings account earns 5% nominal interest while inflation is 7%. What happens?
options: The balance rises in dollars but loses purchasing power
Both the dollar balance and purchasing power fall 2%
Purchasing power rises by 12%
The real return equals the nominal return
q.commonError: Uses the nominal rate alone to infer the purchasing-power return.

q.q: A fixed loan carries 8% nominal interest. Expected inflation is 3%, but actual inflation is 6%. What are the approximate ex ante and ex post real rates?

11% ex ante and 14% ex post

5% ex ante and 2% ex post
q.commonError: Uses actual inflation to describe an expected return or expected inflation to describe the realized return.
q.feedback: Ex ante real interest uses expected inflation; ex post real interest uses actual inflation.

q.q: A loan’s fixed nominal rate is 9%. During its year, CPI rises from 200 to 212. Which conclusion is supported by these observations without a theory of how future loan rates are set?
options: Next year’s nominal rate must rise to 15%
Expected inflation at signing must have been 6%
The realized real return is approximately 3%
The realized real return is approximately 15%
q.commonError: Turns a measurement question into a claim about long-run nominal-rate adjustment.
q.feedback: Observed inflation is (212 - 200)/200 = 6%, so the approximate realized real return is 9 - 6 = 3%. These observations do not reveal prior expectations or determine future nominal rates.

q.commonError: Forgetting to subtract inflation from the nominal interest rate.
q.q: A lender expects 3% inflation and wants a 4% real return. What nominal interest rate should the lender charge approximately?
q.feedback: Nominal interest rate ≈ real interest rate + expected inflation = 4% + 3% = 7%.

It was 4 percentage points higher than expected

q.q: A lender expected a 2% real return on a fixed 7% nominal loan. Actual inflation was 2 percentage points higher than expected. Which inflation and realized real rate follow using the approximation?

q.commonError: Uses actual inflation to describe an expected return or expected inflation to describe the realized return.
q.feedback: Ex ante real interest uses expected inflation; ex post real interest uses actual inflation.

q.q: Use the exact Fisher relation: nominal interest is 10% and inflation is 4%. Rounded to one decimal place, what is the real rate?
q.commonError: Uses the nominal rate alone to infer the purchasing-power return.
q.roundingRule: Use (1.10 ÷ 1.04) − 1 and round to one decimal place.

q.q: A bank pays a fixed 4% nominal rate. CPI inflation during the year is 6%, but no inflation forecast was recorded at signing. What can be established using the Principles approximation?
options: Both expected and realized real returns were -2%
The realized real return is 10%; the expected rate is unknown
The nominal contract must have reset to 6% after inflation was observed
The realized real return is -2%; the expected real return cannot be recovered
q.commonError: Turns a measurement question into a claim about long-run nominal-rate adjustment.
q.feedback: The realized real return uses actual inflation: 4 - 6 = -2%. The expected return needs expected inflation, which was not supplied. A fixed contract does not automatically reset after an inflation surprise.

q.q: Why can a positive nominal interest rate still produce a negative real return?
options: Inflation can exceed the nominal rate
The nominal account balance must decline whenever consumer prices rise faster
Expected inflation must be zero
CPI excludes interest income
q.commonError: Uses the nominal rate alone to infer the purchasing-power return.
q.feedback: For introductory approximation, real interest is nominal interest minus inflation.

q.q: Expected inflation is used to calculate which real rate?
options: The ex post real rate calculated after actual inflation is observed
The GDP-deflator growth rate
The indexed nominal payment
The ex ante real rate
q.commonError: Uses actual inflation to describe an expected return or expected inflation to describe the realized return.
q.feedback: Ex ante real interest uses expected inflation; ex post real interest uses actual inflation.

q.q: Unexpected inflation rises on a fixed-rate loan. What happens to the real burden?
options: It leaves every real outcome unchanged
It converts the loan into an indexed benefit
It shifts downward for the borrower and reduces the lender’s real return
It rises equally for both parties and preserves the lender’s expected purchasing-power return
q.commonError: Misses how unexpected inflation changes the real burden of a fixed nominal loan.
q.feedback: Higher-than-expected inflation lowers the realized real repayment burden and shifts purchasing power from lender to borrower.

q.q: A borrower signs a loan at 7% nominal interest expecting 3% inflation. Actual inflation turns out to be 8%. Who benefits compared with expectations?
options: The lender, because inflation makes repayment more valuable
Neither side, because nominal interest determines all real outcomes
The government, because unemployment must fall
The borrower, because the real repayment burden is lower than expected
q.commonError: thinks_lenders_gain_from_unexpected_inflation
q.feedback: Unexpectedly high inflation reduces the real value of fixed nominal repayments, helping borrowers and hurting lenders.

q.q: A saver earns 6% nominal interest. Inflation is 9%. At the same time, the saver receives a 4% nominal wage increase. Which statement best connects the two effects?
options: Both the real return on savings and the real wage fell
Both the real return and real wage rose
The real return rose but the real wage fell
The real wage rose because any raise beats inflation
q.commonError: analyzes_each_nominal_value_without_adjusting_for_inflation
q.feedback: The real interest rate is about -3%, and the wage increase is below inflation, so both real values fell.

q.q: The Market Marshal says: 'Nominal interest is high, but the real reward for saving is low.' Which situation fits that statement?
options: Nominal interest is 4% and inflation is 0%
Nominal interest is 10% and inflation is 9%
Nominal interest is 3% and inflation is -2%
Nominal interest is 8% and inflation is 1%
q.commonError: chooses_highest_nominal_rate_instead_of_highest_real_rate
q.feedback: A 10% nominal rate with 9% inflation gives only about a 1% real return.

q.q: A loan pays 9% nominal interest while inflation is 4%. What is the approximate real interest rate?
q.commonError: adds_inflation_to_nominal_interest_rate
q.feedback: The approximate real interest rate is nominal interest minus inflation: 9% - 4% = 5%.

q.q: A saver earns 6 percent interest while inflation is 7 percent. Which statement is correct?
options: The saver has fewer dollars but more purchasing power
The saver must be unemployed
The saver has more dollars but less purchasing power
The saver caused a price ceiling
q.commonError: thinks_more_dollars_always_means_more_real_value
q.feedback: The nominal balance rises, but because inflation is higher than the interest rate, purchasing power falls.

q.commonError: Forgetting to subtract inflation from the nominal interest rate.
q.q: Boss Audit: A lender expects 2% inflation and charges 7%. Actual inflation is 9%. What are expected and actual real returns?
options: Expected 5%; actual -2%
Expected 9%; actual 7%
Expected -5%; actual 2%
Expected 7%; actual 9%
q.feedback: Expected real = 7 - 2 = 5. Actual real = 7 - 9 = -2.

q.q: A saver earns a positive nominal rate, but inflation is higher. What is the first real-value diagnosis?
options: The saver gains dollars while losing purchasing power
The saver loses dollars and purchasing power at the same rate
The real return must equal the nominal rate
Expected inflation automatically raises the account balance
q.commonError: Uses the nominal rate alone to infer the purchasing-power return.
q.feedback: For introductory approximation, real interest is nominal interest minus inflation.

q.q: A lender expected 2% inflation on a 7% fixed-rate loan; actual inflation is 8%. What is the complete outcome?
options: Expected return was −5%, realized return 15%, benefiting the lender
Both real returns were 7% because the nominal rate was fixed
The loan automatically repriced to preserve the lender’s return
Expected real return was about 5%, realized return about −1%, benefiting the borrower
q.commonError: Misses how unexpected inflation changes the real burden of a fixed nominal loan.
q.feedback: Higher-than-expected inflation lowers the realized real repayment burden and shifts purchasing power from lender to borrower.

q.q: A lender issues a loan at 11% nominal interest expecting 4% inflation. Actual inflation turns out to be 9%. Which statement is correct?
options: The actual real return is about 7%, so the lender receives exactly what was expected
The actual real return is about 20%, so both borrower and lender gain
The actual real return is about -5%, so the borrower pays more in real terms
The actual real return is about 2%, so the borrower gains relative to what the lender expected
q.commonError: uses_expected_inflation_after_actual_inflation_is_known
q.feedback: Expected real return was about 7%, but actual real return was about 2%. Unexpected inflation helps borrowers and hurts lenders.

q.q: A saver earns 8% nominal interest, inflation is 6%, and their wage rises 4%. Which statement best connects the two real effects?
options: The saver earns a positive real return on savings, but the real wage falls
The saver earns a negative real return, but the real wage rises
Both the real return and real wage rise
Both the real return and real wage fall
q.commonError: treats_all_nominal_increases_as_real_increases
q.feedback: The real interest rate is about 2%, but the wage increase is below inflation, so the real wage falls.

q.q: The Market Marshal offers four economies. Which has the highest approximate real interest rate?
options: Nominal interest 11%, inflation 8%
Nominal interest 7%, inflation -1%
Nominal interest 5%, inflation 2%
Nominal interest 9%, inflation 7%
q.commonError: chooses_highest_nominal_interest_rate
q.feedback: Approximate real interest equals nominal interest minus inflation. With 7% nominal interest and -1% inflation, the real rate is about 8%.

q.commonError: Forgetting to subtract inflation from the nominal interest rate.
q.q: Real interest rate is approximately:
options: Nominal interest rate minus inflation
Nominal interest rate plus inflation
Inflation minus GDP
CPI divided by exports
q.feedback: The real interest rate adjusts nominal interest for inflation.

q.commonError: Forgetting to subtract inflation from the nominal interest rate.
q.q: If nominal interest is 6% and inflation is 2%, real interest is:
q.feedback: Real interest = 6% - 2% = 4%.

q.commonError: Forgetting to subtract inflation from the nominal interest rate.
q.q: Nominal interest is 9% and inflation is 5%. What is the real interest rate?
q.feedback: Real interest = 9% - 5% = 4%.

q.q: The sacrifice ratio measures the output cost of reducing:
options: Inflation
Unemployment
Money demand
Imports
q.commonError: Confusing sacrifice ratio with unemployment rate.
q.feedback: The sacrifice ratio measures how much output is lost when inflation is reduced.

q.q: Credible anti-inflation policy can reduce the sacrifice ratio by causing expected inflation to:
options: Rise faster
Fall faster
Stay above actual inflation forever
Turn into unemployment
q.commonError: Ignoring expectations in disinflation.
q.feedback: If expected inflation falls faster, the short-run cost of disinflation can be smaller.

q.q: What does a sacrifice ratio of 3 mean?
options: About 3% of one year’s output is lost per 1-percentage-point inflation reduction
Inflation falls 3% whenever output falls 1%
Unemployment rises 3 percentage points permanently
The price level falls 3% during every disinflation
q.commonError: Treats the sacrifice ratio as an inflation rate or unemployment change.
q.feedback: The sacrifice ratio measures cumulative output loss per percentage-point reduction in inflation.

q.q: An analyst divides output loss by the final 4% inflation rate after inflation began at 7%. What denominator should replace 4%?
options: The initial 7% inflation rate before policy
The 11% sum of the two inflation rates
The final 4% inflation rate already used
The 3-percentage-point reduction in inflation
q.commonError: Uses the final inflation rate rather than the reduction in inflation.
q.feedback: The denominator is the fall in inflation measured in percentage points.

q.q: Which loss belongs in the usual sacrifice-ratio numerator?
options: The total fall in the price level
The final year’s inflation rate
Cumulative output lost relative to potential during disinflation
The permanent increase in the unemployment rate
q.commonError: Treats the sacrifice ratio as an inflation rate or unemployment change.
q.feedback: The sacrifice ratio measures cumulative output loss per percentage-point reduction in inflation.

q.q: A disinflation has a lower sacrifice ratio than another. Under comparable measurement, what does that indicate?
options: A higher inflation target after policy ends
Less cumulative output loss per inflation point reduced
A larger fall in the price level
A permanently higher natural unemployment rate
q.commonError: Treats the sacrifice ratio as an inflation rate or unemployment change.
q.feedback: The sacrifice ratio measures cumulative output loss per percentage-point reduction in inflation.

q.q: If expected inflation falls quickly after a credible policy announcement, the sacrifice ratio is likely to be:
options: Lower
Higher
Unchanged by expectations
Equal to M1
q.commonError: Ignoring credibility and expectations.
q.feedback: Faster adjustment of expected inflation reduces the output cost of disinflation.

q.q: Cumulative output loss is 12% of one year’s GDP while inflation falls 3 percentage points. What is the sacrifice ratio?
options: 4% of one year’s output per inflation point
3% of output per inflation point
9% of output per inflation point
36% of output per inflation point
q.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
q.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

q.q: A planned inflation reduction is 2.5 percentage points and the estimated sacrifice ratio is 3. What cumulative output loss is implied?
options: 1.2% of one year’s output
5.5% of one year’s output
8.3% of one year’s output
7.5% of one year’s output
q.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
q.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

q.q: The output gap is −1.5% in year one and −2.5% in year two while inflation falls 2 percentage points. Using the sum of annual gaps, what is the sacrifice ratio?
options: 4% of output per inflation point
8% of output per inflation point
2% of one year’s output per inflation point
1% of output per inflation point
q.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
q.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

q.q: Inflation declines from 8% to 5%. Which calculation uses the correct denominator?
options: Final output divided by 13 percentage points
Cumulative output loss divided by 3 percentage points
Cumulative output loss divided by the final 5%
Cumulative output loss divided by the initial 8%
q.commonError: Uses the final inflation rate rather than the reduction in inflation.
q.feedback: The denominator is the fall in inflation measured in percentage points.

q.q: Path A loses 6% of one year’s output to cut inflation 3 points. Path B loses 5% to cut inflation 2 points. Which has the lower sacrifice ratio?
options: Path A has a ratio of 2; Path B has a ratio of 2.5
Path B has a ratio of 2; Path A has a ratio of 2.5
Both paths have a sacrifice ratio of 2
Path A has a ratio of 3; Path B has a ratio of 2
q.commonError: Compares total losses without dividing each by its own inflation-point reduction.
q.feedback: Path A: 6 ÷ 3 = 2. Path B: 5 ÷ 2 = 2.5, so Path A has the lower sacrifice ratio.

q.q: A credible disinflation lowers expected inflation before unemployment rises much. What happens to the sacrifice ratio?
options: It falls
It rises
It becomes infinite
It equals MPC
q.commonError: Ignoring credibility in disinflation costs.
q.feedback: Credibility lowers expected inflation faster and can reduce the output cost of disinflation.

q.q: A student says disinflation has no cost if the Fed announces it. What is the correction?
options: Credibility can lower the cost, not guarantee zero cost
Announcements always raise inflation first
The sacrifice ratio ignores expectations
Unemployment must fall during disinflation
q.commonError: Overstating credibility effects.
q.feedback: Credibility can reduce the sacrifice ratio, but it does not automatically make disinflation costless.

q.q: Potential GDP remains $500 billion in each of the three years. Output is 2% below potential for one year and 1% below for two more years while inflation falls 4 points. What is the loss per inflation point?
options: $2.5 billion per inflation point
$10 billion per inflation point
$20 billion per inflation point
$5 billion per inflation point
q.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
q.feedback: The cumulative loss is $10 billion + $5 billion + $5 billion = $20 billion; $20 billion ÷ 4 = $5 billion per inflation point.

q.q: A disinflation creates cumulative output loss equal to 9% of annual GDP. If the sacrifice ratio is 3, how far did inflation fall?
options: 6 percentage points
27 percentage points
3 percentage points
2 percentage points
q.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
q.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

q.q: Real GDP growth slows from 4% to 1%, but output remains above potential. Why can the 3-point growth slowdown not automatically be the sacrifice-ratio numerator?
options: Only the final inflation rate belongs in the numerator of this measure
The numerator measures an output-level loss relative to a benchmark, not merely slower growth
Any growth slowdown is exactly the cumulative output gap relative to potential
The numerator must be a permanent unemployment-rate change rather than output
q.commonError: Treats the sacrifice ratio as an inflation rate or unemployment change.
q.feedback: The sacrifice ratio measures cumulative output loss per percentage-point reduction in inflation.

q.q: Cumulative output loss is 6.5% of one year’s GDP and inflation falls 3 percentage points. Round the sacrifice ratio to two decimals.
options: 2.17% of one year’s output per inflation point
2.16% of output per inflation point
2.20% of output per inflation point
3.50% of output per inflation point
q.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
q.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

q.q: The Fed announces disinflation, but workers doubt it and expected inflation stays high. What happens to the sacrifice ratio?
options: It is likely higher
It is automatically zero
It becomes the MPC
It shifts LRAS right
q.commonError: Assuming announcements alone make policy credible.
q.feedback: If expected inflation does not fall quickly, reducing actual inflation tends to require more output loss.

q.q: If inflation falls from 12 percent to 7 percent and the sacrifice ratio is 3.5, output loss equals:
options: 17.5 percent of one year's output
15.5 percent of one year's output
8.5 percent of one year's output
5 percent of one year's output
q.commonError: Adding the sacrifice ratio to the inflation reduction.
q.feedback: Inflation falls by 5 points, so output loss is 3.5 x 5 = 17.5 percent of one year's output.

q.q: If cumulative output loss is 14 percent of one year’s potential GDP and inflation falls by 4 percentage points, the sacrifice ratio is:
options: 3.5% of one year’s output per inflation point
4% of one year’s output per inflation point
10% of one year’s output per inflation point
18% of one year’s output per inflation point
q.commonError: Uses the inflation change or output loss alone rather than dividing cumulative loss by the percentage-point reduction.
q.feedback: Divide the 14% cumulative output loss by the 4-percentage-point inflation reduction: 14 ÷ 4 = 3.5% of one year’s output per point.

q.q: A disinflation plan is credible, wage contracts adjust quickly, and expected inflation falls fast. Which path is most likely?
options: Smaller unemployment increase for the same inflation reduction
Larger unemployment increase for the same inflation reduction
No change in expected inflation despite credibility
Permanent unemployment below natural
q.commonError: Ignoring expectations in sacrifice-ratio logic.
q.feedback: Credibility and fast expectation adjustment reduce the output and unemployment cost of lowering inflation.

q.q: A disinflation plan lacks credibility, wage contracts are slow, and expected inflation remains high. Which path is most likely?
options: Larger output loss for the same inflation reduction
Smaller output loss for the same inflation reduction
Immediate movement to lower unemployment
LRPC becomes downward sloping
q.commonError: Assuming disinflation costs vanish without credibility.
q.feedback: If expected inflation stays high, lowering actual inflation usually requires a larger output loss.

q.q: A disinflation lowers inflation from 10 percent to 6 percent. Cumulative output loss is 18 percent of one year’s potential GDP, of which 11 percent occurred before the final year. An analyst reports a sacrifice ratio using only the final-year loss. Which audit correction is needed?
options: Use all 18 percent: the ratio is 4.5; using only the final year would understate it as 1.75.
Use only 7 percent: the ratio is 1.75 because earlier output losses are already over.
Use the final inflation rate: the ratio is 3 because the target is 6 percent.
Add initial and final inflation: the ratio is 1.125 because the full window contains both rates.
q.commonError: Dividing by the wrong inflation change.
q.feedback: The inflation reduction is 4 percentage points. Cumulative loss gives 18/4 = 4.5. Final-year loss is 18 − 11 = 7, giving 7/4 = 1.75 if earlier losses are wrongly omitted. Returning toward potential does not erase earlier lost production.

q.q: A plan must reduce inflation by 5 percentage points with cumulative output loss no greater than 14 percent of one year’s potential GDP. Its first stage has already reduced inflation by 2 percentage points at a cumulative loss of 7 percent. What maximum sacrifice ratio can the remaining stage have if the full plan is to meet both targets?
options: About 2.33 percent of one year’s output per remaining inflation point.
2.8 percent of one year’s output per remaining inflation point.
3.5 percent of one year’s output per remaining inflation point.
7 percent of one year’s output per remaining inflation point.
q.commonError: Adding instead of multiplying.
q.feedback: There are 3 inflation points and 7 percent of output-loss allowance remaining. The remaining-stage ceiling is 7/3 = 2.333..., about 2.33. Applying the overall allowance ratio 14/5 = 2.8 to the remaining stage would exceed the total loss limit because the first stage used more loss per point.

q.q: A disinflation lowers inflation from 9 percent to 5 percent with cumulative output loss of 10 percent of one year’s potential GDP. A second plan is projected to lower inflation by only 2.5 percentage points with loss of 7 percent on the same output benchmark. Which comparison avoids confusing a smaller total loss with a lower loss per inflation point?
options: The completed plan has ratio 2.5 versus 2.8 for the second; the second has less total loss but a higher loss per point.
The second plan has the lower ratio because 7 is less than 10, regardless of the inflation reductions.
Both have ratio 2.5 because the second plan’s inflation reduction is its denominator and also its ratio.
The completed plan has ratio 0.4 and therefore no output cost; the second has ratio 2.8.
q.commonError: Using the ending inflation rate instead of the inflation reduction.
q.feedback: The completed reduction is 9 − 5 = 4 points, so 10/4 = 2.5. The second ratio is 7/2.5 = 2.8. A lower cumulative cost can accompany a higher per-point cost when the inflation reductions differ; neither statistic alone proves a universally better policy.

q.q: Two stages jointly reduce inflation by 6 percentage points with a combined sacrifice ratio of 1.75. The first stage loses 3 percent of one year’s potential GDP while reducing inflation by 2 percentage points. Use the same output benchmark for both stages. What is the second-stage ratio, and how does it compare with the first?
options: 1.875 for the second versus 1.5 for the first; the second has the higher loss per point.
1.75 for both stages, because a combined ratio must equal each stage’s ratio.
3.75 for the second versus 1.5 for the first, using only 2 remaining inflation points.
0.533 for the second versus 0.667 for the first, using inflation reduction divided by loss.
q.commonError: Adding the inflation reduction and sacrifice ratio.
q.feedback: Total loss is 6 × 1.75 = 10.5 percent. The second stage accounts for 10.5 − 3 = 7.5 percent loss and 6 − 2 = 4 inflation points, giving 1.875. The first-stage ratio is 3/2 = 1.5. The combined ratio is weighted by the reductions, not a mandate for equal stage ratios.

q.q: A three-year disinflation produces annual output gaps of −2%, −1%, and 0%, cutting inflation from 6.5% to 4.5%. A faster path produces one year at −4% and cuts inflation the same amount. Which comparison is correct?
options: The gradual path ratio is 3; the fast path ratio is 4
Both paths have a ratio of 2
The gradual path ratio is 2; the fast path ratio is 1.5
The gradual path ratio is 1.5; the fast path ratio is 2
q.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
q.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

q.q: Economy A loses 8% of one year’s GDP while inflation falls from 9% to 5%. Economy B loses 6% while inflation falls from 5% to 2%. What can be concluded?
options: A has a ratio of 0.5 and B has a ratio of 0.67
A has a lower ratio because its inflation drop is larger
A has a ratio of 2 and B also has a ratio of 2
A has a ratio of 4 and B has a ratio of 3
q.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
q.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

q.q: If the sacrifice ratio is 4 and inflation falls by 2 percentage points, the output cost is:
options: 2 percent of one year's output
4 percent of one year's output
8 percent of one year's output
16 percent of one year's output
q.commonError: Adding instead of multiplying.
q.feedback: The output cost is 4 x 2 = 8 percent of one year's output.

q.q: Potential GDP is $400 billion. Cumulative output loss is $24 billion while inflation falls from 8% to 5%. What is the sacrifice ratio?
options: 3% of output per inflation point
6% of output per inflation point
8% of output per inflation point
2% of one year’s output per inflation point
q.commonError: Divides the dollar loss directly by the inflation change without converting loss to a share of potential output.
q.feedback: The $24 billion loss is 6% of $400 billion. Inflation falls 3 percentage points, so the ratio is 6 ÷ 3 = 2.

q.q: If inflation falls by 3 points and the output loss is 12 percent of one year’s GDP, the sacrifice ratio is:
options: 12% of one year’s output per inflation point
4% of one year’s output per inflation point
3% of one year’s output per inflation point
9% of one year’s output per inflation point
q.commonError: Uses the inflation reduction or cumulative output loss alone rather than dividing loss by points reduced.
q.feedback: Divide cumulative output loss by the inflation reduction: 12 ÷ 3 = 4% of one year’s output per inflation point.

q.q: If the sacrifice ratio is 3 and inflation falls from 8 percent to 5 percent, the output cost is:
options: 3 percent of one year's output
6 percent of one year's output
9 percent of one year's output
15 percent of one year's output
q.commonError: Adding instead of multiplying.
q.feedback: Inflation falls by 3 percentage points, so output loss is 3 x 3 = 9 percent of one year's output.

q.commonError: Confusing the sacrifice ratio with the inflation rate itself.
q.q: What does the sacrifice ratio measure?
options: The output cost of reducing inflation
The unemployment rate at zero inflation
The money multiplier after disinflation
The tax increase needed to raise AD
q.feedback: The sacrifice ratio measures the output cost of reducing inflation.

q.commonError: Adding instead of multiplying.
q.q: Inflation falls by 3 percentage points. If the sacrifice ratio is 4, what output loss should be expected?
options: 7 percent of one year's output
12 percent of one year's output
3 percent of one year's output
4 percent of one year's output
q.feedback: Output loss equals sacrifice ratio times inflation reduction, so 4 x 3 = 12 percent of one year's output.

q.q: Which formula states the sacrifice ratio?
options: Price-level decline over the episode ÷ nominal GDP growth
Cumulative output loss ÷ inflation reduction in percentage points
Inflation reduction in points ÷ cumulative output loss relative to potential
Permanent unemployment increase ÷ the final positive inflation rate
q.commonError: Treats the sacrifice ratio as an inflation rate or unemployment change.
q.feedback: The sacrifice ratio measures cumulative output loss per percentage-point reduction in inflation.

q.q: Inflation falls from 6% to 4%. What is the denominator?
options: 2 percentage points
4 percent
6 percent
10 percentage points
q.commonError: Uses the final inflation rate rather than the reduction in inflation.
q.feedback: The denominator is the fall in inflation measured in percentage points.

q.q: A ratio of 2 is best read as what?
options: Inflation falls two percent for every percentage point of unemployment added
Unemployment stays two points above natural after expectations completely adjust
The price level declines two percent in each year of disinflation
Two percent of one year’s output lost per inflation point reduced
q.commonError: Treats the sacrifice ratio as an inflation rate or unemployment change.
q.feedback: The sacrifice ratio measures cumulative output loss per percentage-point reduction in inflation.

q.q: Use the sum of annual percentage output shortfalls as the cumulative-loss convention. Annual output gaps are −1%, −2%, and −1%; inflation falls from 7% to 5%. What is the ratio?
options: 6% of output per inflation point
2% of one year’s output per inflation point
0.5% of output per inflation point
3% of output per inflation point
q.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
q.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

q.q: A report divides cumulative output loss by the final inflation rate. What correction is required?
options: Divide by the percentage-point reduction in inflation
Divide by the initial inflation rate before the policy began
Multiply by the final inflation rate
Use the permanent unemployment rate
q.commonError: Uses the final inflation rate rather than the reduction in inflation.
q.feedback: The denominator is the fall in inflation measured in percentage points.

q.q: Path X loses 7.2% of annual GDP to reduce inflation 3 points. Path Y loses 5% to reduce inflation 2 points. Which is more output-efficient?
options: Path Y, with a ratio of 2 versus 2.4
Path X, with a ratio of 3 versus 2
They are equal because both lower inflation
Path X, with a ratio of 2.4 versus 2.5
q.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
q.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

q.q: Loss is 10% of annual GDP and inflation falls 4 points. What is the ratio?
options: 4% of output per inflation point
14% of output per inflation point
2.5% of one year’s output per inflation point
1.5% of output per inflation point
q.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
q.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

q.q: A two-year policy creates output gaps of −2.4% and −1.8%, lowering inflation from 7.0% to 5.2%. Round the sacrifice ratio to two decimals.
options: 2.34% of output per inflation point
4.20% of output per inflation point
2.33% of one year’s output per inflation point
1.80% of output per inflation point
q.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
q.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

q.q: A credible plan lowers expected inflation and produces a 3% cumulative output loss for a 2-point inflation reduction. A less credible plan loses 7.5% for a 3-point reduction. Which comparison is correct?
options: The plans are equal because both reduce inflation
The credible plan ratio is 1.5; the other is 2.5
The credible plan ratio is 2; the other is 2.5
The credible plan ratio is 0.67; the other is 0.4
q.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
q.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.

q.q: Potential output remains $800 billion each year. Actual output is below potential by 1.5% for two years and 0.5% for one year while inflation falls 2.8 points. What is cumulative loss per inflation point?
options: $10 billion per inflation point
$4 billion per inflation point
$14 billion per inflation point
$28 billion per inflation point
q.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
q.feedback: The cumulative loss is 3.5% of $800 billion = $28 billion. Dividing by 2.8 inflation points gives $10 billion per point.
q.roundingRule: Report the exact dollar amount per inflation point.

q.q: Inflation falls from 8% to 5%. What number belongs in the sacrifice-ratio denominator?
options: 3 percentage points
5 percent
8 percent
13 percentage points
q.feedback: The denominator is the fall in inflation measured in percentage points.
q.commonError: Uses the final inflation rate rather than the reduction in inflation.

q.q: Should annual output gaps be added before calculating a multi-year sacrifice ratio?
options: No, only the worst year counts
No, only the final year counts
Yes, but add inflation rates too
Yes, to obtain cumulative output loss
q.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.
q.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.

q.q: Does the sacrifice ratio normally measure an unemployment increase per inflation point?
options: Yes, but only when inflation stays positive
No, it measures the fall in the price level
No, it measures cumulative output loss per inflation point
Yes, unemployment is always the numerator
q.feedback: The sacrifice ratio measures cumulative output loss per percentage-point reduction in inflation.
q.commonError: Treats the sacrifice ratio as an inflation rate or unemployment change.

q.q: The economy temporarily moves above natural unemployment during disinflation. How is this cost measured?
options: Sum the output losses and divide by the inflation-point reduction
Divide the unemployment increase by the final positive inflation rate
Treat the change in the price level as the cumulative output numerator
Shift LRPC right by the cumulative inflation reduction during policy
q.feedback: Add output-gap losses across the disinflation period, then divide by the percentage-point inflation reduction.
q.commonError: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.

q.q: Expected inflation falls faster after a credible announcement. How can that connect to the sacrifice ratio?
options: A lower final inflation rate automatically raises the ratio even with unchanged loss
Credibility changes the denominator from inflation reduction to unemployment
The ratio must become zero in every credible disinflation plan
A smaller cumulative output loss can lower the measured ratio
q.feedback: Credibility can speed expectations adjustment, but disinflation costs depend on model assumptions and wage-price adjustment.
q.commonError: Assumes credibility mechanically eliminates every short-run output cost.

q.q: Two disinflation paths reach the same inflation target. Which family destination uses their sacrifice ratios to compare costs?
options: GDP component classification
Bank reserve accounting
Disinflation and policy
Short-run curve axis reading
q.feedback: The preferred path depends on credibility, expectations, adjustment speed, uncertainty, and cumulative costs.
q.commonError: Assumes either rapid or gradual disinflation is unconditionally best.

q.q: If government purchases rise by $30 with income and consumption fixed, what happens to national saving?
options: It rises by $30
It remains unchanged
It falls by $30
It falls by net taxes
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Private, Public, and National Saving.
q.feedback: From S = Y − C − G, a $30 increase in G lowers national saving by $30, other terms fixed.

q.q: Why must a saving question define T before using Y − T − C or T − G?
options: T must always mean total federal debt
T must include every government outlay
T must consistently mean net taxes in both expressions
T must equal household consumption
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Private, Public, and National Saving.
q.feedback: The private- and public-saving formulas share T, so a consistent net-tax definition prevents mixing textbook saving with total-budget accounting.

q.q: How does the closed-economy identity imply I = Y − C − G?
options: Subtract consumption and government purchases from both sides
Add net exports to both sides
Set private saving equal to taxes
Replace investment with consumption
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving and Investment in a Closed Economy.
q.feedback: Rearranging Y = C + I + G yields I = Y − C − G.

labels: Saving and Investment in a Closed Economy

q.q: In a closed economy, a student says each household's saving must equal one firm's investment. What is the correction?
options: S = I is an aggregate identity mediated by the financial system
Each saver must buy one physical machine
Only public saving can finance investment
The equality applies only to individual bank accounts
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving and Investment in a Closed Economy.
q.feedback: The equality concerns economy-wide totals; intermediaries and markets pool saving and allocate financing across borrowers.

labels: Saving and Investment in a Closed Economy

q.q: Output is $2,000, consumption is $1,250, and government purchases are $450 in a closed economy. What is investment?
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving and Investment in a Closed Economy.
q.feedback: Rearranging the closed-economy expenditure identity gives I = $2,000 − $1,250 − $450 = $300.

labels: Saving and Investment in a Closed Economy

q.q: Net tax revenue is $240 and government purchases are $290. What is public saving?
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Private, Public, and National Saving.
q.feedback: Public saving is T − G, so $240 − $290 = −$50 under the stated net-tax convention.

q.q: Using the same economy with private saving of $150 and public saving of −$30, what is national saving?
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Private, Public, and National Saving.
q.feedback: Adding the two components gives national saving of $150 − $30 = $120.

q.q: Consumption falls by $25 while income and government purchases remain fixed. What happens to national saving?
options: It falls by $25
It remains unchanged
It rises by net taxes
It rises by $25
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Private, Public, and National Saving.
q.feedback: Because S = Y − C − G, lower consumption leaves $25 more national saving.

q.q: A table lists total federal revenues and total outlays including transfers and interest. What does revenues minus outlays measure directly?
options: Public saving T − G under every definition
The federal budget balance
Private saving Y − T − C
National saving Y − C − G
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Private, Public, and National Saving.
q.feedback: Total revenues minus total outlays is the budget balance; it should not be relabeled T − G unless the specified components match net taxes and purchases.

q.q: Private saving falls by $15 while public saving rises by $35. What happens to national saving?
options: It rises by $20
It falls by $20
It rises by $50
It remains unchanged
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Private, Public, and National Saving.
q.feedback: National saving changes by the sum of component changes: −$15 + $35 = +$20.

q.q: In a closed economy, Y is $1,500, C is $900, and G is $350. What are saving and investment?
options: Both are $350
Saving is $600 and investment is $250
Both are $250
Saving is $250 and investment is $900
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving and Investment in a Closed Economy.
q.feedback: Y − C − G equals $250; in the closed-economy model both national saving and investment equal that amount.

labels: Saving and Investment in a Closed Economy

q.q: Consumption rises by $40 in a closed economy while output and government purchases are fixed. What happens to saving and investment?
options: Both rise by $40
Both fall by $40
Saving falls but investment rises
Neither aggregate changes
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving and Investment in a Closed Economy.
q.feedback: The increase in C reduces Y − C − G by $40, lowering both national saving and investment in the closed-economy identity.

labels: Saving and Investment in a Closed Economy

q.q: Which claim improperly extends the closed-economy identity?
options: National saving equals Y − C − G in the stated closed model
The financial system connects savers and borrowers
Aggregate saving can finance investment through markets
Domestic saving must equal domestic investment in every open economy
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving and Investment in a Closed Economy.
q.feedback: Open economies can finance domestic investment with international flows, so the domestic S = I statement requires the closed-economy qualifier.

labels: Saving and Investment in a Closed Economy

q.q: What role does the financial system play when closed-economy saving equals investment?
options: It requires identical saving from every household
It eliminates all differences in project profitability
It reallocates aggregate saving among borrowers and projects
It turns every security trade into new capital
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving and Investment in a Closed Economy.
q.feedback: Intermediation explains how economy-wide saving can finance investment without one-to-one matching between individual savers and firms.

labels: Saving and Investment in a Closed Economy

q.q: Output rises by $100, consumption rises by $70, and government purchases rise by $10. What happens to national saving and loanable-funds supply?
options: National saving rises by $20, so loanable-funds supply shifts right
National saving falls by $20, so loanable-funds supply shifts left
National saving rises by $180, so investment demand shifts right
National saving is unchanged because output and spending all increased
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Private, Public, and National Saving.
q.feedback: Using S = Y − C − G, the change is +100 − 70 − 10 = +$20. Higher national saving shifts the loanable-funds supply curve right.

q.q: Net taxes are $320 and government purchases are $280. Private saving then falls by $20 while fiscal quantities remain fixed. What follows?
options: Public saving falls to $20, but national saving remains unchanged
Public saving remains $40, while national saving rises $20 and supply shifts right
Public saving rises to $60, shifting investment demand rather than loanable-funds supply
Public saving stays $40; national saving falls $20
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Private, Public, and National Saving.
q.feedback: Public saving remains T − G = $40 because fiscal quantities do not change. The $20 decline in private saving therefore lowers national saving and shifts supply left.

q.q: National saving is initially $420 billion in a closed economy. Improved technology then raises desired investment at every real interest rate. What is the adjustment?
options: Investment stays permanently at $420 billion because the identity prevents demand from shifting
Loanable-funds supply shifts right by exactly the technology improvement, leaving the rate fixed
The identity is violated because desired investment can never differ from saving, even away from equilibrium
Investment demand shifts right, creating upward rate pressure until planned saving and investment are equal again
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving and Investment in a Closed Economy.
q.feedback: The accounting identity does not freeze behavior. Higher expected returns shift investment demand right; the real rate adjusts, inducing movements along both curves toward a new equilibrium equality.

labels: Saving and Investment in a Closed Economy

q.q: Government purchases fall by $25 billion in a closed economy with output fixed and the consumption schedule unchanged at each given real rate, while firms also become more optimistic about future sales. Which market description is complete?
options: Only supply shifts right, so both quantity and the real rate must rise
Only investment demand shifts right, so quantity rises and the real rate falls
Both curves shift right; quantity rises and the rate is ambiguous
Both curves shift left, so quantity falls while the real-rate effect is ambiguous
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving and Investment in a Closed Economy.
q.feedback: At each given real rate, lower purchases raise planned national saving by $25 billion and shift supply right. Stronger sales expectations shift investment demand right. Both raise equilibrium quantity, but their opposing rate pressures make the rate depend on relative shift magnitudes.

labels: Saving and Investment in a Closed Economy

q.q: Private saving is $360 billion and public saving is −$60 billion. If desired investment at the current real rate is $340 billion, what pressure should move the closed-economy market toward equilibrium?
options: Excess saving puts downward pressure on the real rate, increasing the gap
Excess demand raises the real rate toward equilibrium
Investment demand shifts left automatically by $40 billion because S = I is an identity
Loanable-funds supply shifts right automatically until both quantities equal $360 billion
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving and Investment in a Closed Economy.
q.feedback: National saving is $300 billion, below desired investment of $340 billion at the current rate. Excess demand pushes the rate upward, causing movements along the curves toward equilibrium.

labels: Saving and Investment in a Closed Economy

q.q: Households reduce current consumption and buy a firm's newly issued bonds. The firm uses the proceeds for new machinery and to purchase an existing office building. Which chain is economically correct?
options: Both firm purchases are current GDP investment because both use borrowed funds
The bond purchase is physical investment, while neither firm purchase enters GDP
Household saving enters GDP directly, and the machinery is only a financial asset
Saving finances the firm, but only the new machinery is current GDP investment
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving Versus Investment.
q.feedback: The bond market channels household saving to the borrower. New machinery is current production and GDP investment; transferring an existing building is not new production.

q.q: At every given real interest rate, planned private saving increases by $25 billion, but a larger deficit reduces public saving by $40 billion. With investment demand unchanged, which sequence follows?
options: National saving rises by $65 billion; supply shifts right, the real rate falls, and investment rises
National saving falls by $15 billion; supply shifts left, the real rate rises, and investment falls
National saving falls by $15 billion; investment demand shifts left, lowering both rate and quantity
National saving rises by $15 billion; supply shifts right, but investment necessarily falls
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Private, Public, and National Saving.
q.feedback: The public-saving decline is larger than the private-saving increase, so national saving falls by $15 billion. Supply shifts left, raising financing costs and crowding out investment along demand.

q.q: In a closed economy, at every given real interest rate, planned private saving rises by $20 billion while public saving falls by $35 billion. At the same time, new technology raises desired investment. What can be concluded without knowing the investment-demand shift magnitude?
options: Both curves shift right; quantity rises, while the real rate is ambiguous
Supply shifts left only; both the real rate and quantity must fall
Investment demand shifts right only; the real rate rises and quantity must rise
Supply shifts left, demand shifts right; the rate rises and quantity is ambiguous
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving and Investment in a Closed Economy.
q.feedback: At each given real rate, planned national saving falls by $15 billion, shifting supply left. Technology shifts investment demand right. Both shifts raise the real rate, but their quantity effects oppose one another; the final change in realized saving and investment is therefore not fixed at −$15 billion.

labels: Saving and Investment in a Closed Economy

q.q: Which action is saving in the macroeconomic sense?
options: Setting aside current income for future use
Buying newly produced factory equipment
Building a newly constructed apartment
Adding unsold goods to business inventories
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving Versus Investment.
q.feedback: Saving is current income not used for consumption; the other choices are forms of new macroeconomic investment.

q.q: Which purchase is counted as new macroeconomic investment in GDP?
options: A household buys an existing corporate share
A firm buys newly produced machinery
An investor buys an existing government bond
A collector buys a previously owned painting
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving Versus Investment.
q.feedback: New production equipment expands the capital stock and is GDP investment; secondary financial and used-asset trades do not.

q.q: A household buys existing shares from another investor. Later, the corporation issues new bonds and uses the proceeds to build a factory. Which statement correctly distinguishes the transactions?
options: Both securities trades are current GDP investment because money changes hands
Only the existing-share purchase is current GDP investment because it changes ownership
Only the new factory is current GDP investment
Neither the bond issue nor the factory affects saving, financing, or current production
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving Versus Investment.
q.feedback: Existing-share trades transfer financial claims. Newly issued bonds can channel saving to the firm, but the newly produced factory is the transaction counted as current macroeconomic investment.

q.q: A construction company completes a new warehouse for a retailer. What macroeconomic category applies?
options: Household saving without investment
A transfer of an existing asset
Government consumption spending
New investment in a structure
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving Versus Investment.
q.feedback: A newly produced warehouse is a structure added to the capital stock, so it is macroeconomic investment.

q.q: Why does construction of a new home count as investment in GDP?
options: It creates a new long-lived residential asset
Every household purchase is classified as investment
The buyer must have purchased an existing stock
Residential services are excluded from production
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving Versus Investment.
q.feedback: GDP conventions treat new residential construction as investment because it adds a durable structure that yields housing services.

q.q: A firm produces $12 million of goods this year but sells them next year without producing replacements. How are the two years affected, all else equal?
options: Consumption rises this year and inventory investment is unchanged next year
Inventory investment rises this year and falls next year
Inventory investment falls this year and rises again when the goods are sold
The goods count as financial investment in both years because ownership changes
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving Versus Investment.
q.feedback: Unsold current production adds $12 million to inventories this year. Selling those previously produced goods next year reduces inventories, creating negative inventory investment then.

q.q: A household deposits part of its paycheck in a bank. What broad role can that saving play?
options: It automatically becomes the household's GDP investment
It directly creates an equal quantity of physical capital
It can supply funds that the bank channels to borrowers
It removes the funds permanently from the financial system
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving Versus Investment.
q.feedback: Financial intermediaries can channel saving toward borrowers who finance investment, without making the deposit itself physical investment.

q.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes financial investment from macroeconomic investment?
options: Financial assets can change ownership without creating new capital
Every financial-asset trade adds equally to current GDP investment
Macroeconomic investment means purchasing only stocks and bonds
New equipment is saving rather than macroeconomic investment
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving Versus Investment.
q.feedback: Trading an existing claim need not add to current production, while new equipment, structures, inventories, and qualifying intellectual property do.

q.q: How does greater national saving make more investment possible?
options: It guarantees every proposed project will be profitable
It requires each saver to build a specific machine
It makes more resources available through the financial system
It makes the real interest rate irrelevant
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving Versus Investment.
q.feedback: Saving frees resources from current consumption and the financial system allocates funds among potential investment projects.

q.q: An investor buys an existing corporate bond from another household, and the issuer receives none of the sale proceeds. Which inference is justified?
options: The issuer's investment rises automatically by the bond's resale price
National saving falls because every secondary-market trade uses saved funds
The trade creates inventory investment because the bond remains unsold by the issuer
It only reallocates an existing financial claim
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving Versus Investment.
q.feedback: A secondary-market bond sale changes who owns the claim. With no new proceeds to the issuer and no new production specified, it creates no direct GDP investment.

q.q: Which institution is acting as a financial intermediary?
options: A bank accepts deposits and makes business loans
A factory converts steel into new machinery
A retailer sells newly produced consumer goods
A household consumes services from an existing home
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving Versus Investment.
q.feedback: A financial intermediary gathers funds from savers and supplies financing to borrowers rather than producing the capital good itself.

q.q: Why is the statement 'each saver finances one identical investment project' incorrect?
options: National saving is unrelated to available financing
Financial markets pool funds and allocate them among borrowers
Only governments can channel funds to firms
Every saver must purchase newly produced equipment
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving Versus Investment.
q.feedback: The aggregate saving-investment link is mediated through institutions and markets, not one-to-one matching of people and projects.

q.q: Income is $1,000, net taxes are $180, consumption is $650, and government purchases are $220. If government purchases then rise by $30 with the other values fixed, which result follows?
options: Private saving stays $170; public and national saving fall $30
Private saving falls to $140; public saving is unchanged, shifting investment demand left
Private saving stays $170; public and national saving each rise by $30, shifting supply right
Private saving rises to $200; national saving is unchanged because taxes did not change
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Private, Public, and National Saving.
q.feedback: Private saving is Y − T − C = $170. Higher G does not change that amount, but it lowers T − G and national saving by $30, so loanable-funds supply shifts left.

q.q: With T defined as net tax revenue and G as government purchases, which expression gives public saving?
options: Y − T − C
T − G
Y − C − G
G − T + C
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Private, Public, and National Saving.
q.feedback: Under the stated textbook convention, public saving equals net tax revenue minus government purchases.

q.q: Which expression gives national saving in the stated closed-economy accounting model?
options: Y − T − C
T − G
Y − C − G
C + I + G
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Private, Public, and National Saving.
q.feedback: Adding private saving Y − T − C and public saving T − G cancels T, leaving Y − C − G.

q.q: Private saving rises by $25 billion while public saving falls by $40 billion. What happens in the loanable-funds market, all else equal?
options: National saving rises by $65 billion, shifting supply right and lowering the real rate
National saving rises by $15 billion, shifting investment demand right and raising the real rate
National saving is unchanged because private and public saving always offset one another
National saving falls by $15 billion, shifting supply left and raising the equilibrium real rate
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Private, Public, and National Saving.
q.feedback: The two components change national saving by +25 − 40 = −$15 billion. Lower national saving shifts loanable-funds supply left, raising the real rate and reducing equilibrium investment.

q.q: Income is $1,200, consumption is $760, and government purchases are $260. What is national saving?
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Private, Public, and National Saving.
q.feedback: National saving equals Y − C − G, so $1,200 − $760 − $260 = $180.

q.q: If net taxes rise by $20 while income, consumption, and government purchases stay fixed, what happens to national saving?
options: It rises by $20
It remains unchanged
It falls by $20
It becomes equal to net taxes
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Private, Public, and National Saving.
q.feedback: Private saving falls by $20 while public saving rises by $20, so their sum and Y − C − G are unchanged.

q.q: A software firm develops a new platform for long-term use, buys an existing patent from another firm, and issues shares to finance both activities. Which evaluation is most accurate?
options: All three activities are current intellectual-property investment because each has a price
Only the new platform may be current intellectual-property investment
Only the share issue is current GDP investment because it raises financial capital
The existing patent purchase creates new output, while developing the platform is current consumption
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving Versus Investment.
q.feedback: Qualifying development creates a new productive intangible asset. Buying an existing patent and issuing shares transfer ownership or financial claims rather than independently creating current output.

q.q: Initially Y = $900, T = $150, C = $600, and G = $180. Net taxes then rise by $20 and government purchases rise by $35 while Y and C stay fixed. What changes?
options: Private saving rises $20, public saving rises $15, and national saving rises $35
Private saving falls $20, public saving rises $20, and national saving is unchanged
Private saving is unchanged, public saving falls $35, and national saving falls $15
Private saving falls $20, public saving falls $15, and national saving falls $35
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Private, Public, and National Saving.
q.feedback: Higher net taxes reduce private saving by $20. Public saving changes by +$20 − $35 = −$15. Together, national saving falls $35, matching the change in Y − C − G.

q.q: In a closed economy, output is $1,240 billion, consumption is $790 billion and government purchases are $230 billion. Firms planned $250 billion of investment, including planned inventory accumulation. Output and final purchases are realized as stated. Which reconciliation is consistent with national accounting?
options: $220 billion of saving and $250 billion of realized investment, leaving a $30 billion accounting gap
$220 billion of realized saving and investment, including a $30 billion unplanned inventory reduction
$250 billion of realized saving and investment, with consumption automatically $30 billion lower
$220 billion of realized investment, including a $30 billion unplanned inventory increase
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving and Investment in a Closed Economy.
q.feedback: Realized saving is Y − C − G = 1,240 − 790 − 230 = $220 billion. Realized investment includes inventories, so it is also $220 billion. Relative to planned investment of $250 billion, unplanned inventory investment is −$30 billion. Equality of realized aggregates does not require equality of plans at every interest rate.

labels: Saving and Investment in a Closed Economy

q.q: Which activity is macroeconomic investment rather than a financial-asset trade?
options: An investor buys an existing stock
A saver buys an existing bond
A collector resells an old sculpture
A manufacturer installs new production equipment
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving Versus Investment.
q.feedback: New production equipment adds to the capital stock; the other choices transfer ownership of existing assets.

q.q: Net tax revenue is $500 and government purchases are $450. What is public saving?
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Private, Public, and National Saving.
q.feedback: Using the defined quantities, T − G equals $500 − $450 = +$50.

q.q: In the closed-economy model, what aggregate relationship connects national saving and investment?
options: National saving equals investment
Private saving equals consumption
Public saving equals income
Investment equals government purchases
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving and Investment in a Closed Economy.
q.feedback: Both national saving and investment equal Y − C − G in the specified closed-economy model.

labels: Saving and Investment in a Closed Economy

q.q: How does household saving connect to later capital formation?
options: Saving is itself always a newly produced capital good
Saved funds must remain idle outside all markets
Financial channels can direct saved funds to investment projects
Capital formation occurs only through household consumption
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving Versus Investment.
q.feedback: The financial system connects the repaired saving idea to firms and households that borrow for new capital investment.

q.q: How does positive public saving connect the accounting identities to the loanable-funds market?
options: It shifts investment demand by definition
It adds to national saving, the supply of loanable funds
It makes private saving equal zero
It converts government purchases into consumption
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Private, Public, and National Saving.
q.feedback: Public saving joins private saving to form national saving, which supplies funds in the closed-economy loanable-funds model.

q.q: How does the accounting identity connect to the loanable-funds model?
options: Consumption becomes the demand for loanable funds
Government purchases become the real interest rate
Every saver chooses the same investment project
National saving supplies funds that finance aggregate investment
q.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Saving and Investment in a Closed Economy.
q.feedback: The closed-economy identity provides the aggregate connection; the loanable-funds market explains coordination through the real interest rate.

labels: Saving and Investment in a Closed Economy

q.q: A community has one available parcel and can build either an elementary school or a recreation complex this year, but not both. What is illustrated most directly?
options: Scarcity, because one limited parcel has competing valued uses
A shortage, because the community temporarily ran out of buildings
Equality, because both projects would serve the same residents
Abundance, because the parcel can support at least one project
q.commonError: Confusing scarcity with a temporary shortage or simple absence.
q.feedback: The parcel is limited relative to competing valued uses, so the community must choose.

q.q: A clinic assigns its limited nurse-hours to the cases expected to produce the greatest total health benefit. Which goal is the clinic emphasizing?
options: Efficiency in the use of its limited clinical resources
Equality through identical treatment time for every patient
Abundance because the clinic can schedule some patients
A shortage caused by setting the price of care too low
q.commonError: Confusing efficient resource use with equal distribution.
q.feedback: Efficiency asks whether scarce resources generate the greatest total value.

q.q: A scholarship office divides a fixed fund so every eligible student receives the same award. Which goal is it emphasizing?
options: Equality in how the available scholarship funds are distributed
Efficiency measured only by the total number of degrees completed
Abundance created by dividing the existing fund into equal shares
A shortage created by charging students a below-market tuition
q.commonError: Confusing equal distribution with maximum total value.
q.feedback: Equality concerns how benefits or prosperity are distributed across people.

q.q: A student can either study for an exam or work a shift, but not both. What does this illustrate?
options: A tradeoff
A tax wedge
A price ceiling
A surplus
q.commonError: confuses_tradeoff_with_money_cost
q.feedback: A tradeoff exists because choosing one option means giving up another.

q.q: A wealthy city can afford more services than before, yet this year it must choose between expanding transit and replacing aging water lines. Why does scarcity remain?
options: Its budget, crews, and construction time are still limited relative to valued projects
Wealth makes every desired project physically impossible to complete
Higher income automatically creates a temporary market shortage
The city faces scarcity only if both projects charge a money price
q.commonError: Treating scarcity as a problem only for poor societies.
q.feedback: Greater wealth relaxes constraints, but limited resources still have competing uses.

q.q: A free campus workshop still involves scarcity because:
options: It still uses limited seats, instructor time, and student time
A zero price makes every required resource unlimited in supply
Only the workshop topic, rather than its inputs, can be scarce
Free admission creates a legal ceiling on every campus price
q.commonError: Assuming a zero money price means no scarce resources are used.
q.feedback: A zero admission price does not make space, labor, or time unlimited.

q.q: A hospital has eight nurse-hours available for either a vaccination clinic or follow-up calls. What is the scarce resource?
options: The eight available nurse-hours
The number of patients who value care
The absence of a money price for calls
The hospital building in every future period
q.commonError: Naming a want or a price instead of the binding resource constraint.
q.feedback: The limited nurse-hours cannot be used fully for both services.

q.q: A family uses its monthly budget to replace a broken refrigerator, leaving less for a planned vacation. What is the tradeoff?
options: Refrigerator spending leaves less budget for the vacation
The refrigerator creates unlimited future income
The vacation becomes a temporary market shortage
