The family no longer faces scarcity after buying an appliance
q.commonError: Recognizing the purchase but not the displaced use of the budget.
q.feedback: Using the fixed budget for one purpose reduces what remains for another.

q.q: A bakery can use its oven this hour for bread or pastries, but there is not enough oven time for both batches. What choice is forced by scarcity?
options: How to allocate the limited oven time
How to eliminate every customer want
How to create a legal price ceiling
How to make flour an unlimited resource
q.commonError: Overlooking production time as the constrained resource.
q.feedback: Limited oven time with competing uses requires an allocation choice.

q.q: A reservoir currently contains enough water for all essential uses, but not for every lawn, pool, factory, and farm request. Which conclusion is correct?
options: Water is scarce because not every valued use can be satisfied
Water is abundant because essential uses can be satisfied
A shortage exists only because the reservoir charges too much
Scarcity ends whenever some users receive the resource
q.commonError: Treating partial adequacy as proof that a resource is nonscarce.
q.feedback: Scarcity remains when the available amount cannot satisfy every competing use.

q.q: A policy improves equality but reduces total output. What tradeoff is being shown?
options: Efficiency versus equality
Supply versus quantity supplied
Positive versus normative
Ceiling versus floor
q.commonError: misses_policy_tradeoff_between_output_and_distribution
q.feedback: The policy improves distribution but reduces total output, so the tradeoff is efficiency versus equality.

q.q: A city can fund either a new fire station or several neighborhood parks with the same budget. This illustrates:
options: A tradeoff created by competing uses of a limited city budget
An end to scarcity created by collecting and spending local taxes
A temporary shortage produced by fixing a public-service price
A specialization gain created by assigning each project to a district
q.commonError: Missing the tradeoff because both projects are socially valuable.
q.feedback: Limited funds force the city to choose among competing uses.

q.q: A student has three free hours and wants to study, work, exercise, and sleep more. The central economic problem is:
options: The student must choose the option with the highest money return.
The student faces no scarcity because time has no price.
The student cannot fully satisfy all competing uses of time.
Only the work option has a cost.
q.commonError: Ignoring time as a scarce resource.
q.feedback: Time is scarce, so not every desired activity can be expanded at once.

q.q: Which statement best distinguishes efficiency from equality?
options: Efficiency concerns total value; equality concerns its distribution
Efficiency requires equal shares; equality requires maximum output
Efficiency and equality describe the same resource-allocation goal
Efficiency concerns prices; equality concerns physical production
q.commonError: Treating efficiency and equality as synonyms.
q.feedback: Efficiency focuses on the size of the economic pie; equality focuses on its distribution.

q.q: A new technology doubles crop yields. What happens to scarcity?
options: Scarcity disappears because higher crop output satisfies every want
Scarcity becomes a shortage because technology changes only prices
The crop constraint eases, but land, time, and other wants remain
The technology removes the need to choose among all production uses
q.commonError: Assuming productivity growth eliminates scarcity.
q.feedback: Greater productivity relaxes constraints but does not remove limited resources or competing wants.

q.q: After a storm, a store cannot meet customers' bottled-water purchases at its posted price. A delivery then provides enough water to meet those purchases. Producing and delivering the water still uses materials and truck time that could serve other purposes. What changed, and what remains?
options: The stockout ended; using materials and truck time still involves scarcity.
Both stockout and scarcity ended because buyers can obtain water again.
Scarcity ended; the stockout remains because producing water still uses resources.
Neither condition ended because the store still has a finite water inventory.
q.commonError: Confusing a market shortage with the universal condition of scarcity.
q.feedback: The delivery resolves this store's stockout at the posted price. Scarcity remains because materials and truck time have alternative uses and cannot satisfy every want. Duration is not the defining difference, and finite inventory alone does not imply unmet purchases at the prevailing price.

q.q: A university converts two classrooms into laboratories. Science students gain space, while other departments lose course capacity. Which analysis is most complete?
options: The conversion reallocates scarce space and creates gains and losses
The conversion ends scarcity because laboratories are more specialized
Only departments charging lab fees face a resource constraint
Classroom capacity becomes a shortage caused by a legal price rule
q.commonError: Counting the new benefit while ignoring displaced classroom users.
q.feedback: The same limited space cannot simultaneously serve both sets of uses.

q.q: A faster 3D printer doubles output per hour, but every job still requires one technician and the lab has only two technicians. What changed?
options: One constraint eased, while technician time still limits feasible production
All scarcity ended because machine productivity doubled
The technician constraint became a price shortage
The lab can now complete every desired job without choosing
q.commonError: Assuming improvement in one input removes every remaining constraint.
q.feedback: Technology can shift the binding constraint without eliminating scarcity.

q.q: A transit agency moves buses from a lightly used route to an overcrowded route. Which statement best captures the tradeoff?
options: Crowded-route riders gain capacity while other riders lose service frequency
The transfer creates more buses because average ridership rises
Public ownership means the routes do not compete for vehicles
The agency eliminates scarcity by serving the larger group first
q.commonError: Analyzing beneficiaries without identifying who loses the reallocated resource.
q.feedback: Reassigning a fixed fleet benefits one route while reducing capacity elsewhere.

q.q: A larger reservoir expands the region’s water supply. Cities, farms, and ecosystems still request more water than is available in dry years. Which statement follows?
options: The expansion relaxes scarcity but does not remove competing uses
The expansion eliminates scarcity because total water increased
The remaining conflict must be a temporary retail shortage
More capacity means allocation rules no longer affect any group
q.commonError: Assuming a resource increase eliminates all unmet wants.
q.feedback: More resources can ease a constraint while valued uses still exceed availability.

q.q: A delivery disruption leaves a hospital temporarily short of oxygen cylinders, while its limited budget also restricts how many backup systems it can maintain. Which statement is accurate?
options: The disruption is a shortage; the budget tradeoff reflects ongoing scarcity
Both conditions are temporary shortages because money is involved
Both conditions are scarcity only if oxygen receives a market price
The backup budget eliminates scarcity once deliveries resume
q.commonError: Collapsing a temporary supply disruption and a persistent resource constraint.
q.feedback: The disruption leaves fewer cylinders available than the hospital needs under current conditions. The budget constraint requires choices among backup systems and other uses of funds, illustrating scarcity. This particular disruption is temporary; shortages need not be temporary, and scarcity is not limited to the long run.

q.q: During a drought, a city allocates water first to hospitals, then households, and lastly decorative landscaping. The policy most clearly reflects:
options: A market surplus caused by excess supply.
A guarantee that the allocation is both perfectly efficient and perfectly equal.
A scarcity-driven tradeoff among uses with different social priorities.
A claim that water has no opportunity cost.
q.commonError: Focusing on one beneficiary while ignoring displaced uses.
q.feedback: Drought limits the available water, so the city must rank competing uses.

q.q: A hospital has one intensive-care bed and two equally ill patients. Which conclusion follows from scarcity?
options: Any allocation rule leaves at least one valued use of the bed unmet
An equal lottery creates enough capacity to treat both patients fully
No money price means the intensive-care bed is not economically scarce
A medically fair rule removes the physical limit on available treatment
q.commonError: Assuming fairness can remove the underlying constraint.
q.feedback: Scarcity means not every valued use can be satisfied, regardless of the allocation rule.

q.q: A government reserves scarce vaccine doses for people at highest medical risk rather than for those willing to pay most. The rule primarily changes:
options: How the scarce doses are allocated, not whether the doses are scarce.
The definition of scarcity itself
The number of vaccine doses physically available
Whether people still compete for the limited doses.
q.commonError: Believing an allocation rule removes scarcity.
q.feedback: Allocation rules determine who receives scarce goods; they do not erase the resource limit.

q.q: An economy can produce more clean energy only by using engineers and materials currently employed elsewhere. Which statement is strongest?
options: The project still trades off against other uses of engineers and materials
Government financing makes the engineers and materials no longer scarce
Large environmental benefits remove every resource cost from the project
Only privately financed energy projects compete for productive resources
q.commonError: Assuming socially valuable projects are costless in resource terms.
q.feedback: Benefits do not eliminate the need to redirect scarce labor and materials from other uses.

q.q: Which claim commits the clearest scarcity error?
options: Cheap copying means digital production and distribution use no scarce inputs
Higher productivity can relax a binding resource constraint without ending scarcity
A zero money price can still require scarce server capacity and user time
Allocation rules can change who receives access to a capacity-limited service
q.commonError: Equating low marginal copying cost with zero resource use.
q.feedback: Creation, servers, bandwidth, attention, and time remain scarce even when copying is inexpensive.

q.q: A public agency reassigns cybersecurity analysts to clear a benefits-processing backlog. Which consequence must be included even if the backlog is urgent?
options: The forgone security monitoring performed by the same scarce analysts
The analysts become nonscarce because both assignments serve the public
The backlog creates more analyst-hours by increasing social need
Only the agency payroll, not analyst time, has an alternative use
q.commonError: Letting urgency obscure the alternative output of a fixed workforce.
q.feedback: Urgency can affect priorities but does not remove the forgone use of analyst time.

q.q: A government funds both climate adaptation and transit by postponing courthouse maintenance. Officials call the package “tradeoff-free” because two programs expand. What is wrong?
options: The postponed maintenance is a displaced use of scarce public resources
Two expanding programs guarantee that no group bears a cost
Deferred maintenance is not a cost until a courthouse closes
Public borrowing makes labor and materials immediately unlimited
q.commonError: Ignoring a less visible displaced use when multiple visible goals improve.
q.feedback: A package can advance several goals while shifting costs to another use or time.

q.q: A wealthy country can afford either a high-speed rail network or a major hospital modernization program sooner, but construction crews and materials cannot complete both on the same schedule. What does this show?
options: Wealth expands options without eliminating real resource constraints
Wealth eliminates scarcity whenever both projects have positive benefits
Only lower-income countries face tradeoffs involving public infrastructure
The conflict is a temporary shortage caused entirely by incorrect prices
q.commonError: Treating national wealth as freedom from physical and time constraints.
q.feedback: Wealth increases capacity, but real inputs and time remain limited.

q.q: A state has one construction workforce for unsafe bridges, aging schools, and storm-water upgrades. Which proposal most clearly hides the tradeoff?
options: Complete all projects immediately because each has benefits greater than zero
Rank projects by expected benefits, urgency, and displaced work
Phase projects as crews and materials become available
State which communities wait under each feasible schedule
q.commonError: Treating positive benefits as proof that mutually competing projects are jointly feasible.
q.feedback: Positive benefits do not create the crews and materials required to do everything at once.

q.q: A parent can accept additional paid work only by reducing caregiving or rest. A colleague says no tradeoff exists because caregiving has no money price. What is the best correction?
options: Time is scarce even when an alternative use is unpaid
Only lost wages can count as a scarce-resource sacrifice
Unpaid activities use no economically relevant resources
A tradeoff exists only when the household budget falls
q.commonError: Restricting tradeoffs to alternatives with explicit money prices.
q.feedback: Nonmarket time has competing valuable uses and remains scarce.

q.q: A policy increases total output but leaves the lowest-income group worse off. Which judgment is most accurate?
options: It may improve total output while worsening the distribution of gains
It must improve both efficiency and equality because output increased
It eliminates scarcity because the economy can now produce more output
It cannot improve efficiency because at least one affected group loses
q.commonError: Assuming efficiency and equality are the same criterion.
q.feedback: Efficiency and distribution are separate dimensions, so they can move in opposite directions.

q.q: A reform raises average income and narrows the income gap but requires more administrative resources. Which statement is warranted?
options: Efficiency and equality cannot improve at the same time
Publicly funded administrative resources are not scarce
The reform may improve both efficiency and equality while still using scarce resources.
There is no tradeoff because average income and equality both improve.
q.commonError: Treating tradeoffs as proof that every objective must worsen.
q.feedback: Some policies can improve multiple outcomes, but resource use and implementation constraints still matter.

q.q: After a flood, a county can use its emergency fund for temporary housing or immediate levee repairs. Housing aids displaced families now; repairs reduce future risk. What must an economic analysis include?
options: Current beneficiaries, future risk reduction, and the use forgone under either choice
Only the number of residents receiving immediate housing assistance
Only the engineering estimate for the levee repair project
A claim that emergency spending makes the county budget unlimited
q.commonError: Evaluating one time horizon while ignoring the competing use and affected groups.
q.feedback: Scarcity requires comparing both uses, their timing, and who gains or loses.

q.q: Automation reduces the labor needed in a warehouse, but expansion still requires scarce electricity, loading space, and computing capacity. Which conclusion is strongest?
options: Automation changes the constraint mix rather than abolishing scarcity
Automation abolishes scarcity because fewer workers are required
The remaining limits are shortages caused only by incorrect prices
Every expansion becomes feasible once one input requirement falls
q.commonError: Treating a productivity gain as the elimination of all production choices.
q.feedback: Reducing one input requirement can leave other resources as binding constraints.

q.q: A low-income household and a wealthy household both have 24 hours in a day, but very different financial options. Which statement correctly distinguishes poverty from scarcity?
options: Poverty concerns limited material means; both households still face scarce time
Only the low-income household faces scarcity because wealth removes all constraints
Both households are poor because neither can create more hours in a day
Scarcity describes temporary stockouts, while poverty describes every tradeoff
q.commonError: Equating scarcity with poverty and overlooking universal nonmoney constraints.
q.feedback: Poverty and scarcity are different: scarcity persists across income levels.

q.q: A policy expands total production, reduces pollution, and requires a small tax increase. Which statement is most defensible?
options: Several goals may improve, while taxes and inputs still have alternative uses
Several benefits mean the policy uses no scarce resources or public funds
Scarcity matters only when total production falls after the policy change
Any tax increase proves the policy reduces both efficiency and equality
q.commonError: Using a single outcome to judge a multi-dimensional policy.
q.feedback: A complete tradeoff analysis includes gains, resource use, financing, and distribution.

q.q: A government can increase disaster preparedness by diverting engineers from current infrastructure repairs. The preparedness program is highly valuable. What still follows?
options: Public projects do not compete for scarce inputs
Its value does not remove the tradeoff created by limited engineering capacity.
Only money, not skilled labor, can be scarce
A highly valuable program has no resource cost.
q.commonError: Treating high value as proof of no sacrifice.
q.feedback: Even high-value projects require scarce labor, time, and materials that could serve other purposes.

q.q: An allocation rule maximizes total output but concentrates nearly all gains among a small group. Which conclusion is strongest?
options: The rule may be efficient by one criterion while raising serious equality concerns.
Scarcity prevents economists from discussing how gains are distributed
High total output automatically makes the allocation equal
Any unequal allocation must reduce total output.
q.commonError: Using efficiency as a complete moral judgment.
q.feedback: Efficiency and equality are distinct criteria and should be evaluated separately.

q.q: A city can zone a waterfront parcel for housing, a flood barrier, or a public park. A developer claims housing demand makes the other uses economically irrelevant. What is the strongest response?
options: High housing value does not erase the flood and recreation benefits forgone
Market demand makes the parcel physically available for all three uses
Public benefits matter only when users pay an admission price
Choosing housing proves the other uses were not valued by anyone
q.commonError: Treating the chosen use as proof that forgone uses have no value.
q.feedback: Scarcity makes the benefits of mutually exclusive uses economically relevant.

q.q: A factory that builds both emergency generators and defense equipment receives a fixed allocation of skilled machinist-hours. Why does a larger government budget not automatically remove the production tradeoff this quarter?
options: Money cannot instantly create the specialized labor and machine time required
Government purchases never use resources that have alternative civilian uses
A larger budget converts every physical constraint into an accounting entry
Defense production eliminates scarcity whenever national security is valuable
q.commonError: Treating additional financing as immediate creation of specialized capacity.
q.feedback: Nominal funding cannot instantly expand every real resource needed for production.

q.q: A university can admit more students by enlarging lectures, but laboratory space and advising time remain fixed. What does the enrollment expansion demonstrate?
options: Relaxing one capacity limit can intensify other educational tradeoffs
Larger lectures eliminate scarcity throughout the university
Advising time becomes abundant when tuition revenue increases
Laboratory capacity matters only for programs charging separate fees
q.commonError: Ignoring constraints that become more important after another constraint relaxes.
q.feedback: The binding limit can move from lecture seats to labs or advising.

q.q: A fishery can allow a larger catch this season or preserve more breeding stock for future seasons. Which feature makes this a scarcity problem rather than only a biological fact?
options: The limited stock has competing current and future valued uses
The fish have no posted price while still in the ocean
The catch becomes scarce only after a legal quota is adopted
Future fish are unlimited because they have not yet been harvested
q.commonError: Ignoring competing uses across time when the resource is renewable.
q.feedback: The breeding stock cannot simultaneously support maximum current catch and future reproduction.

q.q: An evacuation plan dedicates the only outbound bridge to buses carrying people without cars, delaying private vehicles. Which statement is most complete?
options: The rule reallocates scarce road capacity and changes who bears delay
Prioritizing vulnerable residents creates additional bridge capacity
A fairness goal makes the delay imposed on other users economically irrelevant
The bridge is not scarce because evacuees are not charged a toll
q.commonError: Treating a fairness rationale as elimination of the underlying capacity cost.
q.feedback: The priority rule affects distribution, but the bridge capacity remains fixed.

q.q: A policy improves equity but reduces total surplus. Which answer best frames the issue?
options: It presents an efficiency-equity tradeoff requiring both criteria
It proves the policy is desirable because equity necessarily dominates
It proves the policy is undesirable because total surplus necessarily dominates
It removes scarcity because one distributional goal improves
q.commonError: treats_tradeoff_as_automatic_policy_answer
q.feedback: Policies often involve tradeoffs. A reduction in efficiency may or may not be justified by equity goals.

q.q: A coastal city can use a limited parcel for flood protection, affordable housing, or commercial development. Which analysis best respects scarcity?
options: Compare feasible parcel uses, incremental benefits and displaced uses, making the distribution of gains and losses explicit.
Rank uses by expected cash revenue, counting public benefits only when the city can charge users for them.
Rank uses by the number of beneficiaries, treating benefit size and displaced alternatives as secondary tie-breakers.
Divide the parcel equally among uses, treating equal area shares as sufficient evidence of equal benefit and efficiency.
q.commonError: Listing benefits without confronting mutually exclusive uses.
q.feedback: A scarce parcel requires a feasible comparison of valued uses, including nonmarket benefits and distribution. Cash revenue, beneficiary counts or equal acreage alone can miss opportunity costs and competing criteria.

q.q: A safety process uses the same technicians as production. Managers fund more materials and predict that both safety checks and output can rise without any other change. Which missing condition matters most?
options: Whether technician time can expand or become more productive
Whether the materials budget is recorded as a public or private expense
Whether both activities produce positive benefits in isolation
Whether managers prefer safety checks to output
q.commonError: ignores_tradeoffs_when_policy_goal_is_good
q.feedback: More materials do not relax a binding technician constraint. Expanding both activities requires spare technician capacity, added time or a productivity improvement.

q.q: A wage floor raises pay for workers who keep jobs but reduces entry-level openings. Which economic idea best frames the policy debate?
options: An efficiency-equity tradeoff
A movement along the PPF with no opportunity cost
A nonbinding ceiling
A fixed CPI basket
q.commonError: analyzes_only_winners_or_only_losers
q.feedback: The policy can improve outcomes for some workers while reducing efficiency or job access for others.

q.q: A region faces limited electricity during a heat wave. It can prioritize hospitals, households, or energy-intensive factories. Which response is the most complete economic analysis?
options: Compare marginal benefits and forgone uses across feasible allocations, then show the health, output and distribution tradeoffs.
Prioritize immediate health effects, treating displaced production and later income losses as outside the economic comparison.
Prioritize measured dollar output losses, treating unpriced household and hospital benefits as equal across allocations.
Give each group the same percentage reduction, treating proportional rationing as sufficient evidence of the best allocation.
q.commonError: Reducing a scarcity problem to a single efficiency or fairness rule.
q.feedback: Electricity has competing health, household and productive uses. Economic evaluation compares marginal gains and displaced benefits while stating distributional priorities; health-only, cash-only and proportional rules each impose a particular criterion.

q.q: A breakthrough makes desalination much cheaper, but coastal land, energy, pipelines, and environmental capacity remain limited. Which statement is best?
options: Cheaper desalination reduces water opportunity cost to zero, leaving land and energy limits relevant only for other industries.
Cheaper desalination relaxes one constraint, but land, energy and delivery limits can become the binding sources of tradeoffs.
Cheaper desalination makes physical water abundant, so any remaining scarcity must be explained entirely by monopoly pricing.
Cheaper desalination expands output proportionally at every stage, so pipelines and environmental limits become less binding automatically.
q.commonError: Assuming one technological improvement removes all constraints.
q.feedback: A productivity improvement changes which resource limits output. Complementary land, energy, networks and environmental capacity remain scarce and need not expand with desalination technology.

q.q: Following an earthquake, a hospital has one surgical team for trauma cases, routine emergencies, and patients already scheduled. Which policy best acknowledges scarcity without pretending one criterion settles the decision?
options: Compare expected health gains, urgency and displaced treatment under feasible schedules, stating how the priority rule weights them.
Treat trauma first in every case, using the emergency label as sufficient evidence that postponed care has lower marginal value.
Preserve scheduled order in every case, using earlier commitments as sufficient evidence that urgent arrivals have lower priority.
Allocate equal team time to each group, using equal shares as sufficient evidence of both fair treatment and greatest health gain.
q.commonError: Using one allocation criterion while ignoring displaced care and distribution.
q.feedback: The surgical team has competing uses with differences in urgency, benefits and forgone care. No label or equal-time rule settles every dimension without evaluating the feasible alternatives.

q.q: A laboratory has idle testing machines but fully occupied specialist staff. It buys more machines, then shifts specialists from quality checks to testing. Tests rise and errors rise. What best explains the result?
options: The equipment purchase left the staff constraint; reallocation increased tests at a quality cost
More tests prove the original equipment constraint was the only limit
Idle machines mean the extra tests had no opportunity cost
The rise in errors shows there was no expansion in testing
q.commonError: Assuming expansion of one input removes complementary-input constraints.
q.feedback: Specialist time remained scarce. Reassigning it raised testing by sacrificing quality checks, so the extra machines alone did not remove the tradeoff.

q.q: During a drought, a river authority must allocate water among cities, farms, and minimum ecosystem flows. Which statement avoids both an efficiency-only and a fairness-only mistake?
options: Compare total and ecological benefits while showing how each feasible rule distributes losses among users.
Maximize measured market output while counting ecosystem flows only when the authority can collect a fee.
Equalize percentage cuts across users while treating equal reductions as proof of equal welfare losses.
Preserve historical allocations while treating prior entitlements as evidence of the highest current marginal benefits.
q.commonError: Using efficiency or equality as a complete allocation rule without examining the other.
q.feedback: Benefits, ecosystem effects and distribution must be distinguished. Prices, proportional reductions and historical shares can each omit relevant marginal values or impose a distributional rule.

q.q: A region has surplus generation but a fully used transmission line. A subsidy expands generation again. Delivered power stays flat. Which proposal addresses the observed limit without claiming scarcity disappears?
options: Expand transmission, then reassess other constrained resources and forgone uses
Expand generation further because surplus generation measures delivered capacity
Declare electricity costless because some generated power goes unused
Treat unchanged deliveries as proof that users place no value on power
q.commonError: Treating abundant output at one stage as abundance throughout a system.
q.feedback: Transmission is the observed bottleneck. Relaxing it may expand deliveries, but construction resources and other constraints still have alternative uses.

q.q: Automation frees assembly hours. Managers assign them to inspection, reducing defects, but product development gets no extra staff. Which counterfactual is needed to evaluate the allocation?
options: What those same hours would have achieved in development relative to the inspection gain
What the robot cost before the hours were freed, counted as the entire current tradeoff
The sum of benefits from inspection and development as if both received the hours
Whether inspection has a cash price rather than a nonmonetary benefit
q.commonError: Assuming labor-saving technology eliminates choice over the released resources.
q.feedback: The technology relaxes one constraint; it does not determine the best use of freed labor. Compare inspection with the feasible development alternative.

q.q: A transit authority postpones track maintenance to accelerate a network extension. The extension raises capacity next year but increases breakdown risk now. Which analysis best captures the dynamic tradeoff?
options: Compare current reliability losses with future capacity gains and their distribution
Count only future riders because maintenance creates no new visible service
Treat postponed work as costless until a breakdown actually occurs
Assume future capacity removes the present scarcity of repair crews
q.commonError: Ignoring intertemporal costs because their effects are delayed or uncertain.
q.feedback: Scarcity links present resource use to future benefits and risks.

q.q: Route A delivers more meals but skips isolated households. Route B reaches every district but delivers fewer meals. An official calls A superior because total deliveries are higher. What evidence and judgment are still needed?
options: Who loses access, and how that loss is weighed against additional deliveries
Only more precise meal totals, because totals establish distributional fairness
Only whether either route has positive benefits, because that settles the ranking
Proof that isolated households are costly, which makes their access irrelevant
q.commonError: Using the total output result as a complete judgment about distribution.
q.feedback: A higher total establishes a production advantage under that metric. Ranking the routes also requires the distribution of access and an explicit weight on it.

q.q: A mineral discovery expands deposits, but refining staff are fully occupied. Exporting unrefined ore can fund training; keeping it for later refining forgoes that revenue. Which statement follows?
options: More deposits expand options, while refining and the timing of resource use still involve tradeoffs
The discovery removes scarcity because the mineral stock increased
Keeping the ore has no cost because it remains physically available
Export revenue proves immediate export is best under every future-use objective
q.commonError: Assuming discovery of one resource makes the complete production system unconstrained.
q.feedback: The deposit gain does not eliminate the refining constraint. Holding ore preserves a future option but forgoes a feasible current use, including financing training.

q.q: A machine can make sensors or monitors. A proposal raises both outputs by reducing maintenance time; next period's downtime then rises. Which evaluation avoids a false tradeoff-free claim?
options: Compare current output gains with the future production sacrificed through downtime
Count only current outputs because both increased
Treat maintenance as irrelevant because customers do not buy it
Add current and future output gains without deducting the downtime loss
q.commonError: Ignoring intertemporal costs because their effects are delayed or uncertain.
q.feedback: Maintenance uses capacity now to preserve capacity later. Expanding both saleable outputs by reducing it can shift the sacrifice into the future.

q.q: A school uses idle rooms for smaller classes, but instructor hours stay fixed. More hours per student reduce enrollment unless other teaching duties shrink. Which condition permits higher enrollment and smaller classes without that sacrifice?
options: Additional effective instructor capacity as well as rooms
A larger room budget with instructor hours and productivity unchanged
A statement that smaller classes are educationally valuable
Reclassifying the displaced teaching duties as unpaid work
q.commonError: Looking at quality or access alone instead of their competing use of instructional capacity.
q.feedback: Rooms and instructor time are separate inputs. Idle rooms alone cannot supply the additional teaching capacity needed for both goals.

q.q: An aid aircraft can carry water filters, antibiotics, or shelter materials after a cyclone. Which decision process best applies scarcity reasoning?
options: Compare marginal relief benefits per constrained cargo unit and identify the urgent needs displaced by each feasible load.
Load the items serving the largest headcount, treating differences in treatment benefit and cargo weight as secondary.
Divide weight equally across the three supplies, treating equal shares as proof of the greatest total relief benefit.
Load the highest-priced supplies first, treating purchase prices as complete measures of local marginal relief value.
q.commonError: Using a single rule while ignoring cargo capacity and the supplies displaced.
q.feedback: Scarce payload requires comparing benefits against space or weight and the supplies forgone. Headcounts, equal weights and purchase prices alone do not identify the best load.

q.q: A school has more requests for tutoring than its staff can serve this week. Which fact makes tutoring time scarce?
options: Limited tutor-hours have several valued uses and cannot meet every request
The school has permanently run out of every kind of educational service
Families differ in income even if every tutoring request could be served
The school charges a price below the market-clearing price for tutoring
q.commonError: Confusing scarcity with poverty, high prices, or a temporary stockout.
q.feedback: Tutor-hours are limited relative to the competing requests for them.

q.q: A community center has one gym available tonight. Scheduling a youth league means canceling an adult exercise class. What does that choice show?
options: Using the fixed gym for one valued activity leaves less access for another
The community has permanently exhausted every recreation resource
The gym stops being scarce once managers publish the schedule
Both groups receive equal access because the choice is publicly announced
q.commonError: Ignoring the displaced use of a fixed resource.
q.feedback: Assigning the fixed gym to one activity displaces another valued use.

q.q: Efficiency is primarily about:
options: Giving everyone identical outcomes
Eliminating all tradeoffs
Getting the greatest total value from available resources.
Ensuring that no one ever loses from a change.
q.commonError: Confusing efficiency with equality.
q.feedback: Efficiency concerns how much total value is produced from scarce resources.

q.q: A town spends its entire emergency fund on flood barriers instead of fire equipment. The central issue is:
options: An elimination of scarcity through public spending.
A shortage created by a price floor.
A tradeoff among competing uses of limited funds.
A gain from comparative advantage.
q.commonError: Ignoring the alternative public use.
q.feedback: The same limited fund cannot fully finance both priorities.

q.q: A policy raises total output but widens the income gap. Which pair best describes the possible outcome?
options: Lower efficiency and higher equality.
No change in either criterion.
Scarcity and shortage become identical.
Higher efficiency and lower equality.
q.commonError: Treating efficiency and equality as one measure.
q.feedback: Total output and distribution can move in opposite directions.

q.q: Why does a zero-price service still face scarcity?
options: It still uses limited labor, space, equipment, and user time
A zero price guarantees enough capacity for every possible user
Only services sold for money can require scarce productive inputs
Free access removes every competing use of the service resources
q.commonError: Equating free access with unlimited resources.
q.feedback: Money price and resource scarcity are different issues.

q.q: A city allocates scarce shelter beds by medical vulnerability instead of willingness to pay. What changes?
options: The allocation rule changes, while the limited number of beds does not
The vulnerability rule immediately creates enough beds for every applicant
The beds stop being scarce because recipients do not bid a money price
The rule makes efficiency and equality identical measures of the outcome
q.commonError: Assuming rationing rules remove the constraint.
q.feedback: The rule determines recipients but does not create more beds.

q.q: A technology raises output and reduces input use, yet firms still choose among projects. Why?
options: Remaining capital, skilled labor, time, and wants still create choices
Higher productivity guarantees that every available project can be funded
Only government agencies continue to face tradeoffs after technology improves
Productivity growth changes scarcity into a temporary market shortage
q.commonError: Assuming productivity growth eliminates choice.
q.feedback: Productivity relaxes constraints but does not remove all competing uses.

q.q: Which evaluation is most complete for a policy that increases output but harms a vulnerable group?
options: Reject the policy solely because one group loses
Assume there is no tradeoff because output rises
Evaluate only the change in total output.
Assess both the total gains and the distribution of gains and losses.
q.commonError: Using only one criterion in a multi-dimensional judgment.
q.feedback: Economic evaluation should separate efficiency from distributional effects.

q.q: A classroom has 24 seats and 31 students who want to attend. Which statement identifies the scarce resource?
options: The 24 available classroom seats
The seven students without seats
The tuition paid by every student
The number of courses in the catalog
q.commonError: Naming unmet wants rather than the resource that constrains them.
q.feedback: Seats are the limited resource relative to enrollment demand.

q.q: A county gives more reservoir water to farms during planting season, leaving less for lawn irrigation and some industrial uses. What is the best interpretation?
options: A limited resource is being shifted among competing users
The county has eliminated scarcity by choosing agriculture
Only users paying the highest price face a water tradeoff
The reduced uses prove the reservoir has a temporary leak
q.commonError: Treating a priority decision as elimination of the resource constraint.
q.feedback: Prioritizing farms reallocates water and reduces what remains for other users.

q.q: A space agency has one launch window for a weather satellite or a communications satellite. Both have large benefits. Which claim is least defensible?
options: Large benefits allow both satellites to use the same launch window
Choosing either mission forgoes the other mission’s near-term benefits
The launch window remains scarce even if the agency receives more money
A complete choice compares benefits, timing, and affected users
q.commonError: Assuming positive benefits make mutually exclusive projects jointly feasible.
q.feedback: Value does not allow two missions to occupy one fixed launch window.

q.q: One crew can inspect 18 bridges or repair 6 mains per month at a constant tradeoff. A plan requires at least 6 inspections and proposes 5 main repairs. Extra funding cannot add crew time this month. Which revision is feasible, and what does the limit show?
options: Keep 6 inspections and reduce repairs to 4; money alone does not supply the missing crew capacity.
Keep 6 inspections and 5 repairs; separate maximum outputs can be combined without sacrificing either.
Keep 6 inspections and reduce repairs to 2; one repair displaces six bridge inspections.
Cancel every main repair; any minimum inspection requirement uses the crew’s entire monthly capacity.
q.commonError: Ignoring the displaced use of a fixed resource.
q.feedback: Each main repair costs 18/6=3 inspections. Six inspections use one-third of capacity, leaving two-thirds for 4 repairs. The proposed 6/18+5/6=7/6 of a crew-month is infeasible even with enough funding.

q.q: A stricter safety standard is expected to avoid $12 million of accident losses, require $7 million of real compliance resources and reduce variety valued at $3 million as small firms exit. A targeted alternative avoids $10 million, costs $4 million and loses $1 million of variety. Which evaluation follows from these estimates?
options: The alternative has $5 million net benefit versus $2 million for the stricter rule; neither safety benefits nor entry losses alone settle the comparison.
The stricter rule has $12 million net benefit because a safety benefit should not be offset by lost variety or compliance inputs.
The alternative has $9 million net benefit because only the lost variety is a real opportunity cost.
The stricter rule must be rejected regardless of benefits because any reduction in small-firm entry proves inefficiency.
q.commonError: Using a single outcome to judge a multi-dimensional policy.
q.feedback: The stricter standard nets 12-7-3=2 million; the alternative nets 10-4-1=5 million. Entry-related variety and real compliance inputs are relevant costs, but their existence alone is not enough to reject all safety policies.

q.q: A disaster agency compares feasible stockpiles A: 24,000 meals and 4,000 kits, and B: 12,000 meals and 6,000 kits. Each added kit between these plans has expected relief value equal to 8 meals. A separate proposal C has 24,000 meals and 6,000 kits but exceeds storage capacity. Which decision follows under that valuation?
options: Choose B over A: 2,000 extra kits cost 12,000 meals but are valued at 16,000 meals; C remains infeasible despite its larger gross benefits.
Choose A over B: 2,000 extra kits cost only 2 meals each, making the higher kit allocation wasteful.
Choose C: its larger benefit makes the storage constraint economically irrelevant.
Choose B over A: the extra kits are free because both plans have positive relief benefits.
q.commonError: Ignoring the displaced use of a fixed resource.
q.feedback: The move A→B sacrifices 12000/2000=6 meals per kit. At a value of 8, its net gain is 2000×8-12000=4000 meal-equivalents. Benefits do not make the capacity-violating proposal C feasible.

q.q: A convoy can carry 800 food rations or 500 water rations, with a linear payload tradeoff. Relief requires at least 320 food and 200 water. Above those minima, an extra food ration adds 1 benefit point and an extra water ration adds 2. Which feasible load maximizes the stated benefit?
options: 320 food and 300 water: it meets both minima and gives 200 additional benefit points.
480 food and 200 water: it meets both minima and gives 160 additional benefit points.
400 food and 250 water: equal payload shares necessarily maximize the benefit measure.
480 food and 300 water: the two separate maxima imply enough capacity for this combined load.
q.commonError: Using one visible quantity without comparing benefits and displaced cargo.
q.feedback: The constraint is F/800+W/500≤1. The minima use 0.4+0.4=0.8 of capacity. Remaining capacity yields either 160 food points or 100 water×2=200 points, so choose 320 food and 300 water. The last load requires 1.2 convoys.

q.q: A city has one waterfront parcel. A flood barrier yields net benefits of $30 million; housing yields $28 million; a park yields $12 million. Housing and the park each require the entire parcel. The city chooses the barrier for a stated safety priority. Which analysis correctly describes the tradeoff?
options: The best forgone feasible use is $28 million housing; the safety priority explains the choice but does not erase that sacrificed value.
The forgone value is $40 million because the benefits of every rejected use must be added even when they cannot coexist.
The forgone value is zero because the barrier has the largest net benefit and was chosen for public safety.
The forgone value is $2 million because the difference between chosen and next-best benefits is the entire displaced use.
q.commonError: Treating rejection of an alternative as evidence that it had no value.
q.feedback: Only one use is feasible. Housing is the best alternative at 28, while the barrier’s advantage over it is 2. A safety criterion may guide the decision, but neither public ownership nor superior benefits makes displaced uses valueless.

q.q: A supply chain can deliver at most 10 battery packs weekly because battery assembly is capped at 10, minerals at 15 and transmission installations at 12. Assembly productivity triples with no other capacity change. Demand is 20 packs. Which investment would next expand deliverable output?
options: Transmission capacity: output first rises to 12, then can rise to 15 before minerals become the next bottleneck.
Mineral capacity: output first rises to 30, then mineral expansion is needed only after demand reaches 30.
More assembly capacity: tripling assembly leaves its old 10-pack limit binding until every stage also triples.
No investment: the productivity improvement makes every 20-pack demand feasible despite the other stated limits.
q.commonError: Generalizing one productivity improvement to the entire production system.
q.feedback: Deliverable output is the minimum capacity: initially min(10,15,12)=10; afterward min(30,15,12)=12. Raising transmission to at least 15 then makes the mineral constraint binding at 15.

q.q: A wealthy country has 100 engineer-years available this year. Hospital upgrades require 70 and rail expansion 60; each project must be completed as a whole. Funding covers both, but training extra engineers takes a year. Which plan and interpretation are feasible now?
options: Complete one project now and schedule the other later; the 30-engineer-year shortfall is a current real constraint despite adequate funds.
Complete both now by borrowing more money; financing removes the need for the missing 30 engineer-years.
Assign 50 engineer-years to each and count both completed; equal resource shares satisfy any whole-project requirement.
Complete both now because training expands next year’s workforce, so its future capacity can be used this year.
q.commonError: Equating wealth with unlimited real resources.
q.feedback: The two projects need 70+60=130 engineer-years, exceeding the current 100. Money is not the binding constraint and next-year training cannot instantly supply current labor. A feasible schedule must delay at least one whole project.

q.q: A vaccine program compares two feasible allocations of a fixed stock. A is projected to save 120 lives, including 10 in remote communities. B saves 110, including 30 remotely. A charter requires at least 25 remote lives saved. Which evaluation respects both the estimates and the stated constraint?
options: A saves most overall; only B meets the remote constraint, sacrificing 10 total lives for 20 additional remote lives.
A meets the charter because its larger total automatically compensates remote communities for receiving fewer doses.
B maximizes the stated total because adding its 30 remote lives to 110 produces 140 lives saved.
B removes scarcity because satisfying the charter makes the additional 10 projected total lives costless to obtain.
q.commonError: Treating an efficiency result as a complete distributional judgment.
q.feedback: Remote lives are included in the totals. A has 10 more total lives, while B has 20 more remote lives and meets the threshold. The charter imposes a distributional constraint; it does not change the projections or eliminate the tradeoff.

q.q: A port has one crew for this month. Routine maintenance prevents a certain $40 million loss this year. A resilience project instead avoids $100 million of storm losses with probability 0.6 next year but leaves the $40 million current loss. At a 20% discount rate, ignoring other effects and using expected present value, which allocation is better?
options: Resilience by $10 million: its expected discounted benefit is $50 million versus $40 million for maintenance.
Maintenance by $20 million: the resilience project’s $100 million must be multiplied by the 0.2 discount rate.
Resilience by $60 million: compare the full possible $100 million directly with the certain $40 million.
Maintenance because future benefits are uncertain; a positive probability makes expected-value comparison invalid.
q.commonError: Ignoring either the present or future use of a fixed workforce.
q.feedback: Expected present benefit of resilience is 0.6×100/1.2=50 million. Maintenance provides 40 now. With the specified criterion and no other effects, resilience leads by 10; it still sacrifices the current protection, rather than offering a tradeoff-free gain.

q.q: Scarcity exists when:
options: A seller earns a profit
Limited resources cannot satisfy every competing want.
A store temporarily runs out of one item
A price is legally fixed.
q.commonError: Confusing scarcity with shortage or regulation.
q.feedback: Scarcity is the general condition of limited resources relative to wants.

q.q: Which statement describes efficiency rather than equality?
options: Resources are arranged to generate the greatest total value
Resources are divided into identical shares for every person
Income differences are removed regardless of total production
Every affected group receives the same gain from the policy
q.commonError: Confusing production efficiency with distributional equality.
q.feedback: Efficiency focuses on total value from resources.

q.q: A tradeoff occurs because:
options: Using a limited resource one way restricts another valued use
Every choice requires an explicit payment made with money
Only public agencies must choose among competing resource uses
A high-benefit choice stops using scarce inputs and worker time
q.commonError: Ignoring nonmoney resources and alternative uses.
q.feedback: Tradeoffs arise whenever scarce resources have competing uses.

q.q: A wealthy person must choose how to use one free evening. Why can that person still face scarcity?
options: Time is limited even when the person has substantial income
Scarcity applies only when a person cannot afford basic goods
Wealth makes every nonmoney resource unlimited
A choice among activities is only a temporary shortage
q.commonError: Equating scarcity with poverty.
q.feedback: Poverty concerns limited material means; scarcity also includes universal limits such as time.

q.q: At a shop's posted price, customers want more bottled water than the shop has available. Which distinction correctly describes shortage and scarcity?
options: A shortage concerns unmet buying plans; scarcity concerns choices among limited resources.
Scarcity concerns unmet buying plans; a shortage concerns choices among limited resources.
A shortage concerns limited resources; scarcity begins when goods have a money price.
Scarcity concerns empty shelves; a shortage ends whenever buyers choose another product.
q.commonError: Equating a shortage or stockout with the general condition of scarcity.
q.feedback: The shop has a shortage or stockout because availability is below what customers want to obtain at the posted price. Scarcity means limited resources relative to wants, so choices and tradeoffs remain necessary even when shelves are stocked. The distinction is not how long either condition lasts.

q.q: A faster machine reduces production time but the firm still has limited workers and materials. What did the technology do?
options: It relaxed one constraint without eliminating scarcity
It made every productive input unlimited
It changed scarcity into a retail shortage
It removed the need to choose among projects
q.commonError: Assuming technology eliminates all scarcity.
q.feedback: Technology can expand possibilities while other scarce inputs and wants remain.

q.q: A fair lottery assigns one available treatment slot among two equally eligible patients. What does the lottery change?
options: Who receives the slot, not the number of available slots
The number of slots, because a fair rule creates capacity
Scarcity into abundance, because each patient had an equal chance
Efficiency into equality, because the two ideas are identical
q.commonError: Assuming fairness removes the underlying resource constraint.
q.feedback: An allocation rule can be fair without creating more of the scarce resource.

q.q: A policy tradeoff occurs when:
options: Improving one goal makes another goal harder to achieve
A policy has no consequences
Supply equals demand
A tax is legally paid by sellers
q.feedback: Policies often require balancing competing goals rather than delivering only benefits.

q.q: Scarcity exists because:
options: Resources are limited while wants are unlimited
Market prices sometimes rise
Some goods are provided publicly
Production adjusts slowly to demand
q.feedback: Scarcity is the fundamental condition of limited resources relative to unlimited wants.

q.q: A policy improves efficiency but reduces equality. What does this illustrate?
options: A tradeoff
A shortage
A movement along demand
Perfect competition
q.feedback: A tradeoff requires weighing competing goals; improvement in one dimension can come at a cost in another.

q.q: A library extends weekend hours but must reduce weekday staffing. What does this demonstrate?
options: A market surplus
The end of scarcity
A tradeoff in the use of limited staff time.
A guarantee that everyone benefits equally.
q.commonError: Failing to transfer the tradeoff idea to a service setting.
q.feedback: More staffing in one period leaves less staffing available in another.

q.q: A food bank receives more donations but still cannot meet every request. Which conclusion is best?
options: The food bank now faces only a temporary shortage
The additional resources reduce the constraint but do not eliminate scarcity.
No allocation rule is needed once donations increase
Scarcity disappears whenever supply increases.
q.commonError: Assuming more resources remove all unmet wants.
q.feedback: More resources can ease scarcity while competing needs remain.

q.q: A campus uses its only open parcel for a laboratory instead of student housing. Scarcity creates a tradeoff; which concept names the next-best alternative forgone?
options: Opportunity cost
Market equilibrium
Price elasticity
Monetary neutrality
q.commonError: Recognizing a tradeoff without connecting it to the next-best forgone alternative.
q.feedback: Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best alternative given up when scarcity forces a choice.

q.q: A factory divides fixed labor and machine time between medical devices and water filters. Which model displays the feasible production combinations created by this scarcity?
options: A production possibilities frontier
A consumer price index
A money-demand curve
A Phillips curve
q.commonError: Recognizing limited resources without connecting them to feasible production combinations.
q.feedback: A PPF represents the combinations possible when scarce productive resources have competing uses.

q.q: The short-run aggregate supply curve slopes upward mainly because:
options: Wages, prices, or perceptions do not adjust instantly
Money is neutral in every period
Taxes cannot change
Output is fixed forever
q.commonError: Applying long-run neutrality to the short run.
q.feedback: SRAS slopes upward because sticky wages, sticky prices, and misperceptions allow price-level changes to affect output.

q.q: A decrease in oil prices would most likely shift:
options: SRAS right
AD left
LRPC right
Money demand left
q.commonError: Treating production cost changes as AD shifts.
q.feedback: Lower production costs shift short-run aggregate supply to the right.

q.q: Refer to the graph. Moving from AS2 to AS1 represents:
options: A decrease in short-run aggregate supply
An increase in short-run aggregate supply
An increase in aggregate demand
A fall in money demand
q.commonError: Reversing AS1 and AS2.
q.feedback: AS1 is up and left of AS2, so moving from AS2 to AS1 is a decrease in SRAS.

q.q: An increase in nominal wages, holding productivity and expected prices constant, shifts short-run aggregate supply:
options: Nowhere.
Down along the same SRAS curve.
Right.
Left.
q.commonError: Reversing the effect of higher production costs.
q.feedback: Higher nominal wages raise firms’ costs and reduce output supplied at each price level.

q.q: What change from AS0 to AS1 is shown?
options: A decrease in aggregate supply
An increase in aggregate supply
An increase in aggregate demand
A decrease in aggregate demand
q.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
q.feedback: When the aggregate supply curve shifts left/up, less output is supplied at each price level, which is a decrease in aggregate supply.

These coordinates are approximate readings of hand-drawn curves. No AD or LRAS curve is drawn.

q.q: How should AS1 be classified relative to AS0 in the second aggregate-supply diagram?
options: A decrease in aggregate supply
An increase in aggregate demand
An increase in aggregate supply
A decrease in aggregate demand
q.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
q.feedback: A downward/rightward shift of the AS curve means aggregate supply has increased.

These are approximate readings of hand-drawn curves. No AD or LRAS curve is drawn.

q.q: Sticky-wage theory explains upward-sloping SRAS because unexpected price-level changes affect:
options: Real labor costs and firm production decisions
Only the money multiplier
Only net exports
The vertical position of LRPC
q.commonError: Applying long-run neutrality to short-run wages.
q.feedback: When nominal wages are sticky, price-level changes alter real labor costs and production.

q.q: If expected prices rise, short-run aggregate supply usually shifts:
options: Right because real wages fall
Left because production costs rise
Right because AD increases
Left because LRAS moves
q.commonError: Reversing expected price effects on SRAS.
q.feedback: Higher expected prices push wages and costs upward, shifting SRAS left.

q.q: If workers and firms expect a higher price level before contracts are set, short-run aggregate supply tends to:
options: Become vertical immediately.
Remain fixed because expectations affect only AD.
Shift left.
Shift right.
q.commonError: Reversing the expected-price effect.
q.feedback: Higher expected prices tend to produce higher nominal wages and other input costs.

q.q: A temporary payroll-tax reduction lowers firms’ labor costs. Holding other factors constant, SRAS shifts:
options: AD right only.
LRAS left only.
Left.
Right.
q.commonError: Treating a production-cost change as an AD shifter.
q.feedback: Lower per-worker cost raises short-run output supplied at each price level.

q.q: Why can an unexpected rise in the price level increase output in the short run under sticky-wage theory?
options: Household wealth rises and shifts AD
Potential output permanently increases
Nominal wages immediately rise more than prices
Product prices rise before nominal wages fully adjust, lowering real labor cost.
q.commonError: Confusing short-run wage rigidity with long-run capacity.
q.feedback: With sticky wages, unexpected price increases can make production temporarily more profitable.

q.q: Which event best matches the shift from AS0 to AS1?
options: Higher consumer confidence that boosts spending
A cut in income taxes that raises aggregate demand
A rise in input prices that makes production more costly
A fall in the overall price level causing a movement along AS0
q.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
q.feedback: Higher production costs shift short-run aggregate supply left.

Solid red AS0 slopes upward, near price 70 at GDP 0 and near price 150 at GDP 150, and near price 190 at GDP 230. Dashed red AS1 lies above and left of AS0, near price 115 at GDP 0 and near price 190 at GDP 150. Both lines continue upward to the right. These coordinates are approximate readings of hand-drawn curves. No AD or LRAS curve is drawn.

q.q: If aggregate demand stays put, what equilibrium effect follows from the supply change in the second AS diagram?
options: Real GDP decreases while the price level increases
Both real GDP and the price level increase
Both real GDP and the price level decrease
Real GDP increases while the price level decreases
q.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
q.feedback: A rightward shift of AS increases output and lowers the price level.

These are approximate readings of hand-drawn curves. No AD or LRAS curve is drawn.

q.q: Which favorable production-side change could account for the shift displayed in the second AS diagram?
options: A fall in input costs or an improvement in productivity
A surge in household spending
An increase in government purchases that shifts AD right
A rise in inflation expectations that shifts SRAS left
q.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
q.feedback: Lower costs or better productivity shift aggregate supply right.

Dashed red AS1 lies below and right of AS0, running from approximately (0,35) toward (230,150). At GDP 150, the curves are near price levels 150 and 110 respectively. These are approximate readings of hand-drawn curves. No AD or LRAS curve is drawn.

q.q: Oil prices rise sharply, but firms also adopt a productivity-enhancing technology. What can be concluded about SRAS?
options: SRAS must shift left
The net shift is ambiguous because costs rise while productivity improves.
Only LRAS can change
SRAS must shift right
q.commonError: Allowing one supply shifter to dominate without magnitude information.
q.feedback: Higher oil costs push SRAS left, while higher productivity pushes it right.

q.q: Expected prices rise by 4 percent, but nominal wages are locked in long-term contracts. Compared with a setting where wages adjust immediately, the leftward SRAS shift is likely:
options: Larger.
Smaller in the short run.
A rightward shift of LRAS.
Identical by definition.
q.commonError: Ignoring the mechanism through which expectations affect costs.
q.feedback: If wages cannot yet adjust, expected-price changes have a weaker immediate cost effect.

q.q: The price level rises unexpectedly while nominal wages are fixed. In the short run, firms tend to:
options: Increase production because output prices rise relative to wage costs.
Leave output unchanged because SRAS is vertical
Shift LRAS right immediately
Reduce production because real wages rise
q.commonError: Reversing the real-wage effect.
q.feedback: Unexpectedly higher output prices lower the real cost of contracted wages.

q.q: A government permanently improves transportation infrastructure but finances it with a temporary business-energy surcharge. Which supply effects are possible?
options: Only AD can change.
LRAS may shift right while SRAS shifts left temporarily.
Both LRAS and SRAS must shift left permanently.
LRAS must remain fixed because taxes are involved.
q.commonError: Treating all policy effects as demand-side or same-direction.
q.feedback: Infrastructure can raise capacity while the temporary surcharge raises current production costs.

q.q: Firms revise expected prices downward after a period of unexpectedly low inflation. Holding actual prices fixed, SRAS tends to:
options: Become vertical.
Shift left.
Shift right.
Move upward along the same curve.
q.commonError: Reversing how lower expected prices affect wage and cost setting.
q.feedback: Lower expected prices tend to reduce nominal wage and input-cost growth.

q.q: Refer to the first AS graph. At real GDP of 150, which value is closest to the vertical price-level gap between AS0 and AS1?
q.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
q.feedback: The hand-drawn curves lie near price levels 150 and 190 at GDP 150. Their gap is roughly 40–45 price-level units, so 40 is the closest offered estimate; the graph does not support exact coordinate arithmetic.

Dashed red AS1 lies above and left of AS0, near price 115 at GDP 0 and near price 190 at GDP 150. Both lines continue upward to the right. These coordinates are approximate readings of hand-drawn curves. No AD or LRAS curve is drawn.

q.q: Refer to the second AS graph. At real GDP of 150, which value is closest to the vertical price-level gap between AS0 and AS1?
q.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
q.feedback: The curves lie near price levels 150 and 110 at GDP 150. Their separation is approximately 40 price-level units, the closest offered estimate.

These are approximate readings of hand-drawn curves. No AD or LRAS curve is drawn.

q.q: Which event best matches the joint shift from SRAS0/LRAS0 to SRAS1/LRAS1?
options: A confidence drop that lowers consumer and investment spending
A productivity gain that lowers costs and raises potential output
An energy-price increase that raises costs and lowers output
A government-spending increase that shifts aggregate demand right
q.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
q.feedback: A positive supply-side change can shift both SRAS right and LRAS right.

LRAS0 is vertical at GDP 100 and dashed LRAS1 is vertical to its right at GDP 115. A, the AD0-SRAS0-LRAS0 intersection, is at (100,125). B, the AD0-SRAS1-LRAS1 intersection, is at (115,110). Dashed guides connect A and B to the axes.

q.q: Workers expect 6 percent inflation, but actual inflation is 2 percent and wage contracts reflect the higher expectation. What happens to SRAS relative to contracts based on accurate expectations?
options: SRAS is farther left because nominal labor costs are higher than necessary.
AD shifts right
SRAS is farther right because real wages are lower
LRAS shifts left
q.commonError: Ignoring how excessive expected inflation enters wage contracts.
q.feedback: Higher expected prices can produce higher nominal wages and lower short-run supply.

q.q: A severe storm destroys capital, while emergency deregulation lowers current compliance costs. Which conclusion is strongest?
options: LRAS shifts left, while the SRAS effect is ambiguous because cost relief offsets disruption.
LRAS shifts right because regulation falls
Only AD changes
Both curves must shift left by the same amount
q.commonError: Assuming all supply forces have the same horizon and direction.
q.feedback: Capital destruction lowers capacity; lower compliance cost pushes SRAS right, while storm disruption may push it left.

q.q: A student says, “Any rise in the price level shifts SRAS right.” What is the best correction?
options: Any price-level rise shifts aggregate demand left only
A change in the actual price level causes movement along SRAS; expected prices or costs shift the curve.
Actual prices shift LRAS, not SRAS
The statement is correct in every case
q.commonError: Confusing movement along SRAS with a curve shift.
q.feedback: The actual price level is an axis variable, not a supply shifter by itself.

q.q: With aggregate demand unchanged, which macro outcome is consistent with the AS shift shown?
options: Lower output with a higher price level
Higher output with a lower price level
Higher output with a higher price level

q.q: Expected inflation rises, productivity improves, and oil prices fall. What can be concluded about SRAS?

Right: all three changes shift the SRAS curve right

Ambiguous: expectations shift SRAS left, productivity and oil shift it right

q.q: Nominal wages are fixed for one year. The price level rises unexpectedly, then wage contracts reset to reflect the higher expected price level. What sequence is most likely?

Only aggregate demand changes
An immediate rightward LRAS shift
Movement up along SRAS at first, followed later by a leftward SRAS shift.
q.commonError: Failing to distinguish immediate movement from later expectation adjustment.
q.feedback: Unexpected prices initially raise output along SRAS; higher wage expectations later shift SRAS left.

q.q: An economy’s expected price level falls while actual price level and productive resources are unchanged. At each actual price level, firms are likely to supply:
options: More potential output, so LRAS shifts right.
Less output, so SRAS shifts left.
The same output because expectations never matter.
More output, so SRAS shifts right.
q.commonError: Confusing expected-price effects with long-run capacity.
q.feedback: Lower expected prices tend to lower nominal input costs and raise short-run supply.

q.q: Refer to the first AS graph, treating AS0 and AS1 as short-run supply. A temporary energy bottleneck and a permanent loss of productive equipment could each help explain the shift to AS1. After energy costs normalize, which evidence is needed to predict whether wage adjustment restores the old potential-output level?

Whether productive capacity was restored and LRAS retained its old position; the SRAS-only drawing does not establish that.
Whether actual GDP fell; any actual output loss permanently lowers potential output by the same amount.
Whether demand policy can raise spending; a rightward AD shift by itself restores lost productive capacity.
q.commonError: misreads_graph_or_curve_shift
q.feedback: The drawing establishes a reduction in short-run supply, but contains no LRAS line. Temporary costs may reverse while destroyed capital leaves lower potential output. Wage adjustment returns output toward the applicable capacity level, so the old long-run anchor must be verified.

q.feedback: Restoring expected prices reverses that contribution to SRAS, while improved productivity still supports supply and raises potential output. The graph records only their combined initial effect; without a decomposition it does not locate the final SRAS precisely.

Left.

Nowhere.
LRAS right.
Left.

A rightward AD shift
A leftward LRAS shift
A rightward SRAS shift

Both curves must shift left.

q.commonError: Forcing offsetting SRAS shifters into one predetermined direction.

A rightward SRAS shift, then movement down.

Right
Nowhere
Into AD

Never change at all
Are always real variables
Cancel aggregate demand

Right
Into AD
Into LRPC

Left
Into AD
Into money demand

Aggregate demand rose
Potential output must have increased
The money supply fell by definition

SRAS shifts right
AD shifts right
LRAS becomes horizontal

Rise, so output falls
Stay fixed forever
Become money demand

q.q: Oil prices fall and shift SRAS to the right while aggregate demand is unchanged. What should be done next to determine the macroeconomic outcome?

Move along the old SRAS curve without finding a new equilibrium.
Shift LRAS right automatically because oil became cheaper.
Treat the change as an aggregate-demand shock and ignore SRAS.
q.feedback: A supply shift changes the short-run equilibrium where the new SRAS curve intersects aggregate demand.
q.commonError: Identifies a supply shift but does not translate it into an equilibrium outcome.

q.q: Two episodes produce the same increase in inflation. In one, unemployment falls after aggregate demand expands; in the other, unemployment rises after an adverse supply shock. What explains the difference?
options: Both episodes are movements along one SRPC, but they begin from different unemployment rates.

The supply shock lowers expected inflation and moves the economy down an unchanged SRPC.
The demand expansion moves along an SRPC, while the supply shock shifts the curve.
q.commonError: Assuming every inflation change is a movement along one fixed Phillips curve.
q.feedback: Demand changes can move the economy along a given SRPC; supply shocks alter the inflation-unemployment relationship and shift the SRPC.

q.q: Refer to the graph with A on SRPC0 and LRPC. Later observations show unemployment at A’s rate but persistently higher inflation. One analyst says the SRPC must have become vertical; another says the same vertical LRPC can coexist with a higher SRPC after contracts adjust. Which additional evidence would support the second interpretation?
options: Inflation rose once, which by itself proves that expectations already adjusted fully.
Current unemployment equals the natural rate, which requires every SRPC to be vertical.
The price level is higher, which proves that the natural unemployment rate permanently fell.
Wage-setting expectations have risen to match the sustained inflation while labor-market structure and supply conditions are unchanged.
q.commonError: misreads_phillips_curve_or_natural_rate
q.feedback: An unchanged natural rate locates the same LRPC. Evidence that expected inflation caught up, with other shifters held fixed, supports a higher SRPC crossing it. Equal unemployment and a higher inflation observation alone do not establish the expectations mechanism.

q.q: Which statement best connects diminishing returns and the catch-up effect?
options: Scarce capital has high returns, which fall as capital accumulates
Poor countries grow slower because every new unit of capital has zero return
Rich countries grow faster because diminishing returns help them
Catch-up occurs because inflation is lower in rich countries

q.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
q.q: A factory adds machinery but productivity barely changes. After operator training, output rises with the same machines and labor hours. A manager concludes that machines have no productive value. Which interpretation best fits both stages?

Training proves all earlier spending on machines should be subtracted from GDP
The later gain must be more physical capital because worker skills are unchanged by training
The data prove training raises output equally in every factory, regardless of equipment
q.feedback: The second stage changes human capital while holding physical inputs fixed. Its effect can reflect complementarity between skills and machinery. A weak result before training does not identify a zero contribution from capital.

q.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.

options: Resources alone do not guarantee high productivity
Oil is not a natural resource
Education matters only in service economies

q.q: Two plants initially use the same machines and hours. Plant A adopts a freely available scheduling method and raises output 8%. Plant B trains operators without changing its method and raises output 8%. What can be inferred about productivity sources?

Both added physical capital because output rose without more labor hours
Both changed natural resources because the gain has the same size
A’s gain is human capital and B’s is technology solely because both involve information
q.feedback: A new production method is technological knowledge; skills acquired by workers are human capital. Equal measured gains do not identify a common mechanism or prove the two interventions would have equal effects elsewhere.

q.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.

Only technological knowledge
Only population growth

q.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.

options: The successive gains are 60 and 40; continued diminishing marginal returns would put the next gain below 40
The observed average gain is 50, so 40 machines must yield exactly 250
The capital stock doubled once, proving output must double at 40 machines
The last gain was 40, so every later ten machines must add exactly 40
q.feedback: Equal capital increments add 60 then 40 units while other inputs are fixed. If the diminishing-returns pattern continues, the next increment adds less than 40; the table alone does not supply an exact future output level.

q.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.

options: Catch-up effect followed by diminishing returns
CPI substitution bias followed by inflation
Frictional unemployment followed by cyclical unemployment
Imports followed by exports

q.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
q.q: A poor country and a rich country both add $1,000 of capital per worker. Why might the poor country gain more output per worker?
options: Capital is scarcer
Rich countries never use capital
Poor countries do not face diminishing returns
The CPI is lower in poor countries
q.feedback: The catch-up effect depends on higher marginal returns to capital where capital is scarce.

q.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
q.q: Physical capital includes:
options: Productive equipment and structures
The unemployment rate
Worker education only
The CPI basket
q.feedback: Physical capital is the equipment and structures used to produce goods and services.

q.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
q.q: If workers receive better machinery, what should happen to productivity, other things equal?
options: It should rise
It must fall
It becomes inflation
It no longer depends on output
q.feedback: Better machinery usually allows workers to produce more output per hour.

q.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
q.q: A business has 10 workers and 20 machines. It adds 10 more machines while employment stays the same. What has increased?
options: Physical capital per worker
Natural resources per worker
The CPI
Frictional unemployment
