q.commonError: Confusing worker training and skills with physical equipment.
q.q: Two countries use similar machines, but one invests heavily in worker education and training. Which productivity factor differs most?
options: Human capital
Physical capital
Natural resources
The money supply
q.feedback: Education and training build human capital—the knowledge and skills workers bring to production.

q.commonError: Confusing worker training and skills with physical equipment.
q.q: A country expands technical training and apprenticeship programs. Which productivity factor increases most directly?
options: Human capital
Natural resources
GDP deflator
Net exports
q.feedback: Training programs increase worker skills, which raises human capital.

q.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
q.q: Two factories use the same machines, but one has better-trained workers. Why might that factory produce more?
options: Its workers have more human capital
It has more natural resources by definition
Its CPI is lower
It has fewer final goods
q.feedback: Better-trained workers can use tools and processes more effectively.

q.commonError: Assuming natural resources alone guarantee high productivity.
q.q: Which item is a natural resource used in production?
options: Crude oil in the ground
Worker training
A factory robot
A software patent
q.feedback: Natural resources are inputs supplied by nature, such as land, water, minerals, and oil.

q.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
q.q: A new drilling method allows firms to extract more oil with the same workers and equipment. Which factor changed most directly?
options: Technological knowledge
Labor force participation
CPI inflation
Frictional unemployment
q.feedback: A better method of production is technological knowledge.

q.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
q.q: A country discovers large copper deposits but lacks skilled workers and roads. What is the best interpretation?
options: Resources help, but skills and capital also matter
Natural resources alone guarantee high living standards
Roads reduce productivity
Human capital no longer matters
q.feedback: Natural resources are useful, but they work best alongside skills, infrastructure, and technology.

q.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
q.q: A factory keeps the workforce fixed and adds identical machines. Each new machine raises output by less than the previous one. What principle is shown?
options: Diminishing returns to capital
Catch-up growth
Constant returns to capital
Frictional unemployment
q.feedback: With other inputs fixed, each additional unit of capital eventually adds less output.

q.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
q.q: A worker with no tools gains a hammer and becomes much more productive. A worker with ten hammers gains an eleventh and barely improves. What does this show?
options: Diminishing returns to capital
CPI bias
Cyclical unemployment
Net export accounting
q.feedback: The extra hammer matters more when capital is scarce.

q.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
q.q: Capital per worker doubles, but output per worker rises by only 25%. What does that suggest?
options: Diminishing returns to capital
Capital had no effect
Output per worker doubled
The Rule of 70 failed
q.feedback: Output rose less than proportionally to capital, which is consistent with diminishing returns.

q.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
q.q: The catch-up effect says:
options: Scarce capital can produce faster catch-up growth
Rich countries always grow faster
Growth rates are unrelated to capital
Poor countries cannot grow
q.feedback: The catch-up effect occurs when capital-scarce economies can gain more from new investment.

q.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
q.q: Why might a poor country gain more from one additional machine than a rich country?
options: Scarcer capital can have a higher marginal return
The rich country cannot use machines
The poor country has no workers
Machines count only in poor countries
q.feedback: Capital tends to have a higher marginal product when it is scarce.

q.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
q.q: Country A has very little capital per worker and Country B has abundant capital per worker. If each receives the same new equipment, which country may grow faster from that addition?
options: Country A
Country B
Both must grow equally
Neither can grow
q.feedback: Country A may gain more because capital is scarcer there.

q.q: A worker receives a new machine that raises output with the same labor time. Which productivity input increased most directly?
options: Physical capital per worker
Human capital only
Natural resources only
Population growth
q.commonError: Treats every increase in capital as producing the same output gain.
q.feedback: Providing a new machine increases physical capital per worker; with labor time unchanged, that can raise output per worker.

q.q: In GROWTH-01, why does an equal small addition to capital have greater output potential near point A than near point B?
options: Point A has more output per worker than B
The curve is vertical near B
Capital has no relationship to output near A
The curve is steeper near A
q.commonError: Treats every increase in capital as producing the same output gain.
q.feedback: The curve is steeper near A, so an equal small capital addition produces a larger additional output per worker there.

q.q: A new production method lets the same workers and machines produce more output. Which source of productivity improved?
options: Natural resources only
The unemployment rate
Technological knowledge
Physical capital per worker only
q.commonError: Confuses technological knowledge with merely owning more machines.
q.feedback: Technology raises the efficiency with which available inputs are transformed into output.

q.q: GROWTH-01 is upward sloping but becomes flatter as capital per worker rises. Which concept is represented by that shape?
options: A fixed level of productivity at all capital levels
Diminishing returns to capital
Increasing marginal returns to capital
The Rule of 70
q.commonError: Confuses total output with output per unit of labor.
q.feedback: An upward-sloping curve that becomes flatter means capital still raises output per worker, but each additional unit adds less: diminishing returns to capital.

q.q: A low-capital country buys machinery, but workers lack training and firms cannot reliably obtain electricity. Why might catch-up remain limited?
options: Physical capital works with human capital, infrastructure, and other complementary inputs
Catch-up requires natural resources and nothing else
More machines always guarantee convergence regardless of other conditions
Human capital matters only after a country becomes rich
q.commonError: Treats every increase in capital as producing the same output gain.
q.feedback: Catch-up is limited because capital works with skills, reliable infrastructure, and institutions; machinery alone cannot overcome missing complements.

q.q: Two countries add the same number of machines. One also improves worker training and production methods. Why can its productivity gain be larger?
options: Machines reduce productivity whenever training also rises
Human capital and technology affect only total population
Natural resources must fall when technology improves
Capital can complement human capital and technological knowledge
q.commonError: Treats worker knowledge and skills as physical equipment.
q.feedback: Training and better production methods complement machines, so the same equipment can generate a larger productivity gain.

q.q: A country increases capital per worker for several decades. Growth is strong at first, then slows even though investment continues. What explains the slowdown?
options: Substitution bias in CPI
A discouraged-worker effect
Diminishing returns to capital
A binding price ceiling
q.commonError: expects_constant_growth_from_repeated_capital_investment
q.feedback: As capital becomes more abundant, each additional unit tends to add less extra output.

q.q: A poorer country adopts existing technology and attracts foreign investment. Its growth rate rises above that of richer countries for a time. What concept fits best?
options: Cost-of-living bias because the CPI is fixed
Cyclical unemployment because the economy is in recession
Tax equivalence because buyers and sellers share taxes
Catch-up growth because returns to capital can be higher when capital is scarce
q.commonError: thinks_poor_countries_cannot_grow_faster_than_rich_countries
q.feedback: Poorer countries can grow quickly when they add capital and technology because the return to new investment can be high.

q.q: A country invests in better machines, worker training, and new technology. Which productivity factors are being strengthened?
options: Only natural resources
Only transfer payments
Physical capital, skills, and technology
Only the CPI basket
q.commonError: treats_productivity_as_only_worker_effort
q.feedback: Machines are physical capital, training is human capital, and new production methods reflect technological knowledge.

q.q: A country has more machines per worker, but each additional machine adds less extra output than the one before. What explains this pattern?
options: Substitution bias
Frictional unemployment
A binding price ceiling
Diminishing returns to capital
q.commonError: thinks_more_capital_always_creates_constant_growth
q.feedback: Diminishing returns means each additional unit of capital adds less extra output once capital is already abundant.

q.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
q.q: Boss Audit: A country improves schools but has no reliable electricity, roads, or legal protection for investors. What limits growth?
options: Skills need capital, infrastructure, and reliable institutions
Education never affects growth
Only natural resources matter
Legal institutions matter only for unemployment
q.feedback: Productivity depends on complementary factors, not education alone.

q.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
q.q: Two equal additions to capital per worker produce output gains of 9 and 6 with skills and technology fixed. A later 9-unit gain occurs after a new production method is introduced. Does that last observation refute diminishing returns to capital?
options: No; the first two gains compare capital with other inputs fixed, while technology changed in the third
Yes; any later larger gain refutes diminishing returns regardless of other changes
No; diminishing returns means total output must fall after adding capital
Yes; introducing technology changes physical capital into a natural resource
q.feedback: Diminishing marginal returns concerns additional capital with other determinants held fixed. The first two gains fit that pattern. A technology improvement changes the production relationship, so the larger third gain is not a comparable capital-only experiment.

q.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
q.q: Boss Audit: A poor country with little capital receives basic machinery and output rises sharply. A rich country adds similar machinery and output barely changes. Why?
options: Scarce capital has a higher marginal product
Rich countries cannot use machinery
Poor countries do not need human capital
GDP ignores machinery
q.feedback: The catch-up effect reflects high returns to capital where capital is scarce.

q.q: A poor country attracts capital investment and adopts existing technology. Growth accelerates, but after decades the growth rate slows as capital becomes abundant. Which paired concepts best explain the pattern?
options: Catch-up growth followed by diminishing returns to capital
Substitution bias followed by cyclical unemployment
Price ceilings followed by tax incidence
Discouraged workers followed by CPI quality bias
q.commonError: expects_fast_growth_to_continue_forever
q.feedback: Poorer countries can grow quickly through catch-up, but growth can slow as capital accumulation faces diminishing returns.

q.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
q.q: The catch-up effect says poorer countries may grow faster because:
options: Capital is scarce and may have high returns
They never face diminishing returns
They have no workers
They ignore productivity
q.feedback: Capital may have high marginal returns when it is scarce.

q.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
q.q: Diminishing returns means extra capital eventually adds:
options: Smaller extra amounts of output
Larger extra amounts forever
No output from the beginning
Only inflation
q.feedback: Additional capital still helps, but by smaller amounts as capital becomes abundant.

q.commonError: Confusing worker training and skills with physical equipment.
q.q: Human capital means:
options: Worker knowledge and skills
Machines only
Minerals only
Net exports

q.commonError: Assuming natural resources alone guarantee high productivity.
q.q: Which description defines natural resources as a productivity input?
options: Inputs provided by nature
Worker training

q.feedback: Natural resources include land, water, minerals, oil, and other natural inputs.

q.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
q.q: Which option consists entirely of physical capital?
options: Machines, tools, buildings, and equipment
Worker education only
Oil and land only
Inflation

q.commonError: Confusing better production methods with more labor or more machines.
q.q: Which description defines technological knowledge as a productivity input?
options: Knowing better ways to produce goods and services
Having more unemployed workers
Having higher CPI
Having more used goods
q.feedback: Technological knowledge is production know-how.

q.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
q.q: A poor country gains basic tools and output jumps sharply. What concept does this fit?
options: Catch-up effect
CPI inflation
Labor force exit
Transfer payments
q.feedback: Capital can have high returns where it is scarce.

q.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
q.q: A factory adds more and more machines, but each extra machine adds less output than the previous one. What is this?
options: Diminishing returns
Rule of 70
CPI bias
Cyclical unemployment
q.feedback: Diminishing returns means each extra unit adds less additional output.

q.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
q.q: A firm trains workers to use advanced equipment. Which productivity factor rises?
options: Human capital
Natural resources
Net exports
Inflation

q.commonError: Assuming natural resources alone guarantee high productivity.
q.q: A country discovers rare minerals used in manufacturing. Which productivity factor increased?
options: Natural resources
Human capital
CPI
Frictional unemployment
q.feedback: Minerals are natural resources.

q.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
q.q: Workers receive better machines but no extra labor is added. What should happen to productivity, other things equal?
options: It should rise
It must fall
It becomes CPI
It becomes unemployment
q.feedback: More or better capital helps workers produce more.

q.commonError: Confusing better production methods with more labor or more machines.
q.q: A new production method lets firms make more output with the same inputs. What improved?
options: Technological knowledge
Labor force participation
Imports
Unemployment insurance
q.feedback: Better production methods are technological knowledge.

q.feedback: In a liquidity trap, nominal interest rates are near zero, making traditional monetary stimulus weaker.

A permanent shift of LRAS

Stop all supply shocks

q.q: A policy lag is a reason stabilization policy can be risky because policy actions may

instantly fix every shock
remove the need for aggregate demand
make money supply impossible to change
q.commonError: thinking stabilization policy works instantly
q.feedback: Policy lags matter because by the time policy takes effect, the economy may have already changed.

only policies that shift AD right

q.feedback: When AD is too high and inflation pressure builds, contractionary policy can shift AD left.

all scarcity forever
the need for banks

shift aggregate demand left
reduce output further
raise unemployment intentionally

q.q: If aggregate demand is too high and inflation pressure is building, stabilization policy would most likely try to
options: shift aggregate demand left
shift aggregate demand right
increase government spending
lower interest rates
q.commonError: stimulating AD when inflation pressure is already high
q.feedback: If AD is too strong, contractionary policy can shift AD left and reduce inflation pressure.

q.q: A key argument for active stabilization policy is that policymakers can
options: counteract short-run aggregate demand shocks
eliminate scarcity permanently
make all real variables nominal

q.commonError: thinking stabilization policy is meant to solve every economic problem
q.feedback: Supporters argue that active policy can reduce the damage caused by short-run AD shocks.

q.q: A key argument against aggressive stabilization policy is that
options: policy lags can cause poorly timed interventions
AD never changes
the Fed cannot affect interest rates
government spending is not part of aggregate demand
q.commonError: thinking stabilization policy works instantly and perfectly
q.feedback: Policy lags can cause interventions to arrive after conditions have already changed.

q.q: If policymakers misread a temporary shock as a lasting recession, they risk

making aggregate demand vanish
ending the money multiplier
turning fiat money into commodity money
q.commonError: thinking wrong policy timing has no cost
q.feedback: If policymakers stimulate after the economy is already recovering, they may push AD too far.

q.q: A pandemic reduces production and also weakens spending. Why is stabilization policy harder here than with a simple demand shock?
options: Because both supply and demand may be affected.
Because monetary policy cannot affect interest rates in any economy.
Because fiscal policy cannot affect aggregate demand.
Because money demand must be zero during pandemics.
q.commonError: treating every downturn as only an aggregate demand problem
q.feedback: A mixed shock is harder because policy may support demand, but it cannot instantly fix lost production capacity.

q.q: Congress cuts spending to reduce deficits during a recession. What policy concern is most direct?
options: AD may fall further before recovery
SRAS must shift right instantly
Inflation must rise immediately
LRPC must become horizontal
q.commonError: Ignoring demand effects of spending cuts.
q.feedback: Cutting spending during a recession can reduce AD further and deepen the downturn.

q.q: If interest rates are near zero and output is below potential, why may monetary policy struggle?
options: Rates have little room to fall
Money demand becomes vertical forever
LRAS shifts left automatically
Taxes cannot change AD
q.commonError: Treating monetary policy as equally strong at all rates.
q.feedback: At near-zero nominal rates, standard rate-cut channels have little room to stimulate spending.

q.q: A policy takes six months to pass and another year to affect spending. The main risk is:
options: The shock may reverse before policy hits
The money multiplier must equal zero
LRAS becomes horizontal
M2 stops including near money
q.commonError: Ignoring timing in stabilization policy.
q.feedback: Inside and outside lags can make policy arrive after conditions have changed.

q.q: Congress cuts government spending to reduce the deficit. If the Fed wants to stabilize output, what should it do?

Decrease money supply to raise interest rates and reduce AD further.

Do nothing because fiscal policy cannot affect AD.

q.q: A stock market boom increases household wealth and pushes output above its natural level. If the Fed wants to stabilize output, it should

increase money supply and lower interest rates
increase government spending

q.feedback: A positive AD shock can push output too high, so contractionary monetary policy can stabilize output.

options: Fed buys bonds and Congress increases government spending.
Fed sells bonds and Congress raises taxes.
Fed sells bonds and Congress cuts spending.

q.commonError: mixing expansionary and contractionary tools
q.feedback: Fed bond purchases are expansionary monetary policy, and higher government spending is expansionary fiscal policy.

q.q: Which policy mix is most contractionary for aggregate demand?
options: Fed sells bonds and Congress raises taxes.
Fed buys bonds and Congress cuts taxes.
Fed buys bonds and Congress increases spending.

q.commonError: thinking bond sales are expansionary
q.feedback: Fed bond sales reduce money supply, and tax increases reduce consumption. Both push AD left.

options: Policy lags can make action arrive after conditions change.
Policy always takes effect instantly.
Aggregate demand never responds to policy.
The Fed cannot change the money supply.
q.commonError: thinking timing never matters
q.feedback: Policy lags can make a policy hit after the original problem has faded, creating a new problem.

q.q: A recession is already ending, but expansionary fiscal policy passed months earlier now takes effect. What is the risk?

q.q: A negative AD shock reduces output and the price level. Which policy response best targets the shock without relying on supply-side repair?

q.q: An economy is above potential output because AD is too high. Which response best reduces the boom without increasing AD further?

Higher government spending and lower interest rates

q.q: A government passes stimulus after a recession has ended, and the economy is already above potential. What is the risk?
options: The stimulus may worsen inflation pressure

The stimulus shifts SRAS right automatically
The stimulus lowers expected prices instantly

q.feedback: Because of lags, stimulus can hit after recovery and add excess demand.

q.q: Fiscal stimulus raises AD, but the central bank offsets it with tighter money. Which final outcome is most plausible?
options: AD rises less than fiscal policy alone suggests
AD rises more than fiscal policy alone suggests
SRAS shifts right because interest rates rise
LRPC shifts left because taxes fall
q.commonError: Ignoring policy interactions.
q.feedback: Tighter monetary policy can offset fiscal stimulus by raising interest rates and weakening AD.

q.q: Suppose output is below its natural level because AD is weak. Which Fed action through the money market would move AD in the stabilizing direction?
options: Shift money supply right to lower r and raise investment.
Shift money supply left to raise r and lower investment.
Shift money demand right to raise r and lower investment.
Keep money supply fixed and raise taxes.
q.commonError: choosing tighter money during a demand slump
q.feedback: When AD is weak, expansionary monetary policy shifts MS right, lowers rates, raises investment, and shifts AD right.

q.q: Suppose output is above its natural level because AD is too strong. Which Fed action through the money market would move AD in the stabilizing direction?
options: Shift money supply left to raise r and lower investment.
Shift money supply right to lower r and raise investment.
Shift money demand left to lower r and raise investment.
Cut taxes to raise consumption.
q.commonError: stimulating AD when output is already above natural level
q.feedback: When AD is too strong, tighter money shifts MS left, raises rates, lowers investment, and shifts AD left.

q.q: If the economy is already near full employment and fiscal policy shifts AD right through the multiplier, what risk becomes more important?
options: Inflation pressure from excessive AD
Deflation from collapsing AD
A lower price level from higher government spending
A smaller price level because MPC is positive
q.commonError: thinking all rightward AD shifts are good regardless of starting point
q.feedback: If the economy is already near capacity, more AD can create inflation pressure instead of useful output gains.

q.q: A recession lowers AD by $300 billion. The government increases spending by $100 billion and MPC is 0.5. Ignoring crowding out, what remains of the AD shortfall?
options: $100 billion
$200 billion
$300 billion
q.commonError: not comparing stimulus size to the original AD shortfall
q.feedback: MPC 0.5 gives multiplier 2. A $100 billion spending increase shifts AD by $200 billion, leaving a $100 billion shortfall.

q.q: Congress cuts spending during a recession while the Fed also sells bonds. What is the combined AD effect?
options: Both policies shift AD left or reduce support for AD, worsening the demand problem.
Both policies shift AD right, stabilizing output.
Fiscal policy shifts AD right while monetary policy shifts AD right.
Neither policy affects AD.
q.commonError: missing that Fed bond sales are contractionary
q.feedback: Cutting spending reduces AD, and Fed bond sales raise rates and reduce investment. That is contraction on top of contraction.

q.q: Congress raises spending during an inflationary boom while the Fed buys bonds. What is the combined AD effect?
options: Both policies shift AD right, risking more inflation pressure.
Both policies shift AD left, reducing inflation pressure.
Fiscal policy shifts AD left while monetary policy shifts AD left.
Neither affects AD because output is already high.
q.commonError: thinking expansionary policy is always appropriate
q.feedback: Spending increases and bond purchases both shift AD right. During an inflationary boom, that pours gasoline on the fire.

q.q: A negative supply shock reduces output and raises prices. Why can expansionary AD policy be a blunt tool here?
options: It may raise output somewhat but can worsen the price-level increase.
It directly restores lost productive capacity with no inflation risk.
It shifts SRAS right automatically.
It lowers prices and lowers output at the same time.
q.commonError: treating supply shocks like pure demand shocks
q.feedback: AD stimulus can support spending, but it does not fix the supply loss and may worsen inflation.

q.q: A negative demand shock reduces output and prices. Why is expansionary monetary policy more directly suited to this case than to a pure supply shock?
options: It targets weak spending by lowering r and raising investment.
It directly increases labor, capital, and natural resources.
It shifts SRAS right by changing the reserve ratio.
It lowers AD to reduce output further.
q.commonError: not distinguishing AD shocks from AS shocks
q.feedback: Expansionary monetary policy works through spending, so it is more directly suited to weak AD than to lost productive capacity.

q.q: A policy is passed to fight a recession, but because of recognition, implementation, and impact lags, it takes effect after output has already recovered. What is the likely stabilization problem?
options: The delayed policy can push AD too far right and create inflation pressure.
The delayed policy must shift AD left automatically.
The delayed policy cannot affect AD after recovery.
The delayed policy eliminates crowding out.
q.commonError: thinking late stimulus is harmless because it was originally well-intended
q.feedback: Good timing matters. Late expansion can overstimulate AD after the recession has already passed.

q.q: If the economy initially needed AD to fall by $300 billion and the MS1 to MS2 movement reduces AD by $200 billion, what remains?
options: $100 billion of excess AD remains.
The overheating gap closes exactly.
AD overshoots by $100 billion.
Output rises from Y2 to Y1.
q.commonError: not comparing the graph's AD shift with the size of the gap
q.feedback: The graph shows AD shifting left. If AD needed to fall $300 billion but falls $200 billion, $100 billion of excess AD remains.

q.q: A contractionary monetary-policy move must reduce AD by $240 billion. If MPC = 0.75, what investment decrease is needed to produce that AD movement?
options: $60 billion
$240 billion
$80 billion
$180 billion
q.commonError: not dividing the AD target by the multiplier
q.feedback: The graph shows a leftward AD movement. MPC = 0.75 gives multiplier 4, so investment must fall by $240 billion / 4 = $60 billion.

q.q: The MS1 to MS2 movement causes AD to shift left by $180 billion. A separate fiscal expansion shifts AD right by $60 billion. What is the net AD change?
options: AD falls by $120 billion.
AD falls by $240 billion.
AD rises by $120 billion.
AD rises by $60 billion.
q.commonError: adding both policies in the same direction without checking graph direction
q.feedback: The graph's monetary policy lowers AD by $180 billion. Fiscal policy raises AD by $60 billion. Net AD falls by $120 billion.

q.q: The Fed pushes r high enough to reduce investment by $90 billion, but AD only needed to move left by $240 billion. If MPC = 0.75, what happens?
options: AD falls $360 billion, overshooting by $120 billion.
AD falls $240 billion, closing the gap exactly.
AD falls $90 billion, leaving $150 billion.
AD rises $360 billion.
q.commonError: failing to compare the multiplied AD effect to the needed AD change
q.feedback: The graph shows AD moving left. MPC = 0.75 gives multiplier 4, so a $90 billion investment fall lowers AD by $360 billion, overshooting by $120 billion.

q.q: At a fixed reference price level, desired spending is $250 billion below the policy target. Government purchases rise by $50 billion and MPC = 0.75. Use the simple spending multiplier with no other leakages. Crowding out produces a total $40 billion AD offset, including its induced spending effects. Which decomposition gives the net AD shift and remaining shortfall at that reference price?
options: Direct AD shift $50 billion; multiplied shift $200 billion; net shift $160 billion; gap $90 billion
Direct AD shift $50 billion; multiplied shift $150 billion; net shift $110 billion; gap $140 billion
Direct AD shift $50 billion; multiplied shift $200 billion; net shift $200 billion; gap $50 billion
Direct AD shift $50 billion; multiplied shift $200 billion; net shift $40 billion; gap $210 billion
q.commonError: calculating the multiplier but ignoring the order: initial shift, multiplied shift, crowding-out offset
q.feedback: MPC = 0.75 gives multiplier 4. The $50 billion initial shift becomes $200 billion, then crowding out lowers the net shift to $160 billion, leaving a $90 billion gap. These are horizontal AD distances at the reference price, not actual equilibrium GDP changes; the total offset is not multiplied again.

q.q: At a fixed reference price level, desired spending already exceeds the policy target by $180 billion. Purchases rise by $30 billion and MPC = 0.8. With the simple spending multiplier and no offsets, which interpretation of the policy is correct?
options: The direct $30 billion increase becomes a $150 billion AD shift, raising excess desired spending to $330 billion at the reference price.
The policy shifts AD left by $150 billion, reducing excess desired spending to $30 billion.
Only the direct $30 billion enters AD, raising excess desired spending to $210 billion.
The $150 billion AD shift exactly removes the existing $180 billion excess.
q.commonError: thinking any rightward AD shift is good regardless of the starting gap
q.feedback: The multiplier is 5, so desired spending at the reference price rises by $150 billion. The excess becomes 180 + 150 = $330 billion. An upward-sloping SRAS would divide the equilibrium response between output and prices; these AD distances do not determine the GDP gap.

q.q: The monetary-policy movement shifts AD left by $160 billion. Fiscal expansion shifts AD right by $160 billion. What is the net AD effect?
options: Zero—equal and opposite shifts.
AD falls $160 billion.
AD rises $160 billion.
AD falls $320 billion.
q.commonError: not matching the leftward AD shift in the graph before adding the fiscal offset
q.feedback: The graph shows monetary policy shifting AD left. A fiscal expansion of the same size shifts AD right by the same amount, so the net AD effect is zero.

q.q: At a fixed reference price, desired spending is $400 billion below the policy target. Government purchases rise by $100 billion and MPC = 0.75. Using the simple spending multiplier and ignoring crowding out and other leakages, which decomposition gives the AD shift and remaining horizontal AD gap?
options: AD first shifts right $100 billion, then the multiplier expands the shift to $400 billion, closing the gap.
AD first shifts right $400 billion, then falls back to $100 billion, leaving a $300 billion gap.
AD first shifts left $100 billion, then left $400 billion, worsening the gap.
AD shifts right $100 billion only, leaving a $300 billion gap.
q.commonError: confusing the first AD shift with the final multiplied AD shift
q.feedback: The multiplier is 4. Direct purchases of $100 billion imply a total $400 billion AD shift, closing the stated horizontal AD gap. Without an SRAS relationship, this does not identify an equal equilibrium GDP increase.

q.q: A recessionary gap begins closing without new policy as wage growth slows and SRAS shifts right. A large discretionary stimulus designed for the original gap is still scheduled to take effect several quarters later. What is the strongest stabilization concern?
options: The delayed stimulus may arrive after much of the gap has self-corrected, pushing AD too far right and creating overheating pressure.
The stimulus becomes contractionary once SRAS begins shifting right.
Self-correction guarantees the stimulus has no effect on aggregate demand.
The delayed stimulus automatically shifts LRAS right by the amount of the original gap.
q.commonError: Assumes a policy designed for an old output gap remains correctly sized after self-correction has already reduced the gap.
q.feedback: Policy lags matter because wages, costs, expectations, and private spending can change before discretionary policy takes effect, creating overshoot risk.

q.q: A government authorizes $75 billion of extra purchases when the required rightward AD shift is $300 billion. Before payment, the required shift at the same reference price falls to $100 billion. The simple spending multiplier is 4; no crowding out or other leakages apply. One third of the authorized purchases must now occur, while the rest can still be cancelled. Which implementation decision meets the revised target without overshooting?
options: Pay the entire remaining $50 billion; the original authorization still matches the revised target.
Pay another $25 billion and cancel $25 billion; the unmultiplied purchases must equal the revised target.
Cancel all $75 billion; a revision of the target eliminates the unavoidable payment.
Cancel the remaining $50 billion; the unavoidable $25 billion already produces the required $100 billion AD shift.
q.commonError: Uses the original output-gap estimate even after newer data show a much smaller gap.
q.feedback: The unavoidable purchases are 75/3 = $25 billion, producing 25 × 4 = $100 billion of AD. The remaining authorization is $50 billion and should be cancelled under the stated target. Full implementation would create a $300 billion shift and a $200 billion overshoot. Policy must be evaluated when it takes effect.

q.q: Inflation pressure is being driven by excessive aggregate demand. Policymakers use contractionary stabilization policy and the policy succeeds in lowering aggregate demand. Before inflation expectations fully adjust, which short-run combination is most consistent with the policy mechanism?
options: Higher inflation pressure together with weaker output and higher unemployment.
No change in unemployment because stabilization policy affects only the price level.
Lower inflation pressure together with weaker output and higher unemployment.
Lower inflation pressure together with stronger output and lower unemployment.
q.commonError: Treats lower inflation pressure from contractionary demand policy as costless in the short run.
q.feedback: A contractionary AD policy can reduce inflation pressure while also lowering output and raising unemployment before expectations fully adjust.

q.q: A short recession causes tax receipts to fall and unemployment-benefit payments to rise automatically. Congress also approves an infrastructure stimulus, but construction begins after the economy has already recovered. Which comparison is strongest?
options: The infrastructure program cannot affect aggregate demand once the recession has ended.
The automatic stabilizers cushion the downturn and recede with conditions, while the delayed discretionary program can add demand after the original gap has faded.
Both responses have the same implementation timing because each changes the government budget.
The automatic stabilizers become contractionary during the recession, while delayed infrastructure is always stabilizing.
q.commonError: Assumes automatic stabilizers and discretionary fiscal programs have the same activation and phase-out timing.
q.feedback: Automatic stabilizers respond as income and employment change without new legislation; discretionary programs can arrive later and may outlast the original gap.

q.q: If output is below its natural level because aggregate demand is weak, stabilization policy would usually try to
options: shift AD right
shift AD left
raise unemployment
reduce spending further
q.commonError: using contractionary policy during weak demand
q.feedback: If AD is too weak, expansionary policy can shift AD right.

q.q: The economy has a recessionary AD gap of $500 billion. Monetary policy raises investment by $50 billion and fiscal policy raises government spending by $60 billion. If MPC = 0.75 and there is no crowding out, what happens?
options: AD rises $440 billion, leaving a $60 billion gap.
AD rises $110 billion, leaving a $390 billion gap.
AD rises $500 billion, closing the gap exactly.
AD overshoots by $60 billion.
q.commonError: not applying the multiplier to the combined spending impulse
q.feedback: Initial impulse is $50 billion + $60 billion = $110 billion. Multiplier is 4, so AD rises $440 billion, leaving a $60 billion gap.

q.q: At a fixed reference price, AD must shift right by $500 billion to meet the policy target. A supplied monetary-policy effect raises autonomous investment by $50 billion, government purchases rise by $60 billion, and fiscal crowding out reduces autonomous investment by $40 billion. MPC = 0.75; apply the same simple multiplier to each autonomous change, with no other leakages. What AD shortfall remains?
options: $220 billion remains.
$100 billion remains.
$60 billion remains.
$460 billion remains.
q.commonError: not subtracting crowding out after applying the multiplier
q.feedback: Net autonomous spending rises by 50 + 60 − 40 = $70 billion. The multiplier is 1/(1 − 0.75) = 4, so AD shifts $280 billion and the remaining horizontal shortfall is 500 − 280 = $220 billion. Subtracting only $40 billion after multiplying the gross impulse would omit the lost induced spending.

q.q: Which example is an automatic stabilizer during a recession?
options: The central bank announces a new bond-purchase program.
Congress passes a one-time infrastructure bill.
A state raises sales taxes to balance its budget.
Unemployment-benefit payments rise without a new legislative vote.
q.commonError: Confusing automatic fiscal responses with newly enacted discretionary policy.
q.feedback: Unemployment benefits expand automatically as more workers qualify, supporting income without new legislation.

q.q: Real output is below potential and inflation pressure is weak. Which demand-management direction is appropriate?
options: Expansionary policy that shifts aggregate demand to the right.
Contractionary policy that shifts aggregate demand left.
A policy that shifts short-run aggregate supply left.
No policy can affect output in the short run.
q.commonError: Applying contractionary policy to a recessionary gap.
q.feedback: Expansionary fiscal or monetary policy can raise aggregate demand and reduce a recessionary gap.

q.q: Why can a long implementation lag make discretionary stabilization policy harmful?
options: The policy always reduces aggregate demand before it begins.
It may arrive after conditions change and destabilize the economy.
The lag permanently prevents prices from adjusting.
The lag converts fiscal policy into monetary policy.
q.commonError: Treating delayed policy as harmless regardless of the business-cycle phase.
q.feedback: A delayed response can arrive after recovery or after inflation has eased, creating a procyclical rather than stabilizing effect.

q.q: A sharp oil-price increase raises inflation and lowers real output. Why is stabilization difficult?
options: Both inflation and output automatically improve with any expansionary policy.
The shock shifts aggregate demand, so only tax policy can respond.
Supporting output may worsen inflation; fighting inflation may deepen the output loss.
Monetary and fiscal policy have identical effects on short-run aggregate supply.
q.commonError: Treating a negative supply shock like a pure demand recession.
q.feedback: A negative supply shock creates stagflation, forcing policymakers to weigh competing inflation and output objectives.

q.q: The economy is near potential output, yet fiscal and monetary policy both become strongly expansionary. What is the main risk?
options: Aggregate demand must fall because the policies cancel each other.
Long-run aggregate supply immediately shifts left.
Crowding out guarantees that output and prices do not change.
Aggregate demand may overshoot capacity and increase inflation.
q.commonError: Assuming two expansionary policies cannot create excessive aggregate demand.
q.feedback: When both policies push spending upward near capacity, the combined demand increase can create an inflationary gap.

q.q: The central bank tightens monetary policy while the government enacts fiscal expansion. What can be concluded about aggregate demand?
options: The net effect is uncertain because the policies work in opposite directions.
Aggregate demand must rise because fiscal policy always dominates.
Aggregate demand must fall because monetary policy always dominates.
Both policies shift aggregate demand to the right.
q.commonError: Declaring a definite outcome without comparing the strength of opposing policy impulses.
q.feedback: Fiscal expansion pushes aggregate demand right, while monetary contraction pushes it left; the net change depends on magnitudes.

q.q: AD is weak by $500 billion. Government spending rises by $80 billion, investment rises by $40 billion, and MPC = 0.75. Ignoring crowding out, what happens to the gap?
options: AD rises $480 billion, leaving a $20 billion gap.
AD rises $120 billion, leaving a $380 billion gap.
AD rises $500 billion, closing the gap exactly.
AD overshoots by $20 billion.
q.commonError: not adding investment and government spending before applying the multiplier
q.feedback: Initial spending impulse is $80 billion + $40 billion = $120 billion. Multiplier is 4, so AD rises $480 billion, leaving a $20 billion gap.

q.q: At a fixed reference price, desired spending exceeds the policy target by $360 billion. Contractionary monetary policy is supplied as reducing autonomous investment by $50 billion. MPC = 0.8; use the simple spending multiplier with no other leakages. What excess desired spending remains at that reference price?
options: $110 billion
$250 billion
$50 billion
No gap remains; policy overshoots by $110 billion.
q.commonError: using the investment decrease without applying the multiplier
q.feedback: The supplied investment fall shifts AD left by 50/(1 − 0.8) = $250 billion. Excess desired spending falls to 360 − 250 = $110 billion. This is an AD-distance calculation, not a claim that the equilibrium GDP gap falls one-for-one.

q.q: At a fixed reference price level, desired spending is $600 billion below the policy target. Government purchases rise by $100 billion and MPC = 0.8. Use the simple spending multiplier with no other leakages. Crowding out produces a total $150 billion AD offset, including its induced spending effects. Which decomposition gives the net AD shift and remaining shortfall at that reference price?
options: AD first shifts right $100 billion, then gross shift reaches $500 billion, then crowding out leaves $350 billion net and a $250 billion gap.
AD first shifts right $600 billion, then crowding out leaves $450 billion net and a $150 billion gap.
AD first shifts left $100 billion, then gross shift reaches $500 billion, worsening the gap.
AD shifts right only $100 billion because crowding out cancels the multiplier.
q.commonError: forgetting that crowding out reduces the gross multiplier effect
q.feedback: MPC 0.8 gives multiplier 5, so gross shift is $500 billion. Net after $150 billion crowding out is $350 billion, leaving a $250 billion gap. These are horizontal AD distances at the reference price, not actual equilibrium GDP changes; the total offset is not multiplied again.

q.q: Contractionary monetary policy is used when the economy is already above potential output. What is the likely effect?
options: It may reduce inflation pressure because it shifts AD left when AD is too high.
It worsens inflation pressure because it shifts AD right.
It cannot affect AD because output is above potential.
It directly shifts SRAS right and fixes supply constraints.
q.commonError: reading the contractionary graph as expansionary policy
q.feedback: The graph shows AD shifting left. If AD is too high, that can reduce inflation pressure.

q.q: A contractionary monetary-policy move reduces investment by $60 billion. A separate fiscal expansion raises AD by $400 billion after the multiplier. If MPC = 0.75, what is the final net AD effect?
options: +$160 billion
+$340 billion
+$240 billion
+$460 billion
q.commonError: subtracting only the initial investment drop instead of its multiplied AD effect
q.feedback: The graph shows contractionary monetary policy. A $60 billion investment fall times multiplier 4 reduces AD by $240 billion. Net effect is $400 billion - $240 billion = +$160 billion.

q.q: If policymakers use contractionary monetary policy during a negative supply shock, what is the strongest critique?
options: It may reduce inflation pressure but can worsen the output loss because AD shifts left.
It directly restores lost supply while keeping output unchanged.
It shifts AD right and raises output without inflation risk.
It eliminates the need to consider SRAS.
q.commonError: treating every supply shock as if AD policy has no tradeoff
q.feedback: The graph shows AD shifting left. That can cool inflation pressure, but during a negative supply shock it may deepen the output loss.

q.q: Which policy acts automatically to cushion a recession without a new vote by Congress?
options: Unemployment benefits that rise as workers lose jobs
A one-time discretionary tax bill
A Federal Reserve bond sale
A price ceiling
q.feedback: Automatic stabilizers change with economic conditions; unemployment benefits rise as unemployment rises.

q.q: If output is below potential because AD is weak, policy that shifts AD right is:
options: Expansionary
Contractionary
Neutral
A supply shock
q.feedback: Expansionary policy shifts AD right and can help close a recessionary gap.

q.q: In a liquidity trap, interest rates are often near:
options: Zero
100 percent
The price level
The reserve ratio
q.feedback: A liquidity trap occurs when interest rates are near zero and monetary policy has less room to work.

q.q: Policy lags matter because policy may arrive:
options: After conditions have changed
Before money exists
Only when LRAS shifts
Only when M1 equals M2
q.feedback: Policy can become poorly timed if it takes effect after the economy has changed.

q.commonError: Assumes a delayed policy has the same stabilizing effect regardless of how the economy changes before implementation.
q.q: A stimulus is approved during a recession but takes effect only after output has returned close to potential. What problem should the student diagnose?
options: The delayed stimulus can push aggregate demand too far right after the original gap has faded.
The delay automatically turns the stimulus into contractionary policy.
The policy can no longer affect aggregate demand once recovery begins.
The delay directly shifts LRAS left.
q.feedback: A policy can destabilize the economy if it arrives after the original gap has already narrowed or reversed.

q.commonError: Choosing tighter policy in a recessionary gap.
q.q: A recessionary AD gap can be addressed with:
options: Expansionary monetary or fiscal policy
Contractionary policy only
Higher taxes only
Lower government spending only
q.feedback: Expansionary policy can shift AD right.

q.commonError: Treats a negative supply shock as if policymakers can simultaneously eliminate its inflation and output effects by shifting AD.
q.q: A negative supply shock lowers real output and raises the price level. If policymakers use expansionary demand policy to support output, what tradeoff should the student remember?
options: It can support output while worsening inflation pressure.
It lowers the price level and raises output with no tradeoff.
It directly shifts SRAS right and restores productive capacity.
It must reduce both output and the price level.
q.feedback: Demand stabilization during a negative supply shock involves a tradeoff: supporting output can worsen price pressure, while reducing inflation can deepen the output loss.

q.commonError: Choosing expansionary policy during overheating.
q.q: During an inflationary boom caused by excessive AD, policymakers may use:
options: Contractionary monetary or fiscal policy
Expansionary policy only
Tax cuts and bond purchases
Higher government spending
q.feedback: Contractionary policy shifts AD left and reduces inflation pressure.

q.q: After a negative AD shock, output is below potential, but wages and input costs are already adjusting downward and SRAS is shifting right. What additional question belongs to stabilization-policy analysis?
options: Whether policymakers should deliberately shift AD right rather than wait for the self-correcting SRAS adjustment.
Whether LRAS should be moved left to meet the current level of output.
Whether the multiplier should be redefined as zero during every recession.
Whether unemployment should be excluded from the labor force until recovery is complete.
q.feedback: Long-run adjustment describes endogenous SRAS movement; stabilization policy asks whether policymakers should deliberately change AD instead of waiting.
q.commonError: Treats self-correction and active stabilization as the same mechanism.

q.q: The Fed increases money supply, but rates are already near zero and investment barely responds. What is this problem?
options: Liquidity trap
Crowding out
Inflation tax
Menu cost
q.feedback: A liquidity trap weakens the usual interest-rate channel of monetary policy.

q.q: A stimulus bill takes effect after the recession has already ended. What problem is this?
options: Policy lag
Money multiplier
Inflation tax
LRPC shift
q.feedback: Policy lags can cause stimulus to arrive after economic conditions have changed.

q.commonError: Not comparing stimulus size to the recessionary gap.
q.q: A recessionary AD gap is $300 billion. Policy raises spending by $75 billion and the multiplier is 4. What happens?
options: The gap closes exactly
A $75 billion gap remains
AD overshoots by $75 billion
The gap is unchanged
q.feedback: $75 billion x 4 = $300 billion, so the gap closes exactly.

q.commonError: Stops with an AD shift and does not connect the short-run output response to unemployment and inflation pressure.
q.q: Contractionary stabilization policy shifts AD left to cool an overheating economy. Which short-run labor-market effect connects this policy choice to Phillips-curve analysis?
options: Unemployment tends to rise as output weakens while inflation pressure falls.
Unemployment must fall because lower AD always increases hiring.
Unemployment is unchanged because only the price level responds to AD.
The natural rate permanently falls by the size of the AD shift.
q.feedback: A contractionary stabilization policy that lowers AD can reduce inflation pressure while raising unemployment in the short run, creating the bridge to Phillips-curve analysis.

q.q: A tax levied on sellers and an equal tax levied on buyers are generally:
options: Equivalent in their market effects
Completely unrelated
Opposite in their effect on quantity
Always paid only by sellers
q.commonError: thinks_legal_tax_assignment_determines_full_burden
q.feedback: A tax on buyers or sellers creates the same wedge and similar market effects.

q.q: Refer to the graph. At the post-tax quantity of 60 thousand movies, what price do sellers receive?
options: $10.50 per movie
$13.50 per movie
$7.50 per movie
$6.00 per movie
q.commonError: misreads_graph_or_policy_effect
q.feedback: At quantity 60 thousand, the shifted demand curve intersects supply at $7.50. That is the amount sellers receive before the buyer remits the tax.

q.q: A tax is legally imposed on sellers, but buyers pay most of the burden. What explains this?
options: Legal assignment does not determine economic burden
Sellers always avoid all taxes
Buyers became legally responsible for the tax after prices adjusted.
The market must have a price ceiling
q.commonError: thinks_legal_tax_assignment_determines_full_burden
q.feedback: Tax burden depends on market responses, not just who is legally assigned to pay.

q.q: Refer to the graph. What per-unit tax wedge is created by the buyer-side tax?
options: $3 per movie
$7.50 per movie
$21 per movie
$6 per movie
q.commonError: misreads_graph_or_policy_effect
q.feedback: At the post-tax quantity, read the buyer price and seller receipt from the graph and take the difference: $13.50 − $7.50 = $6.

q.q: Refer to the graph. Which side bears more of the buyer-side tax?
options: Neither; the burden is split equally.
Buyers bear more of the tax than sellers.
Sellers bear more of the tax than buyers.
Neither side bears any economic tax burden.
q.commonError: misreads_graph_or_policy_effect
q.feedback: Buyers pay $3 more than the original $10.50 price, while sellers receive $3 less. The legal placement on buyers does not make buyers bear the entire tax.

q.q: A tax is legally imposed on sellers, but buyers end up paying most of the burden. What does this show?
options: Economic incidence does not depend only on legal assignment
Sellers never pay taxes
Buyers must have become the statutory taxpayers when the market price changed.
The tax must be a price ceiling
q.commonError: thinks_legal_assignment_determines_full_burden
q.feedback: Who legally pays the tax does not determine who bears the economic burden.

q.q: A policy analyst says a tax legally placed on sellers will be paid entirely by sellers. What is wrong with this claim?
options: Legal assignment does not determine economic incidence
Sellers always pass the entire tax to buyers
Buyers always avoid taxes completely
A seller tax is the same as a price floor
q.commonError: thinks_legal_assignment_determines_full_burden
q.feedback: Economic tax burden depends on market responses and elasticities, not only on who legally sends payment.

q.q: A tax causes buyers to pay more, sellers to receive less, and quantity to fall. Which statement is false?
options: The side legally assigned the tax must bear the entire burden
The tax creates a wedge between buyer and seller prices
The market quantity falls after the tax
Buyers and sellers can both be worse off per unit traded
q.commonError: chooses_true_tax_wedge_statement_as_false
q.feedback: The legal assignment does not determine the entire burden. Market elasticities matter.

q.q: Refer to the tax graph. If the same per-unit tax is collected from buyers instead of sellers, with demand and supply unchanged, which outcome follows?
options: Buyers still pay $18 in total, sellers keep $12, and 80 units trade
Buyers pay $21 in total, sellers keep $15, and 80 units trade
Buyers pay $18 in total, sellers keep $18, and 100 units trade
Buyers pay $15 in total, sellers keep $9, and 100 units trade
q.commonError: thinks_legal_assignment_determines_tax_burden
q.feedback: The graph establishes a $6 wedge at quantity 80, with total buyer payment $18 and net seller receipt $12. Changing the remitter preserves this wedge and equilibrium. Under buyer remittance, buyers pay sellers $12 and government $6; that does not make the economic buyer burden $6.

q.q: Refer to the tax graph. If sellers instead remitted the same tax, with both curves fixed, which bundle would give the total buyer payment, net seller receipt and quantity?
options: $7.50 paid, $13.50 received, and 60,000 units traded
$13.50 paid, $7.50 received, and 60,000 units traded
$13.50 paid, $7.50 received, and 100,000 units traded
$10.50 paid, $4.50 received, and 100,000 units traded
q.commonError: misreads_graph_or_policy_effect
q.feedback: Supply intersects Demand with tax at 60,000 units and $7.50 received by sellers. At that quantity, original demand gives the $13.50 total buyer payment. The $6 difference goes to government. Switching remittance to sellers preserves these total and net prices and quantity.

q.q: A seller-side tax shifts the supply curve upward. Which statement best explains why buyers still pay part of the tax?
options: Elasticities determine how the tax is split.
Buyers voluntarily pay taxes for sellers
The demand curve shifts right by the tax amount
The tax creates a price ceiling
q.commonError: confuses_who_remits_tax_with_who_bears_tax
q.feedback: Legal remittance does not determine economic burden. Prices adjust based on supply and demand elasticities.

q.q: A tax is placed on buyers instead of sellers. In a standard supply-demand model, why is the final outcome similar to an equal seller tax?
options: Both taxes create the same buyer–seller price wedge.
Only buyer taxes reduce quantity
Only seller taxes raise prices
The tax disappears if buyers legally pay it
q.commonError: thinks_legal_side_changes_total_wedge_effect
q.feedback: A buyer tax or seller tax of the same size creates the same wedge and reduces quantity similarly.

q.q: A seller tax and a buyer tax of the same size create the same wedge in the same market. What does this imply about the market outcome?
options: The market outcome is equivalent even if the legal payer differs
The seller tax always hurts sellers more
The buyer tax always hurts buyers more
Only the tax on sellers reduces quantity
q.commonError: legal_assignment_controls_outcome
q.feedback: Equivalent taxes on buyers or sellers create the same wedge and market outcome.

q.q: Refer to the graph. Under the buyer-remitted $6 tax, buyers pay the seller $7.50 and remit $6 separately. The tax is now collected from sellers, with unchanged curves and compliance. A cinema proposes charging $13.50 plus another $6 to preserve its receipt. Which corrected invoice and burden calculation fits the same competitive equilibrium?
options: Invoice $13.50 plus $6; buyers bear $9 and sellers bear $3 relative to $10.50.
Invoice $7.50 including tax; buyers gain $3 and sellers bear $9 relative to $10.50.
Invoice $10.50 including tax; buyers bear $0 and sellers bear $6 relative to $10.50.
Invoice $13.50 including tax; buyers bear $3 and sellers bear $3 relative to $10.50.
q.commonError: misreads_graph_or_policy_effect
q.feedback: The $6 wedge remains: buyers pay $13.50 in total and sellers retain $7.50 after remittance, at 60 thousand tickets. Seller remittance means the $13.50 invoice includes the tax. Against the untaxed $10.50 price, each side bears $3. Adding another $6 would double-count the tax and would not be the same equilibrium.

q.q: Refer to the concert graph with Demand with tax. The law changes so sellers remit the same tax instead. With demand and supply fixed, which cash-flow description fits the resulting equilibrium?
options: Buyers pay sellers $8; sellers remit $8 and keep $0; 150,000 tickets trade
Buyers pay sellers $18; sellers remit $8 and keep $10; 200,000 tickets trade
Buyers pay sellers $16; sellers remit $8 and keep $8; 150,000 tickets trade
Buyers pay sellers $16; sellers remit $6 and keep $10; 200,000 tickets trade
q.imageAlt: The concert-ticket market has price vertically and quantity in thousands horizontally. D0 and S0 intersect at A, quantity 200 and price 10 dollars. Demand with tax intersects supply at quantity 150 and seller price 8; original demand there gives buyer price 16.
q.commonError: misreads_graph_relationship
q.feedback: The graph shows buyer cost $16 and net seller receipt $8 at 150,000 tickets, so the wedge is $8. Switching remittance changes the transaction payment, not these net prices or quantity. Sellers now collect $16, forward $8 and retain $8.
q.graphDescription: The concert-ticket market has price vertically and quantity in thousands horizontally. D0 and S0 intersect at A, quantity 200 and price 10 dollars. Demand with tax intersects supply at quantity 150 and seller price 8; original demand there gives buyer price 16.

q.q: A $6 tax is legally remitted by buyers. Before it, 120 repairs sold for $25 each; afterward, 100 repairs sell, buyers pay $29 in total and firms keep $23. A firm says buyer remittance leaves its sales receipts unaffected. What refutes the claim?
options: Net sales receipts fall by $700, although the seller burden is only $2 per remaining repair
Net sales receipts fall by $600, equal to the full government receipt
Net sales receipts rise by $400, because buyers pay $4 more per repair
Net sales receipts remain $3,000, because firms do not remit the tax
q.commonError: assumes_nonlegal_side_is_unaffected
q.feedback: Firms initially receive 120 × $25 = $3,000, then 100 × $23 = $2,300: a $700 decline. Only $200 is the $2 price burden on continuing repairs; $500 reflects lost sales at the old price. Sales receipts are not profit or producer surplus. Legal remittance does not shield firms from price and quantity changes.

q.q: Refer to the tax graph. A proposal shifts remittance to sellers while keeping the tax unchanged. Which forecast correctly combines revenue and economic incidence?
options: Revenue stays $600,000; buyers and sellers each bear $3 per unit
Revenue stays $360,000; sellers now bear the entire $6 per unit
Revenue falls to $180,000; only the new legal remitter has a burden
Revenue stays $360,000; buyers and sellers each bear $3 per unit
q.commonError: misreads_graph_or_policy_effect
q.feedback: The wedge is $13.50 − $7.50 = $6 and 60,000 units trade, giving $360,000 in revenue. Relative to the original $10.50 price, buyer and seller burdens are each $3. The same fixed curves and wedge yield the same equilibrium under seller remittance.

q.q: A $5 tax is legally placed on sellers. After the tax, buyers pay $3 more than before and sellers receive $2 less than before. What does this show?
options: The legal side pays the government, but buyers and sellers share the economic burden
The legal side bears the full burden because sellers are the ones sending in the tax
The buyer side avoids the burden because the law places the payment on sellers
The seller side avoids the burden because buyers now pay a higher market price
q.commonError: confuses_legal_liability_with_economic_burden
q.feedback: Legal assignment does not determine economic burden. Buyers and sellers share the tax through changes in prices.

q.q: A $5 tax is placed on buyers instead of sellers. Supply and demand conditions are unchanged. What should happen compared with an equal tax on sellers?
options: The same wedge, quantity reduction, and burden split occur
Buyers bear all of the tax because they legally pay it
Sellers bear all of the tax because they receive less
The tax disappears because sellers are not legally charged
q.commonError: thinks_statutory_side_determines_burden
q.feedback: A tax on buyers and an equal tax on sellers create the same wedge and the same economic outcome. The legal side does not control the burden.

q.q: Refer to the tax-incidence graph. The tax shown raises the buyer price to $18, lowers the seller price to $12, and reduces quantity to 80. If the same per-unit tax were legally imposed on buyers instead of sellers, what would change?
options: Nothing about the final buyer price, seller price, or quantity
Buyers would pay $12, sellers would receive $18, and quantity would remain 80
Buyers would bear the entire tax, so sellers would still receive $15
The tax wedge would disappear because supply would no longer shift
q.commonError: thinks_legal_assignment_changes_market_outcome
q.feedback: An equal per-unit tax creates the same wedge and equilibrium whether the law assigns payment to buyers or sellers.

q.q: Demand is Qd=100-2Pb and supply is Qs=2Ps, where Pb is the buyer’s total price and Ps is the seller’s net receipt. A $5 unit tax is first remitted by sellers, then by buyers, with unchanged schedules and compliance. Which outcome and interpretation are correct?
options: Seller remittance yields Pb=$25 and Ps=$20, while buyer remittance yields Pb=$30 and Ps=$25; legal assignment fixes who loses.
Both systems yield Pb=$27.50, Ps=$22.50 and Q=45; the legal payer changes but the same wedge determines economic incidence.
Both systems yield Pb=$25, Ps=$25 and Q=50; changing the remitter cancels the wedge from equilibrium.
Both systems yield Pb=$22.50, Ps=$27.50 and Q=45; sellers receive more than buyers pay because the tax is a transfer.
q.commonError: thinks_legal_assignment_changes_market_outcome
q.feedback: Use Pb=Ps+5 and 100-2Pb=2Ps. Then 90=4Ps, so Ps=22.5, Pb=27.5 and Q=45. The untaxed price was 25, giving each side a 2.5 burden. Remittance changes the payment route, not these equations.

q.q: Under a seller-remitted tax, buyers pay $52 and sellers keep $46 per unit. The same tax is reassigned to buyers, with curves unchanged. An invoice then asks buyers to pay sellers $52 plus a separate tax payment. Which correction preserves the original economic outcome?
options: Pay sellers $52 and government $6, for $58 in total
Pay sellers $49 and government $3, for $52 in total
Pay sellers $46 and government $6, for $52 in total
Pay sellers $46 and government nothing, for $46 in total
q.commonError: thinks_legal_assignment_changes_market_outcome
q.feedback: The original wedge is $52 − $46 = $6. Under buyer remittance, the seller transaction payment must be $46, with another $6 sent directly to government. Paying sellers $52 and then adding $6 double-counts the wedge relative to the equivalent equilibrium.

q.q: Labor demand is Ld=120-2Wf and supply is Ls=2Ww. Wf is the employer’s total cost and Ww is take-home pay. An $8 per-worker payroll tax is legally moved from firms to workers without other changes. Which prediction refutes the claim that firms’ economic burden disappears?
options: Wf falls to $30 and Ww to $22, with employment 60; legal reassignment removes all employer burden.
Wf remains $34 and Ww rises to $34, with employment 52; workers now remit the tax from a higher net wage.
Wf remains $34 and Ww $26, with employment 52; each side still bears $4 relative to the untaxed $30 wage.
Wf rises to $38 and Ww stays $30, with employment 44; firms bear all tax whenever labor demand slopes down.
q.commonError: confuses_who_remits_tax_with_who_bears_tax
q.feedback: The wedge is Wf-Ww=8 regardless of remitter. Solve 120-2(Ww+8)=2Ww: Ww=26, Wf=34 and L=52. Without tax W=30. Employer and worker burdens are 4 each, unchanged by the statutory relabeling.

q.q: Whether a tax is legally collected from buyers or sellers, its economic burden depends mainly on:
options: Relative elasticities
Which side writes the check
The number of firms only
The tax's label
q.feedback: Legal incidence does not determine economic incidence; elasticities determine who bears more burden.

q.q: A $4 tax on buyers and a $4 tax on sellers create the same wedge in the same market. What should happen to the market outcome?
options: The outcome should be equivalent
The buyer tax must hurt only buyers
The seller tax must hurt only sellers
Only the seller tax reduces quantity
q.commonError: thinks_legal_tax_assignment_controls_outcome
q.feedback: Equivalent taxes on buyers or sellers create the same wedge and market outcome.

q.q: A student says, 'If sellers legally pay the tax, buyers avoid the burden.' What is wrong?
options: Elasticities, not legal labels, determine burden
The statement is always correct
Sellers cannot change prices
Taxes do not affect buyers
q.commonError: thinks_legal_assignment_determines_full_burden
q.feedback: Legal assignment does not determine who bears the economic burden.

q.q: The law of supply says that, other things equal:
options: As price rises, quantity supplied rises
As price rises, demand rises
As price falls, quantity supplied rises
As price falls, supply shifts right
q.commonError: confuses_supply_with_demand_direction
q.feedback: The law of supply says price and quantity supplied move in the same direction.

q.q: If the price of a good rises, what happens to quantity supplied?
options: Quantity supplied increases
Supply decreases
Demand increases
The supply curve shifts left
q.commonError: treats_own_price_change_as_supply_shift
q.feedback: A change in the good's own price causes movement along the supply curve.

q.q: Which change would shift the supply curve?
options: A change in input costs
A change in the good's own price
A change in quantity demanded
A movement along the demand curve.
q.commonError: thinks_own_price_shifts_supply
q.feedback: Input costs shift supply. The good's own price changes quantity supplied.

q.q: If the cost of steel rises for car producers, what happens to the supply of cars?
options: Supply decreases
Supply increases
Demand decreases
Quantity demanded increases
q.commonError: gets_input_cost_effect_backwards
q.feedback: Steel is an input in car production. A higher steel price raises producers' costs, so the car supply curve shifts left.

q.q: An improvement in production technology usually causes:
options: Supply to increase
Demand to decrease
Quantity demanded to fall because price changed
A binding price floor
q.commonError: misses_technology_as_supply_shifter
q.feedback: Better technology makes production easier or cheaper, shifting supply right.

q.q: Market supply at a given price is the:
options: Sum of the quantities all sellers are willing and able to offer.
Quantity supplied by the single largest seller at that price.
Average quantity each seller plans to produce at that price.
Total quantity buyers are willing and able to purchase at that price.
q.commonError: Confusing market supply with one firm’s supply or with demand.
q.feedback: Market supply horizontally adds the quantities supplied by every seller at each price.

q.q: On the displayed coffee supply curve, what price and quantity are shown at point A?
options: $11 and 225 thousand units
$6 and 225 thousand units
$6 and 100 thousand units
$2 and 100 thousand units
q.commonError: misreads_graph_or_confuses_shift_with_movement
q.feedback: At point A, the supply curve pairs a price of $6 with a quantity supplied of 100 thousand units.

q.q: In the displayed hamburger market, the move from S0 to S1 represents:
options: A decrease in supply
An increase in supply
An increase in quantity supplied caused only by a higher price
A decrease in demand
q.commonError: misreads_graph_or_confuses_shift_with_movement
q.feedback: S1 lies to the left and above S0, showing less quantity supplied at each common price.

q.q: How should the taco supply change from S0 to S1 be classified?
options: A decrease in supply
An increase in quantity supplied caused only by a higher price
An increase in supply
A decrease in demand
q.commonError: misreads_graph_or_confuses_shift_with_movement
q.feedback: S1 lies below and to the right of S0, showing more quantity supplied at each common price.

q.q: The price of a good falls, and sellers produce less of it. What happened?
options: Quantity supplied decreased
Supply decreased
Demand increased
Supply shifted right
q.commonError: treats_own_price_change_as_supply_shift
q.feedback: A change in the good's own price changes quantity supplied, not supply.

q.q: A new machine lowers the cost of producing shoes. What happens to the supply of shoes?
options: Supply increases
Supply decreases
Demand decreases
Quantity demanded decreases
q.commonError: misses_technology_as_supply_shifter
q.feedback: Lower production costs from better technology shift supply right.

q.q: Several sellers leave the market. What happens to market supply?
options: Supply decreases
Supply increases
Demand decreases
Quantity supplied rises
q.commonError: misses_number_of_sellers_as_supply_shifter
q.feedback: Fewer sellers means less market supply at each price.

q.q: An input used to make pizza becomes more expensive. What is the likely effect in the pizza market?
options: Supply decreases and price rises
Supply increases and price falls
Demand increases and price rises
Quantity demanded increases because cost rose
q.commonError: gets_input_cost_equilibrium_effect_backwards
q.feedback: Higher input costs decrease supply, which tends to raise price.

q.q: Refer to the supply and demand graph. Which curve shift is shown when equilibrium moves from Price P2, Quantity Q1 to Price P1, Quantity Q2?
options: A rightward shift in supply
A rightward shift in demand
A leftward shift in demand
A leftward shift in supply
q.commonError: mistakes_supply_shift_for_demand_shift
q.feedback: The move from D1 with S1 to D1 with S2 lowers price and raises quantity, which matches an increase in supply.

q.q: The government begins paying producers a subsidy for every unit sold. What happens to market supply, other things equal?
options: Supply shifts left because the subsidy increases firms’ effective production cost.
Supply shifts right because the subsidy lowers the effective marginal cost of selling output.
Quantity supplied rises along the original curve because only the market price changed.
Demand shifts right because the payment is received directly by buyers.
q.commonError: Treating a producer subsidy as a movement along supply or a demand shifter.
q.feedback: A per-unit producer subsidy raises the return from supplying each unit and shifts supply right.

q.q: Points A and B lie on one supply curve. What economic change occurs between them?
options: Supply increases, shifting S to the right.
Price rises, causing quantity supplied to decrease along S.
Demand increases, shifting D to the right.
Price rises, causing quantity supplied to increase along S.
q.commonError: misreads_graph_or_confuses_shift_with_movement
q.feedback: A and B lie on the same supply curve. The higher price is associated with a larger quantity supplied, so this is a movement along supply, not a shift.

q.q: Moving from point A to point B on the displayed supply curve changes quantity supplied by:
options: An increase of 125 thousand units
A decrease of 125 thousand units
An increase of 5 thousand units
An increase of 225 thousand units
q.commonError: misreads_graph_or_confuses_shift_with_movement
q.feedback: Quantity supplied rises from 100 thousand at A to 225 thousand at B, an increase of 125 thousand.

q.q: At a price of $9 on the displayed hamburger graph, how does quantity supplied change when supply shifts from S0 to S1?
options: It increases from 100 thousand to 200 thousand
It decreases from 200 thousand to 100 thousand
It decreases from 300 thousand to 200 thousand
It stays at 200 thousand
q.commonError: misreads_graph_or_confuses_shift_with_movement
q.feedback: At $9, S0 shows 200 thousand units while S1 shows 100 thousand, a decrease of 100 thousand at the same price.

q.q: Which event is consistent with the shift from S0 to S1 shown in the hamburger market?
options: The price of hamburgers rises and firms move up S0
A new cost-saving grill technology is adopted
The price of a major meat input rises
More hamburger restaurants enter the market
q.commonError: misreads_graph_or_confuses_shift_with_movement
q.feedback: Higher input costs reduce supply, shifting the supply curve left.

q.q: What does the movement from point A to point B on S0 represent?
options: An increase in supply because the supply curve shifts right.
A decrease in quantity supplied because the price is higher.
An increase in demand because buyers move along the demand curve.
An increase in quantity supplied because the price is higher.
q.commonError: misreads_graph_or_confuses_shift_with_movement
q.feedback: A and B lie on the same S0 curve. Price rises from $3 to $4 and quantity supplied rises from 100 thousand to 225 thousand, so this is a movement along supply.

q.q: At a price of $3, the shift from S0 to S1 changes quantity supplied from 100 thousand to approximately:
options: 225 thousand
125 thousand
200 thousand
325 thousand
q.commonError: misreads_graph_or_confuses_shift_with_movement
q.feedback: At $3, point A on S0 is 100 thousand, while S1 crosses the $3 line at about 225 thousand. Supply therefore increases by about 125 thousand units at that price.

q.q: Refer to the graph. What market change is shown from A to B?
options: Supply increases, lowering price and raising quantity
Demand increases, raising price and quantity
Supply decreases, raising price and reducing quantity
Demand decreases, lowering price and quantity
q.imageAlt: The movie-ticket market has price in dollars on the vertical axis and quantity in thousands on the horizontal axis. D0 is a downward-sloping demand curve. S0 and S1 are upward-sloping supply curves, with S1 lying to the left of S0 at each displayed price. Point A is the D0-S0 intersection at quantity 200 and price $10. Point B is the D0-S1 intersection at quantity 150 and price $12.
q.commonError: misreads_graph_relationship
q.feedback: Supply shifts left; price rises from 10 to 12 and quantity falls from 200 to 150 thousand.
q.graphDescription: The movie-ticket market has price in dollars on the vertical axis and quantity in thousands on the horizontal axis. D0 is a downward-sloping demand curve. S0 and S1 are upward-sloping supply curves, with S1 lying to the left of S0 at each displayed price. Point A is the D0-S0 intersection at quantity 200 and price $10. Point B is the D0-S1 intersection at quantity 150 and price $12.

q.q: Refer to the graph. Why is the move from A to B a decrease in supply rather than merely a decrease in quantity supplied?
options: Supply itself shifts left from S0 to S1
Quantity supplied rises along the original S0 curve
Demand itself shifts right from D0 to D1
The market stays at A on the original curves
q.imageAlt: The movie-ticket market has price in dollars on the vertical axis and quantity in thousands on the horizontal axis. D0 is a downward-sloping demand curve. S0 and S1 are upward-sloping supply curves, with S1 lying to the left of S0 at each displayed price. Point A is the D0-S0 intersection at quantity 200 and price $10. Point B is the D0-S1 intersection at quantity 150 and price $12.
q.commonError: misreads_graph_relationship
q.feedback: A quantity-supplied change moves along one curve; here the supply curve itself shifts.
