q.graphDescription: The movie-ticket market has price in dollars on the vertical axis and quantity in thousands on the horizontal axis. D0 is a downward-sloping demand curve. S0 and S1 are upward-sloping supply curves, with S1 lying to the left of S0 at each displayed price. Point A is the D0-S0 intersection at quantity 200 and price $10. Point B is the D0-S1 intersection at quantity 150 and price $12.

q.q: The price of handmade tables rises, and sellers produce more tables. What happened?
options: Quantity supplied increased
Supply increased
Demand increased
Supply shifted right
q.commonError: treats_own_price_change_as_supply_shift
q.feedback: A change in the good's own price causes movement along supply, so quantity supplied changes.

q.q: At a market price of $8, approximately how many units does the displayed coffee supply curve show producers are willing to sell?
options: 100 thousand units
175 thousand units
150 thousand units
225 thousand units
q.commonError: misreads_graph_or_confuses_shift_with_movement
q.feedback: The supply line passes through quantity 150 thousand at a price of $8.

q.q: Refer to the graph. A producer says the move from A to B proves that supply increased by 125 thousand units. What is the correct diagnosis?
options: Any quantity increase counts as an increase in supply.
A and B show a leftward shift of the supply curve.
The higher quantity means the demand curve shifted right.
It is more quantity supplied, not an increase in supply.
q.commonError: misreads_graph_or_confuses_shift_with_movement
q.feedback: A change in the good's own price changes quantity supplied along a fixed supply curve. A supply increase would require a rightward shift of the entire curve.

q.q: A new production method cuts the cost of making solar panels. What happens in the solar panel market?
options: Supply increases, price falls, and quantity rises
Supply decreases, price rises, and quantity falls
Demand increases, price rises, and quantity rises
Quantity demanded decreases because supply rose
q.commonError: confuses_supply_increase_with_demand_increase
q.feedback: Lower production costs increase supply, which lowers price and raises quantity.

q.q: A tax on producers raises the cost of selling bottled water. What is the likely market effect?
options: Supply decreases, price rises, and quantity falls
Supply increases, price falls, and quantity rises
Demand decreases, price falls, and quantity falls
Demand increases because taxes fund public services
q.commonError: does_not_treat_tax_as_cost_increase
q.feedback: A tax on producers raises production cost, shifting supply left and reducing quantity.

q.q: Producers expect the future price of a product to rise sharply, so they hold inventory back today. What happens to current supply?
options: Current supply decreases
Current supply increases
Current demand decreases
Quantity supplied increases because current price changed
q.commonError: gets_producer_expectation_effect_backwards
q.feedback: If sellers expect higher future prices, they may reduce current supply to sell later.

q.q: Refer to the supply and demand shift graph. Which movement shows an increase in supply with demand fixed at D2?
options: From P3, Q2 to P2, Q3
From P2, Q1 to P1, Q2
From P1, Q2 to P2, Q3
From P2, Q3 to P3, Q2
q.commonError: uses_d1_equilibrium_when_question_says_d2
q.feedback: With demand fixed at D2, moving from S1 to S2 changes equilibrium from P3, Q2 to P2, Q3.

q.q: Workers accept lower wages, but producers also expect the product’s future price to rise and hold inventory for later sale. What can be concluded about current supply?
options: Supply must rise because lower wages dominate the decision to withhold inventory.
Supply must fall because withholding inventory dominates the wage reduction.
The net supply shift is uncertain because lower wages and inventory withholding work in opposite directions.
Supply stays fixed because wages and expected future prices only move firms along supply.
q.commonError: Using only one supply shifter when several operate at once.
q.feedback: Lower wages reduce production costs and increase supply. Holding inventory for a higher expected future price reduces current supply. Their relative sizes determine the net shift.

q.q: Refer to the graph. Calculate the quantity response per $1 price increase from A to B, then infer which supply relationship that calculation illustrates.
options: Quantity supplied rises 25 thousand per $1 increase, illustrating movement along an upward-sloping supply curve
Supply rises 25 thousand per $1 increase, illustrating a rightward shift of the supply curve
Quantity supplied falls 25 thousand per $1 increase, illustrating movement down the supply curve
Supply rises 125 thousand per $1 increase because production costs decline
q.commonError: misreads_graph_or_confuses_shift_with_movement
q.feedback: From A to B, price rises $5 and quantity supplied rises 125 thousand, or 25 thousand per dollar. Because the product's own price changes, this is movement along supply rather than a curve shift.

q.q: Refer to the graph. At $9, compare S0 with S1. Which event and quantity change are consistent with that comparison?
options: Lower input costs; 100 thousand fewer units supplied.
A fall in the product’s own price; 100 thousand fewer units at the same $9 price.
Higher input costs; 200 thousand fewer units supplied.
Higher input costs; 100 thousand fewer units supplied.
q.commonError: misreads_graph_or_confuses_shift_with_movement
q.feedback: At $9, supply falls from 200 thousand on S0 to 100 thousand on S1. Higher input costs can cause this leftward shift. A change in the product’s own price cannot explain different quantities at the same price.

q.q: Which comparison correctly distinguishes the two changes visible in the taco graph?
options: A to B is an increase in supply; S0 to S1 is movement along supply
A to B is movement along S0; S0 to S1 is an increase in supply
Both A to B and S0 to S1 are movements caused only by price
Both changes are decreases in supply
q.commonError: misreads_graph_or_confuses_shift_with_movement
q.feedback: A and B are points on one curve, so their difference is quantity supplied. Moving from S0 to S1 shifts the entire curve and changes supply.

q.q: Refer to the graph. Equilibrium moves from A to B after one market determinant changes. Evaluate the graph evidence: which explanation identifies the curve shift and connects it to the new price and quantity?
options: Higher theater operating costs shift supply left, raising price and reducing quantity
A higher substitute price shifts demand left, raising price and reducing quantity
Higher consumer income shifts supply left for a normal good, reducing quantity
A lower ticket price shifts supply left as firms move along the demand curve
q.imageAlt: The movie-ticket market has price in dollars on the vertical axis and quantity in thousands on the horizontal axis. D0 is a downward-sloping demand curve. S0 and S1 are upward-sloping supply curves, with S1 lying to the left of S0 at each displayed price. Point A is the D0-S0 intersection at quantity 200 and price $10. Point B is the D0-S1 intersection at quantity 150 and price $12.
q.commonError: misreads_graph_relationship
q.feedback: Higher operating costs reduce supply, shifting it left from S0 to S1. With demand unchanged, the equilibrium moves from A to B: price rises and quantity falls.
q.graphDescription: The movie-ticket market has price in dollars on the vertical axis and quantity in thousands on the horizontal axis. D0 is a downward-sloping demand curve. S0 and S1 are upward-sloping supply curves, with S1 lying to the left of S0 at each displayed price. Point A is the D0-S0 intersection at quantity 200 and price $10. Point B is the D0-S1 intersection at quantity 150 and price $12.

q.q: Demand rises and the market price increases. Firms respond by producing more with the same technology, input prices, and number of sellers. Which statement is correct?
options: Supply shifts right because firms produce more.
Quantity supplied rises along an unchanged supply curve.
Supply shifts left because the product is now more expensive.
Both supply and quantity supplied must increase.
q.commonError: Calling a price-induced movement along supply an increase in supply.
q.feedback: A change in the good’s own price changes quantity supplied. The supply curve shifts only when a nonprice determinant changes.

q.q: A per-unit input cost falls by $4, but a new per-unit tax raises cost by $6. Holding other determinants fixed, what is the likely supply effect?
options: Supply shifts left because net marginal cost rises by $2 per unit.
Supply shifts right because any input-cost decline dominates a tax.
Supply is unchanged because the two policies offset exactly.
Only quantity supplied falls along the same curve.
q.commonError: Treating unequal per-unit cost changes as if they cancel.
q.feedback: The combined change raises marginal cost by $2 per unit, reducing supply at each price.

q.q: A product gets more expensive because demand increases. Sellers produce more at the higher price. Students say supply increased. What is the error?
options: They confused an increase in quantity supplied with an increase in supply
They correctly identified a supply shift
They confused demand with quantity demanded
They ignored that equilibrium cannot change
q.commonError: calls_quantity_supplied_change_supply_increase
q.feedback: Sellers move along the supply curve when price rises. Quantity supplied increases, but supply does not shift.

q.q: A new machine lowers unit production cost, while a new per-unit environmental fee raises cost. Which conclusion about supply is justified without knowing the size of each change?
options: Supply must shift right because improved technology outweighs any higher per-unit fee.
Supply must shift left because a new per-unit fee outweighs any technological saving.
Supply must remain unchanged because there is one cost decrease and one cost increase.
The net supply shift cannot be determined without comparing the two cost changes.
q.commonError: Assuming one opposing supply shifter automatically dominates the other.
q.feedback: The cost saving increases supply; the fee reduces supply. The net direction depends on the magnitudes, not the number of changes.

q.q: Twenty new firms enter a market, but an essential input becomes more expensive for every firm. What is the most careful conclusion about market supply?
options: Entry pushes supply right and higher input cost pushes it left, leaving the net effect uncertain.
Market supply must rise because entry outweighs the input-cost increase.
Market supply must fall because higher input costs outweigh entry.
Market supply stays fixed because both events only change quantity supplied along the curve.
q.commonError: Ignoring an offsetting change in the number of sellers or input costs.
q.feedback: More firms add supply at each price; a cost increase reduces each firm’s supply. Without magnitudes, the combined shift can go either way or be zero.

q.q: Refer to the graph. Compare the initial point on S0 at $9 with the final point on S1 at $13. Which explanation separates the supply shift from the subsequent price movement?
options: The shift to S1 lowers quantity at each price; moving up S1 then raises quantity back to 200 thousand
The shift to S1 raises quantity at each price; moving up S1 then lowers quantity to 200 thousand
Supply stays on S0 because the price rise accounts for the entire return to 200 thousand
Demand shifts right first, and movement down S1 restores quantity to 100 thousand
q.commonError: misreads_graph_or_confuses_shift_with_movement
q.feedback: The leftward shift from S0 to S1 reduces quantity supplied at each price. The later price rise causes movement up S1 until quantity supplied returns to 200 thousand.

q.q: Refer to the graph. Compare point A on S0 with the final point on S1 at $2. Which explanation separates the supply increase from the later price movement?
options: The shift to S1 raises quantity at each price; moving down S1 then lowers quantity back to about 100 thousand
The shift to S1 lowers quantity at each price; moving down S1 then raises quantity to about 100 thousand
Supply remains on S0 because the price decline explains the entire move
Demand shifts left first, and movement up S1 raises quantity to about 225 thousand
q.commonError: misreads_graph_or_confuses_shift_with_movement
q.feedback: The rightward shift to S1 raises quantity supplied at each price. The later price decline causes movement down S1, offsetting that increase in this particular comparison.

q.q: At $30, three sellers offer 12, 18, and 25 units; at $35 they offer 16, 24, and 30 units. Calculate both market quantities and infer what the comparison represents.
options: Market quantity rises from 55 to 70 units, representing movement along market supply
Market supply shifts right from 55 to 70 units because the number of sellers increases
Market quantity falls from 70 to 55 units, representing movement down market supply
Market supply shifts left by 15 units because individual quantities are aggregated vertically
q.commonError: Using the largest or average firm quantity instead of summing quantities.
q.feedback: Horizontal summation gives 55 units at $30 and 70 at $35. Because only the product's own price changes, the 15-unit increase is movement along the market supply curve.

q.q: At a fixed price, 60 identical firms initially supply 8 units each. An input-cost decline raises each surviving firm’s supply to 10 units, but some firms exit. Total supply at that price is unchanged. How many firms exited, and what does the unchanged total imply?
options: 10 firms; the cost and exit effects offset at this price.
12 firms; neither input costs nor firm exit shifted supply.
15 firms; a higher product price offset the firm exits.
12 firms; the cost and exit effects offset at this price.
q.commonError: Forgetting that market supply depends on the number of active sellers.
q.feedback: Initial supply is 60 × 8 = 480 units. At 10 units each, 48 firms supply 480, so 12 exited. Opposing supply determinants offset at the stated price; this is not a movement caused by an own-price change.

q.q: Producers expect a temporary price spike next month and can store the product cheaply. What pattern is most plausible?
options: Current and future supply both rise because firms expand production immediately and store none of it.
Current supply falls as firms hold inventory, while future supply rises when the inventory is released.
Current supply rises as firms sell inventory before the expected spike, while future supply falls.
Current quantity supplied falls along one curve because the current product price decreases.
q.commonError: Applying future price expectations in the wrong time direction.
q.feedback: When storage is feasible, a higher expected future price can reduce current supply and increase supply when the stored goods are later sold.

q.q: A surge in demand raises the equilibrium price. Firms expand output, and new firms later enter the industry. Which sequence is correct?
options: First supply shifts right; later quantity supplied falls along the curve.
Both responses are movements along the original supply curve.
First quantity supplied rises along the curve; later entry shifts market supply right.
Both responses are supply shifts caused by the good’s own price.
q.commonError: Treating immediate output response and later firm entry as the same kind of change.
q.feedback: The higher price first causes a movement along supply. Entry is a nonprice determinant that later shifts market supply right.

q.q: A drought reduces crop yields, while the market price of the crop rises because demand is unchanged. What is the best description?
options: Supply shifts right because the higher equilibrium price encourages more production after the drought.
Quantity supplied falls along the original supply curve while the curve itself remains unchanged.
Demand shifts left because the drought changes buyer preferences rather than production conditions.
Supply shifts left, and the higher price causes movement upward along the new supply curve.
q.commonError: Using the higher equilibrium price as evidence of an increase in supply.
q.feedback: The drought is a supply shifter. The resulting higher price determines the quantity supplied on the new, left-shifted curve.

q.q: Refer to the graph. Producers start on S0 at $9. Higher input costs move supply to S1, while a purchase contract permits a price no higher than $11. A buyer expects that allowed price increase to restore the original quantity supplied. Which assessment is correct?
options: It succeeds: S1 supplies 200 thousand at $11, restoring the original quantity.
It fails: S1 supplies 150 thousand at $11, still 50 thousand below the original quantity.
It fails: S1 supplies 100 thousand at $11, still 100 thousand below the original quantity.
It succeeds: raising price to $11 shifts supply back to S0, restoring the original quantity.
q.commonError: misreads_graph_or_confuses_shift_with_movement
q.feedback: S0 at $9 supplies 200 thousand. S1 supplies only 100 thousand at $9 and 150 thousand at $11. Returning to 200 thousand on S1 would require $13, outside the contract. The allowed price movement offsets only half the quantity reduction caused by the cost-driven shift.

q.q: Refer to the graph. At a price of $3, technology moves supply from S0 to S1. Half the fixed-price output gain is later lost, leaving a parallel supply curve halfway between S0 and S1. To keep the quantity supplied at its full-improvement level, what price is now needed and what is the mechanism?
options: About $2.50; movement down the halfway curve offsets the lost capacity.
About $3.00; unchanged desired output prevents a supply shift.
About $3.50; movement up the halfway curve offsets the partial supply reversal.
About $4.00; movement up S0 offsets the entire improvement.
q.commonError: misreads_graph_or_confuses_shift_with_movement
q.feedback: At $3, S0 supplies about 100 thousand and S1 about 225 thousand. The halfway curve supplies about 162.5 thousand at $3. At 225 thousand, S0 requires $4 and S1 $3, so the halfway curve requires $3.50. A price movement along that new curve restores quantity; it does not undo the partial technology loss.

q.q: According to the law of supply, how are price and quantity supplied related, other things equal?
options: As price rises, quantity supplied rises
As price rises, supply shifts left
As price falls, quantity supplied rises
As demand rises, supply must rise
q.commonError: confuses_supply_with_demand_direction
q.feedback: The law of supply says price and quantity supplied move in the same direction.

q.q: The price of handmade tables rises, and sellers offer more tables for sale. What is the most precise statement?
options: Quantity supplied increases
Supply increases
Demand increases
Supply shifts right
q.commonError: treats_own_price_change_as_supply_shift
q.feedback: A change in the good's own price causes movement along the supply curve, so quantity supplied changes.

q.q: Steel becomes more expensive for car producers. What happens to the supply of cars?
options: Supply decreases
Quantity supplied increases because car price changed
Demand decreases
Supply increases
q.commonError: gets_input_cost_effect_backwards
q.feedback: More expensive steel raises the cost of producing cars at every output level, shifting car supply left rather than changing demand.

q.q: At one price, Firm A supplies 8 units and Firm B supplies 11 units. Market quantity supplied is:
options: 19 units.
8 units.
9.5 units.
11 units.
q.commonError: Averaging firm quantities instead of adding them.
q.feedback: Market supply adds each seller’s quantity: 8 + 11 = 19.

q.q: The price of oranges rises, and growers offer more oranges while all nonprice determinants stay fixed. This is:
options: An increase in supply.
An increase in quantity supplied.
A decrease in supply.
A decrease in quantity supplied.
q.commonError: Calling a movement caused by the good’s own price a supply shift.
q.feedback: A higher own price causes movement up the existing supply curve.

q.q: The price of an important input falls. What happens to supply, other things equal?
options: Supply shifts left.
Quantity supplied falls along the curve.
Supply shifts right.
Demand shifts right.
q.commonError: Confusing lower production cost with a movement along supply.
q.feedback: Lower input cost makes production profitable at more output levels, shifting supply right.

q.q: A subsidy lowers marginal cost by $3 per unit, while a regulation raises marginal cost by $3 per unit. What happens to supply if those are the only changes?
options: Supply shifts right because the subsidy lowers marginal cost by more than the regulation raises it
Supply shifts left because the regulation raises marginal cost by more than the subsidy lowers it
Quantity supplied rises along the original curve because the product's market price increases
The two per-unit effects offset, so supply is unchanged.
q.commonError: Assuming the label of a policy matters more than its net marginal-cost effect.
q.feedback: Equal and opposite per-unit cost changes leave marginal cost, and therefore supply, unchanged.

q.q: Four firms each supply q=2P units at every price. Demand is Qd=120-4P. One firm exits permanently, with the surviving firms’ schedules unchanged. Which statement correctly compares market equilibrium before and after exit?
options: Price rises from $10 to $12; quantity falls from 80 to 72 as remaining firms move along their unchanged individual schedules.
Price stays $10 and quantity becomes 60; unchanged individual schedules prevent equilibrium price adjustment.
Price falls from $10 to $8; exit shifts each surviving firm’s individual supply curve right.
Price rises from $10 to $12 and quantity rises from 80 to 96 because four firms remain in the aggregate schedule.
q.commonError: Failing to remove the exiting firm’s quantity from market supply.
q.feedback: Before exit supply is 8P, so 120-4P=8P gives P=10, Q=80. Afterward supply is 6P, giving P=12, Q=72. Market supply shifts because a seller exits; survivors respond along unchanged individual supply curves.

q.q: Technology improves while the expected future selling price rises sharply and firms store current output. What is the strongest conclusion about current supply?
options: Current supply increases because improved technology and storing output for future sale both add to current market supply.
The net direction is ambiguous without knowing the strength of each effect.
Current supply decreases because the expected future price rises sharply, which establishes that withholding outweighs the technology improvement.
Quantity supplied moves along one curve because both events change the product's current price.
q.commonError: Declaring a net shift when opposing determinants are not quantified.
q.feedback: Better technology increases current supply, while withholding output for a higher expected future price reduces current supply. The word “sharply” does not quantify the withholding effect relative to the technology effect, so the net direction remains uncertain. Neither determinant is a change in the product’s current price along a fixed curve.

q.q: Bakers pay $4 less in flour cost per loaf, but a new energy levy adds $6 per loaf. At the same time, a health report reduces buyers’ willingness to purchase bread. With unknown shift magnitudes, which conclusion is supported?
options: Net unit cost falls $2, shifting supply right; demand shifts left, so price rises while quantity is ambiguous.
Net unit cost rises $2, shifting supply left; demand also shifts left, so quantity falls while price is ambiguous.
Both changes shift supply left, so price rises and quantity falls with no demand change.
Lower flour cost shifts supply right regardless of the levy, so quantity rises and price is ambiguous.
q.commonError: gets_input_cost_effect_backwards
q.feedback: The cost changes net to +2 per loaf, reducing supply. The health information reduces demand. Both changes lower equilibrium quantity, but their price effects oppose one another.

q.q: Evaluate the competing effects of a cost-saving production technology and a new compliance cost. What can be inferred about the net supply shift without relative magnitudes?
options: Supply must increase because technology reduces production cost.
Supply must decrease because compliance raises production cost.
The net supply direction is ambiguous without relative cost changes.
Supply must stay fixed because the two changes cancel by definition.
q.commonError: Assuming one opposing supply shifter automatically dominates the other.
q.feedback: The two cost effects oppose each other. Supply rises if the saving dominates, falls if the added cost dominates, and is unchanged only if they offset.

q.q: Several firms leave a market, reducing the quantity offered at each fixed price. Demand is unchanged. At the new equilibrium, surviving firms sell more than each sold before, but total market sales are lower. Which explanation reconciles the observations?
options: Market supply shifted left, raising price; survivors move up their own unchanged supply curves even though fewer firms reduce total output.
Market supply shifted right because each survivor sells more; the lower total shows demand must have shifted left too.
Market supply is unchanged because survivor technology is unchanged; exit is only a movement along aggregate supply.
Each survivor’s supply shifted left, lowering price; fewer sellers then raise each remaining firm’s quantity supplied.
q.commonError: misses_number_of_sellers_as_supply_shifter
q.feedback: Exit reduces aggregate supply at any fixed price. Along unchanged demand, price rises and total quantity falls. Higher price induces more output along each survivor’s own curve, consistent with lower aggregate output.

q.q: When only the price of a good changes, what happens on the supply curve?
options: There is movement along the supply curve
The supply curve shifts right
The supply curve shifts left
Demand shifts right
q.commonError: treats_own_price_change_as_supply_shift
q.feedback: A good's own price changes quantity supplied, not supply.

q.q: The price of handmade tables rises. What is the most precise result?
options: Quantity supplied increases
Supply increases
Demand increases
Supply decreases
q.commonError: calls_quantity_supplied_change_supply_change
q.feedback: Because the good's own price changed, sellers move along the supply curve.

q.q: Which event shifts supply?
options: Input costs change
The good's own price changes
Quantity demanded changes
Consumers' income changes
q.commonError: thinks_own_price_shifts_supply
q.feedback: Input costs shift supply. The good's own price causes movement along supply.

q.q: Steel is an input in car production. If the price of steel rises, what happens to the supply of cars?
options: Supply decreases
Supply increases
Demand decreases
Quantity supplied increases
q.commonError: gets_input_cost_effect_backwards
q.feedback: The repair cue identifies steel as an input. A higher input price raises marginal production cost and shifts car supply left.

q.q: Bread's selling price rises, while flour becomes cheaper. Considering each change separately, how does it affect the supply of bread?
options: Higher bread price moves sellers along supply; cheaper flour shifts supply right.
Higher bread price shifts supply right; cheaper flour moves sellers along supply.
Higher bread price moves sellers along supply; cheaper flour shifts supply left.
Both changes move sellers along the same supply curve.
q.commonError: treats_own_price_change_as_supply_shift
q.feedback: Bread's own price changes quantity supplied along a supply curve. Flour is a production input: a lower flour price reduces cost at each output level, shifting bread supply right. These are separate mechanisms.

q.q: The price of concert tickets falls, and venues offer fewer tickets for resale. Which statement is most precise?
options: Quantity supplied decreased, but supply did not necessarily shift
Supply decreased because price changed
Demand increased because price fell
Supply shifted right because sellers offered fewer tickets
q.commonError: calls_quantity_supplied_change_supply_change
q.feedback: A change in the good's own price changes quantity supplied, not supply.

q.q: A new machine lowers the cost of producing shoes. What happens in the shoe market?
options: Supply increases
Supply decreases
Demand increases
Quantity demanded decreases
q.commonError: misses_technology_as_supply_shifter
q.feedback: Better technology lowers production costs, shifting supply right.

q.q: Delivery firms face higher diesel prices and also receive higher prices for each delivery. Consider each change separately. Which change reduces delivery supply at every delivery price?
options: Higher delivery prices; they shift delivery supply left.
Higher diesel prices; they shift delivery supply right.
Higher diesel prices; they shift delivery supply left.
Higher delivery prices; they move firms down the supply curve.
q.commonError: gets_input_cost_effect_backwards
q.feedback: Diesel is an input. Its higher price raises the cost of making deliveries, so firms offer fewer at each delivery price: supply shifts left. A higher price received per delivery instead increases quantity supplied along a curve.

q.q: Tax incidence means:
options: How the burden of a tax is divided between buyers and sellers
The legal maximum price
The number of firms in a market
The quantity demanded at every price
q.commonError: confuses_tax_incidence_with_tax_collection
q.feedback: Tax incidence is about who bears the burden of the tax, not just who sends the payment.

q.q: The side of the market that is less elastic usually bears:
options: More of the tax burden
None of the tax burden
Less of the tax burden because it changes behavior less.
All of the producer surplus
q.commonError: thinks_more_elastic_side_bears_more_tax
q.feedback: The less elastic side bears more of the tax burden because it responds less to price changes.

q.q: If demand is less elastic than supply, who bears more of a tax?
options: Buyers
Sellers
Neither side
Only the government
q.commonError: gets_less_elastic_side_backwards
q.feedback: Buyers bear more because demand is less elastic than supply.

q.q: If supply is less elastic than demand, who bears more of a tax?
options: Sellers
Buyers
Neither side
Whichever side is legally required to remit the tax.
q.commonError: gets_less_elastic_side_backwards
q.feedback: Sellers bear more because supply is less elastic than demand.

q.q: If demand is very inelastic and supply is elastic, who likely bears more of a tax?
options: Buyers
Sellers
Both sides bear exactly zero
The side with more firms always bears it
q.commonError: thinks_elastic_side_bears_more_burden
q.feedback: The less elastic side bears more of the tax burden. Here, that is buyers.

q.q: If supply is very inelastic and demand is elastic, who likely bears more of a tax?
options: Sellers
Buyers
Only the government
No one because demand is elastic
q.commonError: gets_less_elastic_side_backwards
q.feedback: The less elastic side bears more of the burden. Here, that is sellers.

q.q: Why does the more elastic side of a market tend to bear less of a tax?
options: It can adjust its behavior more easily in response to the tax.
A binding price floor absorbs part of the tax.
Elasticity affects only the legal assignment of the tax.
The more elastic side cannot change quantity when price changes.
q.commonError: misses_elasticity_as_escape_ability
q.feedback: The more elastic side can respond more easily, so it bears less of the tax burden.

q.q: Refer to the tax incidence graph. Who bears more of the tax burden?
options: Buyers and sellers share the burden equally
Buyers bear all of the burden
Sellers bear all of the burden
No one bears the burden
q.commonError: assumes_legal_tax_assignment_determines_burden
q.feedback: Buyers pay $3 more and sellers receive $3 less, so the burden is split equally.

q.q: In a competitive cigarette market, demand is less price-elastic than supply. A small per-unit tax is collected from sellers. With other market conditions unchanged, which conclusion about the economic burden follows?
options: Buyers bear more because demand is less price-responsive than supply.
Sellers bear more because the government collects the tax from sellers.
Each side bears half because both participate in the taxed transactions.
Buyers bear the entire tax because demand is less elastic than supply.
q.commonError: Assigning economic tax burden by statutory collection rather than relative elasticity.
q.feedback: Buyers bear the larger share because demand is less elastic than supply: buyers adjust quantity less readily when prices change. Collecting the tax from sellers does not determine economic incidence. The stated comparison does not imply that buyers bear the entire tax.

q.q: In a competitive luxury-boat rental market, demand is more price-elastic than supply. A small per-unit tax is collected from renters. With other market conditions unchanged, which conclusion is best supported?
options: Sellers are more likely to bear more of the tax burden.
Buyers are more likely to bear more of the tax burden.
Buyers and sellers are likely to share the tax burden equally.
Sellers are likely to bear the entire tax because they receive payment.
q.commonError: Assigning economic tax burden by statutory collection rather than relative elasticity.
q.feedback: Supply is less elastic than demand, so sellers are less able to adjust quantity and bear the larger share through lower net receipts. Collecting the tax from renters does not make renters bear the larger share. Relative inelasticity does not imply that sellers bear the entire tax.

q.q: A tax on cigarettes causes only a small drop in smoking even though buyers face a noticeably higher price. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Demand is relatively inelastic
Demand is perfectly elastic
Supply increased after the tax
The tax created a price floor
q.commonError: thinks_small_quantity_change_means_tax_failed
q.feedback: If quantity falls only a little after a tax, demand is likely relatively inelastic.

q.q: A tax is imposed on a market where demand is perfectly inelastic. Who bears the tax burden?
options: Buyers bear the burden because quantity demanded does not respond
Sellers bear the burden because they collect the money
The government bears the burden
No one bears the burden because quantity does not change
q.commonError: thinks_legal_collection_determines_burden
q.feedback: If buyers do not change quantity demanded at all, buyers bear the tax burden.

q.q: If demand is less elastic than supply, why do buyers bear more of a tax?
options: Buyers are less able to reduce quantity demanded when price rises
Buyers legally pay all taxes
Sellers are less able to adjust quantity supplied
Demand shifts right after the tax
q.commonError: misses_why_less_elastic_side_bears_more
q.feedback: The less elastic side adjusts less, so it bears more of the tax burden.

q.q: If supply is perfectly inelastic and demand is elastic, who bears the tax burden?
options: Sellers bear all of it.
Buyers bear all of it
No one bears it
The government bears it because supply is vertical
q.commonError: thinks_buyers_always_bear_tax_when_price_rises
q.feedback: With perfectly inelastic supply, quantity supplied cannot respond to the tax. Sellers therefore bear the entire tax burden through a lower net price received.

q.q: Refer to the tax graph. Using the original equilibrium as the benchmark, how is the per-unit tax burden divided?
options: Buyers bear $3 and sellers $3, so each bears half
Buyers bear $6 and sellers $0, because the buyer price is highest
Buyers bear $0 and sellers $6, because the shifted curve is supply
Buyers bear $18 and sellers $12, equal to the two after-tax prices
q.commonError: uses_after_tax_prices_as_burden_amounts
q.feedback: The original price is $15. Buyers now pay $18, an increase of $3, while sellers keep $12, a decrease of $3. These burdens sum to the $6 wedge. Neither legal remittance nor the full price level measures incidence.

q.q: Refer to the graph. What percentage of the $8 tax burden is borne by buyers?
options: 25 percent
75 percent
50 percent
100 percent
q.imageAlt: The concert-ticket market has price vertically and quantity in thousands horizontally. D0 and S0 intersect at A, quantity 200 and price 10 dollars. Supply with tax intersects demand at quantity 150 and buyer price 16; original supply there gives seller price 8.
q.commonError: misreads_graph_relationship
q.feedback: The buyer price rises by $6. Buyers therefore bear $6 of the $8 tax, or 75%.
q.graphDescription: The concert-ticket market has price vertically and quantity in thousands horizontally. D0 and S0 intersect at A, quantity 200 and price 10 dollars. Supply with tax intersects demand at quantity 150 and buyer price 16; original supply there gives seller price 8.

q.q: Refer to the graph. Relative to the original $10 equilibrium price, how is the $4 tax burden divided?
options: Buyers bear all $4; sellers bear none.
Sellers bear all $4; buyers bear none.
Buyers gain $2; sellers bear $6.
Buyers bear $2; sellers bear $2.
q.imageAlt: The rideshare market has price per trip vertically and quantity in thousands per day horizontally. D0 and S0 intersect at A, quantity 200 and price 10 dollars. Supply with tax intersects demand at quantity 150 and buyer price 12; original supply there gives seller price 8.
q.commonError: misreads_graph_relationship
q.feedback: Buyer price rises to 12 and seller price falls to 8.
q.graphDescription: The rideshare market has price per trip vertically and quantity in thousands per day horizontally. D0 and S0 intersect at A, quantity 200 and price 10 dollars. Supply with tax intersects demand at quantity 150 and buyer price 12; original supply there gives seller price 8.

q.q: A $12 tax causes buyers to pay $7 more and sellers to receive $5 less. Demand is likely less elastic than supply because:
options: Buyers bear more of the tax burden
Sellers bear more of the tax burden
The legal tax must have been placed on buyers
The tax increased quantity sold
q.commonError: thinks_larger_burden_means_more_elastic_side
q.feedback: The less elastic side bears more of the tax burden. Buyers bear $7, so demand is likely less elastic.

q.q: A tax is imposed on a good with elastic demand and highly inelastic supply. Which result is most likely?
options: Sellers bear most of the burden
Buyers bear most of the burden
Demand increases because the tax is high
The legal assignment alone determines burden
q.commonError: thinks_buyers_always_bear_consumption_taxes
q.feedback: The less elastic side bears more. If supply is highly inelastic, sellers bear most of the tax.

q.q: A student says, 'The price rose after the tax, so buyers paid the entire tax.' What is the flaw?
options: Buyers bear only the increase above the old equilibrium price.
Any price increase means buyers pay everything
Sellers cannot bear taxes if buyers pay more
Tax incidence is unrelated to prices
q.commonError: confuses_price_increase_with_full_tax
q.feedback: Buyers bear the part of the tax reflected in the higher price they pay; sellers bear the part reflected in the lower price they receive.

q.q: Before tax, price is $20. After tax, buyers pay $24 and sellers receive $18. Which statement correctly splits the burden?
options: Buyers bear $4 and sellers bear $2
Buyers bear $2 and sellers bear $4
Buyers bear $6 and sellers bear $0
Buyers bear $24 and sellers bear $18
q.commonError: uses_after_tax_prices_as_burden_amounts
q.feedback: Buyers pay $4 more than before, while sellers receive $2 less than before.

q.q: A tax is imposed on a good with highly inelastic demand and elastic supply. Which policy outcome is most likely?
options: Buyers bear most of the burden and quantity falls relatively little
Sellers bear most of the burden and quantity falls dramatically
Buyers bear no burden because sellers legally pay
The tax creates a surplus equal to the tax
q.commonError: separates_elasticity_from_quantity_response
q.feedback: Inelastic demand means buyers bear more and reduce quantity less in response to the tax.

q.q: Before a tax, price is $40 and 500 units trade. Afterward buyers pay $46, sellers keep $34, and 420 units trade. What is the buyers’ tax burden on the units still traded, as distinct from the entire change in consumer surplus?
q.commonError: uses_full_tax_instead_of_buyer_price_increase
q.feedback: The per-unit buyer burden is $46 − $40 = $6. On 420 continuing units, its rectangle is $2,520. The full CS change also includes lost gains from the 80 missing trades; the rectangle alone does not measure that entire loss.

q.q: A market moves from $40 and 500 units before a tax to a buyer price of $46, seller receipt of $34, and 420 units afterward. What is the seller-burden rectangle on units still traded, excluding the surplus lost on missing trades?
q.commonError: uses_full_tax_instead_of_seller_price_drop
q.feedback: The seller loses $40 − $34 = $6 per continuing unit, so the rectangle is $6 × 420 = $2,520. Using 500 applies the burden to trades that no longer occur. The $12 wedge times 420 is total revenue, not the seller share alone.

q.q: A tax is imposed on sellers. Before the tax, price is $20 and quantity is 300. After the tax, buyers pay $24, sellers receive $18, and quantity is 240. Which statement is correct?
options: Tax wedge: $6; buyer burden: $4 per unit; seller burden: $2 per unit; quantity falls by 60 units.
Tax wedge: $6; buyer burden: $2 per unit; seller burden: $4 per unit; quantity falls by 60 units.
Tax wedge: $6; buyer burden: $0 per unit; seller burden: $6 per unit; quantity falls by 60 units.
Tax wedge: $6; buyer burden: $4 per unit; seller burden: $2 per unit; quantity falls by 240 units.
q.commonError: adds_prices_or_ignores_original_price
q.feedback: The tax wedge is $24 - $18 = $6 per unit. Relative to the original $20 price, buyers bear $24 - $20 = $4 per unit and sellers bear $20 - $18 = $2 per unit; these burdens sum to $6. Quantity falls by 300 - 240 = 60 units. The 240 units are the new quantity, not the decrease. Requiring sellers to remit the tax does not make them bear its entire economic burden.

q.q: Refer to the tax graph. A seller argues that its legal duty to remit the tax means it bears the entire revenue rectangle. What do the price changes and continuing quantity show?
options: Each side bears $3 per unit and $240 of the $480 rectangle
Sellers bear $6 per unit and all $480 of the rectangle
Each side bears $3 per unit and $300 of the $600 rectangle
Buyers bear $6 per unit and all $480 of the rectangle
q.commonError: assumes_legal_tax_assignment_determines_burden
q.feedback: Relative to $15, buyers pay $3 more and sellers receive $3 less. At 80 units, each incidence rectangle is $240, together equaling $480 of revenue. Remitting the money is different from bearing the price burden; these rectangles exclude gains lost on missing trades.

q.q: A $4 tax is placed on concert tickets. Buyers pay $2.50 more than before, sellers receive $1.50 less than before, and fewer tickets are sold. Which statement is strongest?
options: The burden is shared, quantity falls, and the side less able to adjust bears more
The burden falls only on sellers because the legal tax is charged to sellers
The burden falls only on buyers because the buyer price increased
The burden disappears because tax revenue offsets the lower quantity sold
q.commonError: ignores_price_changes_when_assigning_burden

q.q: A market has an $8 tax, a total buyer price of $26 and a net seller receipt of $18. Buyers bear 75% of the per-unit burden. What was the untaxed price, and which side is less price responsive over this change?

$24; sellers
$20; sellers
$24; buyers
q.commonError: ignores_price_changes_when_assigning_burden
q.feedback: Buyer burden is 0.75 × $8 = $6, so the old price was $26 − $6 = $20. Sellers bear the remaining $2, since $20 − $18 = $2. Under the standard tax-incidence comparison, the side bearing more of the wedge is less price responsive.

q.q: Supply is perfectly inelastic at 200 units and demand slopes downward. A $6 tax is imposed in a competitive market with no externalities or collection costs. Which combination follows?

Buyers bear $6 per unit, revenue is $1,200, and deadweight loss is zero
Sellers bear $6 per unit, revenue is $1,200, and deadweight loss is $1,200
Buyers and sellers each bear $3, revenue is $600, and quantity falls
q.commonError: thinks_no_quantity_change_means_no_burden
q.feedback: The vertical supply curve holds quantity at 200. Buyers pay the same demand price at that quantity, so sellers absorb the full $6 wedge through lower net receipts. Revenue is $1,200. With no trades lost and no other distortions in the stated model, tax revenue is a transfer and there is no deadweight loss.

q.q: Refer to the graph. The tax is legally imposed on buyers. Which statement correctly describes who remits the tax, who bears the economic burden, and what the burden split implies about elasticity?

q.q: A $5 tax causes buyers to pay $3 more than before and sellers to receive $2 less than before. How is the burden split?

Buyers bear $2 and sellers bear $3

Buyers bear all $5

q.feedback: The buyer burden is the price increase paid by buyers. The seller burden is the price decrease received by sellers.

q.q: Before a tax, buyers pay $30 and sellers receive $30. After a tax, buyers pay $34 and sellers receive $27. Who bears more of the burden?

Sellers

q.q: Refer to the tax incidence graph. What is the buyers’ tax burden on the units still traded, excluding surplus lost on missing trades?
q.commonError: uses_tax_wedge_instead_of_buyer_price_increase
q.feedback: The per-unit buyer burden is $3 relative to the original $15 price. Multiplying by 80 continuing units gives $240. The full welfare loss for that side also includes surplus lost on trades that no longer occur.

q.q: Refer to the tax incidence graph. What is the seller-burden rectangle on the units still traded, excluding surplus lost on missing trades?
q.commonError: uses_tax_wedge_instead_of_seller_price_decrease
q.feedback: The per-unit seller burden is $3 relative to the original $15 price. Multiplying by 80 continuing units gives $240. The full welfare loss for that side also includes surplus lost on trades that no longer occur.

q.q: Refer to the tax incidence graph. What is the combined buyer- and seller-burden rectangle on units still traded, which becomes government revenue?
q.commonError: adds_buyer_and_seller_prices_instead_of_tax_revenue
q.feedback: The $6 wedge applies to 80 continuing trades, so the rectangle is $480. This is the combined per-unit incidence times taxed quantity. Lost gains from the missing trades are additional welfare loss and are not government revenue.

q.q: Refer to the tax incidence graph. For the units still purchased after the tax, what is the total extra payment by buyers relative to paying the original price for those same units? This question excludes the welfare effect of purchases forgone.
options: $300: $3 extra on the original 100 units.
$480: the full $6 tax on the remaining 80 units.
$240: $3 extra on the remaining 80 units.
$540: the change in sellers’ total receipts.
q.commonError: uses_full_tax_as_buyer_burden
q.feedback: The buyer price rises from $15 to $18 and 80 units are purchased after tax. For these continuing purchases, the extra payment is ($18 - $15) x 80 = $240. Using all 100 original units includes purchases no longer made; using $6 assigns the seller burden to buyers.

q.q: Refer to the tax incidence graph. A seller group divides the fall in total net-of-tax sales receipts by the 80 units still sold and calls the result its tax burden per continuing unit. Why is that calculation misleading?
options: The $540 receipt decline includes fewer units sold; the price burden on each continuing unit is $3.
The $540 receipt decline is entirely a price effect; the burden on each continuing unit is $6.75.
The $240 receipt decline includes fewer units sold; the price burden on each continuing unit is $6.
The $300 receipt decline is entirely a quantity effect; the price burden on each continuing unit is $0.
q.commonError: confuses_total_receipts_change_with_per_unit_tax_burden
q.feedback: Receipts fall from $15 x 100 = $1,500 to $12 x 80 = $960, a $540 decline. This combines $300 from 20 fewer units valued at the old price and $240 from receiving $3 less on each of 80 continuing sales. The per-unit seller tax burden is $15 - $12 = $3; gross receipts are not a measure of producer surplus.

q.q: A $6 tax causes buyers to pay $4 more than before and sellers to receive $2 less than before. Who bears more of the tax burden?
options: Buyers
Sellers
Both sides bear zero burden
Only the government

q.q: Refer to the tax incidence graph. How much of the tax burden is paid by buyers?
q.commonError: confuses_total_tax_with_buyer_burden

q.q: Refer to the tax incidence graph. How much of the tax burden is paid by sellers?
q.commonError: confuses_total_tax_with_seller_burden

q.q: A $6 tax is imposed. Before the tax, buyers paid $20. After the tax, buyers pay $24 and sellers receive $18. How much of the tax burden falls on buyers and sellers?

Buyers bear $24 and sellers bear $18

q.q: Demand is much less elastic than supply. A tax is imposed on the good. Who bears more of the tax burden, and why?
options: Buyers bear more because they are less able to reduce quantity demanded
Sellers bear more because supply is more elastic
Buyers and sellers must split the burden equally
Sellers bear more because buyers pay the tax through the market price
q.commonError: assigns_burden_to_more_elastic_side
q.feedback: The less elastic side bears more of the tax because it is less able to change behavior in response to the tax.

q.q: Supply is much less elastic than demand. A tax is imposed. What is the likely result?
options: Sellers bear more of the burden because quantity supplied is less responsive
Buyers bear more of the burden because demand is more elastic
The burden must be equal because the tax wedge is fixed
The side required to remit the tax bears more because statutory payment determines the economic burden
q.commonError: assigns_burden_to_more_elastic_side
q.feedback: The less elastic side bears more of the tax. If supply is less elastic than demand, sellers bear more of the burden.

q.q: In a competitive market, demand elasticity is Ed=-0.25 and supply elasticity Es=1.20 near equilibrium. A small unit tax is introduced. Later, buyers gain substitutes and Ed becomes -1.50 while Es stays 1.20. Which comparison is best, holding the initial price, quantity and tax size comparable?
options: Buyers initially bear more; afterward sellers bear more, and the stronger demand response makes the tax-induced quantity reduction larger.
Sellers initially bear more; afterward buyers bear more, and stronger demand response makes the quantity reduction smaller.
Buyers bear more in both cases because the negative sign makes demand less elastic than every positive supply elasticity.
Burden shares reverse only if the law changes the tax remitter; elasticity changes affect quantity but not economic incidence.
q.commonError: assigns_burden_to_more_elastic_side
q.feedback: Compare absolute elasticities. Initially 0.25<1.20, so buyers are less responsive and bear more. Later 1.50>1.20, so sellers are relatively less responsive. Greater demand responsiveness also increases the quantity response to a comparable small tax.

q.q: Demand elasticity is -1.80 and supply elasticity is 0.20 in a market. A small tax is imposed on sellers. Over time, sellers gain alternative uses for their resources and supply elasticity rises to 2.40, with demand elasticity unchanged. Compare equal small taxes from the same initial price and quantity. Which evaluation is correct?
options: Buyers initially bear more, but sellers bear more later; the legal seller tax becomes binding only in the long run.
Sellers initially bear more, but buyers bear more later; greater supply responsiveness also increases the quantity response to the tax.
Sellers bear more in both periods because the statute requires them to remit the tax, regardless of alternatives.
Burden becomes exactly equal later because both elasticity magnitudes exceed one, making relative sizes irrelevant.
q.commonError: assigns_burden_to_more_elastic_side
q.feedback: Initially supply magnitude 0.20 is below demand magnitude 1.80, so sellers bear more. Later supply magnitude 2.40 exceeds demand, so buyers bear more. More responsive supply permits a greater quantity adjustment under a comparable small tax.

q.q: Before a tax, market price is $40. After a $12 unit tax, buyers pay $43 and sellers receive $31. A reform puts legal remittance on buyers without changing behavior or the tax size. Which combined inference is supported?
options: Buyers bear 75% and sellers 25%; demand is relatively less elastic, and remittance alone reverses the $43/$31 price pair.
Buyers bear 25% and sellers 75%; supply is relatively less elastic, and remittance alone leaves the $43/$31 price pair unchanged.
Buyers bear 25% and sellers 75%; demand is relatively less elastic, so buyer remittance makes buyers bear the entire $12.
Buyers bear 50% and sellers 50%; the $12 wedge must be split evenly once both sides participate in the market.
q.feedback: Buyer burden is 43-40=3 and seller burden 40-31=9, totaling 12. Shares are 3/12=25% and 9/12=75%. In the standard model the less elastic side bears more, indicating relatively less elastic supply. Legal remittance alone does not alter the wedge equilibrium.

q.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
q.q: A survey classifies people as employed, unemployed, or not in the labor force. Which person is most likely misread by the headline unemployment rate as doing better than they are?
options: A part-time worker who wants full-time work
A full-time worker satisfied with their job
A retiree who does not want work
A student not seeking employment
q.feedback: Involuntary part-time workers are counted as employed, even though their labor situation is weak.

q.commonError: Dividing unemployed workers by the whole population instead of the labor force.
q.q: A labor survey starts with 132 employed, 12 unemployed and 56 other adults. Then 4 unemployed find jobs, 3 stop searching, 5 outsiders start searching without finding work, and 2 employed retire. All job seekers are available. What are the new unemployment and participation rates?
options: About 6.9% unemployment and 72% participation
About 5% unemployment and 72% participation
About 6.9% unemployment and 75.5% participation
About 8.3% unemployment and 72% participation
q.feedback: Employment becomes 132 + 4 - 2 = 134 and unemployment 12 - 4 - 3 + 5 = 10. The labor force is 144 of 200 adults, so participation is 72% and unemployment is 10/144 ≈ 6.9%. The entering and leaving flows happen to offset in total participation.

q.commonError: Using unemployed workers instead of the labor force in the participation formula.
q.q: There are 200 adults, labor-force participation is 75%, and unemployment is 8%. Next month 6 unemployed stop searching, 6 employed retire, and 4 outsiders start searching without finding work. With everyone otherwise unchanged and seekers available, which final account is correct?
options: 132 employed; about 7.0% unemployment; 71% participation
138 employed; 4% unemployment; 75% participation
132 employed; 5% unemployment; 71% participation
144 employed; about 6.5% unemployment; 77% participation
q.feedback: Initially LF = 150, U = 12 and E = 138. After the flows E = 132, U = 12 - 6 + 4 = 10 and LF = 142. Thus U/LF ≈ 7.0% and LF/adults = 71%. A lower unemployment rate coexists with fewer people employed.

q.commonError: Dividing unemployed workers by the whole population instead of the labor force.
q.q: An economy has 90 employed, 10 unemployed, and 50 not in the labor force. Five employed workers lose jobs and search; five unemployed workers stop searching. What happens to unemployment rate?
options: It rises slightly to 10.5%
It rises to 15%
It falls to 5%
It becomes 0%
q.feedback: Employed falls to 85. Five newly unemployed workers replace five workers who stop searching, so unemployed remains 10 and the labor force falls to 95. The rate is 10/95 = 10.53%.

q.commonError: Using unemployed workers instead of the labor force in the participation formula.
q.q: A population of 200 adults is unchanged. The unemployment rate stays at 6%, while participation falls from 75% to 70%. Which employment change and interpretation follow?
options: Employment falls by 9.4; a stable unemployment rate does not imply a stable number of jobs
Employment stays at 141; a stable rate fixes employment
Employment falls by 10; every labor-force exit must be an employed worker
Employment rises by 9.4; lower participation indicates more jobs
q.feedback: The labor force falls from 150 to 140. Employment is 94% of each total: 141 initially and 131.6 afterward, a decline of 9.4. The unchanged unemployment rate is a ratio, not an unchanged employment count.

q.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
q.q: A jobless worker applied to three jobs last week. Another jobless worker wants work but last searched two months ago. A third works 3 hours per week but wants full-time work. How are they classified?
options: Unemployed; not in labor force; employed
Unemployed; unemployed; unemployed
Employed; unemployed; not in labor force
Not in labor force; unemployed; employed
q.feedback: Recent active search means unemployed; no recent search means not in labor force; any paid work means employed.

q.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
q.q: Which case makes the headline unemployment rate look better than the actual labor market experience?

A rise in full-time employment
More unemployed workers actively searching
More job openings filled
q.feedback: Discouraged and involuntary part-time workers are not fully captured by the headline unemployment rate.

q.commonError: Dividing unemployed workers by the whole population instead of the labor force.
q.q: A report says unemployment fell from 20 to 12 while employment rose from 180 to 184. Adult population is fixed at 250, and the only flows were unemployed people finding jobs or stopping search. Which decomposition and participation change are implied?
options: 4 found jobs and 4 left search; participation fell from 80% to 78.4%
8 found jobs; participation stayed at 80%
4 found jobs and 8 left search; participation fell to 76.8%
4 left search and none found jobs; the employment rise is unrelated
q.feedback: The employment rise identifies 4 job findings. Of the 8-person unemployment decline, the remaining 4 are exits. LF falls from 200 to 196, so participation falls from 80% to 78.4%. Both hiring and withdrawal contributed to the lower headline rate.

q.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
q.q: Two districts have the same unemployment rate and population. One has lower participation and a larger share of employed people working part time because full-time work is unavailable. Which additional comparison is best before calling their labor markets equally strong?
options: Compare employment per adult and desired versus actual hours; the headline rate omits both differences
Compare only total unemployment; equal unemployment rates guarantee equal counts
Count all involuntary part-time workers as unemployed before applying the official definition
Exclude discouraged workers from every indicator because they are outside the labor force
q.feedback: Unemployment divides job seekers by the labor force. Lower participation can lower employment per adult even at the same rate, while involuntary part-time workers remain employed. Additional participation and hours evidence is needed for the broader assessment.

q.commonError: Using unemployed workers instead of the labor force in the participation formula.
q.q: If measured unemployment falls because 1M unemployed workers become discouraged, while employment is unchanged, what happens to labor force participation?

It rises

q.q: An economy has 120 employed, 12 unemployed, and 68 not in the labor force. Four unemployed workers find jobs, and four employed workers move to part-time work but keep paid jobs. What is the new unemployment rate?

q.commonError: Using unemployed workers instead of the labor force in the participation formula.
q.q: An economy has 200 adults, 120 employed, 10 unemployed, and 70 not in the labor force. Then 10 unemployed workers become discouraged. What are the new unemployment rate and participation rate?

5% unemployment and 65% participation
0% unemployment and 65% participation
10% unemployment and 60% participation
q.feedback: Unemployed becomes 0 and labor force becomes 120. Unemployment = 0%; participation = 120/200 = 60%.

q.commonError: Assuming healthy economies should have zero unemployment.
q.q: An economist synthesizes this evidence: a worker is counted as employed even though they want full-time work, another worker is not counted as unemployed because they stopped searching, and actual unemployment is above the natural rate. What is the combined lesson?
options: The headline rate misses underemployment and discouraged workers; excess unemployment signals cyclical weakness
The headline unemployment rate captures all labor pain perfectly
Actual unemployment above natural unemployment means no recessionary pressure
Discouraged workers raise the unemployment rate
q.feedback: This pulls together underemployment, discouraged workers, and cyclical unemployment.

q.q: A worker has a part-time job but is actively searching for full-time work. How is the worker classified in official labor statistics?

Employed, because the worker has a paid job.
Outside the labor force, because the job is part time.
Discouraged, because the worker is searching for another job.
q.commonError: Classifying an underemployed worker as unemployed.
q.feedback: Official employment status is based on having work, not on whether the worker wants additional hours.

q.q: A jobless adult is available to work but has not searched during the past four weeks. How is this person usually classified?
options: Unemployed.
Employed.
Outside the labor force.
Frictionally employed.
q.commonError: Ignoring the active-search requirement for official unemployment.
q.feedback: A jobless person generally must be available and actively searching to be counted as unemployed.

q.q: Which equation defines the labor force?

Labor force = working-age population - employed people.
Labor force = employed people + unemployed people.

q.feedback: The labor force contains people who are employed plus people who are jobless and actively seeking work.

q.q: A discouraged worker stops searching for a job while no one finds employment. What can happen to the official unemployment rate?

q.q: An economy has 900 employed people, 100 unemployed people, and 200 adults outside the labor force. What are the unemployment and labor-force participation rates?

q.q: An employed worker loses a job and immediately begins an active search. What happens initially?

Unemployment falls because active search counts as employment.
Employment falls, unemployment rises, and the labor force is unchanged.
The worker exits the labor force despite beginning a search.
q.commonError: Treating job loss with active search as labor-force exit.
q.feedback: The person moves from employed to unemployed but remains in the labor force, raising the unemployment rate.

q.q: Employment rises by 100,000, unemployment rises by 50,000, and labor-force participation rises. What likely happened?

More people entered the labor force, and not all found jobs immediately
The unemployment rate must be zero
Everyone who entered the labor force became employed
q.commonError: sees_rising_unemployment_as_always_job_destruction
q.feedback: Unemployment can rise when more people enter the labor force and some are still searching.

q.q: The unemployment rate falls, but employment does not rise and labor-force participation falls. What is the most careful conclusion?

q.q: Adult population is 250 million, employed workers are 155 million, and unemployed workers are 10 million. What are the unemployment rate and labor-force participation rate?

Unemployment rate ≈ 6.5%; labor-force participation rate = 60%
Unemployment rate = 10%; labor-force participation rate = 66%
Unemployment rate ≈ 6.1%; labor-force participation rate = 66%

Not in the labor force

q.commonError: Confusing normal job search with skill mismatch or recession layoffs.
q.q: Frictional unemployment is caused by:

q.q: Structural unemployment is caused by:

A temporary vacation
GDP accounting rules

q.commonError: Confusing recession-driven unemployment with natural unemployment.
q.q: Cyclical unemployment is associated with:

Not in the labor force

Structural unemployment

Structural unemployment

q.commonError: Confusing permanent mismatch with short-run job search or weak demand.

Structural unemployment

Only structural
Only frictional

q.commonError: Confusing permanent mismatch with short-run job search or weak demand.

Frictional unemployment
Cyclical unemployment
Seasonal unemployment only
q.feedback: A mismatch between worker skills and available jobs is structural unemployment.

Both are frictionally unemployed

q.feedback: Short job search is frictional; long-term mismatch after industry decline is structural.

q.q: A worker is laid off when a recession cuts sales. By the time demand recovers, the firm has automated the old job and the worker lacks the new required skills. What best describes the worker’s unemployment now?
options: It began as cyclical but is now primarily structural
It remains purely cyclical because the original layoff occurred in a recession
It is frictional because every unemployed worker is searching
It is no longer unemployment once the original recession ends
q.commonError: Confuses persistent skill or location mismatch with temporary search or weak aggregate demand.
q.feedback: Structural unemployment reflects a durable mismatch between workers and available jobs, skills, or locations.

q.commonError: Confusing permanent mismatch with short-run job search or weak demand.
q.q: A recession closes restaurants temporarily, while automation permanently reduces demand for cashiers. Which unemployment types are present?
options: Cyclical and structural
Only frictional
Only cyclical
Only natural
q.feedback: Recession-related layoffs are cyclical; permanent automation mismatch is structural.

q.commonError: Confusing permanent mismatch with short-run job search or weak demand.
q.q: A worker leaves a job voluntarily to search for a better match during a strong economy. A different worker loses a job because their industry permanently shrinks. Which pairing is correct?
options: Frictional; structural
Structural; frictional
Cyclical; frictional
Natural; cyclical
q.feedback: Voluntary job search is frictional; long-term industry decline creates structural unemployment.

q.commonError: Confusing recession-driven unemployment with natural unemployment.
q.q: Why is cyclical unemployment not part of the natural rate?
options: It reflects short-run downturns rather than normal job search or structural mismatch
It is always caused by unions
It exists only because workers quit to find better jobs
It is another name for frictional unemployment
q.feedback: The natural rate includes frictional and structural unemployment, not recession-driven cyclical unemployment.

q.commonError: Confusing permanent mismatch with short-run job search or weak demand.
q.q: Which worker is most clearly structurally unemployed?
options: A typist whose skills are outdated after firms switch to new software systems
A nurse moving between hospitals in the same city
A waiter laid off during a short recession
A teacher taking summer vacation but returning in August
q.feedback: Structural unemployment involves a mismatch between worker skills and available jobs.

q.commonError: Confusing permanent mismatch with short-run job search or weak demand.
q.q: A worker has the right skills but needs time to find the right employer. Another has obsolete skills and needs retraining. What separates the two cases?
options: Search time versus skill mismatch
Nominal versus real wages
CPI versus GDP deflator
Imports versus exports
q.feedback: Frictional unemployment is search time; structural unemployment is mismatch.

q.commonError: Confusing permanent mismatch with short-run job search or weak demand.
q.q: A worker is laid off because a recession reduces sales. Six months later, the worker's old industry adopts technology that permanently eliminates the job type. How should the unemployment diagnosis change?
options: Cyclical at first; structural if the job type disappears
It is always frictional
It is never unemployment
It must be natural unemployment only
q.feedback: Weak demand causes cyclical unemployment, but permanent skill/job mismatch is structural.

q.commonError: Confusing permanent mismatch with short-run job search or weak demand.
q.q: After a regional downturn ends, one group has suitable job offers but needs time to choose; another cannot meet credentials for expanding occupations. A third group has already accepted paid part-time work while seeking full-time jobs. Which diagnosis respects both cause and official status?
options: The first group is frictionally unemployed, the second structurally unemployed, and the third employed
All three are structurally unemployed because each wants a different job
The first is cyclical, the second frictional, and the third outside the labor force
All three are unemployed until they obtain their preferred full-time jobs
q.feedback: Normal matching among suitable jobs is frictional; a persistent credential mismatch is structural. A paid part-time job makes the third group employed under the official measure, even though underemployment may remain.

q.commonError: Confusing recession-driven unemployment with natural unemployment.
q.q: Spending and total vacancies recover after a downturn, but vacancies concentrate in licensed occupations while displaced workers lack the credentials. Which evidence would most directly strengthen a structural diagnosis over a purely cyclical one?
options: Credential training is followed by placements into the unfilled occupations while overall spending changes little
All vacancies disappear when spending weakens again
Workers have suitable offers and are briefly choosing among them
Unemployment falls only when economy-wide spending rises sharply, with no change in skills
q.feedback: The mismatch between expanding occupations and worker credentials points to a structural barrier. Placements after relevant training, with demand broadly unchanged, strengthen that mechanism rather than a claim based only on weak spending or ordinary search.

q.commonError: Confusing permanent mismatch with short-run job search or weak demand.
q.q: A worker is unemployed because moving to available jobs is too costly, even though jobs exist elsewhere. Which type is most likely?
options: Structural unemployment
Frictional unemployment only
Cyclical unemployment only
Not in the labor force
q.feedback: Geographic mismatch is a form of structural unemployment.

q.q: A regional downturn eliminates jobs at several firms. One year later overall demand has recovered, but many displaced workers remain unemployed because growing industries require different credentials. Which diagnosis is most accurate?
options: Cyclical unemployment fell, while structural unemployment remains
The remaining unemployment must still be entirely cyclical
The recovery eliminates both structural and frictional unemployment
The remaining unemployment is frictional simply because workers are looking for jobs
q.commonError: Confuses persistent skill or location mismatch with temporary search or weak aggregate demand.
q.feedback: Structural unemployment reflects a durable mismatch between workers and available jobs, skills, or locations.

q.q: A city’s jobless population includes skilled movers choosing among local openings and workers whose occupation disappeared. A single faster job-listing service is proposed for both. Which prediction is best supported?
options: It must eliminate both groups’ unemployment because each can read the same vacancies
It affects only cyclical unemployment because information is part of total spending
It turns structurally unemployed workers into employed people as soon as listings are viewed
It can shorten matching for the first group; the second may also need retraining or mobility support
q.commonError: Confuses normal job search with skill mismatch or recession layoffs.
q.feedback: The first group faces search frictions among suitable jobs. The second faces a durable mismatch that information alone may not remove. Diagnosis should guide the intervention without assuming guaranteed placement.

q.commonError: Confusing normal job search with skill mismatch or recession layoffs.
q.q: An economist asks about job search: frictional unemployment is mainly caused by:
options: The time required for workers and firms to find good matches
A permanent mismatch between skills and jobs
A recession reducing total spending
A binding minimum wage only
q.feedback: Frictional unemployment comes from normal job search and matching.

q.commonError: Confusing permanent mismatch with short-run job search or weak demand.
q.q: A software developer quits one job and spends three weeks comparing offers from similar firms. What type of unemployment is this?
options: Frictional
Structural
Cyclical
Discouraged
q.feedback: Short-term search between suitable jobs is frictional unemployment.

q.commonError: Confusing normal job search with skill mismatch or recession layoffs.
q.q: A new job-matching platform helps workers find suitable openings faster. Which unemployment type should fall most directly?
options: Frictional unemployment
Structural unemployment
Cyclical unemployment
Natural resources unemployment
q.feedback: Better matching reduces search time, which lowers frictional unemployment.

q.commonError: Confusing permanent mismatch with short-run job search or weak demand.
q.q: An economist turns to mismatch: structural unemployment occurs when:

q.commonError: Confusing permanent mismatch with short-run job search or weak demand.

options: Structural
Frictional
Cyclical
Seasonal only

q.commonError: Confusing recession-driven unemployment with natural unemployment.
q.q: An economist points to the business cycle: cyclical unemployment is unemployment caused by:
options: Business-cycle downturns and weak demand

A permanent skills mismatch only

q.commonError: Confusing recession-driven unemployment with natural unemployment.
q.q: A hotel lays off workers because a recession reduces travel demand. What type of unemployment is this?
options: Cyclical
Frictional
Structural
Not in the labor force

q.commonError: Confusing permanent mismatch with short-run job search or weak demand.
q.q: An economist presents three workers: a nurse moves cities and searches for a new hospital job. A cashier loses work because checkout automation permanently reduces demand. A waiter is laid off during a recession. What is the correct order?
options: Frictional, structural, cyclical
Structural, frictional, cyclical
Cyclical, structural, frictional
Frictional, cyclical, structural
q.feedback: Search is frictional, permanent automation mismatch is structural, and recession layoff is cyclical.

q.commonError: Confusing permanent mismatch with short-run job search or weak demand.
q.q: A worker first loses a job because of a recession, then the industry permanently changes and the old job does not return. What is the best classification over time?
options: Initially cyclical, then possibly structural
Always frictional
Always not in the labor force
Never unemployed
q.feedback: The cause can shift from weak demand to long-term mismatch.

q.commonError: Confusing recession-driven unemployment with natural unemployment.
q.q: Which unemployment type is most directly reduced by economic recovery from recession?
options: Cyclical unemployment
Structural unemployment
Frictional unemployment
Natural unemployment

q.commonError: Confusing permanent mismatch with short-run job search or weak demand.
q.q: An economist reviews the recovery: a recession ends, but many former workers cannot find jobs because their old industry has permanently shrunk. What should policymakers diagnose?
options: Cyclical unemployment fell; structural unemployment remains
Only frictional unemployment remains

Frictional unemployment from normal search is the only issue
The workers are all employed

options: Frictional unemployment
Structural unemployment from a persistent skill mismatch
Cyclical unemployment caused by a recession
Outside the labor force because the worker is not searching

q.feedback: Frictional unemployment comes from normal search and matching as workers move between jobs or enter the labor market.

q.q: A machinist’s occupation disappears after a permanent technology change, and available jobs require different skills. Which type is most likely?
options: Frictional unemployment
Cyclical unemployment
Discouraged-worker unemployment
Structural unemployment
q.commonError: Confuses persistent skill or location mismatch with temporary search or weak aggregate demand.
q.feedback: Structural unemployment reflects a durable mismatch between workers and available jobs, skills, or locations.

q.q: A restaurant cuts staff because a recession sharply reduces customer spending. Which type is most likely?
options: Structural unemployment from a permanent mismatch
No unemployment because the staffing cut is temporary
Cyclical unemployment
Frictional unemployment from normal job search

q.feedback: Cyclical unemployment is the deviation associated with weak aggregate demand and business-cycle downturns.

q.q: A worker is unemployed for four weeks while comparing similar jobs in a strong labor market. Which fact most strongly supports a frictional diagnosis?

q.feedback: Structural unemployment reflects a durable mismatch between workers and available jobs, skills, or locations.

options: Structural and cyclical unemployment only

q.q: Automation raises output per worker but displaces workers whose skills fit the old production process. What is the best synthesis?

Productivity must fall because some workers lose jobs

q.feedback: Technology can raise productivity while creating structural unemployment for workers whose skills no longer match available jobs.

q.q: A recession reduces demand for restaurant meals, so restaurants lay off workers. Later, demand returns and many are rehired. What type of unemployment best describes the initial layoffs?
options: Structural unemployment
Cyclical unemployment
Frictional unemployment
Discouraged employment
q.commonError: calls_all_job_loss_structural_unemployment
q.feedback: Layoffs caused by a recession or weak demand are cyclical unemployment.

q.q: A worker quits to search for a better job in a growing industry, while another worker loses a job because their old industry has permanently declined. Which pairing is correct?
options: First is structural; second is frictional
Both are cyclical
First is frictional; second is structural
Both are not in the labor force
q.commonError: confuses_job_search_with_skill_or_industry_mismatch
q.feedback: Job search unemployment is frictional. Mismatch caused by lasting industry change is structural.

q.q: A policy raises productivity over time but temporarily displaces workers in old industries. Which statement best describes the tradeoff?

q.commonError: assumes_growth_and_worker_displacement_cannot_coexist
q.feedback: Productivity growth can raise long-run living standards while creating short-run adjustment costs for workers whose skills no longer match available jobs.

q.commonError: Confusing permanent mismatch with short-run job search or weak demand.

options: Initially cyclical, then potentially structural

q.q: A worker quits a suitable job and spends several weeks comparing similar openings. Which unemployment type is the best starting diagnosis?
options: Frictional unemployment
